trace.situation: BMP5 describes layered Ship Protection Measures (SPM) that vessels can implement to reduce the risk of piracy attack, to be identified during voyage planning.
trace.trigger: Voyage planning process when transiting an area of known piracy/attack risk covered by BMP guidance.

procedures.action: Identify and plan applicable SPM during the voyage planning process.
procedures.why: SPM implementation must be decided before transit to ensure layered protection is in place.

procedures.action: Establish primary layer of defence: maintain good look out/vigilance, use motion sensors/CCTV, manage speed and freeboard.
procedures.why: Early detection and deterrence reduce likelihood of a successful approach by attackers.

procedures.action: Establish secondary layer of defence: harden doors, install gates/grates, maintain communication, use manoeuvring.
procedures.why: Delays and obstructs boarding attempts if primary layer is breached.

procedures.action: Establish last layer of defence: internal door hardening, razor wire, citadel/safe muster point, and PCASP if applicable.
procedures.why: Provides final protection for crew if attackers succeed in boarding.

procedures.action: Consider additional alterations, equipment, or personnel beyond BMP scope as determined by the Company.
procedures.why: BMP is a baseline; companies may further reduce risk based on their own risk assessment.

constraints: SPM must be identified during voyage planning, not improvised during transit.
BMP evolves as attack methods change, so guidance should be treated as current best practice, not fixed doctrine.
warnings: BMP is based on regional experience and will continue to evolve as methods change, so reliance on a single static measure may become outdated.
outcomes: Layered SPM implementation provides proven, proportionate protection against attack.
Failure to plan SPM during voyage planning may leave gaps in the ship's defence layers.
key_facts: SPM are organized into three layers: primary, secondary, and last layer of defence.
Primary layer includes look out/vigilance, motion sensor/CCTV, and speed/freeboard management.
Secondary layer includes door hardening, gate/grate, and communication/manoeuvring.
Last layer includes internal door hardening, razor wire, citadel/safe muster point, and PCASP.
Companies may add further measures, equipment, or personnel beyond BMP's minimum scope.

trace.situation: BMP5 guidance on measures a Master should implement to raise vigilance and enhance lookout capability aboard ship as a ship protection measure against piracy threats.

procedures.action: Provide additional, fully-briefed lookouts.

procedures.action: Maintain careful radar watch and monitor navigational warnings and communications, particularly VHF and GMDSS alerts.

procedures.action: Consider placing well-constructed dummies at strategic locations.

procedures.action: Consider using CCTV and fixed search lights for better monitoring.
procedures.why: Fixed search lights can deter approaches from the stern; CCTV aids monitoring coverage.

trace.situation: Guidance on selecting, installing, and securing razor (barbed) wire as a physical ship protection measure to prevent illegal boarding by pirates.

procedures.action: Use high tensile concertina razor wire with coil diameters of 730mm or 980mm.
procedures.why: Lower quality razor wire is less effective and higher quality wire is difficult to cut with hand tools.

procedures.action: Install a double roll of razor wire where possible.
procedures.why: Increases the barrier's effectiveness against boarding attempts.

procedures.action: If a double roll is not possible, place a single high-quality roll outboard of the ship's structure.
procedures.why: Maximizes the deterrent effect of a single roll by positioning it to block access.

procedures.action: Secure razor wire to the ship properly, e.g. attach at least every third wire ring to ship's railings and rig a steel cable through its core.
procedures.why: Prevents attackers from pulling the wire off the ship.

procedures.action: Use personal protective equipment and wire hooks when moving and installing razor wire.
procedures.why: Protects crew from injury while handling sharp wire.

procedures.action: Obtain razor wire in short sections (e.g. 10m lengths).
procedures.why: Makes the wire easier and safer to move and install.

procedures.action: Keep razor wire clear of mooring fairleads when at terminals.
procedures.why: Prevents interference with mooring operations.

procedures.action: Consider other barriers such as hanging swinging obstacles over the gunnels or purpose-built overhanging protection.
procedures.why: These have proven effective at preventing illegal boarding by climbing over the ship's rails.

constraints: Razor wire must be properly rigged and secured to be an effective barrier.
Wire quality varies considerably; low-quality wire is less effective.

trace.situation: Guidance on using water spray and foam monitors as physical ship protection measures to deter or delay unauthorized boarding attempts by pirates/armed robbers.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a near-miss where failure of threaded fuel pressure regulating valve connections on a marine engine caused gas oil to spray over a running engine, with fuel leakage attributed to poor hose fitting during vessel construction.
trace.trigger: Wear and eventual failure of threads securing the fuel pressure regulating valve to the fuel manifold adapter, caused by engine vibration combined with side loading from a poorly fitted hose connection.

procedures.action: Stop the engine immediately upon detecting fuel spray or leakage onto running machinery.
procedures.why: Prevents ignition of sprayed gas oil and fire risk, as occurred successfully in this incident.

procedures.action: Ensure engine manufacturer specifies exact connection requirements for ancillary pipework (pumps, coolers, filters) during vessel build integration.

procedures.action: Inspect hose and pipe connections for correct fitting and alignment to avoid side loading on threaded fittings.
procedures.why: Poorly fitted hose connections combined with engine vibration caused uneven thread wear leading to failure.

constraints: Engine manufacturer connections to ship system pipework must be properly specified, not assumed to be handled competently by the shipbuilder.
warnings: Fuel sprayed onto a running engine presents a serious fire/explosion risk if not addressed immediately.
Side loading from poorly fitted hose connections combined with vibration can cause progressive, undetected thread wear leading to sudden fuel leakage.
outcomes: The engine was stopped immediately and the sprayed fuel did not ignite, avoiding fire.
Root cause identified as inadequate specification of engine-to-ship pipework connections during vessel build.
key_facts: Thread failure occurred at the connection between the fuel pressure regulating valve and the fuel manifold adapter.
Gas oil was sprayed over a running engine but did not ignite because the engine was stopped immediately.
The cause was a combination of engine vibration and side loading from a poorly fitted hose connection.
The report recommends engine manufacturers take greater responsibility for specifying how their connections are made to ship system pipework rather than relying on shipbuilder competence.

trace.situation: CHIRP report highlighting that poor-quality, non-standardized engine operation & maintenance manuals (often generic, photocopied, or using unclear photographs instead of engineering drawings) contribute to improper installation and fitting of engine connections, risking fatigue failure and fire.

warnings: Badly specified or fitted flexible connections can lead to premature failure with potentially catastrophic consequences.

trace.situation: A crew member working on the after deck was engulfed by a wave during an unannounced anti-collision course change, reported the near-miss, and was then pressured by the Master to alter his written statement.
trace.trigger: An emergency anti-collision manoeuvre caused the ship to turn sharply without warning while a crew member was on the after deck, after the bridge had been informed of his presence but had forgotten him.

procedures.action: Inform the Bridge OOW before proceeding to work on exposed deck areas.
procedures.why: So the bridge team is aware of personnel locations during manoeuvres.

procedures.action: Report any incident or near-miss to the Bridge immediately after it occurs.
procedures.why: Ensures timely awareness and investigation of safety events.

procedures.action: Investigate near-miss reports by addressing the reporter's safety concerns, not by challenging the reporter's credibility.
procedures.why: The purpose of near-miss reporting is to identify hazards, not assign blame.

procedures.action: Allow witnesses to submit their own original statement without alteration.
procedures.why: A statement is one person's view of events; Masters/Safety Officers can submit separate statements rather than editing the witness's account.

procedures.action: Refuse to sign a rewritten statement that is not in the witness's own words.
procedures.why: Protects the integrity and accuracy of the incident record.

constraints: Bridge must track and account for all personnel working on deck during manoeuvres.

The true cause of the sudden turn (an anti-collision manoeuvre avoiding closing to within two cables of another vessel) was only revealed much later.
The crew member learned he had simply been forgotten about despite having informed the bridge of his location.

procedures.action: Confirm the ship's automatic distress signal and available radios (VHF, SW, cell phone) are activated/used before abandoning.

trace.situation: A CHIRP follow-up report addressing confusion between the helm orders 'Steady' and 'Steady as she goes' during coastal or river/canal transits, and the risk of a helmsman using a fixed visual mark instead of the compass as a steering reference in areas of strong current or tidal stream.

constraints: Applies specifically to coastal waters and river/canal transits where strong current or tidal stream exists.

warnings: Adoption of a fixed visual mark as a steering reference instead of the compass can be hazardous in areas of strong current or tidal stream.

outcomes: IMO suggested the UK (via MCA) consider submitting an information paper on the issue.

trace.situation: An investigation into a high-speed craft (HSC) near-miss/close-quarters situation examines whether the Master's speed decisions in reduced visibility complied with COLREG Rule 6 safe speed requirements.

procedures.action: Assess vessel manoeuvrability and radar/AIS/electronic chart capability when determining safe speed under Rule 6.
procedures.why: These factors legitimately affect how fast a vessel can proceed while still being able to avoid collision.

procedures.why: In normal circumstances this distance is judged appropriate given the vessel's crash-stop and turning performance (480m in under a minute from 42 knots).

procedures.action: In visibility less than 5 cables, reduce speed unless ALL four conditions are satisfied: bridge team closed up and briefed, both radars at maximum efficiency tracking small contacts at appropriate range, traffic situation carefully assessed (especially small craft concentration and achievable CPAs), and navigational situation reassessed per Operational Manual.
procedures.why: Reduced visibility erodes the advantages HSC normally enjoy, increasing the likelihood that a speed reduction is needed to retain proper and effective collision-avoidance capability.

procedures.action: Consider reducing speed to between 12 and 30 knots in sensitive areas to avoid excessive wash/wake.
procedures.why: Environmental/wash impact in sensitive areas is an additional factor in determining appropriate speed reduction.

procedures.action: Make full, documented assessment of prevailing circumstances and conditions when setting speed in restricted visibility.
procedures.why: Masters remain responsible for this assessment pending forthcoming MCA guidance, as MAIB has flagged recurring incorrect safe-speed assessments.

procedures.why: Bridge teams risk over-confidence in radar/AIS/ECDIS systems, which can mask real limitations in restricted visibility.

constraints: All four listed conditions must be satisfied before maintaining higher speed below 5 cables visibility; failure of any one requires speed reduction.

Company procedures for safe speed adequacy are a matter for individual company assessment, not a fixed external standard.
warnings: Risk of over-confidence in radar/AIS/electronic chart equipment in restricted visibility.

outcomes: The Maritime Advisory Board found the Master's and bridge team's decisions on the night in question appropriate, as all required aspects were duly considered.

Wash/wake concerns in sensitive areas may dictate speeds between 12 and 30 knots regardless of visibility.

trace.situation: A CHIRP confidential report describes concerns that a European ferry company is rushing masters and mates through Pilotage Exemption Certificate (PEC) assessments to save money, resulting in several incidents including touching bottom, close quarters situations, and near misses with berths.

procedures.action: Allow adequate time to assess situations and decide appropriate actions when determining a safe speed, especially for High Speed Craft.

procedures.action: Make proper allowance for leeway on bends and tide when navigating under PEC.
procedures.why: Failure to do so was identified as a direct cause of incidents including touching bottom and close quarters situations.

procedures.action: Proceed at a safe speed and adjust ETA at the bar to account for under keel clearance.
procedures.why: Failure to consider under keel clearance and adjust ETA accordingly was cited as a contributing factor to incidents.

procedures.action: Ensure PEC holders have adequate English comprehension and rely on proper navigation methods rather than over-reliance on VHF.
procedures.why: Lack of English comprehension and over-use of VHF as a substitute for navigation were identified as root causes of incidents.

constraints: PEC requirements must meet the Pilotage Act 1987 and support port marine safety management systems.
Bridge teams must factor in time needed to assess and decide on actions when setting safe speed, particularly for HSC.
warnings: Rushing PEC certification with minimal tripping requirements risks producing under-qualified pilots/masters.
Over-reliance on VHF as a means of navigation is a safety risk.
Lack of English comprehension among PEC holders can compromise safe navigation and communication.
outcomes: Several incidents occurred among PEC holders including touching bottom, close quarters situations, and near misses with berths.

CHIRP continues to raise concerns in support of port marine safety management systems.
key_facts: The reporting port requires only six voyages in and six voyages out before a PEC candidate can sit an area exam.

Six identified causes of incidents: insufficient tripping experience, failure to allow for leeway on bends/tide, failure to proceed at safe speed, little consideration of under keel clearance/ETA adjustment, lack of English comprehension, and over-use of VHF for navigation.
CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board focuses on compliance with the Pilotage Act 1987 when reviewing such reports.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report addresses in-water survey requirements and the obligation to notify Classification Societies of repairs (particularly shell plating) that may affect class, highlighting pressure on senior officers to avoid or delay such reporting.
trace.trigger: When a vessel approaches its docking/survey due date requiring an in-water survey in lieu of docking, or when repairs potentially affecting classification (e.g., shell plating damage) are identified.

procedures.action: Report defects to Class promptly despite commercial or time pressure.

Rev.3 procedural changes are to be uniformly implemented from 1 July 2005.
warnings: If repairs are undertaken without Class supervision, Class status, P&I cover, and Hull and Machinery insurance could be invalidated.

outcomes: Properly implemented Rev.3 amendments appear to significantly address the reported survey concerns.

trace.situation: A 30m beam trawler took on two metres of water in the engine room bilge over a weekend after an incomplete refit job, because the main battery supply was switched off and no bilge alarm was active to alert anyone.
trace.trigger: Vessel laid up alongside after slipping for bottom paint/minor refit, with main battery supply switched off, allowing an undetected leak to flood the engine room bilge unnoticed over a weekend.

procedures.action: Fit a bilge alarm sensor in the propulsion machinery space and fish hold(s), accessible for regular testing.
procedures.why: Code 4.3.3.1 requires sensors in these spaces; existing vessels must retrofit fish hold sensors by first periodical survey.

procedures.action: Do not allow bilge sensors in compartments containing pollutants to automatically start bilge pumps.
procedures.why: Code 4.3.3.2 - prevents pollution from automatic pumping of contaminated bilges.

procedures.action: Fit auto-start bilge pumps serving clean compartments with audible/visual alarm and manual override at control position.
procedures.why: Code 4.3.3.3 - allows investigation of the reason for pumping.

procedures.action: Fit bilge level alarms (or spring-loaded drain valves) in dry compartments where bilge level cannot be readily visually checked.
procedures.why: Code 4.3.3.4 - ensures bilge level monitoring without needing to enter the compartment.

procedures.action: Ensure bilge alarms give audible and visual warning at the control position(s).
procedures.why: Code 4.3.3.5 - so crew/personnel are alerted regardless of location.

procedures.action: Provide each engine room bilge alarm system with either a secondary independent alarm system or a fail-safe warning for circuit faults.
procedures.why: Code 4.3.3.6 - ensures alarm reliability and fault detection; existing vessels must retrofit by first periodical survey.

procedures.action: Fit a permanently live bilge alarm with a strobe flasher visible from the quay/wheelhouse, independent of main vessel power.
procedures.why: Incident analysis: such an alarm would have almost certainly alerted someone on the quay, preventing the flooding and water damage.

procedures.action: Consult MGN 165(F) for further guidance on bilge alarms and pumps.
procedures.why: Code 4.3.3.7 references this as the source of additional technical guidance.

constraints: Applies to fishing vessels 15m LOA to less than 24m registered length under the Code of Safe Working Practice.
Bilge sensors in pollutant-containing compartments must not auto-start pumps.
Existing vessels have a retrofit deadline of the first periodical survey under the Code.
Bilge alarms must remain accessible for regular testing.
regulations: Code of Safe Working Practice for the Construction and Use of 15m LOA to less than 24m Registered Length Fishing Vessels
warnings: Switching off main battery supply disables bilge alarms, removing the last line of defence against undetected flooding.
Lack of a permanently powered, remotely visible alarm (e.g., strobe flasher) can allow flooding to go unnoticed for days.
Bilge sensors must not be allowed to auto-start pumps in pollutant-containing spaces to avoid environmental pollution.
outcomes: Two metres of water accumulated in the engine room bilge over a weekend, causing considerable water damage.
No alarms were active because the main battery supply had been switched off, delaying detection.
A permanently live alarm with a strobe flasher would likely have alerted someone on the quay, preventing or limiting the damage.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a small (5-ton) pleasure craft navigating in restricted visibility/fog among commercial vessels, including a fast ferry, that relied on radar to detect and avoid it, prompting Maritime Advisory Board commentary on safe speed, COLREGS compliance, and small-craft detectability.
trace.trigger: A small craft operates in restricted visibility in proximity to commercial shipping relying on radar/ARPA for collision avoidance.

procedures.action: Make a full assessment of prevailing circumstances and conditions to determine safe speed appropriate to ship type.
procedures.why: Safe speed is defined as the speed at which effective action can be taken, and this varies by ship type; masters are responsible for this assessment.

procedures.action: Use electronic navigation systems (radar/ARPA) fully but guard against over-reliance on the equipment.
procedures.why: Bridge teams risk over-confidence in equipment capabilities, which can mask true collision risk.

procedures.action: Fit a radar reflector or other means of radar detection on vessels under 150 gross tonnage where practicable.

procedures.action: Leisure craft operators should fully weigh risks, skill level, equipment, crew, and passage plans/timings before transiting in restricted visibility, choosing alternative plans if needed.

constraints: Safe speed must allow effective action to be taken in the prevailing circumstances and conditions.

outcomes: All commercial vessels, including a fast ferry, detected the reporter's small craft via radar and took appropriate action, avoiding collision.

trace.situation: A Maritime Advisory Board issues observations following an incident involving a fishing vessel left unattended with its bilge alarm off, addressing how vessels should be secured and alarm systems designed/maintained.
trace.trigger: A vessel is left temporarily unattended (for repair or other reasons) and/or relies on a bilge alarm system, as highlighted by the incident prompting this advisory.

procedures.action: Secure the vessel (e.g. close sea cocks) whenever it will be left unattended for more than a relatively short period, whether for repair or other reasons.

procedures.why: A secondary alarm that fails when main power is off, or that cannot be seen from outside the vessel, will not alert anyone to a developing flooding situation.

procedures.action: Test whatever alarm system is fitted on a regular basis.
procedures.why: Ensures the alarm remains functional and reliable so it will actually operate and warn of a bilge/flooding condition when needed.

constraints: Secondary alarms must remain live when main power plant is shut down.
Alarm condition must be visible externally (not just internally).
Alarm systems must be tested regularly regardless of type.
warnings: Leaving a vessel unattended for more than a short period without securing sea cocks risks undetected flooding.
An alarm system that is not powered independently of the main plant, not externally visible, or not regularly tested may fail to warn of a flooding event.
outcomes: Following these measures reduces the risk of undetected flooding/sinking while a vessel is unattended.

key_facts: The advisory follows a reported incident involving a bilge alarm being off on a fishing vessel.

constraints: Hand bearing compasses are susceptible to local deviation from objects worn or held close to the body

trace.situation: A CHIRP reporter investigated compass safe distance issues after reading about radio equipment interfering with a magnetic compass, and found inconsistent labelling and equipment fitted too close to compasses on boats in his local marina.

procedures.action: Check the equipment or compass manufacturer's plate, notice, or manual for the stated compass safe distance before installation.

procedures.action: Maintain at least the minimum stated distance (e.g. 1m where specified) between radio/electrical equipment and the magnetic compass.

procedures.action: Exercise particular caution when fitting non-marine equipment such as car audio units near the compass.
procedures.why: Such equipment is not designed or supplied with magnetic compass interference in mind.

constraints: Equipment must be installed at or beyond the manufacturer-specified compass safe distance where stated.
warnings: Radio and electrical equipment can interfere with the magnetic compass if fitted too close.

outcomes: Equipment fitted closer than the recommended safe distance can cause magnetic compass deviation, leading to navigational inaccuracy.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report compiling mariner feedback on the hazards of mobile phone use on deck and on the bridge, including distraction from local hazards and crane operations, and interference with smoke detectors/fire alarms on an offshore vessel.

procedures.why: Crew using phones were observed wandering obliviously into areas with local hazards and active crane operations overhead.

procedures.action: Switch off mobile phones (and KU band bridge phone) during pilotage and when bridge team must remain alert and busy.
procedures.why: Phone calls on the bridge are a distraction and pilotage requires full concentration; ringing phones disrupt bridge team alertness.

procedures.action: Keep ship-to-shore calls to a minimum and avoid non-essential calls (ETAs, crew joining, chandlery queries) interrupting bridge operations.
procedures.why: Increased accessibility via mobile phones has led to excessive non-critical calls reaching the Master/Berthing Master compared to the era of Coast Radio Station link calls.

procedures.action: Maintain physical distance from smoke detectors when making or receiving mobile phone calls.
procedures.why: Mobile phones have been found to set off smoke detectors and activate fire alarms on the offshore vessel over a three-to-four year period.

procedures.action: Report any close calls involving mobile telephone use to CHIRP in confidence.
procedures.why: CHIRP is collecting reports to forward to the Maritime and Coastguard Agency for further action.

constraints: No mobile phone use on the main deck.
Mobile phones should be switched off during pilotage.
Crew must not stand too close to smoke detectors when using mobile phones.
warnings: Mobile phone use on deck causes crew to wander obliviously into zones with local hazards and crane operations overhead.
Mobile phones on the bridge are a distraction, especially during pilotage which requires full concentration.
Mobile phones have been known to set off smoke detectors and activate fire alarms on the offshore vessel.
outcomes: Enforcement of the no-phone-on-deck policy reduced hazardous wandering behavior near crane operations.
Bridge teams that keep phones switched off remain busier and more alert without ringing distractions.
CHIRP has forwarded earlier reports to the Maritime and Coastguard Agency and plans further submissions.

trace.situation: A British master of a multinational nine-nationality crew describes using a pantomime-style demonstration during monthly safety meetings to overcome language barriers and teach hazard awareness, particularly around lifeboat drills and thoughtlessness-caused accidents.
trace.trigger: Conducting required monthly safety meetings aboard a ship with a crew speaking multiple languages, none of whom share full fluency with the master.

procedures.action: Learn key helm orders and basic courtesy words in crew members' languages as master.
procedures.why: English remains the language of the sea but not all crew are fluent, so basic bilingual effort builds communication and rapport.

procedures.action: Use senior officers and bilingual crew as intermediaries to translate safety instructions into each man's own language.
procedures.why: Manuals are often ill-written and relying on English alone leaves gaps in understanding critical safety procedures.

procedures.action: Devise visual/physical demonstrations (e.g. pantomime) to convey safety messages at monthly safety meetings.
procedures.why: A physical demonstration crosses language barriers and makes the hazard message memorable and immediate.

procedures.action: Identify and remove common hazards: buckets of water near ladder feet, unchanged lamp bulbs, unroped painted/dangerous areas, loose wood/shackles/spare parts on deck.
procedures.why: Many shipboard accidents are caused by thoughtlessness and preventable clutter/hazards.

procedures.action: Check that a lifeboat is safe to lower before lowering it.
procedures.why: Prevents accidents during lifeboat operations.

procedures.action: Carry out lifeboat and emergency drills frequently so every man knows his role.
procedures.why: So that in a real emergency (e.g. fire, heavy rolling, darkness) crew act by instinct rather than confusion.

procedures.action: Teach all crew in their own language what and how to do via bilingual speakers, under master's direction.
procedures.why: Ensures universal understanding regardless of poorly written manuals or language gaps.

constraints: Monthly safety meetings are required.
Training must reach every crew member regardless of native language.
Lifeboats must be checked as safe before lowering.
warnings: A ship is a potentially dangerous workplace, especially at sea, liable to move in all three dimensions without warning.
Thoughtlessness (leaving hazards unaddressed) is a major cause of shipboard accidents.
Ill-written manuals may fail to convey safety instructions adequately to a multinational crew.
outcomes: The pantomime demonstration successfully got the safety message across, evidenced by crew reacting with concern and rushing to help.
If all hands realise the ship's inherent danger and think about what they are doing, accidents become less common.

English is the language of the sea but fluency varied among senior officers and crew.

trace.situation: A CHIRP casualty report criticizes the practice of locking emergency escape/access hatches for security reasons, noting that such hatches must remain operable from both sides.
trace.trigger: Emergency escape/access hatches being locked or secured for security purposes, restricting their operability in one direction.

procedures.action: Ensure all emergency escape/access hatches are operable in both directions at all times.

trace.situation: CHIRP raised a safety/security conflict concern about ISPS-driven locking of escape routes, and the UK MCA provided guidance on acceptable solutions that balance both requirements.
trace.trigger: A report that escape hatches on a ship were being padlocked shut from the outside, creating a conflict between ISPS security measures and SOLAS escape route safety requirements.

procedures.action: Use digital locks with one-way, fail-open operation on bridge doors, engine rooms, and radio rooms.
procedures.why: Allows security control while ensuring doors can still be used for escape or access in an emergency.

procedures.action: Use fixed locks or bolts where appropriate instead of padlocks on escape routes.
procedures.why: Maintains security without permanently blocking egress.

procedures.action: Install remote locking of car deck doors with fail-to-safe or unlocked status, using hydraulics, compressed air, or electronic systems.
procedures.why: Ensures doors default to safe/unlocked state in a failure, preserving escape capability.

procedures.action: Deploy micro switches, intruder detection systems, CCTV, alarms, seals, or dedicated manual guarding as alternative security measures.
procedures.why: Provides security monitoring/control without physically obstructing escape routes.

procedures.action: Select the appropriate combination of measures based on ship type and trading pattern.
procedures.why: MCA notes a cruise ship's needs differ from a sand dredger's, so no single solution is mandated.

constraints: Escape hatches must not be padlocked shut from the outside on UK ships or ships in UK ports.
Security solutions must not compromise means of escape required for safety.
No single prescribed technique is mandated by MCA; solution choice is pragmatic and ship-specific.
warnings: Padlocking escape hatches shut from the outside is unacceptable on UK ships or in UK ports.
Security measures that block escape routes create an unresolved safety hazard.
outcomes: Properly designed fail-open/fail-safe security systems eliminate the conflict between ISPS security and SOLAS safety requirements.
MCA surveyors provide advice to masters on acceptable security configurations rather than enforcing one fixed solution.
key_facts: The November 1997 explanatory note to AMSA Direction 25A/96 identified valid techniques for balancing safety and security.
Examples include digital fail-open locks, fixed locks/bolts, remote fail-to-safe car deck door locking, intruder detection systems, CCTV, alarms, seals, and manual guarding.
MCA has not mandated one specific solution, leaving choice dependent on ship type and trading pattern.
Padlocking escape hatches shut from outside is explicitly deemed unacceptable on UK ships or in UK ports.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board debated whether reports of crankshaft bearing failures fall within its safety-reporting scope, while a separate reporter raised concern that a new padlock security system on Class A machinery escape trunks may conflict with SOLAS escape/access requirements.
trace.trigger: A report of crankshaft/bearing failure was submitted to CHIRP, and separately a ship had padlocks fitted to machinery escape trunk hatches restricting them to one-way (escape-only) opening.

procedures.action: Issue an open letter to industry membership (via IMarEST/MER) to solicit opinions on whether the issue falls within program scope.
procedures.why: The Advisory Board was initially uncertain whether crankshaft bearing failure fell within the Programme's remit.

procedures.action: Weigh the two safety perspectives raised: immediate personnel risk vs operational viability risk.
procedures.why: Responses identified distinct risk categories, one slight (personnel) and one potentially significant (ship viability).

procedures.action: Classify the issue as falling within the ISM Code based on balance of responses.
procedures.why: The issue was determined to be a safety matter despite initial scope uncertainty.

procedures.action: Gather further data on frequency of bearing/crankshaft failures, contributory factors, and effectiveness of mitigation measures.
procedures.why: To build an evidence base before escalation.

procedures.action: Forward findings to relevant organisations for assessment once enquiries are complete.
procedures.why: To ensure appropriate bodies can act on the safety information.

procedures.action: Verify that any escape trunk locking/security system still permits two-way opening (escape and access) as per SOLAS Reg 13.3.1.5.2.
procedures.why: Padlocking doors to open only in the escape direction may prevent access, contravening SOLAS and endangering crew.

constraints: SOLAS Reg 13.3.1.5: doors in escape routes shall generally open in the direction of escape.
SOLAS Reg 13.3.1.5.2: doors in vertical emergency escape trunks may open out of the trunk to permit use for both escape and access.
Class A machinery spaces require two independent means of access: one stairway and one vertical ladder (the latter also serving as escape).
CHIRP's classification of an issue as ISM-relevant requires a balance-of-evidence determination, not automatic inclusion.
warnings: Locking escape trunk hatches to open only in the escape direction poses a greater threat to vessel and crew than the security risk it is meant to prevent.
A padlocked trunk hatch may prevent access in an emergency, contrary to SOLAS Reg 13 requirements.
outcomes: CHIRP determined the crankshaft bearing failure issue falls within scope of the ISM Code as a safety matter.
Further data collection was initiated to assess frequency, causes, and mitigation effectiveness before forwarding to relevant organisations.
A potential SOLAS non-compliance (padlocked escape trunks) was flagged for review due to risk of trapping crew during emergencies.
key_facts: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board initially was uncertain whether crankshaft bearing failure reports fell within the Programme's scope.
Two risk views emerged: slight immediate personnel risk vs potentially significant operational viability risk.
The issue was ultimately classified as falling within the ISM Code.
A padlock system fitted to Class A machinery escape trunks allowed hatches to open only in the escape direction, raising a possible SOLAS Reg 13 violation.
SOLAS Reg 13 allows vertical escape trunk doors to open outward for both escape and access, but the padlock system defeats the access function.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a report from a single-handed trans-Atlantic sailor who relied on a radar detector as a watchkeeping aid and encountered numerous vessels not operating radar, prompting Board guidance on radar use, lookout, and restricted visibility.
trace.trigger: Vessel operating in or approaching restricted visibility or busy traffic areas where radar reliance or absence must be assessed.

procedures.action: Prepare appropriate measures for restricted visibility based on circumstances and own risk assessment.
procedures.why: Restricted visibility may be encountered at any stage of a voyage.

procedures.action: Do not leave port into restricted visibility conditions without radar if avoidable.
procedures.why: Such a decision is open to criticism by the Maritime Advisory Board.

procedures.action: When radar-equipped, account for the possibility that other vessels, especially leisure craft, may not have or be using radar.
procedures.why: Rule 19 is most effective only when both vessels are radar equipped; otherwise navigation must adapt.

procedures.action: Use sound signals in restricted visibility.
procedures.why: Sound signals compensate when radar cannot be assumed on other vessels.

procedures.action: Maintain a proper look-out by sight, hearing, and all available means appropriate to conditions, per Rule 5.
procedures.why: Radar or other aids may not be in use by other vessels for operational or security reasons (e.g. avoiding detection).

procedures.action: Do not rely on the operation of equipment (e.g., radar) on another vessel to ensure your own safety.
procedures.why: A radar detector only works if the other vessel is transmitting radar, which cannot be guaranteed.

constraints: Rule 19 (COLREGs) assumes both vessels are radar equipped to be most effective.
Rule 5 (COLREGs) requires lookout by all available means appropriate to prevailing circumstances and conditions.
Radar or AIS use by other vessels cannot be assumed or relied upon.
warnings: Leaving port in restricted visibility without radar is open to criticism.

trace.situation: A loaded bulk carrier (stand-on vessel) approaching the western end of a TSS eastbound lane found itself in a developing close-quarters situation with a container vessel (give-way vessel) that failed to take avoiding action despite repeated VHF calls.
trace.trigger: Give-way vessel (container ship) took no action and did not respond to VHF calls as range closed from 3.5 to 2.5 miles in a developing close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Monitor the developing close-quarters situation and call the give-way vessel by name on VHF Ch.16 when action appears overdue.
procedures.why: To prompt the give-way vessel to take required avoiding action before the situation becomes critical.

procedures.action: Repeat VHF calls as range closes if no reply or action is observed.
procedures.why: To give the give-way vessel further opportunity to comply with the collision regulations before stand-on vessel must act alone.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, initiate own avoiding action (round turn to starboard) when it becomes apparent the give-way vessel will not act in time.
procedures.why: To prevent collision when the give-way vessel fails to fulfil her obligation, consistent with the stand-on vessel's right/duty to act when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone.

procedures.action: After the close-quarters situation is resolved, move to a working channel and advise the other vessel of the near-miss and question their understanding of the collision regulations.
procedures.why: To provide feedback and reinforce proper application of the collision regulations to prevent recurrence.

constraints: Stand-on vessel should maintain course/speed until it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action
VHF communication should not be relied upon as a substitute for timely visual/radar assessment and action under the collision regulations
Avoiding action must be taken in good time and be substantial enough to be readily apparent
warnings: Give-way vessel's failure to act or respond to VHF calls created a very close quarters situation that could have resulted in collision
Reliance on VHF communication by the give-way vessel instead of early positive action is unsafe practice
No other vessels were in the immediate vicinity, meaning there was no valid excuse for the container vessel's inaction
outcomes: Stand-on bulk carrier took unilateral avoiding action (round turn to starboard of approximately 60 degrees) averting collision
Give-way container vessel only queried intentions after the stand-on vessel had already altered course substantially
Near-miss was fortunately not compounded by presence of other traffic
key_facts: Vessel A was a loaded bulk carrier with draught 17.3 metres, the stand-on vessel in the encounter
Vessel B was a container vessel altering course after leaving the westbound TSS lane, identified as the give-way vessel
VHF calls to the give-way vessel at ranges of 3.5 and 3.0 miles went unanswered with no action taken
The stand-on vessel initiated a round turn to starboard at 2.5 miles range, eventually turning about 60 degrees off original course
The give-way vessel only queried the stand-on vessel's intentions after the large course alteration had already begun

trace.situation: Guidance on safe practice for vessels crossing or using traffic separation schemes (TSS), emphasizing speed control and right-angle crossing per COLREG rules.

procedures.action: Cross traffic separation schemes or lanes on a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general traffic flow.
procedures.why: Required by COLREG Rule 10(c).

procedures.action: Only cross a TSS/lane if it is safe to do so; otherwise wait until a safe right-angle crossing can be made.

procedures.action: Make right-angle crossing the vessel's regular practice even when the TSS is empty, and draw the passage plan accordingly.

Passage plan must be drawn to always cross a traffic lane at a right angle.
warnings: Monitoring stations such as Dover will prosecute vessels that fail to cross traffic separation schemes at right angles, even when the scheme is empty.
Do not use high traffic density as justification to deviate from a right-angle crossing heading.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report from an ISPS/ISM auditor highlights that engine room and other compartment doors secured from the inside to allow emergency escape often cannot be opened from the outside, preventing fire parties or shore-based emergency services from gaining entry for rescue or fire-fighting purposes.
trace.trigger: Audit observation that all exits from a space (e.g. engine room) are secured only from the inside, blocking external emergency access.

procedures.action: Fit removable hasps on weathertight doors allowing padlocking from outside, releasable from inside via a butterfly nut.
procedures.why: Provides a cheap, effective method that satisfies both security and emergency entry needs.

procedures.action: Fit mechanical keypads on other doors with quick release from inside, and ensure the access code is known to all ship's staff.
procedures.why: Allows the code to be given to shore-based emergency services if required, enabling entry during an emergency.

procedures.action: Monitor keypad performance in weather-exposed locations.
procedures.why: Mechanical keypads may be more vulnerable to weather exposure, though no failures had been reported at time of writing.

constraints: Security/escape arrangements must not hinder emergency escape from inside.
Security/escape arrangements must not hinder authorised emergency entry from outside.
Access codes/keys must be made available to ship's staff for passing to shore emergency services.
warnings: Doors secured only from the inside may prevent fire parties or shore emergency services from accessing a space for cooling or rescue purposes.

trace.situation: CHIRP sought MCA comment on a reported fatigue concern involving working hours on UK harbour tugs with sea-going certificates.

The document is available in all EU maritime states' languages and is supported by a film 'Say No To Bullying, Say No To Harassment' available on DVD with English soundtrack and subtitles in English, French, Polish, and Russian.
A CD-Rom training programme 'Understanding Equal Opportunities' was produced for shipboard and company management to address discrimination law compliance and self-assessment.
Further details can be obtained from the Chamber of Shipping, NUMAST, ECSA, and ETF.

trace.situation: A list of current MAIB (Marine Accident Investigation Branch) investigations into various maritime casualties occurring between September and December 2005, including flooding, collisions, groundings, machinery failures, and lifeboat incidents.
warnings: Freefall lifeboats can accidentally deploy while unmanned and alongside, posing a hazard even without injury or damage.
Lifeboat drills can result in machinery failure causing crew injury.
Gangway collapse can result in fatality.
outcomes: One life lost in flooding of fv Blue Sinata off Weymouth.
Barges sank and cargo vessel holed in forepeak after collision between George Lyras and four barges on the Lower Thames.
One fatality from gangway collapse of Vaermland in Hamburg.
Two crew members injured during lifeboat drill machinery failure on Sammi Superstars.
No damage or injuries sustained when freefall lifeboat dropped from Solent Fisher while alongside.

Multiple collisions occurred involving fishing vessels and larger cargo/container ships in 2005 (e.g., Harvester/Strilmoy, Arctic Ocean/Marie af Hovrik, Golden Bells II/Plato).
Groundings occurred in varied locations including Sweden (Hohebank), the Baltic Sea (Lerrix), and near Newhaven Harbour (Dieppe).

trace.situation: Instructions and confidentiality terms for completing and submitting a CHIRP (Confidential Hazardous Incident Reporting Programme) maritime report form.
trace.trigger: A seafarer wishes to submit a confidential safety report to CHIRP about a maritime hazard, near-miss, or incident.

procedures.action: Complete the report form, adding extra pages if required.
procedures.why: To capture full relevant information about the event/situation being reported.

procedures.action: Place the completed form in a sealed envelope (no stamp required) and send to the CHIRP Freepost address.
procedures.why: Ensures secure, confidential, cost-free submission to CHIRP.

procedures.action: Alternatively contact CHIRP via the confidential 24hr telephone, freefone, or fax numbers provided.
procedures.why: Provides multiple confidential channels for reporting.

procedures.action: For e-mail reports, first request a security certificate from confidential@chirp.co.uk using only 'Certificate' in the subject line, submitting no other information at that stage.
procedures.why: Protects reporter identity and report confidentiality before any report content is transmitted electronically.

procedures.action: Provide name, address, postcode, telephone number, and preferred contact date/method.
procedures.why: Required solely to allow CHIRP to contact the reporter for further details about the report.

procedures.action: Complete the relevant information about the event/situation in the report.
procedures.why: This is the substantive safety content CHIRP needs to assess the hazard.

constraints: CHIRP is entirely independent of any regulatory, operational, manufacturer, or supplier organisation in the maritime sector.
The report will only be seen by CHIRP staff.
No record of the reporter's name and address will be kept.
The report will not be used without the reporter's approval.
The report form will be returned to the reporter or destroyed after processing.
warnings: Do not submit any information other than the word 'Certificate' in the subject line when requesting an e-mail security certificate.
outcomes: Reporter receives an acknowledgement from CHIRP as soon as possible.
Personal details remain confidential and are not retained beyond contacting the reporter.
Report is not used for any purpose without the reporter's prior approval.
key_facts: CHIRP is independent of all other maritime sector organisations (regulatory, operational, manufacturer, supplier).
Completed forms can be mailed postage-free via Freepost to a specified Farnborough, UK address.
Confidential phone (24hr), freefone (UK only), and fax lines are available for reporting.
E-mail reporters must first obtain a security certificate before sending report content.
Personal details are used only to enable follow-up contact and are not permanently recorded.

trace.situation: A near-miss collision occurred when a Third Mate, covering the Second Mate's watch on a short-handed vessel, incorrectly altered course to port as the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation, resulting in a CPA of zero with another ship.
trace.trigger: ARPA tracking of a crossing vessel showed TCPA 10 minutes and CPA 0.35 NM ahead while own ship was the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel in a crossing situation, hold course and speed per Rule 17.
procedures.why: Rule 17 requires the stand-on vessel to maintain course and speed unless the give-way vessel fails to act appropriately.

procedures.action: Do not alter course to port for a vessel on the port side.
procedures.why: Rule 17 explicitly states a power-driven vessel taking avoiding action shall, if circumstances admit, not alter course to port for a vessel on her port side.

procedures.action: If concerned about the other vessel's intentions, attempt communication with that vessel, VTS, or the Master.
procedures.why: No communication was made with the other ship, VTS, or the Master standing nearby, despite the officer's apparent concern, which the company identifies as a missed safeguard.

constraints: Own ship was the stand-on vessel under Rule 15 (crossing situation)
Duty Officer was properly certificated
Master was physically present on the bridge/bridge wing during the incident
Vessel was sailing short-handed after the Second Mate was dismissed
warnings: Altering course to port as the stand-on vessel for a vessel on the port side is a clear violation of Rule 17
Failure to communicate concerns with the other vessel, VTS, or the Master present can lead to near-collision situations
outcomes: Own ship passed very close astern of the other vessel with ARPA showing CPA as zero
No collision occurred but the incident was classified as a serious Near Miss
Incident was circulated company-wide as a lesson on COLREGS compliance
key_facts: The Third Mate was standing the Second Mate's 1200-1600 watch after the Second Mate was sacked for incompetence
The Master had kept the 0800-1200 watch and remained on the bridge wing during the incident
The other ship was tracked on radar from 11:45 with ARPA showing CPA 0.35 NM and TCPA 10 minutes before the incident
No VHF communication occurred with the other vessel, VTS, or the Master despite their proximity
Weather conditions were good (slight sea, BF3 wind, good visibility)

trace.situation: CHIRP analysis of a near-miss collision incident where a Duty Officer altered course to port in a crossing/head-on situation despite the Master being on the bridge, contrary to COLREGs Rule 17(c) and Rule 14.
trace.trigger: Officer perceives risk of collision in a crossing or head-on/near head-on encounter with another vessel and must decide on avoiding action and whether to involve the Master.

procedures.action: Do not alter course to port when taking action under Rule 14 (head-on) or Rule 17(c) (give-way vessel action).
procedures.why: Altering to port in these situations is a direct contravention of the Rules and a common but dangerous error among young officers.

procedures.action: Take a large alteration of course to starboard (a round turn) or reduce speed as the acceptable action under Rule 17(c).
procedures.why: This is the COLREGs-compliant action that avoids close-quarters situations rather than worsening them.

procedures.action: Keep the Master advised of any navigational hazards or developing close-quarters situations, and call the Master whenever in doubt.
procedures.why: The Duty Officer remains in charge of the vessel unless relieved, but is obligated to inform the Master; failure to call the Master when concerned compounds risk.

procedures.action: Make the sound and light signals prescribed by Rule 33(d) when taking avoiding action.
procedures.why: These signals were not made in the incident, representing a missed safety step in collision avoidance.

procedures.action: Do not rely on VHF for collision avoidance.
procedures.why: VHF use in collision avoidance is generally discouraged as it can create confusion or false assurance instead of following COLREGs-based maneuvering.

procedures.action: Consider establishing Company/Master's Standing Orders on acceptable passing distances.
procedures.why: Lack of clear guidance on CPA may have contributed to the OOW's and Master's misjudgement of the ARPA-indicated 'passing ahead' situation.

procedures.action: Discuss this case with deck officers to ensure awareness of the dangers of altering to port and the obligation to call the Master.
procedures.why: To prevent recurrence of this common but dangerous practice among young officers.

procedures.action: If incorrect port alterations are found to be commonplace, investigate the root cause and implement remedial measures such as a fleet circular, additional assessment and training.
procedures.why: Systemic practice issues require fleet-wide corrective action rather than one-off correction.

constraints: The Duty Officer remains in charge of the vessel unless formally relieved, even with the Master present on the bridge.
Rule 17(c) prohibits the give-way vessel from altering course to port for a vessel on her own side in a crossing situation when action is being taken.
Rule 14 governs head-on and near head-on situations and similarly disfavors port alterations.
Rule 33(d) requires sound and light signals during collision-avoidance maneuvering.
VHF should not generally be used as a substitute for COLREGs-compliant collision avoidance action.
warnings: Altering course to port in crossing or head-on/near head-on situations is dangerous and contravenes the Rules.
Over-reliance on apparent ARPA accuracy (e.g., 'passing ahead') can impair judgement in close-quarters decision-making.
VHF should not be used in collision avoidance as a general rule.
Failure to call the Master when in doubt, even with the Master nearby, compounds risk of collision.
outcomes: Incorrect port alteration under Rule 17(c) directly contravened the Rules and created/worsened a close-quarters situation.
Failure to communicate concerns to the Master or use sound/light signals or reduce speed left available safety options unused.
Company identification of recurring incorrect port alterations suggests need for fleet-wide training and standing order clarification.
key_facts: The Duty Officer altered course to port in contravention of Rule 17(c) despite the Master standing close by.
Duty Officers remain in charge of the vessel unless relieved, but must keep the Master advised of navigational hazards or developing close-quarters situations.
The guiding principle recommended is: 'If in doubt whether you are in doubt - call the Master.'
The acceptable action in this case would have been a large alteration to starboard (round turn) under Rule 17(c) or a reduction in speed.
Sound and light signals prescribed by Rule 33(d) were not made, and speed reduction was not considered as an option.

question_seeds.text: Why is altering course to port considered dangerous under Rule 14 or Rule 17(c)?
When should a Duty Officer call the Master even if the Master is already present on the bridge?
What signals should have been made under Rule 33(d) when taking avoiding action in this incident?
How should the Company address a pattern of officers incorrectly altering course to port in crossing situations?

trace.situation: A vessel in restricted visibility detected another ship on radar with an unsatisfactory CPA, attempted to alter to starboard, but the other vessel unexpectedly altered to port based on a VHF agreement made with a different, misidentified ship, creating a near-collision that was averted by the alert watch officer going hard-a-port at the last moment.
trace.trigger: Detection of a radar contact in restricted visibility with a CPA the master was unhappy with, followed by the other vessel's unexpected course alteration contrary to the plotted passing situation.

procedures.action: Continuously monitor radar plot and CPA/TCPA of contacts in restricted visibility, not relying solely on clear-visibility passing margins.
procedures.why: Vessels appear to continue using clear visibility passing values in restricted visibility, reducing safety margins when they are most needed.

procedures.action: Increase sea room and passing distance margins in restricted visibility, and consider speed reduction in confined waters.
procedures.why: Optimum sea room must be adjusted to prevailing circumstances and conditions; in open water margins can be pushed out, in confined waters speed reduction can achieve similar effect.

procedures.action: Avoid using VHF to negotiate deviations from the Collision Regulations.
procedures.why: VHF was used to try to negotiate a deviation from the Rules and resulted in a misidentification and a near-collision.

procedures.action: If VHF communication is deemed necessary, use it only to confirm compliance with the Rules, not to agree alternative passing arrangements.
procedures.why: Confirms adherence to established Rules rather than creating ambiguity or false agreements between unidentified vessels.

procedures.action: Confirm the identity of any vessel communicated with beyond doubt before acting on any agreed arrangement.
procedures.why: The other vessel believed it had agreed a green-to-green passing with 'my ship' but had actually communicated with a different vessel, causing the dangerous situation.

procedures.action: Maintain alertness and be ready to take immediate emergency action (e.g., hard-a-port) if the other vessel's actions contradict the expected passing situation.
procedures.why: The watch officer's alertness in observing the other vessel's unexpected port alteration and reacting immediately salvaged the situation from collision.

constraints: Compliance with the Collision Regulations ('the Rules') is sufficient in almost all circumstances.
VHF conversations should be avoided for negotiating actions; if used, only to confirm Rule compliance.
Passing distance margins used in clear visibility are not adequate for restricted visibility conditions.
Identity of any vessel engaged via VHF must be confirmed beyond doubt before relying on agreed arrangements.
warnings: Using VHF to negotiate a deviation from the Rules can lead to misidentification and dangerous close-quarters situations.
Reversing an initial avoiding alteration after the other vessel detects it often results in collision rather than avoidance.
Continuing to use clear-visibility passing distance values in restricted visibility is an inadequate safety margin.
outcomes: The near-collision was averted only due to the watch officer's alertness in detecting the other vessel's port alteration and taking immediate hard-a-port action.
The vessel passed close enough to read the other ship's name, indicating how close the near-collision came to an actual collision.
The other vessel's VHF-based agreement was with a different, misidentified vessel, demonstrating the danger of VHF negotiation without positive identification.
key_facts: The incident occurred in poor (restricted) visibility with a contact detected fine on the port bow by radar.
The master was unhappy with the plotted CPA and ordered a starboard alteration.
The other vessel altered to port based on a VHF agreement to 'pass green to green' made with a different ship, not the reporting vessel.
An immediate hard-a-port action by the watch officer avoided a close-quarters situation or collision.
The MAIB investigation into the collision between 'Lykes Voyager' and 'Washington Senator' illustrates the consequences of not following best practice in this type of situation.

question_seeds.text: Why did the other vessel alter to port when the plotted CPA indicated it would pass clear down our port side?
How should passing distance margins be adjusted when operating in restricted visibility compared to clear visibility?
What should I do if a VHF conversation with another vessel appears to propose a deviation from the Collision Regulations?
When is it acceptable to use VHF communication with another vessel during a close-quarters or collision-risk situation?

trace.situation: An anchored vessel awaiting a pilot at night was nearly struck when another ship (a gas carrier) entering the anchorage was set down by wind and current and passed close ahead at an estimated 50 metres.
trace.trigger: 3rd Officer observes another vessel's lights closing dangerously while at anchor at night and summons the Master, sounding the whistle.

procedures.action: Keep a continuous anchor watch monitoring other vessels entering the anchorage, especially in strong wind/current conditions.
procedures.why: The 3rd Officer had been monitoring the approaching ship and detected she was being set onto own ship before a collision occurred.

procedures.action: Sound the whistle and immediately call the Master to the Bridge when risk of close quarters develops.
procedures.why: Early warning and Master's presence are needed to assess and respond to a developing close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Keep main engine on short notice (10 minutes) while at anchor in strong wind/current conditions.
procedures.why: Enables rapid engine use if manoeuvring is suddenly required to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Use AIS to identify any vessel involved in a near-miss for reporting and follow-up.
procedures.why: Allows identification of the other vessel (confirmed as a gas carrier) for incident reporting purposes.

constraints: Own ship was anchored with 7 shackles of cable, facing into wind/current, awaiting pilot.
Main engine was on 10 minutes notice of readiness.
Anchorage had strong wind and the usual strong current, requiring vessels to compensate when anchoring or manoeuvring nearby.
warnings: Failure to account for wind and current effects (seamanship) can result in a vessel being dangerously set down onto an anchored ship, risking catastrophic collision.
High freeboard and large windage areas (e.g. deck compressor rooms) significantly increase a vessel's vulnerability to being set down by wind, and must be accounted for by the Master.
Newly assumed management of a vessel can lead to a Master underestimating the ship's handling characteristics in adverse conditions.
outcomes: No collision occurred; the gas carrier passed approximately 50 metres ahead and subsequently anchored further west.
The incident was reported via CHIRP and forwarded to the gas carrier's manager.
The gas carrier's manager found no record of the incident in their company's reporting database, and the Master involved had since left the company and declined to comment.
The gas carrier's manager attributed the near-miss to the Master underestimating the vessel's unusually high windage area from high freeboard and deck compressor rooms.
key_facts: Own ship anchored at 22:00 hrs in the Northern anchorage with 7 shackles of cable, facing south into the wind, awaiting a pilot.
At 23:45 hrs a gas carrier entering the anchorage was set down by wind and current, passing an estimated 50 metres ahead of own ship.
The 3rd Officer had monitored the other vessel's approach and alteration to port before realising she was being set down and calling the Master.
AIS was used to identify the other vessel as a gas carrier, which had unusually high windage due to high freeboard and deck compressor rooms.
The gas carrier's management company had no record of the incident, and the Master involved had since left the company.

trace.situation: A pilot reports a near-miss during port manoeuvring where two vessels ("A" and "B") inadvertently shared the same VHF channel for intership communication, causing a helm/engine order intended for vessel B to be received and nearly acted upon by vessel A.
trace.trigger: Two vessels manoeuvring simultaneously in port use the same VHF channel for intership/internal communication, causing cross-reception of critical orders.

procedures.action: Give manoeuvring orders verbally on the bridge rather than relaying them over open VHF when possible.
procedures.why: Reduces risk of a wrong-ship or third-party receiving a critical helm/engine order.

procedures.action: If internal radio communication is necessary, use a low-power UHF set instead of VHF.
procedures.why: UHF is unlikely to be picked up by other vessels or the public, reducing cross-talk and interference.

procedures.action: Confirm and if necessary change VHF channel before relying on it for intership coordination.
procedures.why: Prevents two vessels manoeuvring nearby from inadvertently sharing the same channel and misreceiving orders.

procedures.action: Where radio is unreliable or risky, use direct shouted commands on the bridge/deck.
procedures.why: The pilot found this the most positive and effective method of ensuring the right crew receives the order.

constraints: Orders relayed over an open public VHF channel can be received by any vessel monitoring that channel.
Helm and engine orders during final approach to a lock or berth require precise timing and cannot tolerate miscommunication delays.
warnings: A wrong-way helm order received from another vessel's channel may not be correctable in time during final approach to a lock or berth.
An inappropriate engine order could be catastrophic for the bow tug and its crew.
Shared VHF channel use during manoeuvring risks accidents from inadvertent cross-reception or malicious third-party interference.
outcomes: The pilot's request to switch to verbal orders averted potential harm from the misreceived "Let go everything" command.
The master's choice to speak in his native language instead of changing channel did not resolve the underlying channel-sharing risk.
The reporter notes this unsafe practice of shared VHF channel use during manoeuvring is common across multiple companies' vessels.
key_facts: Vessel B's order 'Let go everything' was received by vessel A because both were using the same VHF channel for intership communication.
The pilot requested the master of vessel A give orders verbally instead of via VHF.
The master then spoke in his native language internally rather than switching VHF channels.
The reporter recommends low-power UHF sets for internal communication to avoid public/third-party reception.
The reporter considers this type of VHF channel conflict a frequent, industry-wide problem during port manoeuvring.

question_seeds.text: Why is using a shared public VHF channel for intership manoeuvring orders dangerous?
How should I ensure my bridge team's internal orders are not received by another vessel on the same channel?
What alternative to VHF should be used for internal communication during critical manoeuvres?
Which phase of a port approach is most vulnerable to miscommunication from shared VHF channels?

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board comments on a vessel operator's response to a reported near-miss incident involving bridge team management and anchoring.
trace.trigger: A vessel operator submitted a response to CHIRP describing corrective actions taken after a near-miss incident report.

procedures.action: Send a reminder letter to ship's staff emphasizing the importance of near-miss reporting.
procedures.why: To reinforce the safety reporting culture following the incident.

procedures.action: Publish an extensive article on near-miss reporting in the company safety newsletter.
procedures.why: To further educate crew on the value of near-miss reporting.

procedures.action: Reduce the interval between bridge team training courses.
procedures.why: To improve the actions and effectiveness of the bridge team.

procedures.action: Review the familiarisation procedure used when a new ship is taken under management.
procedures.why: The incident indicates a possible concern about the effectiveness of this procedure.

procedures.action: Complete the incident investigation even after the Master involved has left the company.
procedures.why: To ensure lessons are captured and shared for the benefit of other employees.

procedures.action: Incorporate lessons on selecting and proceeding to a safe anchorage, considering leeway, set, drift and windage.
procedures.why: These factors are likely to be of general application across the fleet.

constraints: Investigation completion should not be abandoned due to personnel turnover (e.g., Master leaving the company).
Familiarisation procedures for newly managed vessels must be assessed for effectiveness.
warnings: Possible concern regarding the effectiveness of familiarisation procedures when a new ship is taken under management.
Incomplete investigations risk losing valuable lessons for other employees.
outcomes: Operator made a positive assessment and response to the incident, though with some delay in reporting to CHIRP.
Reduced bridge team training intervals aim to improve bridge team performance.
Gaps remain regarding completion of the investigation and documentation of anchorage-related lessons.
key_facts: The vessel operator sent a reminder letter on the importance of near-miss reporting.
A safety newsletter article extensively covered near-miss reporting.
The interval between bridge team training courses was reduced as a broader improvement measure.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report highlighted difficulties with VHF radio communications in port operations, leading to a comment on risks of misidentification and recommendations for improvement.
trace.trigger: Recurring radio communication confusion/misidentification incidents reported to CHIRP involving harbour/pilotage operations.

procedures.action: Ensure Competent Harbour Authority includes operational communications in its risk assessment.
procedures.why: Operational communications should be covered by a Competent Harbour Authority's risk assessment to identify and mitigate risks.

procedures.action: Ensure radio communications are properly prefixed (e.g., with vessel/station identification).
procedures.why: Proper prefixing limits the risk of misidentification between vessels or stations.

procedures.action: Consider alternative communication methods such as 'Talkback' systems.
procedures.why: Alternative methods can reduce reliance on standard VHF and further limit miscommunication risk.

constraints: Communication risk mitigation must be addressed within the Competent Harbour Authority's formal risk assessment process.
warnings: Improperly prefixed radio communications increase the risk of misidentification between vessels or stations.
outcomes: The report was forwarded to the MCA's Port Marine Safety Code Steering Group for further review.
The UK Maritime Pilots' Association will survey members to assess how widespread the communication difficulty is.
key_facts: The report was escalated to the UK MCA's Port Marine Safety Code Steering Group.

48 hours off required between work periods

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime report describing a near-miss head-on encounter between two fast-moving vessels that were reluctant to take early collision-avoidance action, resolving the situation only at close range via VHF communication.
trace.trigger: Two vessels on reciprocal/near-reciprocal courses closing head-on at high speed (~30 kts) without early alteration of course.

procedures.action: Monitor the developing CPA/TCPA on radar as vessels converge.
procedures.why: The reporting vessel tracked both vessels and calculated a CPA of 1.5 nm, highlighting the need for continuous risk assessment.

procedures.action: Take early and substantial action to avoid a head-on situation rather than waiting.
procedures.why: Both vessel A and vessel B continued on their original tracks without alteration, allowing the range to close to within 2.5 nm before any action was taken.

procedures.action: Use VHF only as a last resort to clarify intentions, not as a substitute for COLREGS compliance.
procedures.why: The vessels only communicated once they were dangerously close (within 2.5 nm), and the exchange of intentions on Ch 16/6 was a reactive rather than preventive measure.

procedures.action: When altering course to avoid collision, make the alteration large enough to be readily apparent, not a marginal 5-degree change.
procedures.why: Radar plot showed both vessels altered by only about 5 degrees to starboard, resulting in a pass of less than 0.5 nm, far closer than intended or safe.

constraints: Head-on situations require both vessels to alter course to starboard (implied by the vessels agreeing to 'pass red to red').
Course alterations must be early and substantial to be effective and unambiguous to the other vessel.
VHF communication should not be relied upon as the primary means of resolving a collision risk.
warnings: Reluctance to alter course early can force last-minute, high-risk maneuvers at close range.
A 5-degree course alteration is insufficient to be obvious to another vessel and does not create a safe passing distance.
Relying on VHF negotiation at close range ('What are your intentions?') is a reactive and risky practice compared to early COLREGS-compliant action.
High closing speeds (around 30 kts combined or individual) drastically reduce the time available to safely resolve a risk of collision.
outcomes: The two vessels passed each other at less than 0.5 nm, far closer than prudent despite initial indications of a 1.5 nm CPA.
After passing, both vessels returned to their original track lines, indicating the alterations were minimal and reactive rather than part of a planned avoidance maneuver.
key_facts: The reporting vessel passed vessel A at about 1.5 nm with no alteration from A.
Vessel B and another vessel (astern) closed in a head-on situation at approximately 30 kts.
Neither vessel altered course until they had closed to within 2.5 nm of each other.
VHF communication on Ch 16 and Ch 6 was used to negotiate a red-to-red (starboard-to-starboard) passing.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a reported near-collision where a vessel's course alteration was too small, too late, and resulted in an unnecessarily close passing distance, prompting discussion of Rule 8 compliance and GPS-driven head-on collision risk.
trace.trigger: A report of vessels passing unnecessarily close in open water due to a late, minimal course alteration.

procedures.action: Take any collision-avoidance action in accordance with the Rules, making it positive, timely, and in keeping with good seamanship.
procedures.why: Rule 8(a) requires action to avoid collision to be positive, made in ample time, and with due regard to good seamanship.

procedures.action: Avoid relying on minimal course alterations (e.g. 5°) made at short range (<2.5nm) and short time (<7 minutes) before closest approach.
procedures.why: Such action failed to be positive, timely, or seamanlike, resulting in a passing distance of <0.5nm in open water.

procedures.action: Consider adopting a 'leave waypoints to port' offset when planning routes.
procedures.why: Modern high-accuracy navigation systems increase the risk of head-on or nearly head-on encounters when vessels track identical routes precisely; offsetting to port reduces this risk, an approach endorsed by the Maritime Advisory Board.

procedures.action: Remain alert to overtaking risk even when using waypoint offsets or following recommended routes.
procedures.why: End-on overtaking encounters remain possible if multiple vessels adopt similar offsets, as illustrated by the MAIB investigation into the Cepheus J / Ileksa collision.

constraints: Collision avoidance action must be positive, made in ample time, and with due regard to good seamanship, if circumstances admit (Rule 8(a)).
Waypoint offsets to port do not eliminate overtaking collision risk if similarly adopted by other vessels or mandated by recommended routes.
warnings: A 5° alteration at under 2.5nm range with under 7 minutes to collision, resulting in a passing distance under 0.5nm in open water, fails to meet Rule 8 requirements on all counts.
Precise modern navigation tracking can increase, not decrease, the risk of head-on or nearly head-on encounters.
Adopting a 'leave waypoints to port' offset can still result in end-on overtaking collisions, as seen in the Cepheus J / Ileksa incident.
outcomes: If the reported facts are true, the vessel's action failed to comply with Rule 8 on all three criteria (positive, timely, seamanlike).
The Maritime Advisory Board's endorsement of port-side waypoint offsets aims to reduce head-on encounter risk from high-precision navigation.
key_facts: The reported alteration was only 5° at a range of less than 2.5nm and less than 7 minutes before closest approach, with passing distance under 0.5nm in open water.
Rule 8(a) requires collision-avoidance action to be positive, made in ample time, and seamanlike.
Modern navigation systems' increased track accuracy has heightened the risk of head-on or nearly head-on encounters in certain areas.
The Maritime Advisory Board endorses a 'leave waypoints to port' offset approach to mitigate this risk.
The UK MAIB investigation into the Cepheus J / Ileksa collision shows that offset waypoints can still lead to overtaking collisions.
