trace.situation: CHIRP bulletin presenting two maritime safety concerns: an MAIB finding on pilot fatigue self-assessment following the 'Orade' collision investigation, and a mariner's report of repeated head-on encounters in a navigation channel where another vessel failed to deviate from its track line despite risk of collision.
trace.trigger: A pilot is ordered for a job and must judge his own fatigue level; separately, a vessel detects risk of collision in a head-on situation with another vessel that is not altering course.

procedures.action: Alter course to starboard when a head-on risk of collision situation is identified.
procedures.why: Standard collision avoidance action; reporting mariner used this to open CPA to 0.4nm.

procedures.action: Use AIS and radar together to identify and track approaching vessels at range (e.g. 10nm).
procedures.why: Allows early identification and continuous monitoring of multiple vessels (vessel A ahead, vessel B astern) to assess developing risk.

procedures.action: Continue monitoring CPA/TCPA even after initial avoidance action, especially with multiple vessels in proximity.
procedures.why: A second vessel astern (vessel B) could compound the risk picture and require further action.

procedures.action: Ports/pilotage authorities should proactively manage pilot working-hour risks rather than relying solely on the pilot's own judgment.
procedures.why: MAIB found individuals are not usually the best judge of their own fatigue condition.

constraints: Pilots' working hours are subject to working time regulations, with some allowance made for recently worked hours.
When ordering a pilot, much is left to the pilot's own view on fitness/fatigue, which MAIB considers unreliable.
In a head-on situation, standard practice is to alter course to starboard even if a navigational hazard (bank) lies to starboard.
warnings: An individual (including a pilot) is not usually the best judge of their own fatigue condition.
Some vessels in head-on situations may be unable or unwilling to deviate from a fixed course line, creating 'line fever' risk and requiring the other vessel to take independent avoiding action.
Altering course toward a bank or hazard to comply with head-on avoidance requires careful risk balancing.
outcomes: QinetiQ analysis concluded the Orade pilot was probably not fatigued, but the investigation still exposed systemic risk in how pilot fitness is assessed.
MAIB recommended development of appropriate working-hour regimes for UK pilots.
CHIRP will monitor and report on the Steering Group's findings.
The reporting mariner successfully increased CPA to 0.4nm by altering course to starboard despite the other vessel holding its course.
key_facts: The MAIB investigated the collision of the general cargo vessel 'Orade' with the Apex Beacon on the River Ouse.
QinetiQ Centre for Human Sciences concluded the pilot was probably not fatigued at the time of the Orade accident.
MAIB recommended the Port Marine Safety Code Steering Group develop appropriate pilot working-hour regimes.
A mariner encountered the same vessel in a head-on 'channel' situation on two consecutive nights, with the other vessel seemingly unable or unwilling to alter course.
On a third encounter, the mariner identified a vessel at 10nm via radar/AIS with a second vessel 5nm astern, and altered course to starboard upon determining risk of collision existed.

question_seeds.text: Why does CHIRP/MAIB consider individual self-assessment of fatigue unreliable, and what should pilotage authorities do instead?

trace.situation: Two CHIRP leisure-sector incident reports: one about a skipper disassembling the throttle assembly while under the influence of alcohol causing a near-loss of reverse power, and a Harbour Authority report on a collision between a cargo ship and a small sailing vessel that had anchored in the main shipping channel at night.
trace.trigger: Unsupervised/unqualified mechanical interference combined with alcohol use, and a leisure vessel anchoring in a main navigation channel without adequate lighting, radar conspicuity, or notification to the Harbour Authority.

procedures.action: Only attempt repairs or modifications you are competent to undertake.
procedures.why: Meddling above one's level of expertise nearly caused a serious maritime incident.

procedures.action: Always check the function of controls and equipment after maintenance or repair.
procedures.why: Prevents undetected loss of critical functions such as reverse power.

procedures.action: Do not undertake mechanical work while under the influence of alcohol; work only under close supervision.
procedures.why: Alcohol slows reactions and distorts self-assessment of ability, as shown in the self-reported incident.

procedures.action: When anchoring, provide additional lighting (e.g., deck lighting) as suggested by Rule 30(c) of COLREGS, especially in areas with background shore lighting.
procedures.why: The vessel's masthead light was lost among street and vehicle lighting ashore, reducing its visibility to approaching traffic.

procedures.action: Ensure the anchored vessel presents a conspicuous radar target (e.g., radar reflector).
procedures.why: The sailing vessel did not show up clearly on either shore-based or ship's radar, removing a key detection safeguard.

procedures.action: Notify the Harbour Authority (not only the Coastguard) when anchoring within or near a main shipping channel.
procedures.why: Lack of notification to the Harbour Authority meant approaching traffic had no advance warning of the obstruction.

constraints: Repairs/modifications must be within the operator's competence.
Controls and equipment must be function-tested after any maintenance or repair.
Anchored vessels must comply with Rule 30(c) of COLREGS regarding additional lighting where necessary.
Anchoring in or near a main shipping channel requires notification to the relevant Harbour Authority, not just the Coastguard.
warnings: Alcohol impairs reaction time and distorts self-assessment of one's own abilities.
Unqualified mechanical interference can cause serious maritime incidents.
Anchoring in line with channel leading lights without adequate lighting/radar conspicuity risks collision with commercial traffic.
Notifying only the Coastguard and not the Harbour Authority leaves a critical gap in collision-avoidance communication.
outcomes: In the throttle incident, a serious maritime incident was narrowly avoided due to quick and decisive crew action.

In the anchoring incident, the combination of poor lighting, lack of radar conspicuity, and failure to notify the Harbour Authority resulted in an actual collision between a cargo ship and the sailing vessel.
key_facts: The skipper disassembled the throttle assembly while apparently under the influence of alcohol, risking loss of reverse power.
Crewmembers' quick action prevented a serious incident from the throttle tampering.
A sailing vessel anchored directly in line with leading lights marking the deep-water channel at night.
The vessel's masthead light was lit but lost among shore lighting, and no supplementary deck lighting per Rule 30(c) was used.
The vessel did not present a conspicuous radar target and had notified only the Coastguard, not the Harbour Authority, resulting in a collision.

question_seeds.text: Why is it dangerous to attempt mechanical repairs while under the influence of alcohol?
What additional lighting should I use if I must anchor near a navigation channel at night?
Who besides the Coastguard must be notified when anchoring in or near a main shipping channel?
How can I ensure my vessel is detectable by radar when anchored in a busy channel?

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime Feedback report discusses a near-miss where an outbound ship scraped a sailing boat anchored in the main navigation channel, narrowly avoiding severe or fatal injury due to the ship's last-minute avoiding action.
trace.trigger: A vessel is anchored in or near a main navigation channel where passing ship traffic creates collision risk, especially in low visibility or at night.

procedures.action: Do not anchor in the main navigation channel.
procedures.why: Anchoring in the channel puts the vessel directly in the path of transiting ships, risking collision.

procedures.action: If anchoring in the channel is unavoidable (e.g. emergency), contact the Harbour Authority immediately and advise position and type of vessel.
procedures.why: Allows the Harbour Authority to warn or coordinate with other traffic to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Study the relevant, corrected and up-to-date chart of the area.
procedures.why: Ensures the anchoring vessel understands channel boundaries and traffic risk before anchoring.

procedures.action: Ensure the vessel is adequately lit, accounting for background lighting and prevailing conditions.
procedures.why: Improves visibility to other vessels, especially at night or in poor ambient light.

procedures.action: Ensure the vessel presents an adequate radar target by hoisting or permanently fixing a suitable radar reflector.
procedures.why: Allows passing ships using radar to detect the anchored vessel in time to take avoiding action.

procedures.action: Keep a good lookout and maintain a listening watch on the appropriate VHF channel throughout.
procedures.why: Enables early detection of approaching traffic and ability to communicate/respond to warnings.

constraints: Vessels should not anchor in the main navigation channel except in emergency.
If anchored in the channel out of necessity, the Harbour Authority must be notified immediately with position and vessel type.
warnings: Anchoring in a main navigation channel risks severe or fatal injury to occupants if a passing ship cannot take avoiding action in time.
Inadequate lighting or radar visibility of an anchored vessel increases collision risk with transiting ships.
outcomes: The outbound ship's last-minute avoiding action prevented fatal injury, resulting only in superficial damage to the anchored sailing boat.
Without the avoiding action, the outcome would likely have been severe or fatal injury to those aboard the anchored vessel.
key_facts: A sailing boat was anchored in the main navigation channel.
An outbound ship scraped along the side of the anchored boat after taking last-minute avoiding action.
The damage was superficial, but the potential outcome without avoiding action would have been severe or fatal injury.
CHIRP Maritime Feedback issue 10 lists reasonable points/best practices following this near-miss.

Who should be contacted immediately if forced to anchor in a navigation channel?

trace.situation: CHIRP editorial for the 10th edition of FEEDBACK discusses trends in reporting, including company-sourced SMS reports, a dominance of near-collision reports, and recurring issues of Colreg competence and confidence in application.

procedures.action: Share near-collision and safety-related information obtained through company SMS with CHIRP or other bodies.
procedures.why: CHIRP's mission is to promote safety by obtaining, distributing and analyzing safety-related reports not otherwise available.

procedures.action: Report near-collision encounters to the other ship's owner/operator and/or Flag Administration's investigation body.
procedures.why: Increases the chances of realising improvements and promoting resolution.

procedures.action: Consider establishing Colreg competence through pre-employment screening rather than relying solely on certification.
procedures.why: Reports suggest certified personnel may not always be adequately competent in Colregs, and Flag Administration certification standards vary.

procedures.action: Consider reducing speed as an option when resolving close-quarters/near-collision situations.
procedures.why: CHIRP has not received a single near-collision report where speed reduction was used or even considered, suggesting it is an underused resolution tool.

constraints: CHIRP offers confidentiality to company report sources in the same way it does to individuals.
Reports must come through recognized channels such as a Safety Management System (SMS) for CHIRP to analyze and distribute them.
warnings: Confidence in Colreg application is highly susceptible to company and shipboard culture factors, not just competence.
Reliance on certification alone may not guarantee actual Colreg competence.
outcomes: Increased sharing of near-collision reports has led to a dominance of such reports in CHIRP's post-bag.
Bringing near-collision incidents to the attention of the 'other' ship's management has achieved some success in promoting positive responses.
Lack of speed reduction as a considered resolution option in near-collision reports indicates a gap in practical Colreg application.
key_facts: This 10th edition of FEEDBACK includes two reports sourced from a ship manager and a harbour authority via their SMS.
CHIRP provides confidentiality to companies submitting reports just as it does for individuals.
Near-collision reports currently dominate CHIRP's incoming reports.
No near-collision report received by CHIRP involved speed reduction as a resolution method.
The Shipping Industry Guidelines on Flag State Performance (marisec.org) can help assess Flag Administration certification reliability.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime feedback report discussing a near-miss overtaking encounter, including a shipping company's response to the report and the Maritime Advisory Board's commentary on relevant COLREGs rules (13, 8, 34).
trace.trigger: A near-miss/incident report involving an overtaking situation was submitted to CHIRP and forwarded to the vessel manager for response and analysis.

procedures.action: Encourage and mandate crew to report all near misses and incidents as frequently as possible through the company Quality system.
procedures.why: Enables root cause analysis and fleet-wide learning.

procedures.action: Consolidate reports at head office, analyze them, and distribute findings back to vessels across the fleet.
procedures.why: Provides guidance and follow-up to prevent recurrence.

procedures.action: Review onboard follow-up actions via Internal Auditing procedures.
procedures.why: Ensures corrective actions are implemented and effective.

procedures.action: As the overtaking vessel, keep clear of the vessel being overtaken per Rule 13.
procedures.why: Rule 13 overrides Part B Sections I and II rules and places sole responsibility on the overtaking vessel.

procedures.action: Take collision-avoidance action that results in passing at a safe distance and continuously monitor its effectiveness until the other vessel is finally past and clear, per Rule 8(d).
procedures.why: Ensures the action remains effective throughout the encounter, not just at the point of initial maneuver.

procedures.action: Use the sound signal prescribed in Rule 34(d), or a recognized version of it, when overtaking.
procedures.why: Demonstrated success in alerting the overtaken vessel and resolving the close-quarters situation.

constraints: CHIRP limits the level of information released to protect individuals from negative consequences.
Rule 13 applies notwithstanding anything in Rules of Part B, Sections I and II.
Effectiveness of avoidance action must be checked continuously until the other vessel is finally past and clear (Rule 8(d)).
warnings: There is a tendency in overtaking encounters to accept a closer CPA than in crossing situations, despite greater risk from prolonged proximity and potential involvement of other vessels.
outcomes: The company sent a general guidance message to all ships following the incident.
The second vessel overtaken successfully used the Rule 34(d) sound signal to resolve the close-quarters situation.
The Maritime Advisory Board acknowledged the company's positive and cooperative response to the CHIRP report.
key_facts: Rule 13 requires any overtaking vessel to keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, overriding Part B Sections I and II.
Rule 8(d) requires avoidance action to achieve a safe passing distance and requires continuous monitoring until the other vessel is finally past and clear.
Studies show mariners tend to accept closer CPAs in overtaking situations than in crossing situations despite greater risk.
The second overtaken vessel used the Rule 34(d) sound signal with success.
CHIRP withholds some reporter information to protect individuals, which can limit a company's root-cause investigation.

trace.situation: An officer on a vessel transiting the south end of a Traffic Separation Scheme at reduced speed due to weather observed another vessel (A) overtaking at high speed on the starboard side, creating a close-quarters situation with a CPA of less than one cable.
trace.trigger: Vessel A, overtaking from 6nm astern at 15.7 kts, was plotted as developing a CPA of less than 1 cable at 2nm range while own vessel was limited to 4 kts due to weather.

procedures.action: Continuously plot and monitor the overtaking vessel's course, speed, and CPA from first detection.
procedures.why: Early detection at 6nm allowed the risk of close quarters to be identified before it became critical.

procedures.action: Contact the overtaking vessel on VHF Ch.16 and request a wider berth.
procedures.why: To attempt to resolve the developing close-quarters situation through direct communication.

procedures.action: Assess the risk of altering course to port against the sea state before taking avoiding action.
procedures.why: Heavy rolling in the prevailing weather made an alteration to port hazardous to own vessel.

procedures.action: Report the incident as a 'Near-miss' through the company Safety Management System after the event.
procedures.why: To formally record the close-quarters encounter and support fleet-wide learning.

procedures.action: Recalculate alternative actions (e.g., altering course away from danger) for future reference.
procedures.why: To identify what could have been done differently to avoid the close-quarters situation.

constraints: Weather had reduced own vessel's speed to 4 kts, limiting maneuvering options.
Altering course to port risked heavy rolling in the prevailing weather conditions.
Another vessel (B) was ahead on the same track, constraining vessel A's room to maneuver away from own vessel.
VHF communication with vessel A was unintelligible/incomplete, leaving the situation unresolved by radio.
warnings: Overtaking vessels passing at less than 1 cable show complete disregard for the effect of interaction between ships.
Reliance on VHF communication to resolve close-quarters situations may fail if the response is unintelligible or inadequate.
Altering course in heavy weather can itself create danger (heavy rolling) and must be weighed against collision risk.
outcomes: Vessel A passed own vessel at a distance of less than 1 cable despite the VHF request.
Vessel A then overtook vessel B at a similarly close distance, prompting vessel B's officer to shine a searchlight and complain, causing vessel A to shear away.
No collision occurred, but a formal near-miss report was filed and corrective reflection on alternative actions was conducted.
key_facts: Own vessel was at the south end of a TSS, reduced to 4 kts, course 230(T), due to weather.
Vessel A was overtaking from 6nm astern at 15.7 kts on the starboard side.
At 2nm range, the calculated CPA was less than 1 cable.
Vessel A's VHF response blamed another vessel (B) on its starboard side and was otherwise unintelligible.
Vessel A eventually passed vessel B as closely as it passed own vessel, prompting a searchlight warning from vessel B.

trace.situation: A CHIRP near-miss report describes two vessels ('A' and 'B') arguing over VHF about whether Rule 13 (overtaking) applied, with a language barrier complicating the exchange, followed by a second overtaking incident in the Terschelling-German Bight TSS where a fishing vessel made an unexpected manoeuvre between an overtaking ship and a car carrier.
trace.trigger: Uncertainty or disagreement between vessels over whether a crossing/overtaking situation exists under the COLREGS, compounded by a non-native English speaking OOW.

procedures.action: If any doubt exists as to whether a vessel is overtaking another, assume that it is and act accordingly (Rule 13(c)).
procedures.why: Rule 13(c) explicitly requires this assumption to remove ambiguity and avoid delayed action.

procedures.action: Use Standard Marine Communication Phrases (SMCP) when communicating with an OOW whose first language is not English.
procedures.why: The incident showed a language issue contributed to confusion; SMCP reduces misunderstanding in critical exchanges.

procedures.action: Take early, decisive action under the Rules rather than debating their application over VHF as vessels close.
procedures.why: The Maritime Advisory Board noted this incident mirrored the Hyundai Dominion/Sky Hope collision, where vessels debated the Rules almost up to the point of collision.

procedures.action: When overtaking another vessel while a third vessel's intentions are unclear, proactively communicate intentions to the vessel being overtaken.
procedures.why: The reporting vessel contacted the car carrier via VHF to make it aware of intentions regarding an unknown crossing fishing vessel, to prevent embarrassment or close-quarters situations.

constraints: Rule 13(c) applies whenever there is doubt about whether an overtaking situation exists.
Communication in a shared working language (or SMCP) must be sufficient for mutual understanding of intended actions under the Rules.
Vessels in a TSS lane must account for multiple crossing/overtaking traffic, including fishing vessels, simultaneously.
warnings: Debating the applicability of the collision regulations over VHF up to the point of near-collision is extremely dangerous.
A lack of basic understanding of the COLREGS by an OOW poses a serious safety concern.
Fishing vessels crossing a TSS can make sudden, extraordinary manoeuvres that create close-quarters situations.
outcomes: Vessel 'A' returned to course, altered to port, and passed around the stern of 'B', avoiding collision after the Rule 13 discussion.
The fishing vessel's extraordinary manoeuvre to pass between the car carrier and the reporting vessel created a hazardous close-quarters situation despite prior VHF coordination.
CHIRP flagged the incident's similarity to a real collision (Hyundai Dominion/Sky Hope) caused by Rule-debating instead of timely action.
key_facts: Rule 13(c) of the COLREGS states that when in doubt as to whether a vessel is overtaking another, she shall assume that this is the case and act accordingly.
The incident involved a language barrier, with the OOW on vessel 'A' stating they did not understand English regarding rule discussion.
The Maritime Advisory Board compared this near-miss to the actual Hyundai Dominion/Sky Hope collision, where rule debate continued almost to the point of impact.
In the Terschelling-German Bight TSS incident, multiple fishing vessels were crossing from port to starboard while the reporting vessel was overtaking a car carrier.
A fishing vessel attempted to pass between the overtaking vessel and the car carrier, creating an unexpected close-quarters situation.

question_seeds.text: Why should a vessel assume an overtaking situation exists whenever there is doubt, per Rule 13(c)?
How should I communicate collision-avoidance intentions with an OOW whose first language is not English?
What should I do if another vessel starts debating the applicable COLREGS rule over VHF as we close distance?

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime near-miss report describes an overtaking encounter in the Irish Sea where two vessels, 'A' (overtaking at 20kts) and 'B', disputed via VHF whether 'A' was in a genuine overtaking position, leading to contradictory verbal course-alteration instructions instead of using sound/light signals.
trace.trigger: Vessels in sight of one another approaching each other, with one vessel failing to understand or being in doubt about the other's intentions/actions regarding collision avoidance.

procedures.action: When in doubt whether the other vessel is taking sufficient action to avoid collision, immediately sound at least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle.
procedures.why: COLREG Rule 34(d) requires an unambiguous doubt signal rather than relying on verbal clarification.

procedures.action: Supplement the whistle signal with a light signal of at least five short and rapid flashes if available.
procedures.why: Provides a visual reinforcement of the doubt signal, especially useful in conditions where sound may not carry or be heard clearly.

procedures.action: Avoid relying solely on VHF conversation to resolve uncertainty about relative bearing or overtaking status.
procedures.why: The report shows a prolonged, ambiguous VHF exchange over bearing ('two points abaft the beam') and light colour that failed to resolve doubt and ultimately led to contradictory course-change statements (starboard then port).

constraints: Applies only when vessels are in sight of one another.
Doubt signal must be given immediately upon failure to understand the other vessel's intentions or actions, not after prolonged VHF negotiation.
warnings: Relying on VHF to negotiate right-of-way/overtaking status instead of sound/light signals can cause dangerous confusion.

Vessel A's contradictory statements (first 'alter to starboard, pass red to red' then 'altering to port, pass green to green') created ambiguity about actual intended maneuver, increasing collision risk.
outcomes: Prolonged VHF dispute over bearing and overtaking status delayed clear, unambiguous collision-avoidance action.
Contradictory verbal course-change statements from vessel A created confusion for vessel B about the actual maneuver being executed, resulting in a near-miss situation.
key_facts: COLREG Rule 34(d) mandates at least five short and rapid whistle blasts (optionally with light flashes) when a vessel is in doubt about another's intentions or actions near collision risk.
The incident occurred in the Irish Sea in NW 5/6 winds with good visibility, afternoon, involving vessel A overtaking at ~20kts on vessel B's starboard quarter.
Vessel A and B disputed via VHF (channels 16 then 6) whether A was more than two points abaft B's beam, which determines overtaking status under COLREGs.
Vessel A first proposed altering course to starboard to pass red-to-red, then reversed and stated it was altering to port to pass green-to-green, creating contradictory instructions.

question_seeds.text: At what point should I sound the five short rapid blasts instead of continuing to negotiate intentions over VHF?
Why is relying on VHF conversation to determine overtaking status and relative bearing considered unsafe practice in this report?
How should I resolve a dispute over whether my vessel is 'more than two points abaft the beam' of another vessel to determine overtaking responsibility?
What should I do if the other vessel's stated maneuver (e.g., pass red-to-red) is then contradicted by a different stated maneuver (pass green-to-green)?

trace.situation: A reporting vessel in hand steering altered course to avoid a fishing vessel while simultaneously being overtaken by another vessel that closed to a dangerously small CPA, prompting VHF contact and eventual independent avoiding action when the overtaking vessel failed to alter course as promised.
trace.trigger: The overtaking vessel's distance off continued to decrease to an unacceptable CPA (2 cables) despite verbal VHF agreement to alter course to port.

procedures.action: Alter course to starboard to avoid the fishing vessel while monitoring the overtaking vessel's position.
procedures.why: To prevent embarrassment/collision risk from the fishing vessel's own alteration while remaining aware of the overtaking traffic.

procedures.action: Make a visual check on the overtaking vessel before executing a large course alteration.
procedures.why: To ensure the alteration to starboard would not impede the overtaking vessel's progress.

procedures.action: Contact the overtaking vessel by VHF (channel 16 then 77) to clarify roles and request course alteration.
procedures.why: The overtaking vessel was identified as the give-way vessel and needed to be alerted that its distance/course was unsatisfactory.

procedures.action: Restate the give-way obligation and the calculated CPA/time to the overtaking vessel, demanding immediate action rather than a delayed alteration.
procedures.why: An 8-minute delay to a promised 12:45 alteration would still result in an unacceptable 2-cable CPA.

procedures.action: When the overtaking vessel maintained course and speed despite verbal assurances, alter own course substantially to starboard to avoid collision.
procedures.why: VHF agreement was not followed by action, so independent avoiding action was required to prevent a close-quarters situation from developing into collision.

constraints: The overtaking vessel is the give-way vessel in all aspects and is obligated to keep clear.
VHF communication does not replace the requirement to take positive, timely avoiding action.

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board review of a near-miss overtaking incident between two vessels (Vessel A and the reporting/overtaking vessel) in the westbound lane of the Terschelling-German Bight Traffic Separation Scheme, where the overtaking vessel altered course to port shortly after passing Vessel A at close range.

constraints: Vessel A was the overtaken and reporting vessel; the other vessel was the overtaking vessel under investigation.

warnings: AIS destination/ETA/draught fields may be blank or unreliable and should not be the sole basis for predicting another vessel's intentions.

outcomes: Closest point of approach was 0.4Nm on almost parallel courses despite the overtaking vessel believing it was 1.3Nm clear when it altered course.

trace.situation: A 10m motor sailer suddenly filled with thick acrid smoke while motoring in calm weather, caused by a shorted diesel cut-off solenoid in the blown-air heater locker whose vaporised packing smoke was drawn into the heater's air intake and dispersed throughout the boat, triggering all three domestic smoke alarms simultaneously.

procedures.action: Identify alternative smoke dispersal path (e.g. heater air intake) when whole-vessel smoke spreads too fast for a single localized fire.

procedures.action: Open the suspect heater locker cautiously with a fire extinguisher ready.
procedures.why: To check for flames or further smoke while being prepared to fight a fire if present.

procedures.action: Determine root cause (shorted diesel cut-off solenoid) once immediate danger is ruled out.
procedures.why: To confirm source and assess whether repair or ongoing risk exists.

constraints: Each of the three smoke alarms (one per cabin) can be individually closed off, but all sounded simultaneously in this incident.

warnings: Loud simultaneous smoke alarm sounding can make it impossible to think clearly or communicate.

A forced-air heater intake can rapidly disperse smoke from a locker fault throughout an entire vessel, mimicking a more serious fire.
outcomes: No fire or flames were found; the smoke originated solely from a vaporised solenoid packing.

procedures.why: Failure to appreciate Vessel B's proximity to the buoys led to Vessel A passing only 2 cables from both Vessel B and the buoy.

procedures.action: Give fixed marks (buoys) a greater distance when passing to leave sufficient sea room for other traffic.
procedures.why: VTS advised Vessel B that it exercised poor seamanship by not passing the buoy at a greater distance to give Vessel A more room.

constraints: Decisions on passing arrangements made over VHF should be confirmed with radar plotting of the other vessel's position and closing distance.

warnings: Agreeing on passing intentions via VHF without radar confirmation can lead to unappreciated close-quarters situations.

outcomes: Vessel A passed only about 2 cables from Vessel B and the buoy, classified as a near-miss.
VTS reprimanded Vessel B for poor seamanship in not giving Vessel A more room.
The reporter acknowledged the situation as a near-miss, highlighting the need for better radar monitoring.

Vessel A intended to alter to starboard once clear of buoys.
Vessel A did not have Vessel B plotted on radar at the time of the VHF exchange.
Vessel B passed about 1/2 mile from the buoy, closer than expected.
Final separation was about 2 cables between Vessel A, Vessel B, and the buoy.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a reported marine accident caused by inadequate work planning and risk assessment during machinery maintenance on a pressurised system, referencing the UK Code of Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seaman (COSWP) sections 1.3 and 22.4.

procedures.action: Conduct a careful risk assessment before beginning the work activity, examining what in the nature of the operation could cause harm.
procedures.why: COSWP 1.3.1 states the aim is to minimise accidents and ill health onboard by deciding whether enough precautions have been taken.

procedures.action: Identify hazards present at the place of work and the significant risks arising from the work activity, including existing precautions such as permits to work, restricted access, warning signs, or PPE.
procedures.why: COSWP 1.3.2 requires this structured hazard/risk identification to determine adequacy of controls.

procedures.action: Implement a permit-to-work system with appropriate double-checking before maintenance begins.
procedures.why: Its absence in the reported accident is cited as a major contributing factor increasing the risk of accident.

procedures.action: Before removing valves or filter covers or performing similar operations on pressurised systems, isolate that part of the system by closing the appropriate valves and open drain cocks to confirm pressure is off.
procedures.why: COSWP 22.4.2 specifies this isolation procedure to prevent exposure to residual pressure.

procedures.action: When breaking joints of pipes or fittings, do not fully remove fastenings until the joint has been broken and it is confirmed that no pressure remains within.
procedures.why: COSWP 22.4.3 prevents sudden release of trapped pressure causing injury.

constraints: A risk assessment should precede hazardous maintenance operations.
A permit-to-work system with double-checking should be used for such work.

warnings: Without risk assessment and permit-to-work systems, the risk of accident is much higher.

outcomes: Failure to perform risk assessment and use permit-to-work procedures contributed to the reported accident.
Applying the general guidance in COSWP 22.4 on machinery maintenance isolation may have prevented the accident even without a formal risk assessment.

procedures.action: Include anticipated fouling hazards and a response plan for fouling in passage planning.
procedures.why: CHIRP notes it is important to know how such fouling will be dealt with as part of required passage planning.

procedures.action: If fouled and disabled with no means of propulsion, call for lifeboat/rescue assistance promptly.
procedures.why: The vessel was fully disabled with no wind to sail and could not clear the net themselves, necessitating external rescue.

procedures.action: Report sightings of unmarked or inadequately marked fishing gear to CHIRP or relevant authority.
procedures.why: Reports provide evidence of a worsening safety-of-navigation problem and help prompt remedial action from the fishing community.

constraints: Incident occurred in a 100m-wide navigation channel at low water slack tide with a pot buoy and 4 metres of floating rope across the channel.
Net fouling occurred despite excellent visibility and careful watch for lobster pot buoys, as the net was floating just below the surface and not visible.
No wind was available, removing the option to sail clear once propulsion was lost.
warnings: Inadequately marked or lost fishing gear poses a high risk of fouling vessels, even those keeping careful watch.
Submerged net/debris may not be visible even in excellent visibility conditions.
Vessels without wind for sailing and with fouled propellers may become completely disabled and require rescue.
outcomes: The reporting vessel was disabled, called out the lifeboat, lost three days but suffered no damage to prop or engine after drying out alongside and untangling the net manually.
A motor cruiser involved in a separate, concurrent rescue (the lifeboat's second that week) sustained severe damage with an enormous repair bill.
The lifeboat station reported this was their third net-related rescue that week, indicating the issue is widespread and recurring.
key_facts: A lobster pot buoy with 4 metres of floating rope was found mid-channel in a 100m-wide navigation channel at low water slack tide.
Dungeness to Beachy Head, particularly off Hastings, is known for very high densities of fishing pots on well-trodden navigation routes.
A vessel fouled a large piece of stray green trawler net (bottom end of a beam trawl) around its propeller while motoring in excellent visibility with no wind.
The local lifeboat reported this was their third rescue that week caused by discarded trawler net.
CHIRP states that some part of the fishing community continues to place or lose gear with inadequate marking and little regard for navigation safety or gear cost.

trace.situation: CHIRP review of a near-miss overtaking incident in the Southwest Safety Fairway, a high traffic density area, between two time-chartered vessels ("B" and "C") managed by separate companies.
trace.trigger: A vessel being overtaken in a high traffic density fairway identifies a risk of close-quarters situation with the overtaking vessel not keeping clear.

procedures.action: Raise the overtaking vessel by VHF early to state destination and intended course alteration.
procedures.why: Vessel B informed Vessel C of her destination and upcoming course change to ensure mutual awareness and avoid confusion.

procedures.action: Programme AIS to display destination.
procedures.why: Provides additional situational information to other vessels in the area.

procedures.action: Repeat/remind the overtaking vessel of the intended manoeuvre if no action is observed.
procedures.why: Vessel B reminded Vessel C at 1225 LT that she would be altering course shortly, since Vessel C had not yet responded with action.

procedures.action: Continuously assess the situation before executing the planned course alteration.
procedures.why: Vessel B assessed the situation again at 1445 LT before actually altering course to port.

procedures.action: Overtaking vessel must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken until finally past and clear, and should overtake from the starboard side per general seamanship practice.
procedures.why: This is the duty of the overtaking vessel under the applicable collision regulations and seamanship norms, which Vessel C failed to follow by overtaking on the port side and not keeping clear promptly.

constraints: Vessels were navigating in a high traffic density safety fairway.
The overtaking vessel is responsible for keeping clear until finally past and clear.
General seamanship practice recommends overtaking from the starboard side.
warnings: Failure of the overtaking vessel to correctly assess the situation and take early action can create a close-quarters/near-miss situation.
Overtaking on the port side instead of the conventional starboard side increases risk in a high traffic fairway.
outcomes: Vessel C eventually altered course to port and made a full turn to keep clear, avoiding collision.
The near-miss could have been avoided if Vessel C had assessed the situation correctly and acted earlier.
Vessel C's own report confirmed CHIRP's account was correct, acknowledging the issue.
key_facts: Vessel B was on a southwesterly course at about 14 knots in the Southwest Safety Fairway, a high traffic density area.
Vessel C was overtaking Vessel B on the port side, contrary to general seamanship practice of overtaking from starboard.
Vessel B communicated her destination and intended course change to Vessel C at 1205 LT and again at 1225 LT, both acknowledged by Vessel C.
At 1445 LT, with Vessel C about 1.3 miles on the port quarter, Vessel B altered course to port after reassessing the situation.
Vessel C only took a full turn to keep clear after Vessel B's course alteration, rather than acting earlier as the overtaking vessel's duty required.

question_seeds.text: Why is the overtaking vessel responsible for keeping clear until finally past and clear, and how does that affect my decision-making when being overtaken?

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime report describing a near-collision incident among several vessels (A, B, C, D) where Vessel 'B' repeatedly disregarded navigation rules and good seamanship, cutting across the bows of other ships and forcing emergency avoidance maneuvers.
trace.trigger: Vessel 'B' cuts across the bows of Vessel 'C' without warning, then sets a collision course with Vessel 'D', apparently steering by a plotted radar track rather than responding to traffic.

procedures.action: Give way or take early, substantial action when risk of collision exists, as required by the rules of the road.
procedures.why: Vessel 'B' gave no warning and no early action, forcing 'C' to make a full 360-degree emergency turn to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Respond promptly to VHF calls or signals from other vessels regarding collision risk.
procedures.why: Vessel 'D' had to call 'B' and still had to hold course for three miles before 'B' altered, despite open water with no other traffic.

procedures.action: Use radar/ECDIS plotted tracks as a planning aid, not as a rigid instruction to be followed blindly regardless of actual traffic.
procedures.why: The navigating officer on 'B' appeared to have been instructed to blindly follow the red line on the radar without deviation, disregarding COLREGS and situational awareness.

procedures.action: Maintain proper lookout and situational awareness independent of plotted navigation lines.
procedures.why: Blind adherence to a planned track without regard to nearby vessels created repeated near-collision situations.

constraints: Officers must apply traffic/collision-avoidance rules regardless of a pre-plotted course line.
Early and unambiguous action is required when risk of collision exists, even in open water with no other traffic to justify delay.
warnings: Blindly following a plotted radar line without deviation is dangerous and can lead to collision.
Failure to give timely warning or take avoiding action constitutes appalling seamanship and creates an accident waiting to happen.
outcomes: Vessel 'C' avoided collision only by executing a full 360-degree emergency turn.
Vessel 'D' was forced to hold course for three miles before 'B' finally altered to port, despite open water.
Vessel 'B' was eventually persuaded to alter course toward her destination, avoiding a second near-collision.
key_facts: Vessel 'B' cut across the bows of Vessel 'C', causing 'C' to execute a 360-degree avoidance turn with no warning given.
Vessel 'B' then set a collision course with Vessel 'D' in open water with no other traffic present.
Vessel 'D' had to call 'B' via VHF and maintain course for three miles before 'B' altered to port.
The report attributes 'B's' behavior to the navigating officer blindly following a plotted radar line without deviation, showing no understanding of traffic rules or seamanship.

question_seeds.text: Why did Vessel 'B' fail to give way or warn 'C' before cutting across her bows?
How should a navigating officer balance following a plotted radar/ECDIS track with real-time collision avoidance obligations?
What immediate actions should Vessel 'D' have taken sooner when 'B' remained on a collision course?
Who is responsible for training or instructing officers who appear to navigate purely by a plotted line without situational awareness?

trace.situation: An officer of the watch recounts a close-quarters near-miss where another vessel (Vessel B) suddenly altered course to port and cut across the bow in open water, followed by a CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board commentary urging proper investigation of such incidents.
trace.trigger: Vessel B suddenly and without notice altered course to port, crossing the reporting vessel's bow and creating risk of collision.

procedures.action: Assess the situation under COLREG Rule 8 and determine the only viable avoidance action.
procedures.why: Rule 8 'Action to avoid collision' requires action to be taken in ample time and in accordance with good seamanship when risk of collision exists.

procedures.action: Put the rudder hard to port immediately to open distance from the other vessel.
procedures.why: Short distance and unknown course/intentions of Vessel B left only one possibility to avoid close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Inform the Master immediately and have him present on the bridge during the manoeuvre.
procedures.why: Ensures command oversight and supports proper decision-making during an emerging collision risk.

procedures.action: Record and report the incident, including closest point of approach and circumstances, for investigation.
procedures.why: Enables analysis of why Vessel B altered course and supports industry learning as recommended by CHIRP.

constraints: Action must comply with COLREG Rule 8 and good seamanship practice.
Master must be informed and present on the bridge during collision-avoidance manoeuvres.
Reported closest distance between vessels was approximately 0.2-0.3 miles.
warnings: Sudden, unexplained course alterations by other vessels in open, clear water can still create serious close-quarters/collision risk.
Conflicting accounts from vessel operators undermine confidence that safety risks have been properly identified or mitigated.
Charterers may use such incidents in commercial dealings and brand-risk assessments with owners, independent of the safety investigation.
outcomes: Collision was avoided but closest point of approach was only 0.2-0.3 miles.
The Charterer used the incident in presentations to vessel Owners and shared it internally, citing brand protection concerns.
The Maritime Advisory Board found the owner/operator accounts conflicting and inadequate for reassurance on safety/brand risk mitigation.
CHIRP recommends such incidents be investigated as if they were accidents to maximize learning benefit.

Vessel B altered course to port suddenly and without notice in open water with clear way, with no apparent navigational reason.

The Master was informed and present on the bridge throughout the manoeuvre.
The Charterer intends to use the case as an example in discussions with vessel Owners regarding brand and safety risk.

trace.situation: A near-miss occurred during a vessel refit when a shipyard contractor was found hot working near the steering compartment while the aft mooring hydraulic system was in operation, creating a potential fire/explosion risk from a possible hydraulic fluid leak.
trace.trigger: Hot work was being conducted in the vicinity of operating hydraulic machinery despite the conflict having been raised at the daily work planning meeting, due to the contractor foreman misunderstanding the instruction.

procedures.action: Immediately suspend the hot work upon discovery of the conflict.
procedures.why: To remove the ignition source before a hydraulic leak could cause fire or explosion.

procedures.action: Report the near miss to the yard safety officer and master without delay.
procedures.why: To ensure prompt awareness and escalation of the safety conflict.

procedures.action: Convene a meeting shortly after the incident with all involved parties.
procedures.why: To determine what went wrong and identify immediate corrective actions.

procedures.action: Hold a mass toolbox briefing the next day with all contractors on the vessel.
procedures.why: To communicate initial findings and prevent recurrence across the whole workforce.

procedures.action: Amend the Safety Management Plan or HSE contractual terms so hydraulic actuation/flammable fluid transfer is included in the yard's permit to work system.
procedures.why: The existing permit system allowed hot work permits to be merely suspended (not cancelled/removed) during hydraulic activation, creating a gap in control.

procedures.action: Review the venue and format of daily work planning meetings (location, noise, seating, attendee list, disturbance policy).
procedures.why: The meeting venue was congested, preventing the contractor foreman from clearly hearing instructions.

procedures.action: Ensure key messages from daily planning meetings are passed to yard workers and sub-contractors via daily toolbox talks.
procedures.why: Communication from the meeting to sub-contractor foremen and workers was poor, causing a lack of understanding.

constraints: Yard's permit to work system allows hot work permits to be suspended but not cancelled/removed from site during hydraulic system activation.
Permits are not returned to the yard HSE Officer when suspended.
Daily work planning meeting outcomes must be effectively relayed down to foremen and workers to be effective.
warnings: Hot work near hydraulic systems in operation risks fire and/or explosion if a hydraulic leak occurs.
Suspended (not cancelled) hot work permits remain a latent hazard if hydraulic systems are reactivated.
Poor communication from planning meetings to frontline workers is identified as the significant root cause of this near miss.
outcomes: No injury or incident occurred because the ship's safety officer intervened and suspended the hot work in time.
Shipyard completed over 400,000 man hours during the refit without injury following the corrective actions.
Lessons learned led to recommendations for permit system, meeting venue, and communication improvements.
key_facts: Hot work was discovered in the steering compartment vicinity while the aft mooring hydraulic system was operating.
The conflicting work had been discussed at the daily planning meeting but was misunderstood by the contractor foreman due to meeting congestion.
The yard's permit to work system does not require cancellation/removal of hot work permits during hydraulic activation, only suspension.
Root cause was identified as inadequate communication, whether verbal or via posted hot work permits.
Daily toolbox talks were identified as the best method to ensure key safety messages reach workers and sub-contractors.

question_seeds.text: Why was the hot work permit not required to be physically removed when hydraulic systems were activated?
How should the daily work planning meeting be restructured to prevent foremen from misunderstanding safety-critical instructions?

Who is responsible for ensuring hot work permits are properly suspended or cancelled during hydraulic system activation?

trace.situation: A CHIRP near-miss investigation finding addresses hazards arising when multiple parties work on a vessel's hydraulic/other systems during shipyard repairs without full awareness of each other's activities.
trace.trigger: Discovery that workers or trades involved in a shipyard repair were not fully aware of other ongoing work or systems still in operation, leading to a near-miss.

procedures.action: Ensure all parties involved in vessel repair work are made fully aware of the work of others and which systems remain in operation.
procedures.why: Lack of awareness between trades/systems still live was identified as a root cause of the near-miss.

procedures.action: Thoroughly vet the efficiency of the shipyard's permit to work system.
procedures.why: The permit to work system is the control mechanism meant to prevent conflicting or unsafe concurrent operations.

procedures.action: Incorporate permit to work system vetting into existing HSE inspections used to maintain shipyards on the approved list.
procedures.why: Leverages an existing inspection process to enforce compliance rather than creating a new one.

procedures.action: Put measures in place to ensure recommendations arising from inspections are actually implemented.
procedures.why: Recommendations without enforcement mechanisms risk being ignored, perpetuating the hazard.

constraints: Shipyards must remain on an approved list, implying inspection compliance is a precondition for continued use
Permit to work system effectiveness must be verifiable, not assumed
warnings: Failure to coordinate awareness of live systems and concurrent work during repairs can lead to near-miss or accident conditions

outcomes: Improved coordination and awareness could prevent recurrence of similar near-misses

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board comments on a submitted incident report involving a collision, commending the merchant ship's crew for standing by to render assistance afterward and praising the reporting company for widely sharing the safety information.

procedures.action: After a collision, stand by the scene ready to render assistance.
procedures.why: This action is reportedly often not taken by vessels involved in collisions, and CHIRP explicitly commends it as good practice.

procedures.action: Share incident report information as widely as possible within the company and industry.
procedures.why: Wider dissemination of lessons learned helps prevent recurrence, which CHIRP is committed to supporting.

warnings: Standing by after a collision to render assistance is reportedly often not done, implying a common failure in industry practice.
outcomes: CHIRP commends the report as high standard and publicizes it to support wider industry learning.
key_facts: The report concerned a collision involving a merchant ship.
The merchant ship stood by after the collision to render assistance, which CHIRP notes is often not done in similar incidents.
The reporting company committed to sharing the incident information as widely as possible.

trace.situation: An operator investigation into a bridge watchkeeping incident in which an OOW misidentified a fishing vessel's lights and mishandled radar settings, following removal of the OOW from watchkeeping duties.
trace.trigger: An OOW failed to correctly identify a fishing vessel's navigation lights against radar, prompting an operator-led investigation using SVDR data and crew interviews.

procedures.action: Remove the OOW from watchkeeping duties and repatriate at the next opportunity following the incident.
procedures.why: Standard response to a watchkeeping failure pending investigation.

procedures.action: Board the vessel at the earliest opportunity, take statements, and secure evidence including SVDR data.
procedures.why: Preserve evidence for accurate reconstruction of events before it is lost or overwritten.

procedures.action: Interview the OOW at the operator's office and review the investigation report alongside VDR data.
procedures.why: Corroborate the OOW's account against objective recorded data to reach sound conclusions.

procedures.action: Positively identify observed targets and lights and compare them against radar targets before acting.
procedures.why: To avoid making assumptions on the basis of scanty information, which caused the misidentification.

procedures.action: Use all available means (sight, hearing, visual bearings, AIS, radar including auto-acquisition/guard rings) to detect and identify navigational hazards.
procedures.why: Relying on a single sensor (3cm radar only) failed to detect the fishing vessel target.

procedures.action: Advise the lookout whenever course alterations are made, especially small autopilot increments.
procedures.why: Small course changes via autopilot are not readily apparent to other vessels or to the lookout, increasing collision risk if unannounced.

constraints: 3cm (X band) radar is optimized for definition at shorter ranges; 10cm (S band) radar is optimized for detection at longer ranges.
Radars should be set to appropriate, complementary ranges rather than inconsistent/incorrect ranges.
Any alteration of course should be communicated to the lookout.
warnings: Do not rely on a single radar band or unverified visual identification of lights to confirm vessel identity/type.
Small autopilot course alterations may go unnoticed by other vessels and by onboard lookouts if not communicated.
outcomes: The fishing vessel's lights were misidentified and its radar target was not detected, due to radar tuning and incorrect range settings.
The investigation concluded the incident resulted from an error in judgment by the OOW, not a reckless violation of procedure or negligence.
The OOW was removed from watchkeeping duties and repatriated as a consequence.
key_facts: The 3cm radar was set to 12nm while the 10cm radar was set to 6nm, an incorrect configuration for optimal detection and definition.
A visual lookout was maintained and lights were observed, but the fishing vessel's lights were incorrectly identified.
Observed lights were not positively verified against a radar target before the OOW acted.
Course alterations were made via autopilot in small increments, not readily apparent to the fishing vessel or lookout.
The OOW did not inform the lookout of the course alteration.

question_seeds.text: Why did the 3cm radar fail to detect the fishing vessel target despite a visual sighting of lights?

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Feedback report on a bridge watchkeeping near-miss involving an OOW and lookout, detailing recommended bridge practices and the corrective/preventative actions taken by the operator following the incident.
trace.trigger: A near-miss incident involving inadequate OOW/lookout communication and radar use, prompting a formal company review and corrective action.

procedures.action: Regularly adjust radar range scale and tuning (gain, sea clutter, rain clutter) throughout the watch.
procedures.why: To increase the probability of detecting weak radar targets.

procedures.action: Establish strong OOW-lookout communication, including discussion of traffic/navigational situation and positive confirmation of reports.
procedures.why: To ensure information is understood and acted upon, reducing risk of missed contacts.

procedures.action: Encourage the lookout to use navigational aids such as radar.
procedures.why: To increase the lookout's situational awareness beyond visual observation alone.

procedures.action: Issue the OOW a written formal warning.
procedures.why: To formally record and address the performance failure identified in the incident.

procedures.action: Target the OOW for additional Bridge Team Management (CRM) training before next appointment.
procedures.why: To correct identified deficiencies in bridge resource management skills.

procedures.action: Require the OOW to undertake a management course to improve leadership and integrated team working.
procedures.why: To address leadership and teamworking shortfalls contributing to the incident.

procedures.action: Promulgate incident details fleet-wide, highlighting mistakes and best practices.
procedures.why: To share lessons learned and prevent recurrence across the fleet.

procedures.action: Raise identified best-practice failures with institutions conducting company CRM courses.
procedures.why: To ensure training providers address real-world gaps revealed by the incident.

procedures.action: Forward incident details to CHIRP and the Nautical Institute's MARS scheme.
procedures.why: To promulgate learning throughout the wider maritime industry.

constraints: Radar settings must be actively and regularly adjusted, not left static.
Lookout reports must be positively confirmed by the OOW, not assumed received.
warnings: Failure to regularly adjust radar tuning reduces probability of detecting weak targets.
Poor OOW-lookout communication and lack of positive reporting confirmation increases collision/near-miss risk.
outcomes: OOW received a formal written warning and was required to undertake further CRM and management training.
Incident details were shared fleet-wide and with CHIRP/MARS to spread industry-wide learning.
Best-practice failures prompted review of CRM training institutions used by the company.
key_facts: The incident stemmed from inadequate radar use, poor OOW-lookout communication, and underuse of navigational aids by the lookout.
Corrective actions included a formal warning, mandatory CRM training, and a leadership/management course for the OOW.
The company promulgated the incident internally and externally via CHIRP and the Nautical Institute's MARS scheme.

trace.situation: A loaded merchant vessel on a clear, calm night collided with a small wooden fishing vessel after the OOW failed to correctly interpret two lookout reports of a red light and radar discrepancies between its 3cm and 10cm units.
trace.trigger: Lookout reported a red light fine to port at 04:41 and again at 04:56, which the OOW assumed was a distant target (>9nm) and did not independently verify.

procedures.action: Reduce to manoeuvring revolutions and turn the vessel around after the collision
procedures.why: To return to the scene and render assistance to the damaged fishing vessel.

procedures.action: Inform the Master immediately after the collision is detected
procedures.why: Command decision-making and overall response coordination require Master's involvement.

procedures.action: Prepare the rescue boat and lifesaving appliances
procedures.why: To be ready to assist the fishing vessel's crew if needed.

procedures.action: Inform the nearest coast radio station and coastguard
procedures.why: Regulatory notification and to enable coordinated search and rescue/assistance.

procedures.action: Attempt radio contact with the fishing vessel
procedures.why: To assess her condition and crew welfare directly.

procedures.action: Call the Operator's 24hr duty phone and advise of the situation
procedures.why: To keep the company informed and enable shoreside support.

procedures.action: Assess own vessel's damage
procedures.why: To confirm seaworthiness and ability to continue operations or assist.

procedures.action: Stand by until a coastguard vessel rendezvoused with the fishing vessel
procedures.why: To ensure the fishing vessel was safely escorted before departing the scene.

procedures.action: Continue voyage only upon instruction from local authorities
procedures.why: To ensure proper release and compliance with coastguard/authority direction before resuming passage.

constraints: Visual sightings reported by the lookout must be verified using all available means, not dismissed on assumption alone.
OOW must cross-check radar returns between available radar units when a target is suspected but not confirmed on one set.
Vessel must stand by and assist a vessel involved in collision until relieved by competent authority.
warnings: Reliance on a single radar band (3cm) can result in missed small/wooden vessel targets that are visible on another band (10cm).
Assuming a reported light sighting is 'further away' without verification can lead directly to collision.
Small wooden fishing vessels may present poor or inconsistent radar returns depending on radar band used.
outcomes: Fishing vessel sustained extensive damage above the waterline but made port safely under her own power.
Fishing vessel's crew suffered minor injuries; merchant vessel sustained only minor scuffing damage.
No fatalities occurred; post-collision response (stopping, assisting, notifying authorities) was executed correctly.
Voyage was resumed only after coastguard escort and authorization from local authorities.

trace.situation: A single-handed yacht skipper using a radar target enhancer (ARTE) and self-steering gear was nearly run down at night in the Channel by a large (approx. 90,000 ton) vessel that approached close before sounding a warning horn blast.
trace.trigger: A very loud horn blast from an approaching large vessel very close astern/alongside while the yacht was under self-steering and the skipper was below.

procedures.action: React immediately to the horn blast by going to the cockpit and visually assessing the situation around the genoa.
procedures.why: The genoa was blocking the view of the approaching vessel, so a quick visual check was needed to understand the threat.

procedures.action: Reject tacking as an option.
procedures.why: Tacking would take too long with the self-steering engaged and would turn the yacht to port, sailing along with the oncoming threat instead of away from it.

procedures.action: Disengage the self-steering by turning the Hydrovane through 90 degrees rather than unclamping the tiller first.
procedures.why: Any helm action taken before disengaging self-steering would be immediately counteracted by the gear, so the vane had to be turned to initiate a bear-away using its own rudder.

procedures.action: Allow the Hydrovane's auxiliary rudder to initiate a turn to starboard.
procedures.why: This provided an immediate, effective course change away from the approaching vessel's path.

procedures.action: Return to the tiller, free it, and use the main rudder to complete the turn.
procedures.why: To finish the avoidance maneuver with full manual control once the vane had started the bear-away.

procedures.action: After the close pass, resolve to look around the genoa more frequently (at least three times) as an ongoing watchkeeping practice.
procedures.why: The genoa had obstructed the skipper's view of the approaching large vessel, contributing to the late detection.

constraints: Self-steering gear response must be accounted for before taking manual helm action, as it will counteract uncoordinated inputs
A continuous and frequent visual lookout must be maintained even when sail trim (e.g., genoa) could obstruct the view

trace.situation: A highly experienced single-handed yachtsman describes his lookout, lighting, and radar-visibility arrangements during an offshore passage toward Ushant, shortly before a near-collision occurred.
trace.trigger: Sailing single-handed overnight on a long passage where the skipper must periodically sleep and cannot maintain continuous visual watch.

procedures.action: Limit sleep breaks to about 20 minutes, often waking earlier.
procedures.why: To maintain a near-continuous lookout despite sailing alone.

procedures.action: Fit two additional forward-facing windows in the coach roof.
procedures.why: To allow a lookout to be kept from inside the cabin without going on deck.

procedures.action: Install an active radar target enhancer on a separate stern-mounted spar, 3m above water.
procedures.why: To present other vessels' radar with a return similar to a super tanker, improving detectability over a passive reflector.

procedures.action: Cover the top section of the mast with fluorescent orange vinyl.
procedures.why: To aid daytime visual detection by other vessels.

procedures.action: Keep genoa and main part-reefed even after wind dropped.
procedures.why: To raise the foot of the genoa and improve visibility from inside the boat.

procedures.action: Exhibit the masthead tricolour light while under sail at night.
procedures.why: To show the vessel's navigation lights appropriate to a sailing yacht underway.

constraints: Skipper is sailing entirely single-handed with no other crew to share watchkeeping.
Vessel is under self-steering (Hydrovane) with tiller lashed, so no one is actively steering or watching continuously.
Lookout checks are only possible during brief waking intervals between short sleep breaks.
warnings: Relying on technology (radar target enhancer, fluorescent mast marking) does not replace continuous effective lookout.
Single-handed sailing inherently limits the ability to maintain a full-time watch, increasing collision risk.
outcomes: Despite extensive precautions (short sleep breaks, enhanced radar visibility, visual aids), a near-collision occurred, indicating these measures alone did not fully mitigate the risk.
key_facts: The yacht was close reaching on port tack at about 4 knots, heading 220° toward Ushant near 49°52'N 003°24'W.
Only the masthead tricolour light was exhibited at night.
The skipper had over 40 years of sailing experience and a Yachtmaster Offshore certificate.
The radar target enhancer's maker claimed its echo would appear similar to a super tanker on other vessels' radar.
The skipper had just completed a 20-minute sleep break and checked around without seeing anything before the incident.

trace.situation: A near-collision occurred when a single-handed yacht crossing the Casquets Traffic Separation Scheme in the English Channel fell asleep for '20 winks' while transiting the westbound shipping lane, with uncertainty over whether a merchant vessel's radar could detect the yacht's radar enhancer.
trace.trigger: A single-handed vessel must cross or navigate near a busy Traffic Separation Scheme, creating fatigue and lookout risk combined with uncertain radar detectability.

procedures.action: Plan single-handed transits of busy traffic areas with particular caution, considering transit length and timing.
procedures.why: To reduce fatigue-related lookout failures during extended exposure to merchant traffic.

procedures.action: Select a course that avoids known areas of dense traffic or crosses them as quickly as possible, ideally near-perpendicular to the traffic flow.
procedures.why: An oblique course (e.g. 220°T crossing lanes running 075°/255°T) increases time exposed to traffic and causes ambiguity over whether the yacht is crossing or following traffic flow.

procedures.action: Shine a light on the sail at night.
procedures.why: To improve visual conspicuity to other vessels, especially where radar detectability of the yacht is uncertain.

procedures.action: Maintain continuous lookout and do not rely solely on radar enhancers.
procedures.why: Radar enhancers are only effective if the other vessel's OOW is using the radar band (10cm) for which the enhancer is tuned; if the OOW is watching 3cm radar, the yacht may be far harder to detect.

constraints: Rule 5 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS) requires a proper lookout at all times by sight and hearing as well as by all available means.
It is not possible to comply with Rule 5 if the watchkeeper is asleep.
Merchant vessel traffic is concentrated along TSS course lines well before and after the scheme itself, extending the zone of risk beyond the charted TSS boundaries.
warnings: Sleeping while on watch is a direct violation of the lookout requirement under Rule 5.
A radar enhancer may be ineffective if the observing vessel's radar is operating on a different frequency band (e.g. 3cm vs 10cm) than the enhancer is designed for.
Crossing a TSS obliquely rather than perpendicularly increases time of exposure to traffic and causes ambiguity about the vessel's intended track relative to traffic flow.
outcomes: The incident nearly became a tragedy but a collision was narrowly avoided.
The merchant vessel involved could not be identified or traced by CHIRP.
The Board highlighted systemic risks for single-handed sailors crossing busy TSS areas without adequate watchkeeping.
key_facts: The incident occurred near the Casquets TSS in the English Channel, one of the busiest commercial waterways in the world.
Eastbound traffic generally follows ~075°(T) and westbound ~255°(T); the yacht's 220°(T) track crossed these lines obliquely.
The skipper took '20 winks' (fell asleep) while crossing the westbound shipping lane.
The yacht's radar enhancer would only be effective if the merchant vessel's OOW was using 10cm radar; it would be ineffective against 3cm radar.
CHIRP was unable to identify or trace the merchant vessel involved.

trace.situation: A CHIRP commentary warns leisure sailors about the limitations of radar enhancers and the reduced visibility of required navigation lights on small craft, emphasizing that collision avoidance is a joint responsibility between large and small vessels.
trace.trigger: A small vessel (under 12m LOA) sailing close-hauled and heeled over 5 degrees in proximity to larger, faster vessels where mutual detection and collision avoidance are required.

procedures.action: Do not rely on radar enhancers (reflectors/transponders) as a substitute for proper lookout.
procedures.why: Manufacturer's own handbook states the equipment does not remove the operator's COLREGs responsibility to keep a good lookout and take avoiding action.

procedures.action: Maintain a continuous, vigilant visual and radar lookout, especially at night or in conditions with reduced light visibility.
procedures.why: Side lights on boats under 12m LOA may be visible only to 0.5nm when heeled over 5 degrees, leaving minimal reaction time.

procedures.action: Be prepared to take independent action (including sound signals) to avoid collision rather than assuming the larger vessel will detect and avoid you.
procedures.why: There is a joint obligation under COLREGs for both vessels to avoid collision; the onus is not solely on the larger vessel.

constraints: Boats under 12m LOA are only required to carry side lights visible to 1nm, reduced to 0.5nm when heeled over 5 degrees while close-hauled.
A ship making 20 knots will cover 0.5nm in approximately 90 seconds, leaving little time to react once spotted.
warnings: Radar enhancers do not relieve operators of their responsibility under COLREGs to keep a good lookout and take avoiding action.
Reduced light visibility on small heeled sailing vessels gives dangerously little warning time to approaching fast vessels.
It is a false assumption that only the larger vessel bears responsibility to detect and avoid the smaller one.
outcomes: Reliance on radar enhancers alone or on assumed detection by larger vessels can result in insufficient time to avoid collision.
A small heeled vessel's reduced light range (0.5nm) combined with a fast ship's closing speed can leave only about 90 seconds of reaction time.
key_facts: Radar enhancer handbooks explicitly state they do not remove the user's COLREGs obligation to keep a lookout and avoid collision.
Vessels under 12m LOA need only carry side lights visible to 1nm.
When close-hauled and heeled more than 5 degrees, that visible light range can drop to 0.5nm.
A vessel travelling at 20 knots covers 0.5nm in about 90 seconds.
Collision avoidance is a joint obligation shared by both the larger and smaller vessel, not solely the larger vessel's duty.

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board commentary addresses a near-miss/incident report involving a racing yacht and the application of COLREGs Rule 17 (stand-on vessel action) in a crossing/give-way situation.
trace.trigger: A vessel finds itself in a potential collision situation with a racing boat where give-way/stand-on obligations under the Collision Regulations apply.

procedures.action: Form an early appreciation of and reaction to the overall traffic situation.
procedures.why: Early assessment may permit avoidance of conflicts with racers before close-quarters situations develop.

procedures.action: Comply with the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs) and ordinary seamanship practice at all times, including while racing.
procedures.why: Racing does not relieve boats from their obligation to comply with the Rules or good seamanship.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, keep course and speed under Rule 17(a)(i).
procedures.why: This is the default obligation of the stand-on vessel when another vessel is required to keep out of the way.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, take action by maneuver alone as soon as it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.
procedures.why: Rule 17(a)(ii) permits early independent action once non-compliance by the give-way vessel is evident, to avoid collision.

procedures.action: If so close that collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone, take whatever action best aids collision avoidance.
procedures.why: Rule 17(b) requires the stand-on vessel to act decisively when collision becomes imminent regardless of right-of-way status.

constraints: Racing activity does not exempt vessels from COLREGs compliance or ordinary seamanship.
Being the stand-on vessel does not confer an absolute right of way.
Action under Rule 17(a)(ii) is only triggered once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not complying with the Rules.
regulations: International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGs)
warnings: Being the stand-on vessel does not confer an absolute right of way.
Failure to act in time when the give-way vessel is not complying with the Rules can lead to collision.
outcomes: Early appreciation and reaction may permit avoidance of conflicts with racers.
Appropriate application of Rule 17 by the stand-on vessel can prevent collision even if the give-way vessel fails to act.
key_facts: The Maritime Advisory Board acknowledges racing is taken seriously but stresses it does not override COLREGs obligations.
Rule 17(a)(i) requires the stand-on vessel to keep course and speed.
Rule 17(a)(ii) allows the stand-on vessel to maneuver independently once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not acting appropriately.
Rule 17(b) requires the stand-on vessel to take best possible action when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone.
The original reporter was not criticized for failing to appreciate or consider action in good time.
