trace.situation: A single-handed sailor on a slow sailing yacht, acting as stand-on vessel on starboard tack, encountered two racing yachts on port tack in a developing close-quarters situation, and had to take emergency avoiding action when the second racing yacht failed to give way.
trace.trigger: The give-way (port tack) racing yacht held its course and speed despite the developing close-quarters situation, making collision inevitable without action by the stand-on vessel.

procedures.action: Assess relative speed and point of sail to decide whether to hold course as stand-on vessel.
procedures.why: Reporter's boat lacked the speed and windward ability to usefully maneuver, so holding course and speed was judged the correct stand-on action.

procedures.action: Continue to hold course and speed while monitoring the approaching give-way vessels.
procedures.why: Standard expectation that give-way vessels (racing yachts) would take timely avoiding action, as the first yacht did by bearing away in good time.

procedures.action: Take independent avoiding action once it became clear the give-way vessel would not act and collision was imminent.
procedures.why: Stand-on vessel's duty to hold course ends when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone.

procedures.action: Turn sharply to port rather than starboard given the specific circumstances (short-handed, disabled crew, no time to transfer helm).
procedures.why: A turn to starboard risked putting the boat in irons or hove-to with no control, possibly still in the path of the oncoming yacht; turning to port allowed a controlled pass starboard-to-starboard.

constraints: Stand-on vessel is expected to hold course and speed until it is clear the give-way vessel will not act.
Short-handed/disabled crew limited the available avoiding-action options (could not handle genoa sheets or transfer helm quickly).
Decision to turn had to account for the boat's own handling limitations (risk of being caught in irons).
warnings: Racing yachts may not reliably comply with stand-on/give-way expectations even when a close-quarters situation is obvious.
Single-handed or short-handed vessels with limited maneuverability have few safe options once a give-way vessel fails to act.
Waiting too long to confirm non-compliance by a give-way vessel leaves very limited time/options for the stand-on vessel to act.
outcomes: The reporter's sharp turn to port avoided collision, passing the give-way yacht starboard-to-starboard at less than 20 metres.
No acknowledgement or response came from the give-way yacht's helm or crew.
Had the turn not been made, a collision was certain, likely sinking the smaller yacht with probable injury or loss of life to both people aboard.
key_facts: Reporter was close-hauled on starboard tack at about 3.5 knots, the stand-on vessel in the encounter.
Two apparently identical racing yachts on port tack approached from several hundred metres away, the second yacht travelling over 15 knots.
The first yacht bore away in good time to pass close astern; the second yacht held its course with no avoiding action.
The reporter's only other crew member was disabled and could not assist with sail handling, preventing a normal tack.
The reporter turned more than 90° to port as a last-resort avoiding action, passing starboard-to-starboard less than 20 metres from the give-way yacht.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report combines a close-quarters crossing incident between a ferry and another vessel in a narrow, busy waterway, with a separate account questioning command authority on dynamically positioned (DP) offshore units when the Master/OIM roles are combined or split.
trace.trigger: Close-quarters situation arising from high-speed crossing traffic in a narrow channel, and the question of whether a non-marine Offshore Project Manager should hold OIM authority over a vessel underway or working.

procedures.action: Make vessel intentions clear to less-frequent transiting vessels even if passing distances are routine for regular traffic.
procedures.why: Other vessels may be concerned by proximity that regular ferry bridge teams consider normal.

procedures.action: Prioritize assessing and reacting to the close-quarters situation over attempting VHF contact.
procedures.why: Time spent trying to establish VHF contact (which may not even be transmitting) could be better used for situational assessment and action.

procedures.action: Make a prompt alteration of course or reduction of speed when approaching close quarters.
procedures.why: This may be the best solution and forces the other vessel to reassess its own actions.

procedures.action: Ensure the person holding Master/OIM authority on a DP unit has competence in navigation, anti-collision rules, and the effects of wind, wave and current.
procedures.why: Lack of such understanding nearly caused a unit to run aground between islands due to a cross current.

constraints: SOLAS Chapter V functions for Master and OIM must be fulfilled as necessary.
The unit must display correct lights and shapes: 'restricted in ability to manoeuvre' when working, plus Morse U lights when maintaining station as an Installation.
The unit is considered 'underway' at all times even when not 'making way'.
warnings: Relying on VHF to establish contact in a close-quarters situation can waste critical reaction time, especially if the other vessel is not transmitting.
Handing control of a DP unit to a non-marine person (e.g., an Offshore Project Manager) who lacks navigation and anti-collision knowledge risks grounding or collision.
outcomes: The operator and coastal state investigation found no significant concerns with the crossing incident.
A similar command-authority arrangement elsewhere nearly caused a unit to run aground between islands due to unfamiliarity with wind, wave, current, and navigation rules.
key_facts: The waterway is narrow with relatively high-speed crossing traffic, limiting time to assess and react to close-quarters situations.
Ferry bridge teams may be accustomed to routine passing distances that alarm less-frequent transiting vessels.
Vessel (C) may not have been transmitting on VHF despite attempting contact.
Some DP offshore units are 'Vessels' when in transit and 'Installations' with a Safety Case when working, requiring both Master and OIM functions.
It has been proposed that an Offshore Project Manager (OPM), without marine qualifications, become the OIM in charge of the unit during well operations.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Feedback discusses the legal and safety concerns of splitting command authority aboard offshore support vessels between a ship's Master and a non-marine Offshore Installation Manager (OIM) during well operations.
trace.trigger: A vessel's command structure is split so that the Master must report to or cooperate with a non-marine OIM while working a well, raising conflict over who holds ultimate authority for vessel safety.

procedures.action: Ensure the Master retains unimpaired authority to exercise personal judgement and discretion in emergencies, including rights under SOLAS Chap. XI-2 Reg 8.
procedures.why: Handing over control to a non-marine person would be illegal and could jeopardise vessel safety by preventing the Master from acting appropriately.

procedures.action: Maintain clear, unambiguous lines of responsibility for who holds the con/overall authority on the bridge.
procedures.why: Errors occur where lines of responsibility become unclear, e.g. OOW assuming the Master has the con when he has not formally taken it.

procedures.action: Resolve conflicts between marine and non-marine managers in favour of the Master's safety authority, especially regarding weather-related suspension of operations.
procedures.why: A non-marine manager with no real knowledge of vessels, weather, or DP principles may disagree with a marine assessment that suspension is necessary, risking disaster.

procedures.action: Refer to the Offshore Installations and Pipeline Works (Management and Administration) Regulations 1995 (MAR), regulation 6, to clarify UK legal responsibility.
procedures.why: The MCA and HSE identified this regulation as the key requirement governing responsibility conflicts on offshore installations.

constraints: The duty holder must not operate the installation in a way that prejudices its integrity (Offshore Installations and Wells (Design and Construction, etc.) Regulations 1996, Reg 7(1)).
Overall responsibility for health and welfare of everyone onboard cannot be split between two persons, particularly when one lacks marine/vessel knowledge.
The Master's rights under SOLAS Chap. XI-2 Reg 8 must not be curtailed by an obligation to cooperate with an appointed OIM.
channels: Offshore Installations and Wells (Design and Construction, etc.) Regulations 1996 Sec. 7
Offshore Installations and Pipeline Works (Management and Administration) Regulations 1995 Reg 6
regulations: Offshore Installations and Wells (Design and Construction, etc.) Regulations 1996
Offshore Installations and Pipeline Works (Management and Administration) Regulations 1995
warnings: Handing over control of the vessel to a non-marine person is both illegal and could jeopardise vessel safety.
Splitting overall responsibility between a marine Master and non-marine OIM is 'a recipe for disaster', risking serious safety and environmental pollution problems.
Unclear lines of responsibility (e.g. who has the con) are a recurring source of errors.
outcomes: If the Master cannot exercise independent judgement, emergency response and SOLAS rights may be compromised.
Conflicting assessments (e.g. on weather suspension of operations) between marine and non-marine managers could lead to unsafe decisions if the non-marine manager's view prevails.
MCA/HSE confirmed regulation 6 of the 1995 Management and Administration Regulations as the key legal reference for resolving such responsibility conflicts.
key_facts: The 1996 D&C Regulations Sec. 7(1) require the duty holder to ensure the installation is not operated in a way that prejudices its integrity.
SOLAS Chap. XI-2 Reg 8 gives the Master discretion to take any action deemed appropriate for ship safety and security.

The complainant argues splitting command between Master and OIM contravenes the D&C Regulations and creates serious safety risk.

trace.situation: A laden vessel (C) transiting a Traffic Separation Scheme encountered two ferries (A and B) crossing simultaneously from opposite directions, both initially showing a 0' CPA with own vessel.
trace.trigger: Simultaneous crossing traffic in a TSS producing zero CPA with two vessels at once, one requiring stand-on action and the other requiring give-way action.

procedures.action: Monitor both crossing vessels' CPA/TCPA closely as the situation develops.
procedures.why: Vessel A's initial actions were insufficient to avoid a close-quarters situation, requiring continuous reassessment.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact vessel A via VHF Channel 16, repeating calls and identifying own vessel.
procedures.why: To alert vessel A's OOW that its inadequate action was creating a conflict with vessel B.

procedures.action: Assess the effect of reducing own speed given vessel's loaded condition and proximity of other vessels.
procedures.why: Being fully laden, a speed reduction was judged to have negligible effect given how close the vessels already were.

procedures.action: Engage hand steering as the close-quarters situation developed.
procedures.why: To enable precise, immediate course control once the final avoidance manoeuvre was needed.

procedures.action: Alter course to starboard by 25 degrees once vessel A was observed ahead.
procedures.why: To clear vessel A and simultaneously allow vessel B, which had correctly maintained course and speed, to pass ahead safely.

constraints: Own vessel was fully laden, limiting the effectiveness of speed reduction as an avoidance option.
Vessel A was on own vessel's port bow, making own vessel the stand-on vessel relative to A.
Vessel B was on own vessel's starboard bow, obliging own vessel to keep out of B's way.
VHF contact with vessel A was attempted multiple times but received no response.
warnings: A vessel's unilateral speed increase to avoid one ship can create or worsen a close-quarters situation with another vessel.
Reliance on VHF communication to resolve a developing close-quarters situation cannot be assumed to succeed.
Reducing speed is not always an effective avoidance option, especially when fully laden and in close proximity to other traffic.
outcomes: Vessel A increased speed and passed ahead at approximately one mile, but this left own vessel still on a 0' CPA with vessel B.
Own vessel altered course 25 degrees to starboard using hand steering, allowing vessel B to pass ahead safely.
The close-quarters situation was successfully resolved despite vessel A's non-response and unhelpful manoeuvre.
key_facts: Own vessel (C) was on course 225(T) in a TSS at approximately 16.5 knots.
Two ferries (A and B) were crossing the channel in opposite directions, each initially 5.5 miles away with a CPA of 0'.
Vessel A was on own vessel's port bow (own vessel stand-on); vessel B was on own vessel's starboard bow (own vessel give-way).
Vessel A's speed increase to avoid own vessel removed own vessel's ability to alter course as required to avoid vessel B.
Vessel B maintained course and speed correctly throughout the encounter, as required of a stand-on vessel.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary explains the UK offshore installation regulatory requirement (MAR regulation 6) that an installation must always have a competent person in charge, commonly the OIM, who may also be the master, and clarifies when this duty applies.
trace.trigger: A question arises over who holds overall charge of an offshore installation, especially where the role of OIM/master transfers between individuals as operations change or during periods when the installation is at or being manoeuvred about its working station.

procedures.action: Duty holder ensures the most appropriate competent person is in charge of the installation at any given time.
procedures.why: Failure to do so is an offence and risks ambiguity over authority, endangering installation safety.

procedures.action: Duty holder demonstrates in the installation's Safety Case that its safety management system ensures compliance with the law, including MAR requirements.
procedures.why: HSE must accept the Safety Case before arrangements become binding and enforceable.

procedures.action: Once HSE accepts the Safety Case, follow its arrangements exactly.
procedures.why: Accepted Safety Case arrangements constitute the compliant operational framework.

procedures.action: Where overall charge is transferable, duty holders should address potential conflicts in the Safety Case and/or operational procedures.
procedures.why: Prevents confusion or gaps in command authority during handovers between roles (e.g. master to OIM or vice versa).

procedures.action: Consult operational staff to identify and resolve conflicts over who holds charge.
procedures.why: Operational staff are best placed to recognize practical ambiguities in command transfer.

constraints: An installation must at all times be under the charge of a competent person appointed by the duty holder.

MAR regulation 6 (and related requirements) apply only while the installation is at or being manoeuvred about its working station; in transit only flag state requirements apply.
HSE regulations do not apply to an installation operating in non-UK waters.
Once HSE accepts the Safety Case, its arrangements must be followed.
warnings: Failure to ensure the most appropriate competent person is in charge of the installation is an offence.
Ambiguity about who is in overall charge compromises installation safety.
outcomes: Clear designation of a competent person in charge ensures installation safety and legal compliance.

key_facts: The OIM is commonly the master where the installation has one, but this is not a formal legal requirement.
The duty holder (installation operator/owner) is responsible for ensuring the appropriate competent person holds charge at all times.
MAR regulation 6 applies only when the installation is at or being manoeuvred about its working station, not during transit.
HSE regulations do not apply to installations operating outside UK waters.
A Safety Case, once accepted by HSE, legally binds the duty holder to follow its stated arrangements.

trace.situation: CHIRP review of an incident involving an electric shock to a crew member, inoperable emergency generator due to a holed sea-water pipe, and inadequate work planning/risk assessment aboard a vessel.
trace.trigger: An electrical shock incident occurred where the emergency generator could not be operated and poor wiring/risk assessment practices were identified.

procedures.action: Consult the Ship Captain's Medical Guide if residual symptoms remain after an electric shock.

procedures.why: Ensures appropriate medical follow-up beyond onboard capability.

procedures.action: Conduct a risk assessment before commencing work and issue necessary permits and notices, including power isolation.

procedures.action: Properly maintain and check wiring runs and temporary cables/extension leads.

constraints: Risk assessment must be completed and permits/power isolation issued prior to work commencing.

Wiring and temporary cables must be properly maintained and checked regularly.
regulations: UK Code of Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seamen
warnings: Individuals should not receive an electric shock even when equipment (GS pump) is running if wiring is properly maintained.

outcomes: The report raised serious issues regarding vessel condition, work planning, and risk assessment processes.

trace.situation: During unmooring from a berth in good weather, a riding turn on the forward mooring winch prevented slacking the remaining spring, yet the Master ordered the bow thruster engaged and the vessel began moving off the berth while the spring was still ashore.
trace.trigger: Officer in Charge reported to the Master that a riding turn prevented providing slack for the spring to be slipped, and the Master nonetheless ordered 'Let go the spring' while bow thruster operation and departure from berth proceeded.

procedures.action: Officer in Charge communicates mooring station status changes (singling up) to bridge via VHF as instructed.
procedures.why: Ensures bridge has accurate picture of remaining lines before further unmooring orders.

procedures.action: Officer in Charge reports the riding turn and inability to provide slack on the spring to the Master.
procedures.why: Bridge must be aware of a line still made fast ashore before initiating vessel movement.

procedures.action: Master should confirm status of all lines before ordering thruster/engine movement.
procedures.why: Moving the vessel with a line still attached ashore risks parting the line, injury to linesmen, or damage.

constraints: All mooring lines must be confirmed clear before vessel movement is initiated from the berth.
Bridge team attention must remain on the unmooring operation during critical maneuvering phases.
Communication between mooring stations and bridge must be acknowledged and acted upon correctly.
warnings: Initiating bow thruster/vessel movement while a mooring line is still ashore risks parting lines, crew injury, or allision damage.
Distraction of the bridge team (multiple persons present, pilots, possible phone call) during unmooring can lead to missed status reports and unsafe orders.
outcomes: The bow began slipping the berth with the spring still ashore, creating a near-miss situation.
The incident raises questions about the quality of bridge team management and situational awareness during unmooring.
key_facts: Vessel was moored starboard side alongside with three headlines, stern lines, and two springs in good weather with slight to moderate wind and slight sea.
The Master ordered singling up progressively to '1 and 2' then '1 and 1', both carried out without issue.
A riding turn on the forward winch prevented providing slack to slip the final spring, which was reported to the Master.
Despite this report, the Master ordered 'Let go the spring' and the bow thruster began operating, moving the vessel off the berth with the spring still ashore.
VHF communication quality between mooring stations and bridge was clear with no interference throughout the operation.
The bridge at the time included the Master, Chief Officer, Docking Pilot, and River Pilot, suggesting divided attention.

procedures.action: Ensure mooring lines are run through split drum winches/reels as designed.

procedures.action: Visually confirm all ropes are clear before using the bow thruster.
procedures.why: Failure to do so constitutes poor seamanship and risks rope entanglement or damage.

procedures.action: Maintain active bridge-to-forecastle communication, with backup via VHF radios held by both Master and Chief Officer.
procedures.why: If the Master is distracted (e.g., talking to the pilot), the Chief Officer should be able to respond to calls from the forecastle.

procedures.action: Report the incident as a near miss under the Safety Management System.
procedures.why: The Officer concerned failed to report this near-miss, which is a required SMS action.

procedures.action: If normal reporting/communication channels fail, contact the DPA directly.
procedures.why: The DPA emphasised that near-miss reporting should go directly to them if the normal process is not possible.

constraints: Near-miss incidents must be reported under the vessel's Safety Management System.

Bow thruster must not be used until ropes are visually confirmed clear.
Vessels are fitted with split drum winches specifically to prevent riding turns; this design must be used correctly.
warnings: Misuse of mooring equipment can cause riding turns and rope damage.
Using the bow thruster before confirming ropes are clear is poor seamanship and a safety hazard.

trace.situation: CHIRP reports on a recurring issue of vessels transmitting incorrect or incomplete AIS data, citing UK MCA notice MIN 231 and a real incident where a vessel's AIS was not transmitting its ship's name and call sign despite correct display locally.
trace.trigger: A vessel's AIS output is found to be transmitting incorrect, incomplete, or missing dynamic/static data (e.g., heading errors, missing ship name/call sign, wrong MMSI/IMO, incorrect destination/ETA or vessel status).

procedures.action: Check AIS display for own ship's transmitted data (name, call sign, dynamic data).
procedures.why: To verify what the unit believes it is transmitting.

procedures.action: Contact a nearby vessel (e.g., by VHF) to confirm what data they are actually receiving from your AIS.
procedures.why: Display information may not match what is actually being transmitted, as occurred in the reported incident.

procedures.action: Reset the AIS unit if a discrepancy is found between transmitted and displayed data.
procedures.why: Resetting resolved the fault in the reported case, restoring correct transmission of ship's name and call sign.

procedures.action: Institute a routine of resetting the AIS unit at the beginning of every watch.
procedures.why: The operator adopted this as a preventive measure, which 'has been a help in improving our Safety on board'.

procedures.action: Report AIS data irregularities to CHIRP and to the equipment manufacturer.
procedures.why: The Board suggests notifying manufacturers so equipment performance and reliability may be improved, and reporting to CHIRP builds industry awareness.

constraints: UK M Notice MIN 231 expired 01 April 2007 but remains available with a reporting format and useful information.
Faulty interfaces, particularly with the gyro compass, are a known cause of AIS dynamic data errors.
Incorrectly entered MMSI or IMO numbers and incorrect destination/ETA/vessel status are known causes of AIS errors.
warnings: Incorrect AIS data transmission can be a danger to navigation and weakens confidence in the system.
A vessel's own AIS display may show correct data even when that data is not actually being transmitted to other vessels.
outcomes: Resetting the AIS unit corrected the fault and restored transmission of ship's name and call sign to a nearby vessel.

trace.situation: A solo night watchkeeper motor-sailing on a clear passage sighted a single red light on the port bow, initially interpreted as a safe passing situation, but the approaching black-hulled yacht was mis-displaying its navigation lights and nearly collided.
trace.trigger: Sighting of a single red light on the port bow at night while standing watch alone, with no other vessel detail visible through binoculars.

procedures.action: Continuously monitor an approaching light's bearing and range rather than assuming safe passage from colour alone.
procedures.why: The watchkeeper initially relied on the mnemonic 'green to green, red to red' but the light was in fact getting closer, indicating a closing/collision risk.

procedures.action: Use radar to confirm the target's course, speed, and closing rate when in doubt.
procedures.why: The watchkeeper felt the light was getting closer but could not leave the cockpit to check radar, leaving the situation unresolved until visual confirmation at close range.

procedures.action: Take immediate avoiding action (take the helm, disengage autopilot, turn hard to starboard) when a close-quarters situation is recognised.
procedures.why: Only a late, sharp turn to starboard (170°) prevented a collision when the other yacht was seen close aboard with no stern light.

constraints: Solo watchkeeping limits ability to leave the cockpit to consult radar or instruments.
Visual identification of navigation lights alone is insufficient to assess collision risk at night.
A vessel's navigation lights must be correctly configured (and visible) for other vessels to interpret its aspect safely.
warnings: Do not rely solely on light colour/aspect to judge a vessel's heading or passing arrangement; the other vessel may be mis-rigged or showing incorrect lights.
Solo night watchkeeping creates risk of being unable to leave the helm/cockpit to verify closing targets by radar.
A vessel showing no stern light and a red light on the wrong (starboard) side can cause dangerous misinterpretation of its course.
outcomes: A last-second hard turn to starboard (170°) avoided a collision as the black yacht slid close by.
The other yacht was found to be showing a red light on her starboard side with no stern light and only a dim cabin light, confirming a navigation light fault or incorrect display.
key_facts: The reporting vessel was motor-sailing alone on watch on a clear night.
A single red light was sighted on the port bow, initially assumed to indicate a safe red-to-red passing.
The approaching black-hulled yacht had no stern light and was showing red on her starboard side, not her port side.
The watchkeeper could not consult radar because leaving the cockpit was not possible while monitoring the closing light.
Evasive action (hard turn to starboard, 170°) was taken only at very close range, narrowly avoiding collision.

trace.situation: A CHIRP correspondence review of a near-miss encounter between a leisure yacht and a tanker in open Channel sea conditions, where the tanker altered course toward the yacht without any visual or sound signal acknowledgement.
trace.trigger: A tanker altering course towards a smaller vessel in open water without giving any visual (Aldis lamp) or sound (siren) indication that it had seen the other vessel.

procedures.action: When altering course near another vessel, give a visual signal (e.g. 2 flashes on Aldis lamp) or sound signal (siren blasts) to indicate awareness of the other vessel.
procedures.why: Confirms to the other vessel that her presence has been noted and the manoeuvre is deliberate, reducing alarm and ambiguity.

procedures.action: A give-way vessel (here the tanker) should alter course to starboard when appropriate rather than toward the other vessel.
procedures.why: Standard practice recommended by the Maritime Advisory Board for avoiding close-quarters situations.

procedures.action: Evaluate close-quarters situations from the other vessel's perspective, asking 'How close would I like someone to be if I were on the other ship/boat?'
procedures.why: Reduces subjectivity in assessing safe passing distance and encourages more cautious manoeuvring.

procedures.action: Do not rely solely on a Radar Target Enhancer (RTE) to assume you have been seen by another vessel.
procedures.why: Most RTEs operate on X band (3cm), but merchant vessels may be using S band (10cm) radar, so the RTE may not be detected by the observing vessel's radar.

constraints: Passing distance assessments are inherently subjective and parties may not agree on what constitutes a safe distance.
Reliance on an RTE's effectiveness assumes the other vessel is using the same radar band, which cannot be guaranteed.
warnings: An unexpected course alteration toward another vessel without acknowledgement signal can cause alarm and is considered thoughtless/perverse seamanship.
RTEs can help detection but should not be relied upon as proof that a vessel has been seen.
outcomes: The yacht crew experienced alarm due to the tanker's unexplained course alteration toward them despite having ample sea room.
The incident generated a CHIRP report highlighting subjectivity in passing-distance judgments between mariners.
key_facts: The tanker altered course towards the yacht in open sea conditions without any visual or sound signal.
The yacht's radar reflector ('blipper') was known to be effective up to 6 miles.
The closest distance off ahead was estimated at around 0.5nm.
Most RTEs operate on X band (3cm) while merchant vessels may use S band (10cm) radar.
The Maritime Advisory Board advised that the tanker should have altered course to starboard.

trace.situation: CHIRP compiles two unrelated small-craft near-miss reports: a comment on over-reliance on navigation-light colour/rhymes for collision avoidance, and a Designated Person's report of rope/tube lighting overheating and charring near a yacht's deckhead, which could have started a fire.
trace.trigger: A crew-reported near miss involving overheated rope/tube lighting fitted close to the deckhead on an ISM-certified private yacht, and separately, a navigational scenario where a vessel's light colour is being used as the sole cue for collision risk assessment.

procedures.action: Do not rely on a single data point (e.g., light colour) to assess collision risk; monitor bearing trend instead.
procedures.why: A steady bearing indicates collision risk regardless of what colour light is observed.

procedures.action: Have the vessel independently checked (e.g., via RNLI free sea check in the UK).
procedures.why: Independent verification improves overall safety beyond relying on crew assumptions or single indicators.

procedures.action: Report recurring equipment hazards (e.g., overheating lighting) through the Designated Person/ISM reporting system.
procedures.why: Enables investigation and systemic risk mitigation across the fleet/industry.

procedures.action: Ensure decorative/hidden lighting installations are fit for the intended purpose and installed per manufacturer's instructions.

trace.situation: A CHIRP editorial urging mariners to practice dynamic 'What if...' risk assessment in everyday navigation, seamanship, engineering, and enclosed space entry scenarios.
trace.trigger: Any vessel operation or evolution (anchoring, navigation, enclosed space entry) where hazards could arise, especially before committing to a risky action.

procedures.action: Mentally or verbally ask 'What if...' before undertaking an operation and think through contingencies in advance.
procedures.why: Good navigation, seamanship and engineering practice entails frequent risk assessment, as formal large documentation is not always required.

procedures.action: Talk through the situation and assessment with someone else where possible.
procedures.why: Discussing the risk assessment improves the quality of decision-making, as modeled by RNLI crew training.

procedures.action: For small craft, assess fouled propeller risk, lee shore proximity, sea-room, anchor/chain/warp holding capacity, and communication means before going to sea.
procedures.why: These are foreseeable hazards that could lead to grounding or loss of vessel if not planned for.

procedures.action: STOP before entering an enclosed space and consider oxygen depletion, presence of gas, breathing apparatus failure, and availability of back-up.
procedures.why: Marine Accident Investigation Branch has reported fatalities from enclosed space entry without proper risk assessment.

procedures.action: Follow the vessel's Safety Management System procedure for enclosed space entry.
procedures.why: SMS procedures codify the safe process to prevent fatalities in this high-risk evolution.

constraints: Risk assessment should be dynamic and ongoing, not a one-time exercise.
Enclosed space entry must STOP and follow the SMS procedure rather than proceeding ad hoc.
warnings: Enclosed space entry has caused fatalities reported by the Marine Accident Investigation Branch.
STOP before entering an enclosed space without assessing oxygen levels, gas presence, and breathing apparatus reliability.
outcomes: Thorough and dynamic risk assessment allowed an RNLI helmsman to remain in control, balance risks to his crew, and commit only when absolutely necessary after exhausting other options.
Failure to risk-assess before enclosed space entry has resulted in reported fatalities.
key_facts: A formal Risk Assessment with large documentation is not always necessary; mental or verbal dynamic assessment can suffice in routine operations.
The RNLI trains crews in dynamic risk assessment, which was credited for a successful difficult rescue.
Key 'what if' questions for small craft include fouled propeller, lee shore distance, sea-room, and anchor gear sufficiency.
Enclosed space entry requires specific what-if questions: oxygen depletion, gas presence, breathing apparatus failure, and back-up availability.
Vessels should follow their Safety Management System procedure for enclosed space entry.

question_seeds.text: How can I incorporate dynamic 'What if...' risk assessment into daily watchkeeping without excessive paperwork?
What specific questions should my crew consider before authorizing entry into an enclosed space?
Why is talking through a risk assessment with another person considered best practice?
Which SMS procedure governs enclosed space entry on my vessel, and have all crew been briefed on it?

trace.situation: A port VTS operator monitoring an adjacent sea area outside its formal responsibility spotted a small cargo vessel entering a safety zone around an outlying island and alerted it to the danger.
trace.trigger: VTS Operator detects a vessel entering a charted safety zone around an outlying island while transiting an area the VTS monitors but has no direct responsibility for.

procedures.action: VTS Operator calls the vessel on VHF channel 16 to warn it is standing into danger.
procedures.why: To alert the vessel before it collides with or grounds near the outlying island.

procedures.action: Repeat the call until a response is received.
procedures.why: The vessel did not respond until the third call, indicating initial lack of bridge watchkeeping attention.

procedures.action: Vessel alters course hard to port upon receiving the warning.
procedures.why: To clear the safety zone and avoid grounding/collision hazard.

procedures.action: Harbour Authority forwards incident details to the local Coastguard office.
procedures.why: To ensure proper reporting and follow-up of a near-miss involving a safety zone incursion.

constraints: VTS monitors the adjacent sea area but has no direct responsibility for vessels transiting it.
Communication relies on VHF channel 16 for safety alerts.
warnings: Vessel was standing into danger by entering a safety zone around an outlying island.
Delayed bridge response (three calls needed) risked a near-miss turning into an actual incident.
outcomes: The vessel cleared the safety zone without incident after altering course hard to port.
The Harbour Authority reported the incident to the Coastguard for record and follow-up.
key_facts: The Harbour Authority's VTS also monitors vessels in the adjacent sea area despite no formal responsibility.
A small cargo vessel entered a safety zone around an outlying island.
The VTS Operator needed three VHF channel 16 calls before the vessel responded.
The vessel took hard-to-port action and exited the zone safely.
A VTS equipment snapshot recorded the vessel's track entering and skirting the island's safety zone.

constraints: A human cannot physically prevent an involuntary gybe once it begins.
Charter boat crews may lack experience or seasoned racing skills, increasing risk.
warnings: Acting as a human boom preventer on the foredeck is dangerous and should not be practiced.

outcomes: Reporter recommends a safety warning be issued regarding this practice.

Crew members on several boats positioned themselves on the foredeck as a 'human boom preventer'.
A human cannot stop an involuntary gybe, making the practice ineffective and hazardous.
The boats involved were charter yachts, possibly crewed by inexperienced individuals.

trace.situation: CHIRP received a navigational near-miss report involving a vessel passing close to an island safety zone, and forwarded it to the ship's manager, who returned the Master's explanation of the circumstances and his navigational decisions.
trace.trigger: A navigational near-miss report was filed concerning the vessel's proximity to an island safety zone, prompting CHIRP to seek the Master's account via the ship manager.
constraints: Master intended to maintain at least 0.5 nm CPA from the island's safety zone as plotted on radar.
Vessel was being set south by tide toward the island, requiring course correction.
Another vessel was ahead on a reciprocal course, adding to the navigational complexity.
warnings: Master's belief that deep water at the location meant 'no risk' did not account for proximity/navigational hazards beyond grounding risk.
Relying on an anticipated but unconfirmed counter-current to correct vessel's set toward the island is a risky navigational assumption.
Uncertainty expressed by the Master about whether his track could be verified ashore suggests lack of confidence in his own CPA assessment.
outcomes: A near-miss was reported despite the Master's belief he maintained the intended 0.5 nm CPA to the safety zone.

key_facts: The Master was on the bridge throughout the passage and considered the area well known to him.
Conditions included a strong following current, a Force 6 following wind, and good visibility.
The vessel was being set south by the tide toward the island, and the Master expected a counter-current to develop closer to the island.
The Master plotted a 0.5 nm CPA to the safety zone on radar and made two 5-degree northward course corrections.
Another vessel was on a reciprocal course ahead, adding to the navigational situation.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a reported navigational near-miss where a vessel's VTS track showed it hugging the starboard outer limit of a fairway, prompting discussion on how ship managers can reduce navigational incident risk.
trace.trigger: A navigational near-miss occurred and was reported, with VTS track data showing the vessel passed close to the fairway's outer limit despite the Master's stated intent to signal clear navigational intentions.

procedures.action: Treat close-quarters track deviations shown on VTS as navigational near-misses with significant risk, even if the Master believed actions were safe and intentional.
procedures.why: Many such events go unreported and can involve otherwise qualified, conscientious mariners.

procedures.action: Conduct navigation audits using a senior Master or navigator riding on vessels to monitor practices and advise improvements.
procedures.why: Mirrors auditing of other critical company activities (technical, financial) to systematically reduce risk.

procedures.action: If a dedicated navigation auditor is not feasible, have a superintendent review the vessel's previous passage plan with the Master during a port visit.
procedures.why: Provides a practical level of assurance on navigational planning quality in smaller companies.

procedures.action: Discuss with the Master and navigation officers how they apply parallel-indexing techniques.
procedures.why: Confirms proper use of a key navigational safety technique in restricted waters.

procedures.action: Check that navigation equipment is functioning and charts are corrected up to date.
procedures.why: Ensures the technical basis for safe navigation is maintained.

constraints: Specialist navigation auditors may not be feasible in small companies, requiring alternative assurance methods.
Assessment should be based on objective VTS track data, not solely on the Master's self-reported justification.
warnings: A near-miss can occur even with properly qualified, conscientious mariners who take pride in their navigation skills.
Many navigational near-misses with significant risk go unreported.
outcomes: CHIRP appreciated the manager's follow-up with the Master but noted the event should still be classified as a significant-risk near-miss.
Navigation audits and superintendent reviews can provide assurance and reduce the likelihood of future navigational incidents.
key_facts: The vessel's VTS track showed it running close to the starboard outer limit of the fairway.
CHIRP assessed this as a navigational near-miss with significant risk, not merely a deliberate safe-intention maneuver.
Large companies may use navigation audits with a senior Master or navigator riding vessels to review practices.
Smaller companies can achieve partial assurance via superintendent review of passage plans, parallel-indexing discussions, and equipment/chart checks.

question_seeds.text: Why did CHIRP classify this event as a significant-risk near-miss despite the Master's explanation of intentional positioning?
How can my company implement navigation audits if we lack a dedicated navigation auditor?
What specific checks should a superintendent perform during a port visit to assess navigational practice?
Who should be reviewing parallel-indexing technique application onboard to ensure proper use?

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary following a Baltic crossing near-miss encounter, commending the Officer of the Watch (OOW) for reporting the incident and the company manager for using it as fleet-wide training material.
trace.trigger: An OOW experienced a close-quarters/crossing near-miss situation and submitted a near-miss report afterward.

procedures.action: Report near-miss incidents promptly through official channels (e.g., CHIRP).
procedures.why: Enables lessons to be captured and shared, illustrating the positive benefit of near-miss reporting.

procedures.action: Company management should review reported near-misses and disseminate them as training material across the fleet.
procedures.why: Promulgating the incident as training material helps prevent recurrence across other vessels in the fleet.

outcomes: The near-miss report led to positive fleet-wide training benefit.
Reporting culture reinforced through CHIRP's public commendation.
key_facts: The OOW of vessel XXXX reported a near-miss crossing encounter.
The manager of company/fleet YYYY followed up on the report and turned it into training material.
CHIRP publicly commended both actions as demonstrating the value of near-miss reporting.

question_seeds.text: Why does CHIRP consider this near-miss report particularly valuable?

trace.situation: A flotilla manager responds to a CHIRP report concerning the use (or absence) of a mainsail boom preventer on charter racing yachts, explaining the company's standard practice for rigging preventers and briefing crews on gybing hazards.
trace.trigger: A CHIRP report was submitted describing an incident or near-miss involving an uncontrolled gybe and lack of a proper boom preventer, prompting CHIRP to contact the flotilla manager for clarification.

procedures.action: Rig the mainsail boom preventer whenever sailing downwind.
procedures.why: Company briefing policy requires it to prevent uncontrolled gybes.

procedures.action: Use a distinctly bright-coloured (orange) line for the preventer so it is clearly identifiable from other lines aboard.
procedures.why: Ensures crew can quickly recognise and correctly deploy the preventer line.

procedures.action: Verify the preventer is listed in the yacht's inventory and check it is present and correct before each charter.
procedures.why: Skipper accountability ensures equipment is actually aboard and serviceable before departure.

procedures.action: Brief clients on the dangers of gybing, including the risk of the boom and mainsheet sweeping the cockpit, before each charter.
procedures.why: Raises client awareness of hazards even though a full drill is not conducted.

procedures.action: Ensure skippers and mates meet MCA code of practice experience requirements prior to charter.
procedures.why: Confirms crew competency standards are maintained for safe operation.

constraints: Preventer line must be a bright colour (orange) distinct from other lines aboard.
Preventer presence must be checked and confirmed correct by the skipper before each charter starts.
Skippers and mates must be experienced in accordance with the MCA code of practice.
Full gybe drill is not conducted with clients, only a verbal briefing on dangers.
warnings: Uncontrolled gybes pose a danger.
The boom and mainsheet sweeping the cockpit during a gybe is a hazard to crew/clients.
outcomes: Flotilla manager confirmed existing safety measures (preventer rigging, briefings, crew experience standards) were already in place.
CHIRP acknowledged and thanked the reporting skipper for raising the safety issue.
The flotilla manager expressed ongoing interest in safety issues, suggesting a positive safety culture response.
key_facts: All racing yachts in the flotilla are supplied with a mainsail boom preventer.
The preventer line is bright orange to distinguish it from other lines.
The preventer is checked by the skipper against the yacht's inventory before each charter.
Clients are briefed on gybing dangers but do not undergo a full gybe drill.
Skippers and mates must meet MCA code of practice experience requirements.

question_seeds.text: What standard equipment and colour-coding does this flotilla use to ensure the boom preventer is correctly identified and rigged?

trace.situation: Officer of the watch on a large commercial vessel in the Baltic monitored a tanker (give-way vessel) on a crossing course near the Anholt crossing/route D, with closing CPA/TCPA, and had to take last-resort avoiding action when the other vessel failed to give way.
trace.trigger: CPA closing to 0.4 miles with TCPA of 9 minutes while the other vessel remained the give-way vessel and did not alter course as required.

procedures.action: Place a vessel calling for pilot services repeatedly under closer radar/visual surveillance once noted as potential crossing traffic.
procedures.why: Enabled early recognition that her CPA was closing and she was the give-way vessel.

procedures.action: Monitor the give-way vessel's progress while maintaining own course and speed.
procedures.why: As stand-on vessel, correct COLREGS action is to maintain course/speed until give-way vessel's inaction makes collision imminent.

procedures.action: Contact the other vessel by VHF (ch16 then ch6) when CPA/TCPA became dangerously close to clarify her intentions.
procedures.why: To confirm whether she intended to give way and warn her of the dangerously close CPA of 0.4 miles.

procedures.action: Alert the captain to the bridge once the other vessel continued to turn the wrong way (port) and remained on a collision course.
procedures.why: Escalation required when verbal VHF agreement was not matched by actual helm action, indicating worsening collision risk.

procedures.action: Execute own last-resort emergency maneuver (hard turn to starboard, full 360-degree turn, speed reduced to 4 knots) when range closed to about 1 mile and collision course persisted.
procedures.why: Stand-on vessel's final action permitted/required when give-way vessel fails to take appropriate action and collision becomes otherwise unavoidable.

procedures.action: Communicate the reason for the maneuver to the other vessel over VHF ch16.
procedures.why: To clarify intentions and avoid further confusion during the avoiding action.

constraints: Stand-on vessel must maintain course and speed until it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action
Give-way vessel is obligated to take early and substantial action to keep clear
VHF agreement does not substitute for actual compliant maneuvering under the rules of the road
warnings: A vessel verbally agreeing to turn on VHF may not actually alter course, requiring continuous monitoring rather than reliance on radio assurances
Waiting too long to take independent action as stand-on vessel can force a last-resort emergency maneuver at very close range (down to ~1 mile)
outcomes: XXXX executed a full 360-degree turn to starboard at close range to avoid collision after YYYY failed to give way
YYYY continued turning to port, maintaining a collision course despite verbal agreement to turn starboard
Situation resolved by 11:12 UTC with YYYY continuing her original route D as if nothing had happened
key_facts: Incident occurred in the Baltic near the Anholt crossing/route D, involving vessels calling Sound Pilot on VHF ch16
CPA reached 0.4 miles with TCPA of 9 minutes before VHF contact was made
XXXX was the stand-on vessel; YYYY was the give-way vessel repeatedly calling for Sound pilot
XXXX's emergency turning circle to starboard had a radius of less than 0.15 miles with speed dropped to 4 knots
Despite verbal agreement to turn starboard, YYYY continued turning to port, forcing XXXX's captain to execute the full 360-degree turn

trace.situation: CHIRP received and investigated a near-miss report concerning two vessels (XXXX and YYYY) in a crossing situation in the Baltic where differing perceptions of an acceptable CPA margin led to XXXX altering course to starboard and reducing CPA to 0.4 miles.
trace.trigger: Give-way vessel YYYY, assessing it was close to crossing XXXX's course, decided to maintain course and speed rather than take early avoiding action, prompting XXXX's OOW to alter course to starboard, which YYYY's Master felt endangered safe passage.

procedures.action: When acting as give-way vessel approaching a crossing situation, take early and substantial action to keep well clear rather than relying on a marginal passing distance.
procedures.why: YYYY's reliance on a 0.6-mile CPA as 'safe' without informing the other vessel created a conflict in perceived safety margins.

procedures.action: Communicate intentions (e.g., via VHF) in advance to the other vessel when planning to pass at a close margin, especially in recommended/high-traffic routes.
procedures.why: YYYY's manager acknowledged that the intended CPA should have been communicated in advance to XXXX's OOW to avoid confusion.

procedures.action: Keep the Master on the bridge and monitoring the OOW's conduct during crossing situations in congested waters.
procedures.why: The excerpt notes the Master of YYYY was on the bridge throughout, indicating oversight was maintained, though communication of intent was still lacking.

procedures.action: Treat differing margin-of-safety perceptions between bridge teams as a recurring hazard and use such incidents as training material.
procedures.why: CHIRP noted this type of issue is reported frequently and YYYY's manager committed to distributing the case for onboard training.

constraints: Give-way vessel must assess whether it is genuinely closing to a point where course alteration is no longer required under COLREGs before deciding not to act.
A reduction of CPA from 0.6 to 0.4 miles was considered unacceptable by the other vessel's bridge team, indicating no universal agreed minimum safety margin exists without communication.
Both bridge teams' assessments were time-critical (9 minutes before CPA at ~4 miles distance), leaving little margin for correction once a differing assessment emerges.
warnings: Differing perceptions of an acceptable safety margin between bridge teams can lead to confusion, reduced CPA, and near-miss situations.
Relying on a 'technically correct' interpretation of give-way obligations without communicating intent can endanger the other vessel's confidence in safe passage.
outcomes: XXXX's OOW altered course to starboard, reducing CPA from 0.6 to 0.4 miles, which YYYY's Master considered endangered safe passage.
YYYY's management ultimately agreed the issue was a near miss and committed to distributing the case for training purposes across managed vessels.
CHIRP identified this as a recurring issue of differing margin-of-safety perceptions, previously addressed in a prior editorial.
key_facts: YYYY was the give-way vessel and decided to maintain course and speed because, at 10:30, it judged itself already close to crossing XXXX's course.
9 minutes before CPA, the vessels were about 4 miles apart; earlier, at 15 miles, YYYY was still the give-way vessel.
YYYY's bridge team considered a CPA of approximately 0.6 miles (half a mile ahead) safe; XXXX's bridge team considered this margin too small.
The Master of YYYY was on the bridge throughout and monitoring the OOW's conduct.
YYYY's manager agreed the intended passing margin should have been communicated in advance to XXXX's OOW.

question_seeds.text: Why did YYYY's OOW decide not to alter course despite being the give-way vessel?
How should differing CPA safety margin expectations between two vessels be resolved before a close-quarters situation develops?
What communication, if any, should have occurred between XXXX and YYYY regarding the intended passing distance?
At what point does a give-way vessel's obligation to alter course change as the crossing situation develops toward CPA?

trace.situation: CHIRP analysis of a near-miss between a ferry departing port and a sailing yacht on a reciprocal course, where the ferry was navigating a draught-restricted, narrow channel and the yachtsman believed he had right of way.
trace.trigger: A power-driven ferry constrained by draught in a narrow/buoyed channel encounters a sailing vessel on a reciprocal course near a port approach.

procedures.action: Treat the ferry as a 'vessel constrained by her draught' (Rule 3h) until clear of the shoal area south of the channel.
procedures.why: Sea bottom configuration restricts the ferry's ability to alter course, both in the buoyed channel and beyond it, until past the shoal.

procedures.action: Treat the passage between the buoyed channel and the 10m depth line to the East as a Narrow Channel under Rule 9(b).
procedures.why: The sea bottom configuration restricts ferries from altering course in this area, invoking narrow channel navigation rules rather than simple give-way/sailing-vessel priority.

procedures.action: Small craft/yachts approaching or departing the port should keep well clear of frequent large vessel movements per local instruction.
procedures.why: Yachts are often not sufficiently aware of the ferry's draught (the 'third dimension') and its resulting manoeuvring constraints.

procedures.action: Maintain watch on VHF Ch 16 in addition to the local working channel (Ch 14).
procedures.why: Lack of communication was identified as a contributing factor in this incident; Ch16 is the distress/calling channel that should not be neglected even when a local working channel is in use.

constraints: The ferry is only to be considered constrained by draught until clear of the shoal area to the South.
The passage between the buoyed channel and the 10m depth line to the East qualifies as a Narrow Channel (Rule 9b), affecting right-of-way interpretation.
In open sea with no restrictions, a power-driven vessel on a reciprocal course with a sailing vessel must give way to the sailing vessel.
Local instruction requires small craft to keep well clear of frequent large vessel traffic at this port.
warnings: Yachts approaching this port are often not sufficiently aware of the draught constraints ('third dimension') of ferries.
Lack of communication between vessels was acknowledged as a factor contributing to the near-miss.
A navigator constrained by a shoal area may be reluctant to alter course to port for fear the yacht will unpredictably alter to starboard, risking a standoff where neither vessel gives way in time.
outcomes: The yacht eventually altered course to get out of the way, avoiding collision in this instance.
The incident highlighted differing perceptions of right-of-way between yacht and ferry bridge crews, with the yachtsman believing he had right of way while the ferry was in fact constrained.
key_facts: The ferry left the berth approximately two hours after low water with NE-ly wind of 1-3 knots.
The ferry is considered 'constrained by her draught' (Rule 3h) until clear of a southern shoal area.
The passage between the buoyed channel and the 10m depth line to the East is classified as a Narrow Channel under Rule 9(b).
Vessels near this port keep watch on VHF Ch 14 but should also maintain watch on Ch 16.

In open sea with no restrictions, a power-driven vessel on reciprocal course with a sailing vessel must give way to the sailing vessel, but this general rule is overridden here by the ferry's constrained-by-draught and narrow-channel status.

trace.situation: Owner of a traditional gaff-rigged yacht reported losing the mast while sailing in 15-20 knot winds due to failure of a shroud splice.
trace.trigger: Failure of a splice on the starboard forward shroud of the main mast during sailing in 15-20 knots of wind

procedures.action: Inspect standing rigging for contact between lightning conductor copper wire and galvanised shroud wires beneath rope serving
procedures.why: Contact between dissimilar metals (copper lightning conductor and galvanised wire) caused galvanic corrosion that led to splice failure and mast loss

constraints: Lightning conductor routing along shrouds must avoid direct contact with galvanised standing rigging
warnings: Copper lightning conductors in contact with galvanised wire rigging can cause galvanic corrosion leading to structural failure
Corrosion within rope serving may be hidden from visual inspection until failure occurs
outcomes: Galvanic corrosion of the galvanised shroud wire at the splice caused the splice to fail and the mast to be lost
key_facts: The yacht was a traditional gaff-rigged vessel
Mast was lost while sailing in wind of 15 to 20 knots
A copper wire lightning conductor was routed down the starboard forward shroud
The conductor touched the splice through the rope serving, causing corrosion of the galvanised wire

trace.situation: A yacht under full sail (goose-winged downwind) approaching port as the stand-on vessel encountered an outbound ferry in a buoyed channel that held a steady, collision bearing and did not respond to VHF calls, forcing the yacht to take last-minute avoiding action.
trace.trigger: Give-way vessel (ferry) failed to alter course in good time, maintained a steady closing bearing, and did not respond to VHF Channel 16 calls as range closed to under 1 mile.

procedures.action: Monitor the other vessel's bearing continuously for signs of risk of collision.
procedures.why: A steady bearing with decreasing range indicates risk of collision under the COLREGs.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the approaching vessel by name on VHF Ch 16 when concern arises.
procedures.why: To prompt the give-way vessel to take action and confirm mutual awareness.

procedures.action: When range closes to under 1 mile with no response and no course change, take independent avoiding action.
procedures.why: Stand-on vessel is permitted/obliged to act alone when the give-way vessel's action is clearly not appropriate to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Choose an avoidance maneuver appropriate to the vessel's configuration (gybe and turn to port rather than attempt a starboard turn).
procedures.why: A rapid turn to starboard was not possible with the genoa poled out, so gybing and altering to port was the only safe, executable option.

constraints: Yacht had no radar or AIS capability, limiting target identification and tracking.
Genoa was goose-winged/poled out, preventing a rapid starboard alteration of course.
Yacht was the stand-on vessel under the COLREGs and initially maintained course and speed.
No known navigational constraint prevented the ferry from altering course in good time.
warnings: Rigging a spinnaker pole/goose-winged sail configuration severely restricts ability to make a rapid course change to starboard in an emergency.
Relying solely on visual observation without AIS or radar limits ability to identify and directly contact approaching vessels.
Stand-on vessels should not assume give-way vessels will act appropriately; be prepared to maneuver independently.
outcomes: Yacht gybed and altered course 90 degrees to port (onto 180T) to avoid collision.
Ferry appeared to alter slightly to port as yacht maneuvered, passing approximately 200m off the yacht's starboard side.
Collision was avoided but only through last-minute action by the stand-on vessel.
key_facts: Yacht was under full sail, goose-winged, on starboard tack, doing 5 knots over ground, course 270T.
Ferry's course appeared to be the reciprocal (090T) with a closing range starting at about 2 miles.

trace.situation: A CHIRP commentary analyzes a near-miss close-quarters encounter between a tug towing a vessel and a small anchored fishing craft, examining whether COLREGS stand-on/give-way obligations and sound signalling were properly applied.
trace.trigger: A tug watch-keeper believing himself to be the stand-on vessel delays action as his tow closes to dangerous proximity with a small anchored craft.

procedures.action: Even if considered stand-on vessel, take action to avoid collision once it is clear the give-way vessel's action alone will not suffice.
procedures.why: Rule 17 requires the stand-on vessel to act when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone.

procedures.action: Make a large alteration of course early rather than slowing down rapidly.
procedures.why: Slowing rapidly risks the tow catching up and running down the towing vessel; course alteration avoids this while still needing care for the towline sweep.

procedures.action: Take avoidance action earlier rather than waiting until very close quarters.
procedures.why: With hindsight the tow came dangerously close to the small craft, indicating action was taken too late.

procedures.action: Sound at least five short and rapid blasts when in doubt about the other vessel's intentions or sufficiency of action.
procedures.why: Rule 34(d) requires this signal to indicate doubt and alert the other vessel to the danger.

procedures.action: The small craft should urgently weigh anchor or let the anchor line go (carefully, avoiding fouling the propeller) and move away from danger.
procedures.why: Immediate self-preservation action is needed once a hazardous close-quarters situation develops.

procedures.action: Don life-jackets as soon as a hazardous situation is arising, per RNLI recommendation.
procedures.why: Personal safety precaution in case the collision risk materializes.

procedures.action: Transmit a Mayday if the situation escalates to imminent danger to life or property requiring immediate assistance.
procedures.why: Mayday is warranted only under conditions of grave and imminent danger requiring urgent assistance.

constraints: Course alteration by the tug must avoid catching the small craft in the sweep of the towline.
The small craft must be careful not to foul its propeller when letting go the anchor line.
Rule 17 obligations apply only once collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone.
Rule 34(d) signal requires at least five short and rapid blasts when in doubt.
warnings: Reluctance to slow down due to the tow catching up can delay necessary avoidance action.
Altering course without care risks catching the small craft in the towline's sweep.
Delaying action until very close quarters increases collision risk.
Failure to don life-jackets in a developing hazardous situation increases risk to life if an incident occurs.
outcomes: The tow came dangerously close to the small craft, indicating action was taken too late.
A near-miss report was submitted instead of an accident occurring, allowing lessons to be learned without injury or loss.
Had circumstances been slightly more severe, a Mayday call would have been justified.
key_facts: The tug watch-keeper believed he was the stand-on vessel but still had a duty under Rule 17 to act once collision could not be avoided by the give-way vessel alone.

The small craft was anchored and should have weighed anchor or slipped the line to escape the danger.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary analyzing a near-miss close-quarters encounter between a small fishing boat at anchor and a tug towing another vessel, examining how ColRegs rules on shapes, stand-on status, and lookout applied.
trace.trigger: A close-quarters situation developing between an anchored/fishing small craft and an approaching tug with tow.

procedures.action: Envisage the encounter from the other vessel's watch-keeping perspective (small craft vs. large vessel and vice versa).
procedures.why: The skipper of a small craft cannot assume the other vessel can identify his status or see his anchor rope/fishing lines from a distance.

procedures.action: Exhibit correct day shapes: fishing vessel (other than trawling) to show two cones apex-to-apex or a basket if under 20m; tug to show a diamond shape if tow exceeds 200m.
procedures.why: Rule 26 and Rule 24 of the ColRegs require these shapes so other vessels can identify restricted/fishing status visually.

procedures.action: Maintain a proper lookout, using binoculars, to assess risk of collision and identify that the tug was towing another vessel while still two to three miles apart.
procedures.why: Rule 5 requires a full appraisal of the situation and risk of collision; VHF is not a substitute for visual lookout.

procedures.action: Prepare to weigh anchor and move out of the tug's track once vessels are within about two miles of each other.
procedures.why: Prudent seamanship to avoid a developing close-quarters situation before it becomes critical.

constraints: A vessel engaged in fishing (other than trawling) must exhibit two cones apex-to-apex by day, or a basket if less than 20 metres long (Rule 26).
A power-driven vessel underway or a vessel fishing when underway must keep out of the way of a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (Rule 18).
A power-driven vessel towing, where the length of tow exceeds 200 metres, must exhibit a diamond shape where it can best be seen (Rule 24).
Every vessel must maintain a proper lookout at all times to assess risk of collision (Rule 5).
VHF communication does not substitute for maintaining a proper lookout under the ColRegs.
warnings: Do not assume another vessel can see your anchor rope or fishing lines from a distance.
VHF should not be relied upon as a substitute for keeping a proper visual lookout.
Failure to recognize a developing close-quarters situation early can lead to a near-tragedy.
outcomes: The incident resulted in a very near miss that could have caused a tragedy.
Proper application of lookout and early recognition of risk of collision could have allowed the small craft to weigh anchor and avoid the close-quarters situation.
key_facts: The fishing vessel was anchored and rod-fishing when the tug approached from several miles away near the Nab Tower.
Rule 26 requires fishing vessels (other than trawling) to exhibit two cones apex-together by day, or a basket if under 20 metres.
Rule 18 makes a power-driven vessel or fishing vessel underway give way to a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, such as a tug with tow.
Rule 24 requires a towing vessel to exhibit a diamond shape if the tow exceeds 200 metres.
Rule 5 requires a proper lookout at all times, and VHF use does not replace this requirement.

procedures.action: Listen on VHF Channel 16 for warnings from approaching commercial/tow vessels.

trace.situation: While transiting the Gulf of Aden Maritime Security Patrol Area (MSPA) at night, a watchkeeper detected a radar contact with no visible navigation lights in good visibility, which turned out to be a merchant vessel that had deliberately switched off all navigation lights to hide from pirates.

procedures.why: A vessel displaying no lights could indicate she had fallen into the wrong hands or was in distress.

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime feedback report describing a sailing vessel's basic receive-only AIS set failing to display multiple large vessels that were visible on radar and by eye during cruises in South Brittany, off the Loire, and across the Channel, and also mis-displaying anchored ships as 'steaming' at zero knots.
trace.trigger: Repeated instances of known, line-of-sight vessels (confirmed by radar and visual sighting) not appearing on the AIS receiver display, prompting the reporter to question the reliability of low-cost AIS receive-only equipment.

trace.situation: CHIRP review of a close-quarters incident between a tug and a motor-sailing yacht, focusing on the yacht's (stand-on vessel's) decision to alter course to port and the applicability of Rule 17 (Action by Stand-on Vessel).
trace.trigger: A give-way vessel (tug) fails to take appropriate action to avoid collision, forcing the stand-on vessel (yacht) to decide whether and how to take independent avoiding action.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, keep course and speed initially.
procedures.why: Rule 17(a)(i) requires the vessel not obliged to give way to maintain course and speed so the give-way vessel can take clear action.

procedures.action: Only take independent action once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not acting appropriately under the Rules.
procedures.why: Rule 17(a)(ii) permits the stand-on vessel to act alone only at that point, to avoid confusing the developing situation.

procedures.action: If collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone, take whatever action best aids collision avoidance.
procedures.why: Rule 17(b) places a duty on the stand-on vessel in extremis to act decisively.

procedures.action: Avoid altering course to port for a vessel on your own port side in a crossing situation (power-driven vessels).
procedures.why: Rule 17(c) prohibits this because it risks both vessels turning towards each other if the give-way vessel belatedly turns to starboard.

procedures.action: Prefer slowing, stopping, or making a large alteration to starboard (up to 180° or 360°) as evasive action.
procedures.why: This is the recommended safe evasive manoeuvre for a stand-on vessel to definitively avoid collision without converging headings.

constraints: Rule 17 does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way (17(d)).
Stand-on vessel may only act independently once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.
A power-driven stand-on vessel should not alter to port for a vessel on her own port side in a crossing situation if circumstances admit otherwise.
warnings: Altering course to port as stand-on vessel risks a head-on convergence if the give-way vessel belatedly turns to starboard.
A vessel's wash, even from a hull form believed to produce less wash, can still pose a considerable hazard to smaller or less robust craft.
outcomes: The yacht's alteration to port, while resolving the immediate incident, created a theoretical risk of converging tracks had the tug turned to starboard.
The tug's wash caused considerable concern to the yachtsman despite the tug operator's belief it did not produce significant wash.

CHIRP's investigation did not establish the underlying cause of the close-quarters situation.

trace.situation: Master of a trailing hopper suction dredger operating in thick fog within a dredging area had to take emergency avoiding action when a radar-tracked vessel failed to respond to VHF calls and maintained a dangerously close CPA of 0.1nm.

procedures.action: Continuously monitor approaching radar target with OOW and identify vessel by name.

procedures.action: When no response received and CPA remained 0.1nm, abort the dredging operation and lift the pipe clear of the seabed.
procedures.why: Regain full maneuverability by ceasing the activity that restricted the dredger's ability to take avoiding action.

procedures.action: Increase speed and alter course approximately 20° to port.
procedures.why: Actively increase separation distance from the approaching vessel since no communication could be established.

procedures.action: Re-attempt VHF contact with the vessel after it had passed clear.
procedures.why: Confirm safe passage and attempt to establish communication post-incident.

outcomes: The approaching vessel (XXXX) passed between the dredger and the navigation buoy at a distance of two cables from the dredger, avoiding collision.

key_facts: The dredger was in thick fog with visibility under one cable while dredging for sand.
The approaching vessel was tracked by radar at 5 miles, bearing a course of 030T at 9 knots, with an initial CPA of 0.1nm.
The dredger was on a northerly run at 340T track (actual track 358T due to ebb tide) and 1.2 knots SOG when the target was detected.

The master aborted dredging, raised the pipe, increased speed, and altered 20° to port to increase separation, resulting in a 2-cable passing distance.

trace.situation: A small sailing boat on passage from Yarmouth (IOW) to Southampton fouled a fishing pot line while proceeding under power and autopilot in an area known to contain pot floats.
trace.trigger: Sighting a small white fender (pot marker) in the water just ahead of the bow with insufficient time to avoid it, resulting in the vessel fouling the pot line.

procedures.action: Select neutral to stop the propeller immediately upon sighting the hazard close ahead.
procedures.why: Prevents the line from wrapping around the propeller if contact cannot be avoided.

procedures.action: Drop anchor, switch on anchor light, and stop the engine once fouled.
procedures.why: Secures the vessel's position and signals its status while stationary in a channel.

procedures.action: Check that the prop shaft rotates freely by hand.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the rope is wrapped around the propeller, informing further action.

procedures.action: Inform VTS of position and intentions, and keep them updated.
procedures.why: Keeps traffic control aware of an obstruction/stopped vessel in a navigable channel.

procedures.action: Use a dinghy grapnel anchor to haul the line to the surface.
procedures.why: Allows the line to be brought under control for safe handling and cutting.

procedures.action: Attach the retrieved end to the aft pulpit and cut the seaward end of the line with a knife.
procedures.why: Secures the line end to prevent it re-fouling while freeing the vessel from the remainder.

procedures.action: Have another vessel's dinghy pull the fender clear of the rudder.
procedures.why: Removes the remaining obstruction from the steering gear.

procedures.action: Check steering for full and free movement and engine in ahead/astern before resuming passage.
procedures.why: Verifies the vessel is seaworthy and safe to continue after the fouling incident.

procedures.why: Returns the vessel to normal passage status and closes out the reported incident with VTS.

trace.situation: A yacht anchored off the west coast of Scotland, alongside a French yacht nearby, was approached at high speed by a motor boat while weighing anchor, resulting in a dangerously close pass and damaging wash to both vessels.

constraints: Visibility was good, so the risk was from speed and lack of communication rather than lack of sighting.
