trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Feedback publishes reader correspondence responding to a previously reported battery explosion incident on a yacht, discussing battery types and gas hazard mitigation.
trace.trigger: A prior CHIRP report (Maritime Feedback No 20) described a battery gas explosion on a yacht causing extensive damage, prompting expert and reader correspondence on causes and prevention.

procedures.action: Use AGM (absorbed glass mat) sealed batteries instead of standard 'wet' lead-acid batteries for marine applications.
procedures.why: AGM batteries gas significantly less during charging and are sealed with a pressure-relief valve, reducing explosive hydrogen/oxygen accumulation.

procedures.action: Install a gas detector in battery compartments, ideally a dual-head unit with one head positioned at the top of the compartment.
procedures.why: Standard gas detectors can detect hydrogen well before it reaches dangerous concentration, and hydrogen rises so a high-mounted head improves detection.

procedures.action: Fit forced ventilation (e.g., a 12v computer fan) that activates when batteries are charging from alternator or shore power.
procedures.why: Forced ventilation disperses explosive hydrogen-oxygen gas mixtures produced during charging, preventing dangerous buildup.

procedures.action: Monitor charging systems/regulators for failure and avoid overcharging batteries.
procedures.why: Overcharging, including due to regulator failure, causes excessive gassing of hydrogen-oxygen mixture that can ignite and explode.

constraints: Wet (flooded) lead-acid batteries require loosening of cell caps to vent gas, unlike sealed AGM batteries.
Hydrogen and oxygen gases produced during charging are odourless, invisible, and highly explosive if not adequately vented.
AGM batteries are more expensive upfront but offer longer working life and maintenance-free operation, offsetting cost over time.
warnings: Both hydrogen and oxygen gas from charging batteries are highly explosive, odourless, and invisible, making them most dangerous if not adequately vented.
Similar battery gas explosions have caused fires that burnt boats to the waterline.
A failed voltage regulator can cause overcharging, leading to excessive explosive gas production.
outcomes: Failure to vent battery compartments adequately can lead to explosive gas buildup and catastrophic fire/explosion damage to the vessel.
Installing gas detectors and forced ventilation can detect danger early and prevent explosions, potentially saving the boat and lives.
Switching to AGM batteries reduces gassing risk and, despite higher initial cost, is more cost-effective over the battery's service life due to maintenance-free, longer operation.
key_facts: Maritime Feedback No 20 reported a battery gas explosion on a yacht causing extensive damage.
AGM (absorbed glass mat) batteries gas less than standard wet lead-acid batteries and are sealed with a safety valve.
Hydrogen gas rises, so dual-head gas detectors with one head at the compartment top improve detection.
A 12v computer fan wired to activate during charging provides simple, effective forced ventilation.
Overcharging, such as from a failed voltage regulator, increases explosive gas production from lead-acid batteries.

trace.situation: A sailor comments on a previous CHIRP Maritime Feedback report about using a rope as a boom preventer, proposing a more practical two-part rigging method to encourage actual use of the safety device.
trace.trigger: Boom preventers being impractical to rig quickly, especially during a race, leading to them rarely being used.

procedures.action: Permanently secure one length of rope to the outboard end of the boom, with its other end clipped temporarily near the inboard end (e.g. to the kicker fitting).
procedures.why: Keeps the preventer pre-rigged and ready without being a constant obstruction.

procedures.action: Run a second rope forward through a block on the gunwale, then back to the cockpit.
procedures.why: Provides a quick-access tensioning line that can be reached from the cockpit under way.

procedures.action: When needed, unclip the first part from the boom-side fitting and re-clip it to the gunwale-rigged line, then tighten.
procedures.why: Allows the preventer to be rigged quickly and easily, overcoming the awkwardness that discourages its use.

constraints: The system requires pre-installation of both rope sections before they can be quickly joined.

warnings: Storm-damaged aids to navigation can leave hazards unlit and unmarked, posing a collision/grounding risk to mariners.
outcomes: Lighted buoys were re-instated at the fish farm following the Commissioners' Inspector visit.
The hazard was resolved through cooperation between the yachtsman, the General Lighthouse Authority, and the fish farm manager.
key_facts: The Commissioners of Irish Lights are the General Lighthouse Authority for Ireland with duty over Local Aids to Navigation.
IALA guidelines require two lighted buoys seaward and two unlighted buoys/beacons shoreside for aquaculture farm marking.
The fish farm's buoys had been damaged by winter storms prior to the report.
Following inspection, the lighted buoys were reinstated.

question_seeds.text: Who is responsible for ensuring aquaculture farm hazards are properly marked in Irish waters?
What is the IALA-recommended buoy configuration for marking a fish farm?
Why were the fish farm's buoys unlit when the yachtsman encountered them?
How should a Captain report an unlit navigational hazard like a fish farm to the relevant authority?

trace.situation: CHIRP analyzes a near-collision at night between a ship (allegedly unmanned watch) and a yacht, examining failures in lookout practice and the actions the yacht's crew should have taken as risk of collision developed.
trace.trigger: A reported near-collision incident where the ship allegedly had no one keeping watch, prompting CHIRP to review both the ship's lookout practices and the yacht's response options.

procedures.action: Maintain a proper lookout visually and by radar at all times, even when briefly engaged in essential duties like plotting position.
procedures.why: A lapse in lookout, especially for routine tasks like chart correcting, risks missing developing collision situations.

procedures.action: Post a dedicated lookout on the bridge during darkness in addition to the OOW.
procedures.why: Darkness reduces visual detection range and reaction time, requiring extra dedicated watchkeeping.

procedures.action: Keep wheelhouse lights off at night.
procedures.why: Interior lighting impairs the OOW's night vision and ability to keep a proper lookout.

procedures.action: When risk of collision becomes apparent (e.g., at ~2 miles/12 minutes before closing), call the skipper immediately.
procedures.why: Command decision-making and experienced judgement are needed once a developing collision risk is identified.

procedures.action: Direct at least five short and rapid flashes of a flashlight toward the approaching ship.
procedures.why: Per ColRegs Rule 34(d), this signal indicates doubt about the other vessel's intentions or that collision risk exists.

procedures.action: Illuminate the yacht's sails with a flashlight.
procedures.why: Per ColRegs Rule 36, this improves the yacht's visibility to the approaching ship.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the ship by VHF.
procedures.why: Direct communication can clarify intentions and prompt avoiding action.

procedures.action: Ensure crew wear lifejackets if not already doing so.
procedures.why: Following RNLI advice to wear lifejackets at all times afloat, especially critical when collision risk is imminent.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, consider action under Rule 17(b) if the give-way vessel fails to act.
procedures.why: Rule 17(b) permits/obliges the stand-on vessel to take action to avoid collision when the give-way vessel's action alone is insufficient.

procedures.action: Consider starting the engine to assist avoiding action.
procedures.why: Engine power provides additional maneuverability beyond sail alone to avoid collision.

constraints: OOW should not be diverted to routine tasks (e.g., chart correcting) at the expense of lookout duties.
A dedicated lookout must be present on the bridge during darkness.
Wheelhouse lights must not be left on at night as this impairs lookout.
Yacht actions should follow ColRegs Rules 34(d), 36, and 17(b) as applicable.
warnings: It would be completely unacceptable for wheelhouse lights to be on as this impairs proper lookout.
Engaging in routine tasks such as chart correcting instead of maintaining lookout is unacceptable.
Failure to keep a proper lookout, visually and by radar, risks missing an approaching vessel and developing collision risk.
outcomes: If lookout is properly maintained, the ship should be visible to the yacht at least 20 minutes before a potential collision given fair weather and estimated relative speed of 10 knots.
Early recognition of collision risk (around 2 miles/12 minutes out) allows time for defensive signaling, communication, and evasive action.
Without proper watchkeeping, alarming close-quarters situations as described can occur, risking collision.
key_facts: The reporting yacht could not be identified, so CHIRP could not verify with the ship's manager whether there was truly no one on watch.
In fair weather, the ship was likely visible from the yacht at least three miles away.
Assuming the ship at 15 knots and yacht at 5 knots in the same direction, relative closing speed was about 10 knots, giving roughly 20 minutes of visibility before the incident.
At about 2 miles (approximately 12 minutes before the incident), a risk of collision should have been apparent to the yacht crew.
CHIRP's summary guidance for small craft in such situations is to 'Sail Defensively.'

question_seeds.text: Why is it unacceptable for an OOW to perform chart correcting duties during a watch, even briefly?
What specific actions should a yacht's crew take once risk of collision with a larger vessel becomes apparent?
How should the yacht signal the approaching ship under the ColRegs if its intentions are unclear?
When should the skipper be called to the bridge/deck in a developing close-quarters situation like this?

trace.situation: A CHIRP near-miss report describes a tanker where a junior officer had the con while the Master was on the bridge but distracted by administrative/communication tasks, resulting in a close-quarters situation with an offshore vessel that required a late, large alteration to port.
trace.trigger: Master, distracted by administrative duties, is alerted late (by personally noticing, not by being warned) to a close offshore vessel and must take emergency avoiding action.

procedures.action: CHIRP refers the report to the tanker's manager while protecting reporter/vessel anonymity.
procedures.why: Standard CHIRP practice to encourage confidential reporting.

procedures.action: Manager investigates and obtains a corroborating report from the Master.
procedures.why: To verify the reporter's account and establish facts.

procedures.action: Manager identifies specific failures (lack of BRM, failure to warn Master, poor judgment/coordination, inadequate incident knowledge, failure to follow rules).
procedures.why: To determine root causes for corrective action.

procedures.action: Master conducts training for all deck officers on company safe navigation procedures in congested waters, separation zones, coastal and open sea areas.
procedures.why: To remediate identified knowledge/procedural gaps.

procedures.action: Case circulated fleet-wide for awareness and corrective action.
procedures.why: To prevent recurrence across the fleet.

procedures.action: Manager arranges further training for officers and Master when next in the office.
procedures.why: To reinforce and formalize the remedial training.

procedures.action: Ensure passage plans account for known fixed hazards such as rig positions.
procedures.why: To prevent close-quarters situations arising from inadequate passage planning.

procedures.action: Masters must ensure their presence on the bridge while doing other tasks does not reduce watch-keeper alertness.
procedures.why: To preserve effective bridge team management and situational awareness.

constraints: Reporter and vessel identity must not be disclosed as per CHIRP standard practice.
Master's bridge orders and company navigational procedures must be followed by the watch-keeping team.
Passage plans must account for known navigational hazards such as rig positions.
warnings: Lack of bridge team management can allow close-quarters situations to develop undetected.
Failure to warn the Master of a developing hazard is a critical safety lapse.
Master's administrative/communication distractions can reduce watch-keeper alertness and overall bridge safety.
outcomes: Large late alteration to port was required to avoid the offshore vessel once the Master noticed it.
Manager implemented training and fleet-wide circulation of the case as corrective action.
CHIRP assessed the manager's and Master's response as positive and open.
key_facts: A junior officer held the con while the Master was present but engaged in administrative/communication tasks.
The Master was not warned of the close offshore vessel and only noticed it himself before taking over and altering course.
The manager identified five specific failure categories including BRM, failure to warn, poor judgment, inadequate incident knowledge, and rule non-compliance.
CHIRP added that the passage plan should have accounted for the rig's position, and Masters must not let other tasks reduce watch-keeper alertness.

question_seeds.text: Why did the bridge team fail to warn the Master of the approaching offshore vessel despite his presence on the bridge?
How should Masters balance administrative duties with maintaining bridge team alertness during watch-keeping?
What corrective actions did the tanker's manager implement after this near-miss was reported?
Which passage planning failure contributed to the close-quarters situation with the rig/offshore vessel?

trace.situation: An offshore support vessel dodging near a Mobile Offshore Drilling Unit observed a tanker whose small course alterations increased its CPA with the rig but put it on a near-collision course (0.03nm CPA at 8 cables) with the support vessel itself.
trace.trigger: Radar plot showing a vessel's succession of small course alterations is not appreciably reducing risk of collision as CPA decreases toward a dangerously close range.

procedures.action: Commence and maintain a radar plot on any approaching vessel whose track threatens the rig or own vessel.
procedures.why: To objectively track the other vessel's course changes and CPA trend rather than relying on visual impression.

procedures.action: Continue monitoring even after the other vessel appears to be taking avoiding action for a different target (e.g. the rig).
procedures.why: Small alterations intended to avoid one object (the rig) can inadvertently create a new collision risk with another vessel (the OSV).

procedures.action: Assess whether the other vessel's actions are producing an appreciable reduction in risk of collision, not just a change in CPA relative to a third object.
procedures.why: A succession of small alterations made little difference to the CPA and did not reduce the risk of collision with own vessel.

procedures.action: When satisfied the give-way vessel is taking no appreciable action and CPA has closed to a dangerous range (0.03nm at 8 cables), take positive remedial action by altering course to starboard.
procedures.why: To avoid collision when the other vessel is not fulfilling its obligation to keep well clear.

procedures.action: Continue turning under increased power once the other vessel makes its own avoiding alteration, until it has passed clear astern.
procedures.why: To maximize separation and ensure the other vessel passes clear under the stern.

procedures.action: Complete a round turn under reduced power until risk of collision has gone.
procedures.why: To fully resolve the close-quarters situation and confirm clearance before resuming normal operations.

constraints: Decision to take own avoiding action should be based on continuous radar plotting showing no appreciable reduction in collision risk.
Own vessel was operating at very low speed (2.5 knots) while dodging near the rig, limiting maneuvering options compared to the fast-moving tanker (14 knots).
warnings: A succession of small course alterations by another vessel may not represent genuine or sufficient avoiding action, even if it appears to improve CPA with one target.
Avoiding action taken to increase CPA with one object (e.g. a rig) can create a new, more dangerous collision risk with another vessel in the vicinity.
Allowing CPA to close to 0.03 miles at 8 cables before taking action represents a very late and high-risk point to initiate avoidance.
outcomes: Own vessel's starboard alteration combined with the tanker's eventual large port alteration resulted in the tanker passing clear under own vessel's stern.
Completing a round turn under reduced power confirmed the risk of collision had been eliminated.
key_facts: Own vessel (OSV) was dodging near a MODU at approximately 2.5 knots heading roughly north.
The tanker was approximately 20,000 tonnes, steaming at about 14 knots on a heading of roughly south east.
The tanker's small course alterations increased its CPA with the rig but placed it on a collision course with the OSV.
Radar plot showed CPA closing to 0.03 miles at a range of 8 cables before the OSV took avoiding action.
After the OSV turned to starboard, the tanker made a large alteration to port, and both vessels cleared each other with the tanker passing under the OSV's stern.

question_seeds.text: At what CPA/range should I decide that another vessel is not taking appreciable avoiding action and I must act myself?
Why did the tanker's course corrections for the rig create a new danger for my own vessel, and how should I have anticipated this?
How should I combine radar plotting with helm/engine action when a give-way vessel's small alterations aren't resolving risk of collision?
What is the appropriate sequence of actions (course, power, turn completion) once I decide to take positive remedial action?

trace.situation: A ship's officer of the watch received a garbled Mayday call on VHF channel 16 in mid-ocean indicating a vessel on fire, and the bridge team had to decide how to respond before escalating to the coastguard.
trace.trigger: Reception of an unclear but apparently genuine Mayday distress message on VHF channel 16 reporting a vessel on fire.

procedures.action: Immediately call the Master to the bridge upon receiving an unclear Mayday.
procedures.why: A potential distress situation on fire requires command-level awareness and decision-making.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the vessel in distress repeatedly via VHF channel 16.
procedures.why: To clarify the nature and location of the distress before taking further action.

procedures.action: Check AIS to identify other vessels in the area who may have also heard the Mayday.
procedures.why: To corroborate the distress call and determine if other ships are responding.

procedures.action: Make contact with the vessel and verify whether it genuinely sent the Mayday.
procedures.why: To confirm if the distress is real before alerting external authorities.

procedures.action: Conduct a follow-up conversation to double-check the vessel's safety status once contact is established.
procedures.why: To ensure the situation is truly resolved and not a disguised real emergency.

procedures.action: Close communications only after confirming the Mayday was not genuine.
procedures.why: Avoids triggering unnecessary escalation once the false alarm is verified.

constraints: Must attempt direct verification with the source vessel before reporting to the coastguard.
Must use AIS and other means to gather supporting information when VHF contact fails initially.
Should not escalate to coastguard until reasonable verification attempts have been exhausted or failed.
warnings: Running a Mayday drill over live VHF channel 16 without clear identification as a drill risks being mistaken for a real distress call.
Failure to verify could lead to reporting a false Mayday to the coastguard, triggering an expensive and unnecessary search and rescue operation.
outcomes: Contact was eventually established and the Mayday was confirmed to be part of a training drill, avoiding escalation.
Had contact not been made, the Mayday would have been reported to the coastguard, resulting in a costly and unnecessary search for a vessel on fire.
key_facts: The Mayday was received on VHF channel 16 and was not clearly distinguishable, but indicated a vessel was on fire.
No other vessel responded to the Mayday for 10 minutes before the reporting ship attempted contact.
AIS was used to identify another vessel in the area before contacting the coastguard.
The Mayday was ultimately traced to a training drill conducted by another vessel using real VHF channel 16 transmission.
The same voice heard transmitting the Mayday was later confirmed on the radio as performing a drill.

question_seeds.text: How long should a bridge team wait for other vessels to respond to a Mayday before attempting direct contact or escalating to the coastguard?
Why is AIS useful for verifying the credibility of a Mayday call before contacting the coastguard?
What steps should be taken if contact with the distressed vessel cannot be established after a genuine-sounding Mayday?
Who should be notified first when an unclear Mayday is received: the Master, nearby vessels, or the coastguard?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes an incident where a vessel transmitted an actual Mayday distress call during what was intended to be a simulated emergency drill, and CHIRP comments on the root causes and broader lessons for exercise planning.
trace.trigger: Conducting an emergency communications drill or multi-party exercise involving simulated external communications.

procedures.action: Clearly instruct whoever handles communications during a drill that external transmissions must be simulated, not actually sent.
procedures.why: The junior staff member delegated to handle communications was not sufficiently briefed that external comms should be simulated, leading to an actual Mayday being transmitted.

procedures.action: Explicitly define and communicate the 'communication boundaries' of any exercise, i.e. which external parties may genuinely be contacted and which must be role-played.
procedures.why: Ambiguity about real vs simulated contacts can cause real-world consequences, as shown by both this Mayday incident and the recalled story of a staff member phoning an actual ship about a fictitious injury.

procedures.action: Do not place sole blame on the individual who made the error; review whether proper instructions were given beforehand.
procedures.why: The error may stem from inadequate briefing/delegation rather than individual negligence.

procedures.action: Continue to credit and encourage realistic drill execution while fixing the procedural gap.
procedures.why: The vessel's drill was presumably realistic and valuable despite the transmission error, so the goal is to correct the boundary-setting process, not discourage realism.

constraints: Simulated emergency messages during drills must not be actually transmitted externally.
All personnel involved in an exercise must understand which contacts are real and which are role-played.
warnings: Delegating communications duties during a drill without clarifying simulation requirements can result in an actual distress transmission.
Using real ship or personnel names/details in an exercise scenario can cause external confusion and consternation if boundaries are not made clear.
outcomes: An actual Mayday was transmitted during a drill, prompting a CHIRP report and referral to the vessel's regional manager, with no response received as yet.
In a past intra-office exercise, use of a real ship's name without proper boundary-setting led to an office staff member phoning the actual ship, causing confusion over a fictitious injury.
key_facts: The report was referred to the vessel's manager in the Asia-Pacific region, and no response had been received at time of writing.
CHIRP surmises a junior staff member was delegated communications duty during the drill without being told external transmissions must be simulated.
The underlying issue is a lack of clarity on communication boundaries in exercises, which can involve both on-board drills and larger multi-party exercises.
A past incident involved a real ship's name being used in an intra-office exercise, causing a staff member to call the actual ship about simulated injuries.

question_seeds.text: How should we brief crew before a drill to ensure external emergency communications are clearly simulated and not actually transmitted?
Who should be responsible for verifying communication boundaries before a multi-party or on-board emergency exercise begins?
What steps should we take on our vessel to simulate the preparation of emergency messages during drills without risking actual transmission?
Why is it important not to simply blame the individual who transmitted the real Mayday, and what systemic fix is needed instead?

trace.situation: A near-collision incident where a single-handed sailing boat with a deep-cut Genoa failed to see an anchored vessel until very close range, prompting a CHIRP comment on defensive sailing principles for vessels at anchor.
trace.trigger: A vessel at anchor perceives risk of being run into by an approaching boat that appears unaware of its presence.

procedures.action: Sound the horn early to attract the attention of the approaching vessel as soon as collision risk is suspected.
procedures.why: Early warning gives the other vessel time to notice and take avoiding action before closing to dangerous range.

procedures.action: Get everyone in the cockpit or on deck.
procedures.why: Ensures crew are positioned to respond and are not trapped below if a collision occurs.

procedures.action: Don lifejackets if not already worn.
procedures.why: Lifejackets stowed below may become inaccessible after collision due to flooding/ingress of water.

procedures.action: Start the engine.
procedures.why: Provides capability for an emergency manoeuvre to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Be prepared to slip the anchor.
procedures.why: Allows rapid repositioning or escape if the approaching vessel does not alter course in time.

procedures.action: Know your vessel's position.
procedures.why: Enables a prompt and accurate call for assistance if a collision does occur.

constraints: Applies when a vessel at anchor assesses a genuine risk of being run into.
A proper lookout must be maintained at all times by any skipper, especially single-handers.
warnings: Deep cut Genoas severely restrict forward visibility and can prevent a skipper from seeing vessels ahead.
There is no excuse for not keeping a proper lookout at all times.
Lifejackets stowed below may be inaccessible after a collision due to water ingress.
outcomes: The approaching boat's skipper, alerted by shouting, luffed up then bore away, narrowly avoiding T-boning the anchored vessel amidships.
No apology or acknowledgement was offered by the approaching skipper, who appeared stunned and possibly without crew.
key_facts: The approaching boat closed to within 50 metres before its skipper became aware of the anchored vessel.
The skipper's visibility was restricted by a deep-cut Genoa sail.
The boat appeared to have no additional crew aboard (single-handed).
CHIRP recommends 'Defensive Sailing' principles apply even when anchored, including horn use, crew mustering, lifejackets, engine readiness, anchor-slipping readiness, and position awareness.

question_seeds.text: What immediate actions should my crew take if an anchored vessel appears to be at risk of being run into?
Why is it important to start the engine even while safely at anchor if another vessel is approaching?
How can poor sail configuration (like a deep-cut Genoa) contribute to a collision risk, and what lookout practices mitigate this?
When should the horn be sounded to warn an approaching vessel of collision risk while at anchor?

trace.situation: During an eastbound Gulf of Aden group transit convoy, the lead vessel in the port column found itself in a dangerous close-quarters situation when an overtaking fully laden tanker in the adjacent column matched her speed on a parallel course at only five cables distance, refusing to overtake normally and instead demanding the lead vessel alter course to let her pass.
trace.trigger: A tanker overtaking in convoy increased speed to match the lead vessel's speed on a parallel track at five cables distance without altering course or communicating, creating a close-quarters risk of collision as the convoy approached the disbandment waypoint.

procedures.action: Call the Master to the bridge when officer of the watch is concerned about another vessel's actions.
procedures.why: To ensure command-level assessment of a developing close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Assess available sea-room and other vessels' positions before maneuvering.
procedures.why: Starboard side was blocked by the lower column lead vessel at six cables, and speed reduction was blocked by a following vessel under 1 mile astern in convoy formation.

procedures.action: Query the overtaking vessel by radio as to why she did not overtake on the correct (starboard) side when free to do so.
procedures.why: To clarify intentions and press the overtaking vessel to fulfill her obligation to keep clear.

procedures.action: Advise the overtaking vessel to reduce her own speed and keep well clear.
procedures.why: As the overtaking vessel, she bears responsibility for keeping out of the way of the vessel being overtaken.

procedures.action: When the overtaking vessel made no response and continued course/speed, reduce own speed to let her pass ahead, then alter hard to port around her stern once clear, returning to intended course.
procedures.why: The situation had become impossible and dangerous, requiring the own-ship master to take avoiding action despite being the stand-on/overtaken vessel, to prevent collision.

constraints: Could not alter to starboard because the lower column lead vessel was on the starboard beam at six cables, same speed.
Could not reduce speed because a following vessel in convoy formation was under 1 mile astern.
Convoy formation and escort warship coordination limited independent maneuvering until the final waypoint disbandment call.
warnings: Overtaking vessel showed no sign of altering away and made no attempt to contact the lead vessel despite closing to five cables at matching speed.
Overtaking vessel failed to overtake on the correct side when ample sea-room existed, instead demanding the overtaken vessel alter course.
Situation described by the Master as 'impossible and dangerous' before he took avoiding action.
outcomes: The Master reduced speed, let the tanker continue ahead, then swung around her stern and resumed his intended course toward the Persian Gulf without collision.
The overtaking tanker made no response to being advised to reduce speed or keep clear, continuing her course and speed unchanged.
key_facts: Vessel was lead ship in the port column of an eastbound Gulf of Aden Group Transit escorted by a warship, approaching the final waypoint where the convoy would disband.
A fully laden tanker bound for Singapore (per AIS) began increasing speed at 0330 LT and by 0430 LT was five cables off the port side, matching speed at 12 knots.
The tanker later requested the lead vessel reduce speed and alter hard to port around her stern so she could increase to her max speed of 14 knots and continue east toward Singapore.
The lead vessel was constrained from altering to starboard or reducing speed due to other convoy vessels' positions (six cables to starboard, under 1 mile astern).
There was ample sea-room for the tanker to have overtaken normally to starboard of both column vessels.

question_seeds.text: Why did the tanker not overtake on the starboard side when there was ample sea-room, instead requesting the lead vessel maneuver for her?
How should a convoy lead vessel balance formation-keeping constraints against the need to avoid an overtaking vessel at five cables?
What options remain for a Master when both course alteration to starboard and speed reduction are blocked by other convoy vessels?
Who bears responsibility for keeping clear when an overtaking vessel refuses to respond to radio calls and continues a converging course?

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime Feedback publication discusses a yachtsman's suggestion to fit forced ventilation to a battery compartment using a 12-volt fan, and a follow-up letter adds technical safety caveats.
trace.trigger: Battery compartments can accumulate flammable/explosive hydrogen gas during charging, creating a need for ventilation; if forced ventilation is considered, the fan itself must not become an ignition source.

procedures.action: If fitting a fan to force-ventilate a battery compartment, select one certified as having a spark-proof fan motor.
procedures.why: A standard fan motor can generate sparks capable of igniting flammable gas accumulated from battery charging.

procedures.action: Choose fan/ventilation units complying with ISO 8846 (Small craft - Electrical devices - Protection against ignition of surrounding flammable gases) or the equivalent US standard.
procedures.why: These standards certify equipment as safe for use in gas-prone environments, reducing ignition risk.

procedures.action: Avoid at all costs any electrical components capable of producing a spark in an area classified as IEC Zone 1 (likely to have an explosive gas mixture).
procedures.why: Zone 1 areas have a higher probability of explosive atmosphere presence, making spark-capable equipment extremely hazardous.

procedures.action: Configure the ventilation system so exhausted gas is directed overboard where it can safely disperse.
procedures.why: Ensures flammable gas does not accumulate within the vessel or vent into enclosed/occupied spaces.

constraints: Fan must be certified spark-proof (ISO 8846 or equivalent US standard) if used in battery compartment ventilation.
No spark-capable electrical components should be used in IEC Zone 1 classified areas.
Ventilated gas must be exhausted overboard, not into enclosed internal spaces.
warnings: A non-certified fan motor may produce a spark capable of igniting flammable gas in the battery compartment.
Electrical components capable of sparking should be avoided at all costs in IEC Zone 1 classified areas.
Exhausted gas must be directed overboard to prevent dangerous accumulation.
outcomes: Properly certified spark-proof ventilation reduces the risk of battery compartment gas ignition and explosion.
Failure to use certified equipment or proper overboard venting could result in an explosive gas ignition incident.
key_facts: A previous Maritime Feedback (No.21) suggested yachtsmen consider fitting forced ventilation to battery compartments.
A 12-volt computer fan was suggested as a possible ventilation solution but requires certification as spark-proof.
ISO 8846 covers small craft electrical devices' protection against ignition of surrounding flammable gases.
IEC Zone 1 classification denotes areas likely to have an explosive gas mixture, where spark-capable components must be avoided.
Ventilation exhaust must be directed overboard for safe gas dispersal.

question_seeds.text: What certification standard should a fan meet before being installed in a battery compartment for ventilation?
Why is a standard, non-certified computer fan potentially dangerous in a battery compartment?
How should the ventilation system be configured to safely handle battery compartment gases?
Which IEC zone classification requires avoiding all spark-capable electrical components?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a tanker in a Gulf of Aden anti-piracy convoy that broke away from the convoy formation two hours before the dispersal point to increase speed, followed by a separate yacht lookout report about a developing collision risk near an anchored vessel.
trace.trigger: The tanker requested and received permission from the escorting warship to leave the convoy early, two hours before the scheduled dispersal point, in order to increase speed and clear the piracy-prone area faster.

procedures.action: Request explicit permission from the escorting warship before leaving the convoy formation.
procedures.why: Convoy operations require coordination with the escort to maintain overall formation safety.

procedures.action: Remain in convoy and maintain lane discipline until formally dismissed by the warship.
procedures.why: Breaking away early creates confusion and risk for other vessels still maintaining convoy discipline.

procedures.action: Communicate course and speed changes clearly to all convoy vessels and the warship during any deviation.
procedures.why: Multiple communications were needed between tanker, warship and other ships after the course change, indicating the maneuver caused uncertainty.

procedures.action: Weigh the actual security/time benefit of leaving convoy early against the risk created for other ships.
procedures.why: The CHIRP review found the time saved was minimal while anxiety and risk were caused to another vessel.

constraints: Vessels should stay in the convoy until formally dismissed by the warship (company policy issued after this report).
Convoy operations require lane discipline, with particular care needed as the convoy disperses.
warnings: Breaking away early from a convoy a few miles from the final waypoint can create collision risk and anxiety for other vessels maintaining discipline.
The apparent security benefit of leaving the convoy early may not be real, while the risk to other ships is.
outcomes: The tanker's manager advised all fleet vessels to stay in convoy until dismissed by the warship following the review.
CHIRP issued a general reminder that convoy operations require lane discipline, especially during dispersal.
key_facts: At 0300, with two hours remaining to the convoy dispersal point, the tanker requested and was granted permission by the warship to leave the convoy.
The tanker altered course to port and increased speed while the rest of the convoy was on her starboard side.
The early breakaway caused anxiety for at least one other vessel properly maintaining convoy discipline.
The overall voyage time saved by leaving early was assessed as minimal.
The tanker's management subsequently instructed all fleet vessels to remain in convoy until officially dismissed.

question_seeds.text: Why did CHIRP conclude that breaking away early did not meaningfully enhance the tanker's security?
What company policy change resulted from this convoy breakaway incident?
When, if ever, is it appropriate for a vessel to leave a Gulf of Aden convoy before the dispersal point?
Who must authorize a vessel's departure from convoy formation before it alters course?

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Feedback discusses reader letters analyzing the probable cause of stainless steel bolt failure that led to a rescue boat lifting lug collapsing during swing-out, dropping two crew 12 metres into the sea.
trace.trigger: Publication of a prior CHIRP report (Issue 22) describing failed stainless steel bolts on a rescue boat lifting lug, prompting readers to submit explanations.

procedures.action: Inspect stainless steel through-bolts, fittings, and wire rigging for signs of anaerobic corrosion, especially where bolts are tightly fitted (e.g., GRP installations) but may allow slight seawater seepage.
procedures.why: Anaerobic corrosion occurs when stainless steel is exposed to seawater seepage while deprived of fresh air, and this can occur with no outward signs until failure.

procedures.action: Check wire rigging inner strands, not just outer strands, when inspecting stainless steel wire for corrosion.
procedures.why: Letter notes anaerobic corrosion can affect inner strands of stainless wire rigging while outer strands appear sound.

procedures.action: Treat any loosening of equipment secured by stainless steel bolts (e.g., radar support tripods) as a potential indicator of underlying bolt corrosion.
procedures.why: A prior case showed a radar tripod became loose and nuts/bolt shanks later fell away due to anaerobic corrosion.

warnings: Anaerobic corrosion of stainless steel bolts/fittings can occur with no outward signs of damage.

trace.situation: A laden tanker approaching a busy anchorage at 225°T and 6 knots encountered a bulk carrier on a converging course abeam to port, which refused to give way despite VHF contact and instead increased speed to cross the tanker's bow, forcing emergency avoiding action.
trace.trigger: A give-way vessel in a crossing situation refuses to alter course/speed and continues to close, while the stand-on/constrained vessel has no room to maneuver to starboard due to anchored ships.

procedures.action: Establish VHF contact with the converging vessel to clarify intentions.
procedures.why: To confirm the other vessel's intended action and request a safe passing arrangement before the situation develops into close quarters.

procedures.action: Request the other vessel to slow down and pass astern.
procedures.why: To secure a safe crossing distance given the reporting vessel's own maneuvering was constrained by anchored ships on the starboard side.

procedures.action: Monitor the other vessel's bearing and range continuously after the request is refused.
procedures.why: To detect when the risk of collision becomes imminent (vessel noted at 4 points on port bow, 6 cables, closing).

procedures.action: Stop engines and go slow astern when the other vessel closed to a dangerous range.
procedures.why: To reduce own speed/way and avoid collision since a starboard alteration was blocked by anchored vessels.

constraints: Starboard maneuvering room was unavailable due to the presence of many anchored vessels.
The give-way vessel refused the requested course of action and maintained/increased speed.
Final passing distance of 3 cables was considered unsafe and too close.
warnings: No attempt was made by the give-way vessel for a safer passing distance, in apparent violation of Rules 15 and 16.
Being boxed in by anchored vessels can eliminate the option of a starboard alteration, forcing reliance on engine action alone.
outcomes: The bulk carrier passed at only 3 cables from the tanker's bow, an uncomfortably close distance.
A collision was avoided only by stopping engines and going slow astern after the other vessel refused to give way.
key_facts: The reporting vessel was a large laden tanker on course 225°T at 6 knots approaching a busy anchorage.

The converging bulk carrier was contacted on VHF and asked to slow down and pass astern but refused, maintaining course and later increasing speed to cross the tanker's bow.

trace.situation: An LNG carrier's Chief Officer informed the terminal Loadmaster that the ship's cargo lines were not yet cooled to the required -110°C temperature, yet the Loadmaster commenced loading anyway while the vessel was not even lined up for loading.
trace.trigger: Loadmaster repeatedly asked if the vessel was ready to load despite being told the lines were not adequately cooled (warmest point at -28°C), then began loading at 1000m³/hr without proper line-up or temperature verification.

procedures.action: Conduct Cold ESD test and pre-loading safety discussion between Loadmaster and Chief Officer before loading commences.
procedures.why: Standard safety check required prior to LNG transfer.

procedures.action: Chief Officer must confirm and communicate actual cooldown status of ship's lines before authorizing loading start.
procedures.why: Lines must reach -110°C to avoid thermal shock from cryogenic LNG introduced into warmer piping.

procedures.action: Refuse/stop loading if vessel is not correctly lined up or lines are not sufficiently cooled.
procedures.why: Loading into an unprepared or unlined-up system risks equipment damage and cargo system failure.

procedures.action: Issue a Letter of Protest to the terminal when loading is commenced in violation of agreed procedure.
procedures.why: Formal record protects the ship/owner and documents terminal's procedural breach for accountability.

constraints: Ship's cargo lines must be cooled to -110°C before loading can safely commence.
Vessel must be correctly lined up for loading before cargo transfer begins.
Loadmaster and Chief Officer must agree readiness before loading starts.
warnings: Commencing LNG loading before lines are adequately cooled risks thermal shock to cargo system.
Loading while the vessel is not lined up for loading is a serious procedural breach with potential for major incident.
Terminal non-compliance with its own stated procedures can occur without the operational and reputational consequences a ship would face for an equivalent error.
outcomes: Terminal eventually admitted its loadmaster did not follow the terminal's own loading procedure.
Terminal stated the issue was discussed with all loadmasters and correction was made for the future.

Reporter notes a perceived double standard: had a ship made the equivalent error, demands for dismissal, retraining, and detailed corrective/preventive action plans would likely have followed, whereas the terminal received no comparable scrutiny.
key_facts: Lines must be cooled to -110°C prior to LNG loading; at the time of the incident the warmest part was only -28°C.
The Loadmaster commenced loading at 1000m³/hr despite the Chief Officer's warning that the system was not adequately cooled.
The vessel was not lined up for loading when the Loadmaster initiated cargo transfer.
A Letter of Protest was issued to the terminal, which later acknowledged its loadmaster failed to follow terminal procedure.

question_seeds.text: Why is it critical that LNG cargo lines reach -110°C before loading begins?

trace.situation: A small motor boat towing a disabled speed boat attempted to pass astern of a large harbour tug assisting a berthing vessel, while an outbound ship with its own tug was transiting the same fairway.
trace.trigger: Motor boat and tow chose the shortest route, passing close astern of the first tug while an outbound ship was proceeding past the berthing operation.

procedures.action: Tug master alerted the outbound ship to the developing problem with the motor boat.
procedures.why: To ensure the larger vessel was aware a small craft was being pushed into its path.

procedures.action: Tug master confirmed it was safe to reduce power before doing so.
procedures.why: Reducing power without checking could itself create a hazard, so safety was confirmed first.

procedures.action: Tug reduced power to lessen the propeller wash.
procedures.why: To reduce the wash effect that was forcing the motor boat across the fairway toward the outbound ship's course.

procedures.action: Motor boat operator continued to distance himself from the area once he recognised the danger, until the outbound ship had passed.
procedures.why: To avoid collision risk and allow safe transit once the fairway was clear.

procedures.action: Near miss reported to the tug company and the Port Authority.
procedures.why: To document the hazard and raise awareness for future prevention.

constraints: Small craft should not assume apparent sea room is sufficient when passing near large tugs under power.
Any reduction of tug power near other vessels must first be confirmed safe.
warnings: Modern tugs generate enormous propeller wash power that can extend considerable distances underwater.
Small boats may lack sufficient power to counteract tug propeller wash and can be spun around or forced off course.
Passing close to large harbour tugs, even with apparent sea room, poses a significant hazard to small craft.
outcomes: The motor boat was spun around by the propeller wash but avoided collision with the outbound ship after the tug reduced power.
The incident was reported as a near miss to the tug company and Port Authority, highlighting the hazard for future awareness.
key_facts: A small motor boat was towing a disabled speed boat back into harbour when it was caught in a tug's propeller wash.
The wash forced the motor boat across the fairway toward the course of an outbound ship.
The tug master alerted the ship and reduced power only after confirming it was safe to do so.

trace.situation: A seafarer reports that their lifejacket inflated accidentally and, upon inspection, found the yellow bladder-covering material had separated at the point where the whistle is sewn on, indicating a manufacturing/sewing defect.
trace.trigger: Accidental inflation of the lifejacket exposing a weak point in the fabric sealing around the whistle attachment.

procedures.action: Inspect the lifejacket bladder cover material after any inflation event, not just at annual checks.

procedures.why: The reporter suspects many jackets of the same type/batch may share this fault, posing a risk if relied upon in an emergency.

warnings: Separation of the bladder cover material at the whistle sewing point is a significant risk factor that could compromise lifejacket performance in a real emergency.
Annual checks alone may not reveal defects that only manifest when the lifejacket inflates under actual pressure/duress.
outcomes: The lifejacket inflated accidentally but not during a serious emergency, allowing the defect to be discovered without endangering the wearer.
The defect revealed a potential fleet-wide issue with jackets of this type purchased around 2004.

The yellow material covering the bladder separated at the sewing point where the whistle attaches.

The reporter suspects the sewing defect is common across many similar jackets.

trace.trigger: Tug powering up during a berthing operation generates propeller wash that creates a hazard for nearby small craft/leisure users.

constraints: Reducing tug power must not compromise the safety of the berthing operation
Hazard awareness relies on skipper alertness and existing local warnings
warnings: Propeller wash from tugs during berthing operations can pose a hazard to nearby leisure/small craft

procedures.action: Maintain a proper lookout at all times by sight, hearing, and all available means.
procedures.why: The International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea are predicated on this fundamental requirement.

procedures.action: Scan the horizon more frequently than perceived, verifying actual intervals rather than assumed ones.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Feedback discusses two separate incidents: a lifejacket that accidentally inflated and failed in a confined locker, prompting general advice on lifejacket maintenance and inspection, and a single-handed yacht skipper's near-collision with an inattentive crew on another yacht while he was the stand-on vessel.
trace.trigger: A lifejacket seam failure was investigated after accidental inflation in a confined space, and a stand-on vessel skipper observed an apparent collision course with a yacht showing no visible lookout.

procedures.action: Regularly inspect lifejacket outer casing and straps for damage.
procedures.why: Visual checks by the user can catch obvious deterioration before failure.

procedures.action: Check that the gas bottle is screwed tight without disturbing the bladder stowage.
procedures.why: Loose gas bottles can prevent proper inflation when needed.

procedures.action: Re-stow an inflated lifejacket's bladder strictly per manufacturer's instructions, seeking advice if uncertain.
procedures.why: Improper re-stowage can cause future malfunction or injury.

procedures.action: Have lifejackets inspected by a competent inspector per manufacturer's recommended schedule, including gas bottle examination and weighing.
procedures.why: Competent inspection detects corrosion and pressure loss not visible to the user, as shown by the severely corroded bottle found in service.

procedures.action: During inspection, inflate the lifejacket to prescribed pressure and verify it holds within allowance, accounting for temperature.
procedures.why: Ensures the lifejacket will perform correctly in an emergency.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, continuously monitor the approaching vessel's heading and crew presence, and take avoiding action when collision is assessed as inevitable.
procedures.why: The give-way vessel's crew were not visible/responsive, so the stand-on vessel had to act to prevent collision despite the 'stand-on' rule.

constraints: Lifejacket inspections must follow the manufacturer's recommended schedule and procedure.
A stand-on vessel must initially maintain course and speed under the collision regulations, but must take action when collision becomes unavoidable.
Lifejacket bladders must not be stowed in confined spaces where they cannot fully expand if inflated.
warnings: Storing an inflated or inflatable lifejacket in a confined space can cause abnormally high seam stress and failure.
A severely corroded gas bottle can compromise lifejacket inflation reliability.
Failure to maintain a proper lookout on a give-way vessel can lead to collision even when the other vessel is the stand-on vessel and attempting to avoid it.
outcomes: Manufacturer inspection confirmed the lifejacket seam failed due to restricted bladder expansion in a locker.
The stand-on vessel skipper avoided collision by altering course to pass astern and to port after confirming the other yacht's crew were not keeping watch.
The skipper hailed the inattentive crew after passing, highlighting the lookout failure.
key_facts: The lifejacket involved had a good track record but failed because it inflated inside a small locker, causing excessive seam stress.
Lifejacket inspections should include checking gas bottle tightness, weighing, and pressure testing to a prescribed standard.
A corroded gas bottle was found still in service at the time of inspection.

trace.situation: A yacht sailing near the Casquets Traffic Separation Scheme encountered dense fog (visibility under 200m) and had to use AIS, radar, and VHF to monitor and communicate with converging merchant ship traffic, including one vessel heading directly at them.
trace.trigger: Fog closed in to less than 200 metres visibility while the yacht was approaching the west-going shipping lane near the Casquets TSS, with large ships appearing on radar/AIS as potential collision risks.

procedures.action: Monitor AIS and radar continuously to identify vessels that may pose a collision danger.
procedures.why: Allows early identification of converging traffic in reduced visibility.

procedures.action: Call merchant ships on VHF at long range (e.g., ~11 miles) to confirm mutual awareness of position and intended course.
procedures.why: Establishes communication early so both vessels can plan safe passing before risk becomes urgent.

procedures.action: Re-contact the vessel at closer range (e.g., 8 miles) if initial contact denied seeing the yacht on radar.
procedures.why: Confirms the situation has been resolved and the other vessel now has the yacht on radar/AIS.

procedures.action: Treat the situation as urgent and decide on avoidance action once range closes to about 6 miles with no confirmed resolution.
procedures.why: A slow yacht has far less time and maneuvering capability than a ship travelling at three times its speed, so decisions must be made early.

constraints: Both vessels in dense fog have a duty to make an early decision to avoid contact.
A slow-moving yacht has significantly less opportunity for effective evasive action than a fast merchant ship.
Course was planned to remain clear of the TSS but still close enough to encounter crossing/converging shipping traffic.
warnings: A merchant ship's radar may not initially detect a small vessel even when AIS data suggests a clear plot, leading to false reassurance or confusion.
Relying only on a single VHF confirmation is not sufficient when the other vessel denies radar contact; follow-up confirmation is necessary.
Fog can persist longer than forecast, extending the period of highest collision risk through a traffic lane.
outcomes: Several merchant ships altered course by 1-2 degrees as a precaution after VHF contact, showing effective bridge-to-bridge coordination.
One merchant ship initially denied having the yacht on radar despite AIS plotting, creating uncertainty about actual detection.
At 6 miles the situation was assessed as urgent, requiring the yacht to consider evasive action due to its speed disadvantage.
key_facts: The yacht was equipped with AIS, radar, VHF, two chart plotters, and a radar reflector.
Visibility dropped to less than 200 metres shortly after departure, persisting until after passing the Casquets.
A merchant ship 12 miles away was tracked heading directly for the yacht's position on AIS and radar.
At 10.9 miles the merchant ship denied seeing the yacht on radar; at 8 miles it confirmed radar contact.
The yacht's slower speed (roughly one-third that of the merchant ship) reduced its evasive maneuvering options.

trace.situation: A small vessel acting as stand-on vessel in a traffic separation scheme encountered a merchant ship that refused to alter course or reduce speed despite repeated radio contact, forcing the small vessel to take evasive action and report the incident to Coastguard.
trace.trigger: A give-way vessel fails to take required avoiding action and explicitly refuses to alter course or speed when contacted by the stand-on vessel at close range (2.9 miles).

procedures.action: Avoid any unpredictable maneuver while remaining the stand-on vessel among other traffic.
procedures.why: Unpredictable action could create confusion or additional collision risk with other vessels in the vicinity.

procedures.action: Attempt repeated radio contact with the approaching vessel to clarify intentions.
procedures.why: To establish communication and confirm whether the other vessel intends to give way as required.

procedures.action: When the give-way vessel confirms it will not alter course or speed, take independent action by turning onto a reciprocal course until the ship has crossed the intended track.
procedures.why: To avoid collision since the other vessel has made clear it will not fulfill its give-way obligation, placing responsibility for avoiding action on the stand-on vessel.

procedures.action: Report the incident to the nearest Coastguard station while maneuvering.
procedures.why: To create a record in case of any mishap and alert authorities to the non-compliant vessel's behavior.

constraints: As stand-on vessel, must not take early or erratic action that could confuse other nearby traffic.
Must still take independent avoiding action if the give-way vessel clearly will not act, to prevent collision.
warnings: A give-way vessel may explicitly refuse to alter course or speed, placing collision-avoidance burden entirely on the stand-on vessel.
Relying solely on radio communication without a contingency maneuver can leave a vessel in a dangerous situation if the other ship is non-compliant.
outcomes: The small vessel safely avoided collision by turning onto a reciprocal course until the ship crossed its track.
The incident was reported to Portland Coastguard as a precaution.
Other merchant captains on the same journey were cooperative and proactively warned of other traffic, including one ship confirming safe passing after losing radar contact.
key_facts: The reporting vessel was the stand-on vessel in a traffic separation scheme with other vessels nearby.
At 2.9 miles range, the merchant ship's captain confirmed he would not alter course or reduce speed.
The stand-on vessel turned onto a reciprocal course and continued until the ship crossed its intended track.

Other encounters on the same voyage involved cooperative merchant captains who warned of other traffic and confirmed safe passing.

trace.situation: CHIRP reviews a near-miss fog encounter between a yacht and a bulk carrier, clarifying correct ColRegs terminology and conduct required in restricted visibility.
trace.trigger: Vessels in restricted visibility (fog) detect each other by radar and must decide on avoiding action.

procedures.action: Apply Rule 19 (Conduct of vessels in restricted visibility), not Section II give-way/stand-on terminology, when vessels are not in sight of one another.
procedures.why: Section II terms do not apply in Section III (restricted visibility) situations per ColRegs.

procedures.action: Take avoiding action in ample time once risk of collision is detected by radar.
procedures.why: Rule 19(d) requires both vessels to act early to avoid collision in restricted visibility.

procedures.action: Proceed at a safe speed appropriate to restricted visibility.
procedures.why: Required by Rule 19; OOW on bulk carrier failed to do so.

procedures.action: Sound appropriate fog signals.
procedures.why: Fog signals were required but not sounded by the bulk carrier.

procedures.action: Avoid using VHF radio for collision avoidance decisions.
procedures.why: ColRegs make no provision for VHF use in collision avoidance; MCA MGN 324 advises against it.

procedures.action: Contact the Coastguard if there is a risk of mishap.
procedures.why: Communication with Coastguard in case of a potential incident was deemed prudent.

procedures.action: Report such near-miss incidents to CHIRP as soon as possible after they occur.
procedures.why: Delay reduces chance of electronic records or crew availability for follow-up, hampering investigation.

constraints: Give-way/stand-on terminology applies only under Section II (vessels in sight of one another), not Section III (restricted visibility).
Avoiding action in restricted visibility must be taken in ample time once risk of collision is identified by radar.
VHF should not be relied upon for collision avoidance communication.
Incident reports to CHIRP should be submitted promptly to preserve evidentiary value.

VHF use for collision avoidance is discouraged and not provided for in ColRegs.
Cavalier attitude by OOW regarding safe speed and avoiding action is unacceptable and unsafe.
Delayed incident reporting risks loss of electronic records and witness availability.
outcomes: The yacht's turn-away action was appropriate but could have been taken earlier.

Rule 19(d) requires both vessels to take avoiding action in ample time in restricted visibility.
The bulk carrier OOW detected the yacht by radar but did not take adequate avoiding action, reduce speed, or sound fog signals.
CHIRP recommends against VHF use for collision avoidance, citing MCA MGN 324.

trace.situation: A yacht motoring in the Solent in force 6 wind suffered sudden engine stoppage and propeller fouling after striking unmarked/poorly visible fishing gear (a white fender marker, weighted anchor warp with fish hooks, and a grapnel).
trace.trigger: Loud bang followed by instant engine stop, with the engine only able to run in neutral but stalling when gear was engaged ahead or astern.

procedures.action: Attempt to restart and diagnose the engine when it stops unexpectedly, testing operation in neutral before engaging gear.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the fault is an internal engine problem or an external obstruction such as fouled fishing gear.

procedures.action: If gear stalls the engine when engaged but it runs fine in neutral, suspect propeller fouling and avoid forcing the drivetrain.
procedures.why: Forcing an already-damaged, fouled propeller/shaft risks further mechanical damage.

procedures.action: Return to berth under sail/alternative means rather than relying on the compromised propulsion.
procedures.why: Avoids further damage and ensures safe return without dependable engine power.

procedures.action: Arrange for divers to inspect and clear the propeller and have the vessel lifted for inspection/repair.
procedures.why: Confirms extent of damage (badly damaged feathering propeller) and allows proper repair (spare propeller fitted).

constraints: Marker buoys for fishing gear may be dragged below the surface in moderate tidal streams, reducing visibility.
White markers are especially difficult to spot among white horses (wind-driven wave crests).

trace.situation: A connecting rod failure in a generator caused major loss of cooling water in a system shared between main and auxiliary engines, leading to shutdown of all main engines shortly after departure from port.

procedures.action: Investigate unusual loud noises from machinery spaces immediately.
procedures.why: Early detection of mechanical failure allows faster response and limits damage.

procedures.action: Start the stand-by generator to maintain electrical power.

procedures.why: Rapid team mobilization is essential for coordinated emergency response.

procedures.action: Follow the technical emergency reaction checklist to isolate the cooling water system using remote isolation valves.
procedures.why: Isolating the damaged generator's cooling circuit prevents complete loss of cooling water to the main engines and other generators, as previously identified as a single-point failure risk.

procedures.action: Rapidly refill the system header tank using the remotely operated high-capacity cooling water pump.
procedures.why: Restores cooling water inventory needed to resume main engine operation.

procedures.action: Restart main engines as soon as cooling water is restored.

outcomes: Main engines shut down within three minutes of the failure due to cooling water loss, but were restarted within two minutes due to rapid isolation and refilling actions.

trace.situation: A sailing yacht acting as stand-on vessel in the English Channel (outside a TSS) detected a constant bearing with a fast-moving ship on a crossing course and had to decide when and how to take avoiding action after attempts to attract attention failed.
trace.trigger: Visual and AIS-confirmed constant bearing/decreasing range (risk of collision) with the give-way vessel showing no response to light signals or VHF calls as the range closed to 1.5 NM.

procedures.action: Visually monitor the bearing of the approaching vessel for signs of change.
procedures.why: A constant bearing indicates a risk of collision under the stand-on vessel's obligation to assess the situation.

procedures.action: Cross-check the visual bearing assessment using AIS receiver data (course, speed, MMSI, name).
procedures.why: AIS data confirmed the ship's course (095°) and speed (17.6 kn), corroborating the constant-bearing observation.

procedures.action: Attempt to attract the other vessel's attention using a large torch directed at the ship, repeated as range closed.
procedures.why: To alert the approaching ship visually when no response was otherwise apparent.

procedures.action: Make a call on VHF Channel 16 to the other vessel.
procedures.why: Standard means to establish communication and warn of collision risk, especially since the yacht had no DSC capability.

procedures.action: Continue observing the other ship's course for any change after signaling attempts.
procedures.why: To determine whether the give-way vessel was taking appropriate action before the stand-on vessel needed to act itself.

procedures.action: When no course change was detected, alter course to port and tack, showing the green sector of the navigation light, to pass behind the vessel.
procedures.why: As stand-on vessel, action was taken only after it became apparent the give-way vessel was not keeping clear, to avoid collision by passing astern.

procedures.action: Continue to monitor the other ship after the avoiding action to confirm no further course change.
procedures.why: To ensure the maneuver was effective and the vessels would safely separate.

constraints: Yacht was not in a traffic separation scheme at the time of the encounter.
Yacht was equipped only with an AIS receiver (not a transponder), tri-lens radar reflector, and non-DSC VHF.
As stand-on vessel, the yacht initially maintained course until it was clear the other vessel was not responding or altering course.
warnings: A ship showed no response to torch signals or VHF Channel 16 calls despite being hailed as the risk of collision developed.

outcomes: The yacht's avoiding action (altering course to port/tacking) resulted in the other vessel passing less than 0.5 NM away, indicating a successful but close-quarters avoidance.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report examines a near-collision between a yacht and a ship, analyzing the yacht's use of a torch and avoiding action under the ColRegs, and discussing how VHF, AIS, and DSC radio could have improved communication and collision avoidance.

procedures.action: Alter course to starboard and gybe away from the approaching ship rather than altering to port and tacking towards it.
procedures.why: This generally takes the yacht away from the approaching danger, provided the gybe can be carried out safely.

procedures.action: Carefully observe the other vessel throughout the avoiding action.
procedures.why: The other vessel may concurrently make a last-minute alteration of course.

procedures.action: Attempt contact with the ship via VHF channel 16.

trace.situation: A yacht's anchor windlass refit (new heavy-duty cables passed through a watertight bulkhead, sealed with compound) failed during a fast heavy-weather coastal passage, causing seawater ingress into a forecabin battery compartment.

procedures.action: Activate bilge pumps and use buckets to reduce water level immediately on discovering ingress.
procedures.why: To control flooding and prevent it worsening before the source is identified.

procedures.action: Systematically check all seacocks, rudder, and prop shaft for ingress sources.
procedures.why: To rule out common known ingress points before investigating further.

procedures.action: Start engine, stow sails, and proceed to a sheltered bay to investigate.
procedures.why: To stabilize the vessel and conduct a safe, controlled inspection away from heavy sea conditions.

procedures.action: Inspect the fore-cabin compartment under the bunks containing the new battery installation.
procedures.why: To locate the actual source of flooding once other ingress points were excluded.

procedures.action: Inspect the watertight bulkhead penetrations for the windlass cables.
procedures.why: To identify that the sealing compound had pulled away due to cable movement/flex.

procedures.action: Secure the cabling and reseal the bulkhead holes.
procedures.why: To restore the watertight integrity of the bulkhead and prevent recurrence.

procedures.action: Empty, wash down with fresh water, dry, and spray electrical components with WD40.
procedures.why: To mitigate corrosion and damage from seawater exposure.

procedures.action: Inspect bilges more frequently going forward.
procedures.why: Lesson learned to detect ingress earlier.

procedures.action: Fully inspect any completed refit/repair work, especially cable runs through watertight bulkheads.
procedures.why: Excess cable length between bulkhead and windlass allowed flex that worked the sealant loose; securing cables would likely have prevented seal failure.

constraints: Bulkhead penetrations for cabling must remain watertight under dynamic flexing/movement in heavy seas.
New installations/refits affecting watertight integrity should be verified under representative sea conditions before relying on them for passage-making.
warnings: Sealing compound alone is insufficient to maintain watertight integrity if cabling is not also mechanically secured against flexing.
An early-season heavy weather 'sea trial' can expose latent faults that calm conditions would not reveal.
Flooding events can disable critical equipment (e.g., solenoid/windlass) even if not immediately apparent.
outcomes: Flooding was contained and traced to a bulkhead cable penetration seal failure rather than hull fittings.
A drowned solenoid was the only lasting damage, rendering the windlass inoperable.
The crew avoided attempting a planned Channel crossing that day, averting a potentially more serious incident offshore.
key_facts: New windlass cables were run through a watertight bulkhead and sealed with sealing compound only, without additional cable securing.
Repeated immersion of the anchor locker in heavy seas caused cable flex that pulled the seal away, allowing seawater ingress.
A full seacock/rudder/prop shaft check excluded other ingress sources before the bulkhead cause was found.

trace.situation: A yacht under power passed close astern of a tanker in a crossing situation, then contacted the tanker by VHF only to learn the tanker had not detected the yacht on radar despite a radar reflector being deployed.

trace.trigger: A crossing situation with risk of collision between a power-driven yacht and a tanker where the give-way vessel delayed taking avoiding action until a late stage.

procedures.action: As the give-way vessel, take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the other vessel.

procedures.action: Alter course to starboard well before the situation becomes critical.
procedures.why: An earlier alteration to starboard would have been prudent, as identified in the yachtsman's Lessons Learned.

procedures.action: If necessary, use light or sound signals, or direct a searchlight beam toward the danger, to attract the attention of another vessel.
procedures.why: Rule 36 permits such signals provided they cannot be mistaken for other authorized signals and do not embarrass any vessel.

procedures.action: Maintain a dedicated lookout in addition to the officer of the watch during hours of darkness.
procedures.why: A tanker underway at night should have a dedicated lookout to detect other vessels' lights in good visibility and smooth sea conditions.

procedures.action: Use attention-attracting signals to be seen, not to intimidate other vessels.
procedures.why: Mariners should treat each other with courteous respect; the aim is to attract attention, not to scare the other vessel.

constraints: The give-way vessel must act early and substantially, so far as possible (Rule 16).

Failure to see a vessel's lights in good visibility and smooth sea calls into question the effectiveness of the lookout maintained.

trace.situation: A yacht crossing the Dover Strait TSS suffered a fouled propeller, losing propulsion and nearly colliding with crossing ships and a ferry near Dover Harbour entrance before being towed to safety by a harbour launch.
trace.trigger: Propeller fouled by trawl net debris while crossing the North bound TSS lane in calm, windless conditions, reducing speed and maneuverability.

procedures.action: Make an advisory call to the Coast Guard as well as Port Control when immobilised.

procedures.action: Prepare the anchor for letting go, with extra warps attached if needed, if being swept toward a hazardous area.

procedures.why: In calm conditions with no wind, sailing to safety was not possible, so in-water clearance was the only option.

constraints: Vessel was transiting a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) lane with crossing traffic that had to be avoided.

Vessel was within 200m of a ferry while immobilised near Dover Harbour entrance.
Rope cutters fitted did not clear net debris, so mechanical aids were insufficient.

outcomes: The yacht was safely towed into harbour by a Harbour launch after being immobilised.
A ferry narrowly avoided the yacht by 200m.
No damage was found to the propeller or shaft after the net was removed by diving.
Three ships had to be avoided with difficulty while crossing the TSS at reduced speed.
key_facts: The propeller was fouled by 1-1.5m of 80mm square mesh green trawl net while crossing the North bound TSS lane in the Dover Strait.

The yacht was in contact with Dover Port Control but had not called the Coast Guard.
