procedures.action: Plan a passing route maintaining at least the recommended safe distance from the salvage operation (1 nm) when converging/overtaking traffic is present.
procedures.why: To avoid entering the salvage safety zone while managing surrounding traffic.

procedures.action: Acknowledge guard vessel's initial advisory on location and recommended safe passing distance.
procedures.why: Guard vessel's legitimate role is to inform vessels of the safety zone extent.

procedures.action: When given a specific course-alteration instruction, move the conversation to a working channel and question the guard vessel's reasoning.
procedures.why: To clarify whether the instruction is based on valid risk assessment and to free Channel 16 for distress traffic.

procedures.action: Independently verify CPA/TCPA with the other converging vessel before accepting or rejecting the guard vessel's instruction.
procedures.why: The master, not the guard vessel, has the equipment and full situational picture to assess collision risk.

procedures.action: Decline the instruction if own assessment shows sufficient sea room, and restate intended track.
procedures.why: Guard vessel's authority is limited to protecting the salvage safety zone, not acting as a VTS directing traffic between other vessels.

procedures.action: Continue to monitor and maintain the planned safe passing distances for both the salvage zone and the other vessel through to completion of the transit.
procedures.why: To ensure safe navigation despite the disputed instruction.

constraints: Guard vessel's authorized role is limited to preventing vessels from entering the salvage operation's safety zone, not general traffic direction.
Minimum passing distance of 1 nautical mile from the salvage operation must be maintained.
Only vessels directly involved have full equipment/information to assess collision risk with other traffic.
VHF Channel 16 should be vacated for working communications, not held for extended instructional exchanges.
warnings: Do not blindly follow navigational instructions from a guard vessel, as it may lack the authority or equipment to properly assess collision risk between other vessels.
Officers unfamiliar with an area may mistakenly interpret guard vessel instructions as coming from an authority with power to direct shipping, which can be dangerous.
Following the guard vessel's instruction in this case would have put the vessel into conflict with at least two other vessels transiting west of the salvage operation.
outcomes: The vessel safely transited east of the salvage operation maintaining a minimum distance of 1.1 nautical miles and a minimum CPA of 1 mile off the other ship.
The guard vessel operator stated he would file a report regarding the master's refusal to comply with his instruction.
key_facts: The ship planned to pass 1 nm east of the salvage operation while overtaking north-bound traffic to the west.
At 2.5 miles from the salvage operation, the planned CPA from the salvage works was 1.4 miles.
The guard vessel instructed an alteration to port, citing an apparent lack of sea room for a vessel 3 miles away on the starboard quarter, whose actual CPA was 0.9 miles.
The guard vessel's role was limited to safety-zone enforcement around the salvage operation, not acting as a VTS.
The master achieved a final passing distance of 1.1 nm from the salvage works and 1 nm CPA from the other vessel.

trace.situation: A sailing yacht acting as stand-on vessel in the Channel, in confused post-storm seas but good visibility, had to repeatedly hail an approaching passenger ship by VHF after it failed to respond or take avoiding action, resulting in a very close quarters situation.

procedures.action: Call the vessel on VHF Ch.16, stating own position and aspect, and request its intentions.

procedures.action: Repeat the VHF call multiple times in quick succession if no response is received.

procedures.action: Escalate messaging to an urgent demand for 'immediate avoiding action' when the close-quarters situation becomes critical.

procedures.action: Log the incident in the ship's log after the encounter.
procedures.why: Creates a record of the near-miss and the other vessel's late avoiding action and acknowledgement of fault.

warnings: Ships do not always keep a good visual lookout.

outcomes: The passenger ship eventually turned hard to starboard, passing ahead of the yacht by only about 20 metres (two boat lengths).

trace.situation: An angling boat at anchor in the Solent approaches, displaying the anchor ball and running AIS with a radar reflector fitted, found itself on a direct collision course with a large ship that failed to respond to VHF calls until Coast Guard intervened.
trace.trigger: A large vessel turned onto a direct collision course with the anchored angling boat and did not respond to repeated VHF calls on Channel 16.

procedures.action: Continuously monitor approaching vessel traffic while at anchor and assess closing range/course for risk of collision.
procedures.why: Early detection (at 4 miles) gave initial reassurance but continued monitoring revealed the closing ship had not deviated, prompting escalation.

procedures.action: Check AIS data on the approaching vessel to confirm speed and course.
procedures.why: Confirmed the ship was on a direct collision course at 12.8 knots, validating the danger.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the approaching ship directly on VHF Channel 16.
procedures.why: Direct hailing is the first line of warning to the other vessel.

procedures.action: When direct calls go unanswered, contact Coast Guard immediately and explain the situation.
procedures.why: Coast Guard can raise the vessel on other channels and has authority/visibility the small craft lacks.

procedures.action: Start engine and prepare to cut the anchor line while awaiting resolution.
procedures.why: Enables immediate evasive action if the ship does not alter course in time.

constraints: Vessel was at anchor and displaying the black ball day shape for a vessel at anchor.
Vessel had AIS Class A and B transmitting and a large commercial radar reflector fitted.
Visibility was excellent (daylight, good conditions) at the time of the encounter.
The approaching ship was reportedly monitoring VHF channels 12, 13 and 16 per its own account.
warnings: A vessel equipped with AIS, radar reflector and day shapes may still not be seen or responded to by a large ship even in excellent visibility.
Large vessels claiming to monitor VHF 12/13/16 may still fail to hear or respond to calls from small craft.
Small craft should not assume early detection (e.g. at 4 miles) guarantees the other vessel will give way or alter course.
outcomes: Coast Guard successfully raised the ship and redirected it to Channel 67 to resolve the situation.
The ship altered course to port and passed approximately 300 yards ahead of the angling boat, avoiding collision.

The angling boat skipper was left with unresolved concerns about why the large ship deviated from the deep water channel, failed to respond to AIS/radar/radio, and did not detect the small vessel or its own course change sooner.
key_facts: The angling boat was at anchor fishing in the approaches to the Solent, displaying a black ball, with AIS Class A and B running and a large commercial radar reflector fitted.
The large ship turned south onto a direct collision course when about four miles away from the anchored boat.
Three VHF calls to the ship on Channel 16 went unanswered; Solent Coast Guard was then contacted and successfully raised the ship, directing it to Channel 67.
The ship's radio operator stated they had been monitoring Channels 12, 13 and 16 but had not heard the angling boat's calls, though Coast Guard did hear them.
The ship turned to port and passed about 300 yards in front of the anchored angling boat, avoiding collision.

question_seeds.text: Why did the large ship fail to respond to AIS, radar reflector returns, and repeated VHF calls despite claiming to monitor the relevant channels?
What should a small anchored vessel do when a large ship on a collision course does not respond to direct VHF hailing?
At what point (range/time) should a Captain escalate a developing collision risk from direct hailing to contacting Coast Guard?
Who on the large ship's bridge should have been responsible for recognizing the course deviation as creating a collision risk sooner?

trace.situation: A sailing yacht under sail entering harbour through a short narrow channel at high speed encountered a commercial vessel leaving harbour from the opposite direction, leading to a dangerous close-quarters near miss.
trace.trigger: Two vessels approaching a narrow channel from opposite directions with one acting as stand-on and the other as give-way vessel under the navigation rules.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, maintain course and speed while situation remains safe to do so.
procedures.why: Standard collision regulation expectation that the give-way vessel will take early action to avoid the stand-on vessel.

procedures.action: As give-way vessel, give way early by slowing or waiting before entering the narrow channel.
procedures.why: Give-way vessel is obligated to avoid impeding the stand-on vessel, especially in constrained waters with shoal hazards.

procedures.action: Sound appropriate sound signals and take avoiding action if collision becomes imminent despite stand-on status.
procedures.why: Final avoidance to prevent collision when the other vessel fails to give way in time.

constraints: Narrow channel with dangerous shoal water on either side limits maneuvering options
Stand-on vessel must hold course unless collision is imminent and avoidance is clearly necessary
Give-way vessel must take early and substantial action, not delay until last moment
regulations: COLREGs (implied: stand-on/give-way rules, narrow channel rules, sound signals)
warnings: Delayed or aggressive give-way action in narrow channels with shoal water creates high collision risk
A collision between a small yacht and a commercial vessel in this situation could easily cause fatalities
outcomes: Near miss occurred: commercial vessel passed approximately 25 yards from the yacht's bows after a late turn
No collision occurred, but crew and vessel were placed in significant danger
key_facts: Yacht was under sail, stand-on vessel, speed over ground 9 knots in strong wind
Commercial vessel was give-way vessel but instead increased speed to 10-15 knots to beat the yacht through the channel
Commercial vessel sounded one short blast and turned to starboard only 50-70 yards from the yacht's bows
Channel had dangerous shoal water on either side, limiting the yacht's options to turn away

question_seeds.text: Why did the give-way vessel increase speed instead of slowing down before the narrow channel?
What should the stand-on vessel do if the give-way vessel fails to take early avoiding action in a narrow channel?

Who bears responsibility for avoiding collision when both stand-on and give-way obligations are in play in a narrow channel?

trace.situation: CHIRP reviews a reported close encounter between an anchored angling leisure boat and an approaching commercial vessel, offering general guidance on anchor-vessel identification, ColRegs status, passing distance perception, and VHF/GMDSS alerting practices.
trace.trigger: A near-miss/close-encounter report submitted to CHIRP involving a leisure angling vessel at anchor and a commercial ship, after the ship's manager concluded no regulatory breach occurred.

procedures.action: Treat an angling vessel at anchor as relying on her anchor ball for identification, not as a vessel 'engaged in fishing' under ColRegs.
procedures.why: An angling vessel does not have fishing-vessel status under the ColRegs, so approaching ships must rely on anchor signals/shapes rather than fishing-vessel rules.

procedures.action: Bridge watchkeepers should identify an anchored small craft as early as possible, ideally beyond about 2 miles.
procedures.why: An anchor ball may only become identifiable at roughly 2 miles or less, and a vessel at 12 knots covers that distance in just 10 minutes, leaving little time to assess and take avoiding action.

procedures.action: Do not assume a small craft's movements are predictable or that holding course/speed while 'watching to see what the boat does' is acceptable without full ColRegs compliance.
procedures.why: Small craft movements can appear erratic to OOWs, but holding course and speed without proper assessment risks non-compliance with the ColRegs.

procedures.action: Consider passing distance from the small boat's perspective, not just from a professional mariner's confined-waters standard.
procedures.why: A passing distance of more than one cable may be deemed adequate by professional mariners but can still appear dangerously close from a small boat's cockpit.

procedures.action: Small craft should not rely solely on a VHF Channel 16 call to alert an approaching commercial vessel; use DSC/GMDSS alerting where possible.
procedures.why: Commercial vessels are no longer required to maintain a Channel 16 listening watch under GMDSS, and a DSC call actively sounds an alert on the bridge, unlike a voice call on Channel 16 which may be missed.

constraints: An angling vessel is not classified as 'engaged in fishing' under the ColRegs.
Commercial vessels have no mandatory requirement to maintain a listening watch on VHF Channel 16 post-GMDSS.
Any guidance given does not condone non-compliance with the ColRegs.
warnings: An anchor ball may only be identifiable at about 2 miles or less, leaving limited time for an approaching ship to react.
Holding course and speed while 'waiting to see' what a small craft does may breach ColRegs obligations.
A small vessel should not assume a Channel 16 call will be heard or acted upon by an approaching commercial ship.
outcomes: The ship's manager reviewed the incident and found no inappropriate action or regulatory contravention by the ship.
CHIRP issued general observations to improve mutual understanding between leisure and commercial mariners in future close-quarters situations.
key_facts: An angling vessel at anchor is not considered a vessel 'engaged in fishing' under the ColRegs.
An anchor ball may only be identifiable to an approaching vessel at about 2 miles or less.
A ship travelling at 12 knots covers 2 miles in approximately 10 minutes, limiting reaction time.
Since GMDSS introduction, DSC is the primary distress/urgency alerting method on VHF, and commercial vessels are not required to keep a Channel 16 watch.
Professional mariners may consider a passing distance of more than one cable adequate in confined waters, though it can appear close from a small boat.

question_seeds.text: Why might my bridge team mistakenly assume an anchored angling boat is underway, and what should change in our lookout practice?
How much time will my vessel have to react once an anchor ball becomes visible at typical approach speeds?
What is the regulatory status of an angling vessel under the ColRegs, and does it affect our give-way obligations?
Which VHF/GMDSS alerting method should I expect a small craft to use, and should my bridge still maintain a Channel 16 watch?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a near-collision in a narrow channel involving a sailing vessel, where the hazardous assumption was that the other vessel would take avoiding action rather than continue on its course.
trace.trigger: A mariner assumes another vessel will act predictably (e.g., give way or alter course) instead of planning for the possibility it will carry on unchanged.

procedures.action: Continuously ask 'What if the other vessel carries on?' when assessing collision risk.
procedures.why: The hazardous assumption in this incident was that the other vessel would not continue on its course, which proved false and created risk of collision.

warnings: Do not assume another vessel will alter course or give way; always consider the worst-case scenario of it maintaining its current action.
outcomes: The lesson from this yacht incident was judged applicable across all parts of the maritime sector, including commercial shipping.
key_facts: The report originated from a yacht but was placed in the Commercial section of the journal because its lessons apply broadly.
The hazardous assumption identified was that the other vessel would not simply carry on.
The incident occurred in a narrow channel involving a sailing vessel and stand-on/give-way considerations.

question_seeds.text: Why would a yacht incident be included in the Commercial section of the CHIRP journal?
How should I apply the 'what if the other vessel carries on' principle when navigating a narrow channel?

trace.situation: A pilot reports observing a pilot ladder manufactured with aluminium 'vee' clamps instead of whipping thread to secure treads to the manila main lines, a design that risks cutting into the ropes over time.
trace.trigger: Pilot boarding a vessel at anchor via pilot ladder and inspecting its condition while climbing.
warnings: Once a pilot has transferred from the service boat onto the bottom of the ladder, they are committed and cannot easily abort if the ladder is defective.
Aluminium clamps with sharp edges can cut into the manila main lines over time, weakening the ladder's structural integrity.
Factory-installed aluminium clamps are a manufacturing defect, not a ship's staff modification, meaning the risk may be present on ladders as supplied new.
outcomes: Potential degradation of the pilot ladder's main lines due to sharp aluminium edges cutting into the manila rope, increasing risk of ladder failure during transfer.
key_facts: The pilot observed aluminium 'vee' shaped clamps used instead of whipping thread above and below the vee block at each tread.
The clamps had wings formed around the main line to seize the integral block and hold the tread in place.
This clamp system was the original manufacturing method, not a later ship's staff modification.
The aluminium blocks had sharp edges at the point of contact with the main line, risking cutting into the rope over time.
This report references an earlier article 'Killer in Manila' in Issue 27 of the same publication.

question_seeds.text: What specific defect did the pilot identify in the pilot ladder's construction?
Why is it particularly dangerous for a pilot to discover a ladder defect only after committing to the climb?
How can inspection procedures catch manufacturing defects like sharp aluminium clamps before a pilot boards?

trace.situation: A power-driven vessel transiting a narrow channel outbound encountered a sailing vessel under sail on the opposite side, and both vessels assumed the other would keep clear, resulting in a close-quarters situation in strong wind conditions.
trace.trigger: A power-driven vessel constrained to a narrow channel approaches or passes a sailing vessel that could potentially cross or impede its track.

procedures.action: Do not assume the other vessel will keep clear; actively assess the situation before committing to the channel.
procedures.why: Both vessels in this case assumed the other would give way, and both assumptions proved unfounded.

procedures.action: If uncertain, hold back and delay entry into the narrow channel until the crossing situation is resolved.
procedures.why: The situation could have been avoided if either or both vessels had held back to assess before committing to the channel.

procedures.action: As a power-driven vessel, anticipate that an approaching yacht may suddenly and unexpectedly alter course due to wind gusts.
procedures.why: Sailing vessels are subject to sudden course changes from wind effects, which can defeat assumptions about their intended track.

procedures.action: As a sailing vessel in strong wind, shorten sail early to retain maneuverability needed to comply with the ColRegs as either stand-on or give-way vessel.
procedures.why: Retaining the ability to manoeuvre is essential to properly execute ColRegs obligations, and the old maxim of shortening sail before difficulty remains valid.

procedures.action: Keep as far to the starboard side of the channel centre as possible and avoid increasing speed while transiting.
procedures.why: This is a prudent precaution taken by the Master in this case in case the yacht stood on into the channel.

constraints: Rule 9(b) of ColRegs restricts vessels (including sailing vessels under 20m) from impeding a vessel that can only safely navigate within a narrow channel.
A vessel's compliance with Rule 9(b) does not guarantee the other vessel will behave as expected.
warnings: It is unusual in collision cases for a court to find that one vessel was 100% liable with no liability attaching to the other.
Assuming the other vessel will keep clear is a hazardous assumption that can lead to close-quarters situations or collision.
A sailing vessel in strong wind may lose the ability to manoeuvre as required by ColRegs if not properly sailed/reefed in time.
outcomes: No collision occurred, but the close-quarters situation likely caused considerable anxiety on both vessels.
Had a collision occurred, there would have been lengthy argument over interpretation of the situation and applicability of Rule 9(b).
key_facts: The power-driven vessel was outbound through a narrow channel and noticed a sailing vessel under sail on the opposite side.
The Master maintained speed without increasing it and stayed to starboard of the channel centre as a precaution.
Both vessels assumed the other would keep clear, and both assumptions were incorrect.
CHIRP's role is not to assign blame but to identify lessons learned from the near-miss.
Strong wind conditions were a contributing factor to the close-quarters situation.

question_seeds.text: Why is it hazardous to assume a sailing vessel will keep clear even when I am constrained to a narrow channel under Rule 9(b)?
How should I adjust my passage plan or speed when I see a sailing vessel on the opposite side of a narrow channel in strong winds?
What precautionary actions should I take as a power-driven vessel if an approaching yacht might alter course due to wind gusts?
When should I hold back and reassess rather than commit to entering a narrow channel alongside a sailing vessel?

trace.situation: CHIRP comments on a 2010 IMPA Safety Campaign survey finding persistent defects in pilot boarding arrangements and urges mariners and pilots to inspect and report such defects.
trace.trigger: Discovery of a defect in pilot ladder or boarding arrangements, or awareness of aluminium grippers/ferrules in ladder construction.

procedures.action: Ensure robust procedures exist for inspecting pilot ladders and that they are actually applied on commercial vessels.
procedures.why: 13.5% of surveyed vessels had defects in pilot boarding arrangements, which is still too high despite improvement.

procedures.action: If a pilot observes a defect in boarding arrangements, report it to the port state authority.
procedures.why: Failure to report tacitly endorses the hazard and allows unsafe conditions to persist.

procedures.action: If reluctant to report directly to port state authority, contact CHIRP instead.
procedures.why: Provides an alternative confidential reporting channel to ensure hazards are not ignored.

procedures.action: Where a pilot ladder uses aluminium grippers or ferrules, carefully inspect the condition of the rope.
procedures.why: The aluminium fittings can cut or chafe the rope, creating a structural failure risk.

constraints: Applies to commercial vessels with pilot boarding arrangements
Reporting should go to port state authority, or to CHIRP if reluctant to report directly
warnings: Aluminium grippers or ferrules can cut or chafe the ladder rope, creating a hazard
Not reporting observed defects tacitly endorses unsafe boarding arrangements
outcomes: 2010 survey showed improvement over previous surveys but defect rate (13.5%) remains too high
Unreported defects risk continued unsafe pilot transfer conditions
key_facts: A 2010 IMPA Safety Campaign survey found 13.5% of vessels had defects in pilot boarding arrangements
This figure, though improved from prior surveys, is still considered too high by CHIRP
Pilots are urged to report observed defects to port state authority or to CHIRP
Aluminium grippers/ferrules on pilot ladders can cut or chafe the rope and require careful inspection

trace.situation: A large yacht's rescue boat, stowed internally via a shell door, suffered a snap shackle failure in its three-leg lifting arrangement while being recovered and slewed into the tender bay, causing two deckhands to fall into the water.
trace.trigger: Port aft snap shackle of the lifting arrangement failed during slewing/recovery of the rescue boat into the tender bay.
constraints: Lifting gear must be certificated for the load being handled.
Regular inspections of lifting gear should be carried out as part of maintenance.
Crew being hoisted in the rescue boat should wear inflatable lifejackets.
warnings: Snap shackles in lifting arrangements can fail due to corrosion in pin bore holes even on relatively new equipment (about 2 years old).
Failure of one leg of a multi-leg lifting arrangement causes the load to swing suddenly, endangering personnel seated in or near the suspended craft.
outcomes: Two deckhands fell into the water when the shackle failed and the rescue boat swung downward and to port.
Both deckhands suffered only minor injuries, remained conscious, and were recovered by other crew, attributed to wearing inflatable lifejackets.
Investigation found the cause was failure of the snap shackle secured to the lifting point, with corrosion evident in the bore of the pin holes despite certification and regular inspection.
key_facts: The rescue boat is stowed inside the hull via a shell door on this large yacht.
The lifting arrangement had three legs/slings (forward, starboard, and port aft).
The port aft snap shackle failed, and the boat was held only by the forward and starboard slings afterward.
The yacht and its fittings were about 2 years old; lifting gear was certificated and had not been subjected to severe loads since new.
Fracture surfaces on the port shackle showed corrosion, particularly in the bore of the holes for the pin.

question_seeds.text: Why did a relatively new, certificated snap shackle fail despite regular maintenance inspections?
How can corrosion in pin bore holes be detected during routine lifting gear inspections before it leads to failure?

trace.situation: CHIRP reports a metallurgical investigation into a failed snap shackle used in a rescue boat lifting bridle, finding the shackle failed due to fatigue cracking initiated at the pin hole bore, with corrosion present on the fracture surface.
trace.trigger: A snap shackle failure in a rescue boat lifting bridle prompted a metallurgical investigation by the vessel's manager.

procedures.action: Replace snap shackles in rescue boat lifting bridles with conventional shackles.
procedures.why: The manager's company took this action after the investigation confirmed fatigue failure originating from corrosion at the pin hole bore.

procedures.action: Report any rescue boat equipment failures to CHIRP.
procedures.why: CHIRP is collecting data on rescue boat equipment failures to identify wider safety trends.

warnings: Corrosion combined with cyclic loading can cause fatigue cracking in snap shackle pin bores, leading to sudden failure of rescue boat lifting equipment.
outcomes: The company replaced snap shackles with conventional shackles in rescue boat lifting bridles to mitigate recurrence of fatigue failure.
key_facts: Metallurgical investigation found corrosion on the fracture surface of the failed snap shackle.
Fracture features indicate failure by a fatigue mechanism.
Cracks initiated at the bore of the hole for the pin.
The manager's company has replaced snap shackles in rescue boat lifting bridles with conventional shackles.
CHIRP requests reports of any rescue boat equipment failures.

trace.situation: A yacht approaching a harbour at night in fresh conditions mistook an uncharted red and blue flashing light on a fish farm buoy for an emergency vehicle ashore, nearly colliding with the buoy before safely entering harbour.
trace.trigger: Sighting of unexpected red and blue flashing lights blending with shore background lighting while on a harbour approach course near a charted fish farm.

procedures.action: Cross-check all charted hazards (e.g. fish farms) against current UKHO charts before approach
procedures.why: Crew had already identified fish farm positions and kept clear of charted locations, but the actual hazard light was uncharted

procedures.action: Investigate any anomalous or unexplained lights near the intended track rather than assuming they are unrelated to navigation
procedures.why: The crew discussed the lights but continued focusing on the harbour entrance, nearly resulting in collision

procedures.action: Report uncharted/unnotified hazardous lights to the Coastguard after the incident
procedures.why: To seek clarification and record a safety concern for wider notification

procedures.action: Retrace the inbound track in daylight to locate and confirm the position of the hazard
procedures.why: To verify the exact location and nature of the light relative to the vessel's course

constraints: Mariners rely on current official charts (UKHO) for hazard positions, but local fish farm lighting arrangements may not be charted or promulgated
Red and blue flashing lights used locally to mark fish farms are not a recognized international convention and are not notified to mariners
warnings: Uncharted and un-notified lights near navigational hazards can cause dangerous confusion, especially when resembling shore-based emergency lights
Red/blue flashing lights marking a fish farm buoy can be mistaken for shore emergency vehicle lights at night, masking a genuine collision hazard
outcomes: The yacht passed within approximately 2 metres of the unlit/unmarked buoy, narrowly avoiding collision
Coastguard confirmed that red and blue lights are a local, non-notified convention for fish farm marking, acknowledging the hazard but not formally logging the issue beyond 'noting' it
The vessel safely entered and berthed in harbour despite the near-miss
key_facts: Conditions were force 4-5 wind, moderate sea state, good visibility
Two fish farms were charted and avoided based on current UKHO charts, but the buoy's warning light was not charted
The fish farm manager confirmed buoys were lit with yellow flashing lights as expected, but the red/blue light causing confusion was separate and unexplained
The buoy was found approximately 5 cables due north of the harbour entrance, directly on the vessel's inbound GPS track
Coastguard stated red/blue flashing lights are a local-only convention for fish farms, not notified to mariners via any official channel

trace.situation: A charter yacht experienced a rigging failure (an unmoused shackle pin coming loose, separating from the furling drum) and the yachtsman shares lessons learned, prompting a CHIRP comment on pre-departure checks and charter company responsibility.
trace.trigger: Discovery that a shackle pin on the furling drum rigging was not moused and worked loose, causing difficulty with the foresail.

procedures.action: Check the obvious bits of rigging when chartering a boat before departure.
procedures.why: A small component failure (shackle pin) can lead to major difficulty at sea.

procedures.action: Mouse all shackles where practicable.
procedures.why: Prevents shackle pins from working loose and causing rigging/furling failures.

procedures.action: Charter companies should identify and correct deficiencies before the client boards.
procedures.why: Faults left uncorrected may cause difficulty at sea, especially for less experienced charter clients.

procedures.action: If conditions allow (not too windy), slacken the foresail halyard, unroll the sail, and pull it down to reunite the shackle with the furling drum.
procedures.why: This is a possible remedy to reconnect a separated shackle, but is weather-dependent.

constraints: Remedial action (slackening halyard, unrolling sail) is only feasible in lower wind conditions.
Shackle mousing should be done 'where it is practicable to do so'.
warnings: Failure of a small rigging component (an unmoused shackle pin) can lead to major difficulty at sea.
Charter companies failing to inspect and correct known deficiencies before clients board poses risk, especially for faults that could cause difficulty at sea.
outcomes: The yachtsman experienced rigging difficulty due to the unmoused shackle pin separating from the furling drum.
CHIRP highlights the incident as a reminder for good seamanship practice (pre-departure checks and mousing shackles) and charter company accountability.
key_facts: The incident involved a chartered boat with a shackle pin on the furling drum that was not moused.
Windy conditions during the charter week prevented the yachtsman from attempting to slacken the halyard and reunite the shackle with the furling drum.
CHIRP considers it good seamanship to check a yacht's rigging before leaving harbour.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report discusses two maritime safety matters: a fish farm's incorrectly lit buoys being corrected after being reported to the General Lighthouse Authority, and a separate near-miss report where a charter yacht crew discovered an unsecured shackle pin on the headsail furling drum before departure.
trace.trigger: A yachtsman reported confusing/incorrect buoy lighting to the Local Aids to Navigation Inspector; separately, another yacht's crew pointed out that the charter yacht's headsail tack shackle pin had fallen out before departure.

procedures.action: Report incorrectly lit or confusing navigation marks to the relevant Local Aids to Navigation Inspector/General Lighthouse Authority.

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime feedback report recounts a near-miss close-quarters incident where a fishing vessel overtook another vessel, then stopped close ahead to haul fishing pots, creating a dangerous situation resolved only when the fishing vessel went astern and passed at approximately 5 metres.
trace.trigger: A vessel engaged in fishing overtakes another vessel and then stops/alters course close ahead to work its gear, creating risk of collision.

procedures.action: Maintain a good, continuous lookout on all vessels in the vicinity, especially small fishing boats.
procedures.why: Without close observation of other vessels, there may not be time to take avoiding action.

procedures.action: Exercise extra caution and allow a wider safety margin when the other vessel is a small fishing boat.
procedures.why: Experience shows fishing vessels may alter course further towards own ship even when own ship alters to open the CPA, and may be preoccupied with gear and unaware of relative positions.

procedures.action: Do not assume an overtaking vessel acquires fishing-vessel give-way rights simply by being close ahead and engaged in fishing activity.
procedures.why: CHIRP/the Regulations hold that an overtaking vessel's obligation to keep clear continues until vessels are well clear of each other, regardless of subsequent fishing activity.

constraints: The obligation of an overtaking vessel to keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken continues until the vessels are well clear of each other.
An overtaking vessel cannot acquire the rights of a 'vessel engaged in fishing' while close ahead of the vessel it has just overtaken.
warnings: An overtaking vessel stopping close ahead to engage in fishing activity can create a dangerous close-quarters situation.
Altering course to open CPA on a small fishing vessel may cause that vessel to alter further towards, worsening the situation.
A passing distance of approximately 5 metres is an inadequate margin of safety and 'too close for comfort'.
outcomes: The fishing vessel went astern and passed down the reporting vessel's starboard side at approximately 5 metres, narrowly avoiding collision.
CHIRP contacted the fisherman, who acknowledged the encounter was too close for comfort and agreed on the importance of an adequate safety margin.
CHIRP concluded the regulations do not permit an overtaking vessel to claim fishing-vessel give-way status while close ahead of the overtaken vessel.
key_facts: The fishing vessel was the overtaking vessel in this encounter.
The overtaking vessel's duty to keep clear persists until vessels are well clear of each other.
The closest passing distance in this incident was approximately 5 metres.
Altering course to open CPA on small fishing vessels can backfire, as they may alter further towards own ship.
CHIRP directly engaged with the fisherman involved and he acknowledged the near-miss.

trace.situation: A TEMPSC (Totally Enclosed Motor Propelled Survival Craft) suffered an air cylinder explosion causing considerable damage, prompting a post-incident investigation into the cause and the adequacy of prior LSA surveys.

procedures.action: Check date stamps on cylinders to verify hydro-test currency.

procedures.action: Assess material wastage/corrosion of cylinder walls.
procedures.why: Approximately 50% wall thickness loss through corrosion indicated the cylinders were dangerously degraded and likely the cause of the explosion.

procedures.action: Determine economic viability of repair versus scrapping the TEMPSC.
procedures.why: The craft was assessed as beyond economical repair due to the extent of damage.

procedures.action: Obtain a replacement lifeboat.
procedures.why: The original TEMPSC was scrapped and could not be repaired.

procedures.action: Raise the matter with the organisation that conducted the LSA survey.
procedures.why: To address the apparent failure to properly hydro-test or even remove the cylinders during the survey.

Cylinders should be removed from the boat during survey for proper inspection and testing.
warnings: Failure to hydro-test air cylinders at required intervals can lead to undetected corrosion and catastrophic cylinder failure.

outcomes: No personnel were injured despite the explosion.
The TEMPSC was deemed beyond economical repair and scrapped.
A replacement lifeboat had to be obtained.
The ship's manager took up the matter with the LSA survey organisation.

trace.situation: A sailing yacht on a port tack in the Solent (wind force 2-3, SOG 4.5 knots) detected a coaster on a steady bearing 20-30 degrees off its starboard bow at 5 miles, and monitored the situation as risk of collision developed while a dinghy fleet was racing nearby with a RIB in attendance.

procedures.action: Take avoiding action (turn to starboard) once it becomes clear the other vessel will not take corrective action.

constraints: Must continue monitoring bearing/course until certain no corrective action will be taken before deviating from own course

trace.situation: A ship's manager responds to a CHIRP report about a near-miss incident in the Solent where a vessel encountered a dense fleet of racing yachts with a control RIB plus an approaching ship on the port bow, and CHIRP comments on the appropriateness of the response.

trace.situation: A vessel departing an Asia Pacific port experienced a minor engine control fault causing pilot boarding delays, and during the subsequent narrow channel transit on a flood spring tide, a trainee pilot began turning too early toward rocky shore, prompting the Master to intervene, which led to the pilots reacting with hostility and poor communication, including a later unexplained course change toward the edge of the buoyed channel.
trace.trigger: A trainee pilot begins altering course too early in a narrow, high-current channel, bringing the vessel close to a rocky shore, and later the pilot instructs a course change out of the buoyed channel without explaining intentions.

procedures.action: Delay departure and remain alongside when a main engine fault is reported, especially during strong spring tides.
procedures.why: Leaving on one engine in strong spring tide conditions was judged unsafe by the Master.

procedures.action: Notify the pilot promptly of delays and give required advance notice once ready.
procedures.why: Maintains coordination and allows the pilot to adjust boarding plans.

procedures.action: Maintain full bridge team roles during pilotage (helmsman, officer logging/charting, Master monitoring courses).
procedures.why: Ensures situational awareness and redundancy during critical narrow channel transit.

procedures.action: Voice concerns immediately to the pilot when vessel position appears unsafe (e.g., too close to shore).
procedures.why: The 1st Officer and Master both recognized the danger of the early turn toward rocky shore and acted to prevent grounding risk.

procedures.action: Request pilot refrain from further course alteration until vessel is clear of hazard.
procedures.why: Direct corrective action to mitigate immediate close-quarters risk with shore.

procedures.action: After the transit, remind pilots of their advisory role and the need to communicate intentions to the bridge team.
procedures.why: To prevent recurrence of unexplained maneuvers and improve master/pilot information exchange, especially for a trainee pilot.

procedures.action: Query the pilot's intentions immediately when an unexplained course change threatens to take the vessel out of the buoyed channel.
procedures.why: Reinforces the Master's overriding authority and responsibility for safety when pilot actions appear inconsistent with safe navigation.

constraints: Vessel should not depart on one engine during strong spring tide conditions.
Pilots act in an advisory capacity only; the Master retains command authority.
Bridge team must maintain monitoring and log/position charting throughout pilotage.
Pilots should communicate intentions to the bridge team, especially trainees.
warnings: Trainee pilot turned too early in a narrow channel with high rocky sides and strong currents, risking close proximity to shore.
Pilots reacted with shouting and verbal abuse when the Master raised safety concerns, undermining bridge resource management.
An unexplained course change by the pilot would have taken the vessel out of the buoyed channel.
outcomes: The vessel exited the narrow cut without incident despite the early turn.
The Master's intervention prevented the vessel from being taken out of the buoyed channel on the second course change.
Communication breakdown and hostility between Master and pilots occurred despite no actual grounding or collision.
key_facts: A minor electrical fault in the engine control system caused a pilotage delay from 1200 to 1430 hours.
The transit occurred during a flood tide in springs with high water at 1653, and strong currents in a narrow channel with rocky sides.
A trainee pilot was conning the vessel while the lead pilot and Master were both present on the bridge.
The pilot later ordered a course change to port that would have taken the vessel out of the buoyed channel, prompting the Master to question his intentions.
The pilots are advisory to the Master, who retains ultimate authority and responsibility for the vessel's safe navigation.

trace.situation: During pilotage in a narrow channel with heavy fishing gear and marker buoys, two pilots (lead and trainee) became agitated, shouted at the bridge team, and issued erratic orders such as 'Stop Engines', prompting the Master to assert control to maintain safe navigation.
trace.trigger: Pilots behaving erratically and aggressively on the bridge, giving contradictory or unsafe orders while the vessel was navigating hazardous waters with fishing gear.

procedures.action: Prioritize safety of navigation over managing pilot behavior, especially given fishing gear hazards.
procedures.why: High concentration of fishing gear with marker buoys made navigation safety the primary concern despite the bridge disturbance.

procedures.action: Placate the agitated pilots to de-escalate the situation.
procedures.why: Allowed the pilots to calm down and depart safely via pilot boat without further disruption to bridge operations.

procedures.action: Resume safe course alteration (back to starboard) once pilots departed.
procedures.why: Enabled the vessel to continue passage without incident after the disturbance was resolved.

procedures.action: Retain full command authority and responsibility throughout the pilotage.
procedures.why: The Master remains legally responsible for the safety of the vessel and personnel at all times, regardless of pilot presence.

constraints: The Master remains in full control and full responsibility for the vessel at all times, even with a pilot aboard.
Pilots are to assist the bridge team, not to take over or hinder navigation.
warnings: Erratic or aggressive pilot behavior (e.g., unjustified 'Stop Engines' orders) can endanger the vessel, especially in areas with fishing gear and marker buoys.
Allowing a pilot to effectively take over or hinder the bridge team compromises navigational safety.
outcomes: Master successfully placated the pilots, who then departed by pilot boat.
Vessel altered course and continued passage safely without incident.
1st Officer and 3rd Officer were stunned and appalled by the pilots' behavior, reinforcing the need for strong Master oversight.
key_facts: Two pilots (lead and trainee) were shouting and making erratic commands including 'Stop Engines'.
The area had a high concentration of fishing gear with marker buoys, increasing navigational risk.
The Master managed to placate the pilots before they departed via pilot boat.
The vessel altered course back to starboard and continued without incident.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a maritime incident report praising a Master's decision to delay departure for engine repairs and a bridge team's assertive questioning of a pilot's course near a harbour entrance.
trace.trigger: A scheduled departure time conflicted with an unresolved technical (engineering) problem, and later a pilot took a course near the entrance that the bridge team considered risky.

procedures.action: Assess risk of departing at the scheduled time against the status of unresolved technical issues.
procedures.why: The Master prudently decided against departing on schedule, giving engineers extra time to rectify the problem.

procedures.action: Maintain continuous, careful monitoring of the vessel's passage by the bridge team.
procedures.why: Active monitoring allowed the bridge team to detect the questionable course being taken near the entrance.

procedures.action: Voice concerns immediately to the pilot when the course or passage appears unsafe.
procedures.why: The 1st Officer and Master demonstrated professionalism and confidence by raising concerns promptly, which is a positive BRM behaviour.

procedures.action: Establish open dialogue with the pilot at the time of boarding during the passage plan discussion.
procedures.why: This is the key opportunity to build a positive working relationship so that there are no surprises during the pilotage passage.

procedures.action: Ensure senior team members remain receptive to questioning and challenge from other team members, including the pilot.
procedures.why: A good team requires that individuals, including senior members such as the pilot, accept being questioned without treating it as a personal insult.

constraints: Pilot's legal liability varies between national legal regimes.
Master's overall responsibility for the vessel remains clear regardless of pilot presence.
Effective pilot-bridge team dialogue must be established at the outset of pilotage, during the passage plan discussion.
warnings: A pilot may perceive legitimate questioning of the course as an insult to professionalism, undermining team communication.
Poor pilot-bridge team dialogue at passage plan discussion increases risk of surprises during pilotage.
outcomes: Master's delay of departure gave engineers time to fix the technical problem, avoiding departure with unresolved issues.
Bridge team's monitoring and prompt challenge of the pilot's course helped flag a potentially unsafe situation near the harbour entrance.
Pilot's negative reaction to being questioned highlighted a breakdown in effective team communication.
key_facts: The Master delayed scheduled departure to allow engineers more time to rectify a technical problem.
The bridge team carefully monitored the vessel's passage throughout.
The 1st Officer and Master raised immediate concerns about the course taken near the entrance.

procedures.why: Improves overall compliance with ColRegs across the manager's fleet.

trace.situation: A vessel navigating near Haisborough Sands while being overtaken by a passenger ferry encountered a head-on vessel (XXX) with a closing CPA of 0.2nm that refused to alter course despite VHF requests, forcing evasive action.
trace.trigger: ARPA plot showed CPA of 0.2nm with vessel XXX approaching from nearly right ahead while own vessel's ability to turn starboard was restricted by an overtaking ferry and shallow water.

procedures.action: Detect and plot approaching vessel early using radar and ARPA.
procedures.why: To monitor CPA/TCPA and assess collision risk in good time.

procedures.action: Identify vessel via AIS and establish VHF contact at 4.0nm to ascertain intentions.
procedures.why: Early communication needed because own vessel's maneuvering options were constrained by the overtaking ferry.

procedures.action: Request XXX to alter course to starboard, citing her open water and own vessel's restricted ability to do so.
procedures.why: Own vessel was limited by the overtaking ferry on the starboard beam and proximity to Haisborough Sands.

procedures.action: When no response was received despite repeated calls and risk persisted (vessel under 3nm), contact Engine Control Room and reduce speed.
procedures.why: To create space to drop astern of the overtaking ferry and regain ability to maneuver.

procedures.action: Engage hand steering and alter course to starboard while reducing speed.
procedures.why: To actively increase CPA and avoid close-quarters situation after XXX failed to give way.

procedures.action: Call the master to the bridge.
procedures.why: Situation escalated to a close-quarters encounter requiring command-level awareness and decision-making.

procedures.action: Once CPA with XXX reached 0.5nm and she was clear, increase speed and resume original course.
procedures.why: Return to normal passage plan once collision risk was resolved.

constraints: Own vessel's ability to turn starboard was restricted by the overtaking ferry on the starboard beam.
Proximity to Haisborough Sands further limited maneuvering room.
XXX had open water available on her own starboard side but did not use it.
VHF communication alone was insufficient to resolve the risk once XXX stopped responding.
warnings: A vessel that confirms 'I will keep my course and speed' may still pose a collision risk requiring independent evasive action.
Relying on VHF agreement from another vessel is not a substitute for taking own avoiding action when CPA remains unacceptably close.
Restricted sea room from multiple vessels/shallow water can compound a close-quarters situation.
outcomes: Reducing speed and altering course under hand steering increased CPA with XXX from 0.2nm to 0.5nm, resolving the immediate collision risk.
XXX did not alter course despite having open water, placing the reporting vessel in a difficult position.
Early radar/ARPA detection and timely VHF contact allowed situational awareness, but ultimately only own vessel's maneuver resolved the risk.
key_facts: Own vessel was on course 310° at 15kts, about 1nm west of Haisborough Sands.
A passenger ferry was overtaking 0.5nm off the starboard beam, restricting own vessel's ability to turn starboard.
XXX approached nearly right ahead with an initial CPA of 0.2nm that did not improve despite monitoring.
XXX acknowledged VHF contact but refused to alter course despite having open water on her own starboard side.
Evasive action (speed reduction, hand steering, course alteration) increased CPA to 0.5nm before resuming original course.

trace.situation: A vessel crossing the Southern North Sea TSS at the Foxtrot 3 junction at night identified a close-quarters crossing situation with another vessel in the scheme and used radar/AIS, Aldis lamp, and VHF to resolve it under COLREGs.
trace.trigger: Radar/AIS plotting approximately 20 minutes before TSS crossing identified a vessel (XXXXX) on a steady bearing constituting a potential close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Conduct a pre-crossing discussion and radar scan 20 minutes before entering the TSS to identify all vessels in the area.
procedures.why: Enables early identification of traffic and potential close-quarters situations before entering the scheme.

procedures.action: Continuously monitor bearings of identified vessels to detect steady-bearing (collision risk) situations.
procedures.why: A steady bearing with decreasing range indicates risk of collision requiring action.

procedures.action: At 4.5 miles, signal the other vessel with an Aldis lamp and follow up with a VHF call on CH16, then move to a working channel.
procedures.why: To establish communication and confirm mutual understanding of intended actions before close quarters develop.

procedures.action: Request the other vessel comply with COLREGs by altering course to starboard and passing astern.
procedures.why: To resolve the crossing situation in accordance with the standard give-way/stand-on responsibilities and avoid ambiguity.

procedures.action: Monitor the other vessel's actual course changes via AIS after agreement is reached.
procedures.why: To verify the other vessel is complying with the agreed action rather than assuming compliance.

procedures.action: When relative speeds and surrounding traffic made the original plan unsafe, execute a controlled full round turn to starboard before resuming passage.
procedures.why: To maintain safe separation given the other vessel's smaller-than-expected course change and the presence of additional nearby traffic.

constraints: Decisions must be made considering multiple vessels simultaneously present in and around the TSS, not just the primary contact.
Agreement over VHF does not replace the obligation to continuously verify actual vessel behavior and maintain safe action.
Following a traffic lane within a TSS does not confer right of way over crossing traffic.
warnings: False belief among some crews that following a traffic lane in a TSS gives right of way over crossing traffic.
Verbal VHF agreements may not be followed by the expected actual maneuver, requiring continued vigilance.
outcomes: Own vessel safely avoided the close-quarters situation by executing a controlled full round turn to starboard.
The other vessel only made a small course alteration rather than the agreed substantial turn, increasing risk if own vessel had not adapted its plan.
key_facts: The crossing situation was identified about 20 minutes before reaching the TSS via radar scanning.
Five vessels were identified in the vicinity of the F3 junction, including three close together and one astern heading westerly.
Own vessel used Aldis lamp signaling and VHF (CH16 then working channel) at 4.5 miles to coordinate with the crossing vessel.
The crossing vessel agreed to alter course to starboard but only made a minor alteration to port (heading 213) at 2 miles.
Own vessel ultimately completed a full round turn to starboard at 1 mile distance to maintain safety given relative speeds and other traffic.

trace.situation: A sailing yacht crossing as the stand-on vessel in the Caribbean was approached by a large power-driven ship on a converging course with a dangerously close CPA, and despite radio contact the ship refused to alter course or speed, insisting the yacht keep clear.
trace.trigger: A large ship maintaining steady course and speed produces a CPA of 0.1-0.3 NM with a sailing vessel that is the stand-on vessel under the collision regulations.

procedures.action: Establish VHF contact with the approaching vessel when CPA is assessed as too close.
procedures.why: To seek confirmation of the other vessel's intentions and clarify the developing close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Assert stand-on vessel status and request the give-way vessel take appropriate action.
procedures.why: The yacht was crossing from the ship's starboard side and was therefore the stand-on vessel under the collision regulations.

procedures.action: If the give-way vessel maintains course/speed and CPA remains unsafe (<0.5 NM), take independent avoiding action by reducing sail and altering course away from the other vessel's track.
procedures.why: Good seamanship requires the stand-on vessel to act when the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, even if not legally required by her status.

procedures.action: After the close-quarters situation resolves, radio the other vessel to register concern over non-compliance and advise the incident will be reported.
procedures.why: To formally document the give-way vessel's failure to comply with the collision regulations.

procedures.action: Report the incident to CHIRP/the vessel's management, with reporter and vessel identity kept confidential.
procedures.why: To alert the ship's manager to unsafe conduct while protecting the reporter under standard CHIRP practice.

constraints: Visibility and weather were good, with deep water (over 1,500m), removing navigational hazard as an excuse for non-compliance.
The yacht was identified as the stand-on vessel per the crossing situation (sailing vessel crossing from the give-way vessel's starboard side).
CPA must be continuously monitored via AIS and visual observation to assess when independent action is required.
warnings: Reluctance to adjust speed is a recurring hazard pattern seen in many CHIRP reports.
"I am going fast – keep clear" is not a valid justification for a give-way vessel to ignore collision regulations.
A vessel maintaining course and speed despite acknowledgment of a close-quarters situation can create a dangerous CPA even in good visibility and open water.
outcomes: The yacht's prudent slowing down and sharp turn to port provided sufficient room for XXXX to pass ahead safely.
XXXX never altered her course or speed as observed on AIS or visually, despite earlier radio assurances.

trace.trigger: A vessel needs to cross a Traffic Separation Scheme and must plan the crossing and brief the bridge team.

trace.situation: CHIRP comment providing guidance on the risks and management of biodiesel-blended diesel fuel storage aboard small vessels.
trace.trigger: Use or storage of diesel fuel containing biodiesel blends on small vessels

procedures.action: Practice good housekeeping and fuel management for biodiesel-blended fuel.
procedures.why: Biodiesel's hygroscopic nature increases water content, causing corrosion, sediment, and filter blocking that can be controlled by proper management.

procedures.action: Conduct regular checks to ensure fuel tanks remain free of water.
procedures.why: Eliminating water prevents bacterial/microbial growth that blocks fuel pipes and filters and increases corrosion.

procedures.action: If a bacterial growth outbreak occurs, empty and clean tanks or treat with biocide additives and filtering.
procedures.why: Bacterial growth at the fuel/water interface causes blockages and corrosion if untreated.

procedures.action: Replace fuel filters once, outside the normal service interval, after 2 to 3 tank throughputs of new biodiesel fuel.
procedures.why: Biodiesel is a stronger solvent and dislodges existing deposits in fuel systems, which can block filters.

procedures.action: Inspect and potentially replace fuel seals in sight gauges on older fuel storage tanks.
procedures.why: Older seals may be incompatible with sulphur-free diesel, with or without biodiesel content.

constraints: Applies specifically to small vessels storing biodiesel-blended diesel
Filter replacement should occur outside the regular service interval after 2-3 tank throughputs
warnings: Prolonged use of contaminated fuel may result in damage to engines
Biodiesel blends are more susceptible to biological (microbial) attack than normal diesel
Older fuel tank sight gauge seals may be incompatible with sulphur-free diesel and may need replacement
outcomes: Good housekeeping and water elimination controls corrosion, sediment formation, and filter blocking
Untreated bacterial growth leads to blocked fuel pipes/filters and increased corrosion

key_facts: Biodiesel blends are hygroscopic and can contain more water than normal diesel
Micro-organisms (fungi, bacteria, yeast) grow at the fuel/water interface; anaerobic species grow on tank sides

trace.situation: Guidance addressing biodiesel fuel quality issues (oxidation, waxing, water contamination) affecting fuel systems, particularly in recreational craft, with recommendations on seal inspection and fuel management.
trace.trigger: Use of biodiesel or biodiesel-blended fuel in a vessel's fuel system, especially where fuel may sit unused for extended periods.

procedures.action: Examine fuel system seals for signs of leakage.
procedures.why: Biodiesel can degrade seals, requiring a one-off replacement if leakage is detected.

procedures.action: Turn over fuel in any tank at least every 6 months and no more than every 12 months.
procedures.why: Minimises oxidation-related solid precipitation that can block filters.

procedures.action: Keep tanks as full as possible when in use, balanced against expected usage/duration.
procedures.why: Reduces condensation inside the tank while avoiding overbuying fuel that won't be used in time.

procedures.action: Drain water off regularly from tanks.
procedures.why: Discourages microbiological contamination (MBC), even though complete removal is rarely possible.

procedures.action: Consider modifying drain facilities to improve effectiveness.
procedures.why: Standard drains may not adequately remove water, increasing MBC risk.

procedures.action: Inspect and replace seals and fuel system components as necessary.
procedures.why: Biodiesel's properties can accelerate wear or degradation of seals.

procedures.action: Check and clean strainers and filters more regularly.
procedures.why: Oxidation byproducts and contamination can clog filters faster than with normal diesel.

procedures.action: Where possible, purchase diesel without biodiesel content.
procedures.why: Avoids the specific oxidation, waxing, and contamination issues associated with biodiesel blends.

procedures.action: Use test kits to check for contamination if concerned about fuel quality.

trace.situation: OOW on vessel 'A' monitored a developing crossing situation in good visibility in the Western Approaches to the English Channel when vessel 'B', initially parallel, altered course to starboard and appeared set to cross about one mile ahead.

procedures.action: Identify the close-quarters situation as soon as the other vessel's aspect/light change indicates a course alteration into a crossing situation.

procedures.why: Continued monitoring ensures the risk of collision is being reduced and allows reassessment if the other vessel fails to act.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary addressing the misuse of Not-Under-Command (NUC) lights/shapes and deck lights by vessels that routinely stop their engines to drift, rather than being genuinely unable to manoeuvre.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Programme Director appeals to readers to submit more near-miss reports, explaining the reporting and review process and acknowledging programme sponsors.

procedures.action: Submit a near-miss report on any hazardous incident encountered, taking only a few minutes to do so.
procedures.why: So others can learn from the lessons of similar circumstances and prevent future injuries.

procedures.why: CHIRP has identified these as priority areas needing more reporting.

procedures.action: Agree with CHIRP on publication terms; CHIRP edits reports only to remove identifying text.

constraints: Reports are published only with the agreement of the reporter.

CHIRP accepts reports from commercial, fishing and leisure sectors only.
warnings: Too many people continue to be injured in maritime activities, some incidents potentially preventable through shared lessons learned.
outcomes: Increased near-miss reporting could help prevent future injuries by sharing lessons learned.
CHIRP comments are reviewed by the Maritime Advisory Board representing a wide range of maritime organisations.

trace.situation: A loaded tanker navigating in dense fog within a traffic separation scheme encountered an approaching vessel on a reciprocal/crossing collision course that initially refused to alter course as required.
trace.trigger: Dense fog reducing visibility combined with an approaching vessel in the opposing traffic lane holding a collision course and refusing to comply with the Collision Regulations when hailed.

procedures.action: Reduce speed to a safe speed for the restricted visibility conditions (11.2 kts).
procedures.why: Dense fog required proceeding at a speed appropriate to prevailing visibility and traffic density.

procedures.action: Continuously plot the approaching vessel's movements using multiple radars.
procedures.why: To monitor a critical and evolving collision risk in real time and assess the other vessel's true course and speed.

procedures.action: Call the approaching vessel on VHF and request they pass astern per the Collision Regulations.
procedures.why: To resolve the crossing situation safely and in accordance with the Rules of the Road.

procedures.action: When the other vessel refused and claimed it would pass ahead despite insufficient speed to do so, independently assess the geometry using radar data.
procedures.why: The bridge team recognized the other vessel's stated intention (passing ahead at 8.7 kts) was not physically achievable, indicating poor situational awareness on the other bridge.

procedures.action: Stop engine to reduce own speed further as the final collision avoidance action.
procedures.why: Own ship's only remaining option to create separation, since the other vessel was not reliably altering course or speed.

procedures.action: Continue monitoring until the other vessel passed clear.
procedures.why: The other vessel eventually altered course to port and passed the bow only once own speed had dropped to about 5 kts, confirming the maneuver was necessary.

constraints: Must comply with the Collision Regulations (Rules of the Road) for crossing/head-on situations.
Must proceed at a safe speed appropriate to restricted visibility.
Cannot assume the other vessel will take correct or timely action.
warnings: Professionalism and competence on ship bridges may be inconsistent despite identical STCW licensing requirements.
Masters and pilots encounter crews and officers lacking basic knowledge of the Rules of the Road or seamanship.
Exhausted Masters remaining on the bridge for extended periods due to lack of confidence in Mates poses a fatigue risk.
One must assume the other vessel's bridge team may have poor navigational knowledge and act accordingly to keep well clear.
outcomes: Collision was avoided only because own ship stopped engines and reduced speed to about 5 kts.
The other vessel eventually altered course to port and passed clear of the bow, as confirmed by radar track plotting.
Had own ship not stopped engines, the other vessel would not have passed the bow safely.
key_facts: Own vessel: loaded tanker, length 242m, breadth 44m, draft 15m, bound Skagen to Rotterdam.
Visibility was dense fog; own speed reduced to 11.2 kts.
Approaching vessel 'A' was on heading 260 versus own heading 220, in a traffic separation lane, speed only 8.7 kts.
Three radars were used for continuous plotting of the other vessel's maneuvers.
The other vessel refused the request to pass astern and claimed (incorrectly) it could pass ahead.

question_seeds.text: Why did stopping engines become the only viable collision avoidance option in this scenario?

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board review of a near-miss crossing situation between two vessels, where a reporting tanker reduced speed near a Deepwater Route and a second vessel (Ship 'A') failed to take early avoiding action despite being the crossing vessel.
trace.trigger: A close-quarters crossing situation arose between two vessels with conflicting visibility reports (fog vs clear), prompting a CHIRP investigation into COLREGS compliance.

procedures.action: OOW must comply with the Collision Regulations and take early and decisive action when identified as the crossing vessel.
procedures.why: Ship A's OOW saw red lights on his starboard side, identifying himself as the crossing vessel obligated to give way.

procedures.action: OOW should call the Master when a close-quarters situation appears imminent.
procedures.why: Timely escalation to the Master is required before risk of collision becomes critical.

procedures.action: Company should undertake OOW training to improve understanding of the Collision Regulations.
procedures.why: The Board expressed concern over the officer's level of competence in applying COLREGS.

procedures.action: Company should audit Bridge operations for adequacy.
procedures.why: Systemic gaps in bridge watchkeeping practice may underlie the incident.

procedures.action: Take early and decisive action rather than subtle speed reductions.
procedures.why: The other vessel may not easily notice a reduction in speed, so action must be unambiguous.

procedures.action: Reassess safe speed in restricted visibility rather than maintaining habitual speed.
procedures.why: The Board questioned whether 11 knots in dense fog was an appropriate speed.

constraints: OOW must not be unnecessarily reluctant to make a large alteration to starboard to avoid a vessel on or near the starboard beam.
Proximity to the edge of a Deepwater Route should not override the obligation to take required avoiding action.
Avoiding action must be large enough and timely enough to be readily apparent to the other vessel.
warnings: Reluctance to alter course to starboard to avoid a vessel on the starboard beam is a recognized unsafe tendency identified in simulator exercises.
Subtle actions like reducing speed may not be noticed by the other vessel and do not substitute for early, decisive, and obvious action.
Maintaining a speed like 11 knots in dense fog may not constitute safe speed in restricted visibility.
outcomes: CHIRP/MAB found the OOW of Ship 'A' failed to comply with COLREGS as the crossing vessel.
The company was advised to conduct OOW training and audit bridge operations.
Inconsistencies between the two ships' statements (fog vs clear visibility) undermined the reliability of the incident reports.
The reporter's proposed lessons learned were rejected by the Board as opinionated and not directly tied to the event.
key_facts: Ship A's OOW saw red lights on his starboard side, confirming Ship A was the crossing (give-way) vessel.
The two ships' statements conflicted: one reported dense fog, the other clear visibility.
The tanker (reporter's vessel) reduced speed instead of taking more decisive avoiding action.
The Board questioned whether 11 knots was a safe speed in dense fog.
The MAB raised concerns about the officer's competence in applying the Collision Regulations.

trace.situation: CHIRP report describing a disputed crossing/near-miss encounter between two ships where the reporting vessel claims thick fog and a stopped engine, while the other ship's (A) OOW disputes the fog and reports altering course to starboard-side traffic with VHF-agreed CPA increase.
trace.trigger: A close-quarters crossing situation developed where the reporter perceived collision risk in claimed thick fog and requested the other vessel pass astern.

procedures.action: CHIRP contacted the shipowner of vessel A to obtain the OOW's account of the encounter.
procedures.why: To verify the reporter's claims of time, position, visibility, and vessel behaviour against an independent account.

procedures.action: OOW on vessel A altered course to port to increase CPA from 1.0 to 1.5 miles after VHF communication with the reporter.
procedures.why: He judged altering course and cooperation more effective than stopping or passing astern, given it was too late to safely pass astern.

procedures.action: OOW declined the reporter's request to pass astern.
procedures.why: He assessed the manoeuvre as unsafe to execute at that stage of the encounter.

constraints: Accounts of visibility conditions (thick fog vs good visibility) conflict between the two ships and could not be independently confirmed
The reporter's claim of stopping the ship was not observed by the other vessel
Sufficient sea room existed with no other vessel closer at the time, which the OOW cites as justification for his chosen manoeuvre

outcomes: CPA was increased from 1.0 to 1.5 miles via a course alteration to port by vessel A
No collision occurred, but the incident highlights unresolved conflicting fog/visibility accounts and the officer's concern this pattern is recurring and worsening

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a Ro-Ro ferry loading private cars on an exposed, wet, windy outer vehicle deck, forcing children and infirm passengers to cross a hazardous obstacle-strewn surface in driving rain while sheltered dry deck space remained unused, followed by the ferry manager's response explaining the deck's certification and assistance arrangements.
trace.trigger: Passengers, including young children and infirm individuals, were required to cross a wet, slippery, obstacle-strewn open vehicle deck during loading in driving rain and very high winds, despite available sheltered deck space.

procedures.action: Plan vehicle loading to account for passenger health and safety, not just space/trailer logistics.
procedures.why: A wet, windy, outside freight deck is hazardous and unfriendly for children and infirm people (Lessons Learned).

procedures.action: Passengers requiring assistance should declare this at check-in or via the company website prior to boarding.
procedures.why: This allows cabin staff to meet them at the vehicle deck or arrange vehicle placement near the lift for easier access, per the ferry manager's response.

procedures.action: Deck crew must assist any passenger who appears to need help or asks for it.
procedures.why: Manning arrangements on vehicle decks are intended to provide assistance to vulnerable passengers, per the operator's stated policy.

procedures.action: When queries arise about hazardous loading decisions, the loading officer or responsible party should be willing to explain the reasoning to a concerned passenger or observer.
procedures.why: The reporter's request for explanation was refused, leaving the hazardous choice unexplained and raising concern the company did not know what it was doing.

constraints: The open deck in question is a certified passenger vehicle deck under Class and Flag rules.
The deck surface has an anti-skid coating and fixtures limited to high-visibility painted elephant-foot fittings.
Space left on the exposed deck was intentionally reserved for a booked trailer to preserve disembarkation order (passenger vehicles to leave before trailers).
warnings: A wet, windy, outside freight deck is a very hazardous and unfriendly place for children and infirm people.
Increased risk of injury, accident, or damage can arise from poor loading planning with no clear safety justification.
outcomes: No actual injury was reported, but the increased risk of injury, accident or damage was noted as unexplained.
The loading officer refused to meet with the reporter and instead issued a complaint form, leaving the hazardous loading decision unaddressed directly.

CHIRP forwarded the report to the ferry manager, who provided an explanation citing deck certification, anti-skid coating, intentional trailer space reservation, and passenger assistance arrangements.
key_facts: Private cars were loaded on the wet, exposed extreme rear outside upper deck of the Ro-Ro ferry during driving rain and very high winds.
Ample sheltered, dry vehicle accommodation remained unused throughout the passage.
The loading supervising crewman could not explain the loading plan, citing uncertainty about vehicle numbers despite check-in occurring about an hour before loading.
The deck is certified under Class and Flag rules, coated with anti-skid material, with elephant-foot fixtures painted in high-visibility paint.
Passengers needing assistance can declare this at check-in or via the company website to receive cabin staff support or favorable vehicle placement.
