trace.situation: A seismic survey vessel towing ten long seismic streamers with tail buoys in the North Sea was approached by an unlit, unmanned-lookout sailing yacht crossing astern directly over the towed equipment at sunrise.
trace.trigger: A sailing yacht with no visible lookout, no navigation lights, and no functional VHF was observed on a crossing course that would take it directly over the towed seismic streamers and tail buoys, 4-5km astern of the seismic vessel.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the approaching vessel by VHF from all survey vessels (seismic vessel, chase and guard vessels).
procedures.why: To warn the yacht of the danger and get it to alter course before entering the towed equipment area.

procedures.action: Dispatch the chase vessel to intercept the yacht.
procedures.why: Chase vessel positioned to reach the yacht physically when radio contact fails.

procedures.action: Escalate signalling methods: searchlight, ship's whistle, then bullhorn.
procedures.why: Yacht had no VHF and no lookout, requiring alternative means to get attention.

procedures.action: Make contact by shouting vessel-to-vessel once in proximity.
procedures.why: All electronic/signal methods failed to raise a response until very close range.

procedures.action: Direct the yacht to motor out of the danger area once contact was established.
procedures.why: To remove the yacht from the zone where it could be struck or entangled by tail buoys.

constraints: Seismic vessel is restricted in ability to manoeuvre due to towed equipment and must display correct lights and shapes.
Tail buoys and streamers represent a significant collision/entanglement hazard to crossing vessels, especially small craft with shallow draft over the gear.
warnings: A vessel crossing astern of a seismic survey vessel at 4-5km may still be directly over 6000m-long towed streamers and at high risk of being struck by tail buoys.
Small craft without functional VHF, no lookout, and no navigation lights pose a serious detection and communication challenge even to vessels with radar and AIS.
Yacht sailed over five of the ten towed streamers before contact was made, indicating a near-miss with high potential for serious damage or entanglement.
outcomes: Yacht was intercepted approximately 150 metres from the line of tail buoys and directed clear of the danger area without incident.
Had the chase vessel failed to reach the yacht in time, there was very high risk of the yacht being struck or entangled by a tail buoy, risking serious damage.
Yacht's identity could not be established due to lack of vessel name marking and crew's limited English.
key_facts: Seismic vessel was towing ten streamers, each 6000m long, spaced 100m apart, at 8m depth, with tail buoys marked by bright yellow colour and flashing light.
The seismic vessel and escort vessels were restricted in ability to manoeuvre and displayed correct lights/shapes per their status.
The yacht (30-40ft, Dutch flag, 2 persons aboard) had no lookout, no visible navigation lights, and no functional VHF.
Contact was only achieved via shouting after the yacht had already sailed over five of the ten towed streamers.
Neither the seismic vessel nor the chase vessels detected the yacht early enough visually or by radar.

trace.situation: CHIRP investigation into a close-quarters/near-miss situation between a seismic survey vessel (with chase vessels) and a sailing yacht, identifying multiple contributing factors to the lack of early detection and intervention.
trace.trigger: A sailing yacht approached or crossed close to a seismic survey vessel's operating area without being detected in time by the chase vessels.

procedures.action: Optimise radar settings for prevailing weather conditions.
procedures.why: Radar settings were not optimised for the conditions, reducing detection capability.

procedures.action: Position chase vessels to maximise early detection and intervention opportunities.
procedures.why: Position of chase vessels could have been improved to assist with early detection and intervention.

procedures.action: Maintain enhanced visual lookout, especially when sun angle and wave height obscure small craft.
procedures.why: The sailing vessel was visually obscured by wave height and a low sun on the horizon behind it.

procedures.action: Ensure project operations are properly promulgated via Navtex/Notice to Mariners.
procedures.why: The project was not correctly notified on Navtex/NTM, limiting awareness among other vessel traffic.

procedures.action: Educate leisure/yacht users on hazards of operating near offshore seismic operations.
procedures.why: There was a lack of understanding of the potential hazards of offshore operations by leisure users.

constraints: Yacht must comply with IRPCS (International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea).
Vessels should maintain a proper lookout at all times.
Small craft should carry operational VHF radio and auxiliary means of detection (AIS, radar reflector, or similar).

warnings: A yacht not complying with IRPCS or maintaining a lookout poses a serious collision risk near operational vessels.
Lack of VHF, AIS, or radar reflector on small craft severely limits detection by larger vessels.
Sun glare and wave height can visually obscure small vessels, requiring radar and lookout adjustments.
outcomes: Failure to detect the yacht early reduced the time available for intervention by chase vessels.
Lack of Navtex/NTM notification meant other vessel traffic, including the yacht, may not have been aware of the seismic operation.
key_facts: The sailing yacht was not compliant with IRPCS and was not keeping a lookout.
The yacht had no operational VHF radio, AIS, radar reflector, or similar detection aid.
Radar settings aboard the seismic/chase vessels were not optimised for the prevailing weather.
The project's offshore operation was not correctly notified via Navtex or Notice to Mariners.
Sun glare and wave height visually obscured the yacht from the chase vessels.

trace.situation: A CHIRP correspondent describes personal practices for managing diesel fuel quality on a boat with older mild-steel tanks prone to rust, contamination, and bio-diesel related issues.
trace.trigger: Presence of mild steel fuel tanks, risk of rust/contamination, and use of bio-diesel fuel that increases risk of water, algae ('black slime'), and dirt in fuel.

procedures.action: Drain off a litre or so of diesel from each tank sump at regular intervals and after every rough passage.
procedures.why: To inspect for water, algae ('black slime'), and dirt before they cause fuel system problems.

procedures.action: Change tank and engine fine filters at least twice a year.
procedures.why: To remove accumulated contamination and maintain fuel flow quality to the engine.

procedures.action: Avoid relying solely on a 'Fuel Polishing' system if its filtration is coarser than the tank filters used.
procedures.why: Coarser filtration (10 micron difference) may not adequately remove fine contaminants, giving false confidence in fuel cleanliness.

procedures.action: Dose tanks liberally with a water dispersant additive and occasionally a biocide.
procedures.why: To control water ingress and prevent/limit microbial (algae) growth in the fuel.

constraints: Applies to vessels with naturally aspirated diesel engines and older mild steel fuel tanks.
Fuel polishing systems should only be relied upon if their filter micron rating is finer than or equal to the tank filters used.
warnings: Mild steel tanks are inherently prone to rust and contamination.
Bio-diesel increases uncertainty in marine fuel quality and may worsen contamination issues.
A fuel polishing system with coarser filtration than tank filters may give a false sense of fuel cleanliness.

trace.situation: A second engineer with 38 years' experience reports persistent, systemic poor quality of technical and operating manuals and computer-based planned maintenance systems aboard a two-year-old freight ferry.

trace.situation: A vessel (CL) in restricted visibility (fog) near the Needles, using a course-up radar display, altered course to starboard to avoid a plotted bulk carrier contact, but the bulk carrier simultaneously altered course to port, resulting in a near-collision at less than 100 yards.
trace.trigger: Radar-plotted risk of collision with another vessel in restricted visibility, prompting an avoiding course alteration.
constraints: Radar plotting must be accurate enough to detect a target's course change before relying on it

trace.situation: Two small sailing yachts crossing the English Channel shipping lanes experienced a sudden onset of dense fog and had to use radar to assess and avoid a close-quarters situation with a westbound bulk carrier.

procedures.action: Plot the concerning contact (3-4 miles, starboard bow) for approximately five minutes before acting.
procedures.why: Plotting over time was needed to determine whether risk of collision existed given inexperience with radar plotting.

procedures.action: Make a bold 90-degree alteration of course to starboard (from north to east) when risk of collision was judged to exist.
procedures.why: A large, unambiguous course change was chosen to clearly resolve the developing risk of collision with the westbound contact.

constraints: Neither yacht was fitted with AIS, limiting situational awareness to radar and visual means only.
D's radar functioned only intermittently, reducing redundancy between the two vessels.
Crew, though experienced yachtsmen, lacked recent practice in radar plotting for collision avoidance.
Vessels were operating near/crossing active shipping lanes used by commercial traffic (not a formal TSS in one case).
warnings: Shutting down radar to conserve power in good visibility left the vessel unprepared for a rapid-onset fog bank.
Lack of recent radar plotting proficiency increases risk when sudden restricted visibility occurs near shipping lanes.
Absence of AIS removes an important tool for identifying and tracking nearby commercial vessel movements.
outcomes: A close-quarters situation developed with a westbound ship (implied bulk carrier) after fog reduced visibility to 100 yards.
A 90-degree bold course alteration to starboard was taken as the chosen collision avoidance action based on radar plotting.
key_facts: Both yachts (CL, 30ft cutter; D, 33ft sloop) had radar and radar reflectors but no AIS.
Visibility dropped from 3-4 miles to 100 yards or less in under ten minutes near the westbound shipping lane.
Radar had been switched off in good visibility to conserve battery current.
Upon switching radar back on at 8 miles range, 6-7 contacts were detected proceeding westward in the shipping lane.
One contact 3-4 miles away on the starboard bow was assessed as posing risk of collision after plotting.

question_seeds.text: Why was the radar shut down during the period of good visibility, and what risk did that create?
How did the crew determine that risk of collision existed with the contact on the starboard bow?
What criteria should guide a decision to make a bold 90-degree course alteration versus smaller incremental changes in restricted visibility?
When should a vessel re-energize and activate radar in anticipation of deteriorating visibility near shipping lanes?

trace.situation: A CHIRP incident report analyses a close-quarters/risk-of-collision situation in restricted visibility (fog) between an ocean yacht (CL) and a bulk carrier (BC), where radar-only detection was used to assess risk of collision under Rule 19.
trace.trigger: A vessel detects another vessel by radar alone in restricted visibility and must determine whether a close-quarters situation or risk of collision is developing.

procedures.action: Determine by radar whether a close-quarters situation and/or risk of collision is developing.
procedures.why: Rule 19 requires this assessment before any avoiding action is taken.

procedures.action: Take avoiding action in ample time if risk of collision exists.
procedures.why: Early action reduces the chance of a close-quarters situation escalating.

procedures.action: Avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam (other than one being overtaken).
procedures.why: This is a specific prohibition under Rule 19 to prevent conflicting maneuvers; BC violated this and was found at fault.

procedures.action: Avoid altering course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.
procedures.why: Prevents closing the range with vessels not directly ahead, reducing collision risk.

procedures.action: Keep an active, continuous radar plot of all contacts (on paper or chinagraph) rather than relying on a quick glance.
procedures.why: CL's head-up radar plotting was weak and proved inadequate once multiple contacts (6-7) and a major course alteration occurred.

procedures.action: Use north-up stabilised radar in preference to course-up/head-up mode.
procedures.why: North-up is easier to interpret, improving situational awareness and plotting accuracy.

procedures.action: Make proper, active use of available radar/AIS equipment regardless of its sophistication.
procedures.why: Colregs require 'proper use... of radar equipment if fitted and operational'; effectiveness depends on usage, not equipment quality.

procedures.action: Maintain close visual, auditory, and radar watch at all times in restricted visibility.
procedures.why: Commercial shipping cannot be relied upon to follow the Colregs, as demonstrated by BC's violation.

constraints: In fog/restricted visibility there are no 'stand-on' or 'give-way' vessels; all vessels must keep clear of others under Rule 19.
Avoiding action by alteration of course must, so far as possible, avoid the two prohibited patterns (port turn for vessel forward of beam; turn towards vessel abeam/abaft beam).
Radar plotting method must be adequate for the number of contacts and complexity of the situation (head-up plotting failed with 6-7 contacts and a major course change).
warnings: Head-up radar plotting is inadequate when multiple contacts and major course alterations are involved.
Commercial shipping cannot be relied upon to follow the Colregs.
Reliance on radar alone without active plotting is insufficient in restricted visibility.
outcomes: BC contravened Rule 19 by altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, contributing to the close-quarters situation.
CL/D complied with Rule 19 by altering course to starboard when risk of collision was assessed.
An independent experienced Merchant Marine Captain/Extra Master confirmed CL was right and BC was wrong, while noting CL's radar plot should have been better kept.
key_facts: The incident occurred in restricted visibility (fog) with 6-7 radar contacts present.
BC altered course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, violating Rule 19.
CL used head-up (non-stabilised) radar plotting which was inadequate for the complex multi-contact situation.
In fog, Rule 19 removes the stand-on/give-way distinction; all vessels must keep clear.
Colregs require proper use of radar equipment, not necessarily the most advanced equipment.

question_seeds.text: Why is a port alteration of course for a vessel forward of the beam prohibited under Rule 19?
How should I maintain an effective radar plot when multiple contacts and a major course change are involved in restricted visibility?
What is the difference in stand-on/give-way obligations in restricted visibility compared to clear visibility?
Which radar display mode (north-up vs course-up) should be used to improve situational awareness in fog?

procedures.action: Contact mars@nauticalinst.org or john.rose@chirp.co.uk if interested in becoming an Ambassador.

Ambassadors will receive briefing material and coaching before taking on the role
outcomes: Increased submission of MARS accident reports and CHIRP hazardous occurrence reports
Improved safety culture among seafarers in regions with active Ambassadors

Ambassadors will encourage MARS (accident) and CHIRP (hazardous occurrence) reporting.
Briefing material and coaching will be provided to Ambassadors.
More detail is available in a Seaways February 2014 article.
Contact emails are mars@nauticalinst.org or john.rose@chirp.co.uk.

question_seeds.text: Who can volunteer to become a MARS/CHIRP Ambassador and what support will they receive?
Why is CHIRP partnering with The Nautical Institute on this Ambassador program?

trace.situation: A vessel's bridge team recounts a near-miss close-quarters encounter with a bulk carrier (BC) in fog, where sound signals were not used and reliance on AIS masked the true collision risk.
trace.trigger: Entering a fog bank and detecting multiple unseen/unheard vessel contacts on radar while approaching a bulk carrier with risk of collision.

procedures.action: Do not rely solely on AIS for situational awareness in restricted visibility.
procedures.why: The reporter noted they now assume 'everybody relies on AIS' instead of sounding fog signals, which left vessels unaware of each other's true intentions.

procedures.action: Avoid altering course to port except for a vessel on the starboard quarter, and only after careful consideration of all other options.
procedures.why: Port alterations in close-quarters situations carry elevated collision risk unless the specific starboard-quarter condition applies.

procedures.action: Consider reducing speed or stopping as an alternative to altering course.
procedures.why: Speed reduction was evaluated but judged less likely to be noticed by the BC than a substantial course change.

procedures.action: Make a large, decisive course alteration (e.g., 90 degrees) rather than a modest change.
procedures.why: A substantial alteration was believed more likely to be visually/radar-evident to the other vessel than a 5-knot speed reduction.

procedures.action: Use own sound signals in fog despite doubts about their effectiveness, rather than conserving them indefinitely.
procedures.why: Reliance on AIS over sound signalling likely contributed to mutual unawareness, echoing a Stockholm/Andrea Doria type situation.

constraints: Foghorn (aerosol canister) was available but reporter chose not to use it routinely to conserve it for emergency use.
No sound signals were heard from the BC before or during the incident.
Decision to alter course to port must only be made with careful consideration except in a last-resort scenario.
warnings: Reliance on AIS instead of mandatory sound signalling in fog can create false sense of security and mutual unawareness.
Believing the other vessel has 'avoided collision by its own action' can be a dangerous misassumption, as in Stockholm/Andrea Doria-type incidents.
Altering course to port without careful consideration (except for a vessel on the starboard quarter) increases collision risk.
outcomes: The BC apparently slowed and may not have seen the reporting vessel's course alteration, believing it had itself avoided collision.
The reporting vessel made a 90-degree course alteration as a last resort, judged more effective than reducing speed.
The near-miss highlighted a widespread over-reliance on AIS and underuse of sound signals in fog among multiple vessels (seven/eight radar contacts, none sounding fog signals).
key_facts: The reporting vessel did not hear sound signals from the bulk carrier (BC) and did not use its own foghorn, fearing it wouldn't be heard and to conserve the aerosol canister.
Seven to eight radar contacts were detected in the fog bank with no sound signals from any of them, suggesting universal reliance on AIS instead.
The reporting vessel made a 90-degree course alteration as a considered last resort rather than reducing speed by five knots.

The BC appeared to slow (reduced wash after passing) but seemingly did not perceive the reporting vessel's alteration, creating a Stockholm/Andrea Doria-type situation where both believed collision was avoided by the other's action.

question_seeds.text: Why did the crew choose not to sound their foghorn despite being in a fog bank with multiple vessel contacts?
How should a Captain decide between altering course versus reducing speed when encountering risk of collision in fog?
What risk arises when vessels rely on AIS instead of sound signals during restricted visibility?
Which COLREGS considerations apply when deciding whether to alter course to port in a close-quarters situation?

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary following a recreational seafarer's end-of-passage review of a close-quarters situation with a bulk carrier, highlighting lessons on AIS limitations, bow wave hazards, and safety equipment redundancy.
trace.trigger: A recreational vessel experienced a close-quarters/quarters situation with a bulk carrier and relied on AIS for situational awareness, prompting CHIRP to issue clarifying guidance.

procedures.action: Use radar, not AIS, as the primary tool for collision avoidance and vessel plotting.
procedures.why: IMO Resolution A.917(22) states AIS is designed to provide identification/basic information automatically, not for collision avoidance purposes.

procedures.action: Remain aware that AIS signals may not be detected due to human error or equipment setup, especially Class B (recreational) transmissions by Class A (SOLAS) receivers.
procedures.why: Research shows AIS-A equipment may not detect AIS-B transmissions and can even have AIS-B reception turned off.

procedures.action: Maintain situational awareness of bow wave risk from large vessels even after they ease off propulsion.
procedures.why: A significant bow wave persists until the vessel has almost stopped in the water.

procedures.action: Review and maintain redundancy in the vessel's safety equipment inventory, e.g. carry a hand- or mouth-operated horn as backup.
procedures.why: The reporting crew had concern over their air supply for the horn and lacked a backup signalling device.

constraints: AIS must not be relied upon as a substitute for radar or as a collision avoidance device.
Recreational craft typically use Class B AIS, which may not be reliably detected by Class A systems on larger vessels.
warnings: AIS is not a substitute for radar or for use as a vessel plotting device.
AIS is not a device to be used for collision avoidance purposes.
Human error or equipment setup can cause an AIS signal to go undetected by another station.
AIS-B transmissions may not be detected by AIS-A equipment, which can even have AIS-B reception turned off.
A significant bow wave will still occur from a large vessel until it has almost stopped in the water.
outcomes: Commendable end-of-passage review and sharing of lessons learned by the recreational seafarers.
Identification of gaps in safety equipment redundancy (lack of backup horn) during the close-quarters incident.
key_facts: IMO Resolution A.917(22) 'Guidelines for the onboard operational use of shipborne automatic identification systems (AIS)' clarifies AIS is for identification and information exchange, not collision avoidance.
Vessels over 300gt are fitted with Class A AIS; many recreational craft use Class B AIS.
AIS-A equipment may not detect AIS-B transmissions in some circumstances and can turn off AIS-B reception.
A large vessel continues to produce a significant bow wave until almost stopped, even after easing propulsion.
The reporting crew had concerns about air supply for their horn and lacked a hand- or mouth-operated backup.

question_seeds.text: Why can't AIS be relied upon as a collision avoidance tool according to IMO guidance?
How might Class A AIS equipment fail to detect a recreational vessel's Class B AIS signal?
What redundancy should be built into safety signalling equipment like horns?
When does the bow wave risk from a large vessel subside after it reduces propulsion?

chapter_title: SAFETY BOAT TRAINING FOR YACHT CLUB

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a race officer overhearing a safety boat crew on VHF M1 asking basic operational questions (ignition key location, kill cord connection, kill cord switch location), revealing a lack of competence and experience among sailing club safety boat crews.
trace.trigger: Observation that safety boat crew members were unfamiliar with basic boat controls and safety equipment while on active duty, raising concerns about their ability to respond effectively in an emergency.

procedures.action: Ensure safety boat crews receive appropriate training and certification (ideally RYA Powerboat Level 2 and RYA Safety Boat qualification) before taking up duties.
procedures.why: Driving a club safety boat is vital to safe running of dinghy racing and sail training; untrained crews risk ineffective or unsafe emergency response.

procedures.action: Provide crews with regular experience using safety boats, not just one-off certification.
procedures.why: The reporter identified lack of regular experience, not just lack of initial training, as a contributing factor.

procedures.action: Remind crews of RYA safety guidance every time they take up safety boat duties.
procedures.why: RYA recommends this practice to reinforce competence, especially where full certification is impractical.

procedures.action: Where full RYA qualification is impractical, adopt RYA's detailed guidance for clubs and volunteers, and consult reference material such as the RYA Safety Boat Handbook (G16).
procedures.why: RYA recognises full qualification is not always achievable for all clubs and volunteers, so alternative guidance exists to maintain safety standards.

procedures.action: Conduct risk assessment and safety auditing of safety boat operations.
procedures.why: Additional free resources on risk assessment and safety auditing are available to support safe operation.

constraints: Clubs should distinguish between 'Patrol' boats and 'Safety' boats, as roles and required competence may differ.
An accredited Safety Boat Course (e.g., RYA) is strongly recommended for all safety boat drivers.
warnings: Lack of competence and limited experience of safety boat crew could significantly affect their ability to operate as a safety boat effectively and safely.
Untrained crews asking basic operational questions over VHF while on duty indicates inadequate preparedness for emergency response.
outcomes: The Yacht Club confirmed they use only 'Patrol' boats, not 'Safety' boats, and have adopted RYA safety guidance for clubs.
CHIRP discussed the report with the RYA to reinforce the need for training and certification standards.
key_facts: The incident was overheard on VHF channel M1, a private channel used by sailing clubs for race control.
The safety boat crew asked their race officer for the location of the ignition key/lock, how to connect the kill cord, and the location of the kill cord switch.
The RYA recommends RYA Powerboat Level 2 and RYA Safety Boat qualification as ideal standards for club safety boat drivers.
The RYA acknowledges full qualification is not always practical for all clubs and has published guidance for such cases.
The RYA Safety Boat Handbook (G16) and British Rowing's risk assessment resources are available as references.

question_seeds.text: Why is it critical that safety boat crews be trained on basic equipment like kill cords and ignition locks before taking up duty?
How should a club ensure safety boat crews maintain competence when full RYA certification isn't practical for all volunteers?
What is the difference in competence requirements between a 'Patrol' boat and a 'Safety' boat as used by yacht clubs?
Who is responsible for reminding safety boat crews of safety guidance each time they take up duties?

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime Feedback report summarizes an MAIB investigation into a collision between CMA CGM Florida and Chou Shan, highlighting failures in VHF-based collision avoidance, language barriers, inadequate standing orders, and AIS misuse.
trace.trigger: Publication of MAIB accident investigation report (1 May 2014) on the CMA CGM Florida / Chou Shan collision, flagged by CHIRP as relevant feedback.
constraints: Collision avoidance manoeuvres must comply with COLREGS, not be negotiated verbally via VHF in place of proper application of the Rules.
VHF communications used for navigational coordination must be fully understood by all OOWs involved, including translation if conducted in a non-common language.
Standing orders must specify clear metrics/thresholds for when the master is to be called to the bridge.
warnings: Do not use VHF radio to negotiate collision-avoidance manoeuvres contrary to COLREGS.
Do not rely on VHF agreements that are not fully understood by all parties due to language differences.
Avoid over-reliance on AIS CPA/range-sorted target lists, which can cause loss of a strategic overview of the overall traffic situation.
outcomes: Reliance on VHF negotiation instead of COLREGS compliance contributed to the collision between CMA CGM Florida and Chou Shan.
Lack of full translation of VHF communications left at least one OOW unaware of what had been tacitly agreed, increasing collision risk.
Absence of specific master-call metrics in standing orders meant the master was not brought to the bridge in time.
Focus on AIS targets with smallest CPA/range caused the OOW to lose strategic situational awareness of overall traffic.
key_facts: MAIB accident reports are freely downloadable from maib.gov.uk.
The CMA CGM Florida and Chou Shan collision investigation report was published 1 May 2014.
VHF radio was used by both vessels to negotiate a manoeuvre that contravened COLREGS.
VHF communications were conducted in Mandarin and not fully translated for the other OOW.
Both vessels' standing orders lacked specific metrics for calling the master.

question_seeds.text: Why is negotiating collision avoidance by VHF considered contrary to COLREGS?
How should standing orders be worded to ensure the master is called in time during a close-quarters situation?
What risk does prioritizing AIS targets by smallest CPA/range pose to the OOW's situational awareness?
Which safeguards could have prevented the language-barrier miscommunication between the two vessels' OOWs?

trace.situation: Editorial introduction to a CHIRP Maritime FEEDBACK newsletter edition announcing new ambassadors and summarizing the issue's themes around underreporting and non-compliance as root causes of accidents.
warnings: Unwillingness to interfere with or stop unsafe working practices or conditions is a recurring root cause of accidents.
Operator non-compliance with procedures is a predominant root cause of reported accidents.
Poor reporting schemes or weak safety culture correlate with higher incident, injury, and fatality rates.
outcomes: Sharing lessons learned from reported accidents aims to reduce future incidents and fatalities.
Contributors who failed to report hazardous occurrences expressed shame for exposing shipmates to risk.
key_facts: CHIRP has appointed eight new ambassadors based in Brazil, Greece, Ghana, South Africa and the UK.
The ambassadors cover oil, bulk, dry cargo, offshore vessels, super yachts and recreational craft sectors.
CHIRP is still seeking additional ambassadors, especially from the Middle and Far East.
65,000 paper copies of CHIRP Maritime FEEDBACK are distributed worldwide.
Accident root causes in this edition are predominantly linked to non-compliance with procedures and failure to stop unsafe practices.

trace.situation: A CHIRP comment addressing the risks of failing to identify and fix the root cause of equipment malfunctions, particularly navigation equipment, and the dangers of a superficial 'tick box' approach to pre-sailing safety checks.
trace.trigger: Identification of equipment malfunction or missing/damaged navigation equipment during pre-sailing checks or bridge safety audits.

procedures.action: Investigate and identify the root cause of any equipment malfunction rather than ignoring it.
procedures.why: Not identifying the cause and leaving the problem unfixed creates ongoing danger to the ship.

procedures.action: Repair or make good any damaged or missing navigation equipment before sailing.
procedures.why: Unaddressed navigation equipment deficiencies jeopardize safe navigation.

procedures.action: Conduct pre-sailing checks and internal bridge safety audits thoroughly, not as a superficial tick-box exercise.
procedures.why: A tick-box approach carries a high risk to the safety of all onboard.

procedures.action: Establish a formal recorded system to follow up on any issues identified during pre-sailing checks.
procedures.why: Ensures identified deficiencies are tracked and resolved rather than forgotten.

procedures.action: Carry out a comprehensive cross-check of all bridge equipment regularly by an officer different from the one who performed the original pre-sailing checks.
procedures.why: Provides a backup to avoid complacency and catches issues the original checker may have missed.

constraints: Pre-sailing checks and internal bridge safety audits must be performed for every sailing.
Cross-checks must be conducted by an officer other than the one who performed the original check.
warnings: Adopting a 'tick box' approach to safety checks carries a high risk to the safety of all onboard the ship.
Failing to identify the cause of equipment malfunctions and leaving them unfixed is dangerous and cannot be understated.
outcomes: Without proper follow-up and cross-checking, equipment deficiencies and malfunctions may go unaddressed, endangering the vessel and crew.
A formal recorded follow-up system and independent cross-checks reduce complacency and improve safety.
key_facts: Pre-sailing checks and internal bridge safety audits exist for valid safety reasons.
Equipment malfunctions must have their root cause identified and fixed, not just noted.
A recommended practice is a formal recorded follow-up system for issues found in pre-sailing checks.
Cross-checks of bridge equipment should be done by a different officer than the one who did the original check to avoid complacency.

question_seeds.text: Why is it dangerous to adopt a tick-box approach to pre-sailing bridge equipment checks?
How should I set up a formal system to track follow-up on issues found during pre-sailing checks?
Who should perform the cross-check of bridge equipment to ensure independence from the original checker?
What is the risk of not identifying the root cause of a navigation equipment malfunction before sailing?

trace.situation: CHIRP received three separate reports of hazardous equipment deficiencies aboard a vessel that went undetected because bridge teams performed checklists and inspections superficially rather than with genuine vigilance.
trace.trigger: Bridge team completing onboard checklists and inspections with a 'tick box' mentality instead of thorough verification, allowing COLREGS-related equipment faults to persist undetected.

procedures.action: Conduct comprehensive handover checks between officers covering all COLREGS-required equipment.
procedures.why: The handover between second officers failed to check all required equipment, allowing the missing ship's bell to go unnoticed for months.

procedures.action: Perform pre-sailing checks and internal bridge audits with genuine scrutiny, not routine box-ticking.
procedures.why: Pre-sailing checks and internal bridge audits failed to identify the missing bell, showing these checks were not effective.

procedures.action: Verify navigation shapes are rigged to exact COLREGS Annex 1.6 dimensions (e.g., 1.5m vertical separation for 'vessel not under command' balls).
procedures.why: The shape was found incorrectly rigged at only 0.40 metres apart, violating Annex 1.6 requirements.

procedures.action: Investigate and read equipment instruction manuals when persistent faults/alarms occur rather than routinely silencing them.
procedures.why: The off-course alarm was cancelled for nine months without anyone reading the manual; the incoming Master read it and found the sensor was fitted 180 degrees out of line.

constraints: Ship must carry and maintain a functioning ship's bell to comply with COLREGS Rule 33 sound signals in restricted visibility.
Navigation shapes must meet exact spacing per COLREGS Annex 1.6 (at least 1.5 metres vertical separation for two black balls).
Alarms such as the off-course alarm must not be routinely silenced without investigating root cause.
regulations: COLREGS (International Regulations for Preventing Collision at Sea 1972)
warnings: Tick-box mentality in checklist completion can mask serious safety equipment deficiencies.
Missing or non-compliant sound signal/shape equipment puts the vessel in breach of COLREGS and risks collision in restricted visibility.
Routinely cancelling alarms without investigation can conceal long-standing navigational faults.
outcomes: Ship's bell was found only after a crewmember admitted hiding it, having intended to remove it from the ship, revealing a gap of several months of non-compliance.
Incoming Captain's inspection caught the incorrectly rigged 'vessel not under command' shape before it caused confusion with other vessels.
Incoming Master read the manual and corrected a nine-month-old off-course alarm fault caused by a sensor light fitted 180 degrees out of line.
key_facts: The ship's bell was missing for several months and only discovered during preparation for a tanker vetting inspection.
A crewmember had hidden the bell intending to remove it from the ship.
The 'vessel not under command' shape balls were only 0.40 metres apart instead of the required minimum 1.5 metres per COLREGS Annex 1.6.
The off-course alarm was switched off and routinely cancelled for nine months after a fault from replacing magnetic compass liquid.
The alarm fault was traced to a sensor light fitted 180 degrees out of line, found only after the incoming Master read the instruction manual.

question_seeds.text: Why did the pre-sailing checks and internal bridge audits fail to detect the missing ship's bell?
How should handover procedures between officers be strengthened to ensure all COLREGS equipment is verified?
What is the correct minimum vertical spacing for 'vessel not under command' shapes under COLREGS Annex 1.6?
Who is responsible for ensuring persistent alarm faults are investigated rather than routinely cancelled?

trace.situation: A pilot boarding a loaded vessel (draft 8.5m) found the pilot ladder incorrectly rigged and secured, causing it to slip as weight was applied.
trace.trigger: Pilot ladder secured to the ship's rail via round turns and a half hitch instead of to the deck via pad eyes, causing failure under load during pilot boarding.

procedures.action: Pilot steps onto ladder to board vessel from pilot boat.
procedures.why: Standard pilot transfer procedure at the pilot station.

procedures.action: Pilot quickly scrambles aboard upon feeling the ladder slip.
procedures.why: To avoid falling into the water as the ladder's securing failed.

procedures.action: Pilot checks and identifies the securing method used (3 round turns and a half hitch around the top hand rail).
procedures.why: To determine the root cause of the near miss.

procedures.action: Pilot reports the incident to the Captain and OOW with a diagram explanation.
procedures.why: To ensure the bridge team understands the failure mode and danger.

procedures.action: Captain instigates a near miss report in the company's reporting system.
procedures.why: To document the event per company safety management system requirements.

procedures.action: Captain plans a toolbox talk with the crew.
procedures.why: To correct crew understanding and prevent recurrence.

procedures.action: Pilot explains the correct securing method is to the deck via pad eyes, not to the rail.
procedures.why: To provide the correct technical standard for future rigging.

procedures.action: Pilot completes a defect report sent to the MCA and local harbour master upon return to the pilot station.
procedures.why: To formally notify the maritime authority and port authority of the unsafe condition.

constraints: Pilot ladder must be secured to the deck via pad eyes, not to the ship's rail.
Securing method must withstand the load of a person's full weight without slipping.
Ladder length and spreader configuration must be adequate for safe transfer.
warnings: A pilot ladder secured by round turns and a half hitch around a hand rail can roll out and fail under load.
Short ladders without spreaders secured incorrectly pose a fall risk during pilot transfer.
Incorrect pilot ladder rigging can result in a pilot falling into the water.
outcomes: The ladder slipped downward as the pilot's weight came onto it, but the pilot managed to scramble aboard without injury.
A near miss report was raised internally and a toolbox talk was planned to prevent recurrence.
A defect report was submitted to the MCA and local harbour master, escalating the safety concern beyond the vessel.
key_facts: Vessel draft was 8.5 metres and the pilot ladder was short (approx. 5-6 rungs, no spreader).
The ladder was rigged on the starboard quarter with a side gate access for the deck.
The AB secured the ladder with 3 round turns and a half hitch around the top hand rail instead of pad eyes on deck.
The round turns rolled out under the pilot's weight until the ladder was held only by the half hitch.
Correct practice is to secure the pilot ladder to the deck via pad eyes, not to the rail.

question_seeds.text: Why did the round-turn-and-half-hitch method fail under the pilot's weight?
How should the crew correctly secure a pilot ladder to prevent this type of failure?
Who is responsible for verifying the pilot ladder rigging before a pilot transfer?
What follow-up actions should the Captain take after a pilot ladder near miss is reported?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report examines an incident where a vessel's pilot ladder was hastily rigged on the wrong (starboard) side without officer oversight after a last-minute change from the agreed port-side boarding arrangement.
trace.trigger: A late change to the pilot boarding side (from port to starboard) led to the ladder being rigged in haste without supervision by a responsible officer.

procedures.action: Master must make a radio declaration before pilot transfer that the pilot ladder meets SOLAS requirements.
procedures.why: Required in UK ports to confirm compliance before transfer.

procedures.action: Officer must fully appraise each pilot embarkation situation and take appropriate action before the pilot boards.
procedures.why: Ship managers instructed the Master that situational changes (e.g., side change) require re-assessment, not hasty action.

procedures.action: Always use a certified, fully compliant pilot ladder.
procedures.why: Ensures the ladder meets SOLAS and IMO/IMPA standards regardless of last-minute changes.

procedures.action: A responsible officer with communication to the bridge must supervise rigging of pilot transfer arrangements and pilot embarkation, and arrange safe escort to/from the bridge.
procedures.why: Required by the 2010 SOLAS 1974 amendment to ensure correct rigging and pilot safety.

procedures.action: Instruct personnel engaged in rigging/operating mechanical equipment in safe procedures and test equipment before use.
procedures.why: SOLAS amendment requires trained personnel and tested equipment to prevent hazardous occurrences.

procedures.action: Report hazardous occurrences to the company so SMS procedures can be reviewed and updated.
procedures.why: The company's MAROPS department reviewed the procedure and incorporated IMO/IMPA recommendations into the SMS, demonstrating a positive safety response.

trace.situation: A cruise ship passenger recounts observing inconsistent lifejacket availability, absent safety announcements, and loosely secured liferafts aboard a tender used to ferry passengers ashore and back during a port call.
trace.trigger: Passenger boarded a tender for shore excursion and return without receiving a safety briefing, then noticed lifejackets were present in the main cabin but absent from the upper deck where they were seated.
warnings: No safety announcement was made on either the outbound or return tender journey.
Lifejackets were available in the main cabin but none were stowed on the upper deck, where passengers would depend on jackets being passed up through only two doors.
Liferafts atop the wheelhouse were tied loosely to the tripod mast and would probably not have floated free in an emergency.
Tender was reportedly carrying over 100 passengers on the upper deck alone, out of a stated total capacity of 250 per tender.
outcomes: The one-mile transit each way was completed in slight sea conditions without incident.
The passenger raised the safety concerns with the Guest Services Director upon re-boarding the liner, who listened attentively.
The passenger observed that two other tenders in the same fleet did carry lifejackets on the upper deck, stowed under the benches, indicating inconsistent practice across the tender fleet.
key_facts: The tender ('Tender X') was approximately 25 metres in length with a glass-bottomed main cabin and an open upper deck.
No safety muster or announcement was conducted aboard the tender despite one having been held before departure from Miami on the main liner.
Lifejacket stowage was inconsistent: present in two piles and on shelves in the main cabin, but completely absent from the upper deck.
Liferafts mounted between the legs of a tripod mast atop the wheelhouse appeared loosely tied and likely would not deploy automatically.
Other tenders in the same operation did stow lifejackets on the upper deck under the benches, showing the deficiency was not fleet-wide standard practice.

trace.situation: A cruise passenger with shipping experience noticed an absence of lifejackets on the upper deck of a tender ('Tender X') used by a cruise liner, raised the concern with onboard officers, and later reported it to CHIRP after receiving no further follow-up.

trace.situation: CHIRP compiled three reported incidents involving faults in rescue boat launching/recovery equipment, including an unauthorized limit switch modification, inadequate crane remote-control cable length, and failed emergency hydraulic accumulators during a drill.
trace.trigger: Launching, recovery, or drill testing of a rescue boat using crane/davit lowering equipment reveals equipment malfunction or inadequate design

procedures.action: Do not modify the design of life saving appliances (e.g. limit switch chain arrangement) without first consulting the manufacturer, Flag State, or Classification Society (if delegated statutory oversight).
procedures.why: An unauthorized modification to the limit switch chain reduced the hole diameter and, combined with hardened grease, caused the crane to stop abruptly during recovery, risking equipment damage and loss of life in heavy weather.

procedures.action: Verify that remote control handle connection wires on the rescue boat crane have sufficient length to allow safe operation from within the rescue boat during lowering.
procedures.why: Two separate incidents found insufficient cable length made it impossible to safely operate the crane from the rescue boat while it was being lowered to the sea surface.

procedures.action: Include rescue boat and crane inspection and maintenance (including hydraulic accumulators and changeover valves) in the ship's Planned Maintenance System (PMS).
procedures.why: A rescue boat failed to launch during a drill because hydraulic accumulator pressure was zero and changeover valves were rusty and non-operational, which in a real blackout emergency would have made lowering the boat impossible.

procedures.action: Develop and implement procedures for lowering the rescue boat without power.
procedures.why: It was noted there were no procedures in place for lowering the rescue boat in the event of a power blackout, compounding the risk when the hydraulic accumulator system failed.

constraints: Crew must not modify life saving appliance design without consulting manufacturer, Flag State, or Classification Society
Rescue boat and crane inspection/maintenance must be part of the ship's PMS
Procedures for powerless lowering of the rescue boat must exist
warnings: A rapid/abrupt stop of the crane during recovery can cause equipment damage and even loss of life in heavy weather
Insufficient remote handle cable length makes it impossible to operate the crane safely from the rescue boat
Rusty, non-operational changeover hydraulic valves and zero accumulator pressure can make it impossible to lower a rescue boat during a power blackout emergency
outcomes: Unauthorized limit switch chain modification plus hardened grease caused the weight to lift and falsely activate the limit switch, stopping the crane rapidly
Rescue boat crane could not be operated safely from the boat due to short connection wires
Rescue boat failed to launch during a drill due to zero accumulator pressure and rusty, non-operational changeover valves, which would have prevented lowering in a real blackout emergency
key_facts: CHIRP received multiple reports on rescue boat launching and lowering equipment failures

Emergency hydraulic accumulators had zero pressure and changeover valves were rusty/non-operational during a drill, and no procedure existed for powerless lowering
Lessons learned emphasize no unauthorized LSA modifications and inclusion of rescue boat/crane maintenance in the PMS

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on lessons learned from rescue boat launching/recovery incidents, focusing on equipment maintenance, drill practice, and fall hook safety for rescue boats.

procedures.why: Ensures equipment changes are tracked and maintained correctly.

procedures.why: Maintains proper documentation and regulatory compliance trail.

procedures.action: Include wires and their inspections in the wire ropes register.
procedures.why: Ensures systematic inspection and traceability of wire condition.

procedures.action: Establish written procedures for lowering the rescue boat without power.
procedures.why: Provides a documented fallback method in case of power failure during launch.

procedures.action: Use safeguards against premature release on fall hooks, such as pins.
procedures.why: Prevents accidental release of the boat during lowering.

procedures.action: Consider rigging a Fall Preventer Device (FPD) sling until the boat is just above the water.
procedures.why: Adds an extra safety layer against premature hook release during descent.

outcomes: Proper drills and maintenance reduce the risk of launching/recovery incidents.

trace.situation: A CHIRP investigation report addresses the correct response when a ship's anchor has or may have snagged a gas pipeline while anchored, following an incident where the pipeline ruptured.

procedures.action: Slip the anchor cable as soon as possible.

warnings: Placing weight on a cable snagged on a gas pipeline risks rupturing the pipeline
outcomes: In the reported incident, failure to slip the cable promptly resulted in the gas pipeline rupturing
Had the cable been slipped in time, the investigation concluded the pipeline probably would not have ruptured

trace.situation: A vessel at anchor in 14 metres of water with 5 shackles out began dragging anchor in a 30-knot NW wind over a mud bottom, risking collision, interference with navigation, or fouling of underwater cables/pipelines.
trace.trigger: Anchor observed to be dragging while vessel at anchor in strong wind and wave conditions.

procedures.action: Keep the main engine on standby with short notice (e.g., 5 minutes) whenever at anchor in marginal conditions.
procedures.why: Allows immediate propulsion response if dragging is detected.

procedures.action: Immediately heave up the anchor upon detecting dragging and re-anchor at a nearby, better position.
procedures.why: To regain a secure holding position before the vessel drifts into danger.

procedures.action: Veer more cable (increase scope, e.g., from 5 to 7 shackles) when re-anchoring.
procedures.why: Greater scope improves holding power in strong wind conditions.

procedures.action: Carefully check and continuously monitor the new anchor position.
procedures.why: To confirm the anchor is holding and detect any further dragging early.

procedures.action: Before anchoring, assess depth, bottom type, nearby vessels, current, wind speed and direction.
procedures.why: These factors determine holding ground quality and collision/dragging risk.

procedures.action: Select an anchorage position near the edge of the anchorage area, clear of vessels in the predicted drift path.
procedures.why: Reduces risk of collision or fouling other vessels if dragging occurs.

procedures.action: Conduct bridge team exercises simulating dragging anchor scenarios, including pipeline fouling.
procedures.why: To prepare the team for low-guidance, high-risk situations not well covered in manuals.

procedures.action: If a pipeline fouling is suspected, avoid placing excessive weight on the anchor/gear.
procedures.why: Excess strain could rupture the pipeline, risking gas release, loss of buoyancy, fire, or explosion.

constraints: Main engine must be ready on standby notice while at anchor in risky conditions
Do not rely solely on charted pipeline locations, as many predate accurate GPS surveys
Avoid applying excessive weight on anchor gear if pipeline fouling is suspected
warnings: Dragging anchor can lead to collision with another vessel in the vicinity
Dragging anchor can impact safe navigation of another vessel in a river, narrow channel, or fairway
Dragging anchor can result in catching an underwater cable or pipeline and causing damage

outcomes: Vessel successfully re-anchored with increased scope (7 shackles) and avoided collision/pipeline fouling

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Feedback commentary on safe anchoring practices following reports of vessels dragging anchor, emphasizing position monitoring and chart management.

trace.situation: CHIRP reviewer comments on a reported incident where a crew boat passed another vessel with only 50 metres clearance at speed near a wind farm, raising concerns about inadequate risk assessment and unsafe transit practices.
trace.trigger: A close-quarters passing incident at high speed with only 50 metres separation was reported for review.

procedures.action: Ensure passing/clearance distances fully account for vessel speed and stopping capability.
procedures.why: 50 metres clearance was judged inadequate at the speed involved.

procedures.action: Conduct a thorough risk assessment before close-quarters manoeuvres that accounts for failure scenarios, especially mechanical failure.
procedures.why: The risk assessment reviewed was inadequate because it did not allow for consequences of mechanical failure.

procedures.action: Verify emergency stopping distance claims against realistic conditions, not assumed ideal performance.
procedures.why: Emergency stopping was described as achievable within the ship's length, which if inaccurate could lead to serious injury to passengers and crew.

procedures.action: Ensure crew boat 'tramlines' to and from wind farms maintain adequate separation distance between transits.
procedures.why: Crew boats often use fixed tramlines without allowance for distance, risking unsafe separation between transits.

constraints: Passing distance and speed must be assessed together, not in isolation.
Risk assessments must consider failure modes including mechanical failure.
Tramline transits near wind farms must maintain safe separation distance.
warnings: 50 metres clearance at speed is inadequate and foolhardy.
Failure to allow for mechanical failure in risk assessment can lead to serious injury to passengers and crew.
Reliance on stopping within the ship's length is a dangerous assumption if untrue.
outcomes: If stopping distance claims are inaccurate, serious injury to passengers and crew is highly likely.
Unsafe tramline use without distance allowance risks unsafe separation between crew boat transits.
key_facts: The incident involved a 50 metre clearance passing at speed deemed inadequate.
CHIRP judged the action foolhardy and below ordinary good seamanship standards.
The risk assessment failed to account for consequences of mechanical failure.
Emergency stopping was claimed to be achievable within the ship's length.
Crew boats commonly use tramlines to/from wind farms without adequate distance allowance for safe separation.

question_seeds.text: Why did CHIRP consider the 50 metre clearance inadequate given the vessel's speed?
What should a proper risk assessment include to account for mechanical failure during close-quarters transits?
How should crew boats manage tramline separation distances near wind farms to avoid unsafe transits?
Which assumptions about emergency stopping distance proved risky in this incident?

chapter_title: MAINTENANCE AND IMPACT ON REST HOURS

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a maintenance-related incident where crew complaints about rest hours were not properly addressed by the Master and Chief Officer, compromising crew rest requirements.
trace.trigger: A crew complaint regarding rest hours arises during or after maintenance/refit work that falls outside the scope of the Safety Management System (SMS).

procedures.action: Fully address and investigate crew complaints about rest hours at the time they are raised.
procedures.why: Failure to do so compromises the requirement for crew to be properly rested.

procedures.action: Adopt a best-practice 'Management of Change' process when work scope falls outside the SMS.
procedures.why: Covers situations such as refit work being incomplete before returning to sea, which the SMS may not otherwise address.

procedures.action: Submit a hazardous occurrence report to CHIRP if a breakdown in the Ship's SMS is encountered.
procedures.why: CHIRP will always make time to review such reports, supporting systemic learning and safety improvement.

constraints: Crew complaints about rest hours must be fully addressed by Master and Chief Officer when raised.
If scope of work is not covered by the SMS, a Management of Change process should be applied.
warnings: Not fully addressing crew rest complaints compromises the requirement for crew to be properly rested.
Returning to sea with incomplete refit work not covered by SMS creates a hazardous gap in safety management.
outcomes: Unaddressed crew complaint led to compromised rest hours and a breakdown in SMS compliance.
Adoption of a Management of Change process would cover gaps such as incomplete refit work before returning to sea.
key_facts: The Master and Chief Officer did not fully address a crew complaint about rest hours.
This failure compromised the crew's required rest.
A 'Management of Change' process is recommended best practice for work scope not covered by the SMS.
CHIRP reviews hazardous occurrence reports related to SMS breakdowns.
Further reading is available in 'ALERT!' edition 13, January 2007, on fatigue consequences.

question_seeds.text: Why is it critical to fully address crew complaints about rest hours at the time they are raised?
How should a Management of Change process be implemented when refit work scope falls outside the SMS?
What should the Master do if a crew complaint reveals a breakdown in the Ship's SMS?
Who is responsible for ensuring crew rest hour complaints are properly resolved before returning to sea?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes two high-speed craft performing a planned close-quarters high-speed pass at approximately 60 knots combined speed within a wind farm safety zone, filmed for video, raising safety concerns from the wind farm client.
trace.trigger: Masters of two vessels agreed to conduct a high-speed pass close to each other in a wind farm safety zone to obtain video footage.

procedures.action: CHIRP contacts all parties involved to investigate the reported incident.
procedures.why: To establish facts and assess safety implications of the observed close-quarters high-speed pass.

procedures.action: Owners of Vessel 'A' conduct an internal enquiry and review the incident.
procedures.why: To determine compliance with the required 50 metre safety zone clearance and address client concerns.

procedures.action: Owners of Vessel 'A' remind staff of the company's Safe Navigation policy and state the activity will not recur.
procedures.why: To prevent recurrence of unnecessary close passes that could lead to a major incident.

procedures.action: Marine Coordinator maps vessel tracks using AIS data for review at a periodic safety meeting.
procedures.why: To objectively verify vessel separation and speeds for future safety discussions.

constraints: A minimum 50 metres clearance must be maintained between vessels within the wind farm safety zone.
High-speed manoeuvres near other vessels require sufficient sea room to avoid close-quarters situations.
warnings: Potential for a major incident when vessels operate at very close quarters at high speed.
Overlapping bow waves indicate inadequate sea room between vessels.
Unnecessary close passes for video/photo opportunities pose serious safety risks.
outcomes: Vessel 'A' owners acknowledged the risk and reinforced the Safe Navigation policy, stating the activity would not happen again.
Vessel 'B' owners closed the incident with no action taken, citing the 50 metre clearance and vessel's stopping ability.
The wind farm Marine Coordinator used AIS track data to inform discussion at a periodic safety meeting.
key_facts: Vessel 'A' and Vessel 'B' are both capable of 30+ knots, with Vessel 'B' confirmed at 35 knots.
The combined closing speed was estimated at around 60 knots based on video observation.
Both masters agreed in advance on headings, speeds, and a 50 metre clearance for the pass.
The wind farm client expressed grave concerns over the activity and potential for a major incident.
AIS data was used by the Marine Coordinator to verify vessel tracks.

question_seeds.text: Why would two masters agree to a high-speed close pass purely for video footage despite safety zone rules?
How can AIS data be used to verify actual separation distance during a high-speed pass?
