trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes deck ratings repeatedly using noisy mechanical scaling equipment at 0200hrs on car decks below accommodation, disturbing crew sleep for three consecutive nights despite the chief officer's instruction to stop.
trace.trigger: Crew members woken by loud machinery noise and vibration (78-86dB) during rest hours, recurring nightly despite instructions to cease.

procedures.action: Report sleep-disrupting noise to the chief officer immediately.
procedures.why: To raise awareness and seek corrective action at the earliest opportunity.

procedures.action: Chief officer to instruct deck ratings to postpone noisy scaling work during crew rest hours.
procedures.why: Noise and vibration during rest hours is unsuitable and disrupts crew sleep.

procedures.action: Escalate persistent noncompliance to the master when instructions are disregarded.
procedures.why: Repeated violation of instructions requires higher authority intervention.

procedures.action: Schedule noisy mechanical work for refit/drydock periods or restricted windows near watch handover instead of mid-rest hours.
procedures.why: Minimizes disturbance to off-watch crew and avoids fatigue-inducing sleep interruption.

procedures.action: Communicate work restrictions and scheduling clearly and unambiguously to deck ratings.
procedures.why: Unclear communication from the Chief Mate was identified as a contributing cause of noncompliance.

procedures.action: Prefer quieter alternative methods (e.g., deck blasting machines) over mechanical scaling needle guns.
procedures.why: Reduces disruption to crew compared to mechanical methods.

constraints: Noisy maintenance work should not be performed during crew rest hours.
Refit duration must be sufficient to accommodate noisy jobs ashore; a 5-day refit was too short.
Instructions from department heads regarding work scheduling must be followed by subordinates.
warnings: Repeated sleep disruption from noise/vibration can impair crew rest and safety.
Deliberate subversion of a superior's instructions undermines shipboard discipline and safety culture.
Commercial pressure to shorten refit periods can force unsuitable work schedules affecting crew welfare.
outcomes: Noise disturbance continued nightly until the reporting crew member left the vessel, despite complaints to the chief officer and informal reports to the captain.
Ship managers acknowledged poor communication of restricted work hours and committed to improving clarity.
Company policy shifted toward preferring deck blasting machines and performing such work during annual drydock to minimize crew disruption.
key_facts: Noise/vibration from mechanical deck scaling measured between 78-86dB in a cabin.
Disturbance occurred at 0200hrs nightly for three consecutive nights, lasting 2-4 hours each time.
The refit was only 5 days long, too short to accommodate the scaling job ashore.
Ship managers stated the scaling was meant to be restricted to 1 hour before to 2 hours after watch handover, but this was not clearly communicated to the crew.
All crew, including the master, agreed the job should have been done during refit.

question_seeds.text: Why did the deck ratings continue the noisy scaling work despite the chief officer's instructions to stop?
What alternative methods or scheduling could have minimized crew sleep disruption during this maintenance task?
How should the master have intervened once informal complaints reached him on the third night?
Who is responsible for ensuring work restrictions are clearly communicated to deck crew performing noisy maintenance?

trace.situation: A vessel at anchor in fine weather observed another vessel making strange manoeuvres while approaching the anchorage, attempted to warn it, but the underway vessel made contact with the anchored vessel causing hull scratches.
trace.trigger: OOW notices an approaching vessel behaving erratically near the anchorage.

procedures.action: Monitor approaching vessel's behaviour from the anchored vessel.
procedures.why: Strange manoeuvres indicated a developing risk of collision despite good visibility and calm conditions.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the approaching vessel by VHF.
procedures.why: To establish communication and clarify intentions before any close-quarters situation develops.

procedures.action: Sound several blasts on the whistle when VHF contact fails.
procedures.why: To provide an audible warning signal to the approaching vessel of danger/collision risk.

procedures.action: Call the captain to the bridge/deck.
procedures.why: To ensure command-level awareness and decision-making as the situation escalates.

procedures.action: Inform the port authority after contact occurs.
procedures.why: To report the incident in line with expected reporting obligations following a collision/contact event.

constraints: Vessel was at anchor with fine weather, good visibility, no strong current or abnormal wind/sea
No VHF response was received from the approaching vessel before contact occurred
warnings: An approaching vessel with a main engine problem may be unable to manoeuvre or stop as expected, increasing collision risk even in good visibility.
Lack of VHF response from an approaching vessel should prompt escalation to sound signals and command notification without delay.
outcomes: The underway vessel made contact with the anchored vessel, causing scratches to the hull.
The port authority was informed of the incident.
The other vessel attributed the contact to a main engine problem.
key_facts: The reporting vessel was safely at anchor in fine weather with good visibility and no abnormal wind/current.
The OOW detected strange manoeuvres by an approaching vessel before contact occurred.
VHF attempts to contact the approaching vessel failed, prompting whistle signals and a call to the captain.
Contact caused only hull scratches; the cause was later identified as a main engine problem on the other vessel.

question_seeds.text: At what point should an anchor watch escalate from VHF contact attempts to sounding whistle signals?
Why might a vessel under way make strange manoeuvres before a main engine failure becomes apparent?
How should the OOW balance monitoring an erratic approaching vessel against immediately calling the captain?
Who else besides the port authority should be notified following a contact incident at anchor?

trace.situation: A CHIRP-style best-practice checklist for vessels anchoring, aimed at preventing collisions/contact incidents while at anchor.
trace.trigger: Vessel preparing to anchor or already anchored, particularly in congested anchorages or areas with strong tidal streams/changing weather.

procedures.action: Evaluate and pay out adequate anchor cable length considering prevailing conditions, holding ground, and sea depth.
procedures.why: Ensures sufficient scope for safe holding given local conditions.

procedures.action: Plot the vessel's swinging circle on GPS, paper chart, and ECDIS if available, and verify adequate clearance to swing.
procedures.why: Confirms the vessel will not swing into hazards or other vessels.

procedures.action: Ascertain actual swing pattern once anchored and adjust ECDIS/Radar/GPS alarm limits accordingly.
procedures.why: Real swing behavior may differ from planned, requiring alarm recalibration.

procedures.action: Monitor swing tendencies of nearby vessels, especially at tidal stream changes.
procedures.why: Other vessels' swings can create collision risk as currents shift.

procedures.action: Calculate and mark tidal streams in known strong-tidal-effect areas.
procedures.why: Helps anticipate swing and dragging risks.

procedures.action: Maintain a robust anchor watch at all times, checking position at regular intervals.
procedures.why: Early detection of dragging or drifting prevents collisions.

procedures.action: Re-adjust echo sounder and anemometer alarm limits after anchoring, where fitted.
procedures.why: Alarms must reflect anchored conditions, not underway settings.

procedures.action: Continuously monitor weather and have an action plan for unexpected adverse weather or unusual swinging.
procedures.why: Enables prompt response to changing conditions that threaten anchor safety.

procedures.action: Insert a visual marker on the windlass to indicate brake slipping.
procedures.why: Provides early visual warning of anchor cable paying out unintentionally (dragging).

procedures.action: Maintain main engine in an appropriate state of readiness.
procedures.why: Allows immediate maneuvering if dragging or collision risk develops.

procedures.action: Use BNWAS while at anchor, if available.
procedures.why: Ensures watchkeeper alertness during anchor watch.

procedures.action: Establish clear standing instructions for calling the Master in time based on the developing situation.
procedures.why: Ensures timely command decision-making for anchorage-specific risks.

procedures.action: Keep emergency contact list of local support services (pilot, tugs, etc.) available at all times.
procedures.why: Facilitates rapid assistance if an emergency arises at anchor.

procedures.action: Include evaluation of these best practices in vessel operator's internal navigation audits.
procedures.why: Promotes continuous compliance and improvement.

procedures.action: Provide Bridge Team Simulator training covering weather changes, congested anchorage approach/anchoring, dragging scenarios, and other vessels drifting toward own vessel.
procedures.why: Prepares deck officers and Masters to handle realistic anchor-related collision risks.

constraints: Swing circle must be plotted with adequate clearance before and after anchoring.
Alarm limits (ECDIS/Radar/GPS/echo sounder/anemometer) must be adjusted appropriately post-anchoring.
Anchor watch must be maintained continuously, not just periodically.
Main engine readiness must be maintained throughout the anchor period.
warnings: Failure to monitor swing tendencies and tidal changes can lead to collision with nearby anchored vessels.
Unadjusted alarm limits after anchoring may fail to detect dragging or other hazards.
Lack of main engine readiness could prevent timely avoidance of a collision while at anchor.
outcomes: Proper application of these practices reduces risk of contact/collision incidents at anchor.
Neglecting anchor watch, alarm adjustment, or engine readiness increases risk of dragging-related collisions.
key_facts: Anchor cable length must account for holding ground, sea depth, and prevailing conditions.
Swinging circle should be plotted on GPS, paper chart, and ECDIS with clearance verified.
A visual marker on the windlass can indicate brake slipping, an early sign of dragging.
Bridge Team Simulator training should include scenarios of dragging and drifting vessels at anchor.
Standing instructions should specify when to call the Master based on the anchorage situation.

question_seeds.text: How should I verify and adjust my vessel's swing circle clearance once anchored?
At what point should alarm limits for echo sounder and anemometer be re-adjusted after anchoring?
Why is it important to monitor other vessels' swing tendencies, especially during tidal stream changes?
What standing instructions should be in place for calling the Master while at anchor?

trace.situation: CHIRP comment summarizing a tanker charterer's Safety Alert Bulletin on rising incidents of vessels colliding while anchored or manoeuvring in congested anchorages.
trace.trigger: Vessel is approaching, anchoring in, or already lying in a congested anchorage area shared with other anchored vessels.

procedures.action: Conduct detailed pre-arrival/departure passage planning (appraisal, planning, execution, monitoring) including contingency and site-specific risk assessment.
procedures.why: Causal factors included inadequate planning and failure to assess local conditions before arrival.

procedures.action: Evaluate the prevailing congestion status of the port's designated anchorage before approach.
procedures.why: Congested anchorages were the setting for the identified contact incidents.

procedures.action: Identify a suitable anchorage position in consultation with Port Authorities/VTS prior to entering the anchorage area.
procedures.why: Reduces risk of anchoring too close to other vessels and supports coordinated traffic management.

procedures.action: While approaching an anchorage, avoid passing close ahead of other anchored vessels.
procedures.why: Directly addresses a vessel's duty under COLREGS Rule 2(a) to keep clear and not endanger anchored vessels.

procedures.action: Correctly assess strength and direction of local tidal currents and winds before, during, and while manoeuvring at anchor.
procedures.why: Failure to do so was identified as a root causal factor in multiple incidents.

procedures.action: Plot and actively use the swinging circle as a monitoring tool, especially when anchored vessels swing in different directions.
procedures.why: Swinging circles were not plotted/used in incidents, removing a key situational awareness tool.

procedures.action: Maintain proper navigational watchkeeping while at anchor, including continuous monitoring of clearances from adjacent anchored vessels during tide changes.
procedures.why: Lack of watchkeeping and clearance monitoring during tide change was a causal factor.

procedures.action: Monitor prevailing weather and forecasts (seasonal winds, thunderstorms, squalls) continuously while at anchor.
procedures.why: Inadequate weather monitoring led to anchor dragging in past incidents.

procedures.action: Ensure main propulsion is available for immediate use while at anchor.
procedures.why: Unavailability of propulsion when required prevented timely response to anchor dragging or close-quarters situations.

constraints: A vessel under way must keep clear of a vessel at anchor as a matter of good seamanship (COLREGS Rule 2(a)).
A vessel approaching an anchorage must not endanger other vessels or anchor too close to other anchored vessels.
Site-specific risk assessments and contingency planning must be part of pre-arrival/departure planning.
warnings: Manoeuvring too close to vessels already at anchor significantly increases risk of contact/collision.
Failure to monitor clearances from adjacent anchored vessels during tide change can lead to contact incidents.
Inadequate weather monitoring can result in anchor dragging and subsequent collision.
Unavailability of main propulsion for immediate use removes the ability to avoid close-quarters situations or dragging.
Some anchorage contact incidents have resulted in breach of the hull.
outcomes: A tanker charterer observed a significant increase in incidents involving contact with other vessels at congested anchorages.
In a few cases, contact incidents resulted in hull breaches.
Identified causal factors and improvement areas were shared industry-wide via CHIRP to help vessel operators update their safety management systems.
key_facts: COLREGS Rule 2(a) requires an underway vessel to keep clear of an anchored vessel as good seamanship.
A major tanker charterer issued a Safety Alert Bulletin after noting rising anchorage contact incidents.

Identified causal factors include poor tidal/wind assessment, anchoring too close to others, lack of watchkeeping at anchor, unplotted swinging circles, poor clearance monitoring at tide change, inadequate weather monitoring, and unavailable main propulsion.

Recommended improvement areas include detailed pre-arrival planning, congestion evaluation, consultation with Port Authorities/VTS for anchorage position, and avoiding passing close ahead of anchored vessels.

question_seeds.text: How should the bridge team verify and continuously monitor the swinging circle relative to other anchored vessels during a tide change?
Why is it critical to have main propulsion available for immediate use even while the vessel is at anchor?
What steps should be taken during pre-arrival planning to reduce risk of contact in a congested anchorage?
Who should be consulted before selecting a specific anchorage position in a congested port anchorage area?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describing a close-quarters situation off McDuff/Banff where a tanker got underway from anchorage, crossed ahead of a vessel on passage, and reached a steady bearing creating collision risk before the stand-on vessel altered course to pass astern.
trace.trigger: A tanker got underway from an anchorage south of the reporting vessel, crossed ahead and increased speed to a point where it was on a constant/fixed bearing, creating risk of a close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Maintain a sharp lookout at all times, including in good visibility and calm conditions.
procedures.why: The close-quarters situation developed on a clear, fine day with good visibility, showing risk is not limited to poor conditions.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, take independent action (alter course) to avoid collision when the give-way vessel's actions create continued risk.
procedures.why: The tanker increased speed and reached a fixed bearing, so the reporting vessel altered course to starboard and passed safely astern despite being the stand-on vessel.

procedures.action: Do not assume another vessel will act in accordance with the ordinary practice of seamen or respond appropriately to a VHF query.
procedures.why: The tanker's OOW apparently believed he had 'nothing to reply to' because the reporting vessel was on his port bow, despite the developing risk.

constraints: Stand-on vessel is expected to hold course under normal circumstances but must act when collision risk persists.
Vessel getting underway from anchorage should ideally allow a crossing vessel to pass before leaving and increasing speed.
warnings: Never trust other vessels to act in accordance with the ordinary practice of seamen.
Always keep a sharp lookout, even in good visibility and calm weather.
outcomes: The reporting vessel altered course to starboard and passed safely astern of the tanker.
The reporting vessel noted it would have been more prudent for the tanker to wait before leaving anchorage/increasing speed.
key_facts: Reporting vessel was on passage from Buckie to Erith, steering 090 at about 8 knots.
Incident occurred about 2 miles north of McDuff/Banff.
Conditions: 1645hrs, force 4 wind ENE, sea height 0.5 metres, good visibility.
The tanker got underway from anchorage south of the reporting vessel and crossed ahead, reaching a fixed bearing.
The tanker called asking the reporting vessel's intentions and whether it would pass astern.

question_seeds.text: Why did the stand-on vessel alter course instead of insisting the give-way vessel maneuver first?
At what point should a stand-on vessel abandon holding course and take independent action under Rule 17?
How should a vessel getting underway from anchorage coordinate with a crossing vessel to avoid creating a close-quarters situation?
Who bears responsibility when the give-way vessel assumes no action is needed because the other vessel is on its port bow?

trace.situation: A CHIRP commentary addresses an Officer of the Watch (OOW) who begins a voyage from a safe, non-hazardous starting position but then gets underway in a manner that creates risk of collision with another vessel.
trace.trigger: OOW commencing a passage/getting underway from a non-hazardous position.

procedures.action: Do not get underway or start a passage in a way that creates risk of collision, even from a non-hazardous starting position.
procedures.why: Starting underway improperly can convert a safe situation into a collision risk.

procedures.action: Comply with the COLREGS at all times when commencing and conducting the passage.
procedures.why: The COLREGS are the governing rules for avoiding collision.

procedures.action: Operate in accordance with the ordinary practice of seamen.
procedures.why: This is the OOW's professional responsibility alongside COLREGS compliance.

constraints: OOW must not put the ship at risk of collision when commencing a passage.
Actions must comply with COLREGS and ordinary seamanship practice.
warnings: Getting underway from a non-hazardous position does not excuse creating a risk of collision.
outcomes: Failure to comply with COLREGS and seamanship practice when commencing a passage risks collision.
key_facts: The OOW bears responsibility for safe commencement of a passage.
A non-hazardous starting position does not eliminate the risk of collision if the OOW mismanages getting underway.
Compliance with COLREGS and ordinary seamanship practice is mandatory for the OOW.

question_seeds.text: Why is it significant that the ship started from a non-hazardous position before the risk of collision arose?
Who is responsible for ensuring the ship does not create a risk of collision when getting underway?
How should the OOW apply COLREGS and ordinary seamanship practice when commencing a passage?

trace.situation: A passenger vessel operator responds to a CHIRP safety report by detailing its compliance with evacuation, signage, lighting, and announcement requirements following concerns about passenger safety awareness and emergency readiness.

trace.situation: A fleet of small boats struggled against a strong ebb spring tide to enter a harbour while two ferries, one inbound and one outbound, elected to pass each other in the narrow harbour mouth, with the departing ferry using bow and stern thrusters that pushed small craft toward rocks.
trace.trigger: A ferry captain chose to leave port and pass an incoming ferry within the confined harbour entrance during an unusually strong ebb tide, while multiple small vessels with limited manoeuvrability were present in the small boat channel.

procedures.action: Avoid passing other vessels (e.g., two ferries) within the narrow harbour mouth; conduct such passing manoeuvres inside the harbour, outside in the main channel, or over the spit bank instead.
procedures.why: Passing in the confined harbour entrance imposes unnecessary danger on small vessels using the adjacent small boat channel.

procedures.action: Before using bow/stern thrusters in confined waters, assess the position and proximity of small vessels abeam.
procedures.why: Thruster wash can create water flow faster than the maximum speed of many small vessels, putting them at risk of being pushed onto hazards such as rocks.

procedures.action: Account for tidal strength and its effect on the manoeuvrability of smaller craft when planning port entry/exit timing and routing.
procedures.why: Unusually strong ebb tide extended the time small boats needed to enter harbour and limited their ability to manoeuvre, increasing collision/grounding risk.

constraints: Vessels using the main channel in and out of port should not normally pass each other in the narrow harbour mouth.
Small vessels in the small boat channel have limited speed and manoeuvrability, especially against strong tidal flow.
warnings: Using bow and stern thrusters in confined spaces when abeam of small vessels can create water flow faster than those vessels' maximum speed, risking them being pushed onto hazards.
Passing vessels (e.g., two ferries) within a narrow harbour entrance during strong tidal conditions endangers small craft operating nearby.
outcomes: The reporting yacht and a 40-foot yacht were pushed sideways dangerously close to rocks only 15m away due to ferry thruster wash.
No collision or grounding occurred in this instance, but the close encounter was assessed as an avoidable, professionally preventable risk.
key_facts: About 10 small boats were attempting to enter harbour on a full ebb spring tide, with only a couple able to make headway.
The reporting vessel made less than half a knot over ground at full throttle due to tidal strength.
An outbound ferry used bow and stern thrusters while passing an inbound ferry in the harbour mouth, pushing nearby small vessels toward rocks.
The rocks bordering the small boat channel were only about 15 metres away from the affected vessels.
The ferry captain was visibly aware of the situation he was creating, as seen through the bridge window indicating thruster use.

question_seeds.text: Why did the ferry captain choose to pass another ferry inside the harbour entrance rather than in open water or over the spit bank?

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary following a close-quarters encounter in a harbour entrance involving a recreational craft and strong tidal conditions.
trace.trigger: Entering or leaving port under strong tidal stream conditions with a recreational craft.

procedures.action: Conduct a simple risk assessment using all available facts before entering or leaving port.
procedures.why: Reveals hazards such as strong tides that increase risk during port entry/exit.

procedures.action: Consult port information books, charts, and tide tables during passage planning.
procedures.why: These sources provide the tidal and local knowledge needed to assess risk accurately.

procedures.action: Consider delaying port entry (e.g., by two hours) if tidal conditions are unfavourable.
procedures.why: Significantly reduces risk and provides a greater margin of safety, especially in case of mechanical breakdown.

constraints: Decision should be based on facts known at the time, including port information, charts, and tide tables.
warnings: Failure to allow for strong tides when entering/leaving port increases risk of close encounters or loss of control.
Mechanical breakdown during an unfavourable tidal window greatly increases danger.
outcomes: Delaying entry by two hours would have significantly reduced risk and increased safety margin.
Lack of proper risk assessment contributed to the close encounter in the harbour entrance.
key_facts: The incident involved a recreational craft in a harbour entrance.
Strong tides were a key contributing factor.
A simple risk assessment using port information, charts, and tide tables could have identified the risk.
Delaying entry by two hours would have reduced risk, particularly in the event of mechanical breakdown.

trace.situation: A small boat reported a near-miss ('nearly wrecked') encounter with a ferry near the perimeter of a 'small boat' channel at a harbour entrance, prompting a CHIRP investigation with the Harbour Master.
trace.trigger: A close-quarters/near-miss encounter between a small boat and a ferry in a harbour entrance is reported to CHIRP.

procedures.action: CHIRP contacts the Harbour Master to request review of the incident.
procedures.why: To obtain an authoritative, evidence-based account of what occurred.

procedures.action: Harbour Master reviews CCTV footage of the encounter.
procedures.why: To verify vessel positions and actions objectively rather than relying on recollection alone.

procedures.action: Harbour Master discusses findings with the ferry company.
procedures.why: Although the ferry acted correctly, it was close to the 'small boat' channel perimeter, warranting corrective guidance.

procedures.action: Ferry company issues an advisory note to its captains to keep a wider berth from the 'small boat' channel.
procedures.why: To increase safety margin for small craft using the adjacent channel.

procedures.action: Harbour Master advises small boat users to be aware of tidal streams and plan transits accordingly.
procedures.why: Because inadequate speed relative to tidal flow was identified as a root contributing factor to the dangerous situation.

constraints: A vessel's engine speed must be sufficient to make headway against the prevailing tidal stream when entering/leaving harbour.
Small boats must remain within the designated 'small boat' channel and be aware ferries may operate close to its perimeter.
warnings: A vessel with only 5 knots engine speed should not attempt to enter against a peak ebb rate of up to 5.5 knots — this is poor navigation.
Operating near the perimeter of a 'small boat' channel reduces safety margins even when technically correct.
outcomes: Ferry company issued an advisory note instructing captains to give wider berth to the 'small boat' channel.

The ferry was found to have acted correctly, but systemic/procedural improvements were still implemented.

Advisory notes were issued to both the ferry company and small boat users following the investigation.

trace.situation: CHIRP feedback analysing a close-quarters situation between a fishing vessel and a yacht, attributing the root cause to inadequate lookout aboard the fishing vessel, compounded by sun glare that may have hidden the yacht.
trace.trigger: A close-quarters situation occurred between a fishing vessel and a yacht in clear visibility conditions.

procedures.action: Maintain a vigilant visual lookout at all times, regardless of visibility conditions.
procedures.why: The root cause of the close quarters situation was the fishing vessel not keeping a vigilant look-out.

procedures.action: Continue radar watch even in clear visibility.
procedures.why: The watch keeper on the fishing vessel probably saw no reason to keep a close radar watch because visibility was clear, which contributed to the missed detection.

procedures.action: Account for sun glare as a factor that can obscure small craft and take anti-glare precautions on the bridge.
procedures.why: A contributing cause may have been the yacht not being seen due to glare from the sun; the vessel owner's anti-glare precautions were noted as prudent.

constraints: Clear visibility does not eliminate the need for radar watch or vigilant lookout.
Sun glare conditions require additional precautions and bridge ergonomic considerations.

trace.situation: A sailing yacht 34nm west of Bishop Rock had a near-collision with an unresponsive fishing vessel that was not keeping a proper lookout, forcing the yacht to take evasive action.
trace.trigger: A fishing vessel on a crossing course approached without altering course, without AIS or VHF response, and with no one visible in the wheelhouse.

procedures.action: Start engine as a safety precaution when a converging vessel shows no sign of giving way.
procedures.why: Allows immediate maneuvering capability if the other vessel fails to act.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the approaching vessel repeatedly via VHF Channel 16.
procedures.why: To alert the other vessel and confirm whether they are aware of the situation.

procedures.action: Take decisive avoiding action (full throttle ahead) when the give-way vessel fails to respond or alter course.
procedures.why: To prevent collision when it becomes clear the other vessel is not keeping a lookout.

procedures.action: Note vessel name/number and follow up by radio once clear, and report the incident.
procedures.why: Enables accountability and allows lessons to be captured for future safety (as done via CHIRP).

procedures.action: Test radar reflector visibility/range periodically with other vessels.
procedures.why: Confirms the reflector's detectability under varying conditions, as done earlier the same day with a cargo ship.

constraints: Fishing vessel displayed no signals indicating fishing activity.
No AIS or VHF contact was received from the fishing vessel prior to close approach.
The yacht's radar reflector was mounted ~10m above sea level and had been confirmed visible at 6nm in rain earlier that day.
The fishing vessel's wheelhouse design placed the watch-keeper in a forward starboard corner near windows, with heat/sunlight exposure, during gear recovery operations.
warnings: Fishing vessels may pass very close even in crossing situations; do not assume they will give way.
A vessel's design (e.g., wheelhouse placement, gear-handling equipment) can create blind spots or reduce lookout effectiveness.
Absence of an AIS/VHF response does not mean a vessel has seen you — verify by other means.
Failure to keep a proper lookout for extended periods can lead directly to near-collisions.
outcomes: The yacht's proactive evasive action (engine start, full throttle, passing 50m ahead) averted a collision.
The fishing vessel crew admitted they had not seen the yacht or noticed it on radar, despite confirmed radar reflector visibility at 6nm earlier that day.
Investigation revealed the fishing vessel's wheelhouse layout and gear operations likely compromised lookout for an extended period (~30 minutes).
key_facts: Incident occurred 34nm west of Bishop Rock in good visibility, SE wind 12 knots.
The sailing yacht was close-hauled at 3.5 knots on a course of 070°; the fishing vessel approached from port at 10 knots on a southerly course.
The yacht's radar reflector, mounted ~10m up the mast, had been verified visible to a cargo ship at 6nm in rain earlier the same day.
The fishing vessel's wheelhouse design placed the watch-keeper in the forward starboard corner near windows, exposed to sun and heat, due to net-hauling gear arrangement.
No one was observed in the fishing vessel's wheelhouse at the time of closest approach.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report recounts a near-miss close-quarters situation in which the fishing vessel 'FV', navigating between two fishing operations, failed to detect an approaching yacht by radar or visually due to late-afternoon sun glare, until alerted by a VHF call when the yacht was already close astern.
trace.trigger: Fishing vessel skipper handed over the watch with 'nothing to report' and briefly left the wheelhouse to top up the engine room service tank, during which period sun glare prevented visual or radar detection of an approaching yacht.

procedures.action: Remove wheelhouse obstructions (e.g. screens) that block vision to port or other critical arcs.
procedures.why: Owner found a screen had been blocking vision when looking to port, contributing to reduced lookout capability.

procedures.action: Investigate and mitigate wheelhouse glare (e.g. through equipment/company enquiry) to improve visibility during low sun conditions.
procedures.why: Late-afternoon sunshine glaring off the sea on the starboard side prevented the crew from seeing the yacht visually or on radar.

procedures.action: As the give-way vessel, detect the other vessel early by any means (visual or electronic) and take action in good time.
procedures.why: FV was clearly the give-way vessel and would have given way in good time had the target been detected earlier.

procedures.action: When crossing the bow of another vessel, consider reducing speed, stopping, or paralleling course until past and clear rather than crossing ahead.
procedures.why: Owner questioned the wisdom of the yacht crossing FV's bow instead of maintaining a safer passing strategy.

procedures.action: Maintain a sharp, continuous lookout at all times, including during watch handovers and brief crew absences.
procedures.why: Good lookout practices (as used routinely to avoid trawler gear conflicts) are key to avoiding close-quarters situations, though direct sunlight remains a limiting factor.

warnings: Sun glare can render both visual and radar lookout ineffective, and this limitation cannot be fully overcome by crew vigilance alone.
Leaving the wheelhouse briefly, even for routine tasks, can result in missed radar/visual contacts during a critical period.
Delaying a warning VHF call to a give-way vessel can allow a close-quarters situation to develop to a dangerous degree.
outcomes: A close-quarters situation developed between FV and the yacht, which was only resolved after a VHF call alerted FV when the yacht was already close astern.

The owner implemented physical changes (removing the obstructing screen) and sought a company solution for glare reduction following the incident.
key_facts: FV was steaming at 192º at 9.5 knots between two fishing operations 8.8 miles apart.
Late-afternoon sun glare off the sea on the starboard side impaired detection of the yacht.
The skipper left the wheelhouse for about 10 minutes to top up the engine room daily service tank after reporting 'nothing to report'.
The yacht was only noticed after a VHF Channel 16 call alerted FV to a close-quarters situation, with the yacht visibly astern.
Static net fishery crews are described as generally skilled with radar due to needing to track trawler activity and avoid gear conflicts.

trace.situation: A vessel approaching Felixstowe via the Sunk TSS identified a crossing situation with a Ro-Pax ferry approaching via North Shipwash channel, with CPA effectively zero, and the ferry (give-way vessel) failed to take appropriate avoiding action.
trace.trigger: ARPA plot showing CPA of zero with a crossing vessel visible on the portside (green sidelight) at good visibility, indicating risk of collision.

procedures.action: Plot contact on ARPA well in advance and monitor CPA/TCPA continuously.
procedures.why: Early detection of a developing close-quarters situation allows time for communication and action.

procedures.action: Contact the other vessel by radio to confirm intentions when CPA is zero.
procedures.why: To establish mutual understanding of the situation and press for the give-way vessel to act.

procedures.action: Clearly state the correct COLREGS classification (crossing, not overtaking) and identify which vessel is give-way.
procedures.why: To correct the other vessel's mistaken assessment and reinforce the obligation to give way.

procedures.action: When the give-way vessel fails to act in ample time, take own avoiding action as stand-on vessel by altering course and reducing speed.
procedures.why: COLREGS permits/requires the stand-on vessel to act alone when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone.

procedures.action: Instruct the other vessel to maintain course and speed while own vessel alters to port and reduces speed to pass astern.
procedures.why: To safely resolve the close-quarters situation decisively once it became clear the give-way vessel would not act in time.

constraints: Do not rely on the other vessel to comply with COLREGS.
Give-way vessel is obligated to take early and substantial action to keep well clear.
Stand-on vessel must act if collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone.
warnings: Never rely on other vessel to obey the collision regulations.
Failure to classify the encounter correctly (crossing vs overtaking) can lead to a close-quarters situation.
outcomes: Own vessel successfully avoided collision by altering course to port and reducing speed, passing astern of the Ro-Pax ferry.
The Ro-Pax ferry, as give-way vessel, did not take timely action and incorrectly claimed the other vessel was overtaking.
key_facts: CPA was effectively zero for at least 30 minutes before the situation was resolved.
Visibility was very good; the Ro-Pax ferry was observed visually at 8nm and its lights at 3nm.

trace.situation: CHIRP incident review covering (1) a close-quarters encounter between a fishing vessel and a sailing yacht where VHF calls were missed and watchkeeping was questioned, and (2) a separate report on a sailing yacht's total electrical power failure caused by a loosened wing-nut battery terminal connection.
trace.trigger: Yacht passed ahead of a fishing vessel after failing to respond to four VHF calls, prompting investigation into watchkeeping; separately, a vessel leaving its berth experienced sudden loss of all electrical accessories.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a near-miss/collision report discussing whether a stand-on vessel took timely action, specifically the effectiveness of early speed reduction versus course alteration under COLREGS Rule 17(a)(ii).
trace.trigger: Risk of collision develops with a vessel approaching from abeam or near the beam, and the give-way vessel fails to take appropriate action in compliance with the Rules.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel OOW, monitor whether the give-way vessel is taking appropriate action in compliance with COLREGS.
procedures.why: Rule 17(a)(ii) permits the stand-on vessel to act independently only once it becomes apparent the other vessel is not complying.

procedures.action: Take early action to avoid collision, using speed reduction in addition to or instead of course alteration.
procedures.why: Early reduction in speed can be as effective as altering course for vessels approaching abeam or near the beam, and CHIRP's simulator study showed 17 of 24 collisions could have been avoided this way.

procedures.action: Weigh the operational cost of slowing down (minor ETA delay) against collision risk.
procedures.why: The study found the average ETA delay from early speed reduction was only 20 minutes, a small cost relative to avoiding collision.

procedures.action: For larger vessels (e.g., bulk carriers), consider engine limitations before executing rapid speed reduction.
procedures.why: Quick speed reduction on large ships risks damage to the main engine, such as cracks to liners and casing.

constraints: Stand-on vessel may only take independent action once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not complying with the Rules (Rule 17(a)(ii)).
Speed reduction must be considered alongside engine mechanical limitations on larger vessels.
warnings: Rapid speed reduction on larger bulk carriers can cause damage to the main engine (cracked liners and casing).

trace.situation: A CHIRP commentary analysing a near-miss/collision risk scenario where two vessels on reciprocal (NW/SE) courses used VHF to negotiate a 'green-to-green' passing agreement instead of applying COLREGS, and a separate collision case where VHF word-dropout during a storm caused a fatal miscommunication.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, consider making allowance for any vessel constrained by its draught.
procedures.why: COLREGS obligations on the stand-on vessel include accounting for vessels constrained by draught.

procedures.action: Avoid using VHF to renegotiate the application of the COLREGS.

outcomes: Reliance on VHF negotiation distracted the OOW from timely COLREGS-compliant action.

procedures.action: Exit the anchorage parallel to and ahead of anchored vessels until well clear.
procedures.why: Avoids passing closely ahead of anchored vessels and being set down onto them.

procedures.action: Keep courses parallel, not converging, with other vessels moving within the anchorage.
procedures.why: Converging or crossing courses at slow speed with difficult-to-manage set inevitably create collision scenarios.

procedures.action: Avoid using VHF to determine another vessel's intent in the anchorage.

constraints: Visual bearings and ARPA-derived CPA data in an anchorage are based on inaccurate, rapidly changing data and cannot be relied upon.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on the MAIB investigation into the RIB 'Milly' incident in the Camel Estuary, where 6 people were ejected from a rigid inflatable boat during a turn, resulting in 2 deaths and 3 injuries, highlighting the dangerous 'hooking' phenomenon identified during reconstruction trials.
trace.trigger: A RIB is turned tightly at certain speeds, causing its heel angle to increase until the aft hull loses grip and slides sideways.
constraints: Modern RIBs are larger, faster, and fitted with very fast-acting engine controls, increasing operational risk.

warnings: A RIB turned tightly at certain speeds can 'hook', sliding sideways until the keel grips and the craft rolls violently upright, generating forces strong enough to eject occupants even if braced.
The hooking action can return the boat 30 degrees to upright in less than 0.5 second.
An increase of only 5 knots in turning speed could be sufficient to eject a prepared, braced driver.
Mishandling fast modern RIBs with quick-action engine controls can result in catastrophic consequences.
outcomes: In the actual incident, 6 people were ejected from the RIB, 3 were injured (2 seriously), and 2 lives were lost.

During reconstruction trials, drivers needed to be seated, braced, and holding handholds to withstand the hooking forces, and even then one driver believed a small speed increase would have ejected him.
key_facts: The incident involved the RIB 'Milly' in the Camel Estuary, Cornwall, England.
The hooking phenomenon occurs when a RIB's heel angle increases during a tight turn until the aft hull loses grip and slides sideways.
The sideways slide stops abruptly when the keel regrips, causing a violent upright roll.
Reconstruction trial drivers reported needing to be well prepared, seated, braced, and holding handholds due to the considerable forces involved.
Modern RIBs are increasingly bigger, faster, and equipped with very fast action engine controls, raising operational risk.

trace.situation: A Chief Officer on a 0400-0800 watch observed an overtaking vessel approaching on a dangerously low CPA (0.3nm) on the port side, which failed to respond to signalling or VHF calls and did not alter course, forcing the stand-on vessel to take avoiding action.
trace.trigger: An overtaking vessel closes to within 1nm with CPA under 0.3nm and does not respond to Aldis lamp signals or VHF calls, indicating it is not complying with COLREGs Rule 13 (overtaking vessel must keep clear).

procedures.action: Continuously monitor CPA/TCPA of an overtaking vessel once first detected astern.
procedures.why: Early detection of a closing, low-CPA contact allows time to assess risk of collision.

procedures.action: Attempt to signal the overtaking vessel via Aldis lamp and VHF when it closes to within about 1nm.
procedures.why: To alert the other vessel and prompt it to take the required give-way action under Rule 13.

procedures.action: If no response or course alteration is received and CPA remains dangerously low, take independent avoiding action (e.g. alter course to starboard) despite being the stand-on vessel.
procedures.why: To increase CPA and reduce risk from a developing close-quarters situation when the give-way vessel fails to act.

procedures.action: Record/document the incident, including screenshots of radar/AIS data.
procedures.why: To provide evidence for reporting and investigation of non-compliant vessel behaviour.

constraints: Under COLREGs Rule 13, the overtaking vessel is the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken.
The stand-on vessel should maintain course/speed until it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, at which point avoiding action is justified.
warnings: Increasing number and size of vessels do not give way under any circumstances, even when required as the overtaking/give-way vessel.
Large vessels (up to 400M) from well-known companies have been observed overtaking at only 3-4 cables in open sea.
When two non-compliant vessels meet in unfavourable circumstances, an accident is inevitable sooner or later.
outcomes: The overtaking vessel passed at 0.36nm after the stand-on vessel's avoiding action, never altering its own heading or responding to communications.
The reporting company briefed the Master, directed a bridge team meeting to discuss the feedback, and ordered a Navigation Audit to ensure compliance with COLREGs.
The Chief Officer involved in the incident had already disembarked by the time of investigation, limiting direct follow-up with that individual.
key_facts: The overtaking vessel approached on the port side with an initial CPA of 0.3nm while still 2 miles astern.
Repeated Aldis lamp signals and VHF calls to the overtaking vessel received no response.
The stand-on vessel altered course 30 degrees to starboard to increase CPA after the overtaking vessel failed to act.
The final passing distance was 0.36nm despite the avoiding action taken.
The reporting officer notes a pattern of large vessels from well-known companies routinely overtaking at 3-4 cables in open sea.

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime safety report discusses an overtaking collision analyzed under COLREGs Rule 13, and separately details a Rigid Inflatable Boat (RIB) 'show boating' incident on the Menai Strait that injured passengers.
trace.trigger: An overtaking vessel failed to keep clear leading to collision risk/incident, and three RIBs engaged in reckless maneuvering with full passenger loads resulting in a capsize-type ejection event.

procedures.action: Overtaking vessel must keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken under Rule 13.
procedures.why: COLREGs Rule 13 places the onus on one vessel to take all necessary action to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Third-party ship managers worked with current officers after the overtaking incident.
procedures.why: To help prevent reoccurrence of the collision-risk behavior.

procedures.action: Report the RIB accident to the Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MAIB) as required.
procedures.why: Mandated under the Merchant Shipping Act 2012 (Accident Reporting and Investigation).

procedures.action: Replace RIBs, improve aft seat securing measures, and issue automatic inflatable lifejackets instead of manual ones.
procedures.why: Remedial action plan addressing identified causal factors in the RIB incident.

procedures.action: Ensure management clearly communicates all safety precautions to employees before taking to the water.
procedures.why: Duty of care obligation highlighted by CHIRP to the film production company.

constraints: Rule 13 overtaking responsibility applies to all vessels, not just power-driven ones.
RIBs operating in this context fall under local authority (Anglesey County Council) jurisdiction, not MCA jurisdiction.
Accidents must be reported per Merchant Shipping Act 2012 (Accident Reporting and Investigation).

warnings: Overtaking vessel bears sole responsibility to avoid collision and must not assume the other vessel will give way.
Reckless 'show boating' maneuvers with passengers aboard risk ejection and injury, as demonstrated by the RIB hooking into a standing wave.

trace.situation: A yacht crossing from Mallorca to Menorca in clear weather experienced a close-quarters situation with a fast ferry that was the give-way vessel but failed to alter course, forcing the yacht to take emergency avoiding action.
trace.trigger: AIS and visual tracking showed the ferry's CPA decreasing to about 0.2 miles as it closed at high speed on a crossing course.

procedures.action: Monitor the other vessel visually and via AIS to track CPA/TCPA as it closes.
procedures.why: Early detection of a decreasing CPA (0.2nm) revealed developing collision risk.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the approaching vessel on VHF Channel 16.
procedures.why: To alert the ferry and prompt it to take appropriate give-way action.

procedures.action: Make an early alteration of course to starboard.
procedures.why: Standard collision avoidance action, attempted but insufficient to clear the ferry given its speed and heading.

procedures.action: Reassess options when initial alteration fails, avoiding a port alteration (risk if ferry turns starboard) or further starboard turn (would put yacht in ferry's path).
procedures.why: Both alternatives carried risk of worsening the close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Apply full throttle and cross ahead of the ferry's bow, then alter to port once clear.
procedures.why: Last-resort maneuver to avoid collision when the give-way vessel took no action and speed differential prevented other options.

constraints: Yacht could only transmit/receive AIS passively (receive only, no transmit).
Yacht's maximum speed was only 6 knots versus ferry's ~20 knots.
Ferry was the give-way vessel under COLREGs but made no course alteration.
VHF Channel 16 calls to the ferry received no reply.
warnings: A give-way vessel may not keep a proper watch and may not respond to VHF calls.
Relying on the stand-on vessel's expectation that give-way vessel will act can be dangerous if it fails to do so.
High speed differential between vessels can rapidly convert a safe situation into a close-quarters emergency.
outcomes: The ferry passed approximately 100m off the yacht's port side after the yacht took emergency evasive action.
No collision occurred, but the encounter highlighted the ferry's apparent lack of watchkeeping and failure to give way.
key_facts: Yacht heading 104°T at 5.5 knots; ferry heading approximately 240°T on a crossing course.
AIS indicated a CPA of about 0.2 miles before evasive action.
Ferry speed was approximately 20 knots or more per AIS.
Two attempts to contact the ferry via VHF Channel 16 received no reply.
Yacht's maximum speed capability was only 6 knots, limiting avoidance options.

trace.situation: CHIRP analysis of a close-quarters crossing encounter between containership 'A' (stand-on) and ferry 'B' (give-way) where the OOWs' actions raised compliance concerns under COLREGs Rule 15 and Rule 17.
trace.trigger: Give-way vessel (Vessel 'B') fails to take early and apparent action to keep clear in a crossing situation, placing the stand-on vessel at risk of collision.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, maintain course and speed per Rule 17(a)(i) and avoid any unexpected action.
procedures.why: Unexpected action by the stand-on vessel can confuse the give-way vessel and increase collision risk.

procedures.action: As soon as it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, take your own action under Rule 17(a)(ii).
procedures.why: A small, hard-to-detect speed alteration (as made by Master of 'A') risks non-compliance because it is unlikely to be noticed by the other ship.

procedures.action: If collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone, take the best action possible under Rule 17(b), executed in time.
procedures.why: Rule 17(b) requires effective, timely action, not a token or late maneuver.

procedures.action: Do not alter course to port in a crossing situation under Rule 17(c); instead use a round turn to starboard.
procedures.why: If the other ship correctly turns to starboard, a port turn by the stand-on vessel would cause both ships to turn towards each other, increasing collision risk.

procedures.action: Assess the 'big picture', including third and fourth vessels in proximity, by mentally placing yourself in the position of other ships.
procedures.why: Nearby vessels may restrict or complicate the available actions of any of the ships involved.

procedures.action: Sound the horn and flash lights at the other vessel per Rule 34(d).
procedures.why: This is the 'wake up' signal intended to alert a give-way vessel that is not taking appropriate action.

constraints: Rule 15 requires the give-way vessel to keep clear in a crossing situation.
Rule 17(a)(i) requires the stand-on vessel to keep course and speed until it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not acting appropriately.
Any action taken under Rule 17 must be substantial enough to be detected by the other vessel.
Action under Rule 17(b) must be taken in time to avoid collision, not left too late.
Rule 17(c) prohibits altering course to port in a crossing situation.
warnings: A small alteration in speed is unlikely to be detected by the other ship and risks non-compliance with Rule 17(a)(i).
Do not go to port in a crossing situation under Rule 17(c), as it may cause both vessels to turn towards each other.
Do not delay action under Rule 17(b) until it is too late to avoid collision.
outcomes: Close encounter between containership 'A' and ferry 'B' occurred due to Vessel B's non-compliance with Rule 15.
Maritime Advisory Board raised concern over actions of OOWs on both vessels.
Honest reporting and third-party cooperation enabled the safety lesson to be identified and shared.
key_facts: Vessel 'B's OOW did not comply with COLREGs Rule 15 as the give-way vessel.
Containership 'A's Master made only a small speed alteration, risking non-compliance with Rule 17(a)(i).
A third and fourth vessel were in close proximity to the starboard side of Vessel 'B', complicating the situation.
Rule 17 has three stages: (a)(i) maintain course/speed, (a)(ii) act when give-way vessel's inaction is apparent, (b) take best action if collision unavoidable.
Rule 34(d) provides for sound and light 'wake up' signals to alert another vessel.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board reviewed a hazardous incident report of a small yacht taking early, substantial avoiding action against a fast-moving ferry to prevent a small CPA, found the ferry company failed to respond to the report, and issued advice to leisure sailors on yacht radar visibility and AIS use.
trace.trigger: A reported close-quarters/small CPA situation between a yacht and a fast-moving ferry, followed by the ferry company's failure to respond to the hazardous incident report.

procedures.action: Recognize that yachts often do not appear on radar beyond about 5 miles due to GRP hull radar wave behaviour, shallow beam angle, wave interception, and inverse-square signal loss.
procedures.why: Radar limitations mean other vessels, including ARPA systems and human observers, may genuinely fail to detect a small yacht at range.

procedures.action: Do not rely solely on radar reflectors for detection enhancement.
procedures.why: RYA and MCA MGN 394 paragraph 4.3 indicate radar reflectors have limited effect in improving identification of small vessels.

procedures.action: Understand that even at closer range a yacht may be hard to detect on radar due to wave clutter.
procedures.why: Wave clutter degrades radar and ARPA plotting/alert performance for small targets.

procedures.action: Install an AIS transponder (or a transponder incorporating a receiver) on the yacht, even at additional cost.
procedures.why: AIS carriage improves identification and situational awareness for other vessels when radar detection is unreliable.

procedures.action: If battery power for AIS is a concern, run the engine to keep batteries charged.
procedures.why: Ensures continuous AIS operation is not compromised by power limitations.

procedures.action: Report failures of proper lookout and VHF Channel 16 listening watch to the Flag State authority when a vessel/company fails to respond to a hazardous incident report.
procedures.why: Severity of the report and the ferry company's non-response warranted escalation to ensure accountability for lookout/watchkeeping failures.

constraints: Advice applies specifically to leisure/yacht users operating near fast-moving vessels such as ferries.
Radar reflector improvements are limited per MCA MGN 394 paragraph 4.3.
Flag State referral occurs only after company failure to respond and due to severity of the report.
warnings: Yachts often do not show up on radar beyond about 5 miles due to hull structure and radar beam geometry.
Radar reflectors have limited effectiveness in improving identification of small vessels.
Wave clutter can prevent detection of yachts even at closer range, affecting both ARPA and human observers.
Failure to maintain proper lookout and VHF Channel 16 listening watch is a serious safety deficiency that can be escalated to Flag State.
outcomes: Ferry company's failure to respond to the hazardous incident report led to Flag State notification regarding lookout and VHF watch failures.
Maritime Advisory Board identified parallels with the Ouzo yacht sinking incident (MAIB 7/2007), underscoring recurring small-vessel detection risks.
Advisory issued to leisure users recommending AIS installation to mitigate radar detection limitations.
key_facts: Yachts typically do not appear on radar beyond approximately 5 miles due to GRP hull effects and radar beam geometry.
Radar reflectors provide only limited improvement in yacht detectability (per RYA and MCA MGN 394 para 4.3).
Wave clutter can obscure yacht detection on radar/ARPA even at closer ranges.
The ferry company did not respond to the hazardous incident report, prompting Flag State notification.
CHIRP drew a parallel to the MAIB's 2007 investigation into the sinking of the yacht Ouzo.

trace.situation: A container ship (Vessel 'A') and a ferry (Vessel 'B') were in a crossing situation with a very small CPA, leading to a VHF exchange over give-way responsibilities and a subsequent disagreement over compliance with COLREGs Rule 15.
trace.trigger: Developing close-quarters crossing situation with initial CPA of 0.57 nm between the two vessels.

procedures.action: Master of Vessel 'A' reduced speed slightly under Rule 8(e) to gain more time to assess the situation.
procedures.why: To allow time to evaluate risk of collision and avoid crossing ahead of Vessel 'B'.

procedures.action: Master of Vessel 'A' contacted OOW of Vessel 'B' via VHF to clarify intentions.
procedures.why: To coordinate collision avoidance action given the small CPA.

procedures.action: Master of Vessel 'A' asserted that Vessel 'B' should comply with COLREGs Rule 15.
procedures.why: As the crossing vessel with the other on her starboard side, Vessel 'B' was the give-way vessel and should alter course to starboard, not expect 'A' to pass astern.

procedures.action: Master of Vessel 'A' attempted to re-contact Vessel 'B' on VHF after no acknowledgement.
procedures.why: To confirm agreement and avoid ambiguity in collision avoidance intentions.

procedures.action: Company instructed Master to refresh COLREGs training (especially Rule 15) with all deck officers.
procedures.why: Corrective action after breach of Rule 15 was identified.

procedures.action: Conduct an extraordinary navigational audit.
procedures.why: To verify navigational practices and prevent recurrence of similar breaches.

procedures.action: Hold extraordinary Safety Committee meeting with all deck officers to discuss the case.
procedures.why: To disseminate lessons learned and reinforce correct COLREGs application across the fleet.

procedures.action: Arrange for Company Port Captain to attend the vessel at next port and debrief officers at sign-off.
procedures.why: To ensure direct oversight and reinforcement of corrective measures.

constraints: Rule 15 requires the give-way vessel (Vessel 'B' in this crossing) to alter course to starboard, not to port.
VHF communication should not replace or override required COLREGs actions.
Monitoring of VHF channels 6 and 16 must be maintained during risk-of-collision situations.
warnings: Altering course to port instead of starboard under Rule 15 constitutes a breach of COLREGs and can create or worsen a close-quarters situation.
Relying on VHF agreement without proper COLREGs compliance can lead to confusion and increased collision risk.
Failure of the give-way vessel to acknowledge and follow correct action can leave the stand-on vessel without clear confirmation of avoidance measures.
outcomes: Vessel 'B' altered course to port, increasing the crossing distance from an initial CPA of 0.57 nm to about 1.6 nm, averting a close-quarters situation.
This action was later found to be in breach of Rule 15, since Vessel 'B' should have altered course to starboard.
Company implemented corrective and preventive actions including COLREGs refresher training, a navigational audit, and a safety committee review.
key_facts: Initial ARPA-derived CPA was 0.57 nm at a range of 1.7 nm, indicating a close-quarters crossing situation.
Vessel 'A' reduced speed under Rule 8(e) and contacted Vessel 'B' via VHF regarding right-of-way.
Vessel 'B' proposed Vessel 'A' pass her stern while 'B' altered to port, contrary to Rule 15, which required 'B' to alter to starboard.
After resulting course alteration, crossing distance and CPA increased to about 1.8 nm and 1.6 nm respectively.
Corrective actions included refresher COLREGs training, an extraordinary navigational audit, a safety committee meeting, and a port captain debrief.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report lists best practices for maintaining a safe anchor watch to prevent contact incidents between vessels at anchor.
trace.trigger: Vessel is at anchor, particularly in a congested anchorage or when adverse weather/dragging anchors is expected.

procedures.action: Maintain a robust anchor watch at all times and check the vessel's position at regular intervals.
procedures.why: To detect dragging or drifting early and avoid contact with other vessels.

procedures.action: Re-adjust echo sounder and anemometer limit alarms after anchoring, where fitted.
procedures.why: Alarm settings used for passage may not be appropriate once anchored, so they must reflect the anchorage conditions.

procedures.action: Continuously monitor weather and have an action plan ready for adverse weather or when nearby anchored vessels are swinging differently.
procedures.why: Changing weather or differential swinging indicates increased risk of dragging or collision.

procedures.action: Insert a visual marker on the windlass to indicate brake slipping.
procedures.why: Provides an early visual cue that the anchor brake is not holding, allowing timely intervention.

procedures.action: Keep the main engine in an appropriate state of readiness.
procedures.why: Enables prompt maneuvering if the vessel starts to drag anchor or another vessel approaches.

procedures.action: Use the Bridge Navigational Watch Alarm System (BNWAS) while at anchor, if available.
procedures.why: Ensures continuous watchkeeping alertness is maintained even at anchor.

procedures.action: Follow clear standing instructions for calling the Master in good time, tailored to the specific anchorage.
procedures.why: Ensures the Master is informed early enough to make decisions before a situation escalates.

procedures.action: Keep an emergency contact list of local support services (pilot, tugs, etc.) available at all times.
procedures.why: Allows rapid access to assistance if an emergency develops at anchor.

procedures.action: Provide Bridge Team Simulator training to deck officers and Masters covering anchoring scenarios including weather changes, dragging anchors, and vessels drifting towards own ship.
procedures.why: Builds practical experience and preparedness for realistic contact-incident scenarios at anchor.

procedures.action: Include an evaluation of anchor-watch best practices in the vessel operator's internal navigation audits.
procedures.why: Ensures ongoing compliance and improvement of anchor watch procedures across the fleet.

constraints: Applicable only while the vessel is at anchor.
Alarm and equipment adjustments should only be made where such equipment is fitted and applicable to the anchorage.
Master must be called in accordance with standing instructions specific to the anchorage location.
warnings: Failure to adjust alarms and maintain vigilant anchor watch can result in contact incidents with other anchored or maneuvering vessels.
Dragging anchor in congested anchorages poses a significant collision risk.
outcomes: Early detection of anchor dragging or brake slippage allows timely corrective action.
Proper training and standing instructions reduce the likelihood of contact incidents in anchorages.
Continuous monitoring and readiness of the main engine enable rapid response to drifting vessels or weather changes.
key_facts: A visual marker on the windlass helps identify when the anchor brake is slipping.
BNWAS should be used at anchor if available to maintain watch alertness.
Bridge Team Simulator training should include scenarios of dragging anchors and vessels drifting towards own ship.
An emergency contact list for pilots, tugs, and other local support should always be accessible.
Internal navigation audits should evaluate anchor watch best practices where possible.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Feedback 41 reports on a rise in contact incidents between vessels at congested anchorages, prompting a major charterer's Safety Alert Bulletin outlining causal factors and good practice for anchoring operations.
trace.trigger: An increase in incidents involving contact between vessels at congested anchorage locations, leading a major charterer to issue a Safety Alert Bulletin.

procedures.action: Conduct detailed pre-arrival/departure planning covering appraisal, planning, execution, monitoring, contingency and site-specific risk assessment.
procedures.why: Prevents poor preparation that contributes to contact incidents at anchorage.

procedures.action: Evaluate anchorage congestion status and select a suitable anchorage position in consultation with Port Authorities/VTS before entering the anchorage area; avoid passing close ahead of other anchored vessels while approaching.
procedures.why: Reduces risk of close-quarters situations with vessels already at anchor.

procedures.action: Evaluate and pay out an adequate length of anchor cable considering prevailing conditions, holding ground and sea depth.
procedures.why: Ensures sufficient holding power to prevent dragging.

procedures.action: Plot the vessel's swinging circle on GPS, paper chart and ECDIS where available.
procedures.why: Ensures adequate clearance to swing about the anchor without contacting other vessels.

procedures.action: Once anchored, ascertain the actual swing pattern and adjust ECDIS/Radar/GPS alarm limits accordingly.
procedures.why: Verifies real swing behavior matches planned clearance and enables early alerting of deviation.

procedures.action: Monitor swing tendencies of other vessels in the immediate vicinity, especially during change of tidal streams.
procedures.why: Adjacent vessel movement during tide change is a known cause of contact incidents.

procedures.action: Calculate and mark tidal streams, particularly in areas known for strong tidal effects.
procedures.why: Supports correct assessment of current strength and direction affecting anchored vessel behavior.

constraints: Swinging circle must be plotted and used as an active monitoring tool, not just a planning exercise.
Main propulsion should be available for immediate use while at anchor when required.
Anchorage position selection should be coordinated with Port Authorities/VTS.
warnings: Bridge team's failure to correctly assess strength and direction of local tidal current and wind prior to arrival and during departure from anchorage can cause contact incidents.
Maneuvering too close to vessels already at anchor increases collision risk.
Lack of proper navigational watchkeeping while at anchor is a causal factor in contact incidents.
Failure to plot or use the swinging circle as a monitoring tool, especially when anchored vessels swing in different directions, is a causal factor.
Lack of monitoring clearances from adjacent anchored vessels during change of tide contributes to incidents.
Inadequate monitoring of prevailing weather and forecasts (local seasonal winds, thunderstorms, squalls) can lead to anchor dragging.
Unavailability of main propulsion for immediate use when required is a causal factor in contact incidents.
outcomes: Increase in contact incidents between vessels at congested anchorages prompted a formal Safety Alert Bulletin from a major charterer.
Anchor dragging can result from inadequate weather monitoring, leading to contact with adjacent vessels.
key_facts: A major charterer issued a Safety Alert Bulletin after noticing an increase in contact incidents between vessels at congested anchorages.
Causal factors include poor tidal/wind assessment, manoeuvring too close to anchored vessels, inadequate watchkeeping, unplotted swinging circles, and unavailable main propulsion.
Good practice includes detailed pre-arrival/departure planning, anchorage position evaluation in consultation with Port Authorities/VTS, and plotting swinging circles on GPS/chart/ECDIS.
Swing tendencies of other anchored vessels should be monitored especially during tidal stream changes.

procedures.action: Ensure the passage plan conforms to local routeing and manoeuvring guidance (e.g. Deep Water Route rules) with alternatives available.
procedures.why: Local routeing guidance exists to prevent conflicts in congested or draught-restricted areas.

procedures.action: Plan the TSS arrival in advance: timing, bridge manning, and Master's presence on the bridge.
procedures.why: Proper preparation avoids being caught unprepared when entering high-traffic zones.

procedures.action: Treat the passage plan as a basis for change, not a rule to follow regardless of real-time circumstances.
procedures.why: Rigid adherence to a plan ('red-line-itis') can cause failure to adapt to developing close-quarters situations.

procedures.action: Begin planning how to slot into traffic flow from at least 10 nautical miles out when approaching or navigating a TSS.
procedures.why: Early planning for large ships gives adequate time and space to manage traffic safely.

procedures.action: Slow down if in doubt, bearing in mind the vessel astern.
procedures.why: Situations can develop very fast; reducing speed preserves options and safety margins.

procedures.action: Do not overtake unless there is ample time to CPA and sufficient space within the safe straight part of the TSS.
procedures.why: Insufficient time/space for overtaking creates close-quarters risk.

procedures.action: Overtake only on the starboard side of the vessel being overtaken where possible.
procedures.why: This preserves flexible options and maximises searoom.

procedures.action: Masters should issue clear order book or verbal instructions on expectations for speed/course alterations, overtaking, and traffic density handling.
procedures.why: Clear calling orders reduce reliance on inexperienced OOW judgment alone.

procedures.action: Maintain visual lookout (look up and out) and use electronic aids as a supplement, not a sole dependency.
procedures.why: Over-reliance on electronic aids without visual confirmation increases risk.

procedures.action: Consider the situation from the other ship's point of view.
procedures.why: Understanding the other vessel's perspective supports better collision avoidance decision-making.

constraints: Overtaking should only proceed if ample time to CPA and space exist within the safe straight part of the TSS.
Overtaking vessel should only pass on the starboard side of the vessel being overtaken.
Bridge should be backed up with extra expertise to manage workload near TSS entrances.
warnings: Inexperienced OOWs can be sucked into close quarters situations that never need to occur.
A collision at this location could have closed the strait to deep draught vessels or obstructed the route with major consequences.
Following a passage plan 'regardless' of circumstances (red-line-itis) is dangerous.
Do not depend on electronic aids alone.
outcomes: The container ship's managers acknowledged she could or should have slowed down.
Failure to plan ahead and adapt the passage plan contributed to a close-quarters/near-collision situation.

trace.situation: CHIRP guidance advises masters and OOWs on how to plan and execute a safe crossing of a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) amid multiple crossing ships.
trace.trigger: A vessel needs to cross a TSS where crossing situations with one or more ships are likely to develop.

procedures.action: Identify and mark a 'crossing window' on the chart in advance.
procedures.why: Provides a planned safe timeframe/location to conduct the crossing.

procedures.action: Plan in advance when and under what circumstances the Master needs to be on the bridge.
procedures.why: Ensures adequate command presence during critical crossing phase.

procedures.action: Assess traffic in the lanes well ahead and choose a moment to cross where a gap is likely or where only one crossing situation arises at a time.
procedures.why: Reduces complexity and risk of multiple simultaneous crossing situations.

procedures.action: Use the Mark 1 eyeball combined with compass bearing assessments (using azimuth rings if fitted).
procedures.why: Provides direct visual confirmation of bearing movement and risk of collision.

procedures.action: Use ARPA trial manoeuvre to decide the moment of turn.
procedures.why: Helps determine optimal timing when not clear by other means.

procedures.action: Use relative tails on radar to quickly confirm new CPAs after the turn.
procedures.why: Verifies the manoeuvre achieved a safe passing distance.

procedures.action: Use AIS to monitor other ships' course changes and track data for destination/intention assessment.
procedures.why: Course alterations become apparent almost immediately and track data indicates probable intentions.

procedures.action: Brief and motivate lookouts; bring an additional officer to the bridge if in doubt.
procedures.why: Guards against bridge overload, which is almost certain in heavy shipping/complex TSS situations.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary following an overtaking near-miss incident, offering guidance on safe overtaking practice and promoting a positive safety culture aboard ship.

procedures.action: Do not approach dead astern when overtaking another vessel.

procedures.action: Keep a good lookout all round, including astern, and be aware of blind arcs.

procedures.action: Monitor all vessels, especially those with unclear intentions.
procedures.why: Early monitoring allows time to react before a close-quarters situation develops.

procedures.action: Act early in unexpected circumstances or worsening conditions.

procedures.action: If urgent/emergency action is needed, stay calm, follow drills, and apply safety procedures deliberately.
procedures.why: Maintains control and reduces error even under pressure.

procedures.action: Promote and maintain a positive safety culture from leadership down.

procedures.why: Provides flotation and rescue capability if the man falls or is trapped.

procedures.action: Station two crew members at the bow to operate the anchor winch and observe the boat.
procedures.why: Ensures supervision and ability to react/winch control during the operation.

procedures.action: Maintain VHF communications between boat, bow, and bridge.
procedures.why: Coordinates actions and allows immediate reporting of problems.

procedures.action: Have one tender crewman work to release the fouled line while confirming it is not electrical, while the other crewman manoeuvres the boat.
procedures.why: Reduces risk of electrocution and allows controlled handling of the line.

procedures.action: If release is unsuccessful, recover boat and crew, let the anchor go again, and seek commercial diver assistance.
procedures.why: Avoids continued exposure of crew to uncontrolled hazards; uses specialist resources instead.

constraints: Man working on the fouled anchor must wear a life jacket.
Man must have a proper lifeline/harness, not just hang from the fouled line.
Crew member must be continuously supervised, ideally visible from the bridge or by dedicated observers.
Vessel propulsion status and anchor line tension must be assessed before manual intervention.
An operational risk assessment should be completed before undertaking anchor-clearing work.
warnings: Entanglement in the fouled line while clinging to the anchor is a particularly serious hazard.
Sudden increase or release in line tension could trap the man underwater or tow him astern near the propellers.
Lack of life jacket and proper lifeline/harness are severe safety lapses.
Relaxed routines akin to recreational boating in good weather can dilute necessary safety procedures on larger vessels.
It was unclear whether the man was continuously supervised, and he was very unlikely to be visible from the bridge.
outcomes: The incident resolved without injury ('all was well'), but it was recognized as a classic near miss with high potential for serious harm.

Vessel management responded positively to CHIRP and developed a comprehensive future procedure for fouled anchor incidents, including rescue boat deployment, bow crew stationing, VHF communication, and diver assistance if needed.
