The vessel was operating propulsion at the time the man was clearing the fouled anchor.
The man had no life jacket and no proper lifeline/harness other than the line he was hanging from.
It is unclear whether the fouled line was under tension or whether the man was under continuous supervision.
The vessel's management has since developed a detailed procedure involving rescue boat, bow crew, VHF comms, and diver assistance as a fallback.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime reporter accounts describe crew/officers being pressured to illegally dump waste overboard, and an introduction to near-miss reports involving dangerous encounters in Traffic Separation Schemes (TSS).
trace.trigger: Officer or shoreside party orders/requests disposal of oily waste, broken equipment, or damaged oil drums at sea, or a vessel is operating within/crossing a TSS.

procedures.action: Refuse unlawful orders to dump oily waste, machinery, or oil drums overboard even if financial recompense is offered.
procedures.why: Such dumping is an environmental/MARPOL violation and places master and chief engineer at legal and professional risk.

procedures.action: Report concerns to authorities at the next port of call if crew are directed to dump waste illegally.
procedures.why: Crew in one case were sufficiently concerned to involve port authorities, indicating the proper escalation path when illegal orders are given.

procedures.action: Exercise heightened vigilance and proper collision-avoidance practice when overtaking or crossing within a TSS.
procedures.why: Reports show overtaking at dangerously close quarters and head-on closing speeds of ~35 knots have occurred within TSS traffic.

constraints: Dumping of oily waste, machinery, or damaged oil drums overboard is not authorized regardless of distance from shore or financial incentive offered.
Crew/officers retain the right and duty to decline unlawful shoreside instructions.
warnings: Dumping oily waste or damaged equipment overboard, even far from shore and even if offered payment, is illegal and unsafe.
TSS transits carry high risk of dangerously close-quarters situations during overtaking and head-on crossing encounters.
outcomes: Master and chief engineer declined the shoreside request to dump oil drums, avoiding an environmental violation.
In the other case, crew escalated concerns to authorities at the next port after an officer ordered overboard disposal of oily waste.
Previously reported TSS incidents included a dangerously close overtaking manoeuvre and a head-on situation with a 35-knot closing speed.

trace.situation: CHIRP incident report analysing a near-collision/close-quarters situation in a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) near West Hinder, where a vessel (ship 2) deviated into the separation zone and nearly collided with another vessel (ship 3, a Ro-Ro) before altering back to starboard.
trace.trigger: A vessel (ship 2) encroached across the TSS separation line into the opposing/southwest traffic lane, bringing three large vessels into close proximity with minimal sea room.
constraints: Vessels in a TSS must not encroach on the separation line or zone (COLREG 10(b)(ii))

trace.situation: CHIRP incident report describing a ship overtaking in a constrained Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS) near the Bergues North buoy where the overtaking vessel encroached on the separation line, plus a separate account of a passenger ship departing a berth and closing to 20 metres from another vessel's stern while crew stood in hazardous positions near mooring lines.
trace.trigger: Overtaking manoeuvre attempted in a highly constrained part of a TSS approaching a corner/buoy, combined with reduced sea-room and inadequate lookout; separately, a vessel departing a berth passing close astern of another moored vessel with crew tending ropes.

procedures.action: Incorporate avoidance of overtaking in constrained TSS sections or near corners into passage planning.
procedures.why: Overtaking in such areas reduces manoeuvring options and increases collision risk, as demonstrated by the reporter's ship having no room to starboard near Bergues North buoy.

procedures.action: Maintain active lookout and anticipate traffic ahead ('look and think ahead').
procedures.why: Failures were exacerbated by overload, tiredness, distraction, undermanning, and failure to look up and out.

procedures.action: Ensure vessels keep clear of the separation line and follow the general direction of traffic flow when navigating a TSS.
procedures.why: Ship 2 contravened COLREG 10(b)(ii) by encroaching on the separation line and nearly contravened 10(b)(i) regarding general traffic direction.

procedures.action: Assess berth suitability and snapback hazard zones before positioning crew to tend mooring lines during close-quarters departures.
procedures.why: Poor berth design, mismatched berths, and snapback hazards combined with crew standing in hazardous positions near ropes can be lethal, even though no injury occurred in this case.

Risk factors cited include overload, tiredness, distraction, undermanning, and failure to look up and out

No actual collision or injury occurred in either reported incident

trace.situation: A reporter's vessel transiting the Westhinder TSS in the NE lane experienced a tight CPA with an opposing-lane vessel that drifted across the separation line while the reporter was simultaneously being overtaken by a third vessel on a steady bearing.
trace.trigger: An opposite-lane vessel (ship 2) turned slowly to port, crossed the separation line into the reporter's lane, and placed itself on a collision course with the overtaking vessel (ship 3), while failing to respond on the working VHF channel.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the errant vessel on the designated VTS/sector working channel (VHF60).
procedures.why: To establish the other vessel's intentions before the situation develops into collision risk.

procedures.action: If no response, escalate to VTS/port approach on VHF16 to intervene and instruct the vessel to monitor the correct sector channel.
procedures.why: VTS intervention via the universal calling channel succeeded in getting the vessel to respond and alter course where direct contact had failed.

procedures.action: Maintain situational awareness of all three vessels (own ship, opposite-lane ship, overtaking ship) and monitor CPA continuously.
procedures.why: Multiple vessels in proximity within a TSS created a compounded close-quarters risk requiring continuous tracking.

procedures.action: Hold course within the lane as far as sea room allows despite being constrained to starboard by a navigational buoy.
procedures.why: Rule 10 requires vessels to keep within their lane; the reporter was limited in his ability to maneuver further to starboard by the Bergues North buoy.

constraints: Vessels in a TSS must comply with COLREG Rule 10 (lane discipline, avoiding crossing separation lines).

Visibility was good, so restricted visibility rules did not apply.
VHF communication standard of English was poor, complicating coordination.

Poor standard of English in VHF communication hampered resolution of the situation.
outcomes: CPA between own vessel and the errant ship (ship 2) was 3 cables with a developing collision course with ship 3.
After VTS intervention on VHF16, ship 2 turned back to starboard to the extreme edge of the separation scheme, averting the close-quarters situation.
The Maritime Advisory Board linked regulatory non-compliance (e.g., MARPOL) to broader indicators of poor management and safety standards aboard vessels/companies.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report covering two separate safety concerns: a moored passenger vessel with poor mooring line leads and crew exposed to a snap-back zone, and a crossing situation where a give-way passenger ship failed to alter course for a container vessel despite a request.
trace.trigger: Departing vessel wake placed excessive strain on poorly-led mooring lines while crew stood in the snap-back zone, and separately a give-way vessel refused to alter course to starboard when requested by the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation.

procedures.action: Maintain course and speed as the stand-on vessel while assessing the give-way vessel's action.
procedures.why: Collision avoidance rules require the stand-on vessel to hold course until it is apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.

procedures.action: Make an independent avoiding action (360-degree turn to starboard) when the give-way vessel fails to alter course despite request.

procedures.action: Pass clear under the stern of the other vessel after taking avoiding action.
procedures.why: Passing under the stern avoids crossing ahead of the other vessel's path, reducing collision risk.

procedures.action: Avoid positioning crew within the after mooring station's snap-back zone during periods of surge loading.
procedures.why: Angled leads and roller leads across the deck increase the risk of mooring lines parting under strain from vessel wake.

procedures.action: Employ available mooring bollards rather than relying solely on roller leads.
procedures.why: Bollards were not used in this case, contributing to poor line leads and excessive strain risk.

Crew standing within the snap-back zone during surge loading are at serious injury risk
A give-way vessel's failure to alter course despite a VHF request leaves the stand-on vessel at risk of collision
outcomes: The reporter's 360-degree turn and passage under the other vessel's stern avoided a close-quarters situation
Excessive strain on mooring lines occurred due to poor berth fit and inadequate line leads
Lack of crew awareness placed personnel in the snap-back zone during a hazardous surge-load period
key_facts: The moored vessel does not fit the berth, preventing stern lines from being run and causing poor back spring and breast line leads
Mooring bollards were not used in this instance
Crew and an officer were positioned within the after mooring snap-back zone during surge loading

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a near-miss style close-quarters crossing situation between the reporting vessel and a passenger ship, where the passenger ship stood on despite a CPA of about 1nm and crossing-ahead distance of about 2nm, followed by a VHF exchange disputing whether COLREG Rule 15 was being breached; the report also comments on the passenger ship's unconventional and unsafe mooring arrangement at a berth too small for its size.
trace.trigger: A crossing situation develops between two vessels with a calculated CPA (~1nm) and crossing-ahead distance (~2nm) considered too small by the reporting vessel, prompting VHF contact to clarify intentions.

procedures.action: Monitor ARPA true vectors to assess CPA and crossing-ahead distance in a developing crossing situation.
procedures.why: Allows objective assessment of risk of collision rather than relying on assumption.

procedures.action: Establish VHF communication promptly to clarify the other vessel's intentions when CPA appears too small.
procedures.why: Enables exchange of information to resolve ambiguity about risk of collision and COLREG compliance.

procedures.action: As Master, exercise professional judgement on whether to stand on or alter course based on observed CPA, vessel conditions, and COLREG obligations.
procedures.why: Judgement on collision risk and COLREG compliance ultimately lies with the ship's Master given all circumstances.

procedures.action: As Master, refuse a berth considered unsafe for the vessel's size based on observation and professional judgement.
procedures.why: The Master has the right and responsibility to refuse a berth where the standard of safety is not met, despite commercial pressure.

constraints: A minimum 2nm CPA in open water is widely accepted as good practice, though final judgement rests with the Master.
Company policy had required a minimum CPA of 2nm 'when reasonable and practical' in the past but now leaves the decision to individual Masters.
Charterer's responsibility is to provide a safe berth for a ship.
Mooring arrangements are designed for conventional long leads forward and aft; reverse-direction stern/head lines greatly increase stress and risk of premature failure.
warnings: A CPA of around 1nm combined with crossing-ahead distance of about 2nm may constitute a breach of COLREG 15 and inappropriate close-quarters situation.
Use of stern (and head) lines in reverse direction greatly increases stress on mooring arrangements and encourages premature failure with safety implications.
Commercial pressures can make refusing an unsafe berth a challenging call, and inappropriate berthing is reportedly increasing with larger ships and trade volumes.
Close-quarters manoeuvring at a berth may amplify danger of mooring failure through interaction and surge.
outcomes: The passenger ship's Master considered the situation safe and stood on, disputing the reporter's assessment of a COLREG 15 breach.
The reporter believed the crossing distance and CPA were too small and inappropriate.

The passenger ship company's prior policy mandated a minimum 2nm CPA 'when reasonable and practical', but this has since been left to individual Master discretion.
A minimum 2nm CPA in open water is widely regarded as good practice.

procedures.action: Free twisted anchor chain links using a chain hook.
procedures.why: Links were found twisted during locker inspection and needed to be restored to proper function.

procedures.action: Update the vessel's list of spaces to be inspected to include the cofferdam adjacent to fuel tanks.

procedures.action: Order replacement D shackles with security pins for enclosed space evacuation stretchers.
procedures.why: Existing D shackles on stretchers from the bow thruster room and engine room lacked security pins, a safety deficiency.

procedures.action: Order a replacement magnetron for the X-band radar.
procedures.why: The magnetron had exceeded its planned life, causing decreasing sensitivity and failure to locate nearest targets.

procedures.action: Rectify all noted bridge defects (wing repeater illumination, water ingress in navigation consoles, speed log interruptions) through remedial maintenance.
procedures.why: These defects were identified during the inspection as affecting bridge equipment reliability.

constraints: All spaces adjacent to fuel tanks, including cofferdams, must be included in the vessel's inspection list.

warnings: A magnetron exceeding its planned life can cause decreasing radar sensitivity and failure to detect nearby targets, a navigation safety risk.
D shackles without security pins on enclosed space evacuation stretchers pose a risk of failure during an emergency rescue.

outcomes: Twisted anchor chain links were freed and restored.
The vessel's inspection list was updated to include the previously omitted cofferdam.
Replacement D shackles were ordered for evacuation stretchers.
A replacement magnetron was ordered for the X-band radar.
All bridge defects were rectified following remedial maintenance.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime FEEDBACK review of several incident lessons, with the principal case examining a stand-on vessel's actions in a crossing situation under COLREG Rule 7 where risk of collision existed and doubt justified a last-resort 360° turn to starboard.
trace.trigger: Doubt about whether risk of collision exists in a crossing situation, per COLREG Rule 7, where the stand-on vessel must decide how to avoid collision without prematurely turning to port.

procedures.action: Treat any doubt about risk of collision as risk existing (COLREG Rule 7).
procedures.why: COLREG 7 states that if there is any doubt such risk will be deemed to exist.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel in a crossing situation, consider slowing down rather than altering course to port.
procedures.why: A turn to port before the other vessel crosses the bow is not permissible while the crossing situation exists.

procedures.action: Only alter course to port once the other vessel has crossed the bow and the crossing situation no longer exists.
procedures.why: At that point the crossing situation has ended, making a port turn appropriate.

procedures.action: Use a 360° turn to starboard only as a last-resort action.
procedures.why: It can buy valuable time to resolve a close-quarters situation when other options are unavailable.

procedures.action: Exercise caution and maintain an alert all-round lookout before and during a 360° turn.
procedures.why: Below a certain range the manoeuvre can become dangerous and must account for all other vessels nearby, including astern and alongside, especially in constrained waters like TSSs.

constraints: A turn to port is not permitted before the other vessel has crossed the bow in a crossing situation.
A 360° turn to starboard is only reasonable as an action of last resort.
The 360° turn manoeuvre must account for all vessels in the vicinity, especially in constrained waters such as TSSs.
Situational awareness and an alert all-round lookout are required before executing such a manoeuvre.
warnings: Twisted anchor chains are extremely hazardous if they 'jump' on the windlass.
A 360° turn can become dangerous below a certain range.
Pressure surges during cargo transfer carry high risk of pipeline damage and pollution.
outcomes: In this instance, the 360° turn was executed safely and bought valuable time, with no criticism implied of the reporter.
Proper application of COLREG principles and caution avoided a close-quarters collision situation.
key_facts: COLREG Rule 7 states that if any doubt exists as to risk of collision, such risk is deemed to exist.
A stand-on vessel cannot legally turn to port before the other vessel crosses its bow during a crossing situation.
A 360° turn to starboard is a valid last-resort collision avoidance manoeuvre under suitable circumstances.
Work inside a chain/cable locker requires careful planning and communication between locker and windlass operator due to risk of twisted chains jumping.
Cargo transfer pressure surges require close monitoring, with reduced rates or suspension if doubt exists about causes.

question_seeds.text: Why was the stand-on vessel prohibited from turning to port before the other vessel crossed the bow?
At what point does a crossing situation cease to exist, allowing a turn to port?
How should a 360° turn to starboard be safely executed as a last-resort collision avoidance manoeuvre?
Which COLREG rule governs the determination of risk of collision when doubt exists?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a fire that broke out during welding (hot work) on the outside of a ship's superstructure, rapidly engulfing the after side within two minutes.
trace.trigger: Welding sparks dropped into a pile of rubbish on deck during hot work operations without a fire watch in place.

procedures.action: Establish a dedicated fire watch before and during all hot work operations, whether conducted by ship's staff or repair yard personnel.
procedures.why: No fire watch was set by either party, allowing the fire to spread undetected and uncontrolled.

procedures.action: Clear combustible debris and rubbish from the vicinity of hot work before starting.
procedures.why: Sparks dropped into a pile of rubbish, which ignited and allowed the fire to spread quickly.

procedures.action: Ensure adequate curing/drying time between successive paint applications and avoid excessive buildup of paint layers.
procedures.why: A dozen layers of paint with inadequate time between applications created flammable components that contributed to the fire's rapid spread.

procedures.action: Verify appropriate firefighting equipment is available and suitable for the type of fire expected during hot work.
procedures.why: An attempt to extinguish the fire with a 'high pressure cleaner' did not work, delaying suppression.

constraints: Hot work procedures must be followed regardless of vessel size or type.
A fire watch must be set whenever welding or similar hot work is performed on or near a vessel's structure.
warnings: Multiple layers of paint with inadequate drying time can create flammable conditions that accelerate fire spread.
Failure to set a fire watch during hot work can result in fire escaping initial control within minutes.
Inappropriate firefighting equipment (e.g., a high pressure cleaner) may be ineffective against certain fires.
outcomes: The entire after side of the superstructure was on fire within two minutes of ignition.
The fire was eventually successfully extinguished after the initial attempt with a high pressure cleaner failed.
key_facts: The fire started from welding sparks dropping into a pile of rubbish during hot work on the outside of the superstructure.
A dozen layers of paint with flammable components from inadequate inter-coat drying time contributed to rapid fire spread.
No fire watch was set by either ship's staff or the repair yard during the welding operation.
An initial attempt to extinguish the fire using a high pressure cleaner was unsuccessful; the fire was later put out by other means.

question_seeds.text: Why did the fire spread across the entire after side of the superstructure within just two minutes?
What hot work precautions were missing that allowed this fire to escalate so quickly?
How should paint application schedules be managed to avoid creating flammable buildup during hot work operations?
Who is responsible for setting a fire watch during hot work—ship's staff, the repair yard, or both?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report summarizes lessons learnt from multiple incidents: tanker cargo pipeline over-pressurisation during tank changeover/discharge, enclosed-space hazard awareness, stretcher shackle safety, radar magnetron maintenance, and general bridge guidance on avoiding collision in crossing situations.

procedures.action: Verify correct cargo line-up before and during tank changeover and discharge operations
procedures.why: Incorrect cargo line-up was identified as a common factor in loss of containment incidents

procedures.action: Maintain reliable ship/shore communication throughout cargo operations, especially during topping-off
procedures.why: Inadequate ship/shore communication was a common factor and caused a communication failure during a topping-off operation

procedures.action: Ensure adequate supervision during changeover of cargo tanks and restart of operations after a stoppage
procedures.why: Inadequate supervision was identified as a contributing factor to over-pressurisation incidents

procedures.action: Manifold watch to immediately report any change of flow or pressure increase to the Cargo Control Room
procedures.why: Prompt reporting enabled the OOW to detect and act on the pressure increase simultaneously

procedures.action: OOW to suspend discharge immediately upon noting abnormal pressure increase
procedures.why: Timely suspension prevented escalation of the over-pressurisation event, later found to be caused by an uncontrolled automatic shore valve closure

procedures.action: Treat partially open spaces as potentially dangerous and include them on the enclosed space list
procedures.why: Partially open spaces may still present enclosed-space hazards

procedures.action: Mouse stretcher shackles as an alternative to using a split pin
procedures.why: Provides a safer securing method for stretcher shackles

procedures.action: Check radar magnetron performance at regular intervals and schedule replacement in the planned maintenance system
procedures.why: Detects fall-off in performance and ensures equipment reliability ('knowing your equipment')

procedures.action: As give-way vessel, alter course if the stand-on vessel expresses concern about risk of collision
procedures.why: If there is doubt, a risk of collision exists; doubt is accompanied by danger and risk of miscalculation

procedures.action: Avoid using VHF to resolve collision risk situations when time is tight
procedures.why: VHF use can be a distraction from taking correct avoiding action

procedures.action: Consider the situation from the other vessel's point of view
procedures.why: What seems safe and reasonable from one bridge may not appear so from the other's

procedures.action: Continuously practice 'what-ifing' scenarios (e.g., steering gear failure)
procedures.why: Maintains preparedness for sudden equipment or situational failures

procedures.action: Conduct thorough, unpredictable inspections and encourage crew alertness at all levels
procedures.why: Promotes noticing and rectifying shortcomings and rewards vigilance

constraints: If there is doubt, a risk of collision exists
Partially open spaces may still be dangerous and qualify for inclusion in the 'enclosed space' list
warnings: Over-pressurisation of pipelines can cause loss of cargo containment
Partially open spaces may still be dangerous despite appearing open
VHF use can distract from correct collision-avoidance actions when time is tight
Doubt in a crossing situation is always accompanied by danger and risk of miscalculation
outcomes: Prompt reporting by the manifold watch and simultaneous action by the OOW allowed discharge to be suspended before the over-pressurisation worsened
Investigation revealed the pressure increase was due to an uncontrolled closing of an automatic shore line valve
Analysis of multiple incidents identified recurring root causes enabling targeted preventive lessons
key_facts: One company noted an increase in loss of cargo containment incidents due to over-pressurisation during cargo tank changeover, line blowing, and restart after stoppage
Common contributing factors were incorrect cargo line-up, inadequate ship/shore communication, and inadequate supervision
A topping-off operation on a tanker experienced a terminal communication failure
Radar magnetron performance should be checked regularly and a replacement schedule built into planned maintenance
In a crossing situation, if the stand-on vessel expresses concern, the give-way vessel should alter course

question_seeds.text: What common factors were identified as causing cargo pipeline over-pressurisation incidents?
How should the OOW and manifold watch coordinate when a pressure increase is detected during discharge?
Why should VHF communication be avoided as the primary means of resolving a developing risk of collision?
Which vessel is obligated to alter course when the stand-on vessel signals doubt in a crossing situation?

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime Advisor closing editorial reflects on the importance of maintaining emergency equipment readiness and fostering a culture of vigilance, referencing recent CHIRP reports and videos on engine control loss, fouled anchor handling, and berthing safety.

procedures.action: Ensure emergency/life-saving equipment (e.g., lifeboats) is maintained and tested so it is operable when needed.
procedures.why: Emergency equipment is 'least used, most needed' and there are no second chances if it fails when a ship founders.

procedures.action: Remain continuously alert to unexpected signs (noise, movement, smell, heat, water) during normal operations.
procedures.why: Early detection of anomalies prevents incidents before they escalate.

procedures.action: Rectify defects immediately upon discovery.
procedures.why: Unaddressed defects can become the basis of future incidents.

procedures.action: Report observations and near-misses to CHIRP.
procedures.why: Shared observations can form salutary lessons for the wider maritime community.

constraints: Lifesaving equipment must be verified operable before an emergency, not during one.
CHIRP reports are accepted in good faith but CHIRP holds no executive authority.
warnings: Do not wait until a ship is foundering to discover that the lifeboat cannot be launched or lowered.
The sea 'endures no makeshifts' — improvised or substandard practices are dangerous.
CHIRP does not possess any executive authority; reports are accepted in good faith only.
outcomes: Continuous vigilance and immediate defect rectification reduce operational risk.
Sharing observed near-misses with CHIRP contributes to broader industry safety lessons.
CHIRP videos and podcasts help bring reported incidents (engine control loss, fouled anchor, poor berthing safety) to life for wider learning.
key_facts: Emergency equipment must be ready at all times since failure cannot be remedied mid-emergency.
CHIRP has published videos on a car carrier losing engine control near a lock, an unsafe reaction to a fouled anchor, and poor berthing safety practices.
CHIRP accepts all reports in good faith but has no executive/regulatory authority.
The editorial encourages mariners to keep submitting observations as they can become valuable lessons.

trace.situation: A CHIRP reporter highlights increasing misuse of VHF radio communications for collision avoidance, illustrated by a case where a company denied any watchkeeping failure despite a vessel passing abaft the port beam and drawing left during a VHF exchange between two vessels, with discrepancies noted in reported positions via an ECDIS/ARPA screenshot.
trace.trigger: A near-miss/close-quarters situation arose where VHF communication was used instead of proper COLREGS-compliant collision avoidance action, prompting a CHIRP report.

procedures.action: Keep suitable fire extinguishers to hand during hot work.
procedures.why: Required precaution per UKCOSWP 2015 Ch 24 to control fire risk during hot work.

procedures.action: Visit all adjacent compartments on completion of hot work.
procedures.why: To check for hidden ignition or smouldering material spreading from the hot work area.

procedures.action: Conduct frequent checks for at least 2 hours after completion of hot work.
procedures.why: Fires from hot work can smoulder and ignite with delay, requiring extended monitoring.

constraints: Always refer to the full text of UKCOSWP 2015, Chapter 24 for complete hot work guidance.
Watchkeepers must rely on proper COLREGS assessment (visual, radar/ARPA, AIS, CPA/TCPA) rather than VHF agreements for collision avoidance.
warnings: Misuse of VHF radio communications for collision avoidance is increasing and is unsafe.
Discrepancies in reported positions can undermine claims about watchkeeping adequacy, as shown by conflicting ECDIS/ARPA evidence.
outcomes: A company denied any failure of watchkeeping by pointing to position discrepancies, despite a vessel passing close abaft the port beam during a VHF-based collision avoidance exchange.
key_facts: The CHIRP report concerns misuse of VHF communications for collision avoidance in place of COLREGS-based actions.
A vessel passed abaft the port beam and was drawing left at about the same time as a VHF exchange occurred between two vessels.
The company involved denied any watchkeeping failure, citing discrepancies in reported positions supported by an ECDIS/ARPA screenshot.
Separately, hot work safety guidance requires fire extinguishers on hand, inspection of adjacent compartments, and monitoring for at least 2 hours post-completion, per UKCOSWP 2015 Ch 24.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report examines a fire that broke out during hot work aboard a vessel, caused by multiple trapped flammable paint layers igniting due to inadequate fire precautions.
trace.trigger: Hot work being carried out in an area with multiple layers of old paint without proper permit-to-work, fire watch, or fire extinguishers in place.

procedures.action: Issue and complete a hot work permit to work before any hot work begins.
procedures.why: UKCOSWP 2015 requires hot work to be subject to a PTW to ensure risks are assessed and controlled.

procedures.action: Verify training for personnel conducting hot work is completed and in date.
procedures.why: Untrained personnel are less likely to recognise or mitigate fire risks.

procedures.action: Clear the hot work area of combustible materials, including old paint, rubbish, and solvents.
procedures.why: Paint layers can trap flammable solvents that ignite rapidly and spread fire when heated.

procedures.action: Post a dedicated fire watch with fire extinguishers readily available during and after hot work.
procedures.why: The incident showed no fire watch or extinguishers were present, allowing the fire to spread undetected and unchecked.

procedures.action: Consult product data sheets and makers' advice on paint/solvent flammability before working near painted surfaces.
procedures.why: Paints are complex substances where solvents and curing characteristics affect fire risk, and incomplete data requires defaulting to safe practice.

procedures.action: Include galleys and similar high-risk areas in routine day and night rounds.
procedures.why: CHIRP recommends particular vigilance in such spaces to catch hazards early.

constraints: Hot work must not proceed without a completed permit to work.
Personnel must have current, valid training before conducting hot work.
No combustible solids, liquids, or gases should be adjacent to hot work.
Supervision and observation must be maintained throughout hot work operations.
regulations: UK MCA Code of Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seafarers (2015)
warnings: Paint in proximity to hot work should always be treated as presenting a high risk of fire.
Trapped solvents in multiple paint layers can ignite rapidly and cause fast-spreading fires.
Incorrect coat thicknesses, fast over-coating, or excess application temperature can trap flammable solvents even in old paint layers.
Absence of a fire watch, extinguishers, and PTW significantly increases fire risk during hot work.
outcomes: Inadequate fire precautions (no cleared area, no fire watch, no extinguishers) led to a rapid and widespread fire during hot work.
The fire was apparently caused by trapped flammable products igniting within multiple layers of paint.
key_facts: The fire occurred during hot work due to ignition of flammable products trapped within multiple paint layers.
No fire watch, no fire extinguishers, and no cleared area were present, indicating the hot work PTW process had not been properly completed.
Paints contain solvents and other constituents that can remain trapped if over-coating is done too fast or under incorrect conditions.
UKCOSWP 2015 Chapter 24 sets out required precautions for hot work including PTW, training, supervision, and exclusion of combustibles.

question_seeds.text: What precautions does UKCOSWP 2015 require before authorizing hot work on a vessel?
Why can old, multiple layers of paint pose a hidden fire risk during hot work even if they appear dry?
How should the hot work area be prepared to minimize fire risk from trapped solvents in paint?
Who is responsible for ensuring a fire watch and extinguishers are in place during hot work?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a near-collision at night between a 33ft catamaran approaching the Ushant TSS and a merchant ship that failed to see the yacht until very close range, followed by unrelated CHIRP guidance on hot work authorisation and galley fire risk.
trace.trigger: The yacht detected a merchant ship on a steady bearing with CPA calculated at zero within 6 minutes via receive-only AIS, with no response to VHF hailing.

procedures.action: Monitor an approaching vessel's bearing and use AIS/CPA data to assess collision risk.
procedures.why: A steady compass bearing and CPA of zero indicated an imminent collision risk.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the other vessel by VHF.
procedures.why: To alert the merchant ship to the yacht's presence when visual sighting appeared uncertain.

procedures.action: Take early and substantial avoiding action (slow down, alter course to starboard/head to wind, illuminate sail with a torch).
procedures.why: To reduce speed and cross-track risk and to increase the yacht's visibility to the approaching ship.

procedures.action: Never conduct hot work without leadership/management knowledge and a comprehensive check-off list (e.g., UKCOSWP 2015).
procedures.why: Hot work carries fire risk that must be authorised, supervised, and checked to prevent accidental ignition of flammable materials.

procedures.action: Switch off galley power at end of use, when unattended, and at end of each working day; fit external galley power breakers.
procedures.why: Galleys are high-risk fire areas and unattended equipment (e.g., a leaking casserole) can become a long-term hazard.

constraints: Hot work must be authorised and supervised by ship's (and yard's) leadership.
A comprehensive check-off list must be followed every time hot work is performed.
Flammable materials must be identified and removed before hot work begins, including in adjacent compartments.
Galley power must be switched off when unattended or at end of shift.
warnings: Receive-only AIS and VHF calls may not be acknowledged or reliable for avoiding close-quarters situations.
Small craft navigation lights may not be seen by merchant ship watchkeepers or detected on radar until very close range.
Hot work should never be treated as routine; failure to control it can lead to fire.
Unattended galley equipment (e.g., a leaking casserole) represents a long-term fire hazard and indicates poor hygiene/risk awareness.
outcomes: The merchant ship passed so close to the yacht that the skipper felt spray from its propeller.
Post-incident VHF exchange revealed the merchant ship had not seen the yacht's lights and had not detected it on radar.
The merchant ship's investigation found its watchkeepers did not see any lights until sighting a red light at about 2 cables, when the yacht was already very close.
The ship denied receiving a DSC call despite the yacht's attempt to contact it.
key_facts: The catamaran was about 33ft, heading north-west for the Scilly Isles at 2 knots at night in good visibility and minimal sea state.
The yacht's receive-only AIS calculated a CPA of zero within 6 minutes for the approaching ship.
A VHF call from the yacht elicited no response from the merchant ship.
The merchant ship's two watchkeepers reported not seeing the yacht's lights until a red light was spotted at about 2 cables distance.
The merchant ship denied having received a DSC call from the yacht.

question_seeds.text: Why did the merchant ship's watchkeepers fail to detect the yacht on radar or visually until it was only 2 cables away?
How reliable is a receive-only AIS CPA calculation for a small craft in assessing collision risk with a larger vessel?
What avoiding action should a small craft skipper take when a VHF call to an approaching ship goes unanswered and CPA is near zero?
Who is responsible for authorising and supervising hot work aboard, and what checklist should be used?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report highlights a watchkeeper's concern over increasing informal VHF 'collision avoidance arrangements' between vessels instead of following COLREGS, illustrated by a case where a merchant ship failed to detect a yacht near Ushant in a close-quarters situation.
trace.trigger: A give-way vessel (yacht) fails to take appropriate action in compliance with COLREGS as a stand-on vessel (merchant ship) approaches in a crossing/close-quarters situation near a busy traffic area such as Ushant.

procedures.action: Rely on COLREGS rules for collision avoidance rather than ad-hoc VHF 'arrangements' between vessels.
procedures.why: Increasing informal VHF chatter to negotiate collision avoidance undermines the clear, rule-based system that COLREGS provides.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, monitor closely whether the give-way vessel is taking appropriate COLREGS-compliant action.
procedures.why: The reporter admitted he should have anticipated the yacht's lack of response earlier.

procedures.action: Take early, positive and ample avoiding action as soon as it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not complying with COLREGS.
procedures.why: The stand-on vessel is empowered under COLREGS to act once non-compliance by the give-way vessel is evident; early action (e.g., placing the ship on the yacht's port bow) would have removed the danger.

procedures.action: Small craft such as yachts should keep engines available for maneuvering, especially in light winds at known dangerous crossing points.
procedures.why: The yacht's manoeuvrability was very limited in light airs, and Ushant is a notoriously dangerous crossing point.

procedures.action: Bridge watchkeepers on larger vessels should account for the poor detectability of yachts (weak radar returns, dim/intermittent lights) when assessing risk at range.
procedures.why: Many passive radar reflectors return poorly even in good conditions, and yacht lights including the masthead tricolour can be dim, intermittent, or obscured by vessel motion.

constraints: COLREGS remain the primary basis for collision avoidance decisions, not informal VHF negotiations.
A stand-on vessel may only take avoiding action once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not complying with COLREGS.
Avoiding action taken must be 'positive and ample'.
warnings: Growing reliance on informal VHF 'collision avoidance arrangements' between vessels is displacing proper COLREGS compliance.
Yachts may be difficult to detect from a ship's bridge due to poor radar reflector returns and dim or intermittent lights.
A yacht's masthead tricolour light may swing through roughly 60 degrees athwartships and 40 degrees fore and aft in a seaway, reducing its visibility.
Ushant is a notoriously dangerous crossing point requiring extra vigilance and maneuvering readiness.
outcomes: The merchant ship did not detect the yacht, creating a close-quarters/collision risk situation.
Earlier anticipation and action by the stand-on vessel would have removed the existing danger.
The incident is cited by CHIRP as a lesson in both communication discipline and vessel detectability.
key_facts: A watchkeeper reported a marked increase over the last 10 years in VHF-based 'collision avoidance arrangements' between vessels instead of COLREGS application.
In the reported incident, a merchant ship did not detect a yacht with very limited manoeuvrability.
Ushant is identified as a notoriously dangerous crossing point, especially in light airs.
Passive radar reflectors on yachts often produce poor returns even in good conditions.
A yacht's masthead tricolour can swing about 60° athwartships and 40° fore-and-aft in a seaway, making it intermittently visible.

question_seeds.text: Why should I avoid relying on VHF arrangements with other vessels instead of standard COLREGS actions?
At what point am I, as stand-on vessel, empowered to take avoiding action if the give-way vessel isn't responding?
How can I better detect small yachts with poor radar returns and dim lighting in a crossing situation like near Ushant?
What early action should I take to remove collision danger when a give-way vessel fails to comply with COLREGS?

chapter_title: What did the reporters tell us?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report and commentary addressing the risks of relying on VHF radio communication and AIS data instead of COLREGS-based visual and radar observation for collision avoidance at sea.
trace.trigger: A close-quarters or potential collision situation where watchkeepers are tempted to use VHF radio or AIS to coordinate action with another vessel instead of applying COLREGS.

procedures.action: Base collision avoidance decisions primarily on visual observation and/or radar information.
procedures.why: Not all vessels transmit AIS data even if they can receive it, so AIS cannot be solely relied upon.

procedures.action: Apply the COLREGS instinctively as the primary basis for bridge watchkeeping decisions.
procedures.why: COLREGS are based on decades of tried and tested practice, are unambiguous, and address circumstances where one ship does not comply.

procedures.action: Avoid spending time attempting VHF communication during a developing close-quarters situation.
procedures.why: Buying up precious time communicating on VHF delays timely collision avoidance action.

procedures.action: If VHF is used for deconfliction, do not assume the other vessel has taken the 'arranged' action until it is independently verified as happening.
procedures.why: Reliance on unverified VHF arrangements is hazardous, especially when the arrangement contradicts COLREGS.

procedures.action: Avoid making 'arrangements' via VHF that are contrary to the COLREGS.
procedures.why: Such arrangements carry the greatest risk in collision avoidance situations.

constraints: Not all vessels are required to transmit AIS data.
COLREGS-based actions must take priority over VHF-arranged actions.
Any VHF-arranged action must be independently verified before being relied upon.
VHF should not be used as a substitute for COLREGS compliance in collision avoidance.
warnings: Not all vessels transmit AIS data even if they can receive it.
Relying on VHF to coordinate collision avoidance wastes precious time.
Never assume an 'arranged' action via VHF has been taken until it is seen to be happening.
VHF arrangements contrary to COLREGS carry the greatest risk.
Language confusion, mis-identification between vessels, distraction of other ships, and distraction of the OOW from primary tasks all add risk when using VHF for collision avoidance.
Even with AIS, mistakes in vessel identification can still occur in busy, heavy shipping situations.
outcomes: Following COLREGS-based visual/radar decision-making leads to unambiguous, effective collision avoidance.
Reliance on VHF-arranged actions without verification can result in hazardous close-quarters situations or collision.
key_facts: Some vessels at sea are not required to transmit AIS data, even if capable of receiving it.
COLREGS were developed before bridge-to-bridge voice communication existed and are designed to be unambiguous.
VHF radio is legitimately used for traffic management, e.g., in traffic separation schemes (TSSs).
The stand-on vessel can be particularly tempted to use VHF to coordinate with a give-way vessel.
CHIRP has repeatedly received reports highlighting the risks of over-reliance on VHF and AIS instead of COLREGS.

question_seeds.text: Why should collision avoidance decisions be based on visual/radar observation rather than AIS or VHF arrangements?
What should the OOW do if a VHF arrangement has been made with another vessel to avoid collision?
When is it acceptable to use VHF radio in a collision avoidance context?
How can over-reliance on AIS lead to misidentification of vessels in busy shipping situations?

chapter_title: What did the reporters tell us?

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime report highlights the danger that a ship's bridge team may fail to see a yacht's navigation lights at night or in poor conditions, particularly when over-relying on AIS and bridge instrumentation instead of visual lookout.
trace.trigger: Night-time or adverse weather conditions where a small vessel (yacht) without AIS is in proximity to a larger vessel, and bridge watchkeepers may be distracted by instrument lights or reliant on AIS for traffic detection.

procedures.action: Maintain an alert visual lookout at all times, not relying on AIS or instrument displays alone.
procedures.why: Bright instrument lights and technical information sources can distract the OOW from the primary duty of visual lookout, and smaller vessels not fitted with AIS transmitters will not be detected by AIS.

procedures.action: Base collision avoidance decisions primarily on visual and/or radar information, not AIS.
procedures.why: There is no provision in the COLREGs for the use of AIS information.

procedures.action: If using VHF radio as a collision avoidance aid, keep the provisions of the COLREGs uppermost.
procedures.why: VHF use may be justified on occasion but must not override COLREGs compliance, per MCA guidance.

procedures.action: Yacht skippers should fit high-power (e.g. LED) navigation lighting conforming to COLREG stipulations, and consider burning normal navigation lights instead of a masthead tricolour.
procedures.why: Yacht lights can appear as faint flashes or be seen at horizon level, giving a false impression of distance, making them easy to miss.

procedures.action: Yachts should consider fitting an active (transmit and receive) AIS system, especially in busy shipping areas.

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime Feedback report describes a near-miss close-quarters situation arising from simultaneous overtaking manoeuvres as ships approached a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS), alongside a brief separate account of electronic chart confusion during Suez Canal passage planning.

procedures.action: Plan well ahead and maintain a complete all-round lookout when approaching a TSS.
procedures.why: To establish an orderly separation of ships before the scheme itself is entered and to assess other ships' manoeuvring options in good time.

procedures.action: If overtaking, complete the manoeuvre as quickly as possible.

procedures.action: If sea room is at a premium, slow down and do not overtake; consider slotting in astern instead.
procedures.why: This can minimise the constraints created by simultaneous overtaking manoeuvres and reduce close-quarters risk.

procedures.action: Apply the COLREGS instinctively and take early and substantial action when circumstances require, rather than relying on give-way vessels to act correctly.
procedures.why: COLREGS clearly state the stand-on/other vessel should 'take action to avoid'; relying on others' compliance is unsafe.

procedures.action: Use VHF in collision avoidance only in exceptional situations and with utmost caution.
procedures.why: VHF communication can increase doubt, misunderstanding, delay and distraction, and erode OOWs' confident, instinctive application of the COLREGS, posing a serious longer-term threat to safety at sea.

procedures.action: Verify chart identity, source and date against the ship's provider when discrepancies are found during passage planning.
procedures.why: Confusion over which electronic chart was correct required resolution by the ship's provider before the correct chart could be confirmed and supplied.

Orderly separation of ships should be established before entering a TSS.
VHF use in collision avoidance must be exceptional and cautious, not routine.

Doubt in collision avoidance situations equates to danger.

procedures.action: Cross-check depth, chart data, ECDIS position, radar information and the ship's estimated position against each other.

procedures.action: If information sources disagree, slow down, stop, or re-check as appropriate to clarify the discrepancy.

trace.trigger: A reported slip/trip/fall hazard from walkway design plus discovery of a homemade tool being used to lift oxy-acetylene cylinders instead of the approved trolley.

trace.situation: A reporter's vessel, transiting a Traffic Separation Scheme while overtaking a slow coaster, was placed in a close-quarters situation when a ferry leaving port altered course 40 degrees to starboard to cross ahead, reducing CPA to 0.2 miles.
trace.trigger: The ferry's 40-degree course alteration to starboard at a range of about 4 miles created a bow-crossing situation with a dangerously small CPA and no prior VHF communication of intent.

procedures.action: Call the other vessel by VHF to clarify intentions when a close-quarters situation develops.
procedures.why: No VHF call had been made by the ferry by the time range closed to 3 miles, leaving the give-way vessel's intentions unclear.

procedures.action: As give-way vessel, take early and substantial action to avoid the other vessel when possible.
procedures.why: Reporter was identified as the give-way vessel but had no room to maneuver due to the coaster being overtaken and other vessel proximity.

procedures.action: Reduce speed promptly to increase CPA/bow crossing range when unable to alter course.
procedures.why: Reporter was able to slow down quickly (from ~10 knots) to increase CPA/bow crossing range from 0.2 to 1 mile, averting the close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Cross a TSS as close to right angles as possible, and shape up for crossing as soon as possible after leaving port.
procedures.why: Allows other vessels time to assess the crossing vessel's intentions and avoid clusters of ships in the TSS.

procedures.action: Maintain a bow crossing distance (BCD) of no less than 1.5 miles when crossing ahead of another vessel, unless heavy traffic prevents it.
procedures.why: Company regulation sets this margin to avoid close-quarters situations; a 40-degree alteration to cross the TSS does not allow this margin to be met.

procedures.action: Consider the situation as perceived from the other vessel's bridge before deciding to pass ahead.
procedures.why: Company policy requires assessing how the maneuver will appear and affect the other vessel's safety margin.

constraints: Own vessel was overtaking a small coaster at 8.5 knots, only 6 cables away on the starboard quarter, limiting room to alter to starboard.
No room existed to pass on the other side of the ferry due to proximity of other vessels.
Company regulation requires BCD of at least 1.5 miles unless heavy traffic prevents it.
The reporter was correctly identified as the give-way vessel under the rules.
warnings: Altering course 40 degrees to starboard at 4 miles range created a close-quarters situation with a 0.2 mile CPA and bow crossing range.
Failure to communicate intentions by VHF in a timely manner increases risk in crossing/overtaking situations.
Being correct as to who is the give-way vessel does not excuse creating a close-quarters situation through a late or excessive course alteration.
outcomes: Own vessel successfully slowed down to increase CPA and bow crossing range from 0.2 to 1 mile, avoiding collision.
Ship manager acknowledged the 40-degree alteration would not meet the company's 1.5 mile BCD safety margin.
Near miss was reported and used to reinforce company BCD policy and crossing procedures.

No VHF call was made by the ferry to communicate intentions until the reporter called at 3 miles range.

Company regulations require a bow crossing distance (BCD) of at least 1.5 miles unless heavy traffic prevents it.

chapter_title: What did the reporter tell us?

trace.situation: A sailing yacht under sail near the Isle of Wight, approaching the Needles Passage in good visibility, was nearly involved in a close-quarters collision with an overtaking car carrier that altered course toward the yacht and did not respond appropriately to radio contact.
trace.trigger: The overtaking car carrier began a turn to starboard putting it on a converging course with the yacht, reducing estimated closest point of approach to less than 200 metres.

procedures.action: Monitor the approaching vessel's course and speed over an extended period using visual observation and AIS.

procedures.action: Call the other vessel by radio to identify own position and ask its intentions when CPA became unsafe.

procedures.action: Take independent avoiding action by starting the engine and turning hard to starboard, completing a 360-degree turn around the car carrier's stern.

procedures.action: Record the AIS track of the other vessel and file an incident report.
procedures.why: To document the other vessel's unusual course changes and support a formal report of the near-miss.

constraints: Visibility was very good, allowing sighting range of at least 10 miles.

Lack of sound signals or radio communication from an overtaking vessel is a serious lookout and compliance failure.
outcomes: The yacht avoided collision by executing a 360-degree turn and passing around the car carrier's stern.

No sound signals or radio calls were made by the car carrier before the close-quarters situation developed.

trace.situation: A company review of a near-miss report found that a ferry OOW, who was the stand-on vessel in a Traffic Separation Scheme (TSS), wrongly altered course to starboard to find a gap through traffic, creating additional collision risk and losing speed over ground in a flood tide.
trace.trigger: A near-miss report was submitted, prompting the company to review the Voyage Data Recorder (VDR) and consult the senior master about the OOW's decision-making in the TSS.

procedures.action: Practice donning the lifejacket and locating the pull cord and sprayhood with eyes closed.
procedures.why: Training the hands builds muscle memory needed under stress or cold-impaired dexterity.

procedures.action: Learn techniques to combat Cold Shock Reflex.
procedures.why: Cold Shock Reflex can kill and seriously limited the casualty's ability to help themselves.

procedures.action: Stay calm, keep thinking, and never give up during an emergency in the water.
procedures.why: Panic reduces the chance of survival; composure allows the casualty to use remaining strength effectively.

procedures.action: Critically examine all safety gear rather than assuming it is serviceable.
procedures.why: Equipment that is 'fit and forget' can fail, as happened with the propeller shaft seal.

procedures.action: Regularly inspect and maintain propeller shaft seals.
procedures.why: The seal is not a 'fit and forget' component and its failure caused the water ingress that led to the casualty entering the water.

constraints: Lifejackets must be worn, not merely stowed, to be effective.
Safety equipment checks should be as routine as engine checks.

Don’t assume safety gear works — check it critically.
The propeller shaft seal is not a 'fit and forget' piece of equipment.
outcomes: The casualty was rescued by nearby dinghies and reached the club pontoon safely, though severely cold-shocked.

key_facts: The incident was caused by failure of a small vessel's propeller shaft seal, leading to water ingress.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board reflects on two incident reports that revealed a lack of self-preservation awareness and safety-culture failings among seafarers, immediately followed by a first-person account of a person in the water clinging to a vessel's boarding ladder while the engine was still running near the propeller.
trace.trigger: Review of two separate incident reports showing seafarers accepting unsafe conditions, combined with a near-miss involving a person in the water close to a running propeller.

procedures.action: Question whether to remain aboard or continue working on a vessel exhibiting poor safety culture.
procedures.why: The Board notes some reports show a complete lack of awareness of self-preservation, risking seafarers' lives.

procedures.action: Mentally consider 'what if' something were to happen on each job and its consequences, without needing a full formal risk assessment.
procedures.why: Prudent informal risk consideration can catch hazards that a lack of SMS compliance, Code of Safe Working Practices adherence, or effective supervision might miss.

procedures.action: When a person is in the water near a vessel's stern, immediately instruct the helm/engine operator to put the engine in neutral.
procedures.why: Proximity to a running propeller poses an immediate life-threatening hazard to a person in the water.

constraints: Seafarers are not required to perform a full written risk assessment for every job.
Judgment should still weigh potential consequences before proceeding with a task.
regulations: Code of Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seafarers 2015
warnings: Possible lack of SMS compliance.
Possible lack of adherence to the Code of Safe Working Practices for Merchant Seafarers 2015.
Possible lack of effective supervision.
A running engine near a person in the water creates a severe propeller hazard.
outcomes: CHIRP encourages seafarers to question whether they should remain on a vessel with poor safety culture, given the stakes for their life and family.

trace.situation: A yacht owner discovered rising seawater flooding the engine space after departing harbour, the bilge pump failed, and the owner took emergency action including contacting MRCC for assistance.
trace.trigger: Discovery of ~1 metre of seawater in the engine compartment above the prop-shaft, gearbox and accessories after starting the engine and opening the floor hatch.

procedures.action: Open floor hatch and visually inspect engine space before/after starting engine.
procedures.why: To detect flooding or water ingress early.

procedures.action: Attempt to start engine-driven bilge pump.
procedures.why: Primary means of removing water ingress.

procedures.action: Inspect hoses and clips for obvious failures.
procedures.why: To quickly identify and potentially stop the source of ingress.

procedures.action: Rig a spare electrical bilge pump when primary pump fails.
procedures.why: Provide backup dewatering capability when main pump is inoperable (likely due to submerged electrics).

procedures.action: Single up mooring lines and prepare to slip and deliberately run aground alongside a nearby pier.
procedures.why: To have an immediate grounding option to prevent sinking if flooding becomes uncontrollable.

procedures.action: Make VHF radio calls for assistance, first to harbour Master, then to MRCC when unanswered.
procedures.why: To summon help; MRCC call succeeded in reaching nearby RNLI crew.

procedures.action: Accept RNLI assistance including salvage pump deployment and tow to boat-lift.
procedures.why: To reduce inflow and remove the vessel from the water to prevent sinking.

procedures.action: Arrange post-incident inspection by an engineer and insurer's surveyor.
procedures.why: To determine root cause of failure (propeller shaft seal/rotor segment coming loose).

constraints: Harbour Master may not respond to VHF calls, requiring escalation to MRCC.
Grub screws securing the shaft seal rotor segment are crucially dependent on proper torque for security.
warnings: Engine-driven bilge pump may fail if electrics become submerged.
Propeller shaft seal rotor segments secured only by grub screws are a known, not-infrequent failure point, including on working and passenger-carrying boats.
Running aground deliberately alongside a pier was considered as an emergency measure if flooding worsened.
outcomes: RNLI inshore rescue boat crew, exercising nearby, heard the MRCC call and swiftly arrived with a salvage pump.
Salvage pump reduced inflow sufficiently to allow a tow to a boat-lift, which lifted the boat out of the water.
Post-incident inspection confirmed failure of the propeller shaft seal due to the rotor segment becoming unsecured from the prop shaft.
key_facts: The flooding was caused by failure of the propeller shaft seal, specifically the rotor segment loosening from the prop shaft.
The rotor segment is held by two pairs of grub screws that depend on correct torque for security.
The engine-driven bilge pump failed to start, likely due to submerged electrics.
Harbour Master did not respond to VHF calls, but MRCC relayed/received the call leading to rapid RNLI assistance.
This type of shaft seal failure is reported as a not-infrequent problem among working boats, including a passenger-licensed vessel.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report and advisory board comment on an incident where a boat's propeller shaft seal failed due to inadequate maintenance, causing down-flooding that nearly cost the reporter's life, with lessons on shaft seal inspection and maintenance.
trace.trigger: Failure or wear of a propeller shaft seal (grub screws, flexible rubber bellows, or lip seal) leading to down-flooding aboard a small craft.

procedures.action: Disassemble and refit shaft seal grub screws with new parts periodically, since no effective inspection method exists otherwise.
procedures.why: Watertight integrity depends crucially on proper fitting of small grub screws which cannot be verified without disassembly.

procedures.action: Fit bespoke locking collars or a pair of stainless steel jubilee clips onto the prop shaft to prevent rotor movement.
procedures.why: Prevents movement of the shaft seal rotor that could lead to seal failure.

procedures.action: Regularly inspect and/or replace flexible rubber bellows (stator) at manufacturer-recommended intervals.
procedures.why: Failures of the bellows have caused resultant down-flooding; few owners inspect them.

procedures.action: Carry and know how to apply temporary 'get-you-home' strapping for the shaft seal.
procedures.why: Few boat owners have a means of effecting emergency repair if the seal fails underway.

procedures.action: 'Burp' lip-seal type shaft seals to release trapped air and ensure water lubrication.
procedures.why: If lip seals dry out from lack of water lubrication they will fail quickly.

procedures.action: Follow manufacturer's instructions for installation and maintenance rather than treating the seal as maintenance-free.
procedures.why: The seal is a precision engineering item that is 'not fit and forget' despite marketing claims.

constraints: Shaft seal proper fitting can only be verified by disassembly and refitting with new parts, not visual inspection alone.
Manufacturer markets units as 'maintenance-free' but its own website recommends both inspection and replacement at intervals.
Only engineers who sail/live aboard tend to perform routine inspections; other owners typically do not.
warnings: Failures of flexible rubber bellows have been reported, resulting in down-flooding.
Lip seals that dry out from lack of lubrication (not 'burped') will fail quickly.
No effective means of inspection exists for grub screw fitting other than disassembly.
outcomes: Reporter survived due to training and risk awareness retained from drills undertaken 30 years earlier.
Boats with inboard engines and shaft seals risk down-flooding if seals are neglected or dry out.
key_facts: Watertight integrity of shaft seals depends on properly fitted and maintained small grub screws.
Locking collars or stainless steel jubilee clips can prevent rotor movement on the prop shaft.
Flexible rubber bellows (stator) should be inspected/replaced periodically; failures cause down-flooding.
Units are marketed as 'maintenance-free' but manufacturer's own website recommends inspection and replacement.
Cheaper rubber hose lip seals rely on water for lubrication and fail quickly if not 'burped' of trapped air.

question_seeds.text: What maintenance steps should be taken on propeller shaft seals to prevent down-flooding?
How can a crew verify that a shaft seal's grub screws are properly fitted without full disassembly?
Why do 'maintenance-free' marketed shaft seals still require periodic inspection and replacement?
Who typically performs routine shaft seal inspections, and why do other owners neglect this?

trace.situation: CHIRP compiles reader feedback including guidance on small-boat visibility/collision avoidance, a near-miss from heating a water-filled tiller bar causing a steam burn, and a report on crew misunderstanding of mooring winch brake terminology.

procedures.action: Fit a radar reflector and a transmit/receive AIS system on small craft, especially when transiting busy shipping lanes
procedures.why: Improves detectability to other vessels using radar and AIS

procedures.action: Maintain a vigilant visual lookout rather than relying solely on radar reflectors or AIS
procedures.why: Small craft may not be detected in sea clutter despite equipment

procedures.action: Drill a hole in the bottom of a sealed tube/pipe before applying heat to check for trapped liquid
procedures.why: Prevents steam/pressure build-up from heated residual water causing a violent release

procedures.action: Brief all relevant personnel on the difference between rendering point and designed brake holding capacity
procedures.why: Officer was unaware of the distinction, risking unsafe mooring operations

procedures.action: Ensure ship's officers are trained in mooring winch brake testing procedures and requirements
procedures.why: Sound knowledge of these terms is essential for safe mooring operations

constraints: Do not assume small craft will be visible to other vessels based on equipment alone
Always check for trapped fluids before applying heat to a sealed or corroded component
Personnel must understand rendering point vs brake holding capacity before conducting mooring operations
warnings: Small boats may not be seen in radar sea clutter even with reflectors/AIS fitted
Applying heat to sealed components with trapped liquid can cause sudden steam release and burns
Lack of knowledge of winch brake rendering point vs holding capacity can compromise mooring safety
outcomes: Unexpected steam release from heated tiller bar caused burns to hands and arm of assistant
Reporter now drills a test hole before heating to prevent pressure build-up
Recommendation issued for crew training on winch brake terminology and testing

The Mk I eyeball (visual lookout) remains the best collision avoidance tool

trace.situation: CHIRP correspondence corrects earlier guidance on radar reflector mounting orientation for yachts and adds advice on maintaining through-hull fittings on small craft.
trace.trigger: A reporter noticed that a radar reflector pictured in a CHIRP Video Broadcast bulletin was incorrectly mounted and would not give a strong return signal.

procedures.action: Mount octahedral radar reflectors in the 'catch rain' position rather than upright.
procedures.why: The catch rain position gives lower but more balanced RCS peaks with consistent performance across azimuth and elevation, whereas upright mounting has large nulls between peaks that worsen with elevation.

procedures.action: Tilt the reflector's axis 45 degrees as recommended by Transport Canada.
procedures.why: This orientation is stated to achieve optimal radar reflection performance.

procedures.action: Check for and follow any preferred-orientation markings on the reflector.
procedures.why: Transport Canada recommends manufacturers clearly mark the preferred mounting orientation to avoid incorrect installation.

procedures.action: Identify and maintain all through-hull fittings (seacocks, breathers, ventilation openings, stern glands).
procedures.why: All such fittings require some degree of user maintenance to work as expected and prevent water ingress/egress issues.

constraints: Reflector performance depends entirely on correct mounting orientation.
Through-hull fittings require regular user maintenance to function safely.
warnings: An upright-mounted octahedral radar reflector produces large nulls between RCS peaks and performance worsens as elevation angle increases, risking the vessel being lost in sea clutter.
Neglected through-hull fittings can fail to perform as expected, risking water ingress.
outcomes: Correct 'catch rain' mounting and 45-degree tilt produce more consistent radar cross-section performance, improving detectability of small craft by radar.
Regular maintenance of through-hull fittings reduces risk of flooding or fitting failure.
key_facts: The UK MAIB commissioned a 2007 report 'Performance Investigation of Marine Radar Reflectors on the Market'.
Upright-mounted small octahedral reflectors have very large RCS peaks but also very large nulls between them.
The 'catch rain' position gives lower but more balanced RCS performance across azimuth and elevation.
Transport Canada's 'Radar Reflectors on Small Vessels' recommends a 45-degree tilt and clear marking of preferred mounting orientation.
Through-hull fittings (seacocks, breathers, ventilation openings, stern glands) all require some degree of user maintenance.

Why does the 'catch rain' orientation outperform the upright mounting for radar reflectors?

trace.situation: A reporter (crew member) aboard a tanker describes repeated MARPOL Annex I/II violations, including direct discharge of noxious liquid substances and oily waste to sea without proper equipment or procedure, falsified Oil Record Book entries, non-functioning pollution-prevention equipment, and company tolerance of these practices even after a vetting inspection identified major deficiencies.
trace.trigger: Observation of repeated illegal discharges of oily waste/noxious liquid substances directly to sea, bypassing oily water separators and underwater discharge outlet requirements, including incidents ordered by the Chief Engineer and witnessed but ignored by the Marine Superintendent.
constraints: Discharge of noxious liquid substance/seawater mixtures must be made below the waterline through underwater outlets per MARPOL Annex II Regulation 13 2.1.2, not exceeding the maximum rate for which the outlet is designed.
Oily waste from the engine room must pass through the oily water separator before any discharge to sea.

warnings: Direct discharge of noxious liquid substances/oily waste to sea without proper treatment or outlet configuration is a MARPOL violation and pollution hazard, even for cargoes perceived as benign (e.g., vegetable oil).

Crew members following unlawful orders under threat of dismissal does not excuse the violation, and company oversight personnel tolerating such acts compounds the non-compliance.

outcomes: Vetting inspection identified multiple major and detainable deficiencies, but findings were reportedly not acted upon by the company, with crew told only that the vessel 'passed' the inspection.
Repeated illegal discharges occurred at multiple anchorages, suggesting a pattern of institutional tolerance rather than isolated incidents.

key_facts: Last cargo was MARPOL Annex II Category Y (pollution hazard), requiring strict discharge controls even though it was vegetable oil.
MARPOL Annex II Regulation 13 2.1.2 requires noxious liquid substance discharges to be made below the waterline through underwater outlets at controlled rates.
Oily water separator was bypassed on at least one occasion for engine room waste discharge directly to sea.

trace.situation: A vessel drifting outside port limits off a port in Vietnam was approached by four fishing boats, two of which may have served as a distraction while the other two facilitated an armed robbery boarding attempt.
trace.trigger: Four fishing boats approaching simultaneously from different directions (two astern asking about scrap, two from the port bow) raising suspicion with the Officer of the Watch.

procedures.action: Assess suspicious approach pattern of multiple small craft and identify possible diversion tactic.
procedures.why: OOW believed astern boats were a distraction while forward boats were suspicious, prompting targeted vigilance.

procedures.action: Dispatch Bosun to carefully check the forward end of the vessel.
procedures.why: To verify the suspected threat without alerting the approaching craft prematurely.

procedures.action: Observe from a safe distance and report findings to the bridge.
procedures.why: Allows confirmation of armed boarders while avoiding personal risk to the crew member.

procedures.action: Activate the general alarm and inform the Master.
procedures.why: Alerts entire crew to the threat and signals to boarders that the vessel is aware, prompting their flight.

procedures.action: Muster all crew and account for personnel.
procedures.why: Ensures crew safety is verified immediately after the incident.

procedures.action: Inform local VTS, IMB Kuala Lumpur, CSO, Alternative CSO, vessel operator, charterers, and local agents.
procedures.why: Ensures full notification chain for incident reporting, investigation, and follow-up support.

procedures.why: Enables organizational learning and review of anti-piracy preparedness.

constraints: Bosun must maintain a safe distance before confirming and reporting an armed threat.

Local VTS may not respond even when contacted during a security incident.
outcomes: Pirates fled and jumped overboard upon hearing the general alarm.

trace.situation: A vessel simultaneously conducted a helicopter pilot disembarkation and a launch-based accommodation-ladder disembarkation of a cargo surveyor while underway, resulting in the launch striking and breaking the ladder and two men falling overboard.
trace.trigger: Decision to disembark the cargo surveyor by launch via the amidships accommodation ladder while vessel remained underway on a course set for the helicopter operation, before the helicopter had arrived.

procedures.action: Avoid conducting two distinct disembarkation operations (helicopter and launch) simultaneously.
procedures.why: Doing both at once caused inadequate situational awareness and conflicting course requirements.

procedures.action: Set vessel course/speed to give the launch a proper lee from sea and swell before commencing ladder transfer.
procedures.why: The course held for the helicopter's wind requirement left the launch without a lee, causing excessive pitching and loss of control during the astern manoeuvre.

procedures.action: Conduct an adequate on-site risk assessment and require proper PPE, including a safety harness, before personnel go over the side onto the accommodation ladder.
procedures.why: Both men stood near the unprotected lower platform without harnesses despite the visibly unsafe approach of the launch.

procedures.action: Keep personnel at the top of the ladder until the launch is safely alongside and secured, rather than waiting at the lower platform.
procedures.why: Standing near the lower platform exposed them directly to the launch's impact when it struck the ladder.

procedures.action: Rig a pilot ladder in combination with the accommodation ladder for underway transfers.
procedures.why: Using only the accommodation ladder posed a hazard for safe boat approach while the vessel was underway at sea.

constraints: Vessel was underway during the transfer operation
Ladder faced aft, affecting approach geometry
Prevailing sea and swell required a lee for safe launch approach
Helicopter operation required wind on the bow, dictating vessel course
warnings: Simultaneous helicopter and launch operations reduce situational awareness and create conflicting vessel course requirements
Personnel should not stand at the lower ladder platform during an unsafe boat approach
Safety harnesses must be used before going over the side onto an accommodation ladder
Using only the accommodation ladder without a combined pilot ladder is hazardous for underway transfers
outcomes: Launch struck the lower platform of the accommodation ladder, breaking the ladder wire
Cargo surveyor and pumpman fell overboard
Both men were rescued from the water by the launch with no injuries, described as extremely lucky

The vessel's course was set for the helicopter's wind requirement, denying the launch a lee

Only the accommodation ladder was rigged, not combined with a pilot ladder, despite the vessel being underway
