trace.situation: During accommodation ladder deployment after berthing, the ladder's winch wire rope parted and the ladder fell freely into the sea while still attached by its retaining bolts/pins, with no personnel injury.
trace.trigger: Crew began lowering the starboard accommodation ladder via winch after it had been moved outboard from its stowed position.

procedures.action: Recover the fallen accommodation ladder from the sea.
procedures.why: Ladder remained connected via two bolts/pins and needed to be retrieved safely after the wire failure.

procedures.action: End-for-end the wire rope that had parted.
procedures.why: To assess/reuse remaining usable wire and understand failure location relative to fittings.

procedures.action: Order replacement wires for both accommodation ladders on board.
procedures.why: The failed wire was two and a half years old, indicating a need to replace aging rigging on both ladders to prevent recurrence.

warnings: Wire rope used for accommodation ladder winching can part suddenly near the davit connection point, causing the ladder to fall freely even while secured by retaining bolts/pins.
outcomes: No personnel injury occurred despite the ladder falling into the sea.

Replacement wires were ordered for both ladders on board as a corrective action.
key_facts: The wire rope parted about 1.8 metres from the permanent connection of the ladder davit.

Replacement wires were ordered for both accommodation ladders on board.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board commentary on an incident involving simultaneous shipboard operations (helicopter operations and ladder-based transfer/boarding), where inadequate risk assessment coordination and ladder/lifejacket practices contributed to a near-miss or incident.
trace.trigger: A vessel conducting simultaneous operations (e.g., helicopter operations requiring a specific heading plus a ladder-based personnel transfer) without cross-checking the risk assessments of each operation.

procedures.action: Conduct a separate risk assessment for each simultaneous operation being carried out on board.
procedures.why: Each operation carries distinct hazards that must be independently evaluated.

procedures.action: Compare the results of the risk assessments against each other before proceeding.
procedures.why: The outcome of one operation (e.g., ship heading required for helicopter ops) may adversely impact the safety of the other (e.g., inadequate lee for ladder disembarkation).

procedures.action: Any crew member should intervene on safety grounds if a hazard is observed, such as inadequate lee for a ladder transfer.
procedures.why: Timely intervention could have prevented the incident.

procedures.action: Rig a combination ladder instead of relying on a standard ladder when conditions warrant.
procedures.why: This would have provided a safer means of transfer and could have prevented the incident.

procedures.action: Ensure personnel receive basic training in the use and hazards of different ladder types before undertaking such operations.
procedures.why: Lack of training in ladder hazards contributed to the risk.

procedures.action: Use a safety harness when rigging a ladder, but not while standing at the boarding platform.
procedures.why: A harness at the boarding platform is inappropriate and potentially dangerous in that specific context.

procedures.action: Always wear a lifejacket during such transfer operations.
procedures.why: Lack of a flotation aid has historically led to far more serious outcomes in similar incidents.

constraints: Vessel heading requirements for helicopter operations (per ICS Guide to Helicopter/Ship Operations 4th Edition) must be reconciled with lee requirements for safe ladder launch/disembarkation.
Harness use is appropriate only during ladder rigging, not at the boarding platform.
Lifejacket wear is mandatory (a MUST) during these operations.

warnings: Using a safety harness at the boarding platform is inappropriate and potentially dangerous.
Lack of a flotation aid (lifejacket) during ladder-based incidents has resulted in far more serious outcomes in other cases.
Failure to cross-check risk assessments of simultaneous operations can create unrecognized compounding hazards.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary following a gangway/accommodation ladder incident, addressing the regulatory basis and recommended maintenance/inspection practices for accommodation ladders and gangways.
trace.trigger: A wire failure occurred on an accommodation ladder, raising concern about structural integrity and maintenance practices.

procedures.action: Ensure accommodation ladder/gangway maintenance and inspection comply with SOLAS II-1 Regulation 3.9 and MSC.1 Circ1331 guidelines.

procedures.why: These points are vulnerable to wear and were implicated in the wire failure.

procedures.action: Thoroughly inspect bolts/pins in the platform before returning the ladder to service after a wire failure.
procedures.why: A shock load may have been placed on the bolts/pins due to the wire failure, risking structural compromise if not checked.

procedures.action: Consult West of England P&I Club guidance on Gangways and Accommodation Ladders for additional best practice.

constraints: Maintenance and inspection must meet SOLAS II-1 Regulation 3.9 requirements

procedures.why: Prevents the ladder from being submerged or accessible when no one is present to supervise it.

trace.situation: CHIRP received a report on a new-build 333m x 48m container ship where, in light (ballasted-up) condition, the pilot boarding ladder/door was positioned aft of the parallel mid-body due to a hull cut-away, preventing safe pilot disembarkation.
trace.trigger: Vessel sailing in light condition with the pilot ladder's last meter not flush with the hull, forcing the pilot boat to operate dangerously under the counter.

procedures.action: Ballast the ship down to bring the pilot door/ladder into the parallel mid-body before pilot disembarkation.
procedures.why: In light condition the cut-away at the quarter left the ladder misaligned, risking the pilot boat operating under the counter.

procedures.action: Conduct a risk assessment and consult the Classification Society and ship designers after the issue was identified.
procedures.why: To formally evaluate and validate corrective design options for a recognized design failure.

procedures.action: Alter the hull/pilot door design and make structural modifications on the final (fifth) vessel still under construction.
procedures.why: To eliminate the design failure at source before delivery.

procedures.action: Retrofit a combination ladder (accommodation ladder plus pilot ladder) on the four already-delivered vessels.
procedures.why: To bring the boarding arrangement into compliance with SOLAS V/23 and IMO Resolution A.1045(27) without full structural rebuild.

constraints: Pilot boarding arrangements must comply with SOLAS Regulation V/23 and IMO Resolution A.1045(27).

warnings: Pilot ladder not flush with hull side in light condition forces pilot boats to operate under the counter, a serious hazard to pilot transfer.

outcomes: Vessel was ballasted down to allow safe pilot disembarkation as an immediate workaround.

trace.situation: A yacht under sail misidentified the navigation lights of a crossing cruise liner, mistaking obscured/confusing deck lights for a green starboard light, leading to confusion about stand-on/give-way status until the vessel had passed a mile ahead.

procedures.action: Cross-check observed light colour against the vessel's relative track/bearing movement for consistency.

procedures.action: Do not assume own vessel's stand-on/give-way status based solely on an uncertain navigation light sighting; treat ambiguous light identification as a risk of collision.
procedures.why: Had the yacht been under power, misreading the lights would have meant not recognising it was the give-way vessel until very close, and only because the track looked wrong, not through correct light identification.

procedures.action: Ensure own vessel's navigation lights are bright enough to stand out against other onboard lighting, and avoid coloured deck lights that could be confused with navigation lights.

constraints: Collision Regulations specify only minimum visibility ranges for navigation lights; they do not address obscuration or misleading effects from other bright lights.

warnings: Bright other-ship lighting (deck/working lights) can obscure or mimic navigation light colours, causing misidentification of colour or vessel heading.

trace.situation: A vessel's main engine failed to respond when ordered astern during a critical inbound passage approaching a turning circle prior to berthing, with tugs not yet connected.

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a master issuing abrupt, non-standard commands to the engine control room during sea preparations, failing to maintain closed-loop communications, and ignoring the company SOP requiring cargo operations to pause before clutching in the main propulsion plant.

procedures.action: Stop cargo operations before clutching in the main propulsion plant and confirm the clutch and pitch system is not causing uncontrolled vessel movement.
procedures.why: Fleet manual SOP exists to prevent uncontrolled vessel movement during propulsion engagement while cargo operations are underway.

trace.situation: CHIRP followed up on a prior near-miss report by writing to the vessel's managers, classification society, flag state, and shipyard about unresolved pilot boarding arrangement failings, noting that previous lessons from a related 2017 report (Issue 48) had not been applied to new-build vessels.
trace.trigger: A new near-miss/hazardous incident report involving pilot boarding arrangements on a newly built vessel, where the same underlying failings from a previous reported incident (Issue 48) had recurred.
constraints: Classification society approval of pilot boarding arrangements must conform to SOLAS requirements.

Choice of which boarding arrangement (aft pilot ladder for drafts above 13m, or combination accommodation/pilot ladder amidships for drafts below 13m) to deploy is an operational decision for the ship's staff based on actual boarding conditions.
warnings: Failings previously identified and acknowledged in connection with modifications to earlier vessels were not carried forward to new builds, allowing similar incidents to continue.
Shore-side parties (ship managers, shipyard, flag state) declined to respond to CHIRP's follow-up, hindering accountability and corrective action.
outcomes: Only the classification society responded, clarifying that its approval of the dual pilot boarding arrangement (aft ladder for drafts >13m, combination ladder amidships for drafts <13m) met SOLAS requirements.

The classification society stated that selecting the correct arrangement for actual conditions is an operational decision left to the ship's staff, implicitly placing responsibility for incidents on crew judgement rather than ship design/approval.
Lack of response from managers, shipyard, and flag state meant the root causes behind recurring incidents were not addressed by those parties.
key_facts: CHIRP wrote to the ship managers, classification society, flag state, and shipyard regarding a repeat pilot boarding arrangement incident.
The vessel has two approved pilot boarding arrangements: an aft pilot ladder for drafts above 13m, and a combination accommodation/pilot ladder arrangement amidships for drafts below 13m.
The classification society and shipyard had both been involved in similar modifications to previous vessels, referenced in Maritime FEEDBACK Issue 48, where lessons were supposedly learned.
Ship managers, shipyard, and flag state all declined to respond to CHIRP's letters; only the classification society replied.
The classification society asserts its approval conforms to SOLAS but frames the choice of actual arrangement used as an operational matter for the ship's crew.

question_seeds.text: Why did the shipyard and classification society fail to carry forward lessons from the earlier Issue 48 incident into the new-build design?
Who is ultimately responsible if the class-approved dual boarding arrangement is misapplied by ship's staff in given draft conditions?

chapter_title: A report highlighting poor practice by shore

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board comments on a reported incident involving a poorly located pilot boarding door near the ship's propellers, tracing the root cause to ambiguous SOLAS wording and lax classification society/shipyard design practices.
trace.trigger: A vessel incident involving pilot boarding arrangements located in the aft quarter length near the propellers, previously reported in Maritime FEEDBACK Issue 48, prompting review of classification society approval and SOLAS wording.

procedures.action: Classification societies should work with shipyards to ensure compliance with both the letter and spirit of SOLAS pilot boarding regulations.
procedures.why: To avoid hazardous situations and potential loss of life arising from ambiguous regulatory wording.

procedures.action: Flag states should ensure compliance with pilot boarding regulations directly or through oversight of classification societies.
procedures.why: Flag states bear ultimate responsibility for regulatory compliance via designated bodies.

procedures.action: Ship owners should actively scrutinise vessel design (including pilot transfer arrangements) at purchase.
procedures.why: To ensure vessels are fit for purpose and do not unnecessarily endanger life.

procedures.action: Avoid using an alternative pilot door located in the aft quarter length near the propellers, even if it requires less rigging.
procedures.why: Such a location endangers both the pilot cutter and the pilot during transfer.

procedures.action: Design out potential hazards at the design stage rather than relying on permissive/ambiguous regulatory wording.
procedures.why: Imprecise wording intended for exceptional cases can be exploited to create unsafe arrangements.

constraints: SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 23.3.1 requires arrangements enabling the pilot to embark/disembark safely on either side of the ship.
Sub-section 3.3.1.2 requires boarding arrangements to be within the parallel body of the ship and, as far as practicable, within the mid-ship half length.
Classification society approval is vessel-specific and does not extend to other vessels or general design practices.
regulations: IMPA Guidance for Naval Architects & Shipyards – Provision of Pilot Boarding Arrangements 2012
warnings: Using an alternative pilot door in the aft quarter length near the propellers endangers both the pilot cutter and the pilot.
Removing or ignoring qualifying wording in SOLAS regulation 23.3.3.1.2 turns a directive requirement into a discretionary choice, enabling unsafe design interpretations.
outcomes: Root cause of the incident and a prior reported incident traced to regulatory ambiguity and inadequate design-stage approval.
Risk of hazardous pilot transfer conditions and potential loss of life if ambiguous wording is exploited by designers.
key_facts: The classification society's approval response applied only to the specific vessel in question, not to the general design practice reported in Issue 48.
SOLAS V/23.3.1 mandates safe pilot embarkation/disembarkation on either side of the ship, and 23.3.3.1.2 further requires positioning within the parallel body, preferably mid-ship half length.
An alternative pilot door option near the propellers in the aft quarter length exists but poses danger to pilot and pilot cutter.
Classification society at vessel design stage may differ from the one in service, complicating accountability.
IMPA has published guidance for naval architects and shipyards on pilot boarding arrangements (2012).

question_seeds.text: Why does locating a pilot door near the propellers in the aft quarter length pose a serious safety risk?
Who is responsible for ensuring pilot boarding arrangements comply with both the letter and spirit of SOLAS V/23?
What does SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 23.3.3.1.2 require regarding the positioning of pilot boarding arrangements?
How can ambiguous regulatory wording be exploited to create hazardous pilot transfer arrangements, and how should this be prevented?

trace.situation: A reporter aboard a cruise ship observed port stevedores and a crane driver removing the gangway using unsafe practices (no hard hats, unclear hand signals, walking under a suspended load) while the ship was preparing to sail.
trace.trigger: Observation of avoidable safety risks during port-managed gangway removal by crane just before ship departure.

procedures.action: Require stevedores and crane crew to wear hard hats when working near suspended loads.
procedures.why: Heads were at times very close to the crane's heavy metal hook, risking head injury.

procedures.action: Use unambiguous, whole-arm hand signals for crane operations.
procedures.why: The stevedore's very slight finger movements created ambiguity in communicating with the crane driver.

procedures.action: Keep personnel clear of and out of reach of a suspended load.
procedures.why: A stevedore walked under the load and placed his hands under it, risking injury if the load descended unexpectedly.

procedures.action: Report observed unsafe port operations to CHIRP and the shipping company for follow-up.
procedures.why: Means of access is generally the master's responsibility by association, even when the unsafe practice originates with the port.

constraints: Means of access to the vessel is generally the responsibility of the master (and company management by association).
This particular report fell squarely on the port's crane/stevedore operations, not ship's crew.
warnings: Stevedores not wearing hard hats near a heavy metal crane hook.
Ambiguous hand signals between stevedore and crane driver increase risk of miscommunication.
Standing or placing hands under a suspended load risks serious injury if the load descends unexpectedly.
Risks were small in likelihood but consequences, if an accident occurred, could be serious.
outcomes: CHIRP wrote to the shipping company, which welcomed the report and passed it to their QHSE department.
The company provided a port contact, but CHIRP's follow-up letter to the port manager received no response.
Unsafe practices by the port's crane crew went unaddressed by the port itself despite company engagement.
key_facts: The gangway was installed and removed by a road crane managed by the port, not the ship's crew.
The reporter had prior experience managing heavy mechanical engineering/crane operations but no maritime background.
No hard hats, ambiguous hand signals, and a stevedore placing hands under the load were the three observed hazards.
The shipping company is in the luxury cruise sector and responded positively, but the port manager did not respond to CHIRP.

question_seeds.text: Who bears responsibility for safety when port-employed crane crews, rather than ship's crew, handle gangway operations alongside the vessel?
What minimum PPE and signaling standards should the master require of port crane crews working near the ship?
How should a master follow up when a port fails to respond to a reported safety concern involving shore-side operations?
Why is 'poor practice by association' a concern for the master even when the unsafe acts are committed by port personnel?

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board comments on a reported near miss involving unsafe stevedore lifting practices in port, addressing shared responsibility for safety and the cruise industry's reliance on port-provided labour.
trace.trigger: A near-miss report describing an unsafe act by stevedores during a port lifting operation observed by ship or shore personnel.

procedures.action: Encourage all personnel, ship or shore based, to intervene if someone is working unsafely (Stop Work Authority).
procedures.why: Everybody is responsible for the safety of all personnel; intervention promotes a higher safety culture.

procedures.action: If a port operates at lower safety standards, have the master 'note protest'.
procedures.why: This can encourage remedial action by the port in response to substandard safety practices.

procedures.action: Alternatively, have the company send a letter to the port raising the safety concern.
procedures.why: May encourage safer behaviour where responsibility for stevedoring lies with the port rather than the ship.

procedures.action: Apply the Code of Safe Working Practices signalling procedures to all lifting operations.
procedures.why: The Reporter's comments and signalling guidance apply generally to all lifting operations, not just this case.

constraints: The cruise industry generally does not subcontract this type of stevedoring job.
Responsibility for stevedore safety usually lies with the port, not the ship.
Some ports operate at lower safety standards than others.
warnings: Failure to intervene in unsafe stevedore practices can allow unsafe conditions to persist.
Some ports operate at lower safety standards, increasing risk to personnel.
outcomes: Encouraging Stop Work Authority promotes a higher safety culture among ship and shore personnel.
Noting protest or sending a company letter may prompt the port to improve safety standards.
key_facts: Everybody, ship or shore based, shares responsibility for personnel safety.
Stop Work Authority encourages mutual intervention when unsafe acts are observed.
The cruise industry typically does not subcontract this job; the port usually holds responsibility.
The Code of Safe Working Practices contains signalling procedures applicable to all lifting operations.

question_seeds.text: What options does a master have if a port's stevedores are working unsafely?
Who is responsible for stevedore safety when the cruise line does not subcontract the work?
How can 'noting protest' be used to encourage a port to improve safety standards?
Why is Stop Work Authority important for both ship and shore personnel?

trace.situation: A sailing yacht in a local race was nearly run down by a large vessel (carrying a pilot) crossing on a collision course outside the normal shipping channel, with the ship failing to respond to VHF calls or take early give-way action.
trace.trigger: Relative bearing of an approaching give-way vessel remains constant/unchanging, indicating a collision risk, and the vessel fails to respond to VHF hailing.

procedures.action: Monitor the relative bearing of an approaching vessel continuously to detect collision risk.
procedures.why: A constant or unchanging relative bearing indicates risk of collision per the reporter's observation.

procedures.action: Attempt to contact the other vessel via VHF Channel 16 to clarify intentions.
procedures.why: Standard practice to establish communication and prompt give-way action, though it may not succeed.

procedures.action: Do not assume the give-way vessel will actually give way; prepare own avoiding action (e.g. crash gybe) as a last resort.
procedures.why: The give-way vessel showed no sign of taking action until very late, despite COLREGS obligations.

procedures.action: Maintain visual/radar lookout independent of VHF contact attempts.
procedures.why: VHF communication is unreliable: no guarantee of correct transmission, that the other party is listening, or that calls to small craft won't be ignored.

constraints: Give-way vessel is obligated under COLREGS to take early and substantial action to avoid collision.
Stand-on vessel (the yacht) must be prepared to take avoiding action if the give-way vessel does not act.
VHF Channel 16 calls provide no guarantee of receipt or response.
warnings: Never assume the give-way vessel will in fact give way.
VHF is a poor and unreliable method of collision-avoidance communication.
Even a vessel carrying a pilot familiar with local sailing traffic may not obey COLREGS or may delay action until very late.
outcomes: The ship altered course to port at the last moment and passed about 100 yards ahead of the yacht, narrowly avoiding collision.
The yacht was on the point of performing a crash gybe to avoid collision when the ship's turn was noticed.
The pilot reported tracking the yacht on ARPA radar and judged (incorrectly, per the yacht's account) that its bearing was always opening.
key_facts: The yacht was sailing downwind at ~6.5 knots in hazy visibility (~2.5 miles) flying a bright cruising chute.
A large vessel crossed from South to North outside the usual shipping channel, an unusual track for that area.
The yacht called the ship three times on VHF Channel 16 without any response.
The ship was carrying a pilot, who stated via ARPA tracking that the yacht's bearing was 'always opening,' contradicting the yacht's observation of a constant bearing and closing risk.
The ship eventually turned to port and passed about 100 yards ahead of the yacht.

question_seeds.text: Why should I never assume a give-way vessel will actually comply with COLREGS, even one carrying a pilot?
How reliable is VHF Channel 16 as a means of resolving a crossing/collision risk situation, and what should I do if calls go unanswered?
What immediate actions should the stand-on vessel take when a constant bearing indicates collision risk and the give-way vessel shows no sign of action?
Who is responsible when a pilot's ARPA bearing assessment differs from the other vessel's visual observation of a closing, constant bearing?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describing a near-collision/close-quarters encounter between a commercial vessel and a small yacht, where differing perceptions of 'sudden' appearance, VHF channel monitoring, and eye-height-dependent visibility led to confusion over the vessel's course and intentions.
trace.trigger: A yacht skipper perceived a commercial vessel's course as 'sudden' and attempted to call it on VHF Channel 16 without response, prompting a CHIRP report and subsequent investigation/reply from the commercial vessel's bridge team.

procedures.action: Maintain a proper visual lookout appropriate to eye height and conditions, recognizing that visibility judged from a low eye height (6 feet) differs significantly from that at higher conning positions (30 feet).
procedures.why: The yacht's effective visibility was only about 2 miles versus the commercial vessel's stated 4+ nautical miles, causing the vessel to appear to arrive 'suddenly' from the yacht's perspective.

procedures.action: Identify and monitor the correct local VTS/working VHF channel (Channel 71) in addition to Channel 16 when operating in an area with published General Directions.
procedures.why: The commercial vessel was correctly monitoring Channel 71 per local General Directions and would have responded immediately, but the yacht called on Channel 16 and received no response, demonstrating a channel-monitoring mismatch.

procedures.action: Be aware that pleasure vessels may be exempt from local General Directions and therefore unlikely to use or expect to use the VTS working channel.
procedures.why: The local General Directions specifically exempt pleasure vessels from channel requirements, meaning commercial vessels cannot assume small craft will call on the VTS channel even though it is scanned.

procedures.action: Seek early VHF confirmation of another vessel's intentions and awareness when bearing appears steady and a risk of collision is suspected.
procedures.why: The reporter's intent in calling was simply to confirm the other vessel's intentions and that it was aware of the yacht's presence, given a steady bearing causing concern.

constraints: Local General Directions designate Channel 71 as the VTS channel for the area and exempt pleasure vessels from its use.
Visibility assessment is dependent on observer eye height; low eye-height vessels have reduced effective visual range compared to higher conning positions.
Channel 16 remains the commonly expected 'safety channel' by many mariners despite local VTS arrangements favoring a different working channel.
warnings: A vessel may appear to 'suddenly' arrive due to differing visibility ranges based on observer eye height, not due to actual last-minute course changes.
Reliance on Channel 16 alone as the default safety channel may fail if local VTS arrangements use a different designated channel.
Assuming other vessels are monitoring the same VHF channel can lead to missed calls and delayed recognition of risk of collision.
outcomes: The yacht's VHF call on Channel 16 went unanswered because the commercial vessel was monitoring Channel 71 as per local General Directions.
The commercial vessel stated that had the yacht called on Channel 71, it would have received an immediate response.
The reporter acknowledged learning a lesson about VHF channel expectations and differing perceptions of the same situation, stating it would not be repeated.
The incident raised questions, in the reporter's view, about the practical reliability of Channel 16 as a safety channel.
key_facts: The commercial vessel maintained a steady course at a maximum speed of 8 knots with visibility reportedly in excess of 4 nautical miles.
The yacht's effective visibility, from an eye height of about 6 feet, was only about 2 miles.
Local General Directions designate Channel 71 as the VTS channel for the area and exempt pleasure vessels from using it.
The commercial vessel scans Channel 71 for situational awareness but does not expect pleasure vessels to call on it.
The yacht skipper called on Channel 16, which went unanswered, and never considered calling on Channel 71.

question_seeds.text: Why did the commercial vessel appear to 'suddenly' emerge from the yacht's perspective despite good overall visibility?
Which VHF channel should small craft prioritize monitoring when local General Directions designate a VTS working channel different from Channel 16?
How should a Master reconcile the assumption that Channel 16 is universally monitored with local VTS arrangements that exempt certain vessel classes?
What should be done when a steady bearing with another vessel causes concern but VHF attempts on Channel 16 go unanswered?

trace.situation: A vessel departing Rotterdam for the Dover Strait was overtaken by two faster ships on its port quarter, with the second (a container feeder) approaching on a collision course and not responding to VHF calls, requiring Pilot Maas relay and a last-minute course alteration to avoid an unsafe close-quarters overtaking.
trace.trigger: A faster overtaking vessel on a collision course failed to respond on VHF Ch16/Ch02 and then began passing at an unsafe distance of 1.5-2 cables.

procedures.action: Call the first (larger) overtaking vessel to state intention to keep to the south side of the traffic lane
procedures.why: To establish mutual understanding and agree on a safe overtaking side before other ships close in

procedures.action: Attempt contact with the second, faster vessel on VHF Channel 16 and then Channel 02
procedures.why: Channel 02 was the working channel of Pilot Maas, covering the area the vessel was transiting, increasing chance of contact

procedures.action: Contact Pilot Maas to report the collision-course situation and inability to reach the other vessel, requesting they advise the vessel to pass on the reporter's starboard side
procedures.why: To use a third party with communication access to relay critical safety information and coordinate a safe passing arrangement

procedures.action: Monitor the other vessel's course alteration and actual passing distance as it closed to 1.2 miles and then attempted to overtake at 1.5-2 cables
procedures.why: To verify the intended safe passing arrangement was actually being executed

procedures.action: Alter own course to starboard under Rule 2 of COLREGs (Article 2) to increase passing distance to 2-3 cables
procedures.why: The achieved 1.5-2 cable distance was judged unsafe given the risk if either vessel lost steerage, requiring independent action per general prudence

procedures.action: Call the first overtaking vessel (now on starboard side) to advise of the course change
procedures.why: To ensure continued safe separation from the other overtaking vessel after altering course

constraints: A passing distance of 1.5-2 cables was considered unsafe given the risk of loss of steerage by either vessel
Action taken must be in accordance with COLREGs Rule 2 (general prudence) when other vessels' compliance is uncertain
Communication relay via Pilot Maas confirmed the other vessel 'had heard' but did not guarantee compliant action
warnings: A passing distance of 1.5 to 2 cables is not a safe passing distance in close-quarters overtaking situations
If either vessel were to lose steerage there would not be enough time for the other ship to react
outcomes: The second vessel altered course to port as advised via Pilot Maas but still attempted to overtake at an unsafe 1.5-2 cable distance
The reporting vessel's own course alteration increased the passing distance to 2-3 cables, still described as 'short' but safer
The first overtaking vessel confirmed it would keep a safe distance after being advised of the course change
key_facts: The reporting vessel was on a course of 270° at about 8.2 knots departing Rotterdam for the Dover Strait
Two faster vessels were overtaking on the port quarter; the second was a container feeder doing about 14 knots
The container feeder did not respond on VHF Channel 16 or Channel 02 (Pilot Maas's working channel)
Pilot Maas relayed the safety request and reported the vessel would alter course to port to pass on the port side
The reporting vessel invoked COLREGs Rule 2 to alter course to starboard, increasing passing distance from 1.5-2 cables to 2-3 cables

question_seeds.text: Why did the master judge a 1.5 to 2 cable passing distance as unsafe in this situation?
How did the master use Pilot Maas as an intermediary when direct VHF contact failed?
What action did the master take under COLREGs Rule 2 when the other vessel's passing distance remained inadequate?
Who confirmed they would maintain a safe distance after the master's course alteration?

trace.situation: A reporter vessel, after being passed by one ship on its port side, altered course to give way to a second vessel approaching on its starboard side, which then crossed its bow at about 1.2nm in a high-density traffic area near a traffic separation scheme.
trace.trigger: A crossing/give-way situation developed with multiple vessels in close proximity while approaching a traffic separation scheme.

procedures.action: Alter course to resume giving way to the vessel approaching on the starboard side once the port-side vessel has passed at a safe distance.
procedures.why: To comply with give-way obligations under COLREGS as multiple crossing situations arise sequentially.

procedures.action: CHIRP follow up with the company and master of the vessel involved to understand their intentions and perception.
procedures.why: To establish why the desired safe passing distance was not maintained and clarify the other vessel's decision-making.

constraints: Give-way vessel must act in accordance with COLREGS when multiple crossing situations occur
Desired safe passing distances may not always be achievable in high-density traffic areas
warnings: A desired safe passing distance of several cables/miles is sometimes not achievable in high-density traffic areas
Masters may deviate from ideal passing distances to prioritize entering a traffic separation scheme or avoiding a third vessel, increasing collision risk
outcomes: The vessel crossed the reporter's bow at approximately 1.2nm and continued on a track about 1 mile north
The other master's perception was that he needed to make for the traffic separation scheme and avoid a third vessel, and he was aware of the reporter's intentions
No collision or near-miss resulted, but the safe passing distance was compromised
key_facts: A vessel passed the reporter's vessel at 2.4 cables on the port side
The reporter then altered course to give way to a vessel on the starboard side
That vessel crossed the reporter's bow at about 1.2nm and proceeded on a track 1 mile north
CHIRP contacted the company and spoke directly with the master of the vessel involved
The master's priority was reaching the traffic separation scheme and avoiding a third vessel

trace.situation: A reporting vessel outbound from Seki Saki pilot station in the Bungo Suido encountered an inbound car carrier that, despite being the give-way vessel under COLREGS, requested starboard-to-starboard passing and failed to take appropriate action, resulting in a near-collision situation.
trace.trigger: Inbound vessel (car carrier), as the give-way vessel in a crossing/head-on situation, requested a starboard-to-starboard passing and continued on a collision course instead of giving way.

procedures.action: Monitor approaching vessel by radar/visual from long range (10 miles) and track bearing/aspect.
procedures.why: Early detection allows time to assess risk of collision and intentions.

procedures.action: Contact the other vessel by VHF to confirm intentions when within a few miles.
procedures.why: Clarify the other vessel's intended actions and resolve ambiguity about passing arrangement.

procedures.action: Assert own vessel's COLREGS status and insist the give-way vessel alter course to starboard for port-to-port passing.
procedures.why: The reporting vessel was the stand-on vessel and had another ship outbound on its port bow, preventing a port alteration.

procedures.action: Continue close monitoring of the target vessel's course and speed as range closes.
procedures.why: To detect failure to give way and determine when stand-on vessel must take independent action.

procedures.action: Re-query the other vessel's intentions as range closed to 2 miles.
procedures.why: Final check before collision became imminent.

procedures.action: Take avoiding action (hard-over to port) when the other vessel confirmed it was maintaining course.
procedures.why: To avoid collision once it became apparent the give-way vessel would not act, per stand-on vessel's obligation to act when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone.

procedures.action: Report the incident and the other vessel's company to CHIRP for formal notification.
procedures.why: To flag unsafe practice and seek accountability for blatant disregard of COLREGS.

constraints: Reporting vessel could not alter to port due to another outbound vessel on its port bow.
The actual pilot boarding ground was located about 5.0 miles west of the normal traffic lane, meaning the car carrier's request was not justified by proximity to the pilot station.
Good visibility existed, so both vessels' sidelights (green/red) were clearly visible, removing ambiguity about aspect.
warnings: Approaching a pilot station does not exempt a vessel from COLREGS give-way obligations, especially when still miles from the pilot boarding ground.
Vessel described as behaving with 'exceedingly bad seamanship' and being a 'navigational hazard' due to blatant disregard of collision regulations.
outcomes: Reporting vessel was forced to take hard-over avoiding action to pass clear after the give-way vessel failed to alter course.
Heated exchanges occurred between the two masters after the near-collision.
CHIRP wrote to the car carrier's company but received no response.
key_facts: Incident occurred 10 Apr 2018 in the Bungo Suido near Seki Saki pilot station.
Reporting vessel was outbound (stand-on vessel); car carrier was inbound and the give-way vessel.
Initial VHF contact made at 6 miles range; car carrier requested starboard-to-starboard passing instead of complying with give-way duty.
Reporting vessel could not deviate to port due to another outbound ship nearby.
Avoiding action (hard to port) was taken only when range closed to under 2 miles and the car carrier confirmed it was maintaining course.

question_seeds.text: Why was the car carrier not justified in requesting starboard-to-starboard passing simply because it was approaching the pilot station?
How should the OOW have escalated the situation sooner, given the other vessel ignored repeated clarifications of intent?
What options did the stand-on vessel have for avoiding action given it could not alter to port?
Who bears responsibility for ensuring compliance with COLREGS when a vessel is near, but not yet at, a pilot boarding ground?

trace.situation: A reporting vessel detected another ship (M/V xx) on radar at about 8 miles on the port bow with a closing CPA of less than 0.35nm and tried to raise them by radio as the TCPA decreased.
trace.trigger: Detection of a target vessel with a CPA less than 0.35nm and a closing TCPA, indicating a developing close-quarters/collision risk situation

procedures.action: Detect and track the target vessel's range, CPA and TCPA from initial detection (8nm, CPA <0.35nm, TCPA ~40min)
procedures.why: To assess collision risk and monitor how the situation develops

procedures.action: Continue monitoring the target's movements as TCPA decreases
procedures.why: To determine whether the other vessel is taking appropriate action or if risk of collision is increasing

procedures.action: Attempt to establish radio communication with the target vessel via voice and DSC on a regular basis
procedures.why: To alert the other vessel, confirm intentions, and coordinate avoiding action

constraints: CPA was assessed as less than 0.35nm, which is a very close passing distance
Radio contact attempts (voice and DSC) were made repeatedly but received no response
warnings: A target vessel not responding to repeated voice and DSC calls as TCPA closes to 25 minutes represents an unresolved close-quarters risk
outcomes: No response was received from the target vessel despite repeated voice and DSC calls, leaving the collision risk unresolved as TCPA closed to approximately 25 minutes
key_facts: Target vessel M/V xx was first detected at approximately 8 miles on the port bow
Closest Point of Approach (CPA) was assessed at less than 0.35nm
Initial Time to CPA (TCPA) was approximately 40 minutes
The reporting vessel attempted radio contact via voice and DSC regularly but received no response until TCPA was about 25 minutes

trace.situation: A 50m/530GT vessel reports a near-miss close-quarters situation in the Mediterranean with a smaller merchant vessel (M/V xx) that appeared to have no one on watch in the bridge, closing to a CPA of about 0.5nm.
trace.trigger: Another vessel on a closing track fails to respond to VHF calls and shows no apparent watchkeeping as range decreases to 1nm and then 0.5nm.

procedures.action: Attempt to establish VHF contact with the approaching vessel as range closes.
procedures.why: To clarify intentions and avoid a close-quarters situation developing further.

procedures.action: Maintain course and speed while monitoring the situation.
procedures.why: Reporter's vessel was the stand-on vessel and other traffic nearby meant altering course/speed could create additional close-quarters situations with other vessels.

procedures.action: Sound horn signals when range reduced to 1nm and continue as range closed to 0.5nm.
procedures.why: To alert the apparently unaware vessel and prompt avoiding action.

procedures.action: Keep engines and steering at immediate readiness and maintain a proper lookout, including binocular observation of the other vessel's bridge.
procedures.why: To be prepared to take avoiding action if the give-way vessel did not respond in time.

procedures.action: Continue attempting VHF contact even after the other vessel altered course.
procedures.why: To confirm understanding and reinforce safe passage communication.

constraints: Reporter's vessel had other traffic nearby limiting safe options to alter course or speed.
M/V xx had unrestricted sea room to pass astern, implying it was the vessel expected to take action.
Horn signals and radio calls were the only means of alerting the other vessel given no response.
warnings: Smaller merchant vessels in this area regularly ignore the rules of the road and rarely respond to VHF in developing close-quarters situations.
Poor watchkeeping standards on some smaller merchant vessels risk undetected close-quarters situations.
An apparent attitude exists that yachts/smaller vessels should always give way regardless of circumstances, which is not correct under the rules.
outcomes: The other vessel made a bold, late alteration of course to port after a crew member was seen rushing to the bridge, indicating no prior watchkeeper.

trace.situation: A sailing vessel crossing the English Channel hard on the wind had a near-collision (CPA near zero) with a ship that ignored multiple VHF and DSC calls, forcing a chain of course changes among several vessels to avoid collision.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board reviewed several submitted near-miss/collision reports and issued consolidated commentary on recurring causal themes: over-reliance on VHF instead of the collision regulations, poor situational awareness, overtaking practice, and underlying competency/qualification issues.
trace.trigger: Pattern identified across multiple independently reported close-quarters/collision situations showing common root causes.

procedures.action: As stand-on vessel, take your own avoiding action or reduce speed as soon as you are in doubt about the other vessel's intentions.
procedures.why: The collision regulations are designed to work without VHF intervention; doubt itself is the trigger for action.

procedures.action: Avoid using VHF to request the other vessel's intentions.
procedures.why: A VHF conversation gives the other vessel the chance to refuse or contradict the expected action, undermining COLREGS-based decision making.

procedures.action: Concentrate on applying the collision regulations rather than engaging in VHF discussion, including heated exchanges.
procedures.why: Heated VHF discussion may feel satisfying but is not advisable and does not resolve the navigational risk.

procedures.action: Identify and monitor the specific VHF working channel appropriate to your operational area, noting whether it is Simplex or Duplex.
procedures.why: GMDSS removed the legal requirement to monitor Channel 16 continuously, though it remains a safety/distress frequency; knowing channel type affects who can hear/communicate with you.

procedures.action: Maintain full situational awareness by putting yourself in the position of the other vessel(s).
procedures.why: Perceptions of safe passing distance differ between observers; full awareness removes the need to query the other vessel's intentions.

procedures.action: Take any avoiding action early and substantially.
procedures.why: Early, substantial action is more reliable than late checks of the other vessel's intentions.

procedures.action: When overtaking, where practicable overtake to starboard keeping your own starboard side open.
procedures.why: This is identified as good overtaking practice by CHIRP.

procedures.action: Investigate root causes such as personnel qualifications and actual experience rather than simply apportioning blame for actions/inactions.
procedures.why: A certificate of competency does not guarantee the holder was actually competent, as seen in the unmanned bridge case.

constraints: Collision regulations should be the primary basis for avoiding action, not VHF communication.
No legal requirement exists under GMDSS to continuously monitor VHF Channel 16, but it remains a safety and distress frequency.
Overtaking to starboard should only be done where practicable.
warnings: Requesting intentions over VHF gives the other vessel the chance to say 'No!' and can create confusion.
Heated VHF discussion is not advisable and distracts from applying the collision regulations.
Holding a certificate of competency does not mean the individual was actually competent.
Simplex/Duplex channel confusion can mean you can be heard by others but can only communicate with the transmitting station.
outcomes: Reliance on COLREGS rather than VHF reduces risk of miscommunication-driven collisions.
Full situational awareness can eliminate the need to check other vessels' intentions mid-encounter.
Focusing only on blame rather than root causes (qualifications/experience) fails to prevent recurrence, as illustrated by the unmanned bridge incident.

trace.situation: A pilot using a Portable Pilot Unit (PPU) noticed the AIS-derived vessel position lagging behind the actual position while navigating in port, and traced the discrepancy to GPS smoothing settings on the vessel's GPS.
trace.trigger: Pilot observes AIS/PPU position data showing the vessel behind its actual position (lagging) while passing a beacon, and the master's visual bearing from ECDIS does not match reality.

procedures.action: Cross-check PPU/AIS displayed position against visual/ECDIS bearings when a discrepancy is suspected.
procedures.why: The pilot noticed the vessel appeared to lag behind its true position on the PPU.

procedures.action: Ask the master/bridge team to verify a landmark or beacon bearing using the ECDIS as an independent check.
procedures.why: To confirm whether the displayed AIS/PPU position was accurate or erroneous.

procedures.action: Request access to and review the GPS settings, specifically the GPS SETUP/GPS SMOOTHING menu.
procedures.why: To identify the technical cause of the positional lag.

procedures.action: Reset GPS smoothing values (Position, Speed, Average Speed) to zero.
procedures.why: Smoothing settings (20s, 30s, 120s) were introducing delay/averaging that caused the displayed position to lag behind the vessel's actual position.

procedures.action: Confirm accuracy of displayed positions after departure following the setting change.
procedures.why: To verify the corrective action resolved the lag and restored accurate real-time positioning.

constraints: Pilot needs Captain's cooperation/assistance to access and adjust GPS settings.
Error was not evident once vessel was secured alongside (only manifest while underway).
warnings: GPS smoothing settings can cause AIS/PPU displayed vessel position to lag significantly behind actual position, creating a navigational hazard during pilotage.
This type of error has been reported before, but in prior cases no assistance was given by the Captains involved, implying the error went unresolved.
outcomes: Resetting GPS smoothing values to zero eliminated the positional lag and produced accurate position display after departure.
Without master cooperation to investigate and adjust settings, the error can persist across voyages.
key_facts: The vessel's GPS had a 'GPS SMOOTHING' setting under GPS SETUP with Position=20s, Speed=30s, Average Speed=120s.
This smoothing caused the AIS data shown on the PPU to lag behind the vessel's real position.
A bearing check (port bow vs. actual beam) confirmed the ECDIS/AIS display was inaccurate while underway.
No error was observed once the vessel was alongside and stationary.
This type of GPS smoothing-induced error had been reported previously without resolution due to lack of Captain assistance.

trace.situation: A pilot using a Portable Pilot Unit (PPU) discovered that a vessel's AIS-displayed position was offset by about 20 metres from its actual position, traced to a GPS antenna offset discrepancy.
trace.trigger: Pilot noticed a mismatch between the vessel's AIS position and the independent PPU position during pilotage.

procedures.action: Compare AIS position against an independent PPU display to detect discrepancies.
procedures.why: The PPU visually showed the 20 metre difference, confirming an error existed.

procedures.action: Check the antenna offsets entered for the AIS GPS antenna against the ship's antenna plan.
procedures.why: The error stemmed from differing offsets between the AIS GPS antenna and the No 2 GPS antenna.

procedures.action: Use the GPS selector switch to change the AIS external GPS source to No 1 GPS, which was located close to the AIS antenna.
procedures.why: No 1 GPS antenna's position closely matched the AIS antenna location, eliminating the offset error.

procedures.action: Post a notice on the AIS requiring the external GPS input to always be sourced from No 1 GPS.
procedures.why: To permanently prevent recurrence of the position error by standardising the GPS source.

constraints: AIS GPS antenna offsets must match the actual antenna installation plan for accurate position reporting.
Multiple GPS antennas feeding the AIS must have their offsets correctly reconciled or a single verified source selected.
warnings: AIS position can be inaccurate by tens of metres if GPS antenna offsets are not correctly configured, posing a navigational safety risk.
outcomes: Switching the AIS external GPS source to No 1 GPS immediately aligned the AIS position with the independent PPU position.
The Captain implemented a standing notice to ensure the correct GPS source is always used, preventing recurrence.
key_facts: AIS position was found to be out by approximately 20 metres.
The AIS GPS antenna was located forward on the bridge front, 3 metres in on the starboard side.
The error arose from differing offsets between the AIS GPS antenna and the No 2 GPS antenna.
No 1 GPS antenna was situated close to the AIS GPS antenna and gave the correct aligned position when selected.
A selector switch allowed the Captain to change which GPS antenna fed the AIS system.

trace.situation: A ferry master reports a near-miss during a head-in berthing manoeuvre when a port engine de-clutch event combined with poor bridge-engine room communication nearly caused the vessel to be blown onto a breakwater.
trace.trigger: Port engine de-clutched during berthing while the vessel was being blown off the berth by strong wind, and the centre-console phone rang unanswered while the Chief Officer was on the opposite bridge wing.

procedures.action: Install a dedicated talk-back communication system with microphones/speakers in the engine control room and at all bridge conning positions (centre and both wings).
procedures.why: Phone-based communication with separate numbers for centre console and bridge wings was slow, noisy, and caused a critical delay in relaying the port engine de-clutch fault to the bridge team.

procedures.action: Use the talk-back system for all verbal bridge/engine room communication going forward, retaining phones only as a backup.
procedures.why: Pressing a button and speaking is physiologically faster and more reliable than relaying orders via a third party answering a phone, especially at moments of maximum concentration during berthing.

procedures.action: Ensure the person conning the ship can broadcast an immediate problem/delay call to the engine room from any position.
procedures.why: Enables instant communication and encourages feedback from both ends, reducing response time to technical faults during critical manoeuvres.

constraints: Manning during the incident was limited to the Master and Chief Officer, both initially on the same bridge wing.
Communication relied solely on phone lines with separate numbers for centre console and bridge wing positions.
High ambient noise from weather and bow thruster impaired verbal communication in the wheelhouse.
warnings: Phone-based bridge/engine communication can introduce dangerous delay when manning is split across bridge wing positions.
High noise levels in the wheelhouse from weather and bow thruster can mask or delay critical phone alerts.
Referenced MAIB Report 18-2012 incident may have been less severe had a talk-back system been fitted.
outcomes: The vessel berthed safely despite the de-clutch event and communication delay, though with 'raised pulse rates on the bridge'.
A dedicated talk-back system was subsequently installed by ship's staff, improving inter-departmental communication.
After installation, technical problems were reported promptly and heard by the entire bridge team using the talk-back system.
key_facts: The incident occurred during a head-in berthing with control on the starboard bridge wing and a strong wind blowing the vessel off the berth toward a breakwater.
The port engine de-clutched, and the Chief Officer had to run to the centre console phone to receive and relay instructions to set pitch to zero and re-clutch the engine.
Bridge/engine communication was originally via phone only, with separate numbers for the centre console and bridge wing positions.
A talk-back system with one mic/speaker in engine control and three on the bridge was installed afterward and became the primary communication method.
The reporter links the incident to concerns similar to those in MAIB Report 18-2012.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary following a pilotage incident involving helmsman error, discussing bridge-to-engine room communication failures and vessel/bridge design deficiencies that contributed to loss of control during a critical manoeuvre.
trace.trigger: An error by the helmsman while under pilotage, linked to inadequate communication systems and vessel design limitations (lighter drafts, reduced astern power) outside original design parameters.

procedures.action: Install instant talkback (closed-loop) communication systems between bridge and engine room instead of relying on third-party relay.
procedures.why: Reduces risk of miscommunication, especially with multinational crews, and prevents loss of control at critical points in an operation.

procedures.action: Apply a systematic risk management programme to identify, analyse, evaluate and mitigate risks in bridge-engine room communications and any retrofit changes.
procedures.why: A sound risk management programme is needed because conversions/retrofits are never ideal and introduce operational risk.

procedures.action: Incorporate Human Centred Design analysis into ship design from concept stage through retirement, including bridge ergonomics and mooring systems.
procedures.why: Mariners' operational expertise is not currently being utilised at the design stage, leaving crews to manage problems created by poor design (e.g., needing to hang out of bridge windows to berth).

procedures.action: Engage ship owners and mariners more actively in new-build design decisions rather than accepting standard 'off the shelf' designs.
procedures.why: Standard designs are used with little owner involvement, and additional design extras addressing human factors are often omitted.

constraints: Design changes (new-build or retrofit) must consider both bridge-engine room communications and change management processes.
Operating a vessel outside its original design parameters (e.g., lighter drafts, reduced astern power) increases susceptibility to manoeuvrability problems.
warnings: Loss of control at a critical part of an operation could have extremely serious repercussions.
Relying on third-party relay communication increases risk of miscommunication, particularly with multinational crews.
Expecting onboard staff to manually compensate for poor design (e.g., hanging out of bridge window) is not an acceptable solution.
outcomes: Without instant closed-loop communication, miscommunication risk increases during critical manoeuvres.
Persistent recurrence of the same communications issues over many years indicates systemic failure to implement lasting fixes.
Lack of Human Centred Design and mariner input at the design stage perpetuates ergonomic and operational hazards on new and retrofitted vessels.
key_facts: Instant talkback communication systems provide closed-loop reporting and reduce miscommunication risk compared to third-party relay.
The vessel involved was operating outside its original design parameters due to lighter drafts and reduced astern power.
Shipyards currently lack human element expertise needed for Human Centred Design analysis.
New-build vessels often use standard designs with minimal owner involvement, limiting incorporation of human-factor 'extras'.
The same bridge communication issues have been discussed for many years without resolution.

trace.situation: A pilot reports that during inbound pilotage, a helm order of Port 10 was verbally acknowledged correctly by the helmsman but only partially executed (5 degrees instead of 10), requiring correction by both pilot and master.
trace.trigger: Helmsman verbally repeats the helm order correctly but applies incorrect rudder angle, creating a discrepancy between verbal readback and actual rudder indicator reading.

procedures.action: Monitor the rudder angle indicator after giving a helm order to confirm it matches the order given.
procedures.why: Verbal acknowledgement by the helmsman does not guarantee correct execution, as shown when the helmsman repeated 'Port 10' but applied only 5 degrees.

procedures.action: Immediately repeat the helm order and point to the rudder angle indicator if a discrepancy is noticed.
procedures.why: To clearly and promptly communicate the error and prompt correction before the vessel deviates from the intended course.

procedures.action: Have the master independently cross-check and reinforce the correction.
procedures.why: A second bridge team member verifying and correcting the helm order adds a layer of safety and ensures the error is rectified.

constraints: Bridge team (pilot and master) must actively monitor rudder angle indicator, not just rely on verbal readback from helmsman.
warnings: Verbal readback/acknowledgement of a helm order does not confirm correct execution; rudder angle must be independently verified.
outcomes: The discrepancy was caught immediately by both the pilot and master, the helm was corrected to Port 10, and the helmsman apologised, with no adverse consequence to the vessel's track.

trace.trigger: Vessel's speed failed to reduce as expected during berthing, and subsequent engine maneuvers caused increasing sternway that put the ship on a course toward a nearby breakwater.

procedures.action: Install a low-cost bridge-to-engine-control-room communication/intercom system.
procedures.why: Allows the whole bridge/control room team to hear instructions simultaneously, reducing the chance of misunderstanding and bridging the gap between deck and engine departments.

procedures.why: Attempt to counteract wind-induced drift of the stern.

procedures.action: If sternway increases and grounding/collision with a breakwater becomes likely, shift the con to the opposite (danger-side) bridge wing.
procedures.why: Gain direct visual control over the side of the vessel facing the hazard.

procedures.action: Establish direct communication with the engine control room during the critical maneuver.

warnings: Reduced astern power due to non-standard (lighter) draft can cause berthing maneuvers to behave unpredictably.

trace.situation: Explanation of human night vision physiology and lighting considerations relevant to bridge watchkeeping and lookout duties during night hours.
trace.trigger: Need to maintain effective visual lookout and alertness during night watches or when transitioning between lit and dark environments.

procedures.action: Allow at least 30 minutes for eyes to fully adapt to night vision before relying on it for lookout duties.
procedures.why: The dark adaptation line shows eyes are fully adapted to night vision only after 30 minutes in the dark.

procedures.action: Avoid rapidly switching between bright light and dim, dark-adapted conditions.
procedures.why: Rapid switching confuses the body's biological clock and reduces alertness on night duty and recovery from shift work.

procedures.action: Adjust lighting levels on the bridge/workplace to suit individual needs, including age and use of spectacles.
procedures.why: Older people need more light and find tasks like motion detection and detecting the unexpected more difficult; individual visual ability varies.

procedures.action: Use peripheral (rod-based) vision for detecting movement at night and direct central (cone-based) vision for detailed tasks or screens.
procedures.why: Rod cells provide light sensitivity and peripheral movement detection in darkness, while cone cells provide colour and fine detail vision, explaining why off-center vision is better for low light and screens flicker less when viewed directly.

constraints: Night vision adaptation takes approximately 30 minutes and is disrupted by exposure to bright light.
Lighting needs vary by individual, particularly with age and corrective eyewear.
warnings: Rapid switching between bright artificial/daylight and dark conditions reduces alertness and disrupts the body's biological clock.
Older crew members and those with reduced visual ability require more light and may struggle more with motion detection, glare, and dim displays.
outcomes: Properly managed lighting and allowance for dark adaptation improves lookout effectiveness and reduces fatigue-related risk on night watches.
Poor lighting management can impair detection of unexpected hazards and reduce alertness, increasing near-miss risk.
key_facts: Full night vision adaptation takes about 30 minutes in darkness.
Rod cells enable peripheral motion detection and light sensitivity in darkness; cone cells enable colour and detailed vision.
Light exposure affects biological clocks, hormones, appetite, body temperature, and alertness, not just vision.

procedures.action: Allow adequate time for the eyes to acquire good night vision before relying on it for navigation decisions.

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a near-miss report showing good bridge resource management between a master and pilot who used closed-loop communication to catch and correct a helm order error, followed by general CHIRP commentary on industry near-miss data collection and on night vision adaptation for bridge watchkeepers.
trace.trigger: A helm order was given on the bridge and needed verification between the master and pilot.

procedures.action: Repeat back any instruction or helm order (closed-loop reporting) to confirm it has been clearly received.
procedures.why: Ensures the message given matches the message understood, preventing execution of a misheard or misunderstood order.

procedures.action: Double-check critical orders by an independent means (e.g. both master and pilot monitoring the execution).
procedures.why: In the reported case, both the master and pilot independently noticed the error and were able to correct it before it caused harm.

procedures.action: Use standard marine vocabulary and be mindful of whether parties are communicating in their native or second language.
procedures.why: Language differences and non-standard phrasing are important factors affecting the reliability of the closed-loop communication cycle.

procedures.action: Avoid overly bright pre-shift environments and overly dim bridge conditions before taking over a watch.
procedures.why: Eyes need time to adapt between bright and dim environments; poorly managed light exposure impairs night vision needed on watch.

procedures.action: Spend time in a reddish-light environment before or during low-light bridge duty.
procedures.why: The eye's rod cells, which are most active at night, are most sensitive to shorter (reddish) wavelengths, so reddish light helps preserve their sensitivity without requiring the full ~30 minutes of dark adaptation.

constraints: Closed-loop communication requires repeat-back of instructions as a minimum standard.
Verification of critical orders should be independent, not reliant on a single person's perception.
Standard marine vocabulary should be used, especially when parties are not communicating in their first language.
Full eye adaptation to darkness takes about half an hour, which is often not practically available.
warnings: Miscommunication risk increases when parties are speaking in a non-native language or not using standard marine vocabulary.
The maritime industry, with few exceptions, does not collect near-miss data consistently, representing a missed safety opportunity.
Insufficiently dimmed light sources (flashlights, screens) and inadequate pre-watch light management degrade night vision, which worsens with age.
outcomes: Because both the master and pilot independently noticed the helm order error, it was caught and corrected before causing harm, demonstrating good bridge/pilot teamwork.

trace.situation: CHIRP reviews near-miss reports highlighting fire risk from inadequately insulated hot engine surfaces, specifically indicator cocks and other hot spots on main engines.

procedures.why: These are known trouble spots where insulation gaps commonly occur, even on water-cooled components exceeding 220°C.

procedures.action: Conduct regular thorough inspections of all engine insulation and hot surfaces.
procedures.why: Enables rectification of deficiencies and identification of potential fuel leakage sources before ignition occurs.

procedures.action: Use infra-red thermal imaging equipment to search for hot spots and insulation defects.
procedures.why: Provides a practical, non-invasive method to detect surfaces exceeding the 220°C threshold or insulation breakdown.

constraints: All surfaces above 220°C that may be impinged by a fuel system failure must be insulated per SOLAS Reg. II-2/15.2.10.

warnings: Indicator cocks are extremely hot during engine operation and can become an ignition source if fuel impinges on them.

outcomes: Properly insulated hot surfaces prevent flammable liquid contact and minimise ignition risk.

trace.situation: A pilot conducting an inward passage discovered during the Master/Pilot Information Exchange that the vessel had multiple undeclared navigational equipment defects, including a non-functioning Rate of Turn Indicator, unstabilised head-up radar displays with no heading information, and failed analogue gyro repeaters.
trace.trigger: Pilot boards the vessel and conducts the Master/Pilot Exchange (MPX) prior to inward pilotage.

procedures.action: Master must declare all equipment defects in advance of pilot boarding, not just verbally minimize them during MPX.
procedures.why: The pilot needs complete and accurate information to assess whether safe pilotage can proceed.

procedures.action: Pilot must independently verify navigation equipment status (radar mode, gyro repeaters, rate of turn indicator) rather than relying solely on the master's assessment.
procedures.why: The master characterized the defects as minor and of no concern, but the pilot's own check revealed multiple safety-relevant failures.

procedures.action: Pilot should assess whether degraded equipment (unstabilised head-up radar with no heading, failed gyro repeaters) permits safe pilotage, or whether transit should be limited to daylight and fair weather.
procedures.why: Loss of heading reference and stabilised radar display can impair situational awareness and safe navigation during pilotage.

procedures.action: Arrange for a technician to attend upon arrival alongside only after confirming the defects do not compromise the immediate inward passage.
procedures.why: Deferring repair to after arrival is only acceptable if the defects truly do not affect safe pilotage, which must be independently confirmed, not assumed by the master.

constraints: All known defects affecting navigation equipment must be declared during the MPX.
Pilot has authority to decide if it is safe to bring the ship into port only in daylight and fair weather conditions given the defects.
The master's subjective opinion that defects are 'minor' and of 'no concern' does not override the need for full disclosure.
warnings: Undeclared navigation equipment defects (ROT indicator, radar heading stabilisation, gyro repeaters) can compromise safe pilotage.
Failure to declare defects in advance during MPX can lead to unsafe or delayed port entry decisions.
outcomes: The defects could delay the vessel's arrival if the pilot determines safe entry requires daylight and fair weather only.
Lack of advance declaration forced the pilot to discover critical equipment failures independently during MPX.
key_facts: The Rate of Turn Indicator was not functioning.
Radars were operating in unstabilised head-up display mode with no heading indication.
All analogue gyro repeaters checked were not working; the helmsman used a digital console display instead.

The master considered the defects minor and of no concern to the inward pilotage, contrary to the pilot's assessment.

trace.situation: A pilot reports two separate incidents on outbound vessels where rudder angle indicators failed or showed incorrect readings during pilotage, requiring verification of actual rudder response and additional precautions before continuing the transit.
trace.trigger: Rudder angle indicator shows no change or gives contradictory/stuck readings after a helm order is given during pilotage.

procedures.action: Order midships (or test helm command) when the rudder angle indicator shows an unexpected or unresponsive reading.
procedures.why: To check whether the indicator is faulty or the rudder itself is not responding.

procedures.action: Verify actual vessel response to helm independently of the indicator (e.g., observe vessel behaviour/heading change).
procedures.why: The indicator may be defective while the rudder itself is functioning correctly.

procedures.action: Continue the transit with additional precautions, such as tug escort, once it is confirmed the rudder is responding correctly despite the faulty indicator.
procedures.why: To maintain safe passage while mitigating risk from the loss of a key steering reference instrument.

procedures.action: Report any rudder angle indicator defects to the pilot/relevant parties during the Master-Pilot Exchange (MPX), including recurring issues from previous ports.

constraints: Rudder angle indicator malfunction must be distinguished from actual loss of steering before proceeding.
Known recurring equipment defects must be disclosed during the Master-Pilot Exchange.
warnings: A faulty rudder angle indicator can mask or mimic a genuine steering failure, risking a wrong assessment of vessel control.
Failure to disclose known recurring indicator defects during MPX withholds safety-critical information from the pilot.
outcomes: In the first incident, the vessel responded correctly to helm despite the faulty indicator, and the transit was completed safely with tug escort.

In the second incident, both bridge wing indicators were found defective at the next port, while the wheelhouse indicator worked correctly throughout the pilotage, but the master had not disclosed the known recurring defect during the MPX.

trace.situation: A tanker's auxiliary boiler suffered a flame failure during cargo discharge, repeated restart attempts caused visible smoke from the funnel that was observed and reported by the shore terminal.

procedures.action: Engineers respond immediately to the flame failure alarm and attempt boiler restart.

procedures.action: Monitor and note shore terminal warnings of smoke emissions correlated with restart attempts.
procedures.why: Smoke emissions during restart attempts indicate the automatic purging cycle is operating, but repeated failures suggest an underlying fault.

procedures.action: If restart attempts fail, remove the burner and replace with an overhauled spare unit.
procedures.why: A clogged burner was suspected as the root cause preventing successful ignition.

procedures.action: Restart the boiler after burner replacement and confirm no further emissions or operational impact.
procedures.why: To verify the fault has been resolved and normal operation restored.

procedures.action: Examine the removed burner after the incident to determine root cause.
procedures.why: To identify why the burner clogged despite recent overhaul and testing, supporting future prevention.

constraints: Boiler had passed a full class surveyor test one month prior with no issues noted.

warnings: Normal automatic purging cycle after flame failure will produce visible smoke emissions from the funnel as gases are cleared from the furnace.

outcomes: Boiler was successfully restarted after burner replacement with no further emissions or operational impact.

trace.situation: During routine chipping/maintenance of the MARPOL cargo drain line at the starboard manifold, an Ordinary Seaman discovered a hole in the line caused by a previous hidden, painted-over temporary repair.

warnings: Hidden, painted-over temporary repairs can mask serious hull/pipework defects and pose pollution risk.

trace.situation: Shortly after departure, a vessel experienced excessive funnel smoke and an opacity monitor high-smoke alarm, traced to a damaged fuel oil sensor on one of the boilers.
trace.trigger: Increased smoke emission observed from funnel coinciding with activation of the opacity monitor's high smoke alarm.

procedures.action: Bridge reports observed increased smoke emission to the engine control room.
procedures.why: Alerts engineering staff to an anomaly requiring investigation.

procedures.action: Engineers start the standby boiler (No 2) and stop the suspect boiler (No 1) to investigate.
procedures.why: Maintains steam/power supply while isolating the malfunctioning unit for safe investigation.

procedures.action: Investigate the cause of the malfunction.
procedures.why: Determine root cause of excessive smoke and alarm activation.

procedures.action: Replace the damaged fuel oil pick-up sensor with an onboard spare.
procedures.why: Restores correct fuel supply and air/fuel ratio to the boiler.

procedures.why: Verifies the repair resolved the smoke/combustion problem before resuming normal operation.

procedures.why: To identify whether recurrence can be prevented through maintenance or design change.

procedures.why: Eliminates the root-cause failure mode fleet-wide since no preventive maintenance exists for the original sensor.

trace.situation: A CHIRP Maritime FeedBack publication presents a human-factors self-assessment framework covering twelve categories (situational awareness, alerting, communication, complacency, culture, local practices, fit for duty, distractions, pressure, capability, teamwork, fatigue) intended to help seafarers critically examine their own and their crew's behaviour and safety practices.
constraints: Each category should be honestly self-assessed rather than assumed to be fine ('REALLY OK')

trace.situation: A vessel departing berth under pilotage navigated a narrow 250m-wide channel in strong wind and swell, and bridge manning was reduced when the OOW left to assist pilot disembarkation, leading to the vessel drifting toward a channel buoy.

procedures.action: Maintain full bridge manning (pilots, Master, Chief Officer, OOW, helmsman) through the pilotage transit.
procedures.why: Supports bridge resource management and redundancy in a narrow, buoyed channel.

procedures.action: Follow pilot's advised course (221°) after passing No.1 buoys to provide lee for safe disembarkation.
procedures.why: Reduces vessel motion and creates safer conditions for pilot transfer in high wind/swell.

procedures.action: Replace the OOW on the bridge if they leave to assist the pilot.
procedures.why: Prevents loss of a dedicated lookout/navigation role during a critical narrow-channel transit — not done in this case, contributing to the incident.

constraints: Channel is nominally 250m wide at seaward end with buoy pairs spaced every mile.
