trace.situation: A vessel struck a navigation buoy in a channel after the pilot disembarked early due to weather conditions without properly handing over the conn, leading to a helm order sequence that failed to clear the buoy.

procedures.action: Ensure the pilot hands over the conn only in a safe navigational position with ample time before the next manoeuvre.
procedures.why: Prevents the bridge team from being left to react to a hazardous situation with insufficient time or positional safety margin.

procedures.action: Conduct a risk assessment for pilot transfer/manoeuvres that accounts for current, wind, and time required to complete the task.

procedures.action: Cross-verify buoy and navigational mark positions with radar during the manoeuvre.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board reviewed a near-miss/incident report in which a pilot and the OOW left the bridge simultaneously during pilot disembarkation, raising bridge resource management and fatigue concerns.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board (MAB) comments on a reported incident where a crew member was required to work aloft without proper permit-to-work, safe platform, or risk assessment procedures being followed.

procedures.action: Issue a permit to work before any working-aloft task begins.
procedures.why: Any working aloft requires a permit to work as a safety control.

procedures.action: Provide a safe platform for the work, using a ladder only for access or inspection, not for two-handed tasks.
procedures.why: A ladder requires three points of contact and cannot safely support tasks needing both hands.

procedures.action: Conduct a formal task/job risk assessment involving the chief engineer, the reporter, and the ship's safety officer.
procedures.why: This would have highlighted hazards, risks, and mitigation requirements and in all probability prevented the situation from arising.

procedures.action: Maintain the ship's chain of command while ensuring senior staff exercise responsible man management and leadership.
procedures.why: Seniority carries responsibility and obligations regarding man management, especially with multi-cultural, multi-lingual, multi-national crews.

procedures.action: Send senior staff from all departments to HELM (Human Element, Leadership and Management) courses before promotion or as periodic refreshers.
procedures.why: Good HELM courses build the leadership and management skills needed to prevent such situations.

constraints: Working aloft tasks must have a permit to work
Working aloft tasks must have a safe platform, not just a ladder, for two-handed work
Risk assessments must involve chief engineer, reporter, and safety officer jointly
Chain of command must not be undermined despite leadership shortcomings
warnings: A ladder cannot safely be used for tasks requiring two hands as it only provides two points of contact when both hands are occupied, violating the three-points-of-contact rule.
Undermining the chain of command on board is not acceptable, but poor leadership/man management can create unsafe conditions.
outcomes: Lack of a formal joint risk assessment allowed an unsafe working-aloft situation to arise.

Any working aloft task requires both a permit to work and a safe platform.

trace.situation: An engine fitter was ordered to perform a high-risk engine room job (installing a steam condenser and fuel coolers 2-5m above deck plates) without a proper permit to work or safety measures such as scaffolding, refused the job, and was subsequently charged with insubordination and dismissed.
trace.trigger: Crew member assigned a job lacking a permit to work and required safety equipment (scaffolding) for work at height in the engine room.

procedures.action: Refuse to carry out a job when no permit to work or adequate safety measures (e.g. scaffolding) are in place.
procedures.why: Protects worker from performing an unsafe task without proper risk controls.

procedures.action: Report the unsafe work demand and subsequent disciplinary action to CHIRP for independent review.
procedures.why: Allows confidential, non-punitive channel to raise safety and welfare concerns.

procedures.action: CHIRP to refer employment/welfare concerns to the reporter's employment office, ITF and ISWAN.
procedures.why: These issues were outside CHIRP's remit but needed appropriate support bodies.

procedures.action: CHIRP to contact the company DPA regarding the reported poor engine room safety regime.
procedures.why: DPA holds responsibility under the safety management system to investigate and act on safety concerns.

procedures.action: Company to investigate safety issues and provide compensation/repatriation support if evidence supports the reporter's safety concerns.
procedures.why: Mitigates harm to the reporter and demonstrates company accountability while investigation proceeds.

constraints: A job involving work at height (2-5m above deck plates) must not proceed without a permit to work and adequate safety measures such as scaffolding.
Disciplinary hearings/investigations should not override legitimate safety refusals.
Employment and welfare matters must be handled through appropriate external bodies (employment office, ITF, ISWAN), not CHIRP.
warnings: Refusing unsafe work can lead to charges of insubordination, incompetence or inefficiency and summary dismissal, even when the refusal is safety-justified.

outcomes: Reporter was summarily dismissed and ordered to be repatriated at his own expense from the next port.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board comments on a reported pollution incident that prompted a flag state administration to carry out an inspection following a CHIRP report.

procedures.action: Treat a flag state inspector's finding of 'no evidence of pollution' as inconclusive rather than exculpatory.

procedures.action: Maintain a dis-identified copy of relevant reports/records for good order.

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime confidential report alleges systematic MARPOL pollution violations, bribery of surveyors, and seafarer financial exploitation aboard a ship ordered by the Master/Chief Engineer, which CHIRP forwarded to the flag state for investigation.

procedures.action: CHIRP assesses the report and offers to refer seafarer welfare/financial abuse elements to ITF and/or ISWAN.

constraints: Reporter's identity and welfare concerns limit further action unless explicit consent is given

trace.situation: A reporting vessel (A), as stand-on vessel in a crossing situation under VTS control, encountered a give-way vessel (B) reluctant to take avoiding action, prompting A to take bold independent action to prevent a close-quarters collision.
trace.trigger: TCPA approaching ten minutes with CPA less than 0.25nm in a crossing situation where the give-way vessel questioned the stand-on vessel's obligations instead of taking action.

procedures.action: Monitor CPA/TCPA continuously as the crossing situation develops.
procedures.why: To assess developing risk of collision and decide when intervention is needed.

procedures.action: Contact the give-way vessel on VHF to ascertain her intentions once TCPA/CPA thresholds are reached.
procedures.why: To clarify whether the give-way vessel intends to comply with her obligations under the Rules.

procedures.action: Decline to alter course as the stand-on vessel and insist on compliance with the Collision Regulations.
procedures.why: As stand-on vessel, altering to port was not the correct action and would violate Rule 15/17 obligations.

procedures.action: Contact VTS to request intervention when in a VTS area with a developing close-quarters situation.
procedures.why: VTS oversight was expected to assist in resolving the crossing conflict within their area of responsibility.

procedures.action: Take a bold, early reduction in speed when the give-way vessel fails to act.
procedures.why: As the stand-on vessel, independent action is required once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Request VTS radar recordings and VHF recordings after the incident for evidentiary purposes.
procedures.why: To support a formal report and provide an objective record of events, as VHF recordings were not available.

constraints: Own vessel was the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation and must not alter course to port as suggested by the give-way vessel.
Action should be taken by the stand-on vessel only when it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.
Vessels operating in a VTS area are expected to report intentions and monitor the designated VHF channel.
warnings: Give-way vessels frequently show reluctance to meet their obligations in crossing/converging-course situations, particularly in the Dover Strait and English Channel.
VTS may not always record VHF communications, limiting post-incident evidence.
outcomes: The stand-on vessel's bold speed reduction alone avoided the close-quarters situation and allowed vessel B to pass well ahead.

key_facts: Vessel A was proceeding westerly at 11kts; Vessel B was proceeding WNW at 11kts, crossing just forward of A's beam.

Both vessels had reported intentions to VTS and were monitoring VHF Channel 12.
Vessel B, the give-way vessel, suggested A (stand-on) alter to port and questioned under which Rule A was declining.
VTS suggested bridge-to-bridge communication rather than directly intervening.
The incident occurred in pilotage waters within a VTS area, with radar recordings available afterward.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board (MAB) commentary on a reported near-miss between two converging vessels in daylight where the COLREGS classification of the encounter (crossing vs overtaking) was ambiguous.
trace.trigger: A reported close-quarters/near-miss situation between two vessels converging in daylight with differing interpretations of which COLREGS rule applied.

procedures.action: Recognise that daylight converging encounters can be ambiguous as to whether Rule 13 (overtaking) or Rule 15 (crossing) applies.
procedures.why: At night, navigation light cut-off angles would clarify the situation, but in daylight this clarity is absent.

procedures.action: As vessels draw closer and risk of collision increases, apply Rule 17(a)(ii) and then Rule 17(b) regardless of earlier rule interpretation.
procedures.why: Both vessels, believing themselves stand-on under different rules, converge toward the point where action-to-avoid-collision rules override the initial classification.

procedures.action: If early collision avoidance action is required, take significant reduction in speed as action under Rule 17(c).
procedures.why: This was the avoiding action taken by Vessel A and was noted as an effective and appropriate response.

procedures.action: Trust that COLREGS will still function as a safety system even where a vessel misinterprets the applicable rule.
procedures.why: The rule structure (15/13 leading to 17(a)(ii) and 17(b)) is designed to resolve ambiguity as risk of collision increases.

constraints: Applicability of Rule 13 vs Rule 15 depends on correct classification of the encounter as overtaking or crossing.
Rule 17(a)(ii) and 17(b) become governing as vessels draw closer, irrespective of the initial classification.
Rule 17(c) permits/requires specific avoiding action (e.g., speed reduction) by the vessel acting under 17(a)(ii).
warnings: Daylight converging encounters can be misinterpreted as either crossing or overtaking situations, risking both vessels believing they are stand-on vessel.
Misinterpretation of applicable rule does not guarantee safety unless Rule 17 provisions are also correctly applied as risk of collision increases.
outcomes: Vessel A acted under Rule 17(a)(ii) and complied with Rule 17(c) by significantly reducing speed, averting a collision.
COLREGS functioned as a safety mechanism despite differing rule interpretations by the two vessels.
key_facts: The encounter was a classic converging vessel situation occurring in daylight.
At night, navigation light cut-off angles would have clarified whether the situation was crossing or overtaking.
Vessel A interpreted the situation under Rule 15 (crossing); Vessel B possibly interpreted it under Rule 13(a) (overtaking).
Both vessels, under their own interpretation, considered themselves the stand-on vessel.
As vessels closed, Rule 17(a)(ii) and ultimately Rule 17(b) would govern regardless of the initial rule interpretation.

trace.situation: During a tank inspection after cargo discharge on a tanker, an AB opened a vapour lock valve on a closed gauging tape arrangement without verifying the cap was secure, causing the cap to be ejected by inert gas pressure and releasing toxic H2S vapour on deck.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime Advisory Board comments on a near-miss incident involving H2S gas exposure during tank inspection/cargo operations, followed by an introduction to a new 'Pilots corner' section in the newsletter.

Reducing IG pressure before the end of cargo operations increases both H2S hazard and pollution risk.

trace.trigger: Shore loader operator confirmed readiness to resume loading with the chief officer and began the loading circuit while a crew member had not yet been confirmed clear of the cargo hold.

procedures.action: Suspend the loading circuit immediately upon observing a crew member in the hold.
procedures.why: To prevent cargo or equipment from being discharged onto or injuring the person still inside.

procedures.action: Order the crew member to exit the hold via the deck officer on watch.
procedures.why: To clear personnel from the hazard area before operations resume.

procedures.action: Resume and complete loading only after the hold is confirmed clear.
procedures.why: Ensures safe continuation of cargo operations once hazard is removed.

procedures.action: Report the Near Miss to the authorities and the company.
procedures.why: Mandatory reporting requirement for near-miss incidents to enable investigation and learning.

procedures.action: Conduct an investigation reviewing the ship/shore safety checklist, entry permit, risk assessment, and communication procedures.
procedures.why: To identify root causes and communication/coordination gaps between ship and shore during hold entry and loading resumption.

constraints: Ship loader must be informed before access is made to any cargo compartment.
Covers of the compartment being entered must be kept partially closed during the period of access.
An entry permit must be issued before personnel enter the cargo hold.
A Risk Assessment must be carried out and communicated to all involved personnel before the operation.
Hold entry must be supervised (in this case by the bosun).
Deck officer on watch must maintain contact with both the chief officer and the terminal during cargo operations.
Main ship/shore communication method was via handheld radios on an agreed channel.
warnings: Resuming cargo loading operations without positively confirming all personnel have exited the hold risks serious injury or fatality.
Reliance on verbal/radio confirmation of hold readiness without physical verification can lead to near misses.
outcomes: No injury occurred; loading was suspended in time and completed uneventfully.
Near miss was reported to authorities and the company as required.
Investigation was triggered to review ship/shore checklist compliance and communication procedures.
key_facts: No6 hold was in ballast condition on arrival and required de-ballasting and mopping before loading.
An entry permit was issued at 05:00hrs for two ABs to carry out hold wiping, supervised by the bosun.
Work in the hold was completed at 06:30hrs and both ABs were ordered to exit.
The shore loader was relocated to No6 hold and readiness to load was confirmed with the chief officer at 06:36, shortly before a crew member was observed still in the hold.
The ship/shore safety checklist specified that the loader be informed before cargo compartment access and that hatch covers remain partially closed during such access.

question_seeds.text: Why was loading readiness confirmed with the chief officer before physically verifying the hold was clear of personnel?
How should the deck officer on watch coordinate exit confirmation from a hold with the shore loader operator before resuming cargo operations?
What checklist and permit controls were in place, and why did they not prevent the near miss?
Who is responsible for giving final clearance to the shore terminal that a cargo hold is empty of personnel before loading resumes?

trace.situation: A reporter describes finding a pilot ladder contaminated with palm kernel expeller (PKE) cargo residue, and an AB being instructed to clean it, resulting in the AB climbing over the side onto the ladder without safety equipment while the vessel was underway.
trace.trigger: The pilot ladder needed to be rigged for pilot disembarkation but was found covered in dry PKE cargo residue from the port stay.

procedures.action: Stow pilot ladders away from cargo contamination and UV exposure when not in use
procedures.why: Recommendations exist for ladders to be stowed away from contamination and protected from UV damage, which was disregarded

procedures.action: Brush dry cargo residue off the ladder while it is still on deck, before rigging
procedures.why: PKE residue becomes slippery when wet, creating a fall hazard once the ladder is lowered and exposed to water/spray

procedures.action: Ensure any crew member working on or near a rigged ladder over the side wears a lifeline, lifejacket and hard hat
procedures.why: The AB climbed to the bottom rung with no lifeline, lifejacket or hard hat while the vessel was underway, risking a fall overboard

constraints: Ladder must be cleaned of contamination before rigging, not after
Any person working over the side on a rigged ladder must use appropriate PPE (lifeline, lifejacket, hard hat)
Ladder maintenance/stowage must prevent exposure to cargo contamination and UV damage
warnings: PKE cargo residue becomes slippery when wet, increasing fall risk on the ladder
Climbing over the side on a pilot ladder without lifeline, lifejacket or hard hat while the vessel is underway is extremely hazardous
Leaving ladders exposed to contamination and UV damage disregards safety recommendations
outcomes: An AB was placed in a dangerous position, climbing down an unclean, slippery ladder over the side with no protective equipment while the ship was underway
The task of cleaning, intended to be done safely on deck, instead created a serious fall-overboard risk
key_facts: The pilot ladder was left on deck throughout the port stay during PKE cargo discharge, becoming covered in cargo residue.
Recommendations call for ladders to be stowed away from contamination and protected from UV damage.
An AB was given a hand brush to clean the ladder but instead cleaned it after it was rigged over the side.
The AB climbed to the bottom rung without a lifeline, lifejacket, or hard hat while the vessel was underway, holding on with one hand while brushing with the other.

question_seeds.text: Why is cleaning a pilot ladder after it has been rigged over the side more dangerous than cleaning it on deck?
What PPE should be mandatory for any crew member required to work on a rigged pilot ladder?
How should pilot ladders be stowed and maintained during cargo operations to prevent this kind of contamination?
Who should have intervened to stop the AB from climbing over the side without safety equipment?

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime reports on a Maritime New Zealand pilot ladder focus campaign that found widespread non-compliance in pilot boarding arrangements (PBAs), prompting NZMPA to push for regulator-endorsed guidance notes on accommodation ladders used with pilot ladders.
trace.trigger: Discovery during Maritime New Zealand's pilot ladder inspection campaign that a high percentage of pilot boarding arrangements were uninspected, non-compliant, unrecorded, or improperly rigged.

procedures.action: Ensure pilot boarding arrangements are properly inspected by crew before use.
procedures.why: 8% of inspected arrangements were found not properly inspected, risking undetected hazards.

procedures.action: Ensure ladder construction complies with regulatory standards.
procedures.why: 9% of arrangements were of non-compliant construction.

procedures.action: Maintain mandatory records for pilot boarding arrangements.
procedures.why: 30% of arrangements lacked mandatory records required by regulation.

procedures.action: Properly rig pilot ladders and ensure they are safe for use, especially combination/trapdoor arrangements.
procedures.why: 40% of arrangements were improperly rigged or unsafe, and trapdoor arrangements have been specifically challenged for non-compliance since 2018.

procedures.action: Secure ladders directly to the ship's structure, not to the accommodation ladder, for combination/trapdoor arrangements.
procedures.why: Local NZ regulatory framework (Maritime Rule Part 53) requires direct securing to ship's structure, not to the accommodation ladder.

procedures.action: Present compliant modified boarding arrangements to NZ ports to retain pilotage services.
procedures.why: A ship was refused pilotage services for repeatedly presenting a non-compliant and unsafe boarding arrangement.

constraints: Must comply with NZ Maritime Rule Part 53 governing pilot ladder regulations.
Ladders must be secured directly to the ship's structure, not to the accommodation ladder.
Guidance notes apply primarily to combination and trapdoor pilot boarding arrangements.
warnings: 40% of pilot boarding arrangements surveyed were improperly rigged or unsafe for use.
Trapdoor arrangements secured to the accommodation ladder rather than ship's structure are non-compliant and unsafe.
Repeated presentation of non-compliant boarding arrangements can result in refusal of pilotage services.
outcomes: NZMPA is developing regulator-endorsed guidance notes on accommodation ladders used with pilot ladders.
Previously non-compliant ships are now presenting modified, compliant boarding arrangements in NZ.
A ship was refused pilotage services by NZ ports in December for repeated non-compliance.
key_facts: Maritime New Zealand's pilot ladder focus campaign results were presented in November last year.
8% of pilot boarding arrangements were not properly inspected by crew, 9% were non-compliant construction, 30% lacked mandatory records, and 40% were improperly rigged or unsafe.
NZMPA has formally challenged trapdoor arrangements since early 2018 based on the rule that ladders must be secured to the ship's structure, not the accommodation ladder.
The first ship was refused pilotage services by NZ ports last December for repeatedly presenting a non-compliant arrangement.

question_seeds.text: What specific deficiencies were found in the Maritime New Zealand pilot ladder campaign?
Why are trapdoor arrangements secured to the accommodation ladder considered non-compliant under NZ rules?
How should my crew ensure our combination pilot ladder/accommodation ladder arrangement meets Maritime Rule Part 53?
Who is responsible for inspecting and recording pilot boarding arrangements before a pilot transfer in NZ waters?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a crewman using a hand brush instead of proper equipment to rig a pilot ladder, watched without objection by a two/three-man team, prompting a CHIRP commentary on safety culture failure, followed by an NZMPA pilot's corner article on pilot boarding safety initiatives.
trace.trigger: A reported incident where unsafe/reckless pilot ladder deployment practice was observed and not challenged by any crew member present.

procedures.action: Engage proactively with maritime regulators on policy, regulation and education regarding pilot boarding safety.
procedures.why: To address non-compliance by design and non-compliance by ignorance at a systemic level.

procedures.action: Operate an online event reporting system for pilot transfer issues.
procedures.why: To identify trends such as pilot ladder issues being the most common report type and container vessels the most common vessel type reported.

procedures.action: Publish a Safe Pilot Transfer Good Practice Guide.
procedures.why: To give masters and crew clear standards for safe pilot boarding arrangements.

procedures.action: Produce educational materials such as the Pilot Ladder Tips calendar and trapdoor PBA advisory notice.
procedures.why: To educate crews and clarify rule requirements, aiding masters and pilots in demonstrating compliance vs non-compliance.

constraints: Crew must not improvise unsafe equipment or methods (e.g. a hand brush) when rigging pilot transfer arrangements.
Crew witnessing unsafe acts have a collective responsibility to intervene rather than watch without comment.
warnings: Reckless or dangerous pilot ladder deployment practices indicate a breakdown of the safety management system and safety culture.
Lack of individual and collective responsibility for safety can allow dangerous practices to continue unchallenged.
outcomes: NZMPA initiatives on pilot boarding safety are starting to show positive results.
Pilot ladder related issues remain the most commonly reported event type, with container vessels most frequently involved.
key_facts: The crewman was issued a hand brush by his supervisor to use in deploying the pilot ladder.
A two or three man team deployed the ladder and watched the dangerous action without comment.
NZMPA has identified two concern areas: non-compliance by design (e.g. trapdoor arrangements) and non-compliance by ignorance (crew disregard for safety/regulations).

chapter_title: Defects, errors and anomalies with equipment

trace.situation: A pilot reported a pilotage operation undermined by severe language-barrier communication failures, an incomplete pilot card, and an undisclosed bow thruster failure, following a separate recent windlass brake malfunction.
trace.trigger: Pilot boards vessel for a routine pilotage/berthing operation and discovers bridge team cannot communicate effectively in English.

procedures.action: Verify bridge team's English proficiency and establish a reliable communication method before commencing pilotage.
procedures.why: Almost complete lack of spoken English made standard communication with the bridge team impossible.

procedures.action: Ensure the pilot card contains complete information including propeller rotation direction, astern power, and maximum consecutive engine starts.
procedures.why: These critical details were missing from the pilot card and could not be obtained due to language problems.

procedures.action: Immediately inform the pilot of any equipment failure affecting maneuvering, such as a bow thruster malfunction.
procedures.why: The master did not disclose the bow thruster failure until pressed, denying the pilot critical information during berthing.

procedures.action: Report and rectify equipment defects (e.g., windlass brake, auxiliary engine) promptly rather than allowing them to persist into subsequent operations.
procedures.why: The windlass brake had failed two days earlier and the bow thruster problem was linked to an auxiliary engine, indicating unresolved equipment issues affecting safety.

constraints: Pilot card information must be complete and accurate before pilotage begins.
Master must disclose all equipment malfunctions affecting ship handling to the pilot without delay.
Effective communication between pilot and bridge team must be established, using translation aids if necessary.
warnings: Lack of effective communication and BRM during pilotage can compromise safe vessel handling.
Non-disclosure of equipment failures (e.g., bow thruster) to the pilot endangers berthing safety.
outcomes: Complete lack of effective BRM and communication during the pilotage operation.
Bow thruster was unusable for the entire berthing operation due to an undisclosed auxiliary engine problem.
Pilot was forced to rely on an online translation app to obtain critical operational information.
key_facts: Bridge crew had almost no spoken English, requiring use of a translation app for communication.
The pilot card omitted propeller rotation direction, astern power, and maximum consecutive engine starts.
The bow thruster failed during the entire berthing operation, reportedly due to an auxiliary engine fault, and the master did not report this until pressed.
The starboard windlass brake had failed two days earlier at the inner anchorage.

question_seeds.text: Why wasn't the bow thruster failure communicated to the pilot immediately?
How should a master handle pilotage when the bridge team has a severe language barrier with the pilot?
What minimum information must appear on a pilot card before pilotage begins?
When should equipment defects like a failed windlass brake trigger a review of other related machinery before the next port call?

chapter_title: Defects, errors and anomalies with equipment

trace.situation: A CHIRP report comments on a pilotage incident where language barriers, reliance on an online translation app, and an undeclared bow thruster defect compromised safety communications between the pilot and bridge team.
trace.trigger: Bridge team and pilot lacked a common working language and used an online translation app instead of proper English communication, while the bow thruster was unavailable and not declared on the pilot card.

procedures.action: Use English as the working language for bridge-to-bridge, bridge-to-shore, and pilot-bridge communications per SOLAS V/14, or IMO SMCP if needed.
procedures.why: SOLAS V-Reg 14 mandates English unless all parties share another common language, ensuring safety-critical communication is understood.

procedures.action: Ensure pilot card information (including equipment status such as bow thruster availability) is complete, accurate, and communicated to the pilot.
procedures.why: Pilot card accuracy is a flag state and class requirement; missing or undeclared defects leave the pilot unaware of vessel limitations.

procedures.action: If safety-critical communication is not possible, the pilot may abort and direct the vessel back to anchor.
procedures.why: Without reliable communication, the pilot cannot safely conduct pilotage, so suspending the operation protects the vessel and port.

procedures.action: Vessel managers must ensure crew have acceptable standards of English for international voyages.
procedures.why: This is both a safety-critical and SOLAS compliance obligation.

constraints: English must be used on the bridge for safety communications unless all parties share another common language (SOLAS V/14).
Pilot card information must be complete and available, including equipment status like bow thruster availability.
Pilots have authority to abort pilotage and return the vessel to anchor if safety communications fail.
warnings: Online translation apps may distract the pilot and fail to accurately translate marine technical terms, especially between languages with different alphabets.
Failure to properly declare equipment defects (e.g., bow thruster) to the pilot is a safety and compliance failure.
Missing pilot card information is a flag state non-compliance issue.
outcomes: Communication breakdown left the pilot unaware of the vessel's bow thruster defect, undermining safe pilotage.
Vessel managers did not respond to CHIRP's inquiry, leaving the bow thruster issue unresolved.
The incident highlighted multiple human element factors (training, communications, local practices, culture) from the Deadly Dozen framework.
key_facts: SOLAS V/14 requires English as the bridge working language unless all parties share a common alternative language.
The pilot used an online translation app, risking distraction and translation inaccuracy for technical terms.
The bow thruster's non-availability was never properly explained or declared to the pilot, possibly linked to an auxiliary generator issue.
Pilot card information, a flag state/class requirement, was missing and never relayed to the pilot due to communication failure.
Pilots have the authority to abort pilotage and anchor the vessel if safety-critical communication is not possible.

question_seeds.text: Why is reliance on an online translation app considered unsafe for pilot-bridge communications?
What should the Master do if the pilot cannot effectively communicate with the bridge team?
Who is responsible for ensuring the pilot card accurately reflects equipment status like bow thruster availability?
When can a pilot legitimately abort pilotage and return the vessel to anchor?

trace.situation: A newly joined Master tested the bridge team's understanding of an echo sounder system with selectable forward/aft transducers during a familiarisation meeting, revealing that officers did not consider which transducer was in use when assessing under-keel clearance.
trace.trigger: A new Master conducting a familiarisation meeting with the bridge team after taking command, using a hypothetical departure scenario with differing forward/aft drafts.

procedures.action: Conduct proper familiarisation of all bridge team members before they assume watchkeeping responsibility.
procedures.why: Ensures watch officers understand ship-specific equipment and avoid dangerous misunderstandings.

procedures.action: Instruct all officers to check which transducer (forward or aft) is in use when reading the echo sounder.
procedures.why: The ship had two transducers feeding a single display; reading depends on which one is selected, and officers failed to recognize this during the test scenario.

procedures.action: Reinforce the company's requirement for under-keel clearance with the bridge team.
procedures.why: The incident revealed officers would have assessed an unsafe situation as safe, risking grounding or contact.

procedures.action: Update the watch officer's handover information template to include transducer selection details.
procedures.why: To institutionalise the lesson and prevent recurrence for future watch officers.

constraints: Familiarisation must occur before an officer takes watchkeeping responsibility.
Officers must verify which transducer (forward/aft) is selected before interpreting echo sounder depth readings.
warnings: Misinterpreting echo sounder readings without knowing which transducer is selected can lead to a false assessment of safe under-keel clearance.
All watch officers in the scenario incorrectly judged the situation as safe without considering transducer selection.
outcomes: The Master identified a critical gap in bridge team knowledge through a hypothetical scenario before any real danger occurred.
Corrective action (instruction, reinforcement of UKC policy, and handover template update) was implemented to prevent future misjudgement.
key_facts: The ship had two echo sounder transducers (forward and aft) sharing a single display, selectable by the operator.
Forward draft was 5 metres and aft draft was 8 metres in the test scenario, with an under-keel reading of 3 metres.
All watch officers tested stated the situation was safe without considering which transducer was active.
The lesson led to updated handover documentation and reinforced company under-keel clearance requirements.

question_seeds.text: Why is it critical to know which transducer (forward or aft) is selected before relying on an echo sounder reading?
How should I structure a familiarisation meeting to test whether my bridge team truly understands ship-specific equipment risks?
What should be included in the watch handover template to prevent transducer-related misjudgements of under-keel clearance?
Who is responsible for ensuring new watch officers are properly familiarised with dual-transducer echo sounder systems before standing watch?

trace.situation: CHIRP received a report about a vessel operating with a known AIS defect for at least three months without repair, and when CHIRP tried to raise this with the ship's ISM managers/DPA, the managers declined to engage, prompting escalation to the flag state and discussion of broader AIS/GMDSS equipment obligations.
trace.trigger: A known critical equipment defect (AIS) persists unresolved despite management being advised, and the company (DPA/ISM managers) refuses to engage with the safety reporting body (CHIRP).

procedures.action: Report equipment defect issues to company management as soon as identified.
procedures.why: There is a limit to what a ship at sea can achieve; advising management is the obvious first step.

procedures.action: If management fails to resolve a known critical equipment defect, escalate the matter (e.g., via MAB/CHIRP) to the vessel's flag state.
procedures.why: When ISM managers decline to engage, flag state involvement provides an alternative route to ensure accountability and corrective action.

procedures.action: Report reportable AIS/VTS issues to Port State Control and appropriate VTS stations.
procedures.why: Allows vessels to be entered onto monitoring databases and ship inspections to be arranged.

procedures.action: Ensure AIS equipment is kept working and transmitting correct data at all times.
procedures.why: AIS is covered by SOLAS and has become a de facto part of GMDSS equipment since the 2010 adoption of AIS SART; incorrect data has been a causal factor in fatal incidents (USCG bulletin 04-20).

constraints: Once management has been advised of a known defect in critical equipment, the onus shifts to management to ensure resolution.
AIS equipment must be operational and transmitting correct data under both SOLAS and de facto GMDSS requirements.
warnings: Failure by management to resolve a known defect in critical equipment could, in the event of an accident, render the vessel unseaworthy and potentially negate the vessel's insurance.
Sailing with a known AIS defect for three months without calling a service technician is completely unacceptable.
Incorrect AIS data has been identified as a causal factor in fatalities in a real incident.
outcomes: ISM managers declined to engage with CHIRP regarding the report.
The flag state positively engaged with CHIRP and received details of the report after MAB recommendation.
Human factors identified included culture, awareness of risk, and communications both on board and ashore.
key_facts: The ISM managers declined to engage with CHIRP on this report; the flag state was contacted instead and responded positively.
AIS is covered by SOLAS and, while not formally a GMDSS requirement, has become a de facto part of GMDSS equipment since the 2010 introduction of AIS SART.
The vessel in question sailed with a known AIS defect for at least three months despite being advised to call a service technician.
USCG Safety Bulletin 04-20 highlighted incorrect AIS data as a causal factor in fatalities in a separate incident.
Issues like unresolved equipment defects are reportable to Port State Control and VTS stations for database monitoring and inspection scheduling.

Why could failing to fix a known AIS defect render my vessel unseaworthy and void insurance?

How should I document that I advised management of a known critical equipment defect to protect myself and the vessel's seaworthiness status?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes a vessel with persistent ECDIS positional errors and incorrect AIS vessel dimension data that fed erroneous information into the pilot's portable piloting unit (PPU) during two consecutive port visits.
trace.trigger: Pilot observed the ECDIS showing the vessel's position halfway over the wharf while alongside, and the AIS transmitting incorrect vessel dimensions through the pilot plug into the PPU.

procedures.action: Request the captain to check and correct the ECDIS antenna offset and AIS dimension errors upon discovery.
procedures.why: Errors feed directly into the pilot's PPU via the pilot plug, corrupting the navigational picture used for pilotage.

procedures.action: Follow up on previously raised issues at subsequent port calls to confirm corrective action was taken.
procedures.why: The same errors had been noted three months earlier and the captain had assured the reporter they would be addressed.

procedures.action: Request port state control to attend the vessel when the master cannot resolve the fault.
procedures.why: The master reported attempts to correct the offset failed, with settings reverting to zero, indicating a possible equipment fault requiring external intervention.

procedures.action: Submit a separate report to port state authorities requesting corrective action.
procedures.why: The AIS dimension data was believed to not be programmable by the vessel's crew and may require a service technician to resolve, and the issue remained unresolved after repeated requests.

constraints: AIS vessel dimension data reportedly requires a service technician to correct, not crew-level adjustment.
Antenna/GPS offset settings must be properly distinguished and applied, not left defaulting to zero.
Corrective action depends on functioning internal battery to retain configured settings.
warnings: Incorrect data coming through electronic navigation aids (ECDIS/AIS) is a potentially high safety risk.
Unresolved equipment errors persisting across multiple visits indicate a systemic failure to address a known safety issue.
outcomes: Port state control was requested to attend the vessel due to the unresolved and recurring nature of the fault.
The known issue remained unresolved to date despite being raised on two separate occasions three months apart.
Errors in ECDIS and AIS were transmitted into the pilot's PPU, degrading the accuracy of navigational information available during pilotage.
key_facts: The vessel's ECDIS displayed the ship's position halfway over the wharf while alongside.
The AIS had significantly incorrect vessel dimensions programmed into it.
AIS data is linked to and feeds the pilot's PPU through the 'pilot plug', propagating errors into the pilot's system.
The same errors were observed on the vessel's previous visit three months earlier, and the captain had assured the reporter they would be fixed.
The master attempted to correct antenna offset settings but they kept reverting to zero, possibly due to misconfiguration or a dead internal battery.

What steps should the master take if antenna offset settings keep reverting to zero instead of holding the corrected value?
Who is responsible for correcting AIS vessel dimension data if it is not programmable by the ship's own crew?
At what point should a captain escalate an unresolved navigation equipment fault to port state control?

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on an incident where bridge watch officers misunderstood echo sounder readings (fore/aft transducers, depth-below-transducer vs total water depth) while operating in shallow water.
trace.trigger: An incident occurred because bridge watchkeepers assumed how the echo sounder was configured instead of verifying it, in the context of reduced/altered bridge manning or procedures noted elsewhere as a COVID-19 consequence.

procedures.action: Ensure bridge watch officers are familiar with all bridge equipment fitted to the vessel, including echo sounder configuration.
procedures.why: Many echo sounders have single or dual transducers and may not clearly indicate which is in use, so unfamiliarity can cause dangerous assumptions.

procedures.action: Verify which transducer (fore/aft) is active and whether the display shows depth below transducer or total water depth.
procedures.why: Display settings vary and misreading depth reference can lead to groundings or shoal water incidents.

procedures.action: Train regularly with bridge equipment to build familiarity.
procedures.why: Greater familiarity and training reduces reliance on dangerous assumptions and improves ship safety.

procedures.action: Minimise sailing draft and trim where possible when operating in areas of shallow water, while still meeting minimum aft draft for propeller immersion.
procedures.why: Good seamanship practice reduces grounding risk in shoal waters; additional ballast can be added later once clear of shallow water.

constraints: Vessels may require a minimum aft draft to ensure propeller immersion.
Echo sounder transducer selection and depth reference display must be understood before relying on readings in shallow water.
warnings: Assumptions about equipment configuration can be dangerous and lead to an incident.
Not all echo sounders with two transducers readily indicate which transducer is in use.
outcomes: Assumption about echo sounder transducer/display settings contributed to an incident.
Improved familiarity and training with bridge equipment increases safety of vessel and crew.
Minimising draft/trim in shallow water with later ballasting reduces shoal water risk.
key_facts: Echo sounders can have single (usually forward) or dual (fore and aft) transducers.
Displays may show depth below transducer or total water depth depending on settings.
Minimum aft draft is required for propeller immersion, but trim/draft should be minimised in shallow water where possible.
Additional ballast can be added once the vessel clears shoal waters.

question_seeds.text: Why is it dangerous to assume which echo sounder transducer is currently in use?
How should the bridge team verify whether the echo sounder is showing depth below transducer or total water depth?
What seamanship practice should be followed regarding draft and trim when transiting shallow water?
When can additional ballast be added after minimising draft for shallow water transit?

trace.situation: A marine pilot wearing a protective facemask during routine pilotage found that the mask muffled his voice, causing the master to repeatedly respond 'yes' inappropriately, raising doubts about whether communications were truly understood.
trace.trigger: Pilot's voice stifled by facemask during verbal exchanges with master, leading to apparent miscommunication during pilotage.

procedures.action: Use closed-loop reporting for all communications between pilot and master.
procedures.why: To ensure that instructions and responses are properly understood and confirmed, especially when voice clarity is degraded by a mask.

procedures.action: Phrase queries in an open manner rather than leading or suggestive form.
procedures.why: Leading or suggestive questions can prompt automatic 'yes' answers that do not reflect true understanding.

procedures.action: Confirm important communications multiple times when in doubt.
procedures.why: To verify the master actually understood the message correctly given the muffled speech.

constraints: Facemask use was required during the pandemic period ('these extraordinary times').
Master's English comprehension was otherwise excellent, so the issue was acoustic, not linguistic.
warnings: Facemasks can stifle voice clarity and lead to misunderstood verbal communications.
Reliance on a simple 'yes' response can mask a lack of true understanding.
outcomes: Pilot had to repeatedly confirm communications to ensure correct understanding, highlighting a risk of miscommunication going unnoticed if not actively checked.
key_facts: The pilot wore a facemask during a routine pilotage, which muffled his voice.
The master's English comprehension was excellent, but understanding the pilot's muffled speech was questionable.
The master frequently answered 'yes' even when it seemed inappropriate, suggesting miscommunication.
The pilot needed to verify several important communications to confirm correct understanding.

Why is it risky to rely on affirmative responses like 'yes' during masked verbal communication on the bridge?

When should a pilot or master insist on repeated confirmation of instructions during masked communication?

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary on a reported incident where mask-wearing during COVID-19 impaired verbal and non-verbal communication (including lip reading and body language) among ship's personnel and pilots during operations.
trace.trigger: Use of masks or face coverings during critical operations such as pilotage/manoeuvring, raising risk of degraded safety-critical communication.

procedures.action: Follow latest WHO and national recommendations on mask/face covering use.
procedures.why: Advice changes rapidly and varies by location; mariners must stay current.

procedures.action: Apply the strictest applicable precautions when guidance varies.
procedures.why: Ensures maximum protection where multiple jurisdictions or standards conflict.

procedures.action: Conduct a ship-specific COVID-19 threat and risk assessment for anyone boarding the vessel.
procedures.why: Accounts for vessel-specific exposure risks and personnel movements.

procedures.action: Comply with any port-specific COVID-19 procedures required for the vessel.
procedures.why: Ports may impose additional mandatory requirements beyond general guidance.

procedures.action: If removing a mask during critical manoeuvring to aid communication, increase social distancing to compensate.
procedures.why: Balances the need for clear safety-critical communication against contagion risk.

trace.situation: A vessel suffered a main engine fuel leak and then a hydraulic pipe leak within minutes of departing berth on an outbound passage through a narrow channel, requiring the vessel to stop twice and rely on tug assistance to hold station.
trace.trigger: Main engine fuel leak detected approximately ten minutes after departing the berth while mid-stream in a channel with limited manoeuvring room.

procedures.action: Stop the vessel immediately upon detecting the fuel leak.
procedures.why: To prevent further engine damage or fire/pollution risk and allow repair in a confined channel.

procedures.action: Use available tugs to hold station in the narrow channel.
procedures.why: The channel does not have much room for manoeuvring, so external assistance was needed to maintain position while stopped.

procedures.action: Repair the fuel leak before attempting to get underway again.
procedures.why: The fault must be cleared before safely resuming transit.

procedures.action: Stop again when a hydraulic pipe leak on the main engine was discovered four minutes after getting underway.
procedures.why: A second mechanical fault required another halt and repair before continuing.

procedures.action: Obtain Chief Engineer clearance before resuming transit, and proceed at reduced speed (max half ahead).
procedures.why: To ensure the engine was fit enough for restricted-speed transit after repairs, given uncertainty over full reliability.

procedures.action: Proceed to anchor after clearing the channel buoys to effect full repairs.
procedures.why: Full repairs could not be completed mid-channel and needed to be done safely at anchor outside the restricted waterway.

constraints: The channel has limited room for manoeuvring, increasing risk when stopped.
Tug assistance was required to hold station during both stoppages.
Vessel was limited to half ahead speed after temporary clearance by the Chief Engineer.
warnings: Repeated mechanical failures occurring shortly after departure in a confined channel pose significant navigational risk.
A vessel should not be considered fully cleared for transit until underlying faults are properly resolved, not just temporarily patched.
outcomes: The vessel was able to hold station safely with tug assistance during both stoppages, avoiding grounding or collision in the narrow channel.
The vessel eventually cleared the channel and anchored to complete full repairs rather than attempting to continue to destination with unresolved issues.

The vessel was stopped for about ten minutes to address the fuel leak, aided by two tugs holding station.

The vessel anchored after clearing the channel buoys to carry out full repairs.

trace.situation: CHIRP correspondence addressing two separate safety topics: discrepancies between the IMPA pilot ladder poster and actual SOLAS/IMO pilot boarding regulations, and a query about the minimum vessel speed required before a main engine can be put astern.
trace.trigger: A seafarer's letter questioning why an engine failed to start astern at 3.5 knots but worked at 3 knots, referencing a prior MFB56 article on a master-pilot exchange incident; also attention drawn to inconsistencies in the IMPA pilot ladder poster versus SOLAS text.

procedures.action: Always refer to SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 23 and IMO Resolution A.1045(27) as the definitive requirement for pilot ladders and boarding arrangements, treating the IMPA poster only as an illustrative starting point.
procedures.why: The poster contains discrepancies with the written regulations and is not authoritative.

procedures.action: Reduce vessel speed to the minimum threshold (approximately 3 knots or less, vessel-dependent) before attempting to engage the main engine astern on non-controllable-pitch-propeller vessels.
procedures.why: With way on, the engine may be mechanically unable to go astern until the ship's speed falls below a critical threshold.

procedures.action: Post the crash astern manoeuvre procedure in the wheelhouse and ensure all bridge officers are familiar with it.
procedures.why: A crash astern is a normal emergency response and officers must know the procedure and expected engine/ship behaviour in advance.

constraints: Applies to vessels without a controllable pitch propeller.
IMPA poster is illustrative only, not a regulatory substitute.
Crash astern procedure must be posted in the wheelhouse and known by bridge officers before an emergency occurs.
warnings: The IMPA pilot boarding poster may not accurately reflect current SOLAS/IMO regulatory requirements.
Attempting to go astern above the vessel's minimum threshold speed may result in the engine failing to respond, creating risk during critical manoeuvres (e.g. pilot approach).
outcomes: Engine failed to start astern at 3.5 knots but engaged successfully once speed was reduced to 3 knots.
A fully loaded 14,000-tonne vessel from 14 knots 'sea speed' remains moving ahead at ~2-3 knots roughly 15 minutes after the 'Stop' order.
Engine rpm falls from 110 to 40 in 7-8 minutes and comes to rest after about 12 minutes.
In a crash stop, the engine can usually be reversed after ~3 minutes (while still running ahead at ~30 rpm) and reach 60% astern power in ~5 minutes.
key_facts: SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 23 and IMO Res A.1045(27) are the definitive sources for pilot ladder/boarding requirements, not the IMPA poster.
Non-CPP vessels often cannot engage astern propulsion until ship speed drops to a minimum threshold (observed as ~3 knots in this case).
A fully loaded 14,000-tonne vessel takes about 15 minutes to lose way from 14 knots after a 'Stop' order.
Crash astern engagement is typically possible after ~3 minutes, reaching 60% astern power by ~5 minutes.
Slower or ballasted vessels achieve stopping/reversing manoeuvres more quickly than fully loaded ones.

question_seeds.text: Why did the main engine fail to engage astern at 3.5 knots but succeed at 3 knots?
What is the minimum speed threshold on my vessel before the engine can be put astern, and is it owner/IMO specified or vessel-specific?
How should the crash astern procedure be documented and communicated to bridge officers?
Which regulation should I rely on for pilot ladder specifications if the IMPA poster conflicts with SOLAS?

trace.situation: A CHIRP reporter follow-up letter discusses two separate safety concerns raised in earlier Maritime Feedback issues: the engine stress risks of crash astern manoeuvres and the lack of drug-testing practices on fishing vessels/superyachts despite STCW requirements.

procedures.action: Master and pilot must determine the maximum ahead speed through the water at which an astern movement can still be obtained.
procedures.why: This capability varies from ship to ship and is essential for safe manoeuvring, especially during crash astern situations.

procedures.action: Make any known engine braking-air limitations (e.g. inability to apply braking air for extended periods at certain speeds/draughts) a prominent opening part of every Master/Pilot information exchange.
procedures.why: The limitation was discovered post-delivery and not obvious from vessel design; failure to disclose it risks dangerous manoeuvring decisions.

procedures.action: Arrange for a braking tug with large bollard pull to be attached as soon as possible when operating a vessel with limited astern braking capability.
procedures.why: Compensates for the vessel's inability to apply braking air for a substantial period, as adopted by the company as standard practice.

procedures.action: Implement screening programmes for crew whose duties involve designated safety, pollution prevention, and security roles, per STCW 2010 Manila amendments.
procedures.why: To identify and prevent drug and alcohol abuse from impairing crew ability to perform safety-critical duties.

constraints: Crash astern manoeuvres cause very high stress levels within the engine and may cause damage.
Astern capability varies from ship to ship and must be individually known by master/pilot.
Some optimised modern engines cannot apply braking air for a substantial period (up to 17 minutes at loaded draught) from slow ahead.
Flag states have adopted zero-tolerance drug policies but lack enforcement mechanisms, relying on management companies.
warnings: A crash astern manoeuvre causes very high stress levels within the engine and may cause damage.
Some vessel engine designs cannot provide braking air for extended periods, creating a manoeuvring hazard if undisclosed.
Many companies are not aware of or are ignoring the STCW 2010 drug/alcohol screening directive.
outcomes: Company practice of disclosing braking limitations in Master/Pilot exchange and using a braking tug became standard, improving manoeuvring safety.
Without proper disclosure of engine braking quirks, masters/pilots risk making unsafe assumptions about astern capability.
Lack of enforcement and awareness of STCW drug screening requirements leaves gaps in crew impairment prevention.
key_facts: Crash astern manoeuvres cause very high engine stress and potential damage.
Maximum ahead speed for obtaining an astern movement varies ship to ship and must be known by master/pilot.
One vessel class could not apply braking air for a full 17 minutes at loaded draught from slow ahead, a design feature discovered post-delivery.
STCW 2010 Manila amendments require screening programmes for crew with designated safety, pollution prevention, and security duties.
Drug testing methods (saliva, urine, hair follicle) have different detection windows: saliva 2-3 days, urine up to 30 days, hair follicle dependent on hair length.

question_seeds.text: Why is it critical for a master to know the maximum ahead speed at which an astern movement can be obtained?
What should be included in the Master/Pilot information exchange regarding engine braking limitations?

Which STCW requirement obligates companies to implement drug and alcohol screening for safety-critical crew?

chapter_title: This reporter sent details of an incident that

trace.situation: A CHIRP comment reflecting on an incident where a vessel's master became distracted while in control, prompting broader discussion of bridge distractions and watchkeeping practices.
trace.trigger: An incident occurred in which the master, who had the conn, became distracted, leading to an adverse consequence.

procedures.action: Designate high-density or obstruction-prone sea areas as 'Red Waters' requiring heightened attention.

procedures.action: Post an additional dedicated lookout or double-up watchkeepers in Red Waters.
procedures.why: Heightened areas require more attention and concentration than normal watchkeeping levels can provide alone.

procedures.action: Follow standing orders to call the Captain or Chief Engineer when required or in doubt, and use an additional person for backup.

Anybody, including the master, can become distracted, with potentially severe consequences.
outcomes: Distraction of the master while in control of the vessel resulted in an incident.
Lack of sufficient manning or backup personnel in high-risk areas may contribute to accidents caused by distraction.
key_facts: Nobody plans to be distracted, but distraction can affect anyone on watch, including the master.
Distractions range from fleeting momentary ones to ongoing long-term ones, exacerbated by COVID-19-related extended tours of duty.
Open bridges have numerous alarm and communication systems (ECDIS, AIS, GMDSS, IAS, fire alarm panel, ballast control, CCTV, email) that can cause distraction.
Some companies use 'Red Waters' designations for high-traffic or obstruction-heavy areas requiring heightened attention, potentially requiring extra lookouts.

trace.situation: A large yacht (100m+) got underway after anchoring with a lower-deck shell door left open, causing rapid flooding down the elevator shaft and stairwell shortly after departure.

procedures.why: Directly stops the source of flooding

procedures.action: Verify checklist tasks are physically completed, not just ticked

chapter_title: The title says it all, but since CHIRP continues to

chapter_title: A report highlighting a complete lack of respect

trace.situation: A ship's master recounts a berthing operation where a pilot-directed tug's winch brake failed to hold during manoeuvring, requiring the master to take independent engine action to stop the vessel safely, and describes a repeat visit weeks later where the same defective tug was still in service unrepaired.
trace.trigger: Tug winch brake fails to hold under pilot-ordered power during a close-quarters berthing manoeuvre in a narrow channel.

procedures.action: Monitor tug performance and communications during pilotage manoeuvres.
procedures.why: The pilot ordered tug power and the master needed to detect the tug master's report that the winch brake was not holding.

procedures.action: When the vessel is not slowing despite pilot orders to the tug and 'slow astern', order full astern on the main engine and advise the pilot of the action taken.
procedures.why: The aft tug was not effectively towing/braking and the ship was not slowing, creating risk of allision near the berth/ferry pontoon.

procedures.action: Proceed very cautiously alongside once the vessel is stopped.

procedures.action: On a subsequent call, ask the pilot whether the defective tug's winch had been repaired.
procedures.why: To verify the known equipment defect from the prior incident had been addressed before relying on the same tug again.

procedures.action: Speak directly with the tug master and chief engineer while alongside to confirm the tug's actual mechanical condition.

constraints: Only two tugs were available on station, limiting the ability to avoid the defective tug.
The pilot retained command of tug orders during the manoeuvre, but the master acted independently when the vessel failed to slow.
