trace.trigger: Riders of a jet ski, who had been drinking and had taken the craft without permission, failed to attach the kill cord; when they fell off, the jet ski continued running unmanned, leaving both occupants in the water.

procedures.action: Investigate an unmanned jet ski running unattended near the shore
procedures.why: An uncontrolled powered craft underway poses a hazard to swimmers, other craft, and itself

procedures.action: Confirm with any witnesses whether additional persons are still missing in the water
procedures.why: Initial recovery of one person did not confirm the full extent of casualties; urgency required verification

procedures.action: Conduct an immediate search for the second person once confirmed missing
procedures.why: A tired, unequipped, intoxicated person in the water is at high risk and time-critical

procedures.action: Transfer recovered casualties to the nearest lifeguard station
procedures.why: Provides appropriate medical/safety follow-up for exhausted and intoxicated survivors

procedures.action: Relay full situational information to the official lifeboat rescue craft when encountered
procedures.why: Prevents duplicated search effort and confirms casualties are already safe and accounted for

procedures.action: Advise the lifeboat crew to liaise with the beach lifeguard station to confirm casualty status
procedures.why: Ensures continuity of care and accurate reporting between rescue parties

constraints: Jet ski kill cords must be worn to prevent runaway unmanned craft
Life preservers/wetsuits should be worn when operating a jet ski
Operating a jet ski while intoxicated and without permission created the hazardous situation
Rescuers must verify full casualty count before assuming a rescue is complete
warnings: Unmanned jet skis running at speed near swimmers/other craft pose a collision and injury risk
Operating watercraft while intoxicated significantly increases risk of falling overboard and drowning
Not wearing a kill cord allows a craft to continue running unmanned after the rider falls off
Absence of a life preserver worsens outcomes for persons in the water, especially when tired or intoxicated
outcomes: Both persons who fell from the jet ski were located and recovered safely by bystanders
Casualties were successfully transferred to the beach lifeguard station
Confusion and uncoordinated search efforts arose at sea level due to multiple rescue parties acting independently
The official lifeboat rescue craft was searching for the same incident and needed information relay to stand down/confirm safety
key_facts: The unmanned jet ski was travelling at approximately 3 knots about 100m offshore
Two persons had fallen off the jet ski after drinking all day and not wearing kill cords
Neither recovered person was wearing a wetsuit or life preserver
The reporter was an off-duty Coastguard SAR pilot, which aided his handling of the incident
A lifeboat rescue craft was independently searching for the same jet ski and missing persons

question_seeds.text: Why is wearing a kill cord critical in preventing incidents like this unmanned jet ski scenario?
How should bystander vessels coordinate with official rescue craft to avoid duplicated or confused search efforts?
What immediate steps should be taken when an unmanned powered craft is sighted running near swimmers or other vessels?
Who should be contacted once casualties are recovered to ensure proper follow-up care and to stand down other searching units?

chapter_title: A fresh pair of eyes identified an incident waiting

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary following a jet ski/personal watercraft incident report highlights that alcohol use on the water, combined with failure to wear safety equipment, was the root cause of risk, and criticises regulatory gaps that let reckless watercraft users escape accountability.
trace.trigger: A reported jet ski incident involving alcohol consumption and inadequate safety gear prompted CHIRP to issue this safety commentary.

procedures.action: Do not consume alcohol before or during water sports activity
procedures.why: Alcohol and water do not mix; if this is ignored, all other safety precautions become compromised ('a little bit blurred')

procedures.action: Always wear the engine kill cord
procedures.why: Prevents an unmanned/unconscious rider's craft from continuing to run out of control

procedures.action: Always wear a PFD (buoyancy aid)
procedures.why: Provides flotation and survival support if the rider falls or is incapacitated in water

procedures.action: Wear suitable clothing, e.g. a lightweight wet suit outside the tropics even in summer
procedures.why: Protects against cold-water exposure and injury appropriate to the environment

constraints: Basic safety fact (no alcohol with water activity) must be observed before other precautions are meaningful
Current regulations have gaps that allow jet skis/personal watercraft to escape proper safety oversight
warnings: Alcohol and water do not mix; ignoring this undermines all other safety measures
A hooligan element among jet ski users disregards rules/regulations meant for everyone's safety, yet still expects rescue when in trouble
Jet skis and personal watercraft slip through regulatory gaps, enabling unprosecuted reckless behaviour
outcomes: Without addressing alcohol use, kill cord, PFD, and clothing, water sports users remain exposed to preventable incidents
Persistent hooligan-type behaviour by some personal watercraft users continues unchecked due to regulatory gaps
key_facts: The top learning point from this incident report is that alcohol and water do not mix
Recommended safety practices include wearing the engine kill cord, a PFD, and suitable clothing (e.g. lightweight wet suit outside the tropics)
Most jet ski owners are responsible, but a hooligan element disregards safety guidance and rules
Organisations are producing educational videos and signage, but regulatory gaps allow reckless personal watercraft behaviour to go unprosecuted
A separate incident outline follows regarding incorrect valve alignment identified as a near-miss on a chemical/oil product tanker

question_seeds.text: Why does CHIRP identify alcohol use as the single most critical learning point in this jet ski incident?
What minimum personal safety equipment should be mandated for jet ski/personal watercraft operators under my command's water sports program?
How can regulatory gaps for personal watercraft be addressed to enable prosecution of hooligan-type behaviour?
Which clothing standards should apply to crew conducting water sports outside tropical waters?

trace.situation: A CHIRP initial report into a human error incident notes that crew were working extended trips of 8-9 months during the COVID-19 pandemic, which the reporter considered a contributory factor.
trace.trigger: An incident involving human error occurred while crew were serving abnormally extended sea periods during the COVID-19 pandemic.
constraints: Crew rest/rotation periods should not be extended indefinitely without accounting for fatigue risk
Contributory factors to human error must be identified and reported honestly in incident analysis
warnings: Extended trips (8-9 months) during pandemic conditions can contribute to human error
Prolonged time away from home/normal rotation may degrade crew performance and judgement
outcomes: Human error occurred, attributed in part to fatigue/stress from extended sea service during COVID-19
key_facts: Crew were working extended trips of 8-9 months during the COVID-19 pandemic
The reporter identified this extended trip duration as a contributory factor in a human error incident
This is drawn from an initial CHIRP report, not a finalized investigation

question_seeds.text: Could extended crew contract lengths during the pandemic be contributing to fatigue-related errors on my own vessel?
What human error occurred, and what specific tasks or watches were affected by crew fatigue?
How should I monitor crew fatigue and rotation when contract extensions are forced by pandemic travel restrictions?

trace.situation: A chemical/product tanker loading multiple cargo parcels across several ports left its spill-collection arrangement lined up to the port slop tank even after that tank had been loaded with fish oil cargo, creating a mismatch discovered by an incoming Captain during a delayed crew change.
trace.trigger: Arrival at the second loading port to load ethanol while spill collection was still lined to the port slop tank, which already contained fish oil cargo from the first port.

procedures.action: Re-verify spill collection lineup (slop tank vs. bulk spill drums) before each new loading operation, especially after a change in cargo tank status.
procedures.why: The port slop tank had been filled with fish oil cargo, making it unsuitable/unavailable for collecting a different cargo's (ethanol) spillage.

procedures.action: During crew handover, have the relieving Captain review current operational arrangements including spill collection lineup.
procedures.why: The new Captain noticed the outdated arrangement only during handover, after a delayed crew change had occurred at the second port.

procedures.action: Change spill collection lineup to the bulk spill drums when the slop tank is occupied by incompatible cargo.
procedures.why: To ensure a safe and appropriate spill containment option remains available for the cargo being loaded.

constraints: Spill collection arrangement must match current tank cargo status, not remain fixed from an earlier port.
Cargo loading plan must be followed, but operational safety arrangements (like spill collection) require active re-checking as tank contents change.
Handover between Captains must include review of safety-critical operational lineups.
warnings: Leaving spill collection lined to a tank already filled with a different cargo risks contamination or loss of spill containment capability.
Delayed crew changes can create gaps where outdated operational arrangements go unnoticed.
outcomes: The new Captain identified the mismatched spill collection lineup during handover and corrected it to the bulk spill drums before further cargo operations.
key_facts: The vessel's design offers two spill collection options: port slop tank (aft) or 1m³ bulk spill drums (starboard midships).
The cargo loading plan was approved by all parties including the shore office before loading began.
The port slop tank was loaded with fish oil cargo at the first port.
At the second port, loading ethanol, spill collection remained lined to the now cargo-filled port slop tank until corrected during a delayed crew handover.

question_seeds.text: Why wasn't the spill collection lineup automatically reviewed when the port slop tank's cargo status changed?
How should handover procedures be structured to catch operational mismatches like this spill collection error?
What checks should be built into the cargo loading plan to confirm spill collection options remain valid at each port?
Who is responsible for verifying spill collection arrangements are updated as cargo tanks are filled across multiple ports?

trace.situation: CHIRP commentary analyzing a human factors near-miss incident in which a mistake during slop tank cargo operations nearly led to a cargo spillage accident.
trace.trigger: A basic human error occurred during routine slop tank cargo operations that bypassed normal checks and balances, narrowly avoiding a spillage accident.

procedures.action: Review procedures, instructions, and operational checklists regarding use of the slop tank to carry cargo.
procedures.why: The mistake slipped through existing checks too easily, indicating the controls are inadequate.

procedures.action: Investigate whether fatigue and distraction from extended tours of duty due to COVID-19 contributed to the error.
procedures.why: Extended tours of duty during COVID-19 are a potential contributory factor to human error that needs to be assessed and addressed.

constraints: Normal checks and balances in the routine operation are expected to catch mistakes but failed in this instance.
warnings: A near miss can bypass the incident stage and turn into an accident when multiple safeguards fail simultaneously (the 'swiss cheese' model).
Even highly reliable personnel can make basic mistakes under contributing conditions such as fatigue.
outcomes: Holes in layered defenses aligned, allowing the error to nearly result in a cargo spillage.
Identification of a need to review slop tank cargo procedures and consider COVID-19-related fatigue as a systemic risk factor.
key_facts: The incident involved a human factors mistake during slop tank cargo operations.
Normal checks and balances failed to catch the mistake on this occasion.
Extended tours of duty due to COVID-19 may have caused or worsened fatigue and distraction contributing to the error.
The near miss almost escalated into an accident involving cargo spillage.

question_seeds.text: Why did the normal checks and balances fail to catch this mistake before it became a near miss?
How should slop tank cargo procedures be revised to prevent this type of error recurring?
What role did COVID-19-related extended tours of duty play in crew fatigue and this incident?
Who is responsible for reviewing and updating the slop tank cargo checklists following this near miss?

trace.situation: A pilot boarding a vessel at a pilot exchange station had a side rope of the pilot ladder snap while he was climbing, with no spare pilot ladder available on board.
trace.trigger: Side rope of the rigged pilot ladder parted during pilot boarding operations.

procedures.action: Inspect pilot ladder and associated ropes for wear/damage before each use.
procedures.why: To prevent failure of equipment during a safety-critical transfer operation.

procedures.action: Ensure spare/backup pilot ladders are carried and available on board.
procedures.why: No other pilot ladders were available after the failure, leaving no immediate safe alternative.

procedures.action: Check existing equipment for fitness for purpose when a new vessel is taken into the fleet.
procedures.why: To ensure inherited equipment meets safety standards before it is relied upon.

constraints: Pilot ladder and side ropes must be fit for purpose and properly maintained
Spare pilot ladder equipment should be available on board
warnings: Failure of pilot ladder side ropes can cause serious injury or death to boarding/disembarking pilots
There are consequences for non-compliance with pilot transfer equipment requirements
outcomes: The pilot jumped clear and avoided injury due to only having climbed two steps
An earlier sea pilot had boarded using the same compromised ladder without incident, highlighting a near-miss that went unnoticed
Lack of spare ladder left the vessel without a safe means of pilot transfer
key_facts: The side rope of the pilot ladder snapped while the pilot was climbing at the pilot exchange station.
The pilot had only climbed two steps and was able to jump back onto the pilot boat uninjured.
No spare pilot ladders were available on the vessel.
A sea pilot had boarded earlier the same night using the same ladder without the fault being detected.

question_seeds.text: Why did the side rope fail, and was it a maintenance or inspection lapse?
What spare pilot ladder equipment should I carry to avoid being left without a safe transfer option?
How should pilot ladder inspections be conducted before each pilot transfer?
Who is responsible for verifying equipment fitness when a new vessel joins the fleet?

trace.situation: CHIRP received a follow-up report that after a non-compliant pilot ladder was flagged, the ship's agent sourced and delivered a replacement ladder the next day, but the vessel still lost 3 days waiting for a berth to become free, and CHIRP commented on the cost/benefit of compliance versus the company's handling of a related query about alternative rope to manila.
trace.trigger: Discovery of a non-compliant pilot ladder requiring replacement before the vessel could safely embark/disembark pilots.

procedures.action: Source and deliver a replacement pilot ladder promptly via the ship's agent.
procedures.why: A non-compliant pilot ladder must be replaced before pilot transfer operations can safely continue.

procedures.action: Follow up with the DPA/company for details of the alternative rope product and manufacturer being used in place of manila.
procedures.why: CHIRP wanted to verify the suitability and compliance of the replacement rope material, but no further correspondence was received from the DPA.

procedures.action: Review the company's procedure for handling non-compliant pilot ladder reports.
procedures.why: Although the company's engagement with CHIRP was comprehensive, CHIRP felt the underlying procedure needed closer review.

constraints: Replacement pilot ladder must meet compliance standards before use.
Vessel could only load cargo at a single suitable berth in the port, limiting scheduling flexibility.
warnings: A non-compliant pilot ladder poses a safety risk and must not be used for pilot transfer.
Delaying compliance action can result in significant commercial loss that may exceed the cost of fixing the equipment deficiency.
outcomes: A new pilot ladder was sourced and delivered within one day.
The vessel lost 3 days of hire waiting for the berth to become available due to port congestion, a cost likely greater than that of a new pilot ladder.
CHIRP received no further correspondence from the DPA regarding the alternative rope product and manufacturer.
key_facts: The ship's agent was able to source and deliver a new pilot ladder the next day after the report.
The port had only a single suitable berth for the vessel's cargo, causing a 3-day delay.
CHIRP believes the cost of 3 days' lost hire is greater than the cost of a new pilot ladder.
The company's response to CHIRP was comprehensive but CHIRP suggested reviewing the procedure further.
No further correspondence was received from the DPA about the alternative rope details.

question_seeds.text: Why did the vessel lose 3 days of hire despite the pilot ladder being replaced within a day?
What alternative rope material was used in place of manila, and was it verified as compliant?
How should the company's procedure for addressing non-compliant pilot ladder reports be improved?
Who is responsible for following up on safety equipment compliance queries raised by CHIRP?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describing two separate pilot ladder rejections at an anchorage due to physical defects, causing pilotage delays and prompting a company review of pilot ladder maintenance.
trace.trigger: Pilot ladder found to have uneven steps and then loose whippings during a pilot boarding attempt, making it unsafe for transfer.

procedures.action: Reject the pilot ladder if steps are uneven or unsafe.
procedures.why: Uneven steps create a fall/trip hazard during pilot transfer.

procedures.action: Request the vessel rig an alternative ladder when the first is rejected.
procedures.why: To attempt a safe boarding arrangement before refusing pilotage entirely.

procedures.action: Refuse pilotage entirely if the alternative ladder also proves unsafe (e.g. loose whippings allowing steps to rotate).
procedures.why: A ladder step that can turn nearly vertical by hand cannot safely bear a person's weight.

procedures.action: Arrange delivery of a new pilot ladder to the vessel at anchor before resuming pilotage.
procedures.why: The vessel could not proceed safely until a compliant ladder was available.

procedures.action: Redirect the pilot to the next vessel in the anchorage queue.
procedures.why: To avoid operational delay while the first vessel sources a new ladder.

procedures.action: For a separate case, allow the sea pilot to remain onboard through the locks and have the exchange pilot board by gangway instead of ladder.
procedures.why: To avoid using a defective or unsuitable replacement ladder while still completing the pilotage safely.

procedures.action: Modify company procedures to include monthly load testing of pilot ladders with crew weight while suspended down the wheelhouse front.
procedures.why: To proactively detect ladder weaknesses before use, following the incident.

procedures.action: Distribute incident information to all company vessels and crew.
procedures.why: To raise fleet-wide awareness and prevent recurrence.

procedures.action: Replace manila rope pilot ladders with better quality rope through a replacement programme.
procedures.why: Manila rope quality was inconsistent and weaknesses were difficult to spot.

constraints: A pilot may refuse to board if the pilot ladder is found unsafe.
Pilotage must not proceed until a safe, compliant ladder is provided.
New ladder must be delivered before pilot transfer resumes.
warnings: Pilot ladder steps found uneven, causing rejection.
Loose whippings allowed steps to turn nearly vertical by hand, making the ladder unsafe.
Manila rope quality was found unreliable and defects hard to detect.
outcomes: First vessel's pilotage was delayed until a new ladder was delivered at anchor.
Pilot boarded the next vessel in the anchorage instead, maintaining schedule for that vessel.
Sea pilot remained aboard through the locks while exchange pilot boarded by gangway, avoiding ladder use.
Company increased ladder maintenance/testing frequency and began replacing manila rope ladders fleet-wide.
A new ladder ordered for the vessel missed its departure and was left waiting at the home port.
key_facts: Multiple ships were anchored awaiting berths when the pilot ladder issues occurred.
Two separate pilot ladders were rejected: one for uneven steps, another for loose whippings allowing steps to rotate nearly vertical.
The vessel involved had only recently been taken into the fleet by the managers.
Following the incident, the company introduced monthly load testing of pilot ladders and began phasing out manila rope ladders.
CHIRP obtained the company's corrective actions directly from the DPA.

question_seeds.text: What specific defects justified rejecting each pilot ladder in this report?
At what point should a pilot refuse to board rather than attempt the transfer?
How did the company change its maintenance routine after this incident to prevent recurrence?
Why was the exchange pilot allowed to board via gangway instead of a ladder in the locks?

trace.situation: A reporter asks CHIRP for guidance on vessels whose rubbing strakes/railings lack a gap, preventing safe pilot ladder deployment and risking damage to pilot boats.
trace.trigger: Vessel constructed with a solid railing (rubbing strake) that prevents the pilot ladder from lying flush against the ship's side, creating unsafe pilot transfer conditions.

procedures.action: Identify the relevant SOLAS and IMO provisions governing pilot ladder arrangements.
procedures.why: The reporter had difficulty finding rules specifically addressing railings/rubbing strakes without gaps.

procedures.action: Review SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 23(3) and IMO Resolution 1045(27) for applicable requirements.
procedures.why: These are the governing instruments CHIRP identified as relevant to pilot ladder compliance.

procedures.action: Check whether the ship's administration has granted an exemption or accepted an alternative arrangement.
procedures.why: Both SOLAS and the IMO resolution permit non-compliance if the administration deems the requirement impractical or an alternative acceptable.

constraints: SOLAS requires the pilot ladder to lay against the ship's side.
Exemptions from the rule are only valid if accepted/deemed impractical by the flag administration.
warnings: A rubbing strake/railing without a gap can press down on and damage the pilot boat in rough seas.
A wide railing can cause the pilot ladder to swing freely underneath it, creating an unsafe boarding condition.
Vessels may be non-compliant by design even though regulations nominally require safe pilot ladder arrangements.
outcomes: CHIRP was able to point the reporter to specific SOLAS and IMO provisions, but these contain exemption clauses that can legally permit the unsafe design to persist.
The regulatory 'get-out clause' allowing administration discretion undermines enforcement of safe pilot transfer standards.
key_facts: Several vessels in the reporter's area have rubbing strakes/railings without gaps for pilot boat access.
SOLAS Chapter V Regulation 23(3) requires the pilot ladder to lay against the ship's side.
IMO Resolution 1045(27) also addresses pilot ladder/boarding arrangements.
Both instruments include a clause allowing non-compliance if deemed impractical or an alternative is accepted by the 'administration'.
A pilot ladder rigged above a wide railing can swing freely, creating unsafe access.

question_seeds.text: What SOLAS and IMO provisions govern pilot ladder arrangements relative to rubbing strakes or railings?
Why do these regulations fail to prevent non-compliant ship-side designs from being used?
Who has authority to accept an alternative arrangement or deem the rule impractical?
How should a Master handle a vessel calling at a port where known non-compliant ships operate as pilot boats or pilotage vessels?

trace.situation: A CHIRP comment argues that non-compliant pilot boarding arrangements are inherently dangerous and pilots may refuse them, then recounts a company investigation into a windlass brake failure that caused loss of a starboard anchor and all 12 shackles of chain on a sister vessel.
trace.trigger: Windlass brake failure resulting in loss of the starboard anchor and chain prompted an investigation of the braking mechanism on the sister vessel.

procedures.action: Secure the anchor and chain using the guillotine bar and a wire rope stopper before removing load from the windlass brake.
procedures.why: To safely remove weight from the brake mechanism for inspection without risking uncontrolled chain run-out.

procedures.action: Remove the brake band adjusting bottle screw and fixing plates to the engine room workshop for thorough cleaning and lubrication of threads.
procedures.why: To restore proper function and rule out thread fouling as a cause of brake failure.

procedures.action: Refit the fixing plates and bottle screw with minimal thread engagement (approx. 5 threads at each end) and fully apply the brake using two able seamen.
procedures.why: To test the brake's holding capability under a controlled, realistic adjustment setting.

procedures.action: Engage the drive clutch and run the hydraulic motor to test for braking effect on the gypsy wheel.
procedures.why: To verify whether the brake mechanism actually arrests movement under load.

procedures.action: Investigate the crosshead position between the brake application shaft and brake tensioning plates.
procedures.why: Contact between the crosshead and windlass foundation was found to prevent any braking effect, explaining the freedom of movement.

constraints: A pilot boarding arrangement (PBA) must be SOLAS-compliant to be considered safe.
Pilots have the right to refuse to use a dangerous/non-compliant PBA.
Naval architects and flag administrations are expected to resolve such design/build problems at the construction stage.
warnings: A non-compliant PBA is dangerous and should not be used.
Windlass brake failure can cause injury to crew, hydraulic oil spills, and vessel damage.
Mechanical contact between the crosshead and windlass foundation can completely negate braking function, risking loss of anchor and chain.
outcomes: Refusal of unsafe PBAs by pilots creates delays and costs that pressure operators/owners to fix design problems.
Investigation revealed the crosshead was in contact with the windlass foundation, which caused total loss of braking effect, explaining the earlier loss of the anchor and chain.
key_facts: A non-compliant pilot boarding arrangement is defined as unsafe and therefore dangerous.
Pilots are entitled to refuse to use a dangerous PBA.
A windlass brake failure led to loss of the starboard anchor and all 12 shackles of chain on a company vessel.
Inspection of a sister vessel's windlass found the crosshead contacting the windlass foundation, eliminating the braking effect even with the brake fully applied.
The brake adjusting bottle screw and fixing plates were cleaned, lubricated, and refitted with minimal thread engagement before testing.

question_seeds.text: Why does CHIRP equate a non-compliant pilot boarding arrangement with being inherently dangerous?
What mechanical fault was ultimately found to cause the windlass brake's failure to hold the anchor?
How should a windlass brake be tested safely after reassembly to confirm it will hold under load?
Who is responsible for resolving design-stage problems with windlass/brake and PBA equipment identified in incident investigations?

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime feedback report discusses two unrelated safety issues: pilot boarding access doors obstructed by ferry rubbing strakes, and incorrect windlass brake band adjustment leading to loss of an anchor on a sister ship.
trace.trigger: Reports of pilots unable to safely access vessels due to low/obstructed pilot doors, and investigation into an anchor loss traced to incorrect windlass brake adjustment.

procedures.action: Modify pilot boats with raised platforms to present the pilot at or above the level of the obstructing rubbing strake/access door.
procedures.why: Allows the pilot authority to control the solution directly rather than relying on multiple vessel operators to modify their ships.

procedures.action: Secure the anchor fully using lashing wire and a compression bar before removing the bottle screw for inspection.
procedures.why: Prevents uncontrolled anchor drop while the brake/bottle screw arrangement is disassembled.

procedures.action: Strip down and clean the internal and external threads of the bottle screw arrangement on all vessels in the class.
procedures.why: Corrosion/fouling of threads can prevent proper brake tension adjustment.

procedures.action: Refit the bottle screw and adjust the brake to give 30–35 mm clearance between the foundation and crosshead plates when the brake is 'Fully On'.
procedures.why: This clearance is the correct setting; deviation (too tight/too loose) caused contact marks on foundations and ultimately anchor loss on the sister ship.

procedures.action: Ensure chief officers and masters actively supervise and verify windlass brake adjustments rather than leaving it solely to the bosun.
procedures.why: Reporter notes officers typically do not pay attention to this adjustment, allowing incorrect settings to persist, causing slow winch speed, brake liner damage, and slackening of ropes.

constraints: Anchors must be fully secured with lashing wire and compression bar before removing bottle screws for adjustment.
Brake must allow the gypsy to rotate freely in the 'off' position but fully restrain it in the 'fully on' position.
Correct clearance between crosshead plates and foundation must be 30–35 mm when brake is fully on.
warnings: Incorrect brake band adjustment can cause anchor loss.
Contact marks on both port and starboard foundations indicate this incorrect brake tension setting is a recurring, possibly systemic issue on this windlass type.
Low pilot access doors obstructed by rubbing strakes pose a safety risk to pilots during boarding.
outcomes: Loss of the starboard anchor on the sister ship was probably caused by incorrect brake adjustment.
Corrective action mandated fleet-wide inspection and readjustment of bottle screw/brake clearance to prevent recurrence.
Raising pilot platforms could resolve access door obstruction without requiring all vessel operators to modify their ships.
key_facts: The windlass brake issue was identified as a likely cause of anchor loss on a sister ship.
Correct brake clearance between crosshead plates and foundation should be 30-35 mm when brake is fully applied.
Both port and starboard foundations showed contact wear, suggesting the incorrect setting is common on this windlass type.
Pilot boats may be modified with raised platforms to address low pilot access doors obstructed by ferry rubbing strakes.
Reporter states that chief officers and masters commonly neglect to check bosun's windlass brake adjustments.

question_seeds.text: How should I verify correct windlass brake clearance before departure to avoid an anchor loss incident?
Who on board should be responsible for checking and approving windlass brake band adjustments, beyond the bosun?
What immediate inspection steps should be taken across sister ships if a brake-adjustment-related anchor loss is reported?
Why might pilot boarding be unsafe on ferries with low access doors, and what modification could mitigate this?

trace.situation: A CHIRP report describes two separate safety lessons: correct testing and brake-gap verification procedure for an anchor windlass before anchoring, and a case where a rescue boat became overweight due to water ingress through damaged buoyancy space covers, risking a fall-wire failure similar to a fatal incident on another vessel.
trace.trigger: Prior to every anchoring operation (for the windlass brake check) and discovery of water inside the rescue boat's buoyancy compartments (for the overweight boat issue).

procedures.action: Engage the drive shaft clutch with the brake fully on and attempt to rotate the drum in the chain-lowering direction using the hydraulic motor to test brake holding ability.
procedures.why: Confirms the gypsy wheel does not move relative to the brake, verifying the brake can hold the anchor chain.

procedures.action: Deck officer in charge on the forecastle applies the brake fully and reports to the master a suitable 30-35mm gap before every anchoring operation.
procedures.why: Ensures correct brake setting is confirmed and communicated to the master prior to anchoring.

procedures.action: Engine department manufacture a two-ended feeler gauge (30mm and 35mm) kept by the bosun, who measures the gap in presence of the deck officer.
procedures.why: Provides a standardized, repeatable method to verify the brake gap measurement.

procedures.action: Chief Engineer and Chief Officer train all personnel involved in anchoring operations and equipment maintenance before they are permitted to operate or work on the equipment.
procedures.why: Ensures competence and correct procedure use, reducing risk of brake failure during anchoring.

procedures.action: Senior personnel include this procedure in handover notes and instruct relieving officers.
procedures.why: Maintains continuity of safe practice across crew changes.

procedures.action: Upon finding water ingress in rescue boat buoyancy spaces, stop all drills with the rescue boat and await instructions from the office.
procedures.why: Overweight rescue boat risks parting the fall wire, as occurred fatally elsewhere.

procedures.action: Add rescue boat weight check (via load cell) to the dry dock job list.
procedures.why: Vessel lacked appropriate equipment on board to verify rescue boat weight.

procedures.action: On newly delivered vessels, fill buoyancy space openings with silicon and close with plastic plugs.
procedures.why: Prevents water ingress into buoyancy compartments from the outset.

procedures.action: Turn the rescue boat upside down for a week to drain water trapped in the foam inside compartments.
procedures.why: Mopping alone was insufficient; inversion allowed trapped water in foam to fully drain.

procedures.action: After draining, turn the boat upright, seal openings with silicone, and fit new plastic caps.
procedures.why: Restores watertight integrity of buoyancy spaces to prevent recurrence of overweight condition.

constraints: Brake gap must be verified as 30-35mm using the dedicated feeler gauge before anchoring.
Only trained personnel may operate or work on the anchoring equipment.
Rescue boat drills must be suspended if buoyancy space integrity is compromised.
Weight verification of rescue boats requires an appropriate load cell, not available on all vessels.
warnings: An overweight rescue boat due to water ingress can part the fall wire, causing it to fall during drills, risking death or serious injury.
Buoyancy space openings must be sealed to prevent water ingress that compromises rescue boat weight and fall wire integrity.
outcomes: Correct brake gap verification prevents uncontrolled anchor chain running out.
Suspending drills and awaiting office instruction prevented a potential fall-wire failure similar to a fatal incident elsewhere.
Inverting the rescue boat for a week successfully drained trapped water from the foam, resolving the overweight condition.
Sealing openings with silicone and new plastic caps restored protection against future water ingress.
key_facts: The brake gap standard is 30-35mm, verified with a dedicated two-ended feeler gauge kept by the bosun.
A similar incident elsewhere involved a rescue boat parting its fall wire due to overweight from water ingress, killing one person and badly injuring two others.
The vessel lacked a load cell on board to check rescue boat weight, requiring the task be added to the dry dock job list.
Mopping out water from the rescue boat for two days was ineffective because water kept re-emerging from the foam inside compartments.
Chief Engineer and Chief Officer are responsible for training personnel on anchoring equipment before they may operate or maintain it.

procedures.action: Consider any developing situation from the other vessel's point of view.

procedures.why: The Collision Regulations provide the answer to any situation but must be applied with awareness of differing perceptions.

constraints: Fire drills and musters must be genuinely conducted and accurately logged, not falsified after the fact.

trace.situation: A large container vessel's main engine failed to start during departure from a berth in a restricted harbour basin after an electrician had disabled the engine while repairing a bow thruster, despite a logged engine test 30 minutes earlier.
trace.trigger: The pilot called for the first engine movement after tugs had pulled the vessel into the middle of the basin, and the main engine failed to start.

procedures.action: Confirm main engine readiness with the engine room immediately before pilot boarding and before calling for engine movements.
procedures.why: The logged engine test 30 minutes prior gave false assurance; the engine had since been disabled by the electrician.

procedures.action: Ensure any engineering work (e.g. bow thruster repair) that could affect main engine availability is communicated to the bridge and recorded before departure.
procedures.why: The electrician disabled the main engine while repairing the bow thruster without this being reflected in the operational status relied upon by the captain and pilot.

procedures.action: If engine failure occurs in a confined basin with insufficient tug control, abandon attempts to re-berth and tow the vessel to a safe anchorage instead.
procedures.why: The pilot judged it too dangerous to attempt putting the ship back alongside with tugs alone given the restricted space (26m ahead, 50m astern, 100m across).

procedures.action: Keep tugs in attendance once the engine becomes operational and vessel proceeds under her own power.
procedures.why: Precautionary measure in case the engine fails again before clearing the restricted basin.

procedures.action: Obtain a clear, truthful explanation from the captain/crew when an engine fails despite a reported successful test.
procedures.why: The pilot's query about the discrepancy was met with an unexplained, confusing answer ('engine too powerful'), leaving the root cause unresolved.

constraints: Main engine status must be verified as truly operational, not just logged as tested, before pilotage commences.
Any work performed on propulsion-related systems by crew/electricians must be communicated to the bridge before departure.
Decision to tow to anchorage vs. attempt re-berthing must weigh available basin clearance and tug capability.
warnings: A logged engine test shortly before pilot boarding does not guarantee the engine remains operational if subsequent unreported work is performed.
Attempting to re-berth a large vessel with tugs alone in a tight basin after engine failure may be too dangerous.
Unexplained or evasive answers from the captain regarding engine failure causes leave underlying risks unaddressed.
outcomes: The vessel was safely towed to anchorage and the main engine became operational five minutes into the tow.
The ship proceeded outward under her own power with tugs standing by as a precaution.
The root cause of the engine failure (electrician disabling it post bow-thruster repair) was not properly explained or resolved with the pilot.
key_facts: The vessel was a 294m LOA container vessel moored in a restricted basin.
Another vessel was moored 26m ahead, the basin end was 50m astern, and another vessel was 100m across the basin.
The main engine had reportedly been tested 30 minutes before the pilot boarded, per the captain and bridge logbook.
The electrician had disabled the main engine while repairing a previously failed bow thruster, without this being reflected in the reported engine status.
The engine failed on the first call for movement after tugs had pulled the vessel off the berth into the basin.

trace.situation: A CHIRP maritime report with a photograph exposed a non-compliant pilot boarding arrangement (PBA) on a vessel, triggering parallel reporting to the port state administration and engagement between CHIRP, the ISM managers, and the company's Designated Person Ashore (DPA).
trace.trigger: Receipt of a report (with photographic evidence) clearly showing a non-compliant pilot boarding arrangement.

procedures.action: Submit the initial non-compliance report with supporting photograph to CHIRP.
procedures.why: Photographic evidence clearly illustrated the non-compliance, strengthening the report.

procedures.action: Have the reporter's professional association send a more extensive report directly to the port state maritime administration.
procedures.why: To ensure formal regulatory action beyond CHIRP's confidential reporting channel.

procedures.action: Port State Control officers attend the vessel at its next port to inspect the reported arrangement.
procedures.why: To verify the compliance status of the PBA following the external report.

procedures.action: CHIRP contacts the ISM managers and corresponds with the DPA about the report.
procedures.why: To ensure the company's safety management system addresses the identified concern.

procedures.action: DPA cross-references the report against prior similar reports (e.g., the 2019 sister ship PBA report).
procedures.why: To identify recurring equipment or arrangement issues across the fleet.

procedures.action: DPA confirms PSC inspection outcome and, even though no deficiency was logged, authorizes modifications to the PBA.
procedures.why: To proactively address perceived compliance risk despite the absence of a formal PSC deficiency.

procedures.action: Instruct the technical department to liaise with class and flag state to carry out the necessary PBA modifications.
procedures.why: To formalize and certify the equipment changes through appropriate regulatory channels.

constraints: Report must include clear supporting evidence (photograph) to illustrate non-compliance.
PSC inspection outcome (no deficiency logged) does not preclude the company from taking further corrective action.

warnings: A sister ship fitted with the same pilot boarding equipment may share the same non-compliance risk even if not yet reported.
Absence of a logged PSC deficiency does not guarantee full compliance or safety adequacy of the arrangement.

PSC officers inspected the vessel the next day at its next port but logged no deficiency.

trace.situation: CHIRP's Maritime Advisory Board reviews an incident where a vessel's main engine did not behave as expected during port departure, requiring tug assistance, and separately raises concern over frequent non-compliant pilot ladder reports.
trace.trigger: An incident report in which the Master described the main engine as 'too powerful', prompting discussion of engine testing practices, master/pilot exchange accuracy, and contingency planning; also a pattern of recurring pilot ladder non-compliance reports under SOLAS.

procedures.action: Ensure the Master/Pilot exchange reflects the actual status and operability of equipment, not assumed or hoped-for status.
procedures.why: Inaccurate exchange of equipment status can lead to mismanaged expectations during pilotage.

procedures.action: Clarify and communicate how the main engine is actually tested (fuel ahead/astern vs. air-only alongside).
procedures.why: Some engines are tested only on air alongside to avoid excess thrust from fuel firing that could damage moorings; ambiguity about this may explain the 'engine too powerful' comment.

procedures.action: Always prepare a Plan B for port arrival and departure passage plans.
procedures.why: If the primary plan becomes unavailable, a backup (e.g., pre-secured tugs) can safely move the ship to an alternate location such as an anchorage.

procedures.action: Account for engine reset-mode delays (20-30 seconds before propeller turns) during first physical start.
procedures.why: Modern engines with reset modes can create a start delay that must be understood by engineers, electricians, and bridge team to avoid confusion.

procedures.action: Use checklists that highlight links/commonalities between remotely located machinery (main engine, bow thruster, etc.).
procedures.why: Checklists aid system familiarity across interconnected machinery controlled from different locations.

procedures.action: Maintain early and open communication between the engine control room and bridge when problems occur, even after rigorous checks.
procedures.why: Early communication minimises the effects of unexpected problems and overcomes cultural reluctance within the control room to report issues.

constraints: Master/Pilot exchange must reflect actual, not assumed, equipment status
Port arrival/departure passage plans must include a contingency Plan B
Pilot boarding arrangements must comply with SOLAS regulations
warnings: Firing an engine on fuel when only tested on air alongside can generate excess thrust capable of damaging moorings.
Cultural reluctance in the control room to volunteer problem reports can delay critical communication.
A steady stream of non-compliant pilot ladder and boarding arrangement reports continues despite SOLAS requirements.
outcomes: Plan B (pre-secured tugs) worked perfectly, safely towing the ship from the confined basin to anchorage.
Early and good communication between control room and bridge can minimise the effects of engine start problems.
key_facts: Some main engines are tested ahead/astern on fuel, while others are tested only on air while alongside due to risk of mooring damage from excess thrust.
Modern engines with reset modes can take 20-30 seconds between first start command and propeller turning.
Checklists help reveal commonality/links between remotely located machinery such as main engines and bow thrusters.
Pilot ladders and boarding arrangements are governed by SOLAS regulations, yet non-compliance reports remain common.
A contingency Plan B for port arrival/departure enabled safe towing of a vessel to anchorage after the primary plan failed.

question_seeds.text: Why is it important that the Master/Pilot exchange reflect actual equipment status rather than assumed status?

trace.situation: A seafarer wrote to CHIRP Maritime asking which organization to report safety concerns to after the flag state failed to respond positively to reports of willful disregard, sabotage, and recklessness aboard a ship, and CHIRP Maritime responded explaining the proper reporting chain and its own limitations.

procedures.action: Escalate to the Captain.

procedures.action: Escalate to the Classification Society, depending on the issue.

CHIRP Maritime operates globally but has no statutory authority or investigative powers.

trace.situation: CHIRP Maritime correspondence presenting three case studies where container ships' pilot boarding (ladder) arrangements were found non-compliant or unsafe, leading to enforcement action, dialogue, and eventual rectification before a pilot would board.
trace.trigger: A pilot or Port State Control inspector identifies a pilot boarding arrangement that is non-compliant or unsafe (e.g. excessive gap, trap-door ladder securing, or other configuration issues).

procedures.action: Inspect and photograph the pilot boarding arrangement on arrival or during pilotage.
procedures.why: To assess whether the configuration meets compliance and safety standards.

procedures.action: Issue formal notice to the vessel requiring rectification before the next port visit.
procedures.why: Arrangement was deemed compliant but not safe, so correction was mandated with pilotage withheld as leverage.

procedures.action: Engage in dialogue with the vessel/owner over several weeks to agree a corrected configuration.
procedures.why: Allows collaborative resolution of a safety deficiency rather than immediate refusal.

procedures.action: Refuse pilotage outright if no adjustments have been made despite prior dialogue.
procedures.why: Trap-door arrangement remained non-compliant and unsafe, so boarding could not proceed.

procedures.action: Hold vessel at anchor until modifications are completed and arrangement reconfigured (e.g. combination arrangement secured to main deck strong points).
procedures.why: Ensures the vessel achieves a safe, compliant arrangement before the pilot boards.

procedures.action: Have the pilot confirm the final arrangement is safe before use.
procedures.why: Direct pilot confirmation is the final safety check after modification.

procedures.action: When ladder-to-platform gap exceeds the permitted maximum, require the vessel to find an onboard solution to reduce the gap to within limits.
procedures.why: A gap greater than 20cm (measured at 50cm) is unsafe for pilot transfer and must be corrected before boarding is allowed.

constraints: The gap between the pilot ladder and the lower platform must not exceed 20cm.
A boarding arrangement must be both compliant and genuinely safe, not merely technically compliant.

warnings: An arrangement can be judged 'compliant but not safe', so compliance alone is insufficient.

outcomes: Case 1: Vessel modified arrangement after weeks of dialogue; pilot confirmed it safe on return and boarding proceeded.

What options does a Captain have if engine problems reduce speed capability in heavy weather on an open ocean passage with no nearby port of refuge?
