outcomes: Vessels of special construction operate under Government-determined alternative compliance provisions when full compliance with lighting/shape/sound-signal rules is not possible.
Traffic separation schemes adopted by the Organization become part of the framework these Rules operate within.

procedures.action: Comply with the Rules while also exercising ordinary seamanship and taking any precaution demanded by the special circumstances of the case.

trace.situation: The excerpt sets out the administrative procedures within the COLREG Convention for convening revision conferences, proposing and adopting amendments to the Regulations, and for a Contracting Party to denounce the Convention.
trace.trigger: A Contracting Party requests a revision conference, proposes an amendment to the Regulations, or wishes to denounce the Convention after the required waiting period.

procedures.action: Organization may convene a revision Conference on its own initiative or must convene one if requested by at least one-third of Contracting Parties.
procedures.why: Ensures sufficient collective support before reopening the Convention/Regulations for revision.

procedures.action: A Contracting Party proposing an amendment to the Regulations requests consideration by the Organization.
procedures.why: Formal channel required to initiate amendment process.

procedures.action: Maritime Safety Committee adopts proposed amendment by two-thirds majority of those present and voting, then communicates it to all Contracting Parties and Members at least six months before Assembly consideration.

procedures.action: Assembly adopts the amendment by two-thirds majority of those present and voting; Secretary-General communicates it to all Contracting Parties for acceptance.
procedures.why: Final adoption step requiring broad consensus before entry into force.

procedures.action: Amendment enters into force on date set by Assembly unless more than one-third of Contracting Parties object by a prior deadline also set by the Assembly (itself decided by two-thirds majority).
procedures.why: Provides an objection mechanism so a significant minority can block entry into force.

procedures.action: On entry into force, the amendment replaces prior provisions for all non-objecting Contracting Parties; Secretary-General informs all Parties/Members of requests, communications, and entry-into-force dates.
procedures.why: Maintains transparency and legal clarity on which provisions apply to which Parties.

procedures.action: A Contracting Party may denounce the Convention only after five years from its entry into force for that Party, by depositing an instrument with the Organization.
procedures.why: Prevents premature withdrawal and ensures formal notice procedure.

procedures.action: Secretary-General informs all other Contracting Parties of receipt and deposit date of the denunciation instrument; denunciation takes effect one year (or longer if specified) after deposit.
procedures.why: Gives other Parties advance notice and time to adjust before the denunciation takes legal effect.

constraints: A revision Conference must be convened by the Organization if requested by at least one-third of Contracting Parties.

Denunciation can only occur after five years from entry into force for that Party.
Denunciation takes effect one year (or longer per instrument) after deposit.
outcomes: Amendments adopted and not objected to by more than one-third of Parties replace and supersede prior provisions for non-objecting Parties.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 5 establishes the universal requirement for all vessels to maintain a proper look-out at all times.
trace.trigger: Applies continuously to every vessel underway or at anchor in navigable waters, regardless of visibility or traffic conditions.

procedures.action: Maintain a proper look-out by sight and hearing at all times.
procedures.why: Enables full appraisal of the situation and detection of risk of collision.

procedures.action: Use all available means appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions (e.g. radar, AIS, binoculars, sound signals).
procedures.why: Sight and hearing alone may be insufficient in restricted visibility, heavy traffic, or at night.

procedures.action: Continuously assess the situation to determine risk of collision.
procedures.why: Early and full appraisal allows timely action to avoid collision under subsequent steering and sailing rules.

constraints: Look-out must be maintained at all times, not only in certain conditions

The standard applies to every vessel without exception
warnings: Failure to maintain a proper look-out by all appropriate means may result in failure to detect risk of collision in time to act.
outcomes: A full appraisal of the situation and risk of collision allows the vessel to take appropriate and timely collision-avoidance action per other steering and sailing rules.
key_facts: Rule 5 requires continuous look-out by sight and hearing as well as all available means.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 6 establishes the obligation for every vessel to proceed at a safe speed at all times, considering listed factors applicable to all vessels and additional factors for vessels with operational radar.
trace.trigger: Applies continuously whenever a vessel is underway, requiring assessment prior to and during any risk of collision.

procedures.action: Maintain a speed that allows proper and effective action to avoid collision and permits stopping within a distance appropriate to prevailing circumstances and conditions.
procedures.why: Ensures the vessel retains the ability to avoid collision given current conditions.

procedures.action: Assess visibility, traffic density (including fishing vessel concentrations), own manoeuvrability/stopping distance/turning ability, background night lighting, wind/sea/current state, proximity of navigational hazards, and draught versus available water depth.
procedures.why: These are the factors all vessels must take into account to determine safe speed.

procedures.action: If operating radar, additionally assess radar equipment characteristics/limitations, range scale constraints, effects of sea state/weather/interference on detection, risk of missing small vessels/ice/floating objects, number/location/movement of radar-detected vessels, and use radar for more exact visibility/range assessment.
procedures.why: Radar has specific limitations and capabilities that must be factored into the safe speed determination.

constraints: Safe speed must be maintained at all times, not just in restricted visibility.
All listed factors (a)(i)-(vi) must be considered by every vessel.
Vessels with operational radar must additionally consider factors (b)(i)-(vi).
warnings: Small vessels, ice and other floating objects may not be detected by radar at an adequate range.
Radar range scale in use may impose constraints on detection and assessment.
Sea state, weather and other sources of interference can degrade radar detection effectiveness.
outcomes: Proceeding at a safe speed enables proper and effective collision avoidance action.
Failure to account for radar limitations or environmental factors could result in missed detections and collision risk.
key_facts: Rule 6 requires safe speed determination at all times, independent of visibility conditions.
Six factors (a)(i)-(vi) apply to all vessels regardless of equipment.
Six additional factors (b)(i)-(vi) apply specifically to vessels with operational radar.
Safe speed must allow the vessel to be stopped within a distance appropriate to prevailing circumstances.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 7 establishes how a vessel must determine whether risk of collision exists with another vessel, including the use of radar and bearing observations.
trace.trigger: Another vessel or object is detected (visually or by radar) that may be approaching the own ship.

procedures.action: Use all available means appropriate to prevailing circumstances to determine if risk of collision exists.
procedures.why: Ensures no reliance on a single method and accounts for environmental conditions.

procedures.action: If any doubt exists about risk of collision, treat risk as existing.
procedures.why: Precautionary principle to avoid underestimating collision danger.

procedures.action: Properly use fitted and operational radar, including long-range scanning and systematic plotting or equivalent observation.
procedures.why: Provides early warning of risk of collision and tracks target movement over time.

procedures.action: Avoid making assumptions based on scanty information, especially scanty radar data.
procedures.why: Incomplete data can lead to incorrect risk assessments and dangerous maneuvers.

procedures.action: Deem risk of collision to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change.
procedures.why: A constant bearing with decreasing range is a classic indicator of a collision course.

procedures.action: Consider that risk may still exist despite an appreciable bearing change, especially near very large vessels, tows, or vessels at close range.
procedures.why: Large vessels, tows, or close-range targets can still result in collision despite bearing drift due to their size or proximity.

constraints: Radar equipment must be fitted and operational for its use to be mandated.
Any doubt about risk of collision must default to treating risk as existing.
Decisions must not be based on insufficient or scanty data.
warnings: Do not assume no risk of collision based on scanty information, especially scanty radar information.
An appreciable bearing change does not guarantee safety, particularly near large vessels, tows, or at close range.
outcomes: Proper assessment of risk of collision enables timely and appropriate collision avoidance action.
Failure to use all available means or over-reliance on scanty data increases risk of collision.
key_facts: Risk of collision must be assessed using all available means appropriate to conditions.
Any doubt about collision risk must be treated as risk existing.
A constant compass bearing of an approaching vessel indicates risk of collision.
Risk of collision can exist even with bearing change when approaching very large vessels, tows, or vessels at close range.
Radar must be properly used, including plotting or systematic observation, when fitted and operational.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 8 sets out general requirements for any action taken by a vessel to avoid collision with another vessel.
trace.trigger: A risk of collision exists between vessels and action must be taken under the Rules of Part B.

procedures.action: Take action to avoid collision in accordance with the Rules of this Part, making it positive, timely, and seamanlike if circumstances admit.
procedures.why: Ensures the action is effective and consistent with good seamanship.

procedures.action: Make any alteration of course and/or speed large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel visually or by radar; avoid successive small alterations.
procedures.why: Small or ambiguous alterations may not be detected by the other vessel and can cause confusion about intentions.

procedures.action: If sufficient sea room exists, consider alteration of course alone as the most effective action, provided it is made in good time, is substantial, and does not create a new close-quarters situation.
procedures.why: A well-timed, substantial course change can resolve risk of collision without further hazard.

procedures.action: Ensure the action results in passing at a safe distance and continuously monitor its effectiveness until the other vessel is finally past and clear.
procedures.why: Initial action may not be sufficient; ongoing verification confirms collision risk is truly resolved.

procedures.action: If necessary, slacken speed, stop, or reverse propulsion to avoid collision or to gain more time to assess the situation.
procedures.why: Reducing speed or stopping way can be essential when other actions are insufficient to avoid collision.

procedures.action: If required not to impede another vessel's passage, take early action to allow sufficient sea room for that vessel's safe passage.
procedures.why: Early action prevents a situation from developing into risk of collision and fulfills the non-impedance obligation.

procedures.action: Even when obligated not to impede another vessel, continue to take action having full regard to the Rules of this Part if risk of collision develops.
procedures.why: The non-impedance duty does not override or replace other collision-avoidance obligations.

constraints: Actions must be positive, made in ample time, and consistent with good seamanship if circumstances admit.
Course/speed alterations must be large enough to be apparent to another vessel; avoid small successive changes.
Course alteration alone as sole action requires sufficient sea room and must not create a new close-quarters situation.
Passing distance must be safe, and effectiveness must be checked continuously until vessels are past and clear.
A vessel required not to impede another's passage remains fully obliged to comply with all Part B rules if risk of collision arises.
warnings: Avoid a succession of small alterations of course and/or speed, as these may not be apparent to another vessel.
An alteration of course alone, if insufficient sea room or substance, may create another close-quarters situation.
The obligation not to impede another vessel's passage does not relieve a vessel of its duty to comply with collision-avoidance rules if risk of collision develops.
outcomes: Positive, timely, and substantial action reduces risk of collision and results in safe passing distance.
Failure to make clear alterations or to monitor effectiveness may result in continued or renewed risk of collision.
Early action by a vessel not to impede another's passage ensures sufficient sea room and avoids escalation to a close-quarters or collision risk situation.
key_facts: Rule 8 governs general action to avoid collision under COLREG Part B.
Course/speed changes must be large enough to be apparent to another vessel by visual or radar observation.
A vessel may need to slacken speed, stop, or reverse propulsion to avoid collision or gain time to assess the situation.
A vessel required not to impede another's passage must still comply fully with collision-avoidance rules if risk of collision arises.
Effectiveness of avoiding action must be checked continuously until the other vessel is finally past and clear.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 9 sets out navigation rules for vessels operating in narrow channels or fairways, covering position-keeping, right-of-way between vessel types, crossing, overtaking, and anchoring.
trace.trigger: A vessel is proceeding along, crossing, overtaking within, or anchoring in a narrow channel or fairway.

procedures.action: Keep as near to the outer limit of the channel/fairway on your starboard side as is safe and practicable.
procedures.why: Ensures predictable traffic flow and safe passage for vessels proceeding along the channel.

procedures.action: If less than 20m in length or a sailing vessel, do not impede vessels that can only navigate safely within the channel.
procedures.why: Smaller/sailing vessels have more maneuvering options and must yield to constrained vessels.

procedures.action: If engaged in fishing, do not impede the passage of any other vessel navigating within the channel.
procedures.why: Fishing activity should not obstruct vessels confined to the channel.

procedures.action: Do not cross a narrow channel if it would impede a vessel that can only navigate safely within it.
procedures.why: Crossing vessels have more sea room and must avoid interfering with constrained traffic.

procedures.action: If in doubt about a crossing vessel's intentions, sound the Rule 34(d) signal.
procedures.why: Alerts the crossing vessel and prompts clarification of intent to avoid collision.

procedures.action: When overtaking requires the overtaken vessel to take action, the overtaking vessel must sound the Rule 34(c)(i) signal to indicate intent.
procedures.why: Communicates intention clearly given the overtaken vessel must actively assist the maneuver.

procedures.action: The vessel being overtaken, if in agreement, sounds the Rule 34(c)(ii) signal and takes steps to permit safe passing; if in doubt, sounds Rule 34(d) signals.
procedures.why: Confirms mutual understanding and enables safe overtaking in confined waters.

procedures.action: Remember that overtaking in a narrow channel does not relieve the overtaking vessel of her Rule 13 obligations.
procedures.why: Rule 13 (overtaking) duties remain in force regardless of channel-specific signaling.

procedures.action: When nearing a bend or obstruction that may obscure other vessels, navigate with particular alertness and caution and sound the Rule 34(e) signal.
procedures.why: Blind bends/obstructions increase collision risk; sound signal warns unseen traffic.

procedures.action: Avoid anchoring in a narrow channel if circumstances permit.
procedures.why: Anchored vessels in narrow channels obstruct the limited navigable width for other traffic.

constraints: Applies specifically to vessels in narrow channels or fairways.
Outer-limit-on-starboard-side rule only applies 'as is safe and practicable'.
Crossing/overtaking restrictions apply only when they would impede a vessel confined to the channel.
Anchoring avoidance is conditional on circumstances of the case admitting it.
warnings: Small vessels (<20m) and sailing vessels must not impede vessels confined to the channel.
Fishing vessels must not impede other vessel passage in narrow channels.
Do not cross a narrow channel if it impedes a constrained vessel.
Overtaking in a narrow channel does not relieve the overtaking vessel of Rule 13 obligations.
Avoid anchoring in narrow channels where circumstances permit otherwise.
outcomes: Predictable, safe traffic flow in narrow channels when outer-limit and non-impedance rules are followed.
Reduced collision risk at bends/obstructions through sound signaling and heightened alertness.
Clear mutual understanding during overtaking maneuvers via prescribed signals, preventing miscommunication.
Failure to follow impedance/crossing restrictions could result in collision or obstruction of constrained vessels.
key_facts: Vessels proceeding along a channel should keep to the starboard outer limit when safe and practicable.
Vessels under 20m, sailing vessels, and fishing vessels must not impede vessels confined to the channel.
Crossing vessels must not impede vessels that can only navigate within the channel.
Specific sound signals (Rule 34 c(i), c(ii), d, e) govern overtaking intent, doubt, and bend/obstruction warnings.
Anchoring in a narrow channel should be avoided if circumstances permit.

When is a fishing vessel required to give way in a narrow channel?
How should overtaking be conducted in a narrow channel when the overtaken vessel needs to maneuver?
Why does Rule 9 still require compliance with Rule 13 obligations during overtaking?

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 10 exemptions for vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre while conducting safety-of-navigation or submarine cable operations within a traffic separation scheme.
trace.trigger: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre is engaged in maintaining safety of navigation or laying/servicing/picking up a submarine cable within a traffic separation scheme.

procedures.action: Determine whether the restricted-in-ability-to-manoeuvre vessel is engaged in a safety-of-navigation maintenance operation or a submarine cable operation within the TSS.
procedures.why: Determines which exemption under Rule 10(k) or 10(l) applies.

procedures.action: Allow such vessel to depart from Rule 10 requirements only to the extent necessary to carry out the specific operation.
procedures.why: The exemption is limited in scope, not a blanket waiver of Rule 10.

constraints: Exemption applies only to vessels classified as restricted in their ability to manoeuvre.
Exemption applies only within a traffic separation scheme.
Non-compliance with Rule 10 is permitted only to the extent necessary to carry out the stated operation.
warnings: Other vessels must recognize that a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre conducting these operations may deviate from normal TSS traffic flow rules.
outcomes: Vessels engaged in safety-of-navigation maintenance or submarine cable operations within a TSS can legally operate outside standard Rule 10 traffic lane requirements while performing their task.
key_facts: Rule 10(k) exempts a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre performing safety-of-navigation maintenance operations in a TSS from Rule 10 compliance, to the extent necessary.
Rule 10(l) provides a similar exemption for vessels engaged in laying, servicing, or picking up a submarine cable within a TSS.
Both exemptions are limited strictly to what is necessary to carry out the specific operation.
This excerpt precedes Section II, which covers conduct of vessels in sight of one another.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 10 sets out the navigational obligations of vessels operating in or near IMO-adopted traffic separation schemes (TSS).
trace.trigger: A vessel is navigating in, crossing, joining, leaving, or operating near a traffic separation scheme or its inshore traffic zone.

procedures.action: Proceed in the appropriate traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow.
procedures.why: Maintains orderly traffic flow within the scheme.

procedures.action: Keep clear of traffic separation lines and separation zones so far as practicable.
procedures.why: Separation lines/zones divide opposing traffic and must not be straddled.

procedures.action: Join or leave a traffic lane normally at the lane's termination; if joining/leaving from the side, do so at the smallest practicable angle to traffic flow.
procedures.why: Minimizes conflict with vessels following the lane.

procedures.action: Avoid crossing traffic lanes where practicable; if crossing is unavoidable, cross on a heading as near as practicable to right angles to traffic flow.
procedures.why: Reduces time spent exposed to opposing/crossing traffic and improves predictability.

procedures.action: Do not use the inshore traffic zone if the adjacent traffic lane can be safely used, unless the vessel is under 20m, a sailing vessel, or engaged in fishing.
procedures.why: Reserves the inshore zone for vessels less able to use the main lanes, keeping lanes clear for through traffic.

procedures.action: A vessel may use the inshore traffic zone when en route to/from a port, offshore installation, pilot station, or other place in the zone, or to avoid immediate danger.
procedures.why: Provides a safety and operational exception to the inshore zone restriction.

procedures.action: Do not normally enter a separation zone or cross a separation line except in emergency to avoid immediate danger or to fish within the zone.
procedures.why: Separation zones exist to physically separate opposing traffic lanes; entry undermines that purpose.

procedures.action: Navigate with particular caution near the terminations of traffic separation schemes.
procedures.why: Termination areas see convergence/divergence of traffic and higher collision risk.

procedures.action: Avoid anchoring in a TSS or near its terminations so far as practicable.
procedures.why: Anchored vessels in high-traffic areas create collision hazards and obstruct flow.

procedures.action: If not using the TSS, avoid it by as wide a margin as practicable.
procedures.why: Reduces interference with vessels properly using the scheme.

procedures.action: Fishing vessels must not impede vessels following a traffic lane.
procedures.why: Lane-following vessels have priority of passage within the scheme.

procedures.action: Vessels under 20m or sailing vessels must not impede the safe passage of power-driven vessels following a traffic lane.
procedures.why: Smaller/less maneuverable vessels must not obstruct larger vessels constrained to the lane.

constraints: Rule 10 does not relieve any vessel of obligations under any other Rule.
Applies only to TSS adopted by the Organization (IMO).
Inshore traffic zone use is restricted unless vessel qualifies (under 20m, sailing, fishing) or meets destination/emergency exception.
Entry into separation zones/lines is restricted except for emergency or fishing exceptions.
warnings: Do not straddle or cross separation lines/zones except as explicitly permitted.
Avoid anchoring in or near TSS terminations.
Fishing and small/sailing vessels must not impede vessels properly using the traffic lane.
outcomes: Compliance maintains orderly, predictable traffic flow and reduces collision risk within TSS.
Non-compliance (e.g., impeding lane traffic, unnecessary anchoring, improper crossing) increases collision risk and may constitute a Rule 10 violation.
key_facts: Rule 10 governs vessel conduct within IMO-adopted traffic separation schemes and does not override other COLREG rules.
Vessels under 20m, sailing vessels, and fishing vessels are permitted to use inshore traffic zones; other vessels generally must use the adjacent TSS lane if safely usable.
Crossing traffic lanes should be avoided, but if necessary must be done as close as practicable to a right angle to traffic flow.
Separation zones/lines may only be entered in emergencies to avoid immediate danger or for fishing.

How should I cross a traffic lane if crossing is unavoidable?
Why must vessels avoid anchoring near the terminations of a traffic separation scheme?
Which vessels are obligated not to impede power-driven vessels following a traffic lane?

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: Two power-driven vessels are meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses, creating risk of collision in a head-on situation.
trace.trigger: A power-driven vessel sees another vessel ahead or nearly ahead with masthead lights in line or nearly in line and/or both sidelights (by night) or the corresponding aspect (by day), or is in any doubt as to whether such a situation exists.

procedures.action: Alter course to starboard so that each vessel passes on the port side of the other.
procedures.why: Rule 14(a) mandates this maneuver to avoid risk of collision when meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses.

procedures.action: Identify a head-on situation by observing the other vessel ahead or nearly ahead with masthead lights in line and/or both sidelights (night) or corresponding aspect (day).
procedures.why: Rule 14(b) defines the visual criteria that establish a head-on situation exists.

procedures.action: If in any doubt as to whether a head-on situation exists, assume that it does and act accordingly by altering course to starboard.
procedures.why: Rule 14(c) requires erring on the side of caution to prevent collision when situational clarity is lacking.

constraints: Applies only to two power-driven vessels meeting on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses involving risk of collision.
Each vessel must alter course to starboard, not port, to ensure port-to-port passing.
Doubt about the situation must be resolved in favor of assuming head-on and acting accordingly.
warnings: Failure to alter course to starboard when in doubt about a head-on situation increases risk of collision.
outcomes: Both vessels pass safely on each other's port side when the rule is correctly applied.
Assuming a head-on situation exists when in doubt prevents collision from uncertainty.
key_facts: Rule 14 governs head-on situations between two power-driven vessels.
The required action is for each vessel to alter course to starboard.
A head-on situation is identified by seeing the other vessel ahead or nearly ahead with masthead lights in line and/or both sidelights visible at night, or the corresponding aspect by day.
If there is any doubt whether a head-on situation exists, the vessel must assume it does and act accordingly.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 13 defines the overtaking situation and establishes the overriding duty of an overtaking vessel to keep clear of the vessel being overtaken.
trace.trigger: A vessel comes up with another vessel from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam, or there is doubt about whether an overtaking situation exists.

procedures.action: Determine whether you are approaching another vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam (i.e., you would only see her sternlight at night, not her sidelights).
procedures.why: This is the defining geometric/visual test for an overtaking situation under Rule 13(b).

procedures.action: If any doubt exists as to whether you are overtaking, assume that you are and act accordingly.
procedures.why: Rule 13(c) requires the more cautious assumption to avoid ambiguity in collision avoidance responsibility.

procedures.action: As the overtaking vessel, keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, regardless of other Part B Section I and II rules.
procedures.why: Rule 13(a) makes this duty override the normal crossing/head-on rules.

procedures.action: Maintain the duty to keep clear even if the bearing between the two vessels subsequently changes, until finally past and clear.
procedures.why: Rule 13(d) prevents the overtaking vessel from reclassifying the encounter as a crossing situation to escape her keep-clear obligation.

constraints: The overtaking definition applies notwithstanding any other rule in Part B, Sections I and II.
The overtaking vessel's duty persists until she is finally past and clear of the overtaken vessel.
A change in bearing after initial overtaking does not convert the situation into a crossing situation.
warnings: Do not assume a subsequent bearing change relieves you of the duty to keep clear if you are the overtaking vessel.
If in doubt whether overtaking applies, you must assume it does - do not default to crossing/give-way ambiguity.
outcomes: Correct application prevents collision by placing unambiguous responsibility on the faster/overtaking vessel.
Failure to recognize an overtaking situation (or to maintain the keep-clear duty) could result in a close-quarters or collision situation.
key_facts: A vessel is overtaking if approaching from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the other vessel's beam.
At night, the overtaking vessel would see only the other vessel's sternlight, not her sidelights.
The overtaking vessel must keep clear regardless of other steering and sailing rules in Part B Sections I and II.
The keep-clear duty continues until the overtaking vessel is finally past and clear, even if bearings change.

trace.situation: Two power-driven vessels are crossing on courses that create risk of collision.
trace.trigger: Another power-driven vessel is detected on the vessel's own starboard side with risk of collision developing in a crossing situation.

procedures.action: Identify that the other power-driven vessel is on your own starboard side.
procedures.why: This determines which vessel is the give-way vessel under the crossing rule.

procedures.action: Keep out of the way of the vessel on your starboard side.
procedures.why: The rule assigns give-way responsibility to the vessel that has the other vessel on her own starboard side.

procedures.action: Avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel if circumstances of the case admit.
procedures.why: Crossing ahead risks close-quarters situation and collision; avoiding it provides a safer, clearer course of action.

constraints: Applies only to two power-driven vessels crossing so as to involve risk of collision.
The give-way vessel must take action only if circumstances of the case admit avoiding crossing ahead.
warnings: Do not assume the other vessel will give way; maintain situational awareness of risk of collision.
Avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel when possible to reduce collision risk.
outcomes: If followed, the give-way vessel maneuvers to keep clear and avoid crossing ahead, reducing collision risk.
If not followed, risk of collision increases as both vessels may fail to coordinate avoidance action.
key_facts: Rule 15 governs crossing situations between two power-driven vessels.
The vessel with the other vessel on her own starboard side is the give-way vessel.
The give-way vessel should avoid crossing ahead of the other vessel if circumstances permit.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 12 establishes which sailing vessel must keep out of the way when two sailing vessels are approaching each other with risk of collision.
trace.trigger: Two sailing vessels are approaching one another so as to involve risk of collision.

procedures.action: Determine which side of each vessel the wind is on.
procedures.why: The give-way obligation depends on which side the wind strikes each vessel.

procedures.action: If each vessel has the wind on a different side, the vessel with wind on the port side must keep out of the way of the other.
procedures.why: Rule 12(a)(i) assigns give-way responsibility based on port-side wind.

procedures.action: If both vessels have the wind on the same side, the windward vessel must keep out of the way of the leeward vessel.
procedures.why: Rule 12(a)(ii) prioritizes the vessel with less maneuvering constraint (leeward) as stand-on.

procedures.action: If a vessel with wind on the port side sees a vessel to windward and cannot determine with certainty which side the other vessel has the wind on, she shall keep out of the way of the other.
procedures.why: Rule 12(a)(iii) applies a precautionary default when wind direction of the other vessel is uncertain, to avoid ambiguity leading to collision.

procedures.action: Determine windward side as the side opposite to where the mainsail is carried (or largest fore-and-aft sail for square-rigged vessels).
procedures.why: Rule 12(b) provides the technical definition needed to apply the windward/leeward rule correctly.

constraints: Rule applies only between two sailing vessels approaching with risk of collision.
Windward side is defined as opposite to the side the mainsail (or largest fore-and-aft sail) is carried on.
warnings: If uncertain which side the other vessel has the wind on, default to keeping out of the way rather than assuming stand-on status, to prevent collision.
outcomes: Following the rule assigns clear give-way responsibility between two sailing vessels, reducing risk of collision.
Failure to correctly assess wind side or windward/leeward status could lead to both vessels assuming stand-on status, increasing collision risk.
key_facts: When two sailing vessels have wind on different sides, the vessel with wind on port side gives way.
When both have wind on the same side, the windward vessel gives way to the leeward vessel.
If a vessel with wind on port side cannot determine the other's wind side and sees her to windward, she must keep out of the way.
Windward side is defined as the side opposite to where the mainsail or largest fore-and-aft sail is carried.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 20 establishes when and how navigation lights and shapes must be displayed by vessels at sea.
trace.trigger: Applies continuously to all vessels in all weathers, specifically from sunset to sunrise for lights and during daylight for shapes, with additional light display required in restricted visibility.

procedures.action: Comply with the shape and light rules in all weather conditions.
procedures.why: Rule mandates compliance regardless of weather.

procedures.action: Exhibit prescribed navigation lights from sunset to sunrise.
procedures.why: Ensures vessels are visible and identifiable to others during darkness.

procedures.action: Do not display any other lights that could be mistaken for, impair visibility of, or interfere with recognition of prescribed lights, or that interfere with proper lookout.
procedures.why: Prevents confusion with navigation lights and preserves lookout effectiveness.

procedures.action: Exhibit prescribed lights (if carried) from sunrise to sunset when visibility is restricted, and may exhibit them at other times when deemed necessary.
procedures.why: Restricted visibility reduces ability to see shapes/day signals, so lights provide better identification.

procedures.action: Display prescribed shapes during daylight hours.
procedures.why: Shapes are the daytime equivalent signal to lights for identifying vessel status/activity.

procedures.action: Ensure all lights and shapes conform to the technical specifications in Annex I.
procedures.why: Standardization ensures lights/shapes are correctly interpreted by other vessels.

constraints: Light rules apply from sunset to sunrise.
Shape rules apply by day.
No extraneous lights may be shown that could be confused with or obscure prescribed lights or hinder lookout.
Lights must, if carried, also be shown during restricted visibility in daytime.
Lights and shapes must comply with Annex I specifications.
warnings: No lights other than those specified may be exhibited if they could be mistaken for prescribed lights, impair their visibility/distinctive character, or interfere with proper lookout.
outcomes: Proper application of lights and shapes ensures vessels can be correctly identified and their status understood by other vessels, reducing collision risk.
key_facts: Light and shape rules must be complied with in all weather conditions.
Lights are required from sunset to sunrise; shapes are required by day.
Lights must also be shown during restricted visibility in daytime if carried.
Extraneous lights that could be confused with navigation lights or impede lookout are prohibited.
All lights and shapes must meet the technical standards set out in Annex I.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 18 establishes the hierarchy of responsibility between vessel types regarding which vessel must keep out of the way of another, absent overriding Rules 9, 10, 13.
trace.trigger: Two or more vessels of different categories (power-driven, sailing, fishing, not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught, seaplane, WIG craft) are underway and encounter each other outside the specific scenarios covered by Rules 9 (narrow channels), 10 (TSS), and 13 (overtaking).

procedures.action: As a power-driven vessel underway, keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, engaged in fishing, or under sail.
procedures.why: Rule 18(a) establishes power-driven vessels as lowest in the responsibility hierarchy among these categories.

procedures.action: As a sailing vessel underway, keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, or engaged in fishing.
procedures.why: Rule 18(b) places sailing vessels below these more constrained categories despite normally having right of way over power-driven vessels.

procedures.action: As a vessel engaged in fishing, keep out of the way of a vessel not under command or restricted in ability to manoeuvre, so far as possible.
procedures.why: Rule 18(c) recognizes fishing vessels still rank above not-under-command and restricted-in-ability vessels.

procedures.action: Unless not under command or restricted in ability to manoeuvre, avoid impeding the safe passage of a vessel constrained by her draught exhibiting Rule 28 signals, if circumstances admit.
procedures.why: Rule 18(d)(i) protects vessels whose manoeuvrability is limited by draught.

procedures.action: As a vessel constrained by draught, navigate with particular caution having full regard to her special condition.
procedures.why: Rule 18(d)(ii) acknowledges this vessel's reduced manoeuvring options still require prudent seamanship, not blind reliance on others.

procedures.action: As a seaplane on the water, keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding navigation generally; comply with Part B Rules if risk of collision exists.
procedures.why: Rule 18(e) treats seaplanes as generally subordinate but requiring full COLREG compliance when collision risk arises.

procedures.action: As a WIG craft taking off, landing, or in flight near the surface, keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding navigation; when operating on the water, comply with Part B Rules as a power-driven vessel.
procedures.why: Rule 18(f) differentiates WIG craft operating modes for collision-avoidance responsibility.

constraints: This hierarchy applies only except where Rules 9, 10, and 13 otherwise require.
Paragraph (f) on WIG craft entered into force 29 November 2003 per Resolution A.919(22).
Vessel constrained by draught must be exhibiting Rule 28 signals for 18(d)(i) to apply.
Fishing vessel's duty to keep clear is qualified by 'so far as possible'.
Avoidance duties under 18(d)(i) are qualified by 'if the circumstances of the case admit'.
warnings: Failure to observe this responsibility hierarchy can lead to incorrect stand-on/give-way assumptions and collision risk.
A vessel constrained by draught must not assume automatic right of way; she must still navigate with particular caution.
outcomes: Clear hierarchy reduces ambiguity about which vessel must give way among differing vessel categories, supporting collision avoidance.
Non-compliance with keep-out-of-the-way duties under Rule 18 increases collision risk among vessels of differing manoeuvrability.
key_facts: Rule 18 sets a hierarchy: not under command and restricted in ability to manoeuvre rank highest, followed by fishing vessels, then sailing vessels, then power-driven vessels.
This hierarchy is overridden by Rules 9 (narrow channels), 10 (traffic separation schemes), and 13 (overtaking).
Vessels constrained by draught receive special consideration but must exhibit Rule 28 signals and still navigate cautiously.
Seaplanes and WIG craft have distinct responsibilities depending on their operating mode (on water, in flight, taking off/landing).
WIG craft provision (paragraph f) entered into force 29 November 2003 via Resolution A.919(22).

How should I navigate my vessel when constrained by draught while another vessel is required to avoid impeding my passage?

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: Conduct required of vessels navigating in or near restricted visibility when not in sight of one another, including radar-only detection scenarios.
trace.trigger: Vessel is navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility and is not in sight of other vessels.

procedures.action: Proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing restricted visibility conditions.
procedures.why: Ensures the vessel can respond appropriately to developing situations in low visibility.

procedures.action: Have engines ready for immediate manoeuvre (power-driven vessels).
procedures.why: Allows rapid speed or course changes if a close-quarters situation or collision risk is detected.

procedures.action: Apply Section I steering/sailing rules with due regard to restricted visibility conditions.
procedures.why: Normal Rules of the Road must be adapted because visual sighting of other vessels is not possible.

procedures.action: When another vessel is detected by radar alone, determine if a close-quarters situation or risk of collision is developing.
procedures.why: Radar may be the only means of detecting other traffic in restricted visibility, so assessment of risk is essential before acting.

procedures.action: If risk exists, take avoiding action in ample time.
procedures.why: Early action reduces the chance of a close-quarters situation developing into collision.

procedures.action: Avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam (unless overtaking), and avoid altering course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.
procedures.why: These alterations could create confusion or worsen a close-quarters situation when the other vessel's actions are unknown (not in sight).

procedures.action: If hearing a fog signal apparently forward of the beam, or unable to avoid a close-quarters situation with a vessel forward of the beam, reduce speed to the minimum at which the vessel can be kept on course.
procedures.why: Reduces speed and reaction distance needed to avoid collision when the other vessel's position/heading is uncertain.

procedures.action: If necessary, take all way off.
procedures.why: Stopping the vessel entirely may be required to avoid collision when danger is imminent and unresolved.

procedures.action: Navigate with extreme caution until the danger of collision is over.
procedures.why: Restricted visibility conditions persist risk until the situation is fully resolved.

constraints: Applies only to vessels not in sight of one another in or near restricted visibility.
Avoiding action via course alteration should avoid turning to port for a vessel forward of the beam (except when overtaking) and avoid turning towards a vessel abeam/abaft the beam.
Speed reduction/stopping is not required if it has been determined that risk of collision does not exist.
warnings: Avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam (other than when overtaking).
Avoid altering course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.
Navigate with extreme caution until danger of collision is over.
outcomes: Proper speed, engine readiness, and cautious course alteration reduce risk of close-quarters or collision situations in restricted visibility.
Failure to reduce speed or take avoiding action when risk exists increases likelihood of collision with an unseen vessel.
key_facts: Rule 19 applies to vessels not in sight of one another in or near restricted visibility.
Power-driven vessels must keep engines ready for immediate manoeuvre in restricted visibility.
Radar-only detection of another vessel requires assessment of close-quarters/collision risk before acting.
Specific course alterations (to port for vessels forward of beam, or towards vessels abeam/abaft beam) should generally be avoided.
Vessels must reduce to minimum steerage speed or stop entirely if they hear a fog signal forward of the beam or cannot avoid a close-quarters situation.

chapter_title: PART B - STEERING AND SAILING RULES

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 17 defines the actions a stand-on vessel must and may take in a crossing or similar encounter where another vessel is required to keep out of the way.
trace.trigger: The give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action to avoid collision, or the situation has developed so close that collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone.

procedures.action: Keep course and speed as the stand-on vessel.
procedures.why: Allows the give-way vessel to predictably maneuver to keep out of the way.

procedures.action: Take action to avoid collision by own manoeuvre alone once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not complying with the Rules.
procedures.why: Permitted deviation to prevent collision when the other vessel fails to act appropriately.

procedures.action: If collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone, take whatever action best aids avoidance of collision.
procedures.why: In extremis, both vessels must act to prevent collision regardless of right-of-way status.

procedures.action: As a power-driven vessel taking action under (a)(ii) in a crossing situation, avoid altering course to port for a vessel on her own port side, if circumstances permit.
procedures.why: Prevents creating a new collision risk or confusing the other vessel's expected maneuver.

procedures.action: Recognize that the give-way vessel remains obligated to keep out of the way regardless of stand-on vessel's actions.
procedures.why: This Rule does not relieve the give-way vessel of her primary obligation.

constraints: Stand-on vessel must maintain course and speed until it is apparent the give-way vessel is not acting appropriately
Deviation under (a)(ii) is only permitted once non-compliance by the give-way vessel becomes apparent
Power-driven vessel acting under (a)(ii) in a crossing situation shall not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side, circumstances permitting
This Rule does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way
warnings: Premature or inappropriate action by the stand-on vessel can increase collision risk
Altering course to port for a vessel on own port side in a crossing situation is prohibited where circumstances admit otherwise
outcomes: Proper adherence allows predictable collision avoidance between give-way and stand-on vessels
Failure of give-way vessel to act appropriately obligates stand-on vessel to take independent action
In extremis, best available action by stand-on vessel aids collision avoidance
key_facts: Rule 17 governs the conduct of the stand-on vessel in a give-way/stand-on encounter
The stand-on vessel may depart from maintaining course and speed once it is apparent the give-way vessel is not complying
When collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone, the stand-on vessel must take the best available action
A power-driven stand-on vessel taking action in a crossing situation must not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side, if circumstances allow otherwise
The give-way vessel's obligation to keep out of the way is never relieved by this Rule

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 22 specifies the minimum visibility ranges required for navigation lights based on vessel length category.
trace.trigger: Determining whether a vessel's navigation lights meet the prescribed minimum visibility (intensity) requirements under the Rules.
constraints: Light intensity must conform to Section 8, Annex I of the Regulations
Vessels of 50 metres or more: masthead light 6 miles, sidelight/sternlight/towing light/all-round light 3 miles
Vessels 12m to <50m: masthead light 5 miles (3 miles if vessel <20m), sidelight/sternlight/towing light/all-round light 2 miles
Vessels less than 12m: masthead light 2 miles, sidelight 1 mile, sternlight/towing light/all-round light 2 miles
Inconspicuous, partly submerged vessels or objects being towed: white all-round light 3 miles
key_facts: Minimum light visibility ranges are tiered by vessel length: ≥50m, 12-50m, and <12m categories
A masthead light on a vessel under 20m (but ≥12m) need only be visible 3 miles instead of 5
Sidelights have shorter required ranges (1-3 miles) than masthead lights (2-6 miles) across all size categories
Partly submerged towed objects require a white all-round light visible at 3 miles regardless of their inconspicuous nature

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 21 provides formal definitions for the arcs of visibility and characteristics of the masthead light, sidelights, sternlight, towing light, all-round light, and flashing light used throughout Part C lighting rules.
constraints: Masthead light must show an unbroken arc of 225 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side.
Sidelights must each show an unbroken arc of 112.5 degrees, from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on their respective side.
Vessels less than 20 meters in length may combine sidelights into a single lantern on the fore and aft centreline.
Sternlight must show an unbroken arc of 135 degrees, 67.5 degrees from right aft on each side.
Towing light must have the same characteristics as the sternlight but shown in yellow.
All-round light must show an unbroken arc of 360 degrees.
Flashing light must flash at regular intervals at 120 or more flashes per minute.
outcomes: Correct understanding of these definitions enables proper interpretation and application of all subsequent lighting rules (Rules 22-31) governing vessel navigation lights.
key_facts: Masthead light: white, 225-degree arc, fore-and-aft centerline placement.
Sidelights: green (starboard) and red (port), each 112.5-degree arc; combinable into one lantern for vessels under 20 meters.
Sternlight: white, 135-degree arc, placed near the stern.
Towing light: yellow, same characteristics as sternlight.
All-round light: 360-degree arc; flashing light: 120+ flashes per minute.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 23 specifies the lights that power-driven vessels of various types and sizes must exhibit while underway.
trace.trigger: A power-driven vessel (including air-cushion vessels and WIG craft) is underway and must determine which navigation lights to display.

procedures.action: Exhibit a masthead light forward, a second masthead light abaft and higher than the forward one, sidelights, and a sternlight.
procedures.why: Standard configuration for power-driven vessels underway to indicate heading and aspect to other vessels.

procedures.action: If the vessel is less than 50 meters in length, the second (aft) masthead light may be omitted, though it may still be carried.
procedures.why: Smaller vessels are not obligated to carry the second masthead light but retain the option.

procedures.action: If operating as an air-cushion vessel in non-displacement mode, exhibit an all-round flashing yellow light in addition to the standard lights.
procedures.why: Distinguishes the unique operating mode of air-cushion vessels from standard power-driven vessels.

procedures.action: If the vessel is a WIG craft taking off, landing, or flying near the surface, exhibit a high intensity all-round flashing red light in addition to the standard lights.
procedures.why: Alerts other vessels to the distinctive flight profile and hazard of WIG craft near the surface.

procedures.action: If the vessel is less than 12 meters in length, may substitute an all-round white light and sidelights in lieu of the standard masthead/sternlight configuration.
procedures.why: Simplifies lighting requirements for small vessels where full configuration may be impractical.

procedures.action: If the vessel is less than 7 meters in length and max speed does not exceed 7 knots, may exhibit only an all-round white light, and should exhibit sidelights if practicable.
procedures.why: Further simplification for very small, slow vessels, balancing visibility needs with practicality.

procedures.action: If centreline fitting of the masthead light or all-round white light is not practicable on a vessel under 12 meters, it may be displaced off-centreline, provided sidelights are combined in one lantern on the centreline or as near as practicable to the masthead/all-round light's fore-and-aft line.
procedures.why: Accommodates physical/structural limitations of small vessels while maintaining a functional light configuration for collision avoidance.

constraints: Paragraph (c) regarding WIG craft lights entered into force on 29 November 2003, per Resolution A.919(22).
Vessels under 50 meters are exempt from carrying the second masthead light but may still choose to do so.
Substituted lighting (all-round white light and sidelights) is only permitted for vessels under 12 meters in length.
The simplest lighting option (all-round white light only) is only permitted for vessels under 7 meters with max speed ≤ 7 knots.
Combined sidelight lanterns must be on the centreline or as near as practicable to the masthead/all-round light line when displacement is used.
outcomes: Proper light exhibition allows other vessels to correctly identify vessel type, size, and aspect, reducing collision risk.
Failure to exhibit correct lights (or incorrect substitution for vessel size) could lead to misidentification by other vessels and increase collision risk.
key_facts: Rule 23 governs lights for power-driven vessels underway, including air-cushion vessels and WIG craft.
Vessels under 50m may omit the second (aft) masthead light.
Vessels under 12m may substitute an all-round white light and sidelights for the standard configuration.
Vessels under 7m with max speed ≤7 knots may use only an all-round white light, with sidelights if practicable.
Paragraph (c) on WIG craft lighting became effective 29 November 2003 via Resolution A.919(22).

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 24 specifies the navigation lights and shapes that power-driven vessels towing or pushing, and the vessels/objects being towed or pushed, must exhibit under different towing configurations.
trace.trigger: A power-driven vessel is engaged in towing (astern), pushing ahead, or towing alongside another vessel or object.

procedures.action: If towing astern, exhibit two masthead lights in a vertical line instead of Rule 23(a)(i)/(a)(ii) lights (three if tow length exceeds 200m), plus sidelights, sternlight, and a towing light above the sternlight.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a vessel engaged in towing from a normal power-driven vessel underway so other vessels can assess the situation and tow length.

procedures.action: If tow length exceeds 200 metres, exhibit a diamond shape where it can best be seen (on both towing vessel and the tow).
procedures.why: Warns other vessels of an unusually long and hazardous tow requiring extra sea room.

procedures.action: If pushing ahead or towing alongside (not a composite unit), exhibit two masthead lights in a vertical line, sidelights, and a sternlight.
procedures.why: Identifies the composite navigation profile of the pushing/alongside-towing arrangement.

procedures.action: If pushing vessel and pushed vessel are rigidly connected as a composite unit, exhibit lights prescribed in Rule 23 as for a single power-driven vessel.
procedures.why: A rigidly connected composite unit functions and maneuvers as one vessel, so single-vessel lighting is appropriate.

procedures.action: Ensure vessels/objects being towed exhibit sidelights and a sternlight, and a diamond shape if tow exceeds 200 metres.
procedures.why: Allows other traffic to identify the towed vessel/object's position and extent independently of the towing vessel.

procedures.action: For vessels towed alongside or pushed in a group, light the group as one vessel, with pushed vessel showing sidelights forward and towed-alongside vessel showing sternlight and forward sidelights.
procedures.why: Simplifies identification of multi-vessel tow/push groups as a single navigational unit while marking true extremities.

procedures.action: Also comply with Rule 23(a)(ii) (additional light requirement) when paragraph (a) or (c) applies.
procedures.why: Ensures full compliance with standard power-driven vessel lighting in addition to towing-specific lights.

constraints: Tow length is measured from the stern of the towing vessel to the after end of the tow.
Three masthead lights in vertical line required only when tow length exceeds 200 metres.
Diamond shape required only when tow length exceeds 200 metres.
Composite unit (rigid connection) exhibits Rule 23 lights, not Rule 24 towing lights.
Any number of vessels towed alongside or pushed in a group must be lighted as one vessel.
warnings: Failure to correctly light a long tow (>200m) with required diamond shape and three masthead lights can lead other vessels to misjudge the length and hazard of the tow.
outcomes: Correct exhibition of lights/shapes allows other vessels to accurately identify a towing/pushing operation, its length, and take appropriate collision-avoidance action.
Non-compliance risks misidentification of the tow as a normal vessel, increasing collision risk, especially with long tows.
key_facts: A towing power-driven vessel shows two masthead lights vertically (three if tow exceeds 200m) plus sidelights, sternlight, and a towing light above the sternlight.
A diamond shape is required when tow length exceeds 200 metres, on both towing vessel and towed object.
Composite units (rigidly connected pushing arrangements) are lighted as a single power-driven vessel per Rule 23.
Vessels towed alongside or pushed in a group are lighted collectively as one vessel.
Towed vessels/objects (not covered by paragraph g) show sidelights, sternlight, and diamond shape if tow exceeds 200m.

trace.situation: Lighting and shape requirements for inconspicuous, partly submerged towed vessels/objects, and exceptions when display is impracticable, under COLREG Rule 24 (Towing and pushing).
trace.trigger: A vessel is towing an inconspicuous, partly submerged vessel or object (or combination thereof), or towing circumstances make normal light/shape display impracticable (including towing a vessel in distress).

procedures.action: If the towed object is less than 25 metres in breadth, exhibit one all-round white light at or near the forward end and one at or near the after end (dracones exempt from forward light).
procedures.why: Marks the extent of a low-visibility, partly submerged tow for other vessels.

procedures.action: If the towed object is 25 metres or more in breadth, add two additional all-round white lights at or near the extremities of its breadth.
procedures.why: Indicates the full width of a wide, low-visibility tow.

procedures.action: If the tow exceeds 100 metres in length, add intermediate all-round white lights so spacing between lights does not exceed 100 metres.
procedures.why: Ensures long tows remain continuously visible along their length.

procedures.action: Exhibit a diamond shape at or near the aftermost extremity of the last vessel/object towed; if tow length exceeds 200 metres, add another diamond shape as far forward as practicable.
procedures.why: Provides daytime shape signals marking the extent of a long tow.

procedures.action: If it is impracticable to exhibit the prescribed lights/shapes for the towed vessel/object, take all possible measures to light it or otherwise indicate its presence.
procedures.why: Safety fallback to prevent collision when standard signals cannot be displayed.

procedures.action: If a vessel not normally engaged in towing cannot display the normal towing lights while towing a vessel in distress or needing assistance, it is exempted from those lights but must take all possible measures (e.g., illuminating the towline) to indicate the towing relationship per Rule 36.
procedures.why: Balances urgency of rescue/assistance towing against the need to warn other traffic of the towing relationship.

constraints: Dracones are exempt from exhibiting a forward light.
Spacing between additional white lights on tows over 100m must not exceed 100 metres.
Exemptions under (i) apply only to vessels not normally engaged in towing and only when towing a vessel in distress or needing assistance.
Even when exempted, all possible measures must still be taken to indicate the towing relationship (e.g., via Rule 36 signals/illuminated towline).
warnings: Failure to adequately light or shape an inconspicuous, partly submerged tow risks collision due to its low visibility.
Exemption from standard towing lights does not remove the obligation to signal the towing relationship by other means.
outcomes: Proper lighting/shape display on wide, long, or submerged tows enables other vessels to recognize and avoid the tow.
Use of fallback measures when standard signals are impracticable reduces collision risk despite non-standard compliance.
Illuminating the towline when distress-towing allows other vessels to understand the vessel relationship despite missing normal towing lights.
key_facts: Inconspicuous, partly submerged towed objects require specific all-round white lights based on breadth and length.
Diamond shapes mark the aftermost extremity of a tow, with an additional one required if tow length exceeds 200 metres.
Vessels unable to comply due to impracticability must still take all possible measures to indicate presence.
Vessels towing a distressed vessel may be exempted from standard towing lights but must indicate the towing relationship via Rule 36, e.g., illuminating the towline.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 25 specifies the lights and shapes a sailing vessel underway (including vessels under oars and vessels under sail with auxiliary machinery) must exhibit.
trace.trigger: A sailing vessel, or a vessel under oars, is underway, or a sailing vessel is simultaneously being propelled by machinery.

procedures.action: Exhibit sidelights and a sternlight while a sailing vessel is underway.
procedures.why: Required baseline lighting configuration under paragraph (a).

procedures.action: If vessel is less than 20 metres, may combine sidelights and sternlight into one lantern carried at or near the masthead.
procedures.why: Permitted simplification for smaller sailing vessels where it can best be seen.

procedures.action: Optionally exhibit two all-round lights in a vertical line (red over green) at or near the masthead, in addition to paragraph (a) lights.
procedures.why: Provides additional identification as a sailing vessel, but must not be combined with the lantern of paragraph (b).

procedures.action: For vessels under 7 metres, exhibit lights of (a) or (b) if practicable; otherwise keep an electric torch or lighted lantern with white light ready at hand and show it in time to prevent collision.
procedures.why: Ensures minimum visibility for small craft unable to carry full light configuration.

procedures.action: For vessels under oars, exhibit sailing vessel lights if possible; otherwise keep a torch/lantern with white light ready and show it in time to prevent collision.
procedures.why: Same minimum collision-avoidance visibility requirement extended to rowed vessels.

procedures.action: When a sailing vessel is also being propelled by machinery, exhibit a conical shape, apex downwards, forward where it can best be seen.
procedures.why: Signals to other vessels that the vessel is under power (and thus a power-driven vessel for COLREG purposes) despite having sails set.

constraints: Red-over-green masthead lights (paragraph c) must not be shown together with the combined lantern of paragraph (b).
Lights/shapes must be positioned where they can best be seen.
Torch/lantern substitute lighting must be shown in sufficient time to prevent collision.
warnings: Do not combine the all-round red-over-green masthead lights with the combined lantern permitted under paragraph (b).
Small sailing vessels and vessels under oars without prescribed lights must be ready to show a white light in time to prevent collision.
outcomes: Compliance ensures sailing vessels are correctly identified and distinguished from power-driven vessels at night or in restricted visibility.
Exhibiting the conical shape when under sail and power prevents other vessels from misapplying sailing vessel right-of-way rules.
key_facts: A sailing vessel underway must show sidelights and a sternlight.
Vessels under 20m may combine these into a single masthead lantern.
An optional red-over-green vertical light pair may be shown at the masthead but not with the combined lantern.
Vessels under 7m and vessels under oars may substitute a ready white torch/lantern if full lights are impracticable.
A sailing vessel also under machinery power must show a downward-pointing conical shape forward.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 26 prescribes the lights and shapes that fishing vessels (trawling and non-trawling) must exhibit whether underway, making way, or at anchor.
trace.trigger: A vessel is engaged in fishing (trawling or other methods) and must determine which navigation lights/shapes to display.

procedures.action: If engaged in fishing, exhibit only the lights/shapes prescribed in this Rule and no others.
procedures.why: Prevents confusion with other vessel light configurations under the Rules.

procedures.action: If trawling, show two all-round lights vertical (green over white) or two cones apex-to-apex vertically.
procedures.why: Identifies vessel as trawling to other mariners for collision avoidance.

procedures.action: If trawling and 50m or more in length, also show a masthead light abaft and higher than the green all-round light (optional if under 50m).
procedures.why: Provides additional indication of heading/orientation for larger trawlers.

procedures.action: If making way through the water while trawling or fishing, add sidelights and a sternlight to the prescribed fishing lights.
procedures.why: Indicates vessel is moving, not stationary, so other vessels can assess risk of collision correctly.

procedures.action: If fishing other than trawling, show two all-round lights vertical (red over white) or two cones apex-to-apex vertically.
procedures.why: Distinguishes non-trawling fishing vessels from trawlers.

procedures.action: If outlying gear extends more than 150 metres horizontally, exhibit an all-round white light or a cone apex upward in the direction of the gear.
procedures.why: Warns other vessels of extended gear hazard beyond the vessel's hull.

procedures.action: When in close proximity to other fishing vessels, apply the additional signals in Annex II.
procedures.why: Additional signals help prevent collisions in crowded fishing grounds.

procedures.action: When not engaged in fishing, do not display fishing lights/shapes; show only lights prescribed for the vessel's length.
procedures.why: Avoids misrepresenting vessel status to other mariners.

constraints: Lights/shapes under this Rule apply whether the vessel is underway or at anchor while fishing.
Vessels under 50 metres in length are exempt from the additional masthead light requirement while trawling, though they may still display it.
Additional sidelights and sternlight are only required when making way through the water.
A vessel not engaged in fishing must not use fishing lights/shapes.
warnings: Do not exhibit fishing lights/shapes unless actually engaged in fishing.
Failure to show outlying gear light/shape when gear extends over 150m creates a collision hazard for vessels unaware of the extended gear.
outcomes: Correct display of lights/shapes allows other vessels to identify fishing vessel status and gear, reducing collision risk.
Incorrect or incomplete signaling (e.g., omitting sidelights/sternlight while making way) could lead to misjudgment of vessel movement by other mariners.
key_facts: Trawling vessels show green-over-white all-round lights or two apex-together cones.
Non-trawling fishing vessels show red-over-white all-round lights or two apex-together cones.
An all-round white light or upward cone indicates outlying gear exceeding 150 metres horizontally.
Vessels under 50m trawling are exempt from the additional masthead light, though it is optional.
A vessel not fishing must only show lights appropriate to her length, not fishing signals.

When is the additional masthead light required for a trawling vessel?

trace.situation: COLREG rule describing the optional additional lights/shapes a power-driven vessel constrained by her draught may exhibit to signal her status to other vessels.
trace.trigger: A power-driven vessel is constrained by her draught and wishes to indicate this status to other vessels at night or by day.

procedures.action: Exhibit the normal power-driven vessel lights required under Rule 23.
procedures.why: The vessel remains a power-driven vessel underway and must show those lights regardless.

procedures.action: Additionally exhibit, where they can best be seen, three all-round red lights in a vertical line (at night) or a cylinder (by day) to indicate constrained-by-draught status.
procedures.why: Alerts other vessels that the vessel has limited maneuverability due to draught in relation to available depth of water, so they can take appropriate action to avoid close-quarters situations.

constraints: This signal is optional ('may'), not mandatory.
Applies only to vessels constrained by their draught, in addition to Rule 23 power-driven vessel lights.
Lights/shape must be exhibited where they can best be seen.
outcomes: Other vessels can identify the vessel as constrained by draught and give appropriate sea room or priority.
key_facts: The signal consists of three all-round red lights in a vertical line at night.
By day, the equivalent signal is a cylinder shape.
This additional signal supplements, not replaces, the standard power-driven vessel lights under Rule 23.
Use of this signal is discretionary ('may exhibit').

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 27 specifies the lights and shapes to be exhibited by vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre, towing vessels severely restricted in deviating course, and vessels engaged in dredging or underwater operations.
trace.trigger: A vessel becomes not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, engaged in a restrictive towing operation, or engaged in dredging/underwater operations requiring exhibition of special lights/shapes.

procedures.action: If not under command, exhibit two all-round red lights in a vertical line and two balls/similar shapes in a vertical line where best seen.
procedures.why: Signals to other vessels that the vessel cannot manoeuvre as required by the Rules.

procedures.action: If not under command and making way through the water, also show sidelights and a sternlight.
procedures.why: Indicates heading/movement in addition to the not-under-command status lights.

procedures.action: If restricted in ability to manoeuvre (except mineclearance), exhibit three vertical all-round lights (red-white-red) or three shapes (ball-diamond-ball) where best seen.
procedures.why: Distinguishes restricted-manoeuvrability status from not-under-command and normal vessels.

procedures.action: If restricted in ability to manoeuvre and making way, add masthead light(s), sidelights, and sternlight to the prescribed lights.
procedures.why: Provides additional navigational information while underway.

procedures.action: If restricted in ability to manoeuvre and at anchor, add the anchor light/shape prescribed in Rule 30 to the restricted-manoeuvrability lights/shapes.
procedures.why: Combines anchor status indication with restricted-manoeuvrability status.

procedures.action: If a power-driven vessel is towing in a manner that severely restricts the tow's ability to deviate course, exhibit Rule 24(a) towing lights/shapes plus the restricted-in-ability-to-manoeuvre lights/shapes (b)(i) and (ii).
procedures.why: Alerts other vessels to the compounded restriction from both towing and manoeuvrability limitation.

procedures.action: If engaged in dredging/underwater operations and restricted in ability to manoeuvre, exhibit (b)(i),(ii),(iii) lights/shapes, and when an obstruction exists, show two red lights/balls on the obstructed side and two green lights/diamonds on the passing side.
procedures.why: Indicates the safe side for other vessels to pass around the obstruction.

procedures.action: If the dredging/underwater operations vessel is at anchor, exhibit the obstruction-indicating lights/shapes in lieu of the Rule 30 anchor light/shape.
procedures.why: Ensures obstruction-side information takes priority over standard anchor signals in this situation.

constraints: Mineclearance vessels are excepted from the restricted-in-ability-to-manoeuvre light/shape requirements in (b).
Lights/shapes must be exhibited where they can best be seen.
Additional lights (sidelights, sternlight, masthead light) are required only when making way through the water.
Anchor light/shape under Rule 30 applies only if not superseded by dredging/underwater obstruction lights.
warnings: Failure to correctly display these signals may cause other vessels to misjudge the vessel's manoeuvring capability, increasing collision risk.
Obstruction side signals must be correctly oriented (red = obstruction side, green = passing side) to avoid misdirecting other traffic.
outcomes: Other vessels can identify the nature of the restriction (not under command vs. restricted manoeuvrability vs. towing vs. dredging) and take appropriate avoiding action.
Correct display of obstruction-side lights allows safe passage around dredging/underwater operation vessels.
key_facts: Not under command vessels show two red all-round lights and two ball shapes vertically.
Restricted-in-ability-to-manoeuvre vessels show three vertical lights (red-white-red) or three shapes (ball-diamond-ball).
Mineclearance vessels are excluded from the Rule 27(b) restricted-manoeuvrability signal requirement.
Dredging/underwater operations vessels must show red lights/balls on the obstructed side and green lights/diamonds on the passable side when an obstruction exists.
At anchor, dredging/underwater vessels use obstruction-indicating signals instead of the standard Rule 30 anchor light/shape.
