Why must a towing vessel severely restricted in course deviation show both towing and restricted-manoeuvrability signals?

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 27 specifies alternative light/shape signals for vessels engaged in diving operations too small to exhibit full signals, and for vessels engaged in mineclearance operations, plus exemptions for small vessels and clarification that these signals are not distress signals.
trace.trigger: A vessel is engaged in diving operations and cannot practicably exhibit the full set of lights/shapes under paragraph (d), or a vessel is engaged in mineclearance operations, or a vessel is under 12 metres in length (other than diving vessels).

procedures.action: If impracticable to exhibit all diving-operation lights/shapes, display three all-round lights in a vertical line (red-white-red from top to bottom) where best seen, plus a rigid replica of Code flag 'A' at least 1 metre high with all-round visibility.
procedures.why: Provides a reduced but visible signal set for small diving vessels unable to carry the full Rule 27(d) signal array.

procedures.action: For mineclearance operations, exhibit power-driven vessel lights (Rule 23) or anchor lights/shape (Rule 30) as appropriate, plus three all-round green lights or three balls positioned near the foremast head and at each end of the fore yard.
procedures.why: Warns other vessels that approaching within 1000 metres of the mineclearance vessel is dangerous.

procedures.action: Do not require vessels under 12 metres (except diving vessels) to exhibit the Rule 27 lights and shapes.
procedures.why: Small vessel exemption recognizes impracticality of carrying these signals.

procedures.action: Do not interpret Rule 27 signals as distress signals; refer to Annex IV for actual distress signals.
procedures.why: Prevents confusion between operational status signals and genuine distress signalling.

procedures.action: When combining Not Under Command (NUC) red lights with Restricted Ability to Manoeuvre (RAM) lights, ensure vertical/horizontal spacing complies with COLREG and that the RAM white light can be switched on independently from the two NUC red lights.
procedures.why: Unified interpretation (MSC.1/Circ.1260) ensures correct and unambiguous signalling when a vessel's status changes between NUC and RAM.

constraints: Applies only when exhibiting full diving-operation signals under paragraph (d) is impracticable due to vessel size.
Mineclearance signal lights/shapes must be positioned near the foremast head and each end of the fore yard.
Exemption for vessels under 12 metres does not apply to those engaged in diving operations.
Electrical system for combined NUC/RAM lighting must allow independent switching of the RAM white light.
warnings: Approaching within 1000 metres of a mineclearance vessel exhibiting the prescribed lights/shapes is dangerous.
The signals prescribed in Rule 27 are not distress signals and must not be mistaken for them.
outcomes: Correct exhibition of reduced diving-operation signals allows small vessels to legally indicate their status despite size limitations.
Other vessels are warned to keep clear of mineclearance operations within 1000 metres, reducing collision/mine-related risk.
Proper independent switching of NUC and RAM lights avoids ambiguous signalling about a vessel's maneuvering status.
key_facts: Small diving vessels unable to show full Rule 27(d) signals must show three vertical all-round lights (red-white-red) plus a 1m+ Code flag 'A' replica.
Mineclearance vessels show three all-round green lights or three balls near the foremast head and fore yard ends, in addition to power-driven or anchor signals.
It is dangerous to approach within 1000 metres of a mineclearance vessel exhibiting these signals.
Vessels under 12 metres (except diving vessels) are exempt from Rule 27 lights/shapes.
Rule 27 signals are not distress signals; distress signals are in Annex IV.

trace.situation: COLREGS Rule specifying the lights and shapes to be exhibited by a vessel engaged on pilotage duty, whether underway or at anchor, and by a pilot vessel when not on pilotage duty.
trace.trigger: A vessel is engaged on, or has ceased, pilotage duty and must display appropriate navigation lights/shapes.

procedures.action: Exhibit two all-round lights in a vertical line at or near the masthead, upper white and lower red, at all times while engaged on pilotage duty.
procedures.why: Identifies the vessel distinctly as a pilot vessel to other vessels.

procedures.action: When underway, additionally exhibit sidelights and a sternlight.
procedures.why: Provides standard underway navigation lights so other vessels can assess aspect and give way appropriately.

procedures.action: When at anchor, additionally exhibit the light(s) or shape prescribed in Rule 30 for vessels at anchor, in addition to the masthead pilotage lights.
procedures.why: Ensures the vessel is recognized both as a pilot vessel and as anchored, per Rule 30 requirements.

procedures.action: When not engaged on pilotage duty, exhibit the lights or shapes prescribed for a vessel of her length instead of pilotage lights.
procedures.why: Avoids misleading other vessels into believing pilotage duty is in progress when it is not.

constraints: Pilotage lights (white over red) must be shown at or near the masthead only while actually engaged on pilotage duty.
Underway pilot vessels must also show sidelights and sternlight in addition to the masthead lights.
At anchor, the Rule 30 anchor light/shape must be added to the pilotage lights.
When not on pilotage duty, the vessel must revert to standard lights/shapes for her length category.
warnings: Failure to switch between pilotage and standard lights appropriately could mislead other vessels about the vessel's status and intentions.
outcomes: Other vessels correctly identify a pilot vessel's status (on/off duty, underway/at anchor) and take appropriate collision-avoidance action.
key_facts: Pilot vessel engaged on pilotage duty shows two vertical all-round lights at/near masthead: white over red.
Underway pilot vessels add sidelights and sternlight to the masthead lights.
At anchor, pilot vessels add Rule 30 anchor lights/shapes to the masthead pilotage lights.
A pilot vessel not engaged on pilotage duty must show lights/shapes for a vessel of her own length, not pilotage lights.

trace.situation: COLREG rule addressing seaplanes and Wing-In-Ground (WIG) craft that cannot practicably comply with the standard light and shape requirements set out in Part C of the Collision Regulations.
trace.trigger: A seaplane or WIG craft finds it impracticable to exhibit lights and shapes with the exact characteristics or in the exact positions prescribed elsewhere in the Rules.

procedures.action: If exhibiting the prescribed lights/shapes in their specified characteristics or positions is impracticable, exhibit lights and shapes as closely similar in characteristics and position as possible.
procedures.why: Ensures the vessel/craft remains as visible and identifiable as practicable to other traffic despite physical/design limitations preventing exact compliance.

constraints: Applies only to seaplanes and WIG craft, not conventional vessels
Deviation from prescribed lights/shapes is permitted only when exact compliance is impracticable
Substituted lights/shapes must be as closely similar as possible to those prescribed
outcomes: Other vessels can still reasonably interpret the craft's lights/shapes despite non-exact compliance, supporting collision avoidance

It specifically covers seaplanes and WIG (Wing-In-Ground) craft
The standard allows approximation of lights/shapes when exact compliance is impracticable due to the craft's characteristics

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS

trace.situation: COLREG Part D defines key terms used in sound and light signalling between vessels, specifically 'whistle', 'short blast', and 'prolonged blast'.
constraints: A whistle must be capable of producing the prescribed blasts and must comply with Annex III specifications.
A short blast must be about one second's duration.
A prolonged blast must be four to six seconds' duration.
outcomes: Consistent definitions ensure all vessels interpret sound signals (e.g. maneuvering and warning signals) correctly and uniformly, reducing collision risk due to signal misinterpretation.
key_facts: 'Whistle' refers to any sound signalling appliance that can produce the prescribed blasts and complies with Annex III.
A 'short blast' is defined as a blast of about one second's duration.
A 'prolonged blast' is defined as a blast lasting from four to six seconds.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 30 specifies the lights and shapes that vessels at anchor or aground must exhibit, with exemptions based on vessel length.
trace.trigger: A vessel is at anchor or has run aground and must display appropriate lights/shapes for visibility to other vessels.

procedures.action: Exhibit an all-round white light or ball forward, and a second all-round white light aft at a lower level, when at anchor.
procedures.why: Rule 30(a) requires these signals where they can best be seen to indicate an anchored vessel.

procedures.action: If vessel is less than 50 metres in length, may exhibit a single all-round white light instead of the two-light configuration.
procedures.why: Rule 30(b) provides a simplified option for smaller vessels.

procedures.action: Use working or equivalent deck lights to illuminate decks; mandatory for vessels 100 metres and more in length.
procedures.why: Rule 30(c) ensures large anchored vessels remain conspicuous and their decks visible.

procedures.action: If aground, exhibit the anchor lights/shape from (a) or (b) plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line and three balls in a vertical line.
procedures.why: Rule 30(d) signals the more hazardous aground condition to approaching vessels.

procedures.action: If vessel is less than 7 metres and not anchored in or near a narrow channel, fairway, or anchorage, or where vessels normally navigate, anchor lights/shapes are not required.
procedures.why: Rule 30(e) exempts small vessels in low-risk anchoring locations.

procedures.action: If vessel is less than 12 metres and aground, the additional red lights/balls under (d)(i) and (ii) are not required.
procedures.why: Rule 30(f) exempts small vessels from the extra aground signals.

constraints: Lights/shapes must be exhibited where they can best be seen.
Vessel length thresholds (7m, 12m, 50m, 100m) determine which signal configuration or exemption applies.
Exemption in (e) only applies if vessel is not in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage, or area of normal navigation.
warnings: Vessels of 100 metres and more in length must use deck illumination lights, not merely optional.
A vessel aground must display both anchor signals and additional red lights/balls, except where exempted by length.
outcomes: Proper display of anchor/aground lights and shapes allows other vessels to correctly identify vessel status and avoid collision.
Failure to exhibit correct signals may lead to misidentification of vessel status by approaching traffic, increasing collision risk.
key_facts: Anchored vessels show a forward all-round white light/ball and a lower-level aft all-round white light.
Vessels under 50m may use a single all-round white light instead of the two-light anchor configuration.
Vessels 100m and more must use working/equivalent lights to illuminate decks while at anchor.
Aground vessels must add two vertical red lights and three vertical balls to their anchor signals.
Vessels under 7m (if not in high-traffic areas) and under 12m (aground) have specific exemptions from signal requirements.

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 33 specifies the sound signalling equipment (whistle, bell, gong) that vessels of various lengths must carry aboard.
trace.trigger: Vessel length determines which sound signalling appliances must be carried; applies at all times a vessel is underway or at anchor requiring sound signals.

procedures.action: Equip vessels of 12 metres or more in length with a whistle.
procedures.why: Minimum sound signalling requirement under Rule 33(a).

procedures.action: Equip vessels of 20 metres or more in length with a bell in addition to the whistle.
procedures.why: Required for larger vessels per Rule 33(a).

procedures.action: Equip vessels of 100 metres or more in length with a gong whose tone cannot be confused with the bell, in addition to whistle and bell.
procedures.why: Ensures distinct signalling capability on very large vessels per Rule 33(a).

procedures.action: Ensure whistle, bell, and gong comply with Annex III specifications.
procedures.why: Standardizes sound characteristics across vessels for recognizability.

procedures.action: If replacing bell or gong with other equipment, ensure manual sounding capability is always retained.
procedures.why: Guarantees signal can be made even if automated equipment fails.

procedures.action: For vessels less than 12 metres, provide some other means of making an efficient sound signal if whistle/bell/gong are not carried.
procedures.why: Ensures all vessels retain capability to signal even if exempt from full equipment requirements per Rule 33(b).

constraints: Paragraph (a) entered into force on 29 November 2003 as amended by Resolution A.910(22).
Bell or gong replacement equipment must preserve manual sounding capability.
Vessels under 12 metres are exempt from mandatory whistle/bell/gong but must have an alternative efficient sound-signal means.
warnings: Gong tone must not be confused with bell tone, to avoid signal misinterpretation.
Manual sounding must always remain possible even if automated equipment is used.
outcomes: Vessels equipped per Rule 33 can reliably produce required sound signals for collision avoidance and navigation under COLREGs.
Non-compliance may result in inability to make required signals, increasing collision risk.
key_facts: Vessels 12m+ must carry a whistle.
Vessels 20m+ must carry a bell in addition to the whistle.
Vessels 100m+ must carry a gong distinguishable from the bell.

Bell/gong may be replaced by equivalent equipment if manual sounding remains possible.

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 34 prescribes sound and light signals power-driven vessels must use when manoeuvring in sight of one another, including overtaking in narrow channels and signalling doubt about another vessel's actions.
trace.trigger: Vessels are in sight of one another and a power-driven vessel is manoeuvring as authorized or required by the Rules, including overtaking situations in a narrow channel/fairway or doubt about the other vessel's intentions.

procedures.action: Sound one short blast when altering course to starboard.
procedures.why: Indicates the manoeuvre being carried out per Rule 34(a).

procedures.action: Sound two short blasts when altering course to port.
procedures.why: Indicates the manoeuvre being carried out per Rule 34(a).

procedures.action: Sound three short blasts when operating astern propulsion.
procedures.why: Indicates the manoeuvre being carried out per Rule 34(a).

procedures.action: Optionally supplement whistle signals with light signals (flashes matching blast counts) during the manoeuvre.
procedures.why: Allows vessels without clear whistle audibility or for added clarity to confirm manoeuvre visually, per Rule 34(b).

procedures.action: Ensure light signal flashes last about one second with one second intervals, and at least ten seconds between successive signals, using an all-round white light visible at least 5 miles complying with Annex I.
procedures.why: Standardizes light signal timing and visibility for unambiguous interpretation.

procedures.action: In a narrow channel or fairway, when intending to overtake, sound two prolonged blasts followed by one short blast (overtake on starboard) or two prolonged blasts followed by two short blasts (overtake on port).
procedures.why: Communicates overtaking intention as required under Rule 9(e)(i).

procedures.action: As the vessel being overtaken, if in agreement, sound one prolonged, one short, one prolonged and one short blast in that order.
procedures.why: Confirms agreement to the overtaking manoeuvre under Rule 9(e)(i).

procedures.action: If either vessel fails to understand the other's intentions or doubts sufficient action is being taken to avoid collision, immediately sound at least five short and rapid blasts.
procedures.why: Alerts the other vessel to the doubt so corrective action can be taken to avoid collision.

constraints: Signals under this Rule apply only when vessels are in sight of one another.
Light signals are optional supplements to whistle signals, not substitutes.
Light used for signalling must be an all-round white light visible at minimum 5 miles and comply with Annex I.
Overtaking signals must be given in compliance with Rule 9(e)(i) and only in narrow channels or fairways.
Doubt signal (five short rapid blasts) must be given immediately upon doubt arising.
warnings: Failure to signal doubt immediately when uncertain of another vessel's actions increases collision risk.
Light signals must meet exact timing specifications to avoid misinterpretation.
Overtaking in narrow channels requires explicit signalled agreement before proceeding.
outcomes: Proper use of manoeuvring signals allows other vessels to anticipate and respond to course changes, reducing collision risk.
Clear overtaking signals and agreement prevent confusion in congested narrow channels.
Prompt doubt signal (five short rapid blasts) prompts both vessels to take additional avoiding action.
key_facts: One short blast = altering course to starboard; two short blasts = altering course to port; three short blasts = operating astern propulsion.
Light signals may supplement whistle signals using flashes of about one second duration with corresponding meanings.
Overtaking vessel signals intention with two prolonged plus one or two short blasts depending on side; vessel being overtaken agrees with a specific four-blast pattern.
Five or more short rapid blasts indicate doubt about the other vessel's intentions or sufficient avoiding action.
These signals only apply when vessels are in sight of one another.

When should I sound five short rapid blasts under Rule 34?

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 34 provisions on sound/light signals for vessels nearing blind bends in a channel and rules for whistle placement on larger vessels.
trace.trigger: A vessel is approaching a bend, channel, or fairway area where an intervening obstruction may obscure other vessels, or a vessel has whistles fitted more than 100 metres apart.

procedures.action: Sound one prolonged blast when nearing a bend or obstructed area of a channel/fairway.
procedures.why: To warn other vessels that may be obscured by the intervening obstruction of your presence.

procedures.action: Answer with a prolonged blast if you are an approaching vessel within hearing around the bend or behind the obstruction.
procedures.why: To acknowledge the warning signal and alert the signaling vessel of your own presence.

procedures.action: Use only one whistle for manoeuvring and warning signals if whistles are fitted more than 100 metres apart.
procedures.why: To avoid sending confusing or duplicate sound signals from widely separated whistle positions.

procedures.action: Optionally supplement the manoeuvring/warning sound signal with a light signal of at least five short and rapid flashes.
procedures.why: To provide an additional visual warning that reinforces the sound signal.

constraints: The bend/obstruction signal must be one prolonged blast, not short blasts.
An approaching vessel within hearing must answer with a prolonged blast.
If whistles are fitted more than 100 metres apart, only one whistle shall be used for manoeuvring and warning signals.
The light signal supplement, if used, must consist of at least five short and rapid flashes.
warnings: Failure to sound a bend signal risks collision with vessels obscured by an intervening obstruction.
Failure to answer a bend signal may result in a vessel around the bend being unaware of an approaching vessel.
outcomes: Proper exchange of prolonged blasts between vessels at a bend reduces risk of collision from blind approaches.
Use of a single whistle when whistles are widely spaced prevents conflicting or overlapping sound signals.
key_facts: A vessel nearing a bend or obstructed area must sound one prolonged blast.
Any approaching vessel within hearing around the bend must answer with a prolonged blast.
If whistles are fitted more than 100 metres apart, only one whistle shall be used for manoeuvring and warning signals.
Sound signals may be supplemented by a light signal of at least five short and rapid flashes.

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 35 specifies the sound signals that different categories of vessels must make when in or near an area of restricted visibility, by day or night.
trace.trigger: A vessel is in or near an area of restricted visibility (e.g., fog, mist, heavy rain, sandstorm) at any time of day or night.

procedures.action: If power-driven and making way through the water, sound one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
procedures.why: Signals to nearby vessels that the ship is underway and moving in restricted visibility.

procedures.action: If power-driven, underway but stopped and making no way, sound two prolonged blasts with about 2 seconds between them, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a stopped vessel from one making way, informing others of its reduced movement status.

procedures.action: If not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre, constrained by draught, a sailing vessel, engaged in fishing, or towing/pushing another vessel, sound one prolonged followed by two short blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes instead of (a) or (b) signals.
procedures.why: Alerts other vessels to the special manoeuvring limitations of these vessel types in low visibility.

procedures.action: If a fishing vessel at anchor or a vessel restricted in ability to manoeuvre while working at anchor, sound the Rule 35(c) signal instead of the anchor signal in paragraph (g).
procedures.why: Communicates that the vessel's operational status creates manoeuvring constraints despite being anchored.

procedures.action: If being towed (last vessel of a tow, if manned), sound one prolonged followed by three short blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, made immediately after the towing vessel's signal when practicable.
procedures.why: Identifies the towed vessel's position and status to vessels in the vicinity.

procedures.action: If a pushing vessel and pushed vessel are rigidly connected as a composite unit, treat the unit as a power-driven vessel and use signals (a) or (b).
procedures.why: The rigid connection means the unit manoeuvres as a single power-driven vessel, so standard power-driven signals apply.

procedures.action: If at anchor, ring the bell rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than one minute; vessels 100m or more in length must also sound the gong in the after part immediately after the bell in the forepart.
procedures.why: Provides an audible indication of an anchored vessel's position and length category to approaching traffic.

constraints: Signals apply only in or near an area of restricted visibility, day or night.
Intervals between signals must not exceed 2 minutes (or 1 minute for anchor bell).
Specific vessel categories must use the prescribed substitute signal instead of the general power-driven vessel signals.
Vessels 100 metres or more in length have an additional gong requirement when at anchor.
warnings: Failure to sound the correct signal for vessel status/type in restricted visibility may lead to collision risk due to misidentification by other vessels.
outcomes: Other vessels in the vicinity are able to identify a vessel's type, status (underway, stopped, anchored, towing, restricted), and approximate position through sound alone in conditions where visual sighting is not possible.
key_facts: Power-driven vessels making way sound one prolonged blast every 2 minutes; if stopped, two prolonged blasts with a 2-second gap.

Vessels not under command, restricted in manoeuvrability, constrained by draught, sailing, fishing, or towing/pushing sound one prolonged plus two short blasts instead of standard power-driven signals.
A towed vessel sounds one prolonged plus three short blasts, ideally right after the towing vessel's signal.
A composite unit of pushing vessel and vessel pushed ahead, if rigidly connected, is treated as a single power-driven vessel for signalling purposes.
Anchored vessels ring the bell rapidly for about 5 seconds every minute; vessels 100m+ also sound a gong aft immediately after the bell forward.

Which signal applies if my vessel is engaged in fishing while at anchor in restricted visibility?

Why do vessels constrained by draught or restricted in manoeuvrability use a different signal than a standard power-driven vessel?

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 35 sound signal requirements in restricted visibility for vessels at anchor, aground, small vessels, and pilot vessels.
trace.trigger: Vessel is anchored, aground, or underway in or near an area of restricted visibility and must make sound signals to warn other vessels of position and avoid collision.

procedures.action: A vessel at anchor may sound one short, one prolonged, one short blast in addition to required signals to warn an approaching vessel of her position and collision risk.
procedures.why: Gives explicit warning of position and possibility of collision to an approaching vessel.

procedures.action: A vessel aground shall give the bell signal (and gong signal if required) plus three separate distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after rapid bell ringing.
procedures.why: Distinguishes an aground vessel's signal from a vessel merely at anchor.

procedures.action: A vessel aground may additionally sound an appropriate whistle signal.
procedures.why: Provides extra audible warning of her grounded, immobile status.

procedures.action: A vessel 12m to <20m in length not giving the prescribed bell signals shall instead make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
procedures.why: Ensures smaller vessels without full signalling equipment still provide regular audible warning.

procedures.action: A vessel under 12m in length not giving the above signals shall make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
procedures.why: Maintains minimum collision-warning capability for the smallest vessels exempted from bell/gong requirements.

procedures.action: A pilot vessel engaged on pilotage duty may sound an identity signal of four short blasts in addition to signals under paragraphs (a), (b) or (g).
procedures.why: Allows other vessels to identify a pilot vessel distinctly during restricted visibility operations.

constraints: Bell/gong signal exemptions apply only to vessels under 20 metres in length.
Vessels exempted from bell signals must still signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes using some other efficient method.
Aground vessel signal must include the distinct bell strokes before and after rapid ringing, not just the standard anchor bell signal.
warnings: Failure to give required or substitute sound signals in restricted visibility increases collision risk with approaching vessels.
Vessels aground must distinguish their signal from anchored vessels to avoid confusion.
outcomes: Approaching vessels are warned of anchored or aground vessel's position and collision risk.
Small vessels remain audible to traffic even without bell/gong equipment.
Pilot vessels are identifiable as such during pilotage operations in restricted visibility.
key_facts: A vessel at anchor may add one short, one prolonged, one short blast as a collision warning.
An aground vessel must give bell signal plus three distinct strokes before and after rapid ringing, and may add a whistle signal.
Vessels 12m to <20m and vessels under 12m are exempt from bell signals but must then signal every 2 minutes by other efficient means.
A pilot vessel on pilotage duty may add four short blasts as an identity signal.

chapter_title: PART D - SOUND AND LIGHT SIGNALS

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 36 permits a vessel to use supplementary light or sound signals to attract the attention of another vessel when necessary, outside the formally prescribed signal set.
trace.trigger: A vessel needs to attract the attention of another vessel, such as to warn of a danger of collision or hazard.

procedures.action: Make light or sound signals that cannot be mistaken for any signal authorized elsewhere in the Rules, if necessary to attract another vessel's attention.
procedures.why: Prevents confusion with prescribed COLREG signals that have specific meanings.

procedures.action: Alternatively, direct the beam of a searchlight toward the direction of danger.
procedures.why: Provides a visual means of drawing attention to a hazard.

procedures.action: Ensure the searchlight beam does not embarrass (dazzle/confuse) any vessel.
procedures.why: Avoids creating a new hazard or impairing another vessel's navigation/visibility.

procedures.action: Ensure any attention-attracting light cannot be mistaken for an aid to navigation.
procedures.why: Misidentification as a navigation aid could mislead other vessels' position-fixing or course decisions.

procedures.action: Avoid using high intensity intermittent or revolving lights, such as strobe lights, for this purpose.
procedures.why: Such lights could be mistaken for authorized signals or otherwise cause confusion/danger.

constraints: Signal must not be mistaken for any signal authorized elsewhere in the Rules.
Searchlight beam must not embarrass any vessel.
Any light used must not be mistaken for an aid to navigation.
High intensity intermittent or revolving lights (e.g., strobe lights) must be avoided.
warnings: Do not use signals that could be mistaken for other authorized COLREG signals.
Do not use lights that could be confused with aids to navigation.
Avoid strobe or similar high intensity intermittent/revolving lights.
outcomes: Proper use of attention-attracting signals helps prevent collisions without creating confusion with standardized signals.
Misuse (e.g., strobe lights or signals resembling authorized ones) could mislead other vessels and increase collision risk.
key_facts: Rule 36 allows any vessel to make non-standard light or sound signals to attract attention when necessary.
A searchlight beam may be directed at a danger but must not embarrass other vessels.
Attention-attracting lights must not be confusable with aids to navigation.
Strobe or similar high intensity intermittent/revolving lights are prohibited for this purpose.

trace.situation: Annex I of COLREG specifies the technical requirements for vertical positioning and spacing of masthead lights on power-driven vessels based on vessel length and breadth.

procedures.action: Measure 'height above the hull' vertically from the point directly beneath the light's position to the uppermost continuous deck.
procedures.why: This defines the standard reference datum for all light height calculations under Annex I.

procedures.action: On a power-driven vessel of 20 metres or more, place the forward (or sole) masthead light at least 6 metres above the hull, increasing to match the vessel's breadth if it exceeds 6 metres, up to a maximum of 12 metres.
procedures.why: Ensures the light is high enough to be visible over the vessel's own structure and proportionate to its size, while capping excessive height.

procedures.action: When carrying two masthead lights, position the after light at least 4.5 metres vertically higher than the forward light.
procedures.why: Allows the after light to be seen over and separate from the forward light, aiding other vessels in determining the observed vessel's heading and distinguishing it as power-driven with two masthead lights.

procedures.action: Ensure vertical separation of masthead lights is sufficient that the after light remains visible over and separate from the forward light at 1,000 metres from the stem, viewed from sea level, in all normal trim conditions.
procedures.why: Maintains reliable visual discrimination between the two lights at operational observation distances despite changes in trim.

procedures.action: On a power-driven vessel of 12 to less than 20 metres in length, place the masthead light at least 2.5 metres above the gunwale.
procedures.why: Provides a scaled-down but still adequate height requirement for smaller vessels.

procedures.action: On a power-driven vessel of less than 12 metres, the uppermost light may be placed at less than 2.5 metres above the gunwale.
procedures.why: Recognizes practical constraints on very small vessels while still requiring an uppermost light.

trace.trigger: A U.S. vessel engaged on a foreign voyage carries more than 12 passengers, or is a tanker, bulk freight vessel, freight vessel, or self-propelled mobile offshore drilling unit of 500 gross tons or more.

procedures.action: Determine if the vessel meets the passenger or gross tonnage/type thresholds requiring an SMC.
procedures.why: Mandatory SMC applies based on vessel type, size, and passenger capacity per paragraph (a).

procedures.action: Ensure the company holds a valid Document of Compliance (DOC) under §96.330.
procedures.why: An SMC can only be issued or renewed if the company has a valid DOC.

procedures.action: Complete a satisfactory safety management audit of the vessel's SMS under §96.320.
procedures.why: SMC issuance/renewal requires a passed audit of the vessel's safety management system.

procedures.action: Carry a copy of the valid SMC on board.
procedures.why: Required for vessels carrying more than 12 passengers, or qualifying tankers/freight vessels/MODUs, when on foreign voyages or operating within U.S. waters.

procedures.action: Optionally obtain an SMC even if not required under paragraph (a).
procedures.why: Voluntary SMC holding is permitted under paragraph (b).

constraints: SMC only issued/renewed if company holds valid DOC under §96.330.
Vessel must have completed a satisfactory safety management audit under §96.320.
Mandatory SMC thresholds: >12 passengers, or tanker/bulk freight/freight vessel/MODU of 500 gross tons or more, on foreign voyages.
outcomes: Vessel without a valid SMC cannot legally engage in foreign voyages if it meets the mandatory thresholds.
Lack of a valid DOC or failed audit prevents issuance/renewal of the SMC.
key_facts: SMC is mandatory for U.S. vessels on foreign voyages carrying more than 12 passengers or certain cargo/drilling vessel types of 500 GT or more.
SMC can be voluntarily obtained by vessels not meeting mandatory criteria.
SMC issuance/renewal depends on company's valid DOC and a satisfactory SMS audit of the vessel.

chapter_title: PART 96—RULES FOR THE SAFE OPERATION OF VESSELS AND SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS

trace.situation: US Coast Guard regulations (46 CFR Part 96) establish the validity period, renewal requirements, and revocation conditions for a vessel's Safety Management Certificate (SMC), and introduce the Interim Document of Compliance certificate for companies setting up or expanding their safety management system.
trace.trigger: A company or vessel seeks to obtain, maintain, renew, or faces revocation of a Safety Management Certificate, or needs an Interim Document of Compliance during company formation/transition or when adding a new vessel type.

procedures.action: Ensure a satisfactory initial safety management audit is completed before the SMC is issued.
procedures.why: The SMC's 60-month validity is based on a satisfactory initial safety management audit.

procedures.action: Request and complete an intermediate verification audit between the 24th and 36th month of the SMC's validity period.
procedures.why: This audit is a required condition for the SMC to remain valid; failure to complete it is grounds for revocation.

procedures.action: Maintain a valid Document of Compliance (DOC) certificate for the company.
procedures.why: The SMC for company-owned vessels becomes invalid automatically if the company's DOC expires or is revoked.

procedures.action: Complete a satisfactory safety management system audit meeting all Subpart B requirements before renewing the SMC.
procedures.why: Renewal cannot be started unless the company holds a valid DOC and the audit requirements are fully met.

procedures.action: Request an Interim DOC through an authorized recognized organization when forming a new company, transitioning companies, or adding a new vessel type.
procedures.why: This certificate helps establish a safety management system in these specific circumstances.

constraints: SMC validity is 60 months.
Intermediate verification audit must occur between the 24th and 36th month.
Renewal of SMC cannot begin unless the company holds a valid DOC certificate.
Only the Coast Guard may revoke a U.S. vessel's SMC.
regulations: 46 CFR Part 96 (US Coast Guard SMS rules)
warnings: SMC will be revoked if the required intermediate safety management audit is not completed.
SMC will be revoked if major non-conformities are found during an audit, survey, or inspection.
SMC becomes invalid automatically upon expiration or revocation of the company's DOC.
outcomes: Failure to complete intermediate audit or maintain a valid DOC results in SMC revocation/invalidity, halting authorized vessel operation under the SMS.
Satisfactory completion of all audits and maintenance of DOC allows continued valid certification and eventual renewal.
key_facts: A Safety Management Certificate is valid for 60 months.
An intermediate verification audit must be completed between the 24th and 36th month of SMC validity.
The SMC becomes invalid if the company's Document of Compliance expires or is revoked.
Only the Coast Guard can revoke a U.S. vessel's SMC, and it does so for missed audits or major non-conformities.
An Interim Document of Compliance may be issued for new/transitioning companies or when adding a new vessel type to an existing SMS.

chapter_title: PART 96—RULES FOR THE SAFE OPERATION OF VESSELS AND SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS

trace.situation: US regulation (33 CFR Part 96) describing the conditions under which a vessel's company may obtain an Interim Document of Compliance certificate and an Interim Safety Management Certificate before full ISM implementation.
trace.trigger: A responsible person/company takes delivery of a new U.S. vessel, or takes over management of a vessel new to them, and needs interim certification while full SMS implementation is completed.

procedures.action: Demonstrate to an auditor that the company's safety management system meets the requirements of § 96.230.
procedures.why: Required to be issued the Interim Document of Compliance certificate.

procedures.action: Provide a plan for full implementation of a safety management system within the validity period of the Interim DOC.
procedures.why: Ensures transition to full compliance within the up-to-12-month interim period.

procedures.action: Apply for an Interim Safety Management Certificate upon taking delivery of a new U.S. vessel or taking responsibility for a vessel new to the company.
procedures.why: Allows vessel to operate under interim certification per § 96.360(a).

procedures.action: Ensure the company's valid (or interim) Document of Compliance applies to the vessel type.
procedures.why: Condition (b)(1) for issuance of Interim SMC.

procedures.action: Ensure the SMS for the vessel includes the key elements set out in § 96.220 applicable to the new vessel type.
procedures.why: Condition (b)(2) for issuance of Interim SMC.

procedures.action: Confirm the SMS has been assessed during the DOC/Interim DOC audit process.
procedures.why: Condition (b)(3), ensures system was properly vetted.

procedures.action: Confirm the Master and senior officers are familiar with the SMS and planned setup arrangements.
procedures.why: Condition (b)(4), ensures operational readiness of key personnel.

procedures.action: Extract written documented instructions from the SMS and provide them to the vessel prior to sailing.
procedures.why: Condition (b)(5), ensures crew has actionable guidance before departure.

procedures.action: Plan an internal audit of the vessel within three months.
procedures.why: Condition (b)(6), verifies SMS implementation shortly after interim certification.

procedures.action: Ensure relevant SMS information is written in English and in any other language understood by the vessel's personnel.
procedures.why: Condition (b)(7), ensures crew comprehension regardless of nationality/language mix.

constraints: Interim Document of Compliance certificate is valid for up to 12 months.
Interim Safety Management Certificate is valid for 6 months.
Interim SMC may only be issued if the company's DOC or Interim DOC applies to the vessel type.
Master and senior officers must be familiar with the SMS and setup arrangements before issuance.
Written instructions must be given to the vessel prior to sailing.
An internal audit must be planned within three months of interim certification.
outcomes: Vessel/company may legally operate under interim certification while completing full SMS implementation.
Failure to meet conditions (a)-(b) precludes issuance of Interim SMC.
Internal audit within three months verifies ongoing compliance during interim period.
key_facts: Interim Document of Compliance certificate is valid for up to 12 months.
Interim Safety Management Certificate is valid for 6 months.
Interim SMC applies when a responsible person takes delivery of a new U.S. vessel or takes over management of a vessel new to them.
SMS-relevant documentation must be in English and any other language understood by the crew.
A company must plan an internal audit of the vessel within three months of interim certification.

chapter_title: PART 96—RULES FOR THE SAFE OPERATION OF VESSELS AND SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS

trace.situation: US regulation specifying ISM-related documentation requirements for foreign vessels operating in U.S. waters whose flag states are not party to SOLAS Chapter IX.
trace.trigger: A foreign vessel carrying more than 12 passengers, or a tanker/bulk freight/freight vessel/self-propelled MODU of 500 gross tons or more, operates in U.S. waters under a flag not party to SOLAS Chapter IX.

procedures.action: Carry on board valid documentation showing the company's safety management system was audited and assessed consistent with ISM Code (IMO Res. A.741(18)).
procedures.why: Demonstrates company-level ISM compliance equivalent to SOLAS Chapter IX requirements even though flag state is not a SOLAS party.

procedures.action: Alternatively, carry valid documentation from the vessel's Flag Administration showing the vessel's SMS was audited and assessed consistent with the ISM Code.
procedures.why: Provides flag-state-level verification of ISM compliance.

procedures.action: Alternatively, show evidence of compliance issued by a SOLAS-party government or an organization recognized to act on behalf of the vessel's Flag Administration.
procedures.why: Allows reliance on third-party or recognized organization verification where flag state itself is not a SOLAS party.

procedures.action: Ensure evidence of compliance contains all information and substantially the same format as a Document of Compliance certificate and a Safety Management Certificate.
procedures.why: Ensures equivalency and consistency with standard SOLAS/ISM certification format for enforcement purposes.

constraints: Applies only to foreign vessels from countries not party to SOLAS Chapter IX.
Applies to vessels carrying more than 12 passengers, or tankers/bulk freight/freight vessels/self-propelled MODUs of 500 gross tons or more.
Evidence of compliance must match the format and content of a DOC and SMC.
Failure to comply subjects the vessel to compliance and enforcement procedures under § 96.380.
warnings: Failure to comply will subject the vessel to compliance and enforcement procedures under § 96.380.
outcomes: Vessel is permitted to operate in U.S. waters if valid ISM-equivalent documentation is maintained on board.
Non-compliant vessels face enforcement action under § 96.380.
key_facts: Applies to foreign vessels over 12 passengers or tankers/bulk/freight vessels/MODUs of 500 GT+ from non-SOLAS Chapter IX countries operating in U.S. waters.

Three alternative means of demonstrating ISM compliance are accepted: company audit documentation, flag administration documentation, or evidence from a SOLAS-party government/recognized organization.
Evidence must match the format and content of a Document of Compliance and Safety Management Certificate.
Non-compliance triggers enforcement under § 96.380.

chapter_title: PART 96—RULES FOR THE SAFE OPERATION OF VESSELS AND SAFETY MANAGEMENT SYSTEMS

trace.situation: Coast Guard enforcement and compliance procedures for vessels operating under safety management system (ISM) regulations while in U.S. jurisdictional waters.
trace.trigger: Coast Guard boards a vessel or discovers noncompliance with Document of Compliance (DOC), Safety Management Certificate (SMC), or SMS procedures.

procedures.action: Coast Guard boards vessel to verify valid DOC and SMC (or equivalent evidence) are on board.
procedures.why: Confirms the company and vessel hold required ISM certification.

procedures.action: Coast Guard verifies crew and shore-based personnel are following SMS procedures and policies during operations or cargo transfer.
procedures.why: Ensures actual practice matches the certified safety management system.

procedures.action: If a foreign vessel's condition/SMS use does not substantially agree with its certificates, COTP or OCMI may order detention at the port or terminal where violation is found.
procedures.why: Prevents vessel from going to sea while presenting an unreasonable threat of harm to port, environment, vessel, or crew.

procedures.action: Detaining authority may allow vessel to move to another area of the port rather than remain at the violation site.
procedures.why: Balances safety/enforcement needs with operational/port logistics.

procedures.action: If vessel lacks required SMC and DOC copy on board, pursue civil penalty against owner, charterer, managing operator, agent, Master, or responsible individual under 46 U.S.C. 3318.
procedures.why: Establishes legal accountability for documentation noncompliance.

procedures.action: For foreign vessels, Coast Guard may request Secretary of the Treasury to withhold or revoke clearance under 46 U.S.C. App. 91.
procedures.why: Provides additional enforcement leverage over foreign-flagged vessels beyond direct detention.

procedures.action: Coast Guard may ask Secretary to permit vessel's departure after a bond or other surety is filed.
procedures.why: Allows release of vessel once financial assurance is provided, balancing enforcement with commercial impact.

constraints: Vessel must have valid DOC and SMC (or equivalent evidence for non-SOLAS Chapter IX countries) on board.
Detention continues until detaining authority determines vessel can go to sea without unreasonable threat of harm.
Civil penalty liability applies under 46 U.S.C. 3318 to owner, charterer, managing operator, agent, Master, or individual in charge.
Clearance withholding/revocation applies specifically to foreign vessels under 46 U.S.C. App. 91.
warnings: Noncompliant foreign vessels may be detained at port or terminal until deemed safe to go to sea.
Lack of required certificates on board can result in civil penalty liability for multiple responsible parties.
Clearance for foreign vessels may be withheld or revoked pending compliance.
outcomes: Vessel detained until it no longer presents unreasonable threat of harm.
Civil penalties may be imposed on owner, charterer, operator, agent, or Master for missing certificates.
Foreign vessel clearance withheld/revoked until bond or surety filed, after which departure may be permitted.
key_facts: Coast Guard can board vessels in U.S. jurisdictional waters to check DOC and SMC validity and SMS adherence.
COTP or OCMI has authority to detain noncompliant foreign vessels at the port/terminal of violation.
Detained vessels may be moved to another port area if needed rather than remain at the violation site.
Civil penalties under 46 U.S.C. 3318 apply to multiple responsible parties, not just the Master.
Foreign vessel clearance can be withheld/revoked via the Secretary of the Treasury under 46 U.S.C. App. 91, with release possible after bond is filed.

trace.situation: U.S. Coast Guard regulation specifying when foreign vessels will be denied entry into U.S. ports/terminals for lack of a certificated safety management system, and the purpose of authorizing recognized organizations to perform SMS audits/certification on behalf of the Coast Guard.
trace.trigger: A foreign-flag vessel on an international voyage, carrying more than 12 passengers or being a tanker/bulk freight/freight vessel/MODU of 500 gross tons or more, attempts to enter a U.S. port or terminal without a properly certificated SMS (per this subpart or SOLAS Chapter IX).

procedures.action: Determine whether the vessel qualifies for the force majeure exception before applying entry denial.
procedures.why: Vessels entering under force majeure are excepted from the SMS certification requirement under §96.390(a).

procedures.action: Verify the vessel holds a safety management system properly certificated under this subpart or SOLAS Chapter IX if it is engaged on a foreign voyage and meets the tonnage/passenger criteria.
procedures.why: Only vessels meeting both the voyage type and size/passenger thresholds are subject to the SMS certification entry requirement.

procedures.action: Cognizant COTP denies port/terminal entry to any non-compliant vessel.
procedures.why: Authority is granted under 46 U.S.C. 3204(c) to enforce the SMS certification requirement.

procedures.action: To obtain a current list of Coast Guard-authorized recognized organizations, submit a self-addressed stamped envelope and written request to Commandant (CG-ENG), Office of Design and Engineering Standards.
procedures.why: Recognized organizations are authorized under 46 CFR part 8 to perform delegated safety management audits and certification functions on behalf of the Coast Guard.

constraints: Exception applies only to foreign vessels entering U.S. waters under force majeure.
SMS certification requirement applies only to vessels on a foreign voyage carrying more than 12 passengers, or tankers/bulk freight/freight vessels/self-propelled MODUs of 500 gross tons or more.
Recognized organizations must be recognized under 46 CFR part 8, subparts A and B, before Coast Guard authorization under this subpart.
channels: 46 CFR part 8 subparts A and B
warnings: No vessel shall enter a U.S. port or terminal without a properly certificated safety management system unless the force majeure exception applies.
outcomes: Vessels lacking required SMS certification will be denied entry into U.S. ports/terminals by the cognizant COTP.
Recognized organizations meeting 46 CFR part 8 criteria may be authorized to perform safety management audits and certification on the Coast Guard's behalf.
key_facts: Force majeure entry by a foreign vessel is excepted from the SMS certification requirement.
The SMS certification requirement applies to foreign-voyage vessels with more than 12 passengers, or tankers/bulk freight/freight vessels/MODUs of 500 gross tons or more.
The cognizant COTP has authority under 46 U.S.C. 3204(c) to deny port/terminal entry for noncompliance.
Recognized organizations under 46 CFR part 8 subparts A and B may be authorized to perform SMS audits and certification for the Coast Guard.
An up-to-date list of recognized organizations can be obtained by written request to Commandant (CG-ENG).

procedures.action: Submit a list of the organization's exclusive auditors qualified to perform safety management audits and their operational areas.

procedures.action: Provide a written statement confirming procedures and records related to SMS audits/certification will be available for annual or on-demand Coast Guard review.

procedures.action: If a foreign classification society, include a government affidavit demonstrating reciprocity under 46 U.S.C. 3316, listing authorized delegations to the American Bureau of Shipping.

procedures.action: Await Coast Guard evaluation of the request; if satisfactory, the organization will receive an on-site evaluation visit per §96.440(b).

outcomes: Satisfactory completion of the Coast Guard's evaluation leads to an on-site evaluation visit as described in §96.440(b).
Missing affidavit results in automatic disapproval of a foreign classification society's request.

trace.situation: STCW-related U.S. regulation (46 CFR Part 13) defining how 'transfers' of liquid cargo are counted toward certification requirements for tank vessel personnel seeking endorsements.
trace.trigger: An applicant is compiling evidence of cargo transfer experience to qualify for a tank vessel certification/endorsement under §13.203(b) or §13.303(b).

procedures.action: Count only transfers involving loading/discharge between a vessel's cargo tanks and a shore facility or another vessel; exclude internal tank-to-tank shifts.
procedures.why: A shift of cargo from one tank to another is not considered a transfer for credit purposes.

procedures.action: Count a transfer lasting beyond 4 hours as only one transfer regardless of actual duration.
procedures.why: Prevents inflating transfer counts based on duration alone.

procedures.action: Ensure the transfer being credited includes both a commencement and a completion.
procedures.why: A transfer is only valid for credit if both phases are documented/participated in.

procedures.action: Limit credit to one transfer, one loading, and one discharge per watch, regardless of number of tanks/products handled simultaneously.
procedures.why: Prevents multiple credits being claimed from a single watch's activity.

procedures.action: For watches under 4 hours, only claim credit if the watch includes either connection/commencement or completion/disconnection.
procedures.why: Ensures meaningful participation in the transfer, not partial/incidental involvement.

procedures.action: For commencement-of-loading credit, participate in pre-transfer inspection, pre-transfer conference (with Declaration of Inspection execution), hose/arm connection, system line-up, start of flow, and rate calculations.
procedures.why: These specific tasks define genuine participation in a loading commencement.

procedures.action: For commencement-of-discharge credit, participate in pre-transfer inspection, conference, connection, line-up, pump start/pressure increase, and discharge rate monitoring.
procedures.why: Parallel requirements ensure genuine participation in discharge commencement.

procedures.action: For completion-of-transfer credit, participate in topping-off (loading port) or stripping/commencement of ballasting (discharge port) as required by the vessel's transfer procedures.
procedures.why: Completion credit requires hands-on involvement in finishing the cargo operation.

procedures.action: For off-duty personnel, accumulate credit through incremental training periods covering transfer segments, totaling the minimum number required.
procedures.why: Allows flexible accrual of experience while still meeting the cumulative transfer requirement.

constraints: A transfer must be between a vessel's cargo tank and a shore facility or another vessel, not an internal tank shift.
Only one transfer/loading/discharge credit per watch regardless of multiple tanks or products.
Short watches (<4 hours) only qualify if they include commencement or completion phases.
Specific listed tasks must be performed to claim commencement or completion credit.
Cumulative transfer counts must meet the minimums specified in §13.203(b) or §13.303(b).
outcomes: Properly counted transfers allow an applicant to accrue valid sea service/experience credit toward tank vessel certification.
Miscounting or double-counting transfers could invalidate credit claims for certification.
key_facts: A transfer excludes tank-to-tank shifts within the same vessel.
Transfers lasting beyond 4 hours still count as only one transfer.
Only one transfer, loading, and discharge credit is allowed per watch.
Specific operational tasks (inspection, conference, connection, line-up, etc.) must be performed to claim commencement/completion credit.
Off-duty personnel can accumulate credit incrementally but must meet the same cumulative minimums.

trace.situation: Regulatory requirements specifying the sea service and supervised cargo transfer experience an applicant must document to qualify for a Tank Vessel Person-in-Charge (PIC) endorsement for Dangerous Liquids (DL) or Liquefied Gases (LG).

procedures.action: Document at least 90 days of service as deck/engineering officer, or 90 days as rating/cadet, or a combination thereof, on tank vessels certified for the relevant cargo (DL or LG).
procedures.why: Establishes minimum sea service experience with the cargo type appropriate to the endorsement sought (§13.203(a)).

procedures.action: Provide evidence of participation under a Tank Vessel-PIC's supervision in at least 10 liquid cargo transfers, including 5 loadings, 5 discharges, 2 commencements/2 completions of loading, and 2 commencements/2 completions of discharge.
procedures.why: Ensures supervised practical experience across the full cargo transfer cycle before independent certification (§13.203(b)).

procedures.action: If already holding a DL (or LG) PIC endorsement and seeking the converse, provide evidence of at least half the service in (a) and comply with (b) but with reduced transfer counts (3 loadings/3 discharges plus the commencement/completion requirements).
procedures.why: Recognizes prior equivalent PIC experience to reduce duplicative requirements when cross-qualifying between DL and LG (§13.203(c)).

constraints: Applicant must satisfy either (a)+(b) together, or (c) alone -- not a mix of (a)/(b) full requirements and (c).
Service and transfers must be on tankships or self-propelled tank vessels certified to carry the DL or LG cargo appropriate to the endorsement applied for.
Cargo transfer participation must occur under supervision of a Tank Vessel-PIC.
Converse endorsement applicants must still meet the commencement/completion counts in (b)(2) and (3) even though loading/discharge counts are reduced.
outcomes: Applicant meeting (a) and (b), or (c), qualifies for issuance of the Tank Vessel-PIC endorsement for the applicable cargo type.
Failure to document required service/transfers results in denial of the requested endorsement.
key_facts: Full endorsement requires 90 days of qualifying service plus 10 supervised cargo transfers meeting specific loading/discharge breakdowns.
Cross-endorsement (DL to LG or LG to DL) requires only half the service days and reduced transfer counts (3 loadings/3 discharges) if already PIC-endorsed for the other cargo type.
