constraints: Speed must allow sufficient time for collision avoidance in reduced visibility and congested traffic.
Bridge team reinforcement alone is insufficient without effective BRM practices.
warnings: High speed in dense fog in a congested TSS leaves minimal time for collision avoidance.
A reinforced bridge team is not a guarantee of faultless operations if situational awareness and BRM are lacking.
outcomes: Vessel B's excessive speed in fog contributed to a near-miss/collision scenario due to insufficient avoidance time.
Vessel A's inadequate BRM and situational awareness negated the benefit of its reinforced bridge team, contributing to the collision.
key_facts: Vessel B was making 11.8 knots in dense fog within a congested TSS.
At that speed and close range, minimal time for collision avoidance was available.
Vessel A had a reinforced bridge team appropriate for reduced visibility conditions.
Despite reinforcement, vessel A's BRM and situational awareness were less than adequate, negating the benefit of the extra bridge personnel.

question_seeds.text: Why did vessel B's speed in fog leave insufficient time to avoid collision?
How should bridge team composition be adjusted for actual conditions rather than standard watch schedules in fog?
What does this incident show about the limits of reinforced bridge teams without effective BRM?
Which specific BRM failures negated vessel A's reinforced bridge team advantage?

chapter_title: 202629 Collision in fog in a TSS

trace.situation: A loaded bulk carrier (Vessel A) underway in fog inside a TSS was struck/nearly struck by an overtaking vessel (Vessel B) whose position was never correctly tracked by either bridge team or VTS.
trace.trigger: Visibility dropped to about 350 m in a Traffic Separation Scheme, prompting a heightened bridge watch and a VTS traffic suspension order.

procedures.action: Master of Vessel A implements a heightened bridge watch regime (Master conning, two navigation officers, helmsperson) when visibility drops to 350 m.
procedures.why: Restricted visibility in a TSS requires increased manning and vigilance to detect other traffic.

procedures.action: Bridge team should positively identify and continuously plot all radar contacts, including intermittent returns.
procedures.why: Vessel B's radar return was intermittent and was never plotted, so Vessel A remained unaware it was being overtaken.

procedures.action: Both vessels should sound the fog signal (one prolonged blast every two minutes) required in restricted visibility.
procedures.why: Neither vessel sounded the signal, removing a key means of mutual detection/awareness in fog.

procedures.action: OOW on Vessel B should inform the Master of reduced visibility and the presence of another vessel being overtaken.
procedures.why: The OOW was aware of Vessel A but failed to notify the Master, so no heightened precautions were taken on Vessel B despite the hazard.

procedures.action: VTS instructs Vessel A to go to anchorage/drift because visibility in the TSS is too low and traffic is suspended.
procedures.why: VTS judged conditions unsafe for continued TSS transit and sought to halt traffic movement.

procedures.action: Master of Vessel A, seeing the opposite lane clear, orders slow ahead and port helm to cross the lane and comply with the suspension order, with VTS agreement.
procedures.why: To comply with the VTS suspension instruction by moving out of the active traffic lane.

procedures.action: VTS should confirm the position of all traffic, including vessels without AIS or with intermittent radar returns, before approving a maneuver.
procedures.why: VTS agreed to the lane-crossing maneuver while remaining ignorant of Vessel B's exact position, since Vessel B had no AIS and an intermittent radar return.

constraints: Visibility was approximately 350 m, a restricted visibility condition under COLREGs.
Neither vessel was transmitting a reliable, continuous AIS signal or radar return for identification/tracking by the other or by VTS.
Sound signalling for restricted visibility was not being used by either vessel.
VTS had suspended traffic in the TSS due to low visibility at the time of the maneuver.
warnings: An intermittent radar return can cause a genuine traffic target to go unplotted and undetected.
Failing to sound required fog signals removes a critical layer of mutual awareness between vessels in restricted visibility.
Crossing a traffic lane in a TSS during a VTS-ordered suspension is hazardous if the position of nearby traffic (especially an overtaking vessel) is not positively confirmed.
A bridge officer withholding information about reduced visibility and nearby traffic from the Master undermines the ship's safety management.
outcomes: Vessel A's bridge team remained unaware of being overtaken by Vessel B, increasing collision risk.
The Master's lane-crossing maneuver, agreed by VTS, was executed without knowledge of Vessel B's actual position.
The situation described culminated in a collision in fog within the TSS.
key_facts: Vessel A: loaded bulk carrier, speed ~7.6 kts, visibility ~350 m, Master conning with two officers and a helmsperson.
Vessel B: overtaking at full ahead, ~11.8 kts, manned only by OOW and lookout with autopilot steering engaged.
Vessel B had no AIS transmission and an intermittent radar return, making it hard to track.
Neither vessel sounded the fog signal required under the collision regulations in restricted visibility.
VTS ordered traffic suspension in the TSS and agreed to Vessel A's lane-crossing maneuver without knowing Vessel B's exact position.

question_seeds.text: Why did Vessel A's bridge team fail to plot Vessel B as a radar target despite a heightened watch regime?
What should the OOW on Vessel B have done upon recognizing reduced visibility and an overtaking situation?
How should VTS have verified Vessel B's position before approving Vessel A's lane-crossing maneuver?
Which COLREG sound-signal requirement did both vessels fail to comply with in this fog encounter?

trace.situation: A company investigation into an incident involving a heavy inspection cover found that the risk assessment and toolbox talk failed to identify the lifting hazard, no two-person lifting requirement was specified, and warning signage near the cover was absent, contributing to unsafe solo handling.
trace.trigger: Dismantling or mounting a heavy inspection cover without an adequate risk assessment, lifting procedure, or signage in place.

procedures.action: Always dismantle and mount heavy covers using two persons, whether or not a chain block is used.
procedures.why: Prevents unsafe solo handling of a heavy inspection cover.

procedures.action: Fit two long studs at the top position of every cover before dismantling/mounting.
procedures.why: Keeps the cover in a secure position during the lifting operation.

procedures.action: Ensure work permits and toolbox talks explicitly cover safe lifting techniques and assign roles.
procedures.why: Reinforces correct practice and prevents solo handling that was missed in this incident's risk assessment.

procedures.action: Exercise Stop Work Authority whenever unsafe actions are observed.
procedures.why: Allows any crewmember to halt work before an unsafe act leads to injury.

procedures.action: Maintain supervisory presence during potentially hazardous tasks.
procedures.why: Supervision helps catch hazards and unsafe practices that risk assessments may have missed.

constraints: Risk assessments and toolbox talks must explicitly identify heavy cover lifting hazards.
Two-person lifting must be specified as a requirement, not left to crew discretion.
Warning signage must be posted near hazardous covers.
Stop Work Authority must be actively exercised when unsafe actions are observed.
warnings: Lack of warning signage near the cover contributed to unsafe practices.
Solo handling of heavy inspection covers, even with a chain block, is unsafe.
Failure to specify two-person lifting in procedures increases injury risk.
outcomes: Unsafe lifting practice occurred because the hazard was not identified in the risk assessment or toolbox talk.
Lack of two-person lifting requirement and signage contributed to the unsafe condition that led to the incident.
key_facts: The investigation found the heavy inspection cover hazard was not identified in the risk assessment or toolbox talk.
No requirement for two-person lifting had been specified for the task.
Lack of warning signage near the cover contributed to unsafe practices.
Best practice is to always use two persons to dismantle/mount heavy covers, regardless of chain block use.
Fitting two long studs at the top of the cover helps keep it in position during dismantling/mounting.

question_seeds.text: Why did the risk assessment and toolbox talk fail to identify the heavy cover as a hazard?
How should work permits be revised to mandate two-person lifting for heavy covers?
What physical measures (e.g., long studs) should be fitted to secure covers during dismantling?
Who is responsible for exercising Stop Work Authority if solo lifting of a heavy cover is observed?

trace.situation: During an assisted unberthing manoeuvre, a pilot transposed tug names on his radio card, causing tug orders meant for the aft tug to go to the bow tug and vice versa, resulting in the vessel's stern swinging into the pier in a quartering current and damage to both ship and berth.
trace.trigger: Pilot issuing tug commands using tug names rather than position or number during a multi-tug assisted manoeuvre, with no bridge team member independently verifying the orders.

procedures.action: Establish and maintain a shared mental model of the planned manoeuvre among all bridge team members and the pilot.
procedures.why: Allows inconsistencies in tug orders or vessel behavior to be detected early enough to prevent negative consequences.

procedures.action: Refer to tugs by position (fore/aft) or number (tug 1, tug 2) rather than by name.
procedures.why: Using names introduces a weak link in a multi-person operation since crew must separately remember which name corresponds to which position.

procedures.action: Monitor vessel response against the briefed plan (e.g., expected stern or bow movement) and query the pilot immediately if the vessel behaves contrary to the plan.
procedures.why: The Master only queried 'What is going on?' after the vessel was already moving incorrectly; earlier detection could have prevented the contact.

constraints: All bridge team members must share the same understanding of the manoeuvre plan before and during execution.
Tug identification method (name vs. position/number) must be unambiguous to all parties involved in the manoeuvre.
warnings: Using tug names for vessel manoeuvres introduces a weak link in a multi-person operation.
An undetected miscommunication in tug assignments can cause the vessel to move opposite to the intended direction, risking contact with the berth.
outcomes: The bow was rapidly pulled away from the pier while the stern moved toward the pier in a 1.9-knot quartering current, contrary to the plan to pull the stern off faster than the bow.
Significant damage occurred to the port side of the vessel and some damage to the berth.
Investigation found the pilot had transposed tug names on his radio card, reversing orders between the forward and aft tugs.
key_facts: The pilot's radio card had the tug names transposed, so orders for the aft tug went to the bow tug and vice versa.
The plan was for the vessel's stern to come off the pier faster than the bow, but the opposite occurred.
A 1.9-knot quartering current was present during the manoeuvre, exacerbating the stern's swing toward the pier.
Neither the Master nor other bridge officers detected the pilot's tug order error before contact occurred.
The incident resulted in damage to the vessel's port side and to the berth.

question_seeds.text: Why did none of the bridge officers catch the pilot's transposed tug orders before the vessel contacted the pier?
How should the bridge team verify tug identities and commands during a pilot-directed multi-tug manoeuvre?
What should the Master do immediately upon observing the vessel behaving contrary to the briefed manoeuvre plan?
Which method of tug identification (name, position, or number) reduces the risk of miscommunication during berthing operations?

trace.situation: During a tanker's unberthing from a pier assisted by two tugs (DC and DD), the pilot maneuvered the vessel using engine orders and tug positioning while anticipating an ebb current, resulting in a close-quarters situation when a tug's angle was misjudged.
trace.trigger: Pilot ordering tug DD to adjust to a 90° angle while the vessel was backing off the berth under ebb current conditions.

procedures.action: Order main propulsion to dead slow astern in anticipation of the ebb current.
procedures.why: To control the vessel's departure from the berth while accounting for the current's effect on vessel movement.

procedures.action: Order tug DC to stop once the vessel was off the berth.
procedures.why: Tug DC's assistance was no longer needed at that stage of the maneuver.

procedures.action: Radio tug DD and instruct the operator to maintain a 90° angle with the tug line relative to the tanker.
procedures.why: A 90° angle was the pilot's desired tug configuration for safe control during the maneuver.

procedures.action: Correct the tug operator when the actual angle (45°) and position did not match the requested configuration.
procedures.why: Operator's self-assessment ('pretty darn close') was inaccurate, requiring the pilot to clarify the discrepancy.

procedures.action: Stop the main propulsion immediately when the Master reported 'aft is too close'.
procedures.why: To prevent contact or a close-quarters incident involving the stern area.

procedures.action: Order tug DD to pull 'full away' and put the rudder hard to port.
procedures.why: To actively increase separation and regain control of the vessel's position relative to the tug and other hazards.

constraints: Pilot and tug operators must maintain accurate, unambiguous communication regarding tug position and angle.
Master must monitor vessel clearances independently and report hazards promptly to the pilot.
warnings: Miscommunication or misjudgment of tug angle/position can lead to a close-quarters situation during unberthing.
Operator's self-reported position ('pretty darn close') may not reflect actual vessel geometry and should be independently verified.
outcomes: The Master's timely warning allowed the pilot to stop propulsion and order corrective tug and rudder action before the situation worsened.
key_facts: The pilot ordered dead slow astern anticipating the ebb current as the tanker left the berth.
Tug DC was stopped once the vessel was off the berth.
Tug DD was found to be at a 45° angle instead of the requested 90°, and out of position relative to the line.
The Master alerted the pilot that the 'aft is too close', prompting the pilot to stop main propulsion and order tug DD full away with rudder hard to port.

question_seeds.text: Why did the pilot need tug DD to be at a 90° angle rather than 45°?
How did the Master's report of 'aft is too close' change the pilot's maneuvering decisions?
What immediate actions did the pilot take once the close-quarters situation was identified?
Who is responsible for verifying tug position accuracy during an unberthing maneuver?

trace.situation: A bulk carrier loaded with cassava chips underwent shore-based fumigation with aluminium phosphide tablets placed in the holds before departure, with hatches closed and coamings taped, resulting in fatal phosphine gas poisoning during the voyage.
trace.trigger: Shore-based fumigators treat cargo holds with aluminium phosphide tablets and depart without adequately briefing the crew on fumigation risks.

procedures.action: Ensure fumigation personnel verbally brief all crew (not just written handover to Chief Officer) on the risks, gas properties, and precautions associated with the fumigant used.
procedures.why: A written handover alone was provided and apparently did not explain the risks associated with the fumigation to the crew, leaving the crew unaware of the hazard.

procedures.action: Treat sealed/taped hatch coamings as an indicator of an active toxic gas hazard requiring restricted access and gas monitoring before any entry near or into holds.
procedures.why: Hatches were closed and coamings taped specifically to contain phosphine gas released by the fumigant tablets placed on the cargo.

constraints: Crew must be fully informed of fumigation hazards before getting underway with an actively fumigated cargo.
Aluminium phosphide fumigation releases toxic phosphine gas that can accumulate in and escape from sealed holds.
warnings: Aluminium phosphide tablets release phosphine gas, a fatal poison, when exposed to moisture/air.
Written handover documentation is insufficient if the crew is not verbally informed of the actual risks involved in fumigation.
Taped/sealed hatch coamings indicate the presence of a hazardous fumigated atmosphere that can pose a fatal risk if breached without precautions.
outcomes: Fatal phosphine gas poisoning occurred during the underway voyage due to inadequate crew awareness of fumigation risks.
key_facts: The cargo was cassava chips loaded before fumigation.
Aluminium phosphide tablets were placed on top of the cargo in each hold by shore-based fumigators before departure.
Hatches were closed and hatch coamings were taped by the crew before departure to seal in the fumigant gas.
Fumigation personnel gave only a written handover to the Chief Officer and apparently did not verbally explain the risks to the crew.
The incident resulted in fatal phosphine gas poisoning.

question_seeds.text: Why did the written handover to the Chief Officer fail to prevent a fatal poisoning incident?
What precautions should the crew have taken given that hatch coamings were taped to seal in fumigant gas?
Who is responsible for ensuring the entire crew, not just the Chief Officer, understands fumigation hazards before departure?
How should a Captain verify that fumigation risks have been properly communicated before sailing with a fumigated cargo?

trace.situation: A fumigation incident highlighted that phosphine poisoning symptoms in crew were mistaken for seasickness or illness due to inadequate safety briefings and management of fumigated cargo.
trace.trigger: Vessel is carrying or about to carry cargo treated with a fumigant such as phosphine.

procedures.action: Ensure crew receive a clear, specific safety briefing on the risks of the fumigant used, not merely paperwork sign-off.
procedures.why: Phosphine poisoning symptoms overlap with seasickness, food poisoning and viral illness, risking misdiagnosis and delayed response.

procedures.action: Post warning signs at treated holds.
procedures.why: To alert crew to the hazard and prevent inadvertent exposure.

procedures.action: Implement dedicated company safety management procedures for fumigation, including risk assessment, equipment provision and shore support.
procedures.why: Fumigation should not be treated as a routine cargo operation given its distinct toxic hazards.

constraints: Safety briefing must cover fumigant-specific risks, not just documentation sign-off.
Warning signs must be posted at treated holds.
Company procedures for fumigation must include risk assessment, equipment, and shore support.
warnings: Phosphine poisoning symptoms (nausea, vomiting, chest tightness, breathlessness) can be mistaken for seasickness, food poisoning, or viral illness.
Treating fumigation as a routine cargo operation increases risk of crew poisoning.
outcomes: Without clear briefings and warning signs, crew may misattribute poisoning symptoms to common illnesses, delaying recognition and treatment.
Dedicated fumigation safety management procedures reduce risk of crew exposure to toxic fumigants.
key_facts: Phosphine poisoning symptoms closely resemble seasickness, food poisoning, and viral illness.
Fumigation contractors and ship's officers are responsible for crew safety briefings on specific fumigant risks.
Warning signs must be posted at treated holds.
Company-level safety management procedures for fumigation should include risk assessment, equipment provision, and shore support.

question_seeds.text: How can I ensure crew properly understand the risks of a fumigant rather than just signing paperwork?
Why is it dangerous to treat fumigated cargo as a routine cargo operation?
What symptoms should alert me to possible phosphine poisoning among crew rather than seasickness?
Who is responsible for providing shore support and risk assessment for fumigation operations?

trace.situation: Underway fumigation of cargo with aluminium phosphide poses an ongoing phosphine gas hazard that must be monitored and managed throughout the voyage, not just at the time of loading.
trace.trigger: A vessel is conducting or has conducted underway fumigation with aluminium phosphide while laden and underway.

procedures.action: Carry phosphine gas detection equipment on board for the duration of a fumigated voyage.
procedures.why: Underway fumigation with aluminium phosphide is inherently hazardous and gas levels must be verifiable at any time.

procedures.action: Check gas concentrations regularly throughout the voyage, not only at the point of loading.
procedures.why: Phosphine gas hazard persists and can change over the course of the voyage, not just at loading.

procedures.action: Maintain weathertight integrity of accommodation doors to the same standard as hatch covers.
procedures.why: Recirculation-mode air conditioning can draw contaminated outside air into the entire accommodation block if door/hatch seals are imperfect.

procedures.action: Plan route and speed after fumigation with consideration of wind direction and relative vessel speed.
procedures.why: Wind direction and relative vessel speed determine whether fumigant gas escaping from holds disperses safely or accumulates near the accommodation.

constraints: Vessel must carry phosphine gas detection equipment if undertaking underway fumigation.
Gas concentration checks must be continuous/regular, not limited to the loading stage.
Accommodation door and hatch seals must be weathertight to prevent gas ingress via recirculation AC.
warnings: Underway fumigation with aluminium phosphide is inherently hazardous.
Recirculation-mode air conditioning can pull contaminated outside air into an entire accommodation block if door and hatch seals are imperfect.
Fumigant gas escaping from holds may accumulate near accommodation depending on wind direction and relative vessel speed.
outcomes: Proper gas detection and door seal integrity prevent contaminated air from entering accommodation spaces.
Poor seal integrity or inattentive route/speed planning can allow phosphine gas to accumulate in or be drawn into accommodation spaces.
key_facts: Aluminium phosphide fumigation underway is inherently hazardous and requires continuous monitoring.
Phosphine gas detection equipment must be carried and used regularly throughout the voyage, not just at loading.
Accommodation door seals are as critical as hatch cover seals in preventing gas ingress via recirculation air conditioning.
Wind direction and relative vessel speed influence whether escaping fumigant gas disperses or accumulates near accommodation.

question_seeds.text: What equipment must be carried on board when conducting underway fumigation with aluminium phosphide?
How does recirculation-mode air conditioning increase the risk of phosphine gas exposure in accommodation spaces?
Why should gas concentration checks continue throughout the voyage rather than only at loading?
Which factors should be considered when planning route and speed after fumigation to avoid gas accumulation near accommodation?

trace.situation: A tanker was preparing to depart its berth at night using two assist tugs, with the Master and pilot having briefed the plan including tug placement and differential power settings to use current to swing the stern off the pier, when the pilot later discovered he had transposed the two tug names on his personal radio reference card.
trace.trigger: Investigation after the manoeuvre revealed the pilot's radio card had the tug names transposed relative to their actual placement (forward/aft) recorded on the mooring plan and in his notebook.

procedures.action: Exchange and agree the full manoeuvre plan between Master and pilot, including tug numbers, placement, and intended use
procedures.why: Ensures both bridge team and pilot share a common understanding of how the departure will be executed

procedures.action: Record tug names and placements on the mooring plan diagram and in the pilot's notebook
procedures.why: Creates a documented reference of which tug is assigned to which position (bow/stern)

procedures.action: Prepare a separate 'radio card' listing tug names and placements for quick reference on the bridge wing
procedures.why: Allows the pilot rapid recall of tug identities during time-critical manoeuvring commands

procedures.action: Direct both tugs to push against the pier while mooring lines are let go fore and aft
procedures.why: Keeps the vessel stable alongside while lines are released in preparation for departure

procedures.action: Order the tugs by name to pull away at progressively increasing/differential power (e.g. dead slow, half, three-quarters for one tug; minimum for the other)
procedures.why: Uses differential tug pull combined with the current to open the stern off the pier for a controlled, safe departure

constraints: The departure plan depended on accurate identification of which tug was forward and which was aft
The plan assumed a current of about 1.9 knots running from stern to bow to assist the manoeuvre
Tug commands were issued using tug names from the radio card rather than direct visual/position confirmation
warnings: Transposing tug names on a quick-reference card risks directing the wrong tug to perform a critical action during a differential-power manoeuvre
Reliance on a single written reference without cross-verification against the mooring plan/notebook can allow transcription errors to go undetected until after the fact
outcomes: The tug name transposition was not caught at the time and was only discovered during the subsequent investigation
Orders given using the mismatched radio card risked commanding the wrong tug to pull at the wrong power/direction during the departure
key_facts: Two tugs were used for departure: one forward near the bow (tug DD) and one aft (tug DC)
The plan called for the aft tug to pull faster than the forward tug to open the stern using an expected 1.9-knot stern-to-bow current
The pilot kept tug names/placements in three places: notebook, mooring plan diagram, and a radio card for bridge-wing reference
The radio card had the two tug names transposed relative to their actual positions
At 0400, the pilot ordered tug DD to pull away at increasing power (dead slow, half, three-quarters) and tug DC to pull at minimum power, using the names from the radio card

question_seeds.text: Why did maintaining multiple separate reference records (notebook, mooring plan, radio card) not prevent the tug name transposition?
How should a pilot cross-verify tug identities before issuing differential power commands during an unberthing?
What could have alerted the pilot or Master to the tug name mix-up before orders were executed?
Who should have confirmed tug name-to-position accuracy before the manoeuvre began — pilot, Master, or tug operators?

trace.situation: A cargo ship fumigated with phosphine gas experienced a gas leak that entered the accommodation through faulty ventilation and weathertight doors, causing mass crew illness and death before the crew recognized the cause.
trace.trigger: Wind astern with vessel speed slightly exceeding wind speed caused fumigant gas escaping through hatch and access covers to accumulate on the forward deck instead of dispersing, while accommodation air conditioning ran in recirculation mode under negative pressure.

procedures.action: Familiarize crew with the IMO Recommendations on the Safe Use of Pesticides on Board Ships before and during fumigation voyages
procedures.why: Investigation found crew were not familiar with these recommendations, leaving them unable to recognize or respond to the hazard

procedures.action: Equip the vessel with phosphine gas detection equipment
procedures.why: Vessel had no detection equipment, preventing early identification of toxic gas presence

procedures.action: Conduct safety inspections and concentration monitoring of phosphine gas after departure
procedures.why: No monitoring was performed, so gas accumulation and ingress into accommodation went undetected

procedures.action: Ensure weathertight doors fully close and ventilation is not left in recirculation mode during fumigant cargo carriage
procedures.why: Doors that could not fully close allowed contaminated air to be drawn into accommodation and recirculated through all served spaces

procedures.action: Treat unexplained, spreading crew illness (chest tightness, nausea, vomiting, breathlessness, fatigue) as a possible toxic gas exposure rather than defaulting to food poisoning or Covid-19
procedures.why: Repeated negative antigen tests and misattribution to food poisoning delayed recognition of the real cause, allowing exposure to continue

procedures.action: Stop the vessel, anchor, and request SAR resources once the severity of crew incapacitation becomes apparent
procedures.why: This was the action taken once the Chief Engineer recognized the scale of illness, though it came very late relative to onset of symptoms

constraints: Wind conditions (vessel speed relative to wind speed) can prevent fumigant gas dispersal from deck openings
Accommodation ventilation in recirculation mode spreads contaminated air throughout all served spaces
Weathertight doors must fully close to prevent contaminated air ingress
Phosphine gas detection equipment and monitoring are necessary safeguards that were absent
regulations: IMO Recommendations on the Safe Use of Pesticides on Board Ships
warnings: Gas escaping through hatch/access covers can accumulate on deck instead of dispersing under certain wind/speed conditions
Recirculation-mode air conditioning combined with imperfectly sealed weathertight doors can draw and spread toxic gas throughout accommodation
Symptoms of phosphine poisoning can closely mimic food poisoning or Covid-19, leading to dangerous misdiagnosis
Lack of gas detection equipment and monitoring can allow fatal exposure to go unnoticed for hours
outcomes: 13 of 21 crew members died, including the Master, from toxic pulmonary oedema consistent with phosphine poisoning
Rescue services arrived approximately 12 hours after the Master first felt unwell, by which time he had died
Investigation found crew unfamiliarity with IMO pesticide safety recommendations and absence of phosphine detection equipment and monitoring contributed to the disaster
key_facts: The vessel had no phosphine gas detection equipment aboard
Crew conducted no safety inspections or gas concentration monitoring after departure
Wheelhouse watchkeepers, exposed to the highest air-change rate, fell ill first
The Master and Chief Mate both became incapacitated before the cause was identified
Forensic findings confirmed toxic pulmonary oedema consistent with phosphine poisoning

question_seeds.text: What onboard conditions allowed fumigant gas to enter and recirculate through the accommodation spaces?
Why did the crew and Master initially misattribute the symptoms to food poisoning or Covid-19 rather than gas exposure?
How could early use of phosphine gas detection equipment have changed the outcome of this incident?
At what point should the Master have ordered the vessel stopped and requested SAR assistance given the progression of crew symptoms?

trace.situation: A combination bulk/container carrier loading iron ore developed a torsional twist in the hull due to uneven cargo distribution, causing the forward hatch covers to jam and preventing closure.
trace.trigger: Hatch cover rollers skewed off their guiding trackway and could not close because the hatchway had deformed from a rectangle into a parallelogram during cargo loading.

procedures.action: Take freeboard measurements at various points on both sides of the vessel.
procedures.why: To confirm whether the vessel has developed a torsional twist.

procedures.action: Take diagonal measurements of the hatch coamings.
procedures.why: To further verify and quantify the twisting of the vessel's structure.

procedures.action: Re-open the affected holds and inspect the cargo stow.
procedures.why: To identify whether cargo is unevenly distributed off centreline, causing the twist.

procedures.action: Use bulldozers to level the cargo in each hold.
procedures.why: To redistribute the heavy cargo evenly and correct the hull torsion.

procedures.action: Periodically re-take diagonal measurements during levelling.
procedures.why: To monitor progress and confirm the torsion is being corrected.

procedures.action: Close the hatch covers once torsion is corrected.
procedures.why: To restore watertight integrity of the holds once the hatchway returns to a true rectangle.

constraints: Cargo must be evenly distributed port/starboard and fore/aft to avoid inducing torsional twist.
Loading/discharge plans should account for the possible need to close hatch covers at any time (e.g., rain).
Vessels with broader than normal hatch squares (combination bulk/container type) are more susceptible to torsional deflection.
warnings: Even a slightly uneven distribution of heavy cargo can twist the vessel enough to prevent hatch closure.
Vessels with broader than normal hatch squares are more susceptible to torsional forces and coaming deflection.
Manuals often address maximum trim/heel but may omit guidance on cargo trimming/ballasting to avoid coaming deflection during loading.
outcomes: After levelling the cargo with bulldozers and monitoring diagonal measurements, the vessel's torsion was corrected and the hatch covers were successfully closed.
key_facts: The vessel had six holds with McGregor-type hydraulically operated sliding hatch panels.
Freeboard and diagonal coaming measurements confirmed the vessel had torsionally twisted.
Iron ore in the three aft holds was slightly to starboard of centreline while cargo in the three forward holds was slightly to port of centreline.
The vessel was a combination bulk/container type with broader than normal hatch squares, making it more prone to torsional twisting.
Bulldozers were used to redistribute cargo and correct the twist, verified by repeated diagonal measurements.

question_seeds.text: Why did uneven cargo distribution cause the hatch covers to jam rather than just affecting trim?
How can freeboard and diagonal coaming measurements be used to detect hull torsion during loading?
What loading plan precautions should be taken to avoid torsional twist in bulk/container combination vessels?
Which ship types are most susceptible to this kind of torsional deflection during cargo loading?

trace.situation: A bulk carrier was overtaking multiple vessels including an oil tanker in a Traffic Separation Scheme at night in good visibility, closing from astern at over 16 knots.
trace.trigger: The range to the tanker ahead closed to under a mile and the CPA tightened, prompting Master concern.

procedures.action: Maintain continuous long-range radar and ECDIS scanning of the overall traffic picture, not just the immediate vessel being overtaken.
procedures.why: The bridge team had instead focused on each overtaking situation individually, reducing awareness of the developing close-quarters situation with the tanker.

procedures.action: Keep the lookout continuously on the bridge during overtaking in a busy TSS.
procedures.why: The lookout had briefly left the bridge, reducing the team's visual monitoring capacity during a critical phase.

procedures.action: When CPA tightens to a concerning range, contact the other vessel by VHF to establish intentions.

procedures.action: On detecting a radar contact with apparent risk of collision, take avoiding action in ample time.
procedures.why: Early action reduces the chance of a close-quarters situation developing.

procedures.action: Avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, unless overtaking.
procedures.why: Prevents converging maneuvers that could worsen a close-quarters situation.

procedures.action: Avoid altering course toward a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.
procedures.why: Prevents closing the distance with a vessel whose bearing is not well monitored visually.

procedures.action: On hearing a fog signal forward of the beam, or if close-quarters cannot be avoided with a vessel forward of the beam, reduce speed to the minimum at which course can be maintained.
procedures.why: Minimizes closing speed and buys time to assess and avoid collision.

procedures.action: Stop engines completely if necessary.
procedures.why: Provides maximum avoidance margin when risk of collision remains high.

procedures.action: Treat both vessels as having a shared duty to navigate with caution; do not assume a stand-on role.
procedures.why: In restricted visibility there is no stand-on/give-way distinction, so mutual caution is required.

constraints: Applies only when vessels are not in sight of one another in or near restricted visibility.
No vessel has stand-on privileges under this rule.
Avoid turning to port for a contact forward of the beam unless overtaking.
Avoid turning toward a contact abeam or abaft the beam.
warnings: Do not alter course to port for a vessel forward of the beam unless overtaking it.
Do not alter course toward a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.
Failure to slow or stop when a close-quarters situation cannot be avoided can lead to collision.

There is no stand-on vessel in restricted visibility; both vessels must act with caution.
Avoiding action should be taken early upon radar detection of risk of collision.
Course alterations to port (for vessels forward of beam, not overtaking) or toward vessels abeam/abaft the beam are prohibited.

trace.situation: COLREG Rules 20-22 establish when vessels must show navigation lights versus shapes, and specify minimum visibility ranges for lights based on vessel length.
trace.trigger: Period from sunset to sunrise, or any time during restricted visibility (including daytime), requiring lights to be displayed; shapes are required only during daytime.

procedures.action: Display navigation lights from sunset to sunrise and during restricted visibility even in daytime.
procedures.why: Rule requires lights to run continuously through darkness and whenever visibility is reduced, not just at night.

procedures.action: Display shapes only during daylight hours as the shape equivalent of required lights.
procedures.why: Shapes are a daytime-only substitute/complement to night lights.

procedures.action: Verify masthead light visibility range matches the vessel's size class minimum (e.g., 6 nm for 50m+, 2 nm for sub-12m vessels).
procedures.why: Bigger vessels require lights visible from further away to allow adequate reaction time for other traffic.

procedures.action: If an observed light's visible range falls below the minimum required for that vessel's size class, flag it as a possible equipment fault rather than assuming it is compliant.
procedures.why: A masthead light visible from only 2.5 nm on a 20m vessel is below the 5 nm minimum required for her size class, indicating a deviation from spec that needs investigation.

constraints: Lights must be shown from sunset to sunrise and during restricted visibility during the day.
Shapes apply only during daylight hours.
Minimum light visibility range scales with vessel length (e.g., 50m+ vessel: 6 nm masthead light; sub-12m vessel: 2 nm).
A vessel's actual light visibility range must meet or exceed the minimum for its size class.
warnings: A masthead light visible from less distance than required for the vessel's size class may indicate an equipment fault, not merely a conditions-related shortfall.
outcomes: Correctly displayed lights/shapes ensure other vessels can identify size, type, and aspect at a safe distance.
Undetected substandard light range increases collision risk by reducing other vessels' early-warning time.
key_facts: Lights are required from sunset to sunrise and also during restricted visibility in daytime.
Shapes are the daytime-only equivalent of night lights.

A 20m fishing vessel requires a minimum 5 nm masthead light visibility per her size class.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 23 specifies the navigation lights a power-driven vessel underway must display, with a simplified configuration for small vessels, and provides a worked example of identifying vessel type from observed lights.
trace.trigger: A vessel is observed underway at night and its type/status must be determined from its displayed lights.

procedures.action: Display a forward masthead light.
procedures.why: Required light configuration for a power-driven vessel underway.

procedures.action: Display a second, higher masthead light further aft if the vessel is 50 m or more in length.
procedures.why: Larger power-driven vessels must show an additional masthead light to indicate size/aspect.

procedures.action: Display sidelights, green to starboard and red to port.
procedures.why: Indicates vessel orientation and right-of-way status to other vessels.

procedures.action: Display a sternlight.
procedures.why: Completes the all-round visibility of the vessel's heading/status at night.

procedures.action: If vessel is under 12 m, simplify to a single all-round white light plus sidelights.
procedures.why: Allows small vessels a simplified lighting scheme while still conveying necessary information.

procedures.action: When observing a contact showing only sidelights and a sternlight with no masthead light, classify it as a sailing vessel under Rule 25 rather than a power-driven vessel.
procedures.why: A power-driven vessel underway is required to show a masthead light; absence of one indicates it is not under power per Rule 23.

constraints: Masthead light is mandatory for power-driven vessels underway (except small vessel exception).
Second masthead light required only if vessel is 50 m or more in length.
Vessels under 12 m may use a single all-round white light plus sidelights instead of masthead/stern light combination.
warnings: Absence of a masthead light on an underway vessel at night should not be assumed to indicate malfunction; it may indicate the vessel is a sailing vessel, not power-driven.
outcomes: Correct identification of vessel type (power-driven vs. sailing) based on observed light configuration, supporting safe collision-avoidance decisions.
key_facts: Power-driven vessels underway must show a forward masthead light, sidelights, and a sternlight.
Vessels 50 m or more must show a second, higher masthead light aft of the first.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 25 specifies the lights and shapes a sailing vessel underway (and a sailing vessel also under engine power) must display.
trace.trigger: A sailing vessel is underway at night or in restricted visibility, or is simultaneously under sail and engine power.

procedures.action: Show sidelights and a sternlight (no masthead light) while sailing underway.
procedures.why: Rule 25 defines the standard light configuration for a sailing vessel underway.

procedures.action: If under 20 m, may combine sidelights and sternlight into a single tricolour lantern at the masthead.
procedures.why: Rule 25 permits a simplified lighting option for smaller sailing vessels.

procedures.action: If the engine is also being used to make way, show power-driven vessel lights and display a cone shape, apex down, forward.
procedures.why: Using the engine while sailing legally reclassifies the vessel as power-driven under COLREG, requiring corresponding lights and day shape.

constraints: Tricolour lantern combination option only applies to vessels under 20 m.
A vessel under both sail and engine power must be treated as power-driven, not as a sailing vessel.
Cone shape must be displayed apex down, forward, when motor-sailing.
warnings: Failing to show power-driven lights/shape while motor-sailing misrepresents vessel status and risks collision due to incorrect right-of-way assumptions by other vessels.
outcomes: Correct lighting ensures other vessels correctly identify vessel type and apply appropriate collision avoidance rules.
Incorrect classification (e.g., showing sailing lights while motor-sailing) could lead to navigational misjudgment by other traffic.
key_facts: A sailing vessel underway shows sidelights and sternlight, with no masthead light.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 24 specifies the light and shape signals required for vessels engaged in towing or pushing another vessel or object.
trace.trigger: A vessel is towing or pushing another vessel/object and must display identifying lights and shapes to other traffic, especially at night or in restricted visibility.

procedures.action: Display two masthead lights in a vertical line when towing (instead of the normal one or two).
procedures.why: Distinguishes a towing vessel from a normal power-driven vessel so other vessels recognize the towing operation.

procedures.action: Display three masthead lights in a vertical line when the length of the tow exceeds 200 metres.
procedures.why: Signals specifically that the tow is a long tow exceeding 200 m, warning other vessels to keep extra clearance.

procedures.action: Show a yellow towing light above the sternlight.
procedures.why: Identifies the vessel as the towing vessel and helps indicate the direction of the tow.

procedures.action: Ensure the towed vessel or object shows its own sidelights and sternlight.
procedures.why: Allows other vessels to perceive the extent and orientation of the towed object independently from the tug.

procedures.action: Display a diamond shape on the towed vessel or object when the tow exceeds 200 m.
procedures.why: Provides a daytime shape signal equivalent to the three-masthead-light night signal, warning of a long tow.

constraints: Three masthead lights (instead of two) apply only when the tow exceeds 200 m in length.
The towed vessel/object must independently display sidelights and a sternlight.
A diamond shape is required on the tow only when the tow length exceeds 200 m.
warnings: Misreading the number of masthead lights could cause a vessel to underestimate the length of the tow and pass too close.
Failure to display correct towing lights/shapes creates collision risk by misleading other vessels about the vessel's status.
outcomes: Correct display of lights and shapes allows other vessels to accurately assess the towing vessel's status and the length of the tow, enabling safe passing distances.
Three masthead lights correctly interpreted indicate a tow exceeding 200 m, prompting wider berth from other traffic.
key_facts: A towing vessel shows two masthead lights vertically stacked normally, or three if the tow exceeds 200 m.
A yellow towing light is shown above the sternlight on the towing vessel.
The towed vessel/object shows its own sidelights and sternlight.
A diamond shape signals a tow exceeding 200 m in length.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 26 specifies the lights and shapes fishing vessels must display depending on their method of fishing (trawling vs. other gear).
trace.trigger: A vessel engaged in fishing (trawling or using other gear such as static/line gear) needs to display identification lights/shapes, or another vessel must identify a fishing vessel's activity from its lights/shapes.

procedures.action: Identify a trawling vessel by green-over-white all-round lights (or two cones point-to-point by day).
procedures.why: Rule 26 designates this specific light/shape combination for vessels engaged in trawling.

procedures.action: Identify a vessel fishing with other gear (e.g., static or line gear) by red-over-white lights instead of green-over-white.
procedures.why: Rule 26 distinguishes trawling from other fishing methods using a different light color combination.

procedures.action: Look for an additional white light in the direction of any outlying gear extending more than 150 m from the vessel.
procedures.why: This extra light warns other vessels of the direction and extent of gear that may be a hazard beyond the vessel's hull.

procedures.action: When observing red-over-white lights, anticipate that gear may extend in a fixed direction rather than trailing astern, and maneuver to keep clear accordingly.
procedures.why: Unlike trawling gear (which trails astern), static/line gear may extend outward in a fixed direction, changing the practical collision-avoidance implications.

constraints: Trawling vessels must show green-over-white all-round lights or two cones point-to-point by day.
Vessels fishing with other gear must show red-over-white lights instead of green-over-white.
An extra white light is required only if outlying gear extends more than 150 m from the vessel.
warnings: Misidentifying trawling vs. other-gear fishing vessels can lead to incorrect assumptions about gear direction and length, increasing collision/entanglement risk.

outcomes: Correct identification of light configuration allows other vessels to anticipate the direction and extent of fishing gear and maneuver safely to keep clear.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 27 describes the distinctive all-round light and shape signals used by vessels not under command (NUC) and vessels restricted in their ability to manoeuvre (RAM), and how to distinguish between them.
trace.trigger: A Captain sighting a vessel displaying two or three stacked all-round red/white lights (or balls/diamond shapes by day) needs to classify the vessel's status.

procedures.action: Observe the vertical light/shape configuration of the contact.
procedures.why: The number and color sequence of lights/shapes indicates whether the vessel is NUC or RAM.

procedures.action: Count the lights: two red lights (or two balls by day) = NUC.
procedures.why: NUC vessels display exactly two all-round red lights stacked vertically, or two balls by day.

procedures.action: Identify three lights in red-white-red sequence (or ball-diamond-ball by day) = RAM.
procedures.why: The middle white light/diamond shape is the specific feature that distinguishes a RAM vessel from an NUC vessel.

procedures.action: Adjust expectations of the contact's behavior based on classification.
procedures.why: A RAM vessel may still be manoeuvring, just in a constrained way, whereas an NUC vessel is fully unable to manoeuvre — the practical implications for risk assessment differ.

constraints: Lights/shapes must be correctly counted and sequenced to avoid misclassification
Day shapes (balls/diamond) must be used in place of lights during daylight
warnings: Misidentifying a RAM vessel as NUC (or vice versa) could lead to incorrect assumptions about the vessel's ability to manoeuvre and improper risk assessment
outcomes: Correct identification allows the Captain to accurately assess whether the contact can take any evasive action
Incorrect identification could lead to a collision-risk misjudgment
key_facts: NUC vessels display two all-round red lights stacked vertically, or two balls by day.
RAM vessels display three lights stacked red-white-red, or ball-diamond-ball by day.
The middle white light or diamond shape is the key distinguishing feature between RAM and NUC.
A RAM vessel may still be capable of some manoeuvring, unlike an NUC vessel which cannot manoeuvre at all.

trace.situation: COLREG Part C rules describing the lights and shapes used by vessels constrained by their draught and vessels engaged in pilotage duty.
trace.trigger: A vessel is constrained by her draught in a shallow channel or is engaged in pilotage duty and must display identifying lights/shapes.

procedures.action: Display three red lights in a vertical line (plus normal power-driven vessel lights) if constrained by draught.
procedures.why: Signals to other vessels that the ship has very limited ability to deviate from her track due to draught restrictions.

procedures.action: Show a cylinder shape by day in place of the three red lights for a vessel constrained by draught.
procedures.why: Provides a daytime equivalent signal when lights are not visible.

procedures.action: Display white-over-red lights at the masthead when engaged on pilotage duty.
procedures.why: Identifies the vessel's special status as a pilot vessel to other traffic.

constraints: Three red vertical lights are shown in addition to, not instead of, normal power-driven vessel lights.
The cylinder shape is the daytime signal; lights are used at night.
Pilot vessel signal is white-over-red specifically at the masthead.
warnings: Other vessels must recognize that a ship showing the draught-constrained signal has very limited ability to deviate from her track regardless of what COLREG category would otherwise apply.
outcomes: Other vessels correctly identify a draught-constrained vessel and avoid forcing her to maneuver, reducing grounding or collision risk.
Pilot vessels are correctly identified allowing appropriate right-of-way and communication.

By day, a draught-constrained vessel shows a cylinder shape instead of lights.
The draught-constrained lights/shape are shown in addition to normal power-driven vessel signals.
A vessel on pilotage duty shows white-over-red lights at the masthead.

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 30 specifies the lights and shapes that anchored vessels and vessels aground must display to indicate their status to other vessels.
trace.trigger: A vessel is anchored or aground and must display appropriate lights/shapes, or an observer must interpret a contact's lights/shapes to determine vessel status.

procedures.action: If a vessel is anchored and under 50 m in length, display a single all-round white light at night (a ball shape by day).
procedures.why: Rule 30 mandates this minimal signal for smaller anchored vessels.

procedures.action: If a vessel is anchored and 50 m or more in length, display one all-round white light forward and a lower one aft.
procedures.why: Larger anchored vessels require two lights to indicate their length and orientation to other traffic.

procedures.action: If a vessel is aground, display the normal anchor lights plus two red lights in a vertical line at night (three balls in a vertical line by day).
procedures.why: The additional red lights/balls distinguish a grounded vessel from a normally anchored vessel.

procedures.action: When assessing a contact showing a single all-round white light with zero speed over multiple position updates, classify it as an anchored vessel under 50 m rather than a power-driven vessel with a light fault.
procedures.why: Zero speed over successive reports combined with the single white light signature is consistent with Rule 30's anchored-vessel-under-50m lighting, not a malfunctioning underway vessel.

constraints: Anchored vessel light configuration depends on whether length is under or 50 m and above.
Vessel aground must show anchor lights in addition to the two vertical red lights/three balls.
Day shapes (ball, three balls) must correspond to the night light configurations.
warnings: Do not misidentify a stationary anchored vessel as a power-driven vessel with a malfunctioning light; verify against successive position reports and light configuration.
outcomes: Correct identification of vessel status (anchored vs. aground vs. underway) enables appropriate collision-avoidance and navigational decisions.
key_facts: Anchored vessels under 50 m show a single all-round white light (ball by day).
Anchored vessels 50 m or more show one forward and one lower aft all-round white light.

Zero speed over successive position updates combined with a single white light indicates an anchored vessel under 50 m, not a light-faulted power-driven vessel.

chapter_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals

trace.situation: COLREG Rule 35 specifies the sound signals vessels must sound in or near restricted visibility to indicate their type and movement status to other vessels relying on sound alone.
trace.trigger: Vessel is operating in or near an area of restricted visibility (e.g., fog) where visual identification of other vessels is not possible.

procedures.action: If a power-driven vessel making way, sound one prolonged blast every 2 minutes.
procedures.why: Signals presence and movement of an ordinary power-driven vessel to others relying on sound in restricted visibility.

procedures.action: If a power-driven vessel stopped and not making way, sound two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a stopped power-driven vessel from one still making way.

procedures.action: If NUC, RAM, constrained-by-draught, sailing, fishing, or towing/pushing, sound one prolonged plus two short blasts, regardless of making way status.
procedures.why: Identifies the vessel as a special-category vessel requiring different navigational consideration, independent of its motion state.

procedures.action: On hearing one prolonged plus two short blasts from another vessel, identify it as a special-category vessel before visual contact.
procedures.why: Allows early recognition of vessel type and appropriate collision-avoidance response based on sound alone.

constraints: Signal pattern must be repeated every 2 minutes as specified.
Special-category vessels use the same signal (one prolonged plus two short) whether or not they are making way.
Power-driven vessels must differentiate their signal based on making-way status (one vs two prolonged blasts).
outcomes: Correct sounding of signals allows other vessels to identify a vessel's type and movement status in restricted visibility without visual contact.
Hearing one prolonged plus two short blasts correctly identifies the source as a special-category vessel (NUC/RAM/CBD/sailing/fishing/towing).
key_facts: Power-driven vessel making way: one prolonged blast every 2 minutes.
Power-driven vessel stopped, not making way: two prolonged blasts every 2 minutes.
NUC, RAM, constrained-by-draught, sailing, fishing, and towing/pushing vessels: one prolonged plus two short blasts regardless of making way status.
The one-prolonged-plus-two-short pattern alone identifies a special-category vessel before any visual sighting.

trace.trigger: A vessel was constructed before a specific COLREG amendment date and cannot fully meet a newly introduced technical specification (e.g., exact light placement).

procedures.action: Verify the vessel's construction/build date against the relevant rule amendment date to determine exemption eligibility.
procedures.why: Exemptions under Rule 38 apply only to genuinely older construction, not to all vessels.

procedures.action: Apply the exemption only to the specific technical detail affected (e.g., light positioning), not broadly.
procedures.why: The exemption is narrow and specific, covering only particular technical non-compliance items.

procedures.action: Continue full compliance with Rules 4-19 (steering and sailing conduct rules) regardless of exemption status.
procedures.why: Rule 38 exemptions never extend to the actual conduct rules governing navigation and collision avoidance.

constraints: Exemptions apply only to vessels built before the relevant rule change took effect.
Exemptions cover only narrow, specific technical items like exact light positioning, not general compliance.
Rules 4-19 (steering and sailing rules) must be followed by all vessels, exempted or not.
warnings: Do not assume an older vessel is exempt from steering and sailing conduct rules just because it holds a technical light-positioning exemption.
outcomes: An older vessel retains a specific, limited exemption for a technical detail like light positioning while remaining fully liable for compliance with navigational conduct rules.

Exempted vessels remain fully bound by Rules 4-19 governing steering and sailing conduct.

trace.situation: COLREG Rules 32-34 define sound signals power-driven vessels must use when manoeuvring in sight of one another, including a danger signal when a vessel is unsure of another's actions or doubts collision avoidance.
trace.trigger: A vessel alters course/speed while in sight of another vessel, or a vessel becomes unsure whether another vessel's actions are adequate to avoid collision.

procedures.action: Sound one short blast when altering course to starboard.
procedures.why: Signals intended maneuver to the other vessel per Rule 34.

procedures.action: Sound two short blasts when altering course to port.
procedures.why: Signals intended maneuver to the other vessel per Rule 34.

procedures.action: Sound three short blasts when operating astern propulsion.
procedures.why: Signals intended maneuver to the other vessel per Rule 34.

procedures.action: Sound at least five short rapid blasts (the danger signal) immediately if unsure of another vessel's intentions or doubtful their action is sufficient to avoid collision.
procedures.why: Alerts the other vessel to the uncertainty/danger so corrective action can be taken before close-quarters develops into collision risk.

constraints: Danger signal must be sounded immediately upon doubt arising, not after continued observation.
Applies to vessels in sight of one another and maneuvering under Rule 32-34.
warnings: Do not merely keep watching if bearing/range trend is unchanged and TCPA is shrinking despite the other vessel's reported maneuver — sound the danger signal without delay.
outcomes: Example: a give-way vessel begins a starboard turn but the stand-on vessel sees no change in bearing/range trend and TCPA keeps shrinking; the stand-on vessel should sound five short rapid blasts rather than continue passive observation, to prompt corrective action and avoid collision.
key_facts: One short blast = altering course to starboard.
Two short blasts = altering course to port.
Three short blasts = operating astern propulsion.
Five or more short rapid blasts = danger/uncertainty signal, to be sounded immediately when doubtful of the other vessel's action or intentions.

chapter_title: Part D - Sound and Light Signals

trace.situation: COLREG Rules 36-37 govern the use of light and sound signals to attract another vessel's attention, distinguishing them from the specific distress signals listed in Annex IV.
trace.trigger: A vessel needs to attract the attention of another vessel (e.g., one that appears distracted or on a risk-of-collision course) without an actual emergency being present.

procedures.action: Select a light or sound signal that cannot be confused with any signal already defined elsewhere in the Rules.
procedures.why: Avoids misleading other vessels into thinking a different signal (e.g., a maneuvering or distress signal) is being given.

procedures.action: Aim any attention-getting light (e.g., searchlight) carefully so as not to embarrass or blind any vessel.
procedures.why: Rule 36 requires such signals not endanger or confuse navigation by dazzling other vessels.

procedures.action: Do not improvise or use actual distress signals for non-emergency attention-getting purposes.
procedures.why: Distress signals are a separate, specific list under Annex IV reserved only for genuine emergencies.

constraints: Attention signal must not be confusable with any signal already defined elsewhere in the Rules.
Lights used to attract attention must not blind or embarrass other vessels.
Distress signals are limited to the specific list in Annex IV and must not be improvised for other purposes.
warnings: Do not sound or display a signal that could be mistaken for an actual distress signal when no emergency exists.
Do not aim searchlights in a way that blinds or embarrasses another vessel.
outcomes: Proper use of Rule 36 signals alerts a distracted vessel to risk without causing false alarm.

trace.situation: UK retained EU law sets out the rules governing the periods of validity, renewal timing, and extension of Documents of Compliance (DOC) and Safety Management Certificates (SMC) issued under the ISM regime.
trace.trigger: A DOC or SMC is due for initial issue, renewal verification, or has expired before a new certificate can be issued/placed on board.

procedures.action: Issue initial DOC/SMC for a validity period not exceeding five years from the date of satisfactory completion of the initial verification/ship verification.

procedures.action: If renewal verification is completed within three months before expiry of the existing certificate, issue the new certificate starting on completion date but set it to expire no later than five years after the old certificate's expiry.

procedures.action: If renewal verification is completed more than three months before expiry, issue the new certificate from the completion date, valid for up to five years from that date.

procedures.action: If renewal ship verification for an SMC is completed after the existing SMC has expired, issue the new SMC to run from the day after the old expiry date, for up to five years.

constraints: Maximum validity of any DOC or SMC is five years.

An SMC extension by endorsement cannot exceed five months.
Verification must be 'satisfactorily completed' before any certificate can be issued or extended.
regulations: UK Retained EU Law (Merchant Shipping regulations)
warnings: A new SMC must not be issued or relied upon before satisfactory completion of the required verification.

outcomes: Continuous, valid DOC/SMC coverage is maintained for the company and ship when renewal timing rules are followed.

key_facts: DOC and SMC validity periods cannot exceed five years from initial verification.
Renewal completed within three months of expiry preserves the full five-year cycle from the old expiry date.

procedures.action: Notify the ISM company in writing of the grounds for suspension or cancellation.

procedures.action: Ensure the notice specifies the effective date, and for suspensions, the terms of suspension.

trace.situation: This excerpt sets out the arbitration mechanism available under UK Merchant Shipping ISM regulations when disputes arise over additional ISM company or ship verifications, including arbitrator powers, Scottish-specific terminology, and qualification requirements for arbitrators.

trace.trigger: A ship to which the regulation applies has completed an initial or renewal survey, or a ship transfers from the flag of another Contracting Government while holding a valid IAPP Certificate.

procedures.action: Carry out an initial or renewal survey of the ship's equipment, systems, fittings, arrangements and materials.
procedures.why: To confirm compliance with Part 3 requirements or an approved alternative under regulation 4 before certification.

procedures.action: Issue an appropriate certificate once satisfied the ship fully complies as at the date of survey.
procedures.why: Certification confirms the ship meets Annex VI air pollution prevention standards.

procedures.action: For a ship transferring flag, verify an IAPP Certificate was issued and still valid immediately before transfer.
procedures.why: Ensures continuity of compliance status across flag change.

procedures.action: Cause a survey to be carried out on the transferring ship and confirm its condition conforms with Annex VI.
procedures.why: To ensure the ship is fit to proceed to sea without unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.

procedures.action: Confirm no unapproved changes have been made to equipment, systems, fittings, arrangements or material since the last survey, other than direct replacement with conforming equipment.
procedures.why: Unapproved modifications could invalidate the ship's compliance status established at last survey.

procedures.action: Issue the IAPP Certificate in English using the form in Appendix 1 to Annex VI, or the UKAPP Certificate in the form prescribed by the Secretary of State in Appendix 5 to MSN 1819 (M+F).
procedures.why: Ensures standardized, legally recognized documentation of compliance.

constraints: Certificate issuance is subject to payment of applicable fees.
Certifying Authority must be satisfied equipment/systems/fittings/arrangements/materials fully comply with Part 3 or a permitted alternative under regulation 4.
For transferred ships, the prior IAPP Certificate must have been valid immediately before the transfer date.
No change to covered equipment/systems/fittings/arrangements/material is permitted without Contracting Government approval, except direct replacement with conforming equipment.
IAPP Certificate must be in English and in the Appendix 1 form to Annex VI.
UKAPP Certificate must follow the form prescribed in Appendix 5 to Merchant Shipping Notice 1819 (M+F).
warnings: Unapproved changes to certified equipment/systems/fittings/arrangements/material (other than direct conforming replacement) can prevent certificate issuance.
Ship must not present an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment to be certified fit to proceed to sea.
outcomes: A compliant ship receives an IAPP or UKAPP certificate enabling it to proceed to sea without unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
A ship with unapproved, non-conforming changes or lapsed prior certification may be refused certification upon flag transfer.
key_facts: Certificates are issued only after survey confirms compliance with Part 3 or an approved alternative under regulation 4.
On flag transfer, the ship must have held a still-valid IAPP Certificate immediately before transfer.
Direct replacement of equipment/fittings with conforming equipment is an allowed change not requiring separate approval.
IAPP Certificates must be in English per Appendix 1 to Annex VI; UKAPP Certificates follow Appendix 5 to MSN 1819 (M+F).

trace.situation: UK regulation describing the process by which the Secretary of State may survey a ship and issue, authorise, or endorse an IAPP Certificate under MARPOL Annex VI at the request of a Contracting Government.
trace.trigger: A Contracting Government requests the Secretary of State to survey a ship and issue/endorse an IAPP Certificate under Annex VI.

procedures.action: Receive request from Contracting Government to survey ship and issue/authorise/endorse an IAPP Certificate under Annex VI.
procedures.why: Secretary of State can only act upon such a request.

procedures.action: Cause a survey to be carried out on the ship to confirm compliance with Annex VI requirements.
procedures.why: Certificate may only be issued if satisfied the ship complies with Annex VI.

procedures.action: Issue the IAPP Certificate in English using the form in Appendix 1 to Annex VI, stating it was issued pursuant to the request.
procedures.why: Ensures certificate format and content meet Annex VI and legal requirements.

procedures.action: Treat the Secretary of State as the Certifying Authority for that certificate.
procedures.why: Establishes legal responsibility and reference point for the issued certificate.

procedures.action: Send a copy of the IAPP Certificate and the survey report to the requesting Contracting Government as soon as possible.
procedures.why: Keeps the flag State informed and maintains record continuity.

procedures.action: Refuse to issue an IAPP Certificate if the ship is registered in, or entitled to fly the flag of, a country whose Government is not a Contracting Government.
procedures.why: Certificates can only be validly issued under Annex VI for ships linked to Contracting Governments.

constraints: Issuance is subject to payment of applicable fees.
Certificate must be in English and follow Appendix 1 to Annex VI format.
Certificate has same effect as if issued by the requesting Contracting Government, not the Secretary of State.
Must not issue certificate for ships registered in, or flying the flag of, a non-Contracting Government.
warnings: Must not issue an IAPP Certificate to a ship registered in, or entitled to fly the flag of, a country whose Government is not a Contracting Government.
outcomes: A validly issued IAPP Certificate has the same legal effect as one issued directly by the requesting Contracting Government.
The requesting Contracting Government receives a copy of the certificate and survey report for its records.
key_facts: The Secretary of State can act as Certifying Authority only when requested by a Contracting Government.
An IAPP Certificate issued this way must be in English and follow the Appendix 1 to Annex VI format.
The Secretary of State must send copies of the certificate and survey report to the requesting government.
Certificates cannot be issued for ships linked to non-Contracting Governments.

trace.situation: UK MARPOL Annex VI implementing regulations set out the validity period, renewal, and cessation conditions for a ship's International Air Pollution Prevention (IAPP) appropriate certificate.
trace.trigger: A ship holding an appropriate certificate under these Regulations approaches a renewal survey, certificate expiry, flag transfer, or an uncompleted repair/renewal/survey/endorsement requirement.

procedures.action: Ensure the appropriate certificate is issued for a period not exceeding five years from completion of the initial or renewal survey.
procedures.why: Regulation caps certificate validity at five years beginning with the date of completion of the relevant survey.

procedures.action: If the renewal survey is completed within the final three months before expiry, or after expiry, issue the new certificate valid from completion of that survey to a date not exceeding five years from the expiry of the latest certificate.
procedures.why: Regulation ties the new validity period to the expiry date of the previous certificate to maintain continuous coverage without extending beyond five years from that prior expiry.

procedures.action: Treat the certificate as ceasing to be valid upon transfer of the ship to another State's flag, uncorrected repairs/renewals under regulation 10(1) without compliance with regulation 10(3), failure to complete a required survey under regulations 5-8, failure to endorse the certificate, issuance of a new certificate, or reaching the certificate's expiry date — whichever occurs earliest.
procedures.why: These conditions represent events that invalidate the basis on which the certificate was originally issued.

procedures.action: When a ship is transferred to the flag of another Contracting Government and that Government requests it within three months of transfer, the Secretary of State must send a copy of the IAPP certificate and, if available, the survey report.
procedures.why: Ensures the receiving flag State has the necessary documentation to assess the ship's compliance history.

constraints: Certificate validity cannot exceed five years from the date of completion of the initial or renewal survey.
Renewal survey completed in the final three-month period or after expiry must result in a new certificate valid only up to five years from the prior certificate's expiry date.
The 'final three month period' is defined as the three months ending on the certificate's expiry date.
Request for certificate/survey report copies by a new flag State must be made within three months of the transfer date.
warnings: A certificate ceases to be valid if required repairs/renewals under regulation 10(1) are made without complying with regulation 10(3), even if the certificate has not formally expired.
Failure to complete a required survey or endorse the certificate per the Regulations invalidates the certificate regardless of its stated expiry date.
outcomes: Timely renewal survey completion preserves continuous valid certification without exceeding the five-year cap from the prior certificate's expiry.
Failure to meet survey, repair-compliance, or endorsement requirements results in loss of certificate validity, potentially affecting the ship's ability to proceed to sea.
Proper notification to a new flag State ensures continuity of compliance records upon transfer.
key_facts: An appropriate certificate (IAPP) is valid for up to five years from completion of the initial or renewal survey.
The 'final three month period' is the three months ending on the certificate's expiry date.
Certificate validity ends at the earliest of: flag transfer, non-compliant repair/renewal, incomplete survey, missing endorsement, issuance of a new certificate, or expiry date.
Upon flag transfer to a Contracting Government that requests documentation within three months, the Secretary of State must send the IAPP certificate and survey report if available.
