trace.situation: Regulatory provisions governing how a Certifying Authority may extend or endorse the validity of an appropriate certificate (e.g. IAPP certificate under MARPOL Annex VI) issued to a ship when surveys or renewals cannot be completed on schedule.
trace.trigger: The period of validity of an appropriate certificate is less than five years, expires before a renewal survey/new certificate can be completed, or the ship is engaged solely on short voyages at the time of expiry.

procedures.action: If the certificate's validity period is under five years, the Certifying Authority may extend it to a maximum of five years, provided the required survey under regulation 7 or 8 has been carried out.
procedures.why: Allows alignment of certificate validity with the standard five-year term once compliance surveys are confirmed.

procedures.action: If a renewal survey is completed but the new certificate cannot be issued/placed aboard before expiry, have the surveyor endorse the latest certificate.
procedures.why: Bridges the administrative gap between survey completion and certificate issuance without leaving the ship uncertificated.

procedures.action: Treat an endorsed certificate as valid for the specified further period, not exceeding five months from the original expiry date.
procedures.why: Caps the temporary extension to prevent indefinite reliance on an endorsement.

procedures.action: If the renewal survey has not been completed by expiry and the ship is not in the survey port, request the Certifying Authority to extend validity by up to three months solely to allow the voyage to the survey port.
procedures.why: Ensures the ship can reach the port where the survey is to occur without voyage interruption, while limiting the extension's purpose and duration.

procedures.action: Do not depart the port of survey until a new appropriate certificate has been issued after a paragraph (4) extension.
procedures.why: Prevents the ship from continuing operations on an extended certificate without completing the overdue survey.

procedures.action: For ships engaged solely on short voyages, the Certifying Authority may extend the latest certificate's validity by up to one month, subject to paragraph (7).
procedures.why: Accommodates short-voyage operational patterns while still requiring eventual compliance.

procedures.action: Do not permit a one-month short-voyage extension (paragraph 6) if the certificate has already been extended under paragraph (1), (3), or (4).
procedures.why: Prevents stacking multiple extensions, which would undermine the certification regime's integrity.

procedures.action: Once the renewal survey is completed and a new certificate issued for a ship under paragraph (5) or (6), the new certificate is valid for up to five years from the original expiry date of the previous certificate, subject to paragraph (9) and regulations 16(3) and 18(1).
procedures.why: Restores the standard five-year certification cycle while anchoring it to the original expiry date rather than the actual issuance date.

constraints: Extension under paragraph (1) requires that the survey under regulation 7 or 8 has been carried out.
Endorsement-based extension under paragraph (3) cannot exceed five months from the original expiry date.
Extension under paragraph (4) cannot exceed three months and is granted solely to allow the ship to reach its port of survey.
A ship with an extension under paragraph (4) must not leave the port of survey until a new certificate is issued.
Short-voyage extension under paragraph (6) cannot exceed one month.
Paragraph (6) extension is barred if the certificate was already extended under paragraph (1), (3), or (4).
New certificate validity under paragraph (8) is subject to paragraph (9) and regulations 16(3) and 18(1).
warnings: A ship must not leave its port of survey after a paragraph (4) extension until a new appropriate certificate has been issued.
Multiple extensions cannot be stacked (paragraph 6 extension barred if already extended under paragraph 1, 3, or 4).
outcomes: Properly extended or endorsed certificates allow continued lawful operation of the ship pending survey completion.
Failure to complete the renewal survey or obtain proper extension could leave a ship without valid certification, risking non-compliance.
New certificates issued after extension periods are backdated in validity to the original expiry date, maintaining the five-year cycle.
key_facts: Certificates with validity under five years can be extended to a maximum of five years if required surveys are completed.
Surveyor endorsement can extend validity by up to five months when a new certificate isn't ready by expiry.
A three-month extension is available solely to let a ship reach its survey port if the renewal survey wasn't completed before expiry.
Short-voyage ships may get a one-month extension, but not if already extended under other paragraphs.
New certificates after extensions are valid up to five years from the original expiry date of the previous certificate.

trace.situation: UK MARPOL Annex VI regulations specifying how the validity period of an appropriate air pollution prevention certificate (IAPP/UKAPP) is set, extended, and endorsed following renewal, annual, or intermediate surveys.
trace.trigger: A renewal, annual, or intermediate survey is completed either after the expiry of the previous certificate or before the scheduled survey period, requiring a new certificate validity period or an endorsement/anniversary date amendment.

procedures.action: When a renewal survey is completed after the expiry of the latest appropriate certificate, issue a new certificate valid for the period specified therein, not exceeding five years from the date the renewal survey was completed.
procedures.why: Ensures certificate validity reflects the actual completion date of the renewal survey rather than an expired prior certificate.

procedures.action: When the period of validity is extended under paragraphs (1), (4) or (6), or an endorsement is required under paragraph (2), the Certifying Authority must endorse the appropriate certificate per paragraph (11).
procedures.why: Maintains an auditable record on the certificate itself of any extension or required endorsement.

procedures.action: Use the correct endorsement form: Appendix 1 to Annex VI for an IAPP certificate, or Appendix 5 to Merchant Shipping Notice 1819 (M+F) for a UKAPP certificate.
procedures.why: Ensures endorsement is in the legally recognised format corresponding to the certificate type.

procedures.action: If an annual survey (regulation 7) or intermediate survey (regulation 8) is completed before its due survey period, amend the anniversary date by endorsement to a date no more than three months later than the survey completion date.
procedures.why: Keeps the survey cycle aligned with the actual survey date while limiting drift in the anniversary date.

procedures.action: After amending the anniversary date, schedule subsequent annual/intermediate surveys at the prescribed intervals measured from the new anniversary date.
procedures.why: Preserves the regulatory survey interval requirements going forward.

procedures.action: Alternatively, where a survey is completed early, leave the certificate's expiry date unchanged provided subsequent required surveys are still carried out within the maximum prescribed intervals.
procedures.why: Allows flexibility in survey timing without altering certificate expiry, as long as compliance intervals are respected.

constraints: New certificate validity must not exceed five years from the date of completion of the renewal survey.
Anniversary date amendment must not be more than three months later than the date the early survey was completed.
Endorsements must use the correct form depending on certificate type (IAPP vs UKAPP).
Maximum intervals between surveys prescribed by the Regulations must not be exceeded even if certificate expiry date is left unchanged.
outcomes: Certificates issued or endorsed correctly maintain continuous, valid compliance documentation for air pollution prevention requirements.
Failure to endorse or amend anniversary dates correctly could result in surveys falling outside prescribed intervals, risking certificate invalidity.
key_facts: A new appropriate certificate issued after a renewal survey completed post-expiry is valid for up to five years from the survey completion date.
Endorsements for IAPP certificates use Appendix 1 to Annex VI; UKAPP certificates use Appendix 5 to MSN 1819 (M+F).
Anniversary date amendments for early surveys are capped at three months later than the survey completion date.
Certificate expiry may remain unchanged if early surveys are completed, provided maximum survey intervals are not exceeded.

trace.situation: A surveyor identifies deficiencies aboard a ship requiring corrective action under UK MARPOL Annex VI air pollution regulations, triggering a notification and certificate suspension process.
trace.trigger: A surveyor determines that corrective action is required on a ship holding a valid appropriate certificate.

procedures.action: Surveyor advises the owner or master of the corrective action required.
procedures.why: The surveyor's professional opinion identifies a deficiency needing remedy.

procedures.action: Surveyor notifies the Certifying Authority that issued the certificate that the owner/master have been advised.
procedures.why: Keeps the issuing authority informed of the compliance issue.

procedures.action: Surveyor notifies the Certifying Authority if the corrective action is not taken.
procedures.why: Enables the Certifying Authority to act on non-compliance.

procedures.action: Certifying Authority may suspend validity of the certificate until corrective action is taken.
procedures.why: Ensures the ship does not operate under a certificate that no longer reflects its compliant condition.

procedures.action: Certifying Authority immediately gives notice of suspension to the ship's owner, and to the appropriate maritime authorities of the foreign port if applicable.
procedures.why: Ensures all relevant parties, including port state authorities, are aware of the suspension.

procedures.action: Owner notifies the master of the suspension upon receiving notice.
procedures.why: Ensures the master, who commands the vessel, is aware the certificate is no longer valid.

constraints: Applies only where an appropriate certificate has been issued in respect of the ship and is still valid.
Certifying Authority must give notice immediately upon suspension.
Owner must notify the master upon receiving suspension notice.
warnings: Failure to take corrective action can result in suspension of the ship's appropriate certificate.
A suspended certificate remains invalid until corrective action is completed.
outcomes: If corrective action is taken, the certificate presumably remains valid without suspension.
If corrective action is not taken, the Certifying Authority may suspend the certificate, affecting the ship's compliance status.
Suspension notice flows from Certifying Authority to owner to master, and to foreign port authorities if applicable.
key_facts: The surveyor is responsible for advising the owner/master of required corrective action.
Notification obligations exist between surveyor, Certifying Authority, owner, and master.
Certificate suspension is tied specifically to failure to take corrective action.
Foreign port maritime authorities must be notified if the ship is outside the United Kingdom when suspension occurs.

trace.situation: UK MARPOL Annex VI (air pollution) regulations set out the procedure for an applicant to dispute the outcome of a ship survey and have the dispute referred to arbitration.
trace.trigger: An applicant is dissatisfied with the outcome of a survey carried out in respect of a ship to which the regulation applies.

procedures.action: Serve written notice on the responsible person within 21 days of receiving notification of the survey outcome.
procedures.why: This is the statutory time limit for raising a dispute under the regulation.

procedures.action: State in the notice that a dispute exists and request referral to a single arbitrator.
procedures.why: Formal notice is required to trigger the arbitration process.

procedures.action: Select an arbitrator meeting the qualification criteria (certificated master/chief mate, chief/second engineer officer, equivalent certificate holder, naval architect, qualified person, person with shipping/fishing/port industry experience, or Chartered Institute of Arbitrators member).
procedures.why: Ensures the arbitrator has relevant competence to adjudicate the technical dispute.

procedures.action: In Scotland, if no agreement on an arbiter is reached, apply for appointment by a sheriff.
procedures.why: Provides a default appointment mechanism under Scottish law equivalent provisions.

procedures.action: Apply the arbitration rules in Merchant Shipping Notice M 1613 unless both parties agree alternative procedures before arbitration begins.
procedures.why: Establishes a default procedural framework for consistency unless parties opt out.

constraints: Written notice must be served within 21 days of receiving notification of the survey outcome.
Only persons meeting specified qualification criteria may act as arbitrator.
In Scotland, 'arbitrator' is construed as 'arbiter' and default appointment is by a sheriff if no agreement.
MSN 1613 rules apply by default unless alternative procedures are agreed before arbitration commences.
channels: Section 259 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995
warnings: Failure to serve notice within the 21-day period may bar the dispute from being referred to arbitration (implied by strict time limit).
outcomes: A qualified arbitrator (or arbiter in Scotland) is appointed to resolve the survey dispute.
The arbitrator is granted the same powers of an inspector under section 259 of the 1995 Act to investigate the matter.
Arbitration proceeds under MSN 1613 rules unless the parties agree otherwise beforehand.
key_facts: An applicant has 21 days from notification of a survey outcome to serve written notice disputing it.
Arbitrators must hold specific maritime certificates or relevant industry/arbitration qualifications.
An appointed arbitrator has the powers of an inspector under section 259 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995.

The 'responsible person' is the Certifying Authority that issued or is responsible for the relevant certificate.

trace.situation: UK MARPOL Annex VI regulations governing cancellation, surrender, integrity, availability, and conditions for a ship to proceed to sea in relation to the IAPP (International Air Pollution Prevention) certificate.
trace.trigger: Secretary of State has reason to believe the appropriate certificate was issued on false/erroneous information, or the ship's equipment/machinery has become deficient/damaged since survey; or a ship intends to leave a UK port without valid certification.

procedures.action: Cancel the appropriate certificate if issued on false/erroneous information or if equipment/machinery is deficient since last survey.
procedures.why: To prevent a ship operating under a certificate that no longer reflects its true compliance status.

procedures.action: Require surrender of an expired or cancelled certificate within a specified time and manner.
procedures.why: To ensure invalid certificates are not retained or misused.

procedures.action: Owner and master must keep the appropriate certificate readily available on board for inspection at all times.
procedures.why: To enable port state or flag state verification of compliance at any time.

procedures.action: Do not allow the ship to proceed to sea from a UK port unless a valid IAPP certificate exists, a surveyor confirms no unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment, or a person with detention power permits transit to the nearest repair yard.
procedures.why: To prevent ships with invalid or deficient certification from sailing and posing environmental risk.

procedures.action: Where Annex VI survey documentation is required but no certificate issued, ensure equivalent valid documentation showing survey completion and surveyor satisfaction exists before departure, or obtain permission to sail to nearest repair yard.
procedures.why: To maintain equivalent assurance of environmental safety even without a formal certificate.

constraints: Certificate cancellation only applies where false/erroneous information was used or equipment/machinery deficiency arose since last survey.
Surrender of expired/cancelled certificates must occur within the time and manner directed in writing by the Secretary of State.
No person may alter, falsify, knowingly/recklessly provide false survey information, misuse, lend, fail to surrender, or (in Scotland) forge an appropriate certificate.
Certificate must be readily available on board at all times for inspection.
Ship must not proceed to sea from a UK port without valid IAPP certificate, surveyor clearance, or detention-authority permission to sail to repair yard.
Where no certificate is issued, equivalent survey documentation confirming no unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment is required instead.
warnings: It is an offence to intentionally alter, falsify, or forge an appropriate certificate.
It is an offence to knowingly or recklessly provide false information in connection with a required survey, with intent to deceive.
It is an offence to use, lend, or permit use of an appropriate certificate by another person.
Failure to surrender a cancelled or expired certificate when required is an offence.
A ship must not proceed to sea without valid certification or documented survey clearance, except to proceed to the nearest repair yard under permission.
outcomes: Ships with falsified, erroneous, or deficiency-affected certificates can have certification cancelled, preventing continued unverified operation.
Owners/masters who fail to maintain certificate availability or who misuse certificates are subject to prosecution.
Ships without valid certification or survey clearance are barred from departing UK ports except under controlled repair-yard transit conditions.
key_facts: The Secretary of State can cancel an appropriate certificate for false information or post-survey equipment deficiency.
Expired or cancelled certificates must be surrendered as directed in writing.
Multiple certificate-related offences are defined, including forgery (specific to Scotland), falsification, and misuse.
Owner and master are jointly responsible for keeping the certificate available on board at all times.
A ship cannot leave a UK port without a valid IAPP certificate or equivalent survey documentation, unless permitted to sail to a repair yard.

trace.situation: UK Merchant Shipping regulations govern the operation of vapour emission control systems (VECS) for volatile organic compounds (VOCs) at harbours and terminals, and the corresponding equipment requirements for tankers calling at designated ports.
trace.trigger: A harbour authority, terminal operator, or tanker owner/master operates in or calls at a harbour/terminal designated for vapour emission control of VOCs.

procedures.action: Harbour authority or terminal operator must obtain written approval from the Secretary of State before operating a VOC vapour emission control system.
procedures.why: Operation without approval is prohibited under the regulation.

procedures.action: Harbour authority or terminal operator operating a VECS must comply with Schedule 4 of Merchant Shipping Notice 1819 (M+F).
procedures.why: Schedule 4 sets the required technical/operational standards for such systems.

procedures.action: Owner and master of a UK tanker subject to vapour emission control at an IMO-notified designated harbour/terminal must comply with Schedule 4 of MSN 1819 (M+F).
procedures.why: Ensures consistency with the Convention's designated-port regime.

procedures.action: Owner and master of a non-UK tanker in UK waters subject to vapour emission control at a Secretary of State-designated harbour/terminal must ensure the tanker is fitted with an approved, fully operational vapour emission collection system.
procedures.why: Equipment must be flag-state approved under Annex VI to ensure safe handling of VOC emissions.

procedures.action: Master must produce evidence of the flag-state approval of the vapour emission collection system on demand to the harbour authority, terminal operator, or surveyor.
procedures.why: Enables verification of compliance by port authorities/surveyors.

constraints: VECS operation by harbour authority/terminal operator requires prior written Secretary of State approval.
Compliance with Schedule 4 of MSN 1819 (M+F) is mandatory for UK tankers and harbour/terminal operators under the designated regime.
Non-UK tankers in UK waters must have a flag-state-approved (per Annex VI) vapour emission collection system that is fully operational.
The regulation on gas carriers applies only if the loading/containment systems allow safe retention or safe return ashore of non-methane VOCs.
warnings: Operating a VOC vapour emission control system without Secretary of State written approval is prohibited.
Tankers without an approved, fully operational vapour emission collection system may be in breach when calling at a designated harbour/terminal.
outcomes: Compliant harbour authorities/terminal operators and tankers avoid regulatory breach and support safe VOC vapour management.
Masters unable to produce approval evidence on demand may face enforcement action by harbour authority or surveyor.
key_facts: Approval for a VOC vapour emission control system must be given in writing by the Secretary of State.
Schedule 4 of MSN 1819 (M+F) sets the compliance standard for both shore-side systems and UK tankers.
Non-UK tankers in UK waters need a flag-state-approved (Annex VI) vapour emission collection system, fully operational, at designated harbours/terminals.
Gas carrier applicability is conditional on safe retention/return-ashore capability of loading and containment systems for non-methane VOCs.

trace.situation: UK MARPOL Annex VI regulations prohibiting deliberate emission of ozone-depleting substances from ships and governing new installations and nitrogen oxide (NOx) emission limits for ship engines.
trace.trigger: Any maintenance, servicing, repair, disposal of shipboard systems/equipment containing ozone-depleting substances, or installation of new equipment/engines on a ship.

procedures.action: Do not deliberately emit ozone-depleting substances during maintenance, servicing, repair or disposal of ship systems/equipment.
procedures.why: Deliberate emission, including releases during such operations, is prohibited by regulation.

procedures.action: Allow only minimal releases associated with recapture or recycling of ozone-depleting substances.
procedures.why: These are explicitly excluded from the definition of prohibited 'deliberate emission'.

procedures.action: Do not install new equipment containing ozone-depleting substances on non-UK ships.
procedures.why: New installations involving introduction of an ozone-depleting substance are prohibited for ships other than UK ships.

procedures.action: For installations before 1 January 2020, treat hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) as excepted from the installation ban.

trace.situation: UK NLS (Noxious Liquid Substances) ship regulations set conditions governing when a ship may proceed to or remain at sea after an important repair or renewal has been made.
trace.trigger: An important repair or renewal has been made to the ship, or a repair resulting from an investigation under regulation 13(5) has been made.

procedures.action: Determine if the repair/renewal qualifies as 'important' (addresses a defect substantially affecting ship/equipment integrity or efficiency, or is needed for Annex II compliance).
procedures.why: Only important repairs/renewals trigger the mandatory additional survey requirement under paragraph (1)(b).

procedures.action: Arrange for a relevant additional survey of the ship before proceeding to sea or continuing at sea.
procedures.why: The ship must not be enabled to proceed to sea or remain at sea unless the survey requirements in paragraph (3) are met.

procedures.action: Ensure the surveyor confirms the repair/renewal was made effectively, materials and workmanship are satisfactory, and the ship complies fully with the Regulations.
procedures.why: These are the specific satisfaction criteria the surveyor must verify under paragraph (3)(b).

procedures.action: Obtain a surveyor's written report expressing this satisfaction.
procedures.why: The report is a precondition for the ship being allowed to proceed or remain at sea.

procedures.action: If there is a dispute about whether a repair/renewal is 'important', the owner or master may serve a written request on the Secretary of State for advice.

procedures.action: Treat the repair/renewal as not important unless the Secretary of State advises otherwise within 21 days of the request.
procedures.why: Establishes a default outcome and time limit to prevent indefinite uncertainty.

constraints: Ship must not proceed to sea or remain at sea unless the additional survey requirements are met.
Surveyor must be satisfied on all three points: effective repair, satisfactory materials/workmanship, and full regulatory compliance.
Dispute resolution request must be made in writing to the Secretary of State.
Secretary of State has 21 days from receipt of the request to advise that a repair is important; otherwise it defaults to not important.
warnings: A ship with an unresolved important repair/renewal must not proceed to sea or remain at sea without the required survey and satisfactory surveyor report.
outcomes: If the survey and surveyor report confirm compliance, the ship may proceed to or remain at sea.

key_facts: This regulation applies to a UK NLS ship after an important repair/renewal or a repair from a regulation 13(5) investigation.

Owners/masters can dispute the classification of a repair as 'important' by writing to the Secretary of State.

trace.situation: UK MARPOL regulations impose duties on owners and masters of NLS (noxious liquid substance) ships to maintain the ship's condition and equipment, control post-survey modifications, and report accidents or defects affecting ship or equipment integrity.
trace.trigger: An accident occurs to the NLS ship, or a defect is discovered that substantially affects the integrity of the ship or the efficiency/completeness of required equipment.

procedures.action: Maintain the ship and its equipment in conformity with relevant requirements at all times.
procedures.why: To ensure the ship remains fit to proceed to sea without presenting an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment, including UK territorial waters.

procedures.action: Do not alter structure, equipment, systems, fittings, arrangements or materials covered by a completed survey, except by direct replacement, without approval.
procedures.why: Unauthorized changes after survey could invalidate the certified condition verified by the Certifying Authority.

procedures.action: Obtain approval from the Certifying Authority that appointed the surveyor, or from the Secretary of State where the survey was carried out by a Contracting State other than the UK pursuant to regulation 16, before making non-replacement changes.
procedures.why: Ensures the correct authority sanctions changes affecting the validity of the NLS certificate.

procedures.action: Report any accident or defect affecting ship/equipment integrity to the Certifying Authority that issued the NLS certificate at the earliest opportunity.
procedures.why: Enables the Certifying Authority to determine whether an additional survey or repair is necessary.

procedures.action: If the ship is in a port outside the United Kingdom, immediately report the accident or defect to the appropriate maritime authorities in that country as well.
procedures.why: Local port state authorities need immediate notice of conditions affecting marine pollution risk.

procedures.action: Certifying Authority must initiate an investigation upon report of accident/defect to determine need for additional survey or repair, and carry it out if necessary.
procedures.why: Confirms the ship's continued compliance and fitness to proceed without environmental risk.

procedures.action: Certifying Authority must take steps to confirm that the port state notification requirement was fulfilled when the ship is in a foreign port.
procedures.why: Ensures compliance oversight is not lost when the ship is outside UK jurisdiction.

constraints: Changes to surveyed structure/equipment are only permitted by direct replacement unless approved.
Approval must come from the Certifying Authority that appointed the surveyor, or the Secretary of State in specified cross-border cases.
Reporting must occur at the earliest opportunity to the issuing Certifying Authority.
If in a foreign port, immediate reporting to local maritime authorities is also required.
warnings: Unauthorized modification of surveyed equipment without approval may compromise certification validity.
Failure to report accidents/defects affecting ship integrity could allow the ship to proceed while posing an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
outcomes: Ship remains fit to proceed to sea without presenting an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
Certifying Authority investigation may result in additional survey or repair before the ship continues operation.
Port state and flag/certifying authorities maintain oversight of ship condition even when the vessel is abroad.
key_facts: Owners and masters of NLS ships must keep the ship and equipment conforming to applicable requirements at all times.
Post-survey changes to surveyed items require approval except for direct replacements.
Accidents or defects affecting ship/equipment integrity must be reported to the issuing Certifying Authority at the earliest opportunity.
If the ship is in a foreign port, the local maritime authorities must also be immediately notified.
The Certifying Authority must investigate reported accidents/defects and arrange additional survey or repair if needed.

trace.situation: Regulation specifying the conditions under which a Certifying Authority must issue a Noxious Liquid Substances (NLS) certificate to a United Kingdom ship, including ships newly flagged to the UK following transfer from another Contracting State.
trace.trigger: A surveyor notifies the Certifying Authority of completion of an initial or renewal survey confirming compliance, or a ship is transferring its flag to the UK from another Contracting State while holding a valid Annex II certificate.

procedures.action: Issue a relevant NLS certificate once notified by a surveyor that a relevant initial or renewal survey has been carried out and compliance confirmed.
procedures.why: Certificate issuance depends on surveyor confirmation that the ship meets relevant requirements at the survey date.

procedures.action: Confirm any fee due has been paid before issuing the certificate.
procedures.why: Fee payment is a precondition stated alongside survey notification.

procedures.action: For a ship transferring from another Contracting State's flag, verify an Annex II-compliant certificate was issued and valid immediately before transfer.
procedures.why: Ensures continuity of compliance status from the previous flag state.

procedures.action: Cause a survey to be carried out on the transferring ship and confirm its condition poses no unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
procedures.why: The Certifying Authority must independently verify fitness to proceed to sea before issuing a new certificate.

procedures.action: Verify no unapproved structural or equipment changes have been made since the last Annex II survey, except direct replacement with conforming equipment.
procedures.why: Unapproved changes could invalidate the ship's compliance basis established under the previous flag's certificate.

constraints: Surveyor's notification must confirm compliance at the date of survey.
Any applicable fee must be paid before certificate issuance.
For transferred ships, the prior Annex II certificate must have been valid immediately before transfer.
No changes other than direct replacement of equipment/fittings with conforming equipment are permitted without approval of the prior Contracting State.
The Certifying Authority must be satisfied the ship can proceed to sea without unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
warnings: Certificate must not be issued if ship's condition presents an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
Unapproved structural or equipment changes (beyond conforming direct replacements) preclude certificate issuance on transfer.
outcomes: Ship receives valid NLS certificate enabling lawful carriage of noxious liquid substances under UK flag.
Failure to meet survey, fee, or change-approval conditions results in certificate not being issued.

trace.situation: UK regulations set out procedures for mutual survey and certification arrangements for Noxious Liquid Substance (NLS) ships between the Secretary of State and other Contracting States to MARPOL.
trace.trigger: A Contracting State requests the Secretary of State (or vice versa) to carry out a survey of an NLS ship not registered in their own state.

procedures.action: Secretary of State may request another Contracting State to survey a UK NLS ship.

procedures.action: If the requested State is satisfied requirements are met, it must issue/authorise issue of an NLS certificate or endorse an existing one.
procedures.why: Ensures certification reflects compliance with notified requirements.

procedures.action: Treat the Secretary of State as the Certifying Authority for any certificate issued under this arrangement.

outcomes: A UK NLS ship can obtain a valid NLS certificate via survey conducted by another Contracting State, with the Secretary of State retained as Certifying Authority.

trace.situation: UK regulation governing extension, endorsement, and validity periods of NLS (Noxious Liquid Substances) certificates issued for United Kingdom NLS ships under MARPOL-related domestic law.

procedures.action: If certificate validity is less than five years, Certifying Authority may extend it up to a maximum of five years, provided the required survey under regulation 11 or 12 has been carried out.
procedures.why: Ensures certificate validity aligns with survey completion while capping total validity at five years.

procedures.action: If a renewal survey is completed but the new certificate cannot be issued/placed on board before expiry, the surveyor may endorse the existing certificate.
procedures.why: Allows continuity of valid certification despite administrative delay in issuing the new document.

procedures.action: Treat an endorsed certificate as valid for the further period stated on it, not exceeding five months from the original expiry date.
procedures.why: Provides a bounded bridge period until the new certificate is produced.

procedures.why: Permits safe transit to the survey location without operating under an expired certificate.

procedures.action: Do not allow the ship to leave the port of survey until a new relevant NLS certificate has been issued, once validity has been extended under paragraph (4).
procedures.why: Prevents the ship from operating indefinitely on an extension once it has reached the survey port.

procedures.action: For ships engaged solely on short voyages, the Certifying Authority may extend certificate validity by up to one month.
procedures.why: Accommodates short-voyage operational patterns while limiting extension duration.

procedures.action: Do not grant a short-voyage extension under paragraph (6) if the certificate has already been extended under paragraph (1), (3), (4), or (6).

warnings: A ship must not leave the port of survey on an extended certificate until a new relevant NLS certificate has been issued.

outcomes: Properly extended or endorsed certificates allow continued lawful operation of the ship pending survey or certificate issuance.

trace.situation: Regulatory provisions governing how a Certifying Authority or surveyor must endorse a relevant NLS (Noxious Liquid Substances) certificate when its validity period is extended or when annual/intermediate surveys are completed early.

procedures.action: Endorse the relevant NLS certificate when its validity period is extended under paragraph (1), (4) or (6).

procedures.action: Alternatively, where an early survey is completed, leave the certificate's expiry date unchanged provided subsequent regulation 11/12 surveys are carried out and endorsed so that maximum intervals between surveys are not exceeded.

constraints: Anniversary date amendment must not exceed three months later than the date the early survey was completed.

warnings: Failure to endorse or amend the certificate correctly could result in survey intervals being exceeded, invalidating the certificate's compliance status.
outcomes: Certificate remains valid and compliant with survey interval requirements when properly endorsed and surveys scheduled per the new or retained anniversary/expiry date.

trace.situation: UK statutory regulation specifying how an arbitrator is appointed to resolve disputes arising under marine pollution (NLS-related) provisions, and the qualifications such an arbitrator must hold.
trace.trigger: A dispute arises between an applicant and a responsible person requiring arbitration under this regulation.

procedures.action: Verify the appointed arbitrator holds one of the specified qualifications (master/chief mate STCW II/2 certificate, chief/second engineer STCW III/2 certificate, equivalent certificate, naval architect, qualified person, special shipping/port experience, or CIArb membership).
procedures.why: Regulation restricts eligibility to ensure the arbitrator has relevant competence.

constraints: The CIArb appointment route does not apply in Scotland.

procedures.action: Treat all discharge of noxious liquid substances or NLS-containing mixtures as prohibited by default.
procedures.why: Baseline rule under the regulation prohibits such discharge unless conditions are met.

procedures.action: Discharge only below the waterline through underwater outlet(s) at or below the designed maximum rate.

procedures.action: Discharge only at least 12 nautical miles from nearest land and in water depth of at least 25 metres.
procedures.why: Distance and depth thresholds required to permit lawful discharge.

procedures.action: Ensure discharge complies with conditions in Annex II regulation 13, paragraphs 1.2 and 4 to 7.

procedures.action: Prohibit any NLS discharge in polar waters regardless of other conditions met.

Discharge must occur below waterline via designed underwater outlet(s).

trace.situation: UK MARPOL regulations define exceptions to the prohibition on discharging noxious liquid substances (NLS) from certificated NLS ships, and define key terms such as 'Category Z substance' and 'NLS ship'.
trace.trigger: A certificated NLS ship needs to discharge noxious liquid substances, ballast water, tank washings, or mixtures containing NLS into the sea, or water has been introduced into a tank following ventilation procedures.

procedures.action: Treat water introduced into a tank after ventilation procedures under paragraph (5) as not being a noxious liquid substance.
procedures.why: Post-ventilation water is excluded from NLS classification under this regulation.

procedures.action: If discharge is necessary to secure the safety of the ship or to save life, proceed without violating paragraphs (1) and (3).
procedures.why: Safety of ship and life-saving discharges are exempted from the general discharge prohibition.

procedures.action: If discharge results from damage to the ship or equipment, take all reasonable precautions after the damage or discovery to prevent or minimise the discharge.
procedures.why: The exemption only applies if the master and owner acted to minimise discharge following the damage event.

procedures.action: Ensure the owner or master did not act with intent to cause damage or recklessly with knowledge that damage would probably result.
procedures.why: The exemption is void if there was intentional or reckless conduct leading to the discharge.

procedures.action: Obtain Secretary of State approval if discharging to combat a specific pollution incident in order to minimise pollution damage.
procedures.why: Approved pollution-response discharges are exempted from the general prohibition.

constraints: Exemptions under this regulation apply only to discharges from a certificated NLS ship.
Damage-related discharge exemption requires reasonable precautions taken after the damage occurred or was discovered.
Damage-related discharge exemption is invalid if intent or recklessness is shown by owner or master.
Pollution-incident discharge must be approved by the Secretary of State.

warnings: Discharge exemptions do not apply if the owner or master acted with intent to cause damage or recklessly with knowledge that damage would probably result.
Category Z substances and mixtures containing them remain subject to classification and discharge controls unless an exemption applies.
outcomes: Lawful discharge exemption applies if safety/life-saving, accidental damage with reasonable precautions, or Secretary of State-approved pollution response.

trace.situation: UK Merchant Shipping Regulations implementing MARPOL Annex II set out master's duties regarding noxious liquid substances (NLS) cargo operations, including unloading, categorisation, tripartite agreements, and the Procedures and Arrangements Manual.

procedures.action: Do not permit loading or carriage of an NLS subject to a tripartite agreement unless a valid NLS certificate is in force and loading/carriage complies with its terms.
procedures.why: Ensures compliance with the tripartite agreement between producing country, receiving country, and flag State, and certification requirements.

procedures.action: Maintain an approved Procedures and Arrangements Manual on board in the standard Appendix 4 format, in English (UK ships) or English/French/Spanish (other NLS ships).

outcomes: Compliance prevents unlawful discharge of hazardous residues back onto the ship or into the sea.

Tripartite agreement substances require a valid, matching NLS certificate for loading and carriage.

trace.situation: Regulatory requirements under MARPOL Annex II (NLS - Noxious Liquid Substances) governing the maintenance of the Cargo Record Book and the carriage of a Marine Pollution Emergency Plan aboard NLS ships.
trace.trigger: Completion of any cargo operation listed in Appendix 2 to Annex II, an accidental discharge of a noxious liquid substance, or a discharge made under regulation 3 of Annex II; also applies continuously to NLS ships of 150 gross tonnage or more regarding carriage of the emergency plan.

procedures.action: Record promptly in the Cargo Record Book the completion of any Appendix 2 operation.
procedures.why: Ensures operational traceability required by the regulation.

procedures.action: On accidental discharge or discharge under regulation 3, enter the circumstances and reason for the discharge in the Cargo Record Book.
procedures.why: Provides documented justification for any non-routine discharge.

procedures.action: Have the officer(s) in charge of the relevant operation sign each entry.
procedures.why: Establishes accountability and authenticity of the record.

procedures.action: Write the Cargo Record Book in English (UK NLS ships) or in/translated into English, French or Spanish (other NLS ships).
procedures.why: Ensures international readability for inspection purposes.

procedures.action: If an entry is also written in the ship's national language, treat that national-language entry as prevailing in case of dispute or discrepancy.
procedures.why: Preserves the authoritative version for the flag State in legal disputes.

procedures.action: Keep the Cargo Record Book readily available for inspection and on board the ship (except unmanned ships under tow).
procedures.why: Facilitates port State/flag State verification.

procedures.action: Retain the Cargo Record Book for three years after the last entry.
procedures.why: Statutory retention period for compliance verification.

procedures.action: Carry an approved Marine Pollution Emergency Plan on board if the NLS ship is 150 gross tonnage or more.
procedures.why: Mandatory preparedness measure for pollution incidents.

procedures.action: Ensure the plan is developed per relevant Guidelines, written in a language understood by master and officers, and contains the minimum information per regulation 17.2.1-17.2.4 of Annex II.
procedures.why: Guarantees the plan is usable and complete in an emergency.

procedures.action: Where combined with another required plan, title it 'Shipboard Marine Pollution Emergency Plan'.
procedures.why: Standardizes documentation when plans are merged.

constraints: Cargo Record Book entries must be made promptly after each relevant operation.
Each entry must be signed by the officer(s) in charge.
Language of the Cargo Record Book must be English (UK NLS ships) or English/French/Spanish (other NLS ships).
National language entry prevails only in case of dispute or discrepancy.
Cargo Record Book must stay on board except for unmanned ships under tow.
Retention period is three years after the last entry.
Marine Pollution Emergency Plan required only for NLS ships of 150 GT or more.
Plan must be approved by the flag State administration and written in a language understood by master and officers.

outcomes: Properly maintained Cargo Record Book provides evidence of compliant operations and discharges during inspections.

Accidental or regulation-3 discharges require a recorded explanation of circumstances and reason.

trace.situation: UK regulation (under the Merchant Shipping Act 1995, applied to noxious liquid substances enforcement) describing the procedure for detaining a ship and notifying relevant authorities.

procedures.action: Serve a detention notice on the master of the ship stating the grounds for detention.

procedures.action: Ensure the notice requires compliance with its terms until the ship is released by a person mentioned in section 284(1) of the 1995 Act.

trace.situation: UK regulation defines the scope and limits of inspection powers under sections 258 and 259 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1995 as applied to ships regarding noxious liquid substance (NLS) pollution prevention compliance.

procedures.action: Verify whether documentation referred to in regulation 21 has been issued and is still valid.

procedures.action: Inspect the Cargo Record Book.

procedures.action: Inspect the Marine Pollution Emergency Plan only where there are clear grounds the ship or equipment condition does not substantially correspond with the certificate/documentation particulars.

procedures.action: Only board the ship if it is in a UK port or at an offshore installation in UK waters or controlled waters.

procedures.action: If corrective action is not completed within the specified reasonable period, withdraw the IOPP or UKOPP Certificate and notify the owner/master and Secretary of State.
procedures.why: Certificate validity depends on the ship actually meeting the standards it attests to.

procedures.action: If the ship is in a port of another Convention Country when withdrawal occurs, notify that country's appropriate authorities.
procedures.why: Allows the port state to take appropriate control action under the Convention.

procedures.action: If a foreign Convention Country ship in a UK port needs its IOPP Certificate withdrawn, the Certifying Authority must notify the Secretary of State.
procedures.why: Enables UK port state control measures to be invoked.

procedures.action: On receiving such notification, the Secretary of State must ensure the ship does not sail until it can proceed without presenting an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment, or may only leave for the nearest appropriate repair yard.
procedures.why: Protects the marine environment while allowing necessary transit to a repair facility.

procedures.action: If dissatisfied with a survey outcome, serve written notice on the responsible person within 21 days requesting referral of the dispute to a single arbitrator.
procedures.why: Provides a formal, time-bound dispute resolution mechanism for survey disagreements.

constraints: The corrective action period specified by the Certifying Authority must be reasonable.
Dispute notice must be served within 21 days of receiving notification of the survey outcome.
Ship must not sail (except to nearest repair yard) while presenting an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
warnings: Ship must not proceed to sea if it presents an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
Failure to complete corrective action within the specified period results in certificate withdrawal.
outcomes: IOPP/UKOPP Certificate is withdrawn if corrective action is not taken in time.
Ship may be detained in port until safe to sail or limited to transit to nearest repair yard.
Dissatisfied applicants can escalate survey disputes to arbitration within 21 days.
key_facts: Certifying Authority can require corrective action or withdraw IOPP/UKOPP certificates for non-compliant or unsafe ships.
Withdrawal notifications must go to owner/master, Secretary of State, and foreign port authorities where relevant.
Secretary of State has authority to prevent a ship sailing until environmental risk is resolved or it reaches a repair yard.
A survey dispute can be referred to a single arbitrator if written notice is given within 21 days.

trace.situation: UK MARPOL regulations define arbitration qualification criteria and set conditions under which a non-UK ship requiring an IOPP certificate may be permitted to leave a UK port.
trace.trigger: A non-United Kingdom ship subject to Annex I regulation 7 IOPP certificate requirements seeks to depart from a UK port.

procedures.action: Confirm a Contracting State has issued and (where appropriate) endorsed a valid IOPP certificate for the ship.
procedures.why: Satisfies the first recognized basis for allowing the ship to proceed to sea under the regulation.

procedures.action: If not a Contracting State, confirm a non-Contracting State's IOPP certificate is deemed by the Certifying Authority to have equivalent force and remains valid.
procedures.why: Provides an alternative recognized certification basis equivalent to Annex I requirements.

procedures.action: If no valid certificate exists, arrange for a surveyor of ships to carry out a survey as if regulation 10(4)(a) applied.
procedures.why: Allows verification of the ship's condition in the absence of a valid foreign certificate.

procedures.action: Obtain surveyor's satisfaction that the ship can proceed without presenting an unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
procedures.why: Ensures environmental protection standard is met before departure is authorized.

procedures.action: Alternatively, obtain authorization from a person with power to detain the ship, confirming the ship can proceed only to the nearest appropriate repair yard without unreasonable threat of harm, and that permission has been granted.
procedures.why: Provides a limited departure route for ships needing repair while still safeguarding against marine pollution risk.

constraints: A non-UK ship requiring an IOPP certificate under Annex I regulation 7 must not be enabled to proceed to sea from a UK port unless one of the specified certificate/survey/permission conditions is met.

Arbitrators under the regulation must meet judicial-appointment eligibility (England/Wales per Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007 s.50) or be an advocate/solicitor in Scotland of at least seven years' standing, or a Bar of Northern Ireland member/solicitor of the Court of Judicature of Northern Ireland of at least seven years' standing.
The Certifying Authority responsible under regulation 12 or 13 is defined per the certificate connected to the survey, with a specific rule for additional surveys under regulation 10(4)(e).
channels: Tribunals, Courts and Enforcement Act 2007 s.50
warnings: A non-UK ship must not be allowed to proceed to sea without valid IOPP certification or equivalent survey/permission to avoid unreasonable threat of harm to the marine environment.
outcomes: Compliance with one of the listed conditions permits the non-UK ship to legally depart a UK port.
Failure to meet any condition results in the ship being prohibited from proceeding to sea, or restricted to proceeding only to the nearest repair yard under detention authority permission.
key_facts: The regulation governs non-UK ships subject to IOPP certificate requirements under Annex I regulation 7 departing from UK ports.

Four alternative pathways exist for authorizing departure: valid Contracting State certificate, valid non-Contracting State certificate deemed equivalent, surveyor assessment, or detaining authority permission to proceed to a repair yard.
Arbitrator eligibility criteria reference statutory qualification standards across England/Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland.
The Certifying Authority is defined by reference to which authority issued the certificate connected to the survey in question.

Who qualifies as the 'Certifying Authority' for a dispute involving an additional survey under regulation 10(4)(e)?

Which qualifications must an arbitrator hold under this regulation in Scotland versus Northern Ireland?

trace.situation: UK MARPOL implementing regulations specify when ships must carry and complete an Oil Record Book (ORB) Parts I and II for machinery space and cargo/ballast operations.
trace.trigger: An oil tanker of 150 GT or above, or any ship of 400 GT or above, conducts machinery space operations (reg 17.2 Annex I) or cargo/ballast operations (reg 36.2/3 Annex I), or any discharge of oil/oily mixture occurs.

procedures.action: Ensure the ship carries an Oil Record Book Part I (Machinery Space Operations) if it is an oil tanker of 150 GT+ or any other ship of 400 GT+.
procedures.why: Mandated by the regulation based on tonnage thresholds.

procedures.action: Ensure the ship carries an Oil Record Book Part II (Cargo/Ballast Operations) if it is an oil tanker of 150 GT+.
procedures.why: Additional requirement specific to oil tankers for cargo/ballast tracking.

procedures.action: Complete ORB Part I on a tank-to-tank basis whenever a listed machinery space operation (reg 17.2 Annex I) occurs.
procedures.why: Ensures accurate, traceable record of machinery-related oil operations.

procedures.action: Complete ORB Part II on a tank-to-tank basis whenever a listed cargo/ballast operation (reg 36.2 or 36.3 Annex I) occurs.
procedures.why: Ensures accurate, traceable record of cargo/ballast oil operations.

procedures.action: Record the circumstances and reasons for any discharge of oil or oily mixture (reg 17.3 or 36.4 Annex I), or any accidental/exceptional discharge not excepted, in the relevant ORB part.
procedures.why: Provides documented justification and accountability for discharges to demonstrate compliance or investigate incidents.

constraints: ORB Part I required for oil tankers 150 GT+ and other ships 400 GT+.
ORB Part II required only for oil tankers 150 GT+.
Entries must be made on a tank-to-tank basis where appropriate.
Discharge entries must specify circumstances and reasons, even for accidental/exceptional discharges not otherwise excepted.
warnings: Failure to record discharges accurately may constitute a violation of MARPOL requirements.
outcomes: A complete, auditable record of oil-related machinery and cargo/ballast operations exists for inspection and compliance verification.
Documented justification is available for any discharge event, supporting regulatory defense or investigation.
key_facts: Oil Record Book Part I is required for oil tankers 150 GT and above and all other ships 400 GT and above.
Oil Record Book Part II is required only for oil tankers 150 GT and above.
Entries must be tank-to-tank where appropriate, tied to specific operations listed in Annex I regs 17.2 and 36.2/3.
Any oil discharge, including accidental or exceptional ones not excepted under regs 17.3/36.4, must be recorded with circumstances and reasons in the relevant ORB part.

trace.situation: UK statutory regulation detailing requirements for recording oil-related operations and equipment failures in the Oil Record Book and the rules governing its retention and inspection.
trace.trigger: Completion of an oil transfer/discharge operation referred to in paragraph (5), or failure of oil filtering equipment or the oil discharge monitoring and control system.

procedures.action: Fully record each oil operation in the Oil Record Book without delay.
procedures.why: Ensures all entries appropriate to that operation are completed accurately and promptly.

procedures.action: Have the officer(s) in charge sign off the completed entry and page.
procedures.why: Confirms accountability and verification of the recorded operation.

procedures.action: Record any failure of oil filtering equipment in Oil Record Book Part I, and any failure of the oil discharge monitoring and control system in Part II.
procedures.why: Maintains a traceable record of equipment malfunctions affecting pollution prevention systems.

procedures.action: Keep the Oil Record Book readily available on board for inspection at all reasonable times.
procedures.why: Allows authorities to inspect compliance without delay, except for unmanned ships under tow.

procedures.action: Preserve the Oil Record Book for three years after the last entry.
procedures.why: Ensures records remain available for regulatory review and potential judicial proceedings.

procedures.action: Allow the Secretary of State or authorised person to inspect, copy, and request certification of entries.
procedures.why: Supports enforcement and evidentiary use of Oil Record Book entries.

procedures.action: Perform inspections and certified copying as expeditiously as possible.
procedures.why: Prevents undue delay to the ship during regulatory inspection.

constraints: The Oil Record Book must be kept on board the ship (except unmanned ships under tow).
Entries must be signed off by the officer(s) in charge of the operation.
The book must be preserved for three years after the last entry.
Inspections must not cause the ship to be unduly delayed.
warnings: Failure to record oil filtering equipment or discharge monitoring system failures breaches recordkeeping requirements.
Oil Record Book must not be withheld or delayed from inspection beyond what is reasonable.
outcomes: A properly maintained Oil Record Book provides admissible evidence in judicial proceedings.
Non-compliance with recording or retention requirements could expose the ship to regulatory and legal consequences.
Efficient inspection procedures minimize disruption to ship operations.
key_facts: Oil operations must be recorded without delay and signed off by the responsible officer(s).
Equipment failures (filtering equipment, discharge monitoring/control system) must be logged in the respective Oil Record Book Part.
The Oil Record Book must be preserved for three years after the last entry.
Authorised inspectors can inspect, copy, and require certification of Oil Record Book entries, and must do so without undue delay to the ship.

question_seeds.text: What must be recorded in the Oil Record Book if the oil discharge monitoring and control system fails?
How long must the Oil Record Book be preserved after its last entry?
Who is authorised to inspect and copy entries from the Oil Record Book while in port?

trace.situation: UK MARPOL regulations set out exceptions under which discharge of oil or oily mixtures into the sea is not a contravention of regulations 25 and 26 (and Polar Code part II-A paragraph 1.1.1).
trace.trigger: A discharge of oil or oily mixture occurs due to safety/life-saving necessity, damage to the ship or its equipment, approved anti-pollution operations, or damage caused by a third party unconnected with an excepted ship's business.

procedures.action: Discharge oil or oily mixture if necessary to secure the safety of the ship or to save life at sea.
procedures.why: This type of discharge is explicitly excepted from regulations 25 and 26.

procedures.action: After damage to the ship or equipment causes a discharge, take all reasonable precautions to prevent or minimise further discharge.
procedures.why: Precautionary action after the occurrence is a required condition for the exception to apply.

procedures.action: Ensure owner/master do not act with intent to cause damage or recklessly with knowledge that damage would probably result.
procedures.why: The exception only applies if neither the owner nor master acted with culpable intent or recklessness.

procedures.action: Use only approved substances containing oil when combating specific pollution incidents to minimise pollution damage.
procedures.why: Only approved discharges for pollution-combating purposes are excepted from the regulations.

procedures.action: For an excepted ship within UK or controlled waters, document that any damage-caused discharge was caused by a person unconnected with the ship's business acting with intent, recklessness, or serious negligence.
procedures.why: This third-party causation condition, combined with reasonable precautions and absence of owner/master intent/recklessness, is required for the exception to apply to excepted ships in UK waters.

constraints: All reasonable precautions must be taken after damage or discovery of discharge to prevent or minimise it.
Owner or master must not have acted with intent to cause damage or recklessly with knowledge damage would probably result.
For excepted ships in UK or controlled waters, the damage must have been caused by a person not connected with the ship's business acting with intent, recklessness, or serious negligence.
Discharges for combating pollution incidents must be approved substances used specifically to minimise pollution damage.
warnings: Discharges resulting from owner/master intent to cause damage or reckless conduct with knowledge of probable damage are not excepted and remain a contravention.
The exception for excepted ships in UK waters does not apply unless the damage was caused by an unconnected third party acting with intent, recklessness, or serious negligence.
outcomes: Discharges meeting the stated conditions are not treated as contraventions of regulations 25 and 26.
Failure to meet the precaution or intent/recklessness conditions removes the benefit of the exception, exposing owner/master to liability.
key_facts: Regulations 25 and 26 (and Polar Code II-A para 1.1.1) do not apply to discharges necessary for safety of the ship or saving life at sea.
Discharges resulting from damage to the ship or equipment are excepted only if reasonable precautions were taken and owner/master did not act intentionally or recklessly.
Approved discharges used to combat specific pollution incidents to minimise damage are also excepted.
For excepted ships in UK or controlled waters, an additional condition requires the damage to have been caused by an unconnected third party acting with intent, recklessness, or serious negligence.

Why would the exception not apply if the master acted recklessly with knowledge that damage would result?

trace.situation: UK MARPOL-implementing regulations define limited exceptions to the oil/oily mixture discharge prohibitions (regs 25 and 26) when a discharge results from damage to a ship or its equipment outside UK controlled waters.
trace.trigger: An oil or oily mixture discharge occurs as a result of damage to a UK excepted ship or non-UK excepted ship or its equipment while outside the United Kingdom or its controlled waters.

procedures.action: After damage occurs or the discharge is discovered, take all reasonable precautions to prevent or minimise the discharge.
procedures.why: This is a mandatory condition for the discharge to qualify for exemption from regulations 25 and 26.

procedures.action: Establish whether the damage was caused by a person not connected with the ship's business acting intentionally, recklessly, or with serious negligence (for UK excepted ships).
procedures.why: This is a required condition distinguishing exempt discharges on UK excepted ships.

procedures.action: Confirm that neither owner nor master acted with intent to cause damage, or recklessly with knowledge that damage would probably result.
procedures.why: This condition must be satisfied for both UK and non-UK excepted ships to retain the exemption.

procedures.action: Identify who counts as a 'person connected with the ship's business' (seafarer, master, owner, cargo owner, classification society) when assessing fault under regulations 21 to 23.
procedures.why: This definition determines whose conduct is relevant in applying the exemption tests.

constraints: Exemption only applies to discharges occurring outside the United Kingdom or its controlled waters.
Exemption only applies to discharges resulting from damage to the ship or its equipment, not routine or deliberate discharges.
For UK excepted ships, the damage must have been caused by a person unconnected with the ship's business acting with intent, recklessness, or serious negligence.
All reasonable precautions must have been taken after the damage or discovery of discharge to prevent or minimise it.
Neither owner nor master may have acted with intent to cause damage or recklessly with knowledge damage would probably result.
warnings: A discharge will NOT be exempt if the owner or master acted with intent to cause damage or recklessly with knowledge that damage would probably result.
Failure to take all reasonable precautions after damage or discovery of discharge voids the exemption.
outcomes: If conditions are met, the discharge is exempted from the prohibitions in regulations 25 and 26.
If conditions are not met (e.g., owner/master acted recklessly or precautions were not taken), the discharge remains a breach of regulations 25 and 26.
key_facts: Regulations 25 and 26 prohibit certain oil/oily mixture discharges, but exceptions exist for damage-caused discharges outside UK controlled waters.
UK excepted ships require a more detailed fault test (third-party intent/recklessness/serious negligence) than non-UK excepted ships.
Both ship categories require that all reasonable precautions were taken post-damage/discovery and that owner/master did not act with intent or knowing recklessness.
'Person connected with a ship's business' includes seafarers, the master, the owner, cargo owners, and the classification society that issued the ship's class certificate.

trace.situation: Regulatory text governing the prohibition and limited exceptions for discharge of oil or oily mixtures into the sea from the cargo area of an oil tanker.
trace.trigger: An oil tanker's cargo area generates oil or oily mixture that may be discharged into the sea.

procedures.action: Treat discharge of oil/oily mixtures from the cargo area as prohibited by default.
procedures.why: Paragraph (1) establishes a general prohibition subject to specified exceptions.

procedures.action: Before discharging outside a special area (except Arctic waters), confirm all conditions of regulation 34.1 of Annex I are satisfied.
procedures.why: This is the only exception permitting discharge on a voyage outside a special area.

procedures.action: For a voyage only partly within a special area, ensure the discharge occurs outside the special area (except Arctic waters) and that all regulation 34.1 Annex I conditions are met.
procedures.why: The exception applies only when both the location and condition requirements are satisfied simultaneously.

procedures.action: Within a special area, prohibit any discharge of oil or oily mixture from the cargo area, subject only to regulations 21 and 27 and paragraph (4).
procedures.why: Special areas receive stricter protection with a near-absolute discharge prohibition.

constraints: Discharge prohibition is subject to regulations 21 to 23 and paragraphs (2) and (4).
Exceptions do not apply in Arctic waters even if otherwise outside a special area.
All conditions of regulation 34.1 of Annex I must be satisfied for any permitted discharge.
Within a special area, discharge is prohibited subject only to regulations 21 and 27 and paragraph (4).
warnings: Discharge of oil or oily mixtures from an oil tanker's cargo area is prohibited by default.
No discharge is permitted in Arctic waters under the general outside-special-area exception.
Any discharge in a special area is prohibited except under the narrow exceptions in regulations 21, 27, and paragraph (4).
outcomes: Compliant discharge only occurs outside special areas (excluding Arctic waters) when regulation 34.1 Annex I conditions are fully met.
Non-compliant discharge within a special area or in Arctic waters constitutes a MARPOL violation.
key_facts: The baseline rule prohibits discharge of oil or oily mixtures from an oil tanker's cargo area into the sea.
An exception exists for voyages outside special areas (excluding Arctic waters) if regulation 34.1 Annex I conditions are satisfied.
For voyages partly within a special area, discharge must occur outside the special area and outside Arctic waters, with regulation 34.1 Annex I conditions met.
Discharge within a special area is prohibited except as allowed by regulations 21 and 27 and paragraph (4).

trace.situation: UK MARPOL regulations governing the prohibition and limited exceptions for discharge of oil, oily mixtures, and hazardous chemicals into the sea from a ship's machinery space, plus the Secretary of State's duty to investigate reported oil traces.
trace.trigger: A discharge of oil/oily mixture or chemicals from machinery space occurs, or visible traces of oil are reported near a ship or its wake.

procedures.action: Do not discharge oil or oily mixtures from machinery space unless an exception applies.
procedures.why: Discharge is prohibited by default under paragraph (1), subject to regulations 21-23 and specified exceptions.

procedures.action: For ships 400 GT and above, verify vessel's voyage type (outside special area, part in special area, or wholly in special area) and apply the corresponding condition set (Annex I reg 15.2 or 15.3) before any discharge.
procedures.why: Different discharge conditions apply depending on voyage area to ensure compliance with Annex I thresholds.

procedures.action: For ships under 400 GT outside Antarctic/Arctic waters, apply conditions in regulation 15.6 of Annex I before discharge.
procedures.why: Smaller ships have a separate exception threshold under Annex I.

procedures.action: Never discharge oil or oily mixtures in the Antarctic area, regardless of other exceptions.
procedures.why: Antarctic area discharge is absolutely prohibited and paragraph (2)(c) exceptions do not apply there.

procedures.action: Retain oil residues on board for discharge to reception facilities if they cannot be discharged in compliance with regulation 15.
procedures.why: Ensures non-compliant residues are not released to the sea.

procedures.action: Report and cooperate with any investigation launched upon observed visible oil traces, providing wind/sea conditions, track/speed, and discharge records.
procedures.why: The Secretary of State must investigate reports of visible oil traces to determine contravention, and the ship's records/data are key evidence.

constraints: Discharge prohibition is subject to regulations 21 to 23 and the stated exceptions in paragraph (2).
Exceptions for 400 GT+ ships depend on voyage area (outside special area, partly in special area, or in special area) and satisfying Annex I regulation 15.2 or 15.3 conditions.
Ships under 400 GT may only use the regulation 15.6 exception, and not in the Antarctic area or Arctic waters.
No exceptions apply to discharge in the Antarctic area.
Discharge of hazardous chemicals, or substances used to circumvent regulation 15 conditions, is prohibited.
Oil residues not dischargeable under regulation 15 must be retained on board.
warnings: Discharge of oil or oily mixture from machinery space is prohibited unless specific conditions are met.
Discharge in the Antarctic area is absolutely prohibited with no exceptions.
Discharge of chemicals/substances hazardous to the marine environment, or used to circumvent discharge conditions, is prohibited.
Non-compliant oil residues must not be discharged and must be retained on board.
outcomes: Compliant ships avoid illegal discharge by correctly applying voyage-area-specific exception conditions.
Reports of visible oil traces trigger an investigation examining wind/sea conditions, ship's track/speed, other possible sources, and discharge records.
Non-compliant residues retained on board are discharged to shore reception facilities instead of the sea.
key_facts: Default rule: discharge of oil or oily mixture from machinery space is prohibited.
Exceptions depend on ship size (400 GT threshold) and voyage area relative to special areas, Arctic, and Antarctic waters.
No exceptions exist for discharge in the Antarctic area.
The Secretary of State must investigate reports of visible oil traces near a ship or its wake, examining specific factors including discharge records.
Oil residues that cannot be legally discharged must be retained on board for reception facility disposal.

question_seeds.text: Which Annex I conditions (15.2, 15.3, or 15.6) apply to my ship's discharge given its GT and current voyage area?
Under what circumstances, if any, can oil residues be discharged while transiting a special area?

Why is there no exception for oil discharge in the Antarctic area when similar exceptions exist elsewhere?

trace.situation: UK regulation implementing MARPOL Annex I requirements for construction, equipment and operation of a ship's machinery space to prevent oil pollution.
trace.trigger: A ship to which these Regulations apply has a machinery space that must be assessed for compliance based on its size and description.

procedures.action: Determine ship size/description and identify which Annex I requirements apply to its machinery space.
procedures.why: Requirements referred to in paragraph (2) apply only as relevant to a ship of its size and description.

procedures.action: Comply with regulation 12 (tanks for oil residues/sludge), regulation 12A paragraphs 1-11 (oil fuel tank protection), regulation 13 (standard discharge connection), regulation 14 paragraphs 1-3, 6 and 7 (oil filtering equipment), and regulation 16 (segregation of oil and water ballast and carriage of oil in forepeak tanks).
procedures.why: These are the prescribed construction, equipment and operation requirements of Annex I that machinery spaces must meet.

procedures.action: For ships under 400 GT, equip the vessel to retain oil/oily mixtures on board for discharge to reception facilities, or discharge in accordance with regulation 15.6 of Annex I.
procedures.why: Smaller ships have an alternative compliance route reflecting practicability limits on equipment.

procedures.action: Apply for or confirm any Secretary of State waiver of regulation 14.1/14.2 if operating exclusively in special areas/Arctic waters or meeting regulation 14.5.3 conditions.
procedures.why: Certain operating profiles qualify for waiver of oil filtering equipment requirements under specified conditions.

constraints: Requirements apply subject to paragraphs (3) and (4) of the regulation.
Only the requirements relevant to the ship's size and description apply.
Waiver under regulation 14.1/14.2 only available for ships exclusively on voyages within special areas/Arctic waters, or compliant with regulation 14.5.3 conditions.
Ships under 400 GT must meet one of the two specified alternative compliance routes.
outcomes: Compliant machinery space construction and equipment reduces risk of unlawful oil discharge.
Non-compliance could result in failure to meet statutory construction/equipment standards for oil pollution prevention.
key_facts: Machinery space construction, equipment, and operation must comply with specified Annex I regulations based on ship size and description.
Ships under 400 GT have an alternative compliance pathway: retain oil on board or discharge per regulation 15.6.
The Secretary of State may waive regulation 14.1 and 14.2 requirements for ships operating exclusively in special areas/Arctic waters or meeting regulation 14.5.3 conditions.
